units.la: NVlla animi arrogantia, vel ut ait ille, ἰπποδυφία, eò assurgere non extimesco, ut quem patriæ primores in sublimi loco collocarunt, ad eum familiarius accedam: quasi de illa familiaritate posthac gloriaturus, veluti Ἐ Διὸς σάνδαλον, Iovis sandalium, secundum proverbium vetus. Longè aliud, huic epistolæ causam præbet. Quum Heroi assiduis Belgii Confœderati negotiis maximè distracto, quod debebam offerendum esset;quid molirer, quidque exhiberem, fuit exponendum. Idque epistolio: quod non tantum cum ipso opere manet, & subinde legi potest; sed verbis etiam & alloquio censetur tanto commodius, quo minus occupatissimum remoratur. utpote quod membratim, & momentis magis vacuis legi possit: cum alloquium tempore etiam minimè opportuno, errore vel casu, sæpe instituatur. Itaque epistola defungens, codicem quendam legum forensium divinæ reipublicæ ostendo,ac transmitto. Rempublicam dico divinam,quam Deus ipse suo ore, providentia singulari constituit, quæque legibus Divinis νεσμοθέτητας (Ebr.8.11.)Etenim inconstantiam & perversitatem voluntatis humanæ cognoscens omnium Dominus, Israëliticam rempublicam legibus potius, quam magistratuum arbitrio regi voluit: voluntas enim lubrica est, inque proclivi ut per devia oberret. cum lex certior sit norma & tutior vitæ Canon. Quò Aristoteles l.2. Politic. lit. c. 8. refpexit, cum propofitis quibufdam in republica fieri folitis, fubjunxit, ταῦτα δὴ πάντα βέλλιον γίνεσθαι τῷ νομον ἢ τῷ ἀνθρώπων βελτιον· ἃ ᾧ ἀσφαλὴς ὁ κανών. hac fane omnia fieri praftiterit lege, quam hominum voluntate: non enim tutus eft canon. Quocirca certiorem legis canonem praetulit Legiflator. Adeo quidem, ut poteftatem quoque legum condendarum fummo fenatui permiferit Deut. 17. quód differtatione ad fecundum codicem demonftro. Nihil novi vel praecipere, vel vetare, Ifraelitis conceffum: imò plane interdictum. Verum ea quae in genere à Deo praefcripta erant, ad fpeciales applicare cafus, adeoque ex generali lege multas quandoque fancire fpeciales, minimè primatibus interdictum. Vel etiam (fi quid hic video) media certa, accommodatis ad legem Dei canonibus, definire & praefcribere. Praeterea lubricum humanae indolis omninò poftulat directionem: qua modi, viaeque divinam praestandi legem oftenduntur. Vnde tres oriuntur legum fpecies, quas legiflator fummus fummo permiififfe Ebraeorum magiftratui videtur: quum tamen suis præceptis nihil novi, quod iis nullo modo contineretur, assui concederet. Prima erat eorum, quibus generalia restringebantur; secunda, definiens media, quibus ad scopum, puta legem Dei observandam, collimabant; tertia, viam, rationem ac modum præscribens, quibus actio mandato Divino imperata, commodissime peragi posset. Atque has leges in pandectas suas (Misnajoth vocant) congesserc Iudæi. Idcirco hinc patet, quantum momentum ad sacras percipiendum Mosis paginas afferant libri ﬠ Misnajoth. Cum istorum codicum compages sit Mosis explicatio: licet subinde cæcutientis tandem populi vestigia isthic deprehendere liceat. Illa est ratio, quare plures hujusmodi codices verterim, ac commentariis illustraverim. quorum nonnulli jam editi, & plures, Deo volente, edendi. Ex istorum numero hunc ex volumine Nezikim (ita Iudæis dicitur) in præsentiarum desumpsi: idque eodem scopo ac fine, quo cæteros adorno. Fermè enim singulos ad pentateuchi intelligentiam plurimum facere arbitror, partim propter fructum; {ētum}; de quo jam actum fuit. Deinde & alia in novi fœderis voluminibus penitius intelligendis utilitas ex iisdem illis promanat. Stilum enim ac phrasin in N. T. scriptis usitatam, nobis exhibent. Sed quò id melius pateat, ἀπὸ βαλλίδων sive, à carceribus (ut loquitur Aristophanes) rem arcessam. Lingua Græca ulterius tandem propagata fuit, & post Alexandri Magni expeditionem Asiaticam, longe lateque in plurimas Asiæ regiones dispersa. Ut alios mittam, Plutarchus in vita Crassi satis aperte, Parthos & Armenios Græce scivisse testatur: quum Hyrodem Parthum & Artuasdem Armenium in convivio post Crassi obitum, ei insultasse narrat (pag. 1030. edit. Henr. Steph.) hæc ipsius sunt verba, Ἐπάσῆς τε ἢ πότοι δ' ἀλλήλων ἦσαν αὐτοῖς, ἐ πολλὰ παρεισηγέ ὑπὸ τὸ Ἑλλάδ ἀκεσμάτων, convivia & symposia inter se agitabant, & multa proferebantur ex Græcis dicta. quandoquidem superato hosti illudere volebant, quis dicteria ignotâ linguâ tegere voluisse credat? Sane in eodem convivio, Iason quidam Tralliănus, ἦδεν Εὐριπίδης Βακχῶν τὰ περὶ τῶν Ἀγαύων. εὐδο-
units.tr: I am not afraid, from no arrogance of spirit (or, as that man puts it, horse-pride [ἰπποδυφία]), to rise so high as to approach more familiarly one whom the leading men of his country have placed in a lofty position. I do not mean that I will later boast of that familiarity, like Zeus's sandal [Ἐ Διὸς σάνδαλον], Jupiter's sandal, as the old proverb has it. Something quite different prompts this letter. Since the hero is most of all distracted by the constant business of the United Netherlands, I had to say what I was offering, what I was undertaking and what I was presenting. I have done this in a short letter. It remains with the work itself and can be read again from time to time, and in words it is more convenient than a spoken address, which would detain a man so occupied. It can be read piece by piece, in spare moments, whereas a conversation is often arranged at an inopportune time, by mistake or by chance. So, to finish with the letter, I show and send you a certain code of forensic laws of the divine commonwealth. I call it the divine commonwealth because God himself constituted it by his own mouth and singular providence, and it is ruled by divine laws [νεσμοθέτητας] (Heb. 8.11). For the Lord of all, knowing the inconstancy and perversity of the human will, wished the Israelite commonwealth to be governed by laws rather than by the discretion of magistrates. The will is slippery and prone to wander off the path, whereas law is a surer norm and a safer rule of life. Aristotle had this in view when, in Politics 2, chapter 8, after listing certain matters that commonly come up in a commonwealth, he added: all these things are better done by law than by the best of men, since the rule is safe [ταῦτα δὴ πάντα βέλλιον γίνεσθαι τῷ νομον ἢ τῷ ἀνθρώπων βελτιον· ἃ ᾧ ἀσφαλὴς ὁ κανών]. Indeed, all these things are better done by law than by human will, for the will is not a safe canon. For this reason the Lawgiver preferred a surer canon of law. So much so that he also granted the power of enacting laws to the supreme senate (Deut. 17), which I show in a dissertation on the second code. Nothing new was granted to the Israelites either to prescribe or to forbid, but indeed it was plainly forbidden. But to apply to particular cases what had been prescribed in general, and so sometimes to enact particular laws from a general law, was by no means forbidden to the leaders. Or again, if I see anything here, to define and prescribe certain means, suited to the canons of God's law. Moreover, the frailty of human nature absolutely requires direction, by which the manner and way of performing the divine law are shown. From this arise three kinds of laws, which the supreme Lawgiver seems to have granted to the magistrate of the Hebrews, although he would not have allowed anything new in his precepts that was not in some way contained in them. The first kind restricted the general commands; the second defined the means by which they aimed at the goal, namely the observance of God's law; the third prescribed the way, method and manner by which the act commanded by the divine precept could be carried out most conveniently. The Jews gathered these laws into their collection of rules, which they call the Misnajoth. Hence it is clear how much weight the books of the Misnajoth carry for understanding the sacred pages of Moses. For the structure of these codes is an explanation of Moses, although one may from time to time detect there the traces of a people groping in the dark. That is the reason I have translated several codes of this kind and illustrated them with commentaries, some of which are already published and more of which, God willing, will be published. From this number I have for the present taken this one from the volume called Nezikim, as the Jews name it, and I prepare it for the same scope and end as the others. I believe that nearly each of them contributes much to the understanding of the Pentateuch, partly because of their usefulness, which I have already discussed. Then also another benefit for understanding more deeply the volumes of the New Covenant flows from those same codes. For they show us the style and phrasing customary in the writings of the New Testament. But to make this clearer, I shall take my matter from far back, from the starting-gates [ἀπὸ βαλλίδων], or, from the starting-gates, as Aristophanes says. The Greek language was at last spread further, and after Alexander the Great's expedition into Asia it was dispersed far and wide into most regions of Asia. To pass over others, Plutarch in the life of Crassus testifies quite clearly that the Parthians and Armenians knew Greek, since he relates that Hyrodes the Parthian and Artuasdes the Armenian insulted Crassus at a banquet after his death (p. 1030, ed. Henri Estienne). His own words are: They passed the time with feasts and drinking-parties among themselves, and many things were said in Greek. Since they wished to mock their defeated enemy, who would believe they wished to hide their taunts in an unknown language? Certainly at that same banquet a certain Iason of Tralles sang from Euripides' Bacchae the lines about Agave [ἦδεν Εὐριπίδης Βακχῶν τὰ περὶ τῶν Ἀγαύων. εὐδο-]

units.la: εὐδοκιμῶν ... ἐξ αὐτῆς, &c. canebat ex Euripidis Bacchis &Agaven. quumque placeret ipse, &c. quasi dixisset, Græcos versus convivis placuisse: unde intellexisse constat. Sequentia ejusdem historici verba rem certissimam esse comprobant. Nam ubi Iasonem scenico ludo Crassum lusisse scripsisset, & hæc pronuntiasse carmina, Φέρομεν ἐξ ὄρεος ἔλικα νεότομον, Ἐπὶ μέλαθρα, μακαρίαν ἥπαν: Ferimus ex monte capreolum recens casum, In atria, felicem prædam:
units.tr: [he was] pleasing ... from it [εὐδοκιμῶν ... ἐξ αὐτῆς], etc. He sang from Euripides' Bacchae and Agave. And when he himself pleased [the company], etc., as if he had said that the Greek verses pleased the guests, from which it is plain that they understood them. The following words of the same historian confirm that this is quite certain. For after writing that Iason, with a theatrical show, mocked Crassus and recited these verses, We bring from the mountain a young tender kid [Φέρομεν ἐξ ὄρεος ἔλικα νεότομον, Ἐπὶ μέλαθρα, μακαρίαν ἥπαν], We carry a fresh kid from the mountain into the halls, a happy prey:

units.la: tandem subjicit, καὶ ταῦτα μὲν πάντας ἔτερπεν, atque hæc omnes oblectaverunt. Ludus ille scenicus & carmina ista voluptatem crearunt omnibus. At Artuasdes suos habebat Armenios, rex Hyrodes Parthos suos. Longinqua igitur loca procul à Græcia Græcus pervaserat sermo. Nam ita fieri solet, ut victoris lingua atque idioma ad victos promanet. magis si coloniæ eò deducantur. maximè si artes & scientiæ hujusmodi lingua peregrina conscriptæ subjugatis placeant. Quæ in Asia observare licet. Verum id docet experientia in patria nostra, aliisque locis quamplurimis: si vulgus peregrino sermoni assuescat; quia sollicita cura, & παιδείας τρο-πῳ non accedit, semper quædam ex patria lingua peregrinæ immisceri. Duo inprimis: vocum simplicium notionem minus usitatam; & stylum ac phrasin. Vbi vocabulum regionis in communiori significatione respondens peregrino, apud indigenas ad alia transferri consuevit, contingit sæpe, ut vocabulum peregrinæ linguæ eadem latitudine extendatur. Pariter phrasēs illi idiomati peculiares, propter ruditatem vulgi, ad linguam recenter assumptam sæpissime transeunt. Id linguæ Græcæ apud Asiaticos evenisse, documento sunt, ut alia prætermittam, sacri N. Testamenti codices. Rudes isti Orientis plebeii perfecte linguam Græcorum addiscere nequiverunt: sed modo jam enarrato συγχυσιν ex utraque, patria & peregrina, instituerunt facillimam. Quæ cum postea sub iis, qui Alexandri imperium inter se partiti sunt, diu permaneret, linguam nobis Hellenisticam loco elegantioris Græcæ exhibuit. Licet & Hellenistica suam habeat elegantiam: quemadmodum Italica, quamvis ex Latina & aliis mixta. Vt nihil habeant, quod arrodant nasutuli quidam, quum Apostolos & Euangelistas imperitiæ insimulant. Quasi nemo possit eleganter scribere vel loqui Italicè; sed potius ad ornatum, Italis Latinè scribendum vel loquendum esset. Ita isti mortales Demosthenicè potius ad Orientales scribendum fuisse judicant; quum L. Hellenistica multo essent in Asia & Oriente usitatior. Neq; hoc prætereundum: quoniam Orientalium linguæ, naturæ ordinem in syntaxi & phraseologia sua admodum imitantur; cum Asiæ populi linguam Græcam propriæ quique attemperarent, inde stylum linguæ Græcæ intellectu facilimum fuisse exortum. Quem cum elegantiores Græci, tum rudiores Asiatici intelligerent. Si quando enim propter elegantiorem idiotismum linguæ Ebrææ, Syræ, Chaldææ, similisve, significatio extensa, vel phrasis Orientalis in Hellenistica comparens, obscuritatem parere videretur, Græcis tamen nullam creavit difficultatem. quandoquidem sacri scriptores & oratores quum ita à simpliciori dicendi genere disce-
units.tr: And these things delighted all [καὶ ταῦτα μὲν πάντας ἔτερπεν], and these things delighted everyone, he finally adds. That theatrical show and those verses gave pleasure to everyone. Artuasdes had his own Armenians, and King Hyrodes had his own Parthians. So the Greek language had spread to distant places far from Greece. For it usually happens that the language and idiom of the victor spread to the conquered, the more so if colonies are settled there, and most of all if arts and sciences written in a foreign tongue are pleasing to the subjugated. This can be observed in Asia. Indeed, experience in our own country and in very many other places shows that when the common people grow accustomed to a foreign speech, and no careful attention or education is applied, some features of the foreign tongue are always mixed into the native one. Chiefly two: the less usual meaning of simple words, and the style and phrasing. When a word of the native tongue corresponding to the foreign one in its more common sense has been extended to other meanings by the natives, it often happens that the word of the foreign language is stretched to the same breadth. Likewise, phrases peculiar to that idiom, because of the crudeness of the common people, very often pass over into the language recently adopted. That this happened to the Greek language among the Asiatics is attested, to mention nothing else, by the codices of the sacred New Testament. Those rough common people of the East could not learn the Greek language perfectly, but by the mixture just described they made a very easy blend of the two, the native and the foreign. Since this lasted for a long time under those who divided among themselves the empire of Alexander, it gave us the Hellenistic language in place of a more elegant Greek. Yet Hellenistic has its own elegance, just as Italian has, although it is mixed from Latin and other tongues. So let those cavilling little noses have nothing to gnaw on when they accuse the Apostles and Evangelists of incompetence, as if no one could write or speak Italian elegantly, but rather Italians ought to write or speak Latin for ornament. In the same way those mortals judge that the Orientals ought to have written in the manner of Demosthenes, although the Hellenistic language was far more in use in Asia and the East. Nor must this be passed over: since the languages of the Orientals closely imitate the natural order in their syntax and phraseology, and since the peoples of Asia adapted the Greek language to their own, a style of Greek easy to understand arose from this. The more elegant Greeks as well as the cruder Asiatics understood it. For if sometimes, because of the more elegant idiom of the Hebrew, Syriac or Chaldee language, or something similar, a meaning stretched or an Oriental phrase appearing in the Hellenistic tongue seemed to produce obscurity, it nevertheless created no difficulty for the Greeks, since the sacred writers and speakers departed from the simpler manner of speaking in this way.

units.la: . discederent; quod rarissimum quidem inter Græcos, nonnunquam tamen usitatum, adhibuerunt. Eatenus saltem, ut ab iis quibuscum loquerentur intelligi potuerint, ne audirent ὡς ἀέρα λαλοῦντες. (1 Cor.14.9.) Quod evincunt orationes Pauli in Actis Apost. Ex quibus & illud liquet, Hellenisticam linguam inde non traxisse originem, quod complures minorem Asiam & Ægyptum aliaque ab ultimo Oriente remotiora loca incolentes, versioni Septuaginta interpretum Græcæ assuevissent. Etenim Paulus Hellenistico sermone eos etiam alloquebatur, qui an Vetus Testamentum extaret, ignorabant: uti quum ad Lystrenses gentiles & idololatras orationem habuisse legitur Act.14. Similiter ad ignaros verbi divini Athenienses c.17. Quod & passim in convertendis gentibus observavit. Profecto Evangelistæ Hellenistica, non Græca usi sunt, quum ab Asiaticis plerisque intelligi vellent: neque salutem tamen eorum tantum intenderunt, qui versionem πρὸ 70. lectione continua sibi familiarem reddidissent, adeoque inde linguam dedicissent Hellenisticam.
units.tr: ...they departed from them; this, though very rare among the Greeks, they sometimes did use. At least so far that they could be understood by those with whom they spoke, lest they should be heard speaking as into the air (1 Cor. 14:9). The speeches of Paul in the Acts of the Apostles prove this. From them it is also clear that the Hellenistic language did not take its origin from this, that many who inhabited Lesser Asia, Egypt and other places more remote from the farthest East had grown accustomed to the Greek version of the Seventy interpreters. For Paul addressed in Hellenistic speech even those who did not know whether the Old Testament existed, as when he is read to have spoken to the Gentile and idolatrous Lystrans (Acts 14). Likewise to the Athenians, ignorant of the divine word (ch. 17). He observed this too in converting the nations throughout. Certainly the Evangelists used Hellenistic, not classical Greek, since they wished to be understood by most Asiatics; nor did they aim only at the salvation of those who had made the version of the Seventy familiar to themselves by continual reading, and so had learned the Hellenistic language from it.

units.la: Quin etiam idcirco isti V.Testamenti interpretes isto stylo usi sunt, quod jam ista lingua Hellenistica esset vulgaris. Eoque libentius, quod phrasin Spiritus sancti hoc pacto presius exprimere voluerint. Quum jam naturam & originem istius linguae habeamus, neminem latere potest, quantum prosit & expediat, Ebraeorum & Chaldaeorum phrasin percepisse. Quamvis enim propter sermonis simplicitatem, sensus cuivis in Oriente degenti, saltem intra Tigrin & mare Mediterraneum (ubi primae ecclesiae, reliquarum matres) pateret: nobis tamen Orientalium linguarum genium non assequutis, neque in Graecis ita versatis, ut quod semel atque iterum in hoc vel illo authore Graeco occurrit, perspectum habeamus; nihil utilius, ne dicam necessarium, quam linguam Ebraeam Talmudicam & vicinas didicisse. Alioqui verba fortassis cognoscces; minime phrases ac stylum novi foederis. ubi stylus est Hellenisticus, id est, voces Graecae, significatio subinde Talmudica, ut & phrases quamplurimae, quemadmodum & ritus, quo Scriptores isti saepe respiciunt.
units.tr: Indeed those interpreters of the Old Testament used this style for the reason that this Hellenistic language was already common. And they were the more willing to do so because they wished to express the phrasing of the Holy Spirit more closely in this way. Since we now have the nature and origin of that language, no one can fail to see how much it profits and helps to have grasped the phrasing of the Hebrews and Chaldeans. For although, on account of the simplicity of the speech, its meaning lay open to anyone living in the East, at least between the Tigris and the Mediterranean Sea (where the first churches, the mothers of the rest, were), yet for us, who have not attained the genius of the Oriental languages, nor are so versed in Greek that we have a thorough grasp of what occurs once or twice in this or that Greek author, nothing is more useful, not to say necessary, than to have learned the Talmudic Hebrew language and its neighbours. Otherwise you may perhaps know the words, but by no means the phrases and style of the New Testament, where the style is Hellenistic, that is, Greek words with a meaning often Talmudic, and very many phrases, as well as the rites to which those writers often refer.

units.la: Itaque cum plures sint libri Ebraici & vicinarum linguarum; inprimis post V. T. volumina, Talmudica laudo. quia isto seculo, in Iudæa & vicinis locis, primi doctores, istis formulis, phrasibus, ritibus, sanctionibus (etsi in unum corpus nondum congestis) innutriti fuerant. Quocirca vel ista saltem de causa me operæ pretium facturum credebam, si subinde codicem quendam Talmudicum publici juris facerem, vertendo & illustrando. quo phrasi illa, aliisque inde perceptis, Novo Testamento lucem quandam afferrem. Necnon quo lingua ista Talmudica plenius cognita, & Ebræa planior fieret, librique isto idiomate conscripti intelligerentur magis magisque. Ista mente hunc primum librum Nezikim edendum & orbi Christiano propinandum statui. Sed quo, pro more passim recepto, augusto alicujus nomine, decorem & authoritatem quandam obtineat; eum tibi, maxime Vosbergi, consecro & primum in debiti officii testeram offero. Quem enim hic quererem, qui æquari tecum posset? De jure legibus præscripto agitur: de jure ex legibus sententiam per multos annos dixisti, in supremo Hollandiae & Zelandiae δικαστηρίῳ. Vbi omnes ὁμοθυμαδὸν dotibus instructum agnoverunt & testati sunt, quas Iethro vir prudentissimus judici necessarias autumabat: quum (Ex. 18:21.) judices exigeret, strenuos, timentes Dei, veraces, osores avaritiae. Tὸ δρασυηεῖον sive strenuitatem, vel vultus totiusque corporis habitus naturalem quandam promptitudinem & majestatem prae se ferens, atque viri cordati ac excitati sermo ostendunt. ut quamplurimorum καλοκαγαθωμάτων γνω-μῶν τῷ ἔθνῃ τύτῳ (quemadmodum loquitur Tertullus Act. 24. 3.) seriem praetermittam. Timor autem Domini vestrae familiae est haereditarius. Hac virtute, ut & reliquis, praecelluit pater tuus l. m. Quem vere exprimis, dictumque comprobas notissimum:
units.tr: Therefore, since there are many books in Hebrew and the neighbouring languages, especially after the volumes of the Old Testament, I commend the Talmudic ones. Because in that age, in Judea and the neighbouring places, the first teachers had been nourished on those formulas, phrases, rites and sanctions (although not yet gathered into one body). For this reason, at least, I believed I would be doing a worthwhile work if from time to time I made some Talmudic code public by translating and explaining it, so that I might throw some light on the New Testament by that phraseology and other things learned from it. Also so that, with this Talmudic language more fully known, Hebrew would become clearer, and books written in that idiom would be understood more and more. With this intention I resolved to publish this first book, Nezikin, and offer it to the Christian world. But so that, according to the custom widely accepted, it might obtain some dignity and authority from the name of some eminent person, I dedicate it to you, most noble Vosbergius, and offer it as a first testimony of my due respect. For whom else should I seek who could be compared with you? The subject is law as prescribed by the laws: you have pronounced judgment for many years on law arising from the laws, in the supreme court of Holland and Zeeland. There all unanimously have acknowledged and testified that you are endowed with those qualities which Jethro, that most prudent man, thought necessary for a judge, when he required judges (Ex. 18:21) strenuous, fearing God, truthful, hating covetousness. Your strenuousness, or a natural readiness and dignity displayed in face and whole bodily bearing, and the speech of a man of sound and lively mind, show this. I will pass over the long series of your many noble qualities and maxims, to this nation (as Tertullus says, Acts 24:3). The fear of the Lord is hereditary in your family. In this virtue, as in the others, your father of blessed memory excelled. You express him truly, and you confirm the very well-known saying:
Brave men are born of brave and good men.

units.la: Atque non tantum fortitudinem, sed & reliqua refers paterni animi bona, ut parentis pietatem. Cui cum vix parem invenirent majores nostri prioribus istis libertatis temporibus, summa commiserunt. Ipsum enim vigilantissimum
units.tr: Nor do you show only courage, but also the other good qualities of your father's spirit, such as his devotion to duty. Our ancestors, in those earlier times of liberty, could scarcely find his equal, and they entrusted him with the highest offices. For the most vigilant man

units.la: Zirizææ urbis & totius infulæ, ac Beoofterfcheldæ Satrapam, multos annos Ordinum Zelandiæ partem, & Senatus Thalassiarchici esse voluerunt, & Zelandorum nomine inter Ordines Generales confidere. Legationem procerum totius Confœderati Belgii nomine ad Galliarum Regem ejusque fratrem suscepit. In qua, dexteritate summa, arduum illud negotium cum regis fratre Andegavensium Duce, feliciter peregit. Et quum difficilima inciderent tempora post dissolutum fœdus, quod Gandavense dicebatur; Ordines eum Vltrajeƨum miserunt, quò arƨius Provinciarum fœdus iniretur. quod summâ viri prudentiâ Deus secundavit. Ad pietatem regressus, oblivisci nequeo fratris tui, qui in timore Dei à teneris educatus, inter Zelandos ista virtute, tanquam corufcante fidere effulget. quem etiam in utroque senatu primario confidere voluerunt, Thalassiarchico, & Deputatorum Provinciæ Ordinum. Qualis parens & frater, tales & generi tui. Nobilissimus vir Iohannes à Berchem Cameræ rationum in Zelandia, Celsissimi Principis nostri nomine præfectus, & David Goddyn Hagesteinii Toparcha ex Nobili, in Saltu carbonario, stemmate parentibus meis notissimo oriundus. qui pietate & strenuitate cum reliquis liberis tuis præfulget. Inter quos Casparus Vosbergius primogenitus, propter dotes suas, cum in Galliis degeret, Cardinali de Richelieu non ignotus, ubi nec prætermittendus Nob. Vir Johannes Hes Dominus in Piershil & VVeena, magister equitum promptissimus ac fortissimus. Itaque vos omnes hanc vobis esse mentem ostenditis aberrare incessum ejus, qui sperat absque Deo Excelso. Tuam Veritatem quod attinet, eam clamat longa sententiarum series per multos diducta annos: quarum nullam reprehendit rerum intelligens. Denique δωροφάγος, munerum acceptores, quique pretio jus dicunt, adeo detestabaris, & etiamnunc aversaris maximè; ut te hujusmodi lucri oforem, secundum Ichthronis præceptum, agnoscant omnes, qui non laborant invidia. Sed hæc viri præstantiam arguit, nedum ut famæ detrahat. Quod in
units.tr: of the city of Zierikzee and of the whole island, and the governor of Beoosterschelde, they wished to serve for many years as a member of the Zeeland States and of the Admiralty Senate, and to sit among the General States in the name of Zeeland. He undertook an embassy to the King of France and his brother on behalf of the nobles of the whole Confederated Netherlands. In it, with the greatest dexterity, he successfully carried through that difficult business with the King's brother, the Duke of Anjou. And when the most difficult times followed the dissolution of the league called the Pacification of Ghent, the States sent him to Utrecht, so that the union of the Provinces might be entered into more firmly; God blessed this with the highest prudence of the man. Returning to piety, I cannot forget your brother, who, brought up from tender years in the fear of God, shines among the Zeelanders by this virtue, like a glittering star. Him too they wished to serve as a leading member in both senates, the Admiralty and the Deputies of the Provincial States. Such as the father and brother, such are also your sons-in-law: the most noble Johan van Berchem, prefect in Zeeland of the Chamber of Accounts in the name of our most exalted Prince, and David Goddyn, lord of Hagestein, of noble birth, descended from the Carbonarius Saltus, a family well known to my parents, who, with the rest of your children, excels in piety and vigour. Among them Casparus Vosbergius, the firstborn, because of his gifts, while he lived in France, was not unknown to Cardinal de Richelieu; and the noble Johan Hes, lord of Piershil and Weena, a most ready and brave master of horse, must not be passed over here. So you all show that your mind is that the course of him errs who hopes without God Most High. As for your Veritas, a long series of opinions, stretching over many years, proclaims it, and no one who understands affairs has censured any of them. Finally, you have always most strongly detested and still shun the bribe-takers [δωροφάγος], those who take gifts and pronounce judgement for a price, so that all who are not labouring under envy acknowledge you, following the precept of Ichthron, as a foe of such gain. But these things demonstrate the excellence of the man, far from detracting from his reputation. What

units.la: Apprehendit bonos semper, sed cum deterioribus non contendit. nam odit præclara. Cæterum, vir summe, virtutes tuæ eo præclariores sunt, & coruscant magis, quo munus postea impositum altius: ubi tanquam è cœlo radios in omnium conspectum demittunt. Hoc volo, anni sunt duodecim & quod excurrit, ex quo in consessu Ordinum Generalium, Zelandorum vices perpetuo sustines. Plerunque fit, ut alii aliis in supremo isto senatu succedant. Verum Heroica tua indoles, sapientia, subactum judicium, singularis sagacitas, experientia multis annis, & longè pluribus præclaris factis acquisita, nullo pacto permittebant, ut proceres quenquam substituendum censerent. quem enim suffecissent, qui tecum paria, vel saltem majora facerent? Et sanè in supremo isto consessu, unde dependent omnia, dirigente omnia omnium Domino, quid magis requiras, quam cum reliquis jam recensitis, zelum gloriæ divinæ ardentissimum, anxiam & perennem Ecclefiæ Christianæ curam, æquissimam animi moderationem, hoc seculo in tanta animorum dissensione, fi unquam, necessariam? de qua olim Imperator Muflimicus, Ali: moderatio viri auxilium ejus. Quod ita accipi queat, ac fi dixisset, auxiliari demum quenquam posse, moderatione sua. Porro hæc omnia in uno summa non tantum primates; sed & omnes agnofcunt, imò qui minus favere videntur. Cujufmodi fi forte inveniantur, eos esse credo, qui illam totius familiæ in Deum reverentiam, in proximos charitatem, tot tantisque documentis cum publicè, tum privatim demonstratam, susque dequè habent: vel patriæ ac publici boni amorem & studium, cum singulari prudentia, (quæ aliis exemplo esse potest, & vel sola perficit maxima in magnis etiam turbis) non agnoscunt.
units.tr: He always lays hold of the good, but does not contend with the worse. For he hates what is excellent. Moreover, most noble sir, your virtues are all the more excellent and shine the more brightly, the higher the office later laid upon you, where like rays from heaven they send their light into the view of all. This I wish to say: it is twelve years, and a little more, since you have sustained the place of Zeeland continuously in the assembly of the States General. It often happens that one succeeds another in that supreme council. But your heroic character, wisdom, sound judgment, singular shrewdness, and experience gained over many years and by far more distinguished deeds, by no means allowed the nobles to think of substituting anyone. For whom would they have appointed who could do equal or even greater things with you? And indeed, in that supreme assembly, from which everything depends, with the Lord of all directing all things, what more do you require than, along with the others already listed, the most ardent zeal for the glory of God, an anxious and unceasing care for the Christian Church, and the most equitable moderation of mind, which in such great dissension of minds in this age is necessary, if ever? Of this the Muslim emperor Ali once said: the moderation of a man is his help. This can be taken as if he had said that anyone can at last help others only by his moderation. Moreover, all these qualities, in sum, are acknowledged not only by the leading men, but even by those who seem least favourable. If by chance such are found, I believe they are those who make light of that reverence for God of your whole family, and of charity towards neighbours, so many and great proofs of which have been shown both publicly and privately, or who do not recognise the love and zeal for the country and the public good, which is exemplary to others with its singular prudence, and which alone accomplishes great things even amid great disturbances.

units.la: Itaque illa cum expenderent patriæ proceres, sæpissimè tantum virum ad primarias obtundas legationes sollicitandum exiftimarunt. Quocirca non una, sed tribus vicibus in Germaniam ad maxima negotia expedienda dimiserunt. Ad Galliarum etiam Regem legati nomine profici-sci sci placuit: imo secundo legationem repetendam. Accidit etiam, ut toties ad Daniæ Regem, publico decreto Ordines, optatum eventum animo præsagientes, eadem dignitate ornatum, eundem te, vir admirande, legandum censuerint. Eundem legatum & Sueciæ Rex atq; proceres commodissimum experti sunt. Quid ea commemorabo pluribus, quæ feliciter, aspirante Numine, istis legationibus tuis peracta sunt? Epistolæ ratio istum catalogum non admittit. Id certo certius: nisi Præpotentibus Ordinibus peracta negotia omninò placuissent, toties eundem legatum ad Imperium Germanicum, totque reges mittendum non judicassent. Hoc argumento est, quod agendum erat, bene semper succesisse. Memini etiam quum Princeps Mauritius, (cujus venerandâ in bonorum animis memoria) Araufiacum Principatum à fratre defuncto, hæreditario jure accepisset, Amplitudinem tuam Araufionem cum summa potestate ab ipso Principe legatam, ut non tantum ejus nomine juramentum fidelitatis exigeret, & Principis initiatio perficeretur; sed etiam omnia quae inibi collapsa erant, vel corrigenda essent, repararentur. Qua occasione ibi hoc quoque effectum dedisti in gratiam gentis ex qua natus Christus, quaeque Deo adhuc propter maiores (Rom.11.28.) dilecta est, adeoque & nobis esse debet: ut cum in fluminis ponte quoda transeundo vectigal solveretur, & quidem aequalia penderent Iudaeus & porcus, Iudaea praegnans & sus foeta; authoritate concessa a Principe, qui factum postea maxime probavit, Iudaei non amplius porcis, sed hominibus caeteris aequarentur. quo indigenae & Iudaei, quos Deus homines, non porcos nasci voluit, aequalia penderent. Quum itaque in Iudaeos tantam benignitatem ostenderis, & eos sic in tutelam tuam receperis; nullus dubito quin hunc Iudaeorum codicem simili favore amplexurus sis, & hoc probaturus munusculum: ab eo oblatum, cui nihil magis in votis, quam ut istiusmodi primariis viris placere detur, quorum judicio stant vel cadunt subditi. Inter quos emines, vir N. & A. quapropter tuam amicitiam tibiq; probari ambiunt omnes boni. Quidni & ego? Qui in magna felicitatis parte censeo, vel remotissima affinitate stirpem tuam attigisse; & familiaritatem cum tanto Heroë colere; amorisque documenta experiri. Quibus etiam animus meus hanc παῤῥησίαν concepit, longiori epistola compellandi occupatissimam N.& A.tuam; simul & nomen tuum meo operi praemittendi Ἀρχομένῳ ἔργῳ, πρόσωπον χρὴ ἐφὶ̈ ὁ̈ ἡλιοφεγγὴς, incipiente opere, frontispicium oportet ponere praefulgidum.
units.tr: Accordingly, when the leaders of the fatherland weighed these matters, they very often judged that so great a man should be called upon for the chief and most difficult embassies. For this reason they sent you not once but three times into Germany to carry out the greatest business. They also decided that you should set out as envoy to the King of the French, and a second embassy to him was to be undertaken. It also happened that the Estates, by public decree, foreseeing the desired outcome in their minds, several times resolved to send the same man, adorned with the same dignity, you, admirable sir, to the King of Denmark. The King of Sweden and his nobles likewise found the same envoy most convenient. Why should I recount at length what, with the Divine Power breathing upon them, was happily accomplished through your embassies? The form of a letter does not admit such a catalogue. This is more certain than certainty itself: unless the business carried out had wholly pleased the Most Powerful Estates, they would not have judged it right to send the same envoy so often to the German Empire and to so many kings. By this argument, whatever had to be done has always gone well. I also remember that when Prince Maurice (whose venerable memory lives in the hearts of good men) received the Principality of Orange by hereditary right from his deceased brother, your Eminence was sent to Orange with the highest authority by the Prince himself, so that not only would you take the oath of fidelity in his name and complete the Prince's installation, but also everything that had fallen into ruin there would be corrected or repaired. On that occasion you also brought about this, in favour of the nation from which Christ was born, and which is still beloved by God for the sake of the fathers (Rom. 11.28), and so ought to be dear to us also: when a toll was being paid for crossing a certain bridge over a river, and Jew and pig paid equal amounts, a pregnant Jewess and a pregnant sow alike, by authority granted by the Prince, who afterwards greatly approved the deed, the Jews were no longer equated with pigs but with other men, so that natives and Jews, whom God willed to be born men and not pigs, would pay equal amounts. Since, therefore, you have shown such great kindness toward the Jews and have received them into your protection, I do not doubt that you will embrace this codex of the Jews with similar favour and will approve this little gift, offered by one who desires nothing more than to please such leading men, on whose judgment subjects stand or fall. Among these you stand out, sir N. and A.; for this reason all good men strive to win your friendship and to be approved by you. Why should I not do the same? I think that in a great part of my happiness I have touched your family, though by a very distant kinship, and cultivate familiarity with so great a hero and experience the proofs of his affection. Emboldened by these things, my mind has conceived the freedom to address your most busy N. and A. in a longer letter, and at the same time to prefix your name to my work: "at the beginning of a work one must set out a brilliantly shining frontispiece" [Ἀρχομένῳ ἔργῳ, πρόσωπον χρὴ ἐφὶ̈ ὁ̈ ἡλιοφεγγὴς].

units.la: Quò igitur abeundum, nisi ad tui nominis splendorem? ut liber ad omnes regiones distrahendus, illum initio in fronte ostenderet, cujus fulgorem conspexerunt regiones longissimè à se invicem disjunctæ, dum iis tot legationum radios dispergeres. Huc collimo ut Amplitudinis & N. tuæ facta mentione, lucubrationibus meis aliquid ponderis addam: ne quis hunc mihi solum præstitutum scopum arbitretur, tua conscribere encomia. Majores sunt virtutes tuæ, majora facta, quam ut ea me exprimere brevi scripto posse sperem: modesto potius silentio ista mirarer & suspicerem; quam impari stylo omnia ista adumbrare, nedum describere conarer. Mihi hoc frontispicio consulere volui.Id statuens cum animo meo, hunc librum tanto Heroi sacratum, longè tutiorem fore à susurris & latratibus imperitorum; quam ædes Herculis Romæ in foro boario, à muscis & canibus tuta fuit, quod consecrata esset Herculi (referente Plinio l.10. Nat. hist. c.29.) Et si lucubrationes meæ propter auctorem forte minoris æstimentur, tui saltem causa magis lectum iri spero. Qui dum coruscó tuo nomine principium illustrari benignè pateris, illas probare videberis omnibus, qui te norunt. Neque aliter animum inducent suum, quam bona esse, quæ probat; probare autem, quæ benigno vultu accipit vir tantus, eorumque quæ hic tractantur peritissimus. Ita quæ operis commendatio à tenuitate mea (uti forte censebit lector) non suppeditabitur, eam tuæ debebit magnitudini, favori, judicio. Vigiliæque meæ reddentur acceptæ per eum, unde id inprimis fieri exopto: cum & ipse ei acceptissimus esse allaborem. Vtpote qui id in votis habeam, ut quantum dotes tuas admirari, tantum tuo favore lætari contingat. Quem cum & parentes mei p. m. experti sint, & ego eorum hæres, adeoque persolvere damnas, ἀντάξιον affectui, quo familiam nostram amplecteris, persolvere non queam; hunc rependo legum codicem. Quem in se si spectes, observabis exiguitatem; sin animum meum unde promanat, affectus debiti amplitudinem. Quæ licet nihil tuo fastigio satis dignum edere queat; perpetuum tamen in te tuosque observantiæ pignus prodere gestit. Vtinam, vir nobilissime, tantum placere & probari possit labor meus, quantum ipse cum meis omnibus N.&A. vestræ placere & probari annitor. Votis etiam apud Deum contendens, ut Pater illi Iesu Christi, Spiritum suum cum omnibus quæ expediunt bonis, in dies magis magisque effundat, vitamque in Reipublicæ & in ea Ecclesiæ incolumitatem, quam diutissime proroget
units.tr: Where, then, should I go but to the splendour of your name? So that the book, to be distributed to all regions, might show at its front that splendour whose brightness regions far separated from one another have seen, while you scattered so many rays of embassies over them. I aim at this: by mentioning your Eminence and N., to add some weight to my labours, lest anyone think that my only purpose is to write your praises. Your virtues are greater and your deeds greater than I could hope to express in a brief writing; I would rather wonder at and admire them in modest silence than attempt to sketch or describe them with an unequal pen. I wished to provide for my work with this frontispiece, resolving in my mind that this book, consecrated to so great a hero, will be far safer from the whispers and barking of the unlearned than the temple of Hercules at Rome in the Cattle Market was safe from flies and dogs, because it was consecrated to Hercules (as Pliny reports, Nat. Hist. bk. 10, ch. 29). And if my labours are perhaps valued less on account of their author, I hope they will be read more for your sake. While you graciously allow the beginning to be illuminated by the shining light of your name, you will seem to approve them in the eyes of all who know you. Nor will they form any judgment other than that they are good, since such a man approves them; and he approves what he receives with a kindly countenance, being most expert in the matters treated here. Thus whatever recommendation the work lacks from my lowliness (as perhaps the reader will judge) will be owed to your greatness, your favour and your judgment. My vigils will be accepted through him from whom I most desire this above all else, since he too is most welcome to me in his labour. For I have this wish: that I may take as much delight in your favour as I admire your gifts. Since both my parents of blessed memory have experienced this, and I as their heir, and since I cannot repay an equivalent [ἀντάξιον] for the affection with which you embrace our family, I offer in return this codex of laws. If you look at it in itself, you will notice its smallness; but if you look at the spirit from which it springs, you will see the greatness of the affection owed. Though it can produce nothing sufficiently worthy of your eminence, it nevertheless eagerly offers a lasting pledge of respect toward you and yours. Would that, most noble sir, my labour might please and be approved as much as I strive to please and be approved by you and all your N. and A. Also, praying earnestly to God that the Father of Jesus Christ may pour out his Spirit, with all things that are profitable, upon you more and more each day, and may prolong your life as long as possible for the safety of the Commonwealth and of the Church within it.

units.la: Vm toties nostras, Cæsar, miramur Athenas, Quâ nimium placido vortice Rhene fluis, Dum toties doctos nostris amplectimur ulnis, Quos tulit è gremio Leida beata suo: Te tamen ante alios, Musarum numina testor, Ingenio divis vidimus esse parem. Ac veluti fluvius nitidis argenteus vndis, In mare perpetuas ejaculatur aquas, Haud secus ingenii torrens è divite venâ Profluit, & nunquam deficis ipse tibi. Sive in divinis spatiosa volumina currunt, Tota cohors juvenum pendet ab ore tuo, Sive tuo cerebro vastum comprendis Olympum, Et quicquid nobis docta Stagira dedit, Seu linguas aperis Mithridates unicus ævi, Credite prodigium est, terra Batava, tuum. Nec tamen hoc satis est totiès egisse triumphum, Sunt tamen hæc regno cuncta minora tuo. Ipsa Themis placuit: placuit collatio legum, Quas Israël & quas Itala terra dedit. Cæsaris atque Dei conferre oracula, Cæsar, Cæsareum & dignum est nobilitate tuâ.
units.tr: Though we so often marvel at our Athens, Caesar, and you flow, Rhine, in too gentle an eddy, while we so often embrace in our arms the learned men whom blessed Leiden has brought forth from her own bosom, yet before all others, I call the divine powers of the Muses to witness, I have seen you matched with the gods in genius. And as a silvery river with its bright waves pours its unfailing waters into the sea, so the stream of your genius flows from its rich vein, and you yourself never fail. Whether in divine matters your wide volumes run on, and the whole company of young men hangs upon your lips; whether with your mind you grasp vast Olympus and whatever learned Stagira gave us; or whether you unlock tongues, the sole Mithridates of the age: believe it, Batavian land, this is your wonder. Yet it is not enough to have celebrated so many triumphs; all these things are less than your realm. Themis herself was pleased; she was pleased by the comparison of laws, which Israel and which the Italian land gave. To set the oracles of Caesar and of God side by side, Caesar, is imperial and worthy of your nobility.
ANTONIVS THYSIVS F., Professor.

units.la: DAmnorum fontes, bos; puteus; depascens; & incendium: eorumque inter se discrepantia & convenientia. Annotat.¹ Mos Talmudistarum omnia ad certa capita revocandi. Eadem dicta פּתח patres; quæ eò reducuntur קולוּת generationes. quæ ex prioribus jura sua recipiunt, nisi distent longius. ² Ad fontes istos tantum revocari damna, quæ semper perfectè compensanda. Quid bos hoc loco sit. Vbi primò incessus consideratur. Quid רבּיץ & כּמיסט . quæ ad incessum pertineant. קוּ quid. מרנץ. Illustratur Mag. sententia ex ff. Si quadrupes. l. 1. §. 9. Sive autem. ³ Puteus quæ complectatur. ⁴ Depascens quò se extendat. quid primo contineat. Obadias à Chal. expositus. ⁵ Incendium quò traducatur. Compensatio damni duplex, & in quibus. Qui varietur. ⁶ Fontes damnorum plures sunt ob causam dupl. Explic. Ex. 21. 33. Bos & depascens quatenus distinguantur. Quid Talm. רי. ⁷ Ambulando quæ nocere dicantur. Phrasis יה רלי יה כרלי יה. ⁸ Membra divisionis Misnicæ collata cum jure Rom. è Cod. li. 3. tit. 35. leg. sin. è Dig. li. 9. tit. 2. l. 28. item li. 43. l. Si filius. è ff. Ad le. Aqu. l. 27. §. 8. Si quis. ⁹ quid. Explicatur Ex. 22. 5. Optimum agri & vineæ quomodo rependatur, & in quibus. Antiquorum de eo sententia. Ad communem cum Hebraïs æquitatem respicere Rom. Dig. li. 9. t. 1. princ.
units.tr: The sources of damage: the ox, the pit, the grazing animal, and fire; and their agreements and differences with one another. Annotation.¹ The Talmudists' custom of referring everything back to fixed headings. The same sayings, called "openings" [פּתח], are "fathers"; those traced back to them are "generations," which take their rights from the earlier ones unless they are separated by a longer interval.² Damages are referred back only to these sources, and they must always be fully compensated. What the ox means in this place. Where the manner of walking is considered first. What the terms for lying down and treading [רבּיץ and כּמיסט] mean, and which things pertain to the manner of walking. What [קוּ] means. What [מרנץ] means. The saying of the Mishnah is illustrated from the Digest, Si quadrupes, l. 1, §9, Sive autem.³ What the pit comprises.⁴ How far the grazing animal extends, and what it primarily covers. Obadiah as explained by the Chaldee.⁵ To what extent fire is carried over. The double compensation for damage, and in what cases. Who is varied.⁶ The sources of damage are several, for a double reason. Explanation from Exodus 21:33. How the ox and the grazing animal are distinguished. What the Talmud [רי] says.⁷ Which things are said to do harm by walking. The phrase [יה רלי יה כרלי יה].⁸ The members of the Mishnaic division compared with Roman law: from the Code, book 3, title 35, leg. sin.; from the Digest, book 9, title 2, l. 28; likewise book 43, l. Si filius; from the Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam, l. 27, §8, Si quis.⁹ What [...]. It is explained from Exodus 22:5. How the best of a field and a vineyard is repaid, and in which cases. The opinion of the ancients on this. To look to the fairness common to the Hebrews, see the Roman Digest, book 9, title 1, principium.

units.la: Quis damni author statuatur. Vltimum in damno, reatum inducere. In quibus facultatibus & ubi datum damnum compensandum. Annot.¹ כפּצרוּי duas admittit expositiones. Damnum stabistabilire quomodo dicatur. 2 Damnum & pauperiem præstandam ab eo tantum, qui ultima causa fuit. Quod ex legibus Romanis rejiciendum. 3 Facultates in quibus non est מפולה. 4 כני כרית. De damno iis dato qui tales non sunt. 5 מיוחדים varie acceptum. 6 Locorum distinctio in damno restituendo attendenda. Confirmatur Dig. li. 9. t. 2. l. Quintus. 7 In communi etiam ditione læsi & ladentis, distinctio adhibenda.
units.tr: Who is to be held the author of the damage. The last cause in the damage brings on guilt. In which goods, and where the damage given is to be compensated. Annotation.¹ [The word] כפּצרוּי admits two interpretations. How it is said that damage is "established." ²Damage and poverty are to be made good only by the one who was the ultimate cause; this is to be rejected by the Roman laws. ³Goods in which there is no [מפולה]. ⁴[כני כרית]. Concerning damage given to those who are not such persons. ⁵[מיוחדים] taken in various ways. ⁶The distinction of places must be considered in restoring damage. This is confirmed by Digest, book 9, title 2, l. Quintus. ⁷Even within the common jurisdiction of the injured and the injuring party, a distinction must be applied.

units.la: Taxatio rerum, quæ compensari debent, coram judicibus fit. Testes cujusmodi requirantur. De damno à mulieribus dato. Communio inter eum qui dat & patitur damnum. Annot. 1 Initium Misna confirmatur ff. li. 2. t. 1. l. 1. §. 2. פוס. Damni valor ad pecuniam in mobilibus revocatus. Mobilia veluti argentum. Taxatio argenti. 2 Argento aquivalens, quid. Pupilli è fundis debitum solvebant. quod mutarunt נוחנים. 3 Testium conditiones. Etiam ex jure Rom. כני חורים. ἡρως unde. De servorum testimonio ex jure Romano. Testimonium in pecuniariis apud Ebr. & Rom. 4 Mulieres de damno teneri, defenditur ex utrorumque legibus. Quibus legibus solutæ sint mulieres ex placito Magistrorum. 5 Variè exponitur communio damni, de qua in Misna. Exod. 21. 35. ex Ebræorum mente illustratus.
units.tr: The valuation of the things which must be compensated is made before the judges. What kind of witnesses are required. Concerning damage done by women. The shared responsibility of the one who gives and the one who suffers the damage. Annotation. ¹The beginning of the Mishnah is confirmed by Digest, book 2, title 1, l. 1, §2 [פוס]. The value of the damage is reduced to money in movable goods. Movables such as silver. The valuation of silver. ²What is equivalent to silver. Wards used to pay debts from their estates, which they changed [נוחנים]. ³The conditions of witnesses. Also from Roman law [כני חורים]. [ἡρως]: whence. Concerning the testimony of slaves from Roman law. Testimony in monetary matters among the Hebrews and the Romans. ⁴That women are liable for damage is defended from the laws of both peoples. By what laws women are released, according to the decision of the masters. ⁵The common responsibility for damage, which is spoken of in the Mishnah, is variously explained. Exodus 21:35 illustrated from the mind of the Hebrews.

units.la: De innocentibus & convitiis. Pecus, quorum respectu non censeatur convitia. Dens & pes qui se hic habeant. Similiter bos, homo, lupus, leo, ursus, pardus, pardalis, & serpens. Innocentis à convicto sive contestato differentia. Annot. 1 Nocua animalia ad petulci bovis leges examinantur; innocua ad mansueti. פחמ qua. 2 Explicantur convicta sive contestata. 3 Qui animalia non convicta censeantur. 4 Eadem bestia quomodo convicta & innocens. de quo Not. 6. amplius. 5 Dupliciter explicatur סור. 6 Mos multa omittendi, in Misnis. פקורי. Quis fit bos ladentis in ditione læsi. & ס definiuntur. 7 De ס, פס, נבע. Pardalis & panthera differunt.
units.tr: Concerning the harmless and the reported (animals). Livestock, in relation to which a goring is not reckoned. How the tooth and the foot stand here. Likewise the ox, the man, the wolf, the lion, the bear, the leopard, the pardalis, and the serpent. The difference between the harmless animal and the one that has been convicted or formally charged. Annotation. ¹Harmful animals are examined by the laws of the wanton ox; harmless ones by those of the gentle ox. [פחמ] what. ²What "convicted" or "charged" means. ³Which animals are reckoned not convicted. ⁴The same beast, how both convicted and harmless; see note 6 below for more. ⁵The word [סור] is explained in two ways. ⁶The custom of omitting many things in the Mishnah. [פקורי]. Who is the ox of the one who causes harm within the jurisdiction of the one injured. The [ס] are defined. ⁷On [ס], [פס], [נבע]. The pardalis and the panther differ.

units.la: Rependere ex praestantissimo, & ex ipso corpore bovis. Ex.21. v.35. contra Iudaeos vindicatur. Distinctio Ebraeorum inter animalia nocua & innocua ex ff. Si quadrupes illustrata.
units.tr: To make restitution from the choicest part, and from the body of the ox itself. Exodus 21:35 is defended against the Jews. The Hebrew distinction between harmful and harmless animals is illustrated from the Digest, Si quadrupes.
Chapter II, §1.

units.la: Damnum pede datum diversimode compensatur. Vas fractum, & deinde frangens. Gallinacei quandoque totius, quandoque dimidii damni tenentur. Annot. Pauperies bestiarum distinguitur, ejusque in compensando diversitas. Consectaria principii sui leges ubique non imitari. כדרכה duo includit. מסדם quid. Misna cum leg. Romanorum in conv. & discrimine collata.
units.tr: Damage done by a foot is compensated in different ways. A vessel broken, and then the one who breaks it. Poultry are sometimes liable for the whole damage, sometimes for half. Annotation. The liability of beasts is distinguished, and the variety in compensating it. The consequences of their principle are not everywhere imitated by the laws. [כדרכה] includes two meanings. [מסדם]: what. The Mishnah is compared and contrasted with the Roman laws on the agreement and the difference.

units.la: Dens ubi & quando convictus censeatur. Quandoque quantum percepti commodi, quandoque quantum damni dati, expenditur. Ann. Exod. 22. 5. ex Iudaorum mente. Qui pretium in aestimando commodo percepto minuatur. Locorum publicorum & privatorum discrimen ex ff. Ad legem Aquiliam.
units.tr: Where and when a person is deemed convicted. Sometimes the compensation is weighed by the advantage received, sometimes by the damage done. Note on Exodus 22:5 according to the Jewish understanding. How the price is reduced in estimating the advantage received. The distinction between public and private places, from the Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam.

units.la: Canis & haedus desiliendo confringentes vasa. Placentâ abreptâ accensa meta. Ann. Misna ex Plat. de leg. confirmata. Quomodo placentâ incendatur meta. Qui multa major in placenta compensanda, quam frumenti meta. Leges Rom. mitiores. Accursii explic. aberrare videtur.
units.tr: A dog and a kid leaping down and breaking vessels. A cake snatched away and a stack set on fire. Note: the Mishnah confirmed from Plato's Laws. How a cake sets a stack on fire. Whether the damage to the cake is greater in compensation than the damage to the stack of grain. The milder Roman laws. The explanation of Accursius seems to go astray.

units.la: Quodnam innocens animal, quodnam convictum. Diversa de eo Magistr. sententia. Annot. Tres dies non uno modo in exhibendo testimonio explicantur. שמ & תפמ. explicantur. Exod. 21. 36. enarratur. Vbi D. Indas, ubi Meir sequendus.
units.tr: What animal is innocent and what is convicted. The different opinions of the teachers on this. Note: the three days are not explained in one way in giving testimony. tam and mu'ad [תם & מועד] are explained. Exodus 21:36 is expounded. Where R. Judah, and where Meir, is to be followed.

units.la: Bos cornu, pede, dente ladens in loco publico & privato. Modus argumentandi à majori, qui in hisce multis procedat. Annot. Tria loca in hac causa sunt distinguenda. Derivatorum jura in fonte damni quaerenda. Quae excipiantur. Tarphonis de damno cornu dato sententia. Mens regula juris, דין כפתן כהנין ... Exceptio in jure usitata contra argum. ab impari. Quando obtineat, diversa sententia. Num. 12.14. exponitur. Sapientes ex ff. sublevantur.
units.tr: An ox injuring with horn, foot or tooth, in a public and a private place. The method of arguing from the greater, which proceeds in many such cases. Note: three places must be distinguished in this case. The rights of derivative matters are to be sought in the source of the damage. What exceptions are admitted. Tarphon's opinion about damage done by a horn. The meaning of the rule of law, the judgment of the priests' tunic [דין כפתן כהנין]. The exception used in law against argument from the lesser. When it holds, a different opinion. Numbers 12:14 is explained. The wise men are relieved by the Digest.

units.la: Homo semper conteslatus ac convictus. Totum damnum præstat. Ann. Quis error excusat: quis secus. Confirmatur è ff. li. 9. tit. 4. leg. 3. Dormientis oculum excæcans quando teneatur. Exod. 21. 14. explicatur. Vbi de מור, ejusque requisitis.
units.tr: A man always a witness and convicted. He pays the whole damage. Note: what error excuses, and what does not. Confirmed from Digest, book 9, title 4, law 3. When a person who blinds the eye of a sleeper is liable. Exodus 21:14 is explained, where there is discussion of the mor [מור] and its requirements.

units.la: De amphora ac cado, quum franguntur, vel iis prateriens laeditur. Cum adhibita distinctione. Annot. Homines anxiè ad vias attendere non tenentur. כר & חבית ex Gemara & Additamentis explicantur. Quid sit sudario acquirere. Multitudinem sequi. Aqua lubricum labendi occasionem prabens. קרמית. Quanti sit, ad liquorem effusum & fragmina animum non advertere. Misna ex Dig. illustrata & confirmata.
units.tr: Concerning a jar and a cask, when they are broken, or when a passer-by is hurt by them. With a distinction applied. Note: people are not bound to attend anxiously to the roads. The jar [כד] and the cask [חבית] are explained from the Gemara and the Additions. What it is to acquire by a handkerchief. To follow the crowd. Water, providing an occasion for slipping on a slippery surface. The potsherd [קרמית]. How far one is bound not to take notice of spilt liquid and fragments. The Mishnah illustrated and confirmed from the Digest.

units.la: De damno dato per effusam aquam, spinam aut vitrum occultatum. Item si sepes in locum publicum decidat. Ann. Quo loco occultata, si ledant, reatum inducant. De eo priscorum sedulitas. Sepes quomodo fieri tuto possit, è Gemara docetur. Sepes decidens qui accipienda. Misna ex ff. Adl. Aquiliam illustrata.
units.tr: Concerning damage done by spilt water, or by a thorn or glass hidden away. Likewise if a hedge falls onto a public place. Note: if things hidden in such a place cause injury, they induce guilt. The diligence of the ancients on this point. How a hedge can be made safely, is taught from the Gemara. Who is to receive a falling hedge. The Mishnah illustrated from the Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam.

units.la: Damnum datum per stramen & paleam. In loco publico aliquid inquinantes, ut stercus eò effundentes. Ann. כוכב quid, ex Glossa & Plinio. Nonnulla nocentia, occupantis fiunt. Quandoque teneri qui faciunt quod licet. Misna ex Dig. lucem mutuata.
units.tr: Damage done by straw and chaff. Those who foul something in a public place, such as by throwing dung there. Note: what a kokhav [כוכב] is, from the Gloss and from Pliny. Some harmful things become the property of whoever takes them. Sometimes those are held liable who do what is permitted. The Mishnah illustrated, borrowing light from the Digest.

units.la: Figulus in quem cadentem alter inpingit, de secundi lesione tenetur. Ann. Id quidem si stare potuerit. Figuli & vitriarii plures, quomodo cadentes de damno teneantur. Quid sit cadere propter primum. Misna comparatur cum casu quodam è Digestis. §. 5. Va-
units.tr: A potter whom another person knocks into when he falls is liable for the injury to the second man. Note: this indeed if he has been able to stand. Potters and glaziers, several, how those who fall are liable for damage. What it is to fall because of the first. The Mishnah compared with a certain case from the Digests, §. 5. Va-

units.la: Varii casus, quibus amphora ad tignum frangitur, eorumque jura. Item de lino lucernâ accenso. Annot. ¹ Maritus uxorem in concubitu ledens. ² Fortuitus casus quando excusat. Fortuiti casus differentia ex Iure civili Rom. probatur.
units.tr: Various cases in which a jar is broken against a beam, and their legal consequences. Likewise concerning flax set alight by a lamp. Note. ¹ A husband injuring his wife in intercourse. ² When a chance event excuses. The difference of chance events is proved from the Roman civil law.

units.la: De eo qui celeri cursu alterum ledit. Ann. Innocens est qui pridie diei festi, cursu ledit. [?]
units.tr: Concerning one who by running swiftly injures another. Note: He is innocent who on the day before a festival injures by running. [?]

units.la: Varii modi, quibus ligna findens alterum ledit, expenduntur. Ann. Ab eis differunt quae ē ff. ad leg. Aquiliam citantur.
units.tr: Various ways in which one who splits wood injures another are weighed. Note: they differ from those cited from the Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam.

units.la: Proponitur damni compensatio, cum boves alter alterum vitiant; similiter homines; & tandem homo bestiam, & vicissim bestia hominem ledit. Annot. ¹ Plene explicatur exuperantia compensatio in mutuo damno, & quid [?] ² Diversa sententia de bestia ledente hominem. Vindicatur contra Iud. Exod. 21. 31. Misna cum variis legibus Rom. confertur.
units.tr: The compensation for damage is set forth when oxen injure one another; likewise men; and finally a man injures a beast, and conversely a beast a man. Note. ¹ The excess compensation in mutual damage is fully explained, and what [?] ² A different opinion about a beast injuring a man. It is defended against the Jews, Exodus 21:31. The Mishnah is compared with various Roman laws.

units.la: Boum cornu ferientium valor diversus, diversum compensandi modum exigit. Exod. 21. 35. quomodo accipiatur. Annot. ¹ Plenius agitur de com. 35. & 36. cap. 21. Exodi. ² Qui verba illa accipienda, cadaver valet 50 drachmis.
units.tr: The value of oxen striking with their horns is different, and demands a different method of compensation. How Exodus 21:35 is to be understood. Note. ¹ The matter is treated more fully in verses 35 and 36 of Exodus chapter 21. ² What those words are to be understood as meaning, the carcass is worth fifty drachmas.

units.la: Quibus casibus quis in sui ipsius facto, liber fit, ob factum vero bovis sui teneatur; & contra. Annot. ¹ Regula juris, [?] ² Dedecorantis crimen qui non fit sine intentione. ³ Qui restringant Exod. cap. 21. 26. comma. ⁴ Ladens parentes quomodo dicatur [?] insons. ⁵ Explicatur è Gem. quis bos [?] sapiens. Misna distinctio tanta, non probata Dig. Si quadr. &c.
units.tr: In which cases a man is free by reason of his own act, but is liable for the act of his ox; and conversely. Note. ¹ The rule of law [?] ² The crime of injuring by insult is not committed without intention. ³ Those who restrict the clause in Exodus chapter 21:26. ⁴ How one who injures his parents is said to be [?] innocent. ⁵ Explained from the Gemara: which ox is [?] wise. A Mishnaic distinction so great, not proved by the Digest, Si quadrupes, etc.

units.la: Quum dubium est quis bos laserit, magnus an parvus, convictus an innocens. Regula, Exigenti incumbit probatio. Ann. ¹ Quid in in bove sit יתר. Magni referre, parvusne an magnus, petulcus an mansuetus laserit. Merito altercantur, quis quem bovem laserit. Regula, affirmanti incumbere probationem, ex Inst. & ff. probatur.
units.tr: When it is doubtful which ox gored, a large one or a small one, a convicted one or an innocent one. Rule: The burden of proof lies on the one who demands it. Note. What is meant by יתר in an ox. It matters whether the ox that gored was small or large, wanton or tame. People rightly dispute which ox gored which. The rule that the burden of proof lies on the one who affirms is proved from the Institutes and the Digest.

units.la: Quomodo, si bos cornu feriat plures boves diversis temporibus, damnum compensandum sit, variis casibus exponitur. Illud de pluribus laesis ex Gemara enarratur. Mansuetus bos a petulco distinguitur. Compensatio ex eo quod restat, exemplo elucidatur. Alius casus ex R. Simeone. Mina. Denarius aureus, cujus valoris. Misna ex ff. & Instit. illustratur.
units.tr: How, if an ox gores several oxen at different times, the loss is to be compensated, is set out in various cases. That point about several injured parties is explained from the Gemara. A tame ox is distinguished from a wanton one. Compensation from what remains is illustrated by an example. Another case is taken from R. Simeon. The mina. The gold denarius, and its value. The Mishnah is illustrated from the Digest and the Institutes.

units.la: Bos <bl>שור</bl>, convictus sive contestatus respectu quorundam animalium & dierum; non omnium. Annot. Casus propositi ratio. Minora animalia, quae censeantur. Quid hic in dubiis faciendum. Boves qui sabbathum discernant. Qui petulcus mansuetus postea censeatur. Quatenus distinctio inter שור & op cum leg. Rom. conveniat, vel ab iis discrepet. Mansuetus bos Ebraeis.
units.tr: Ox [שור]: convicted or proven, with respect to certain animals and days, though not all. Note. The reason for the case proposed. Which minor animals are reckoned as such. What is to be done here in doubtful cases. Oxen that distinguish the Sabbath. Which wanton ox is afterwards reckoned tame. How far the distinction between [שור] and [op] agrees with Roman law, or differs from it. The tame ox among the Hebrews.

units.la: Bos sacer cornu feriens, & cum cornu feritur. Bovem idololatra cornu petit impune bos Israelita. Annot. Idololatrae Iudaeis. Praecepta Noachi posteris data. Gentilium bona, occupantis Iudaei fieri. Deut. 33. 2. prolixè exponitur. Item Hab. 3. 6. Lex Mosis primum aliis gentibus oblata. נגר: Seir, Paran mons. Itineris Isr. ordo in deserto. Iudaei gentiles judicant ex commodo suo. Gentiles à Iudaeis cum mactandis bestiis collati. Num. 15. 16. גר peregrinus quis sit: ejus distinctio. רע proximus, ὁ πλησίον, quis, prolixè probatur contra Iudaeos. Luc. 10. 33. explicatio, probatur. Romani aequiores in Iudaeos, quam hi in illos: ex li. 1. Codicis.
units.tr: A sacred ox that gores, and an ox that is gored by a horn. An ox of an idolater gored by an Israelite's ox goes unpunished. Note. Idolaters and Jews. The precepts of Noah given to posterity. The goods of the Gentiles become the Jew's by occupation. Deut. 33:2 is expounded at length, and likewise Hab. 3:6. The law of Moses was first offered to the other nations. [נגר]: Seir, Mount Paran. The order of Israel's march in the wilderness. Jews judge the Gentiles by their own advantage. Gentiles compared with Jews regarding the slaughter of animals. Num. 15:16. Who is a stranger [גר], and its distinction. Neighbour [רע, ὁ πλησίον]: who he is, proved at length against the Jews. Luke 10:33, explanation, proved. The Romans were fairer to the Jews than the Jews were to them: from book 1 of the Code.

units.la: Bos surdi, fatui, pupilli, quoad damnum consideratur. Istis curatores praefecti. Bovis in theatro pugnantis conditio. Ann. & quid. Legis ratio sumitur e modo quo pupilli satisfaciunt. Obtestatio Exodi 21.29. quando coram Ἀληθείας. Dominium mutat bovis conditionem. Pupilli non censentur proprietarii. תוקף, פותם, ויקףי, בחוקיהם, quid in jure Hebr. denotent. Hinc illustrata Gem. Maccoth. Bos ταῦρος describitur. Leges Rom. etiam consultum voluisse surdis, furiosis, pupillis.
units.tr: The ox of a deaf man, a fool, or a ward is considered as regards damage. Curators are appointed for these. The condition of an ox fighting in the theatre. Note, and what it means. The rationale of the law is taken from the way wards make satisfaction. The adjuration of Exodus 21:29 when before Ἀληθείας. Ownership changes the ox's condition. Wards are not counted as owners. What the terms תוקף, פותם, ויקףי, and בחוקיהם denote in Hebrew law. Illustrated from the Gemara Makkoth. The bull [ταῦρος] is described. The Leges of the Romans also intended to provide for the deaf, the insane, and wards.

units.la: Bos homicida occidendus. quando hic λύτρον solvendum. Quid si servum aut ancillam feriat. Ann. Bos homicida si aliis immisceatur. Exod 21. 31. ad alia animalia quae homines occidunt extendi. Conviciusne cadis bos, antequam λύτρον solvant domini. Bos si occiderit hominem, an domino mortem creet, disputatur. Exod. 21. 29. & 30. fuse enarratur. Iudaeus explicando contradicit Scriptura. Siclus. Servi pretium. λύτρον quo casu solvendum, ex sent. Maim. Varii casus & jura, quae in bove occidente considerantur. Supplicium bestiarum, ob necem, ex Solone. De solvendo pretio, si homo per bestiam interierit, ex jure Romano. Ex eodem, occisor cum eo, qui causam mortis praebet, collatus.
units.tr: An ox that kills a man is to be stoned. When the λύτρον is to be paid here. What if it gores a male or female slave? Note. A homicidal ox if it is mixed with others. Exodus 21:31 is extended to other animals that kill human beings. Whether the oxen are stoned before the owners pay the λύτρον is disputed. Whether, if an ox kills a man, it brings death upon the owner, is also disputed. Exodus 21:29 and 30 are expounded at length. The Jew, by his explanation, contradicts Scripture. The shekel. The price of a slave. In what case the λύτρον is to be paid, from the judgment of Maimonides. The various cases and laws considered in the case of the goring ox. The punishment of beasts for killing, from Solon. On paying the price if a man has perished by a beast, from Roman law. From the same source, the killer is compared with one who provides the cause of death.

units.la: Bos sese parieti affricans. Bos alium occidens quam intenderat. Ann. Idololatra Ebraeis. Cades gentilium ne quidem pecuniā compensanda, ex sententia Iudaeorum. Abortivus quis: ubi de שבת. Hebrew: ubi de Ier. 37. 13. 14. ista phrasis tres sensus admittit. ὁ ἐπὶ ἀναστάσεως. Luc. 20. v. 36. Filius alicujus rei, quomodo dicatur. Filius domus. Filius mortis. Filius hujus seculi. Resurrectio impiorum an, & qua, Iudaeis. Ex ff. Si quadrupes convenientia & discrepantia leg. Rom. à Mishna.
units.tr: An ox rubbing itself against a wall. An ox killing someone other than the one it had aimed at. Note. Idolater and Hebrew. The carcasses of the Gentiles are not even to be compensated with money, according to the opinion of the Jews. What an abortive is: where it concerns שבת. In Hebrew, where Jer. 37:13-14. This phrase admits three senses. ὁ ἐπὶ ἀναστάσεως: Luke 20:36. How someone is called a son of a thing: son of the house, son of death, son of this age. Whether and how there is a resurrection of the wicked, according to the Jews. From the Digest, title "Si quadrupes": agreement and disagreement with Roman law, from the Mishnah.

units.la: Bos mulieris, orphanorum, ac aliorum; bos sacer, si occiderint quendam.Ann. Bos orphanorum, & curatorum quis. Ἀντεῖον hic pro quibus solvatur. Peregrini mortui, nisi filios proselytus genuerit, bona occupantis fiunt, Iudaeis. ita Exod. 22. com. 21. contradicunt: quod explicatur. Vox saepius repetita quid valeat in leg. de bove.
units.tr: The ox of a woman, of orphans, and of others; a sacred ox, if they have killed someone. Note. Who the ox of orphans and of guardians is. Ἀντεῖον here, for whom it is paid. Foreigners who die, unless they have begotten sons as proselytes, have their goods become the property of whoever occupies them, according to the Jews. Thus they contradict Exodus 22:21, which is explained. A word repeated very often, and what it means in the law about the ox.

units.la: Consideratio bovis lapidandi. ejus caro an licita. Ann. Lapidandus educebatur. Consecratio illegitima. Quod de carne bovis, id ad alias bestias extendi. Quantopere Ebraei scandalum fugiendum moneant. in quo cum Servatore faciunt, Matt. 18. Explicatur Exod. 21. 28. Neque comeditor caro ejus. E bove lapidando nullum remanet commodum. Fraus facta legi Exod. 21. 28. refellitur. Illicita consecratio authoritate Inst. l. 2. ti. 1. rejicitur.
units.tr: Consideration of the stoned ox, and whether its flesh is lawful. Note. The stoned ox was led out. An illegitimate consecration. What is said of the flesh of the ox applies to other beasts. How greatly the Hebrews urge that scandal be avoided. In this they agree with the Saviour, Matt. 18. Exodus 21:28 is explained. Nor is its flesh to be eaten. No benefit remains from the stoned ox. A fraud committed against the law of Exodus 21:28 is refuted. An illegitimate consecration is rejected on the authority of the Institutes, book 2, title 1.

units.la: Commodatarius, conducens, similes in locum Dominorum succedunt. Qui praestanda culpa, cum bestia debite conclusa fuerit. Asservatio per cultrum. Annot. Discrimen inter commodatarium & similes. Diversa Misna lectio. Praestanda culpa, quomodo intelligatur. Exod. 21. 36. exponitur. Bovis petulci conditio an melior quam mansueti. Idem comma examinatur. Amplius de asservata bestia. De ipsa custodia. Tertio de sensu Exod. 21. 36. Illud de secespita unde desumtum. Reatus ex non asservata bestia; damnumque rependendum: licet quadrupes alteri commodata, &c. ex leg. Rom. Custos, quis.
units.tr: The borrower, the hirer and similar persons succeed to the place of owners. Who must answer for fault, when the beast has been duly shut up. Keeping by a knife. Note. The difference between the borrower and similar persons. A different reading of the Mishnah. How "answering for fault" is to be understood. Exod. 21. 36. is expounded. Whether the condition of a wanton ox is better than that of a gentle one. The same clause is examined. Further on the beast kept. On the keeping itself. Thirdly, on the sense of Exod. 21. 36. Whence that about the knife is derived. Liability arises from a beast not kept, and the damage must be made good, even if a quadruped lent to another, etc., from Roman law. Custos: who?

units.la: Si bos vaccam, ad cujus latus foetus inveniatur, feriat. Quum vacca cum qua foetus, bovem ferit. Ann. Foetus quis. Vacca consideratur ante & post partum. Quum ignoratur tempus, an antea, an postea ediderit partum. Regula juris qua in dubiis dimidium actori adjudicatur. Similis casus, quum vacca, quae foetum edidit, bovem ferit. Quid hic juris sit, ubi res certa est. Quid, si de tempore iterum non constet. Regula juris de de probatione. Collatio Misna cum jure Rom. Quid faciendum deficiente probatione, ex A. Gellio.
units.tr: If an ox gores a cow at whose side a calf is found. When the cow with the calf gores an ox. Note. What a calf is. The cow is considered before and after giving birth. When it is not known whether she brought forth the young before or after. The rule of law by which, in doubtful cases, half is adjudged to the claimant. A similar case, when a cow that has borne a calf gores an ox. What the law is here where the matter is certain. What if the time again is not established. The rule of law about proof. Comparison of the Mishnah with Roman law. What is to be done when proof is lacking, from Aulus Gellius.

units.la: Ollas in alterius area si frangat pecus; & iis laedatur. Fructus similiter si edat; vel iis laedatur. Ann.¹ Impetrare inferendi veniam, jus immutat.² Figulum accepta ingrediendi venia absolvi, qui cum ceteris cohareat: ex Gem.³ Fructuum proprietarius dato damno quando teneatur, è Gem. Veneno jumentum si quis perdat, quo judicio teneatur: è Gem. סבים, quis. פרוּתפּ, & פחוּם. In alterius aream quid importans, quo damnum inferatur: ex leg. Rom.
units.tr: If livestock break pots in another's yard and are harmed by them. Likewise if it eats fruit, or is harmed by them. Note. To obtain permission to enter changes the law. A potter who, having received leave to enter, is acquitted, being bound together with the others: from the Gemara. The owner of fruit, when he is liable for damage given: from the Gemara. If someone loses a beast by poison, by what judgement he is liable: from the Gemara. סבים [sabim], who? פרוּתפּ [peruta] and פחוּם [pahum]. What it means to be "entering into another's yard" by which damage is inflicted: from Roman law.

units.la: Quum bos introductus in alterius aream, damnum infert; vel eum ferit aut mordet alterius bestia. Ann.¹ Si bovem introductum in aream tuam, alterius bos feriat. חיוּב & פסוּר ad diversos & diversa referri potest. חיבּח רשׁמוּ, quid in Gemara.² פּוּרח רמלי, quid. De bove patrem tuum in puteo opprimente.³ Verba etiam ad remotiora referri.⁴ Misna ex jure Rom. confirmatur.
units.tr: When an ox introduced into another's yard inflicts damage, or another's beast gores or bites it. Note. If another's ox gores an ox you have introduced into your yard. חיוּב [chiyuv] and פסוּר [pasur] can be referred to different persons and different things. חיבּח רשׁמוּ [chayyav rishmu]: what in the Gemara? פּוּרח רמלי [purach ramli]: what? Concerning an ox that crushes your father in a well. The words may also be referred to more remote things. The Mishnah is confirmed from Roman law.

units.la: Bos intendens bovem, si mulieris foetum ejiciat. Si homo id faciat, proximum intendens. Ut foetuum pretium solvatur, quomodo aestimatio fiat. In ancillam manumissam & peregrinam inclementia. Ann.¹ Specialis loquendi modus in Misna.² Ex. 21. v. 22. 23. exponitur.³ Mulier cum foetu, & ubi foetum edidit, comparatur.⁴ Mulierem post partum praestantiorem videri.⁵ Quaenam sit illa peregrina & ancilla. Misna Scriptura contradicit. Peregrinus alterius religionis, haredes non habere censetur Iudaeis. Vxor mariti heres non est. Multa excussi foetus nomine debita, ex leg. Rom. confirmatur.
