Hence it is now clear what is meant by these four sources of damage, or by οπνη ηιαϸ, and that many other things are referred to each of the sources or heads, which follow their laws and imitate their conditions (although here too the reason and condition are often different: insofar as animals are now deemed dangerous for these or those works and not for others; this is to be weighed in the earlier examples from Maimonides, cod. οπνη, c. 1, §5; or because a change (ννϲ) intervenes in the act, as in some examples in c. 2, §1 of this tractate). Then, apart from these damages, there are indeed others, which require full compensation only in certain cases. 6 Moreover, lest anyone object that one source, or at least some of them, is enough, so that the remaining damages and the pauperies (as the Roman laws call it) may be referred to them, Rabbi Judah in this Mishnah proceeds and indicates that each source is necessary. He shows that they differ from one another, and therefore cannot be reduced to one or fewer than those he has named: for their nature is not the same, and the laws to be observed in them also differ. For the Masters are accustomed to infer one species from another; here one species might seem to suffice, but at once an exception would be given. For example: "If the Merciful had written only about the tooth, I would say that the tooth binds, because a benefit is perceived from the damage done by it; but the foot does not bind, because there is no benefit from its damage." Many such examples could be offered on this subject. Besides, in these sources of damage the rule of law is not the same. For example, God is said in the Gemara, f. 5, to have made mention of the pit in such a way as to exempt the man by it: because it is read in Exodus 21:33, "If an ox or an ass falls into it." From this they conclude that if a man has fallen in, who could have foreseen it, the other (the owner) is not liable. Thus, for these and similar reasons, the individual cases are set out distinctly, since some things are excepted here which are not excepted elsewhere. Moreover, when the ox is distinguished from the grazing animal, take this of the foot of the walking ox and the tooth of the grazing ox (as is partly clear from what has been said): namely, that the damage given by the foot is unlike that done by the tooth. Furthermore, as far as the phrase goes, one might say of מזק that it is not Chaldee, but that the Talmudists express it by שור from the same root, except that מזק comes from the Hiphil. This is confirmed by the following phrase, ושור; if you compare our version of Halichoth olam from p. 127 onward, you will have no doubt about it once you have done so. 7 But where he says, "this one and that one, who are accustomed to harm by walking," he means the ox walking and grazing, and the fire which seems to walk by creeping and consuming further; and he distinguishes both from the pit, since the pit remains immovable in its place. The Gemara explains this difference by the phrase, "there is not the aspect of this one as of that one," that is, the status and condition of each is different. This formula is most common in comparative arguments: for there, after various objections against equality and likeness, they finally, drawing out some agreement amid this difference, inequality and unlikeness, are accustomed to add: "the condition of this one is not as of that one; the status is equal, because, etc." (On these matters consult my Talmudic Key, where I have set out all such things at length for readers.) 8 Just so here, although there is no argument, the latter formula is used when it is said, "the side is equal," that is, the common status and condition, or the equal law, which is found in the four said sources. Perhaps it will not be unwelcome to readers if this Jewish division of damages is compared with the Roman division on the same matter. I confess that I do not recall here a division expressly set out in four members, yet individual parts are to be found. And indeed the first and third member of the earlier division, joined by the author in the first difference, namely as regards the ox harming with its foot and tooth, compare the final words of the second note, and likewise that sentence where Diocletian and Maximian write: "Concerning those things which you claim were grazed by wrong, you are by no means forbidden to sue under the sense of the Aquilian law" (Cod. lib. 3, tit. 35, last law). And the words ex sententia sufficiently show that, just as the Jews had certain heads from which they judged the rest, so the Romans did not have everything defined by fixed laws, but some things were also deduced from others. Here, however, I do not quote the whole law, Si quadrupes pauperiem, from the Digest, lib. 9, tit. 1, because that law also contains cases of this sort which are not covered by this Mishnah. Moreover, the remaining two, pit and fire, are likewise considered by the same authorities, so that damage may be prevented: the pit or ditch indeed (Dig. lib. 9, tit. 2, l. 28): "Those who dig pits for catching bears or stags, if they have made them on roads, and something has fallen into them, and the thing has been made worse, are bound under the Aquilian law." Likewise, Digest lib. 43, law "Si filius": "Moreover, if he has dug a ditch in a public wood, and my ox has fallen into it, I can sue, etc." Finally, that fire is treated in the laws of the Romans no one can be ignorant, if he has read even these words (Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam, law 27, §8): "If anyone has wished to burn down my island, and the fire has reached the island of a neighbour, he will be liable under the Aquilian law even to the neighbour." As for the fine, the one imposed here in our Mishnah is that defined in the sacred letters: for God commands in Exodus 22:5, "If anyone grazes a field or vineyard, and lets his beast loose to feed in the field of another, he shall repay with the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard." For compensation from the best and most excellent is commanded in one kind of damage, but the rabbis extend it by analogy to the other kinds. Hence, in general, Abrabanel, on the passage of Exodus: "Hence the sages of blessed memory say that they estimate damages at the most excellent: that is, when he wishes to repay, they estimate the thing damaged as if it equalled the most excellent thing that is found in the possession of the one who caused the damage." Moreover, because the words of the divine law, when it is said ..., seem ambiguous, therefore, as we read here in the Gemara, f. 6, פלוגי

units.la: Dissentiunt. Doctor Ifmael existimat, nos aestimationem facere in bonis damnum passi; at D. Akiba existimat, nos aestimationem facere in iis quae sunt authoris damni. Itaque sicut apud Latinos dicitur, rependere damna, id est, aliquid pro damnis; & rependere pramium; sic etiam apud Ebraeos oło duobus modis adhibetur. unus rependere optimum, ad eum retulit qui damnum passus erat, ut licet optimum agri & vineae depastum non esset; tamen ne minus reciperet quam amisisset, restitutio ad optimum & pretiosissimum conformaretur: alter vero laedentis agrum designari antumavit, scilicet eum hac lege teneri, ut ex praestantissimo suo rependat, ne ullo modo alter minus quam amiserit, recipiat. Verumenimvero distinctione adhibet Gemara, cum inquit f.7.p.2. [Hebrew] Omnes res censenda optimum; quia si non vendantur hic, vendantur in civitate alia: excepto agro, quem compensare debet optimo, quo maturet in ipso venditionem. Hoc sibi Doctores isti volunt, in hunc sensum Dei verba, optimo agri, optimo vinea, accipienda; si pro agri vel vineae proventu solvatur, praestantissimum agri & vineae dandum esse, quo statim in ipso agro vel vinea adhuc remanens fructus vendi queat: at si damnum in mobilibus quis compenset, quodlibet censeri optimum; quia si pretium conveniat, vel hic vel alibi, quo facile transfertur, vendi poterit. cum in agro & vinea secus se res habeat: utpote quorum pretium saepe vilius sit, nec ita commode transferatur; quamvis agri laesi spatium aequale sit agro, quo compensatio instituitur. Sane hujus damnum non semper alterius, i. laedentis segetibus aut uvis compensari posse, in confesso est: quandoquidem laedens aliquando agrum non habet. Quocirca illa Misnae explicatio fundamento non destituitur. Non tamen de nihilo est, quod de optimo agri, &c. in lege ponatur: quia ubi quis pretium. pecunia præstare nollet, facile exciperet se fruges frugibus compensare velle; & deteriores, licet ejusdem quantitatis, rependeret. Cujusmodi rationem bene expressit D. Bechai comment. in Pentateuchum quatern.15. f. 4. col.2. מן הערית טשם קייח לזומר כביכול או כוכורית ויהי כל אחד ואחד נזול את חכרו ערית טלו ויטלם מן הוכורית או מן הכינוכית Ex optimo: nam si diceres, ex mediocri, aut è vilissimo; unusquisq; proximo suo eriperet optimum ipsius, & è vilissimo, vel è mediocri rependeret. Quamvis ergo casus hujusmodi darentur, ubi pecuniâ vel aliis modis pretium æquale restituerent; si quis agro agrum, i. ejus proventum læsum compensare posset; optimo proventu id fieri oportebat: quò semper & ubiq; injustitiæ obviam eundum ostenderetur. Eoque etiam collimarunt leges Romanorum: uti videre est Digest.l.9. tit. 1. in principio. Si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicetur, aliò ex lege duodecim tabularum descendit. qualex voluit: aut dari id quod nocuit, id est, animal quod noxiam commisit; aut æstimationem noxiæ offerre. Noxia autem est ipsum delictum. Et quamvis hic de omnibus Misnæ nostræ capitibus non agatur (licet alia etiam comprehendantur) quin in cæteris etiam parem restitutionem exegerint, dubium non est: idque docent leges citatæ in præcedentibus.
units.tr: They disagree. Doctor Ismael holds that we make the estimate from the goods of the one who suffered the damage; but Rabbi Akiba holds that we make the estimate from the things belonging to the author of the damage. So, just as among the Latins one speaks of rependere damna, that is, making good losses, and rependere pretium, so also among the Hebrews the phrase oło is used in two ways. In the first, rependere optimum refers to the one who had suffered the loss: even if the field or vineyard that was eaten was not of the best quality, the restitution is nonetheless fixed at the best and most valuable, so that he does not receive less than he lost. In the second, the field of the one who causes the harm is meant, namely that he is bound by this law to make good from his best produce, so that the other does not in any way receive less than he lost. Indeed the Gemara draws a distinction when it says at folio 7, page 2: All goods are to be valued at the best, because if they are not sold here, they may be sold in another city; except the field, which he must compensate with the best, so that he may hasten its sale on the spot. Those teachers mean by this that the words of God, of the best of the field, of the best of the vineyard, are to be understood thus: if payment is made from the yield of a field or vineyard, the most excellent part of the field or vineyard must be given, so that the fruit still remaining on that very field or vineyard can be sold at once. But if someone makes good a loss in movable goods, anything may be valued as the best, since if the price is agreed, it can be sold here or elsewhere, to which it is easily carried. It is otherwise with field and vineyard, whose price is often lower and which cannot be so conveniently transferred, although the area of the injured field is equal to the field by which the compensation is made. Certainly it is agreed that the loss of this kind cannot always be compensated from the crops or grapes of the other party, that is, of the one causing the harm, since sometimes the one causing the harm has no field. Therefore that explanation of the Mishnah is not without foundation. Nor is it for nothing that the law says of the best of the field, etc.: for when someone did not wish to pay the price in money, he could easily plead that he wished to make good crops with crops, and would restore inferior ones, though of the same quantity. Lord Bechai, in his commentary on the Pentateuch, quaternion 15, folio 4, column 2, expressed this reasoning well: "From the best: for if you said, from the middling, or from the very worst, each man would snatch the best of his neighbour's and make good with the worst or the middling." Therefore, although cases of this kind were given, where people restored an equal value in money or in other ways, if someone could make good a field with a field, that is, with its injured produce, it had to be done with the best produce, so that it might always and everywhere be shown that injustice must be opposed. The laws of the Romans also aimed at this, as may be seen in Digest 9, title 1, at the beginning: If a four-footed animal is said to have done damage, an action arises from the Law of the Twelve Tables, which allows either that the thing which did the harm, that is, the animal which committed the injury, be surrendered, or that the estimated value of the injury be offered. The injury, moreover, is the wrongful act itself. And although this passage does not deal with all the chapters of our Mishnah (though other matters are included as well), there is no doubt that in the rest too they required equal restitution; and the laws cited in the preceding passages teach this.

units.la: Cujuscunq; curam gerere teneor, ab eo illatum damnum ¹ stabilio. quum in eo partem ² damni ultimam stabilio, ejus damnum præstare debeo, ac si totum ejus damnum stabilivissem. In facultatibus in quibus non est ³ prævaricatio, facultatibus ⁴ fœderatorum, facultatibus ⁵ certaהסיוחרים
units.tr: Whoever's property I am bound to take care of, I guarantee the damage inflicted by him. When I guarantee the last part of the damage in it, I must make good its damage as if I had guaranteed the whole of its damage. In property in which there is no prevarication, the property of allies, the property of certain persons scattered about, outside the injurer's own jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction common to the injured party and the injurer, wherever harm is done to someone, the one causing the harm is bound to pay the price of the damage from his most excellent produce.

units.la: הֵמִיּוּחָדִים בְּכָל מָקוֹם חַיָּב מְשׁוּרָה הַמִּיּוּחָדִי לְמִזִּיק ד וּרְשׁוּת הַנִּזֵּק וְהַמַּזִּיק וּכְשֶׁמִּזִּיק חַב הַמַּזִּיק לְשַׁלֵּם הַשְּׁלוּמִי נִזָּק בְּמֵיטַב הָאָרֶץ׃
units.tr: Whoever is in charge of the property of others, in every place, is bound by the measure of the one who damages, and by the authority of the injured party and the injurer; and when the injurer causes damage, the injurer must pay the compensation for the damage from the best of the land. [Hebrew: "הַמִּיּוּחָדִים בְּכָל מָקוֹם חַיָּב מְשׁוּרָה הַמִּיּוּחָדִי לְמִזִּיק ד וּרְשׁוּת הַנִּזֵּק וְהַמַּזִּיק וּכְשֶׁמִּזִּיק חַב הַמַּזִּיק לְשַׁלֵּם הַשְּׁלוּמִי נִזָּק בְּמֵיטַב הָאָרֶץ"]

units.la: rum personarum passim, extra ditionem ledentis 6 propriam; & ditio- nem lasi & 7 ledentis communem; ubi alicui nocetur, nocens damni pretium solvere tenetur praftantiffimo proventu.
units.tr: …in the property of certain persons scattered about, outside the injurer's own jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction common to the injured party and the injurer; where harm is done to someone, the one causing the harm is bound to pay the price of the damage from the most excellent produce.
Annotations.

units.la: In originali textu est הכִּשְׁרוּתִי Rectum feci, vel direxi: verum hoc loco nonnihil à communi significatione deflectit, idque diversimodè secundum diversas interpretum sententias: quæ hic non conveniunt. Quidam (ut ex Maimonide liquet initio Comment. ad codicem) hunc sensum esse tradunt, Eum, qui bestiæ aliarumve rerum curam gerere debet, si ejus incuriâ contingat ut ab illis damnum inferatur, damnum hoc suum facere & in causa esse ut quod factum est revera non infortunium, sed voluntarium damnum esse censeatur; licet ipso ignorante datum sit: ipsum enim occasionem præbere ut quod damni legibus non subjiceretur, jam hujusmodi esse statuatur, in quod animadverti debeat. itaq; eum stabilire damnum & efficere (quemadmodum loquitur Mishna) ut non fit obliquum; sed rectum damnum. Alii quamvis vocis proprietati magis adhærere videantur; nihilominus ab ipsius in Talmude usu recedentes magis, ita enarrant, ac si id sibi vellet Mishna, Cujuscunque curam gerere teneor, ab eo illatum damnum corrigere, quodque depravavi rectum facere, & ad rectam justitiæ ac æquitatis regulam revocare, id est, damnum compensare debeo. Addit Mishna, eum qui isto modo vel partem damni stabilit, id est, ex parte tantum damni & pauperiei causa fuit; totius damni teneri. Quod sanè sano modo accipiendum & intelligendum est; alioqui plurima absurda secum traheret. ut si quis à te accensum ignem qui nocere nequeat, ita augeat ut proxima quæq; consumat,
units.tr: The original text reads Rectum feci, or direxi [הכשרותי]. Here, however, the word departs somewhat from its usual meaning, and it is taken in different ways according to the different opinions of the interpreters. These do not agree with one another here. Some (as is clear from Maimonides at the beginning of his commentary on the code) hold that the sense is this: if a man who is bound to look after a beast or other property, through his carelessness allows harm to be done by it, he makes that harm his own, and it is as though the damage were not an accident but a voluntary wrong, even though it was done without his knowledge. For he gives the occasion for something that would not be subject to the laws of damage to be regarded as of that kind, and so it ought to be treated as such. Therefore he must establish the damage and make it (as the Mishnah puts it) not a slanting but a straight damage. Others, though they seem to cling more closely to the proper meaning of the word, nevertheless depart further from its use in the Talmud and explain it as if the Mishnah meant this: whoever is bound to take care of a thing must correct the harm done by it, and must make straight what he has made crooked and bring it back to the right rule of justice and equity; that is, he must make good the damage. The Mishnah adds that the man who establishes only part of the damage, that is, who was the cause of only part of the damage and of the loss, is liable for the whole damage. This must certainly be understood in a sound sense, otherwise it would lead to many absurdities. For example, if someone enlarges a fire you have lit, which could not have harmed anyone by itself, so that it consumes everything nearby, the whole loss is to be made good by you. Or if someone digs to ten or more palms a well that you had sunk only a palm or a foot deep, the whole loss that follows is to be charged to you.

units.la: {1} Ex Maimonide. fumat, tuum esse totum præstare damnum; aut si puteum quem palmo vel pedis profunditate depresseras, alius ad decem vel ultra fodiat, tibi totum quod subsequitur damnum imputari. Quapropter in Gemara cum aliis exemplis, tum scamno legem declarant: si quinque in scamno sedentibus accedat sextus, cujus pondere aggravante scamnum frangatur, damnum huic imputabitur; cum nisi accessisset, integrum mansisset. Nam si objiceret quis, absque eo fuisset, etiam frangendum (scil. longiori temporis spatio) responderent, nisi tu fuisses, minori tempore sedissemus: & illo instante, nisi vos fuissetis mecum, non fuisset fractum; regererent alii, simulac adfuit ipsis, enim confregisse. Ex qua disputatione liquet, hanc legis mentem esse, non quemvis qui culpam participat tanti obligari quanti est damnum totum; sed eum qui colophonem addidit. Quemadmodum vulgare hoc exemplum etiam ostendit: si quis (ajunt) per alios depresso ad novem palmos puteo, decimum addat (cum hæc sit demum justa putei profunditas ex illorum definitione) is ubi in puteum aliquid decidens fractum fuerit, ad totum damnum compensandum tenebitur. Ita D. Judas existimat, si quis à decem hominibus singulatim percussus baculis ad ultimum ictum moriatur, hunc qui ultimum ictum infligit tantummodo teneri. At Romanorum leges secus statuere mihi videntur: dig. lib. 48. tit. 8. leg. 15. Nihil interest, occidat quis, an causam mortis præbeat, quæ sententia cum R. Judæ opinione non convenit. Sed ut Misnæ nostræ magis congrua verba proferam, quæ scilicet ad quodvis damnum pertinent; Ad leg. Aqu. 1. Qui occidit, §. In hac, generale dictum occurrit, Et qui occasionem præstat, damnum fecisse videtur. Adeo ut ei soli qui rem perficit culpa non imputetur; sed sæpe iis etiam qui in opere perpetrando antecedentia fecere. 3 Subjiciuntur deinde restrictiones quinque, ne multa commemorata ad quævis damna extendatur. Prima est, ut ea damnum patiantur in quibus non est שור, id est, ne consecrata sint: nam si quis commodum aliquod ex horum jactura ac detrimento percipiat, שור committere dicitur. Exceptionis ratio est, quod ejusmodi delictum alio modo coerceatur: adduntque, Exod. 21. 35. ubi de bove læso agitur, non dicibovem simpliciter; sed proximi sui; ne illa damni pœna ad factum ejusmodi extendatur, quo bos sacer læd​itur. Cum istis consecratis una excipiuntur facultates eorum qui non sunt כהן, גוי (ut Petrus phrasin reddit act. 3.) Confœderati: non quod alia pœna damnum istis, qui Israëlitis confœderati non sunt, illatum puniatur; sed quia istis alienis à fœdere nocens culpa non teneatur ulla, & insons ex Judæorum mente censendus sit. Requiritur etiam ut damnum passa sint certarum personarum bona: etiam quæ lædunt; nam si quis כפר, communem fecerit bovè suum, ut occupantis esse queat, de dano à bove illato non tenetur. Maimonides aliud quoq; innui autumat: ista voce יחיד singulares, simul hunc casum excludi, si duorum alteruter quidem nocuerit, sed incertum sit, uter damnum dederit, quod duorum proprietarii, alter in alterum culpam conferant. Sic enim certæ personæ factum imputari non poterit. Attamen si facultates læsæ sint in loco privato lædentis, licet certarum sint personarum, multam sub finem positam non respiciunt: etenim non permittit æquitas, ut si bovi tuo in meam aream ingressò noceatur, ego tenear; quia secundum Gemaram dicere possem, תוך כרמי, bos tuus in mea ditione quid quærit? Si tamen non bos meus tuo noceat, sed ipse ego, damni teneor: nam regerere posses, נכי fit ita, ut tibi liceat abigere; ut noceas, tibi non licet. Huic exceptioni optimè convenit cum verbis Pomponii Digest. lib. 9. tit. 2. le. Quintus. §. 1. Quamvis alienum pecus in agro suo quis deprehendisset, sic illud expellere debet, quomodo si suum deprehendiffet: quoniam, fi quid ex ea re damnum cepit, habet proprias actiones. Itaque qui pecus alienum in agro suo deprehenderit, non jure id includit: nec agere illud aliter debet, quam (ut supra diximus) quasi suum; sed vel abigere debet sine damno, vel admonere dominum ut suum recipiat. Denique Misna nostra excipit, ne certarum istarum personarum facultates sint tali loco qui duobus dominis communis est: si enim eo casu unius bos bovi alterius noceat, istum ad alterius damnum compensandum non teneri. Quod hac conditione obtinet, כלכר פתהיה קרסות מזותפת בינייםם מיוקדת לפירות ולטוריים לכל אם היתה מיוקדת לפירות וּמבר לחר מן הסותפין והכניים כו מורי והזיק כגן ורגל חייב
units.tr: {1} From Maimonides. Therefore in the Gemara, along with other examples, they explain the law by means of a bench. If five men are sitting on a bench and a sixth comes up, and the bench breaks under the added weight, the damage is charged to him, since it would not have happened had he not come. For if someone objected, it would have been broken even without him (namely, after a longer period of time), they would answer, if you had not been here, we would have sat for a shorter time. And at that moment, if you had not been with me, it would not have been broken; others would reply, as soon as he was there, he broke it. From this discussion it is clear that the intention of the law is not that everyone who shares in the fault is bound for the whole amount of the damage, but only the one who added the final straw. The common example also shows this: if (they say) someone has had a well sunk by others to nine palms, and adds the tenth (since by their definition this is the true depth of a well), he will be bound to make good the whole damage if anything falls into the well and is broken. So too Judah holds that if a man is struck separately by ten men with staves and dies at the last blow, only the one who gives the last blow is liable. But the laws of the Romans seem to me to decide otherwise: Dig. bk. 48, tit. 8, law 15: It makes no difference whether someone kills or provides the cause of death; which opinion does not agree with the view of Rabbi Judah. But to bring forward words more suited to our Mishnah, which apply to any damage whatever: in the law of Aquilius, Dig. 9, 2, 1, §. In hac, a general saying occurs: And he who provides the occasion seems to have done the damage. So that the blame is not imputed only to the one who carries out the act, but often also to those who did earlier things in committing the deed. Next, five restrictions are added, so that the many cases mentioned are not extended to every kind of damage. The first is that the things which suffer damage must not be sacred [שור], that is, not consecrated; for if someone gains some advantage from the loss or injury of such things, he is said to commit shor. The reason for the exception is that such an offence is punished in another way; and they add, citing Exod. 21.35, where the case of a wounded ox is discussed, that the text does not say simply ox but of his neighbour, so that the penalty for damage is not extended to such an act by which a sacred ox is injured. Along with these consecrated things, the property of those who are not priests [כהן] or gentiles [גוי] (as Peter renders the phrase in Acts 3) is excepted, and also confederates. This is not because a different penalty is imposed for damage done to those who are not confederates of the Israelites; rather, because the guilty party is not bound by any fault towards such outsiders to the covenant, and in the mind of the Jews the innocent man is to be judged accordingly. It is also required that the property of certain persons suffer the damage, even of those who do the harm. For if someone has made his ox common [כפר], so that it might belong to whoever takes it, he is not liable for damage done by the ox. Maimonides maintains that something else is also implied by the word individual [יחיד]: this case is excluded too, where one of two owners has indeed done harm but it is uncertain which of them caused the damage, the owners of the two animals each imputing the fault to the other. For in this way the act cannot be imputed to a certain person. However, if the property damaged was in a private place of the one who did the harm, then even though it belongs to certain persons, the fine set at the end does not apply. For equity does not allow that if your ox enters my yard and is harmed, I should be liable; because, according to the Gemara, I could say, what business has your ox in my domain? But if my ox does the harm to yours, or I myself do it, I am liable for damages. For you could reply, it is so arranged that you may drive it out; you are not permitted to do harm. The words of Pomponius in Digest, bk. 9, tit. 2, law 5, §1 agree well with this exception: Although someone has caught another's herd on his own land, he ought to drive it out just as if he had caught his own, since, if he has suffered any loss from it, he has his own actions. Therefore whoever has caught another's herd on his own land does not lawfully shut it up, nor ought he to deal with it otherwise than (as we said above) as if it were his own; but he ought either to drive it off without harm, or to warn the owner to take it back. Finally, our Mishnah excepts the case where the property of those certain persons is in a place held in common by two owners. For if in that case one man's ox harms another man's ox, the former is not bound to make good the loss of the latter. This holds on condition that [Hebrew: Modo ut ditio utrique communis, fructibus & bobus fit accommodata, see below].

units.la: Modo ut ditio utrique communis, fructibus & bobus fit accommodata; sed si designata sit fructibus, & progressus sociorum unus eo bovem suum introduxerit qui dente vel pede noceat, tenetur. Quo docetur, si in locum ad alia quidem communem, non vero ad boves recipiendos, introductus bos noceat alii; damnum praestandum esse. רשות, cujus aliquoties facta est mentio, locum denotat, qui in alicujus, vel quorundam, vel omnium potestate & dominio est. Ita רשות הרבים est locus publicus. Sed de hoc vocabulo alibi actum fuit. גיו שום כסף ושוה כסף בפני בית דין ועל פי עדים בני חורין ובני ברית והנשים בכל הנזק והניזק והמזיק בחשלומין
units.tr: Provided the domain is common to both, and is suited to fruits and to oxen; but if it is set apart for fruits, and one of the partners brings his ox into it, which harms with its tooth or foot, he is liable. By this it is taught that if an ox, introduced into a place common to the partners for other purposes but not for receiving oxen, does harm to another, the damage must be made good. The word reshut [רשות], which is mentioned several times, denotes a place that is in the power and dominion of one person, or of several, or of all. Thus reshut harabim is a public place. But this word has been discussed elsewhere. [Mishnah: Gaiu shum kesef ushvah kesef, befnei beit din ve-al pi edim, benei horin uvenei verit, vehanashim bekol hanezek vehanizak vehamazik bahashlumin.] The valuation of silver and of what is equivalent to silver is made before the judges, on the testimony of witnesses who are free and confederates. Women too are taken into account in the matters that are said concerning damage. The one who does the damage and the one who suffers it sometimes share in the payment…

units.la: Taxatio argenti & ejus quod argento aequivalet, coram judicibus fit: secundum testes qui ingenui, & faederati sint. Mulieres etiam in iis quae de damno dicuntur, considerantur. Dans damnum & passus quandoque solutionem participant.
units.tr: The assessment of silver, and of whatever is equivalent to silver, is made before the judges, on the testimony of witnesses who are free-born and in covenant. Women too are taken into account in those matters that concern damage. The one who causes the damage and the one who suffers it sometimes share in the payment.
Annotations.

units.la: In hac Misna judicibus etiam taxatio in litibus pecuniariis tribuitur, secundum Digest. l.2. t.1. leg.1. §.2. Cui jurisdictio dictio data est: ea quoque concessa esse videntur, sine quibus jurisdictio explicari non potuit. Primò autem in textu orig. occurrit םיב א םב, posuit, statuit: hinc per synecdochen creberrimè pretium statuere: unde םימב & hoc loco םיב taxatio. Latinis inde fit summa, summatim, summarium. Quæ in præcedentibus de compensando damno dicta fuere, & dicentur in sequentibus, ita Judæi accipiunt, ut damnum, saltem in mobilibus datum, æstimari debeat, & valore ad pecuniam revocari, quò quot numis valeat definiatur, summaque ista reo imponatur. Ergo qui ex lege Dei optimo agri proventu satisfacere tenetur, ex hac interpretatione (prout à quibusdam concipitur) argentum debere videtur, quanti optimus proventus æstimabitur. Mobilia autem omnia quæ hic considerari queunt, veluti qɔɔ argentum censentur in hac Misna: quia, ajunt, si non hoc loco, alibi vendi queunt, & in argentum & nummos redigi. Hic vides, quid sit Taxatio argenti: nempe taxatio rei, ut argento vel iis quæ veluti argentum habentur, compensetur. Est quidem hæc dura loquendi formula: quam tamen Maimonides aliique hic observant.
units.tr: In this Mishnah the judges are also granted assessment in monetary disputes, according to Digest 2.1.1 §2: To whom jurisdiction is given, those things are also thought to be granted without which jurisdiction could not be exercised. First, in the original text the word posuit, statuit [םיב א םב] occurs: hence, by synecdoche, very often to set a price, and from this taxatio [םיב] in this place. From this the Latin summa, summatim, summarium arise. The rabbis take what has been said above about compensating damage, and what will be said below, to mean that damage, at least when done to movable goods, must be estimated and reduced to its value in money, so that it is fixed how many coins it is worth, and that sum is imposed on the defendant. Therefore, on this interpretation (as some conceive it), a man who is bound by God's law to make restitution from the best produce of a field seems to owe silver to the amount that the best produce would be valued at. All movable goods that can be considered here are counted in this Mishnah as silver, because, they say, if they cannot be sold here they can be sold elsewhere and turned into silver and coins. Here you see what the assessment of silver is: namely, the assessment of a thing so that it is compensated in silver, or in those things that are held as silver. This is indeed a harsh form of expression, yet Maimonides and others observe it here.

units.la: ² Unde ipsis, quod argento æquivalet, est fundus: quippe unde pecunia difficilius quam ex mobilibus conficiatur; quia aliò deportari non potest, ut nisi his, illis saltem placeat. Atque de fundo propter pupillos agitur, è quorum immobilibus solvitur, si quid ob datum damnum, patris nomine debeant: nam Judæi, cum pupillorum conditionem meliorem reddere vellent, pecuniam immobilibus, saltem agris, prætulerunt. Ideoque coram judicibus, quantum agri, damno dato responderet, decernebatur. Ratio est: quia de mobilibus excipi posset, pupillos ista post mortem patris acquisivisse, ideoque creditoribus non obligari: vide Gemaram hoc loco. Hoc autem postea à Doctoribus םויפא dictis iterum mutatum in pupillorum facultatibus, docet Maimonides Cod. de damnis pecuniariis c.8.§.12. cum in præcedentibus aliam etiam veteris legis rationem annotasset. ¹ Testes qui coram tribunali de damno testimonium perhiberent, nonnisi eos admittebant, qui essent cum מורים בני מורים, tum בני ברית. Quorum illo, nempe בני מורים, in sacris illustrium filii, id est, nativi illustres, noratentur: nam מור ibi saepè illustres à מור. Unde praepositio demonstrativo ѻ est מור: sc. ѻ respondente spiritui aspero, & ѻ in numero literali τῷ η; Graecorum ἥρως, heros. nisi quod ω ad faciendam terminationem Gr. literæ ϱ postponatur; cum י in Ebraeo praecedat. at in legibus Talmudicis designantur homines liberi sive ingenui: sic enim expresse Gemara subjicit, בני מורים לאמורי עברים, nativi ingenui, ad excludendum servos. Isto vero posteriori, scilicet בני ברית, confederati, מורים לאמורי גוים, opus fuisse ad excludendum gentiles, ait eadem Gemara. adeo ut solos Israelitas eo nomine venire liqueat. Quamvis hæ testium conditiones ita non requiruntur lege Rom. ut ex eo quod de foederatis hic dicitur liquet, & quum Digest. li.22.t.3.l.7. & lib.22.tit.5.leg.7. aliquo casu saltem admittuntur servi; tamen non omninò alienæ requiruntur.li.eodem t.eodem l.2. In testimoniis autem dignitas, fides, mores, gravitas examinanda est. Has conditiones in ingenuis Ebræis maximè inveniri, ipsi putabant. Imò & Romani servos utplurimum idcirco etiam exclusisse videntur. Ad Hebraeos pertinet illud Josephi de antiquitat. Jud. l. 4. c. ult. ubi de legibus Dei. Γυναιξὶν μὴ ἐξεῖναι μαρτυρεῖν διὰ κουφότητα καὶ θρασύτητα τῆς φύσεως αὐτῶν· μαρτυρεῖσθαι δὲ μὴ τε δοῦλοι διὰ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀγεννίαν, Mulieribus non liceat testimonium dicere, propter levitatem & temeritatem sui generis; neque testimonium dicant servi, propter animum degenerem. At quemadmodum in pecuniariis litibus Judaei testes exigunt; ita eadem illa lege §. Testimonium, legimus; Adhiberi testes quoque possunt non solum in criminalibus causis, sed etiam in pecuniariis litibus, ubi res postulat. ⁺ Porrò damnum datum & acceptum an in mulieribus etiam locum habeant, dubitari poterat; quia non omnia mulieribus quæ viris imposita cenfentur: uti disertè statuit Gemara c.3. Berachoth f. 20. p.1. יוםר כל מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה omni lege de opere faciendo, quæ ex tempore dependet (quia certo tantum & designato tempore observanda)solvuntur mulieres. Ideo cum de damno etiam teneantur mulieres, & vicissim damnum illis datum præstari debeat; Misna nostra mulieres hic etiam speƈtari distinƈtè annotat. Similiter Paulus jurisc. ut videre est ff. Ad leg. Aq.1. ult. Mulier si in rem viri damnum dederit pro tenore legis Aquiliæ convenitur. ' Tandem illa hoc addit, læsum etiam & lædentem in solutione concurrere. Cujus duplex sensus est: vel enim docetur, non semper evenire ut totum damnum compensetur; sed sæpenumerò contingere ut cui nocetur tantummodò dimidium recipiat: ut si bovem, qui alterum interfecit, antea petulcum non fuisse constet, vel eò respicit quod in Gemara his exprimitur verbis, proprietarii distinutionem patiuntur in cadavere, sive bestia sit innocens, sive convicta., q. d. si inter mortem, exempli gratia, bovis tui, & judicium ferendum contingat, ut pretium occisi minuatur; passus & inferens damnum, hoc ferent simul: quanti occisus depretiatus fuerit, tantum non decedet damnum inferenti; sive bos alter petulcus, sive non petulcus fuerit. Vt si ex lege Exod. 21. ɣf. 35. partiantur mortuum, eumque admodum depretiatum, & secundum Judæorum sententiam, lædens hoc posterius damnum solus non ferat; longe minus quam æquum videbatur in mortuo habebit læsus. Eo casu fiet, ut licet in damno compensando solvat lædens, unà tamen in depretiato bove læsus solvere partem censeatur.
units.tr: ² Hence what is equivalent to silver is land for them, since money can be raised from movable goods only with more difficulty, because movables cannot be carried elsewhere unless these or those parties are willing. The question of land arises for the sake of orphans, from whose immovable property payment is made if they owe anything on account of damage done in their father's name. For the Jews, when they wished to make the orphans' condition better, preferred to set money against immovables, at least fields. Therefore, before the judges, the amount of land that would answer for the damage done was decreed. The reason is that, with movables, it could be objected that the orphans had acquired them after their father's death, and so they could not be bound to the creditors. See the Gemara on this passage. Later, however, the Teachers called (םויפא) changed this again with regard to orphans' property, as Maimonides teaches in the Code, on pecuniary damages, chapter 8, §12, having earlier noted in the preceding sections another reason from the older law. ¹ Witnesses who gave testimony about damage before the court were admitted only if they were both (בני מורים) and (בני ברית). Of these, the first, namely (בני מורים), is understood in sacred usage as the sons of illustrious men, that is, illustrious by birth, for (מור) there often means illustrious, from (מור). Hence the demonstrative preposition is (מור), namely the aspirate corresponding to the Greek (ῷ) and the letter (η) in numerical value; compare the Greek (ἥρως), hero, except that (ω) is placed after it to form the Greek ending, whereas (י) comes first in Hebrew. But in the Talmudic laws, free or freeborn men are meant, for the Gemara adds this explicitly: (בני מורים לאמורי עברים), freeborn, to exclude slaves. The second condition, namely (בני ברית), confederates, (מורים לאמורי גוים), was necessary to exclude Gentiles, says the same Gemara, so that it is clear that only Israelites come under that name. Although the Roman law does not require these conditions for witnesses, as is clear from what is said here about those in covenant, and although, in the Digest, book 22, title 3, law 7, and book 22, title 5, law 7, slaves are admitted at least in some cases, yet they are not altogether excluded in the same book, title and law 2. In testimony, however, dignity, faithfulness, morals and seriousness must be examined. The Hebrews themselves thought these qualities were found chiefly in freeborn Hebrews. Indeed the Romans also seem to have excluded slaves for the most part on this ground. To the Hebrews belongs that statement of Josephus in the Antiquities of the Jews, book 4, last chapter, where he speaks of God's laws: (Γυναιξὶν μὴ ἐξεῖναι μαρτυρεῖν διὰ κουφότητα καὶ θρασύτητα τῆς φύσεως αὐτῶν· μαρτυρεῖσθαι δὲ μὴ τε δοῦλοι διὰ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀγεννίαν), women are not permitted to give testimony, because of the lightness and rashness of their nature; nor may slaves give testimony, because of their base spirit. But just as the Jews require witnesses in monetary suits, so in that same law, in the section Testimonium, we read: Witnesses may be admitted not only in criminal cases but also in monetary suits, where the matter requires it. ⁺ Furthermore, it could be doubted whether damage done and received also applies to women, since not everything imposed on men is imposed on women; as the Gemara expressly states in chapter 3 of Berachoth, folio 20, page 1: (יוםר כל מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה), women are released from every law about doing work that depends on time (since such laws are to be observed only at a fixed and appointed time). Therefore, since women are also liable for damage, and damage done to them must likewise be made good, our Mishnah expressly notes that women are to be considered here too. Similarly, the jurist Paul, as may be seen in the Digest, on the Lex Aquilia, law 1 at the end: If a woman has caused damage to a man's property, she is sued under the terms of the Lex Aquilia. ' Finally, the Mishnah adds that the injured party and the one who caused the injury share in the payment. This can be read in two ways: either it is taught that the whole damage is not always made good, but that it often happens that the one who was harmed receives only half, as when it is established that the ox which killed another was not previously known to be dangerous; or it refers to what the Gemara expresses in these words: the owners undergo a division in the carcass, whether the beast is innocent or convicted. That is, if, for example, between the death of your ox and the holding of the judgment, the price of the dead animal falls, the one who suffered the damage and the one who inflicted it bear it together: however far the dead animal has lost value, that much loss will not fall on the one who inflicted the damage, whether the other ox was dangerous or not. For if, under the law of Exodus 21, verse 35, they divide the dead animal, and it has become much depreciated, and according to the opinion of the Jews the one who caused the injury does not bear this latter loss alone, the injured party will have far less than seems fair in the dead animal. In that case it comes about that, although the one who caused the damage pays in compensating for the damage, the injured party is nevertheless considered to pay a part in the depreciated ox.
C
Five [חמשה]
Rabbi

units.la: חמשה חמין וחמשה מועדין הכהמה אינה מועדת לא ליגח ולא ליגוף ולא לשוך ולא לרכוב ולא לבעוס הסן מועד לאכול את הראוי לה הרגל מועדת לשבר בורך הלוכה ושור המועד ושור המזיק ברשות הניזק והאדם הזאב והאריה והדוב והנמר והברולם והנחש הרי אלו מועדין רבי אליעזר אומר בזמן שהן בני הרבות אינן מועדין והנחש מועד לעולם מה בין הם למועד אלא שההם משלם חצי נזק סגופו ומועד משלם נזק שלם מן העליוה:
units.tr: There are five kinds of animals and five kinds of forewarned damagers. A beast is not forewarned to gore, to kick, to bite, to lie down on people, to ride, or to kick out with its hind legs. It is forewarned to eat what is fit for it. A foot is forewarned to break a jar on its path. A forewarned ox and an ox that causes damage on the property of the injured party are forewarned, as are a man, the wolf, the lion, the bear, the leopard, the hyena and the snake. Rabbi Eliezer says: when they are in a multitude they are not forewarned, but the snake is always forewarned. What is the difference between these and the forewarned animal? Only that the former pay half damages from their own body, whereas the forewarned pays full damages from the best of its property.
Annotations

units.la: Quia Exod. c. 21. ÿf. inferente mitius statuitur esse constet; rectè Ebraorum bovem, qui absque isto vitio cum, Scripturam distinguen secum reputarunt, Dei, c dato inter hunc bovem m nociturum non credebamu Quinque sunt innocentia; quinque convicta. Pecus non censetur convicta, nec quod cornu feriat, nec quod impellat, vel mordeat, vel incumbat, vel recalcitret. Dens convictus sive conteflatus est quod sibi convenicns comedat; pes conteflatus est quod obvia incedendo frangat. Bos conteflatus, bos laedentis in ditione lasi, homo, lupus, leo, vrsus, pardus, pardalis, & serpens, ecce haec animalia convicta censentur. Et Doct. Eliezer inquit, quum domi educantur, non censeri convicta; serpentem vero semper convictum haberi. Quid innocenti convictum interest? Nonnisi quod innocens suo corpore dimidium damni rependat; convictum vero totum damnum rependat è praestantissimo.
units.tr: Because Exodus 21 states the law more mildly than the inference seems to require, it is clear that the Hebrews rightly reckoned, as they distinguished in Scripture, that the ox which had no such vice was not to be believed likely to do harm to a neighbour, given God's ordinance. There are five innocent creatures; five that are known to be dangerous. Cattle are not regarded as dangerous, whether they strike with the horn, push, bite, lean on something, or kick. A tooth is dangerous if it eats what suits it; a foot is dangerous if, in walking, it breaks whatever lies in its path. An ox known to be dangerous, an ox that injures in the territory of the one injured, a man, a wolf, a lion, a bear, a leopard, a pardalis, and a serpent: these animals are regarded as dangerous. And Rabbi Eliezer says that when they are raised at home they are not regarded as dangerous, but the serpent is always regarded as dangerous. What, then, is the difference between the innocent and the dangerous? Only this: the innocent animal makes good half the damage from its own body, but the dangerous animal makes good the whole damage from the best of its property.
Annotations

units.la: 35. & 36. de bove casu damnum dedit, quam de bove quem petulcum ... m jurisconsulti, non tantum inter ... cio simpliciter spectatur, & petulantem ... ere voluisse autumant. Sic enim ... um in praestando damno à bove ... magnum discrimen faceret quem ... is, & illum quem cornu ferire consueverat; ... stabat; eam fuisse mentem, ut in similibus distinctio hujufmodi obtineret. Quo factum est, ut non tantum ea inter fe distinguerent, quæ nocua & innocua sunt; sed etiam quæ & in quibus nocua, vel innocua habeantur, adderent: ut nocua ad bovis petulci leges, innocua ad alterius conditionem examinarentur. Æquitas enim postulat, ne ea quæ nonnisi casu absque indole & dispositione interna nocent, iisdem legibus premamus, quibus vulgò & naturæ dispositione ac conditione nocentia constringuntur: siquidem absque lata culpa minor illorum cura geritur; cum hæc diligenter curari debeant. Itaque primò quinque enumerantur, quæ integra dicuntur, five innocentia: non quasi tanta ipsis integritas competat, ut nunquam noceant (ita enim de ipsorum damnis non ageretur:) sed quia alias lædere non consueverunt, integra habentur. A quibus distinguuntur convicta: quæ suæ ad nocendum dispositionis testimonio, vel quasi testimonio convincuntur. Quamvis enim fit testimonio comprobatum, five testibus adhibitis denunciatum, ex illo com.29. cap.21. Exodi, & denunciatum fit testibus adhibitis domino ejus; tamen de iis etiam hic passim usurpatur, quæcunque noxia esse certa ratione constat. Vt leo convictus habetur, quia experientia & ex natura ejus cognoscitur lædendi ardor. hominemque similiter pro convicto habent: quia licet adhibitis testibus nihil de eo denunciaverint; multis rationibus noxia ipsius natura innotescit. Pergit Mifna, & pecudem five animal brutum quod sub imperio, terræ pabulo pascitur, respectu quinque actionum ad priorem classem refert: non quasi bos cornu non feriat, nec impellat, &c. verum antequam hujusmodi actiones quæ numerantur aliquoties ediderit, bovem petulcum non haberi, ideoque nec anxiè custodiendum esse statuit. Nihilo secius idem ille bos alio respectu, posteriori classi annumerandus: nam ut alia mittam, dentem ejus conveniens
units.tr: 35 and 36 concern an ox that did damage by accident, rather than an ox that is butting. The jurists not only among ... are considered simply, and they maintain that the ox was wanting to be butting or mischievous. For in making good the damage done by an ox, the law drew a great distinction between the ox that ... and the one that was accustomed to gore with its horn; ... stood. The intention was that in similar cases this kind of distinction should hold. Hence they distinguished not only between things that are harmful and harmless, but also added in which things, and in what cases, they are regarded as harmful or harmless: harmful things were examined under the laws of the butting ox, and harmless ones under the condition of the other. For equity requires that we should not subject to the same laws those things that harm only by accident, without any inclination or inner disposition, as we subject those that are commonly harmful by their nature and constitution. Indeed, without gross fault less care is taken of them, whereas these must be carefully guarded. Therefore first five are listed that are called integra, or innocent. This is not because they have such perfect integrity that they never do harm (for then their damages would not be in question), but because they are not accustomed to injure others, and so are held to be integra. From these are distinguished the convicta, which are proved convicted by the evidence, or quasi-evidence, of their disposition to harm. For although that which is testimonio comprobatum, or denunciatum fit testibus adhibitis domino ejus, is proved by testimony, as in Exod. 21. 29, "and it be testified to its owner, with witnesses present," yet here the term is used loosely for anything that is known with certainty to be harmful in a certain way. Thus a lion is held to be convicted, because its fierce readiness to harm is known from experience and from its nature; and they treat a man in the same way as convicted, because, even if no witnesses have reported anything about him, his harmful nature is made known by many considerations. The Mishnah goes on: it refers a beast, or brute animal that is under command and feeds on the produce of the earth, to the first class with respect to five kinds of action. Not as if an ox does not gore or push, and so on; but it lays down that before it has performed such actions as are listed several times, a butting ox is not regarded as such, and therefore it need not be guarded anxiously. Nevertheless the same ox, in another respect, is to be counted in the second class. For, to pass over other things, it is agreed that its tooth consumes fodder. Therefore, as regards fodder, it must be guarded, lest it consume anything of others; so that it is compared in this respect with a butting ox, which has been declared to be such, and for whose whole damage compensation must be made.

units.la: C pabulum consumere, in confesso est. Quapropter quoad pabulum servandus, ne aliorum quicquam consumat: ut qui hac ratione cum bove petulco, quem talem esse denunciatum fit, conferatur; cujus totum damnum praestandum est.
units.tr: It is agreed that its tooth consumes fodder. Therefore, as regards fodder, it must be guarded, lest it consume anything of others; so that it is compared in this respect with a butting ox, which has been declared to be such, and for whose whole damage compensation must be made.

units.la: ⁵ Quum inter convicta bos contestatus recensetur; observa de quovis bove, qui aliqua ratione nocere solet, sermonem non esse; quis enim convictum inter animalia convicta numerandum ignorat? quin etiam eo sensu non מור המועד, sed מור מועד dicendum fuisset. Verum hic est sensus, inter convicta semper & ubique eum bovem censeri, cujus mentio Exod.21. 29. & 36. ideoq; ante מועד praefigitur ה designandi ac demonstrandi particula, ut ille bos intelligatur, שנגיחתו של (ut cum Maimonide loquar) cujus est ut plurimum cornu ferire. Attamen si Gemaram & interpretes quosdam sequamur, idem fuerit ac si author dixisset, Quinque sunt ab initio innocentia; sed ob ternas laesiones convicta etiam habentur: adeoque istud מועד, convictum, ad quinque praecedentia pertinuerit. ⁶ Quocirca antequam pergamus, modus quidam Misnae familiaris considerandus, quo nonnulla brevitati studens omittere solet. Vt quum dicunt חסורי מיחסרא deficiendo deficit: cujus rationem addunt, quia homo in lectione errat, ut rem omittat per oblivionem. quemadmodum docetur in nostro Halichoth Olam p.60. Verum quae tum omittuntur, ספי מחר, plura quam unum esse solent. Eodem modo in hac Misna si Gemaram sequamur, quum bos laedens in loco & dominio alterius privati alicujus, cum sequentibus numeratur, alius ordo recensetur: nempe istorum animalium quae semper convicta habentur. Ideoque praecedentia ita accipere oportet, quasi hoc modo loqueretur Misna, Quinque sunt innocentia, quae eadem si ter illas actiones ediderint pro convictis habentur. alia denique sunt, quae ab initio pro convictis censentur, ut bos ladentis in ditione lasi, (secundum quosdam) quosdam) homo, lupus, &c. ubi multa habemus quæ in Mišna subintelliguntur. Hoc obseruatu dignum: alioqui in multis Mišnæ dictis hallucinaberis. Simul etiam hoc attende, si tam violenter Apostolorum aliorumque dicta interpolare & intercalare liceret; infinitis responsis Judæorum cavillationes retundi posse, multoque magis verisimilia nobis suppeterent. Cæterum quia פּ & מועד hic passim occurrunt, ut dicta & dicenda penitius intelligantur, hæc paulo distinctius expendamus. מועד ex Maim. Jad t. 4. נ"כ c. 1. §. 4. propriissime est faciens opus, quod solet facere semper secundum indolem naturæ suæ. פּ vero est Res quæ nocet absque consuetudine, cujusque mos non fert ut inde damnum ipsum oriatur; sed ut casu contingat. Hic bestia convicta מועדת dicitur, ubi agit quod agere solet, & hac ratione nocet; innocens תמים, quum præter morem quid peragit, itaque damnum infert. Superius dicta quæ huc faciunt, non repetam: observa tantum, unum idemque animal quandoque esse & convictum, & innocens sive innocuum diversarum actionum, ad quas diversimodè se habet, respectu. Vbi hoc actionis genere nonnisi casu nocet; altero autem ex naturæ instinctu. Bos naturaconculcat obvia: ideoque si hoc spectes, est מועד. ut mordeant, multis nonnisi casu contingit: ideoque licet ita noceant, censentur תמים. Quin etiam pecus antea פּ innocua in quodam actionis genere; postea, ubi aliquoties eo modo nocuerit, מועד convicta habetur: ut si ea ratione damnum det, integrum damnum præstari debeat. Qui denique jumentum certorum dierum & animalium ratione convictum censeatur, docet Maimonides de damnis pecun. c. 6. §. 8. & seqq. 7 Porrò quid sit כרמלם (vel ut alii scribunt פרדלם) docetur in Gemara: ubi dicitur פרה, & פסח, nec non זבוע. Nomen פסח mari ac fœminæ commune est, ut & זבוע: coque pardalis notaretur, si literarum convenientia in illo פרד tantummodo spectaretur; vel in hoc שנ etymologia, quasi coloratum dicas, à macularum diversitate. (nam שש potius est colorum diversitas vel diversorum colorum congeries, quam color; imò quæcunque ad istam radicem pertinent, diversitatem connotant: ita ut שש dicatur digitus, quia multi ac diversi sunt.) Verumenimverò licet παρδαλις & פנתר sono conveniant; hoc posteriori panther significatur: sed quia vulgata hæc est sententia pardalin & pantheram eandem esse bestiam, hinc panthera & pantheram Judæi dixerunt פנתר. At differentes inter se bestias facit Xenophon, ubi ab ipso in Cyneg. distinctè recensentur, λεοντες, παρδαλεις, λυγκες, πυνδρες. Quin etiam hic à נמר pardo (in quo genere fœmina pardalis dicitur) ut species diversa separatur. Magni refert unde damnum rependatur: nam si illatum damnum è præstantissimo מיטב rependatur; nullam læsus ulteriorem jacturam patitur. at si è corpore quo ipsius bovis, læso rependatur; sæpe multo minus quam speraverit, recuperabit. Exempli gratia, si cum bos unius minæ bovem minarum trium occidit, deinde damni dimidium מחצית è corpore bovis compensetur; nocens ubi suum bovem alterius dimidio non valere videbit, alteri totum suum bovem tradens liber erit. Hoc colligunt è c. Exod. 21. v. 35. Vendita eo qui vivit, partientur pecuniam pretii ejus, & similiter mortuum partientur. Judæorum jurisconsulti hæc proprie accipienda negant: siquidem inde absurda sequi dicunt. Nam fieri posse, ut si bos duarum (exempli gratia) minarum bovem quinquaginta drachmarum occidat; damnum patiens in morte bovis, in compensatione lucretur multum: quandoquidem dimidium pretium bovis occidentis altero tanto occisum vincit. Propter hujusmodi inæqualitatem alio legem detorquent: scilicet hoc sibi velle, ut ex corpore bovis compensatio æstimetur; hoc etiam, ut læsus tantum damni dimidium accipiat. Nam cum שור Exod. 22. 31. vesci prohiberentur, cadaveris illius nulla fere ratione habita, ad bovis vendendi pretium dimidium respiciunt. Itaque si ad solvendum damni dimidium (ubi ulterius reus non tenetur) bos laedens non sufficit, damno affectum isto tamen bove contentum esse debere contendunt. At sua interpretatione vim legi faciunt. Quasi vero Deus ad ea quae plerumque fieri solent non respexerit, & ubi nimis magna disparitas inveniretur, prudentiam judicum ad legis scopum collimare non voluerit.Sane lex laeso duplex dimidium attribuit,unum pretii vivi bovis; alterum occisi: quo laedens & laesus rerum suarum curam gererent: utpote qui ex lege damnum participarent. Verum Judaeos nimis aberrare, attentus lector facile observabit. Caeterum quod distinctionem illam attinet, quam ex lege hauserunt, inter animalia quae noxia esse constat, eaque in quibus nocendi impetus non deprehenditur; eam & jus Romanorum agnoscit. Etenim ff. Si quadrupes, l.1. §. 4. Tunc haec actio locum habet, cum commota feritate nocuit quadrupes. puta si equus calcitrosus calce percusserit: aut bos cornu petere solitus, petierit. Cum dicit haec actio, intelligit actionem de aestimatione noxiae offerenda, ut loquitur §. 1. vide similia paragrapho septimo ejusdem legis.
units.tr: When the ox is listed among the convicta with witnesses, observe that the discussion is not about any ox that commonly does harm in some way; for who does not know that an ox which is known to gore is to be counted among the convicted animals? Indeed, in that sense it should have been called not "the ox that is a gorer" [מור המועד], but "the goring ox" [מור מועד]. The true sense is that the ox always and everywhere counted among the convicted is the one mentioned in Exod. 21. 29 and 36. Therefore the particle ה, used to designate and point out, is prefixed before מועד, so that that particular ox is understood, "whose goring" (to speak with Maimonides) is for the most part to gore with the horn. Yet if we follow the Gemara and certain interpreters, it would amount to the same as if the author had said: five are innocent from the beginning, but they are also held to be convicted after three injuries; and so that word מועד, convictum, would pertain to the five preceding. Therefore, before we proceed, a certain manner of speaking familiar to the Mishnah must be considered, by which it, studying brevity, is accustomed to omit some things. For example, when they say חסורי מיחסרא [deficiency: it is deficient], they add the reason, "because a man errs in reading, so that he omits the matter through forgetfulness," as is taught in our Halichoth Olam, p. 60. But the things omitted in such a case are usually more than one. In the same way in this Mishnah, if we follow the Gemara, when an ox that does harm in the place and property of some private person is counted together with the following, a different order is recited: namely, that of those animals which are always held to be convicted. Therefore the preceding must be understood as if the Mishnah spoke in this way: "Five are innocent, but if they have performed those actions three times, they are held to be convicted." Finally, there are others which from the beginning are reckoned as convicted, such as an ox that injures in the domain of one injured (according to some), a man, a wolf, etc., where we have many things that are understood in the Mishnah. This is worth observing; otherwise you will go astray in many of the Mishnah's sayings. Note also this: if it were permitted to alter and interpolate the sayings of the Apostles and others so violently, the cavils of the Jews could be refuted by countless answers, and much more probable arguments would be available to us. Moreover, since פּ and מועד occur here everywhere, so that the things said and to be said may be understood more thoroughly, let us weigh these a little more distinctly. מועד, according to Maimonides, Jad t. 4, נ"כ c. 1, §. 4, most properly means doing a work which it is accustomed always to do according to the disposition of its nature. פּ, however, is a thing which harms without habit, whose custom does not bring it about that damage arises from it, but that it happens by chance. Here a beast is called convicted מועדת when it does what it is accustomed to do, and in this way harms; innocent תמים, when it does something beyond its custom, and so inflicts damage. I shall not repeat what was said above that bears on this; observe only that one and the same animal is sometimes both convicted and innocent or harmless, with respect to different actions, to which it stands in different relations. Where it harms by a kind of action only by chance, but in another by the instinct of its nature: an ox by nature tramples whatever is in its way, and so, if you regard this, it is מועד. As for biting, for many animals it happens only by chance; so although they harm in this way, they are counted as תמים. Indeed, a beast that was previously פּ, innocuous, in a certain kind of action, afterwards, when it has harmed in that way several times, is held to be מועד, convicted; so that if it does damage in that way, the whole damage must be made good. Finally, Maimonides, De damnis pecun. c. 6, §. 8 and following, teaches when a beast of burden is counted as convicted by reason of certain days and animals. Further, what כרמלם (or, as others write, פרדלם) is, is taught in the Gemara, where פרה, פסח and also זבוע are mentioned. The name פסח is common to male and female, as is זבוע; and it would denote a leopard if the resemblance of letters were considered only in that פרד, or in the etymology of this שנ, as if you said "coloured," from the diversity of spots. (For שש is rather the diversity of colours or a gathering of various colours, than a colour; indeed whatever pertains to that root connotes diversity, so that שש is called a finger because there are many and various ones.) Yet although παρδαλις and פנתר agree in sound, the latter means the panther; but because the common opinion is that the pardalis and the panther are the same beast, the Jews have called the panther פנתר. But Xenophon, in the Cynegeticus, makes them different beasts, where λεοντες, παρδαλεις, λυγκες, πυνδρες are distinctly listed by him. Indeed here the נמר, the leopard (in which kind the female is called pardalis), is separated off as a different species. It matters greatly from what the damage is made good. For if the harm done is compensated from the most excellent part, מיטב, the injured party suffers no further loss; but if it is compensated from the body, that is, the carcass, of the ox itself, the injured party will often recover much less than he hoped. For example, if an ox worth one mina kills an ox worth three minas, and then half the damage, מחצית, is compensated from the body of the ox, the offender, when he sees that his ox is not worth half of the other's, will be free by handing over his whole ox to the other. They gather this from Exod. 21. 35: They shall sell the living ox and divide the price of it, and likewise they shall divide the dead. The Jewish jurists deny that these words are to be taken strictly, since they say absurdities would follow from it. For it could happen that if an ox worth two minas (for example) kills an ox worth fifty drachmas, the one suffering the damage gains much in the compensation of the dead ox, since half the price of the ox that did the killing exceeds twice the value of the ox killed. Because of this kind of inequality they twist the law another way: namely, that the compensation is to be valued from the body of the ox, and also that the injured party receives only half the damage. For since Exod. 22. 31 forbade eating the flesh, they took almost no account of the carcass, and looked to half the selling price of the ox. Therefore, if the ox that did the harm is not enough to pay half the damage (where the offender is not further bound), they contend that the injured party must be content with the ox that remains. But by their interpretation they do violence to the law. As if God had not regard to what commonly happens, and, where too great a disparity was found, did not wish the prudence of judges to be directed to the purpose of the law. Certainly the law gives the injured party a double half: one of the price of the living ox, the other of the slain; so that the offender and the injured party both take care of their property, as those who share the damage by the law. But that the Jews stray too far, the attentive reader will easily observe. Moreover, as to that distinction which they drew from the law, between animals that are known to be harmful and those in which an impulse to harm is not detected, Roman law also recognises it. For in the Digest, Si quadrupes, l. 1, §. 4: This action has its place when the quadruped has harmed with its wildness aroused; for example, if a kicking horse has struck with its heel, or an ox accustomed to gore has gored. When it says this action, it means the action for offering the estimate of the harm, as it speaks in §. 1; see similar things in paragraph seven of the same law.
