CHAPTER II. §. 1.

units.la: Quomodo pes convictus est, quod incedendo obvia frangat? Pecus eatenus convictus est, quod more suo incedens, frangat. Si recalcitrans, aut scrupis e vestigiis pedum suorum disjectis, fregerit vasa, dimidium damni praestabitur. Si conculcans vas aliquod, id fregerit; idque vicissim in aliud incidens illud fregerit: כיצור הרגל מועדת לשבר בדרך הלוכה הבהמה מועדת להלך כורכה ולשבר היהד מבעטה או שהיו צרורות מנחזין מחחת רגליה ושברה את הכלים משלם הנ דרסה על הכלי ושברו ונפל על כלי את' ושברו על
units.tr: How is a beast's foot held liable for breaking what it meets as it walks? A beast is held liable so far as it breaks things as it goes about in its usual way. If it kicks out, or if it scatters stones from under its feet and breaks vessels, it shall pay half the damage. If it tramples some vessel and breaks it, and then falls on another vessel and breaks it, [כיצד הרגל מועדת לשבר בדרך הלוכה הבהמה מועדת להלך כורכה ולשבר היהד מבעטה או שהיו צרורות מנחזין מתחת רגליה ושברה את הכלים משלם חצי נזק דרסה על הכלי ושברו ונפל על כלי אחר ושברו] (the Hebrew text as printed is garbled here).

units.la: פרק בין הלכי א. הראשון משלם נזק שלם ועל האחרון משלם חצי נזק הרגנולים םועין להלך כורכן ולשנר היה דליל קשור כרגליו או שהיה מהום ושבר את הכלים משלם חנ ו
units.tr: The first vessel: full damage is paid; for the last one, half damage is paid. [Hebrew: the beast that was tied at its feet, or was lame, and broke the vessels, pays half damage.] (The Hebrew as printed is garbled.)

units.la: gerit: pro priori totum damnum rependetur; pro posteriori damni dimidium. Gallinacei contestati sive convicti sunt, quod more suo incedentes obvia frangant. quod si gallus tricis adhærentibus pedibus suis, aut insultans fregerit vasa, damni dimidium præstabitur.
units.tr: ...it breaks: for the first, the whole damage shall be repaid; for the second, half the damage. Hens are held liable, or convicted, for breaking what they meet as they walk in their usual way. But if a cock, with straws clinging to its feet, or by leaping upon them, breaks vessels, half the damage shall be paid.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: {1} Licet in primæ periodi versione à Talmudistarum syntaxi recedam, versionem satis contextus probat. Porrò ut hæc omnia, similiaque intelligantur, nec sæpius repetenda ac inculcanda sint; jam plenius monendi lectores: anxiè inter damna illata distingui, an à pecude proficiscantur quatenus convicta est, id est, quæ ita nocere solet eoque nomine innotuit, an verò ab ista eadem pecude inferantur, quatenus ita lædere non consuevit; (vel per interveniens medium det damnum aliquod:) nam eadem pecus illo modo nocere sæpe solet; hoc modo nonnisi casu & inopinato nocet. Quemadmodum hoc loco de pede constat, eo obvia quæque calcari solere; at si forte pecus incedens pedibus suis scrupos è pavimento ob eorum rotunditatem & lubricitatem excutiat, quibus vas aliquod frangatur; id casu fieri dicemus. Itaque ne pede obvia proteratcavendum; adeoque incuria nostra datum damnum, in solidum compensandum: at si scrupi ex incessu disjecti obvium vitrum frangant, dimidium damni rependetur; quia ut ista anxiè præcavere homo non tenetur: quippe qui fortuita prævidere non possit, vel anxia cura istiusmodi incommodis omnino occurrere. Hæc si ad sequentia applicentur pro negotiorum diversitate, omnia plana erunt. Si modo hoc adjiciatur (de quo etiam aliquid in præcedentibus) animalia quoad hanc, vel illam actionem innocentia, id est, quæ istas actiones patrare non solent, ideoque si eo modo pauperiem faciant, dominum ad dimidium damnum præstandum obligant; hæc inquam eadem quod ad easdem actiones convicta reddi posse; id est, talia haberi quæ istis actionibus ut plurimum lædant. Nam quadrupes recalcitrans, fi eam aliquoties ita læsisse constet, jam calcitrosa habebitur: & nisi custodiatur, cjus proprietarius de toto damno tenebitur. Itaque quum pecus, ejusve dens, pes, &c. fecundum varias actiones inter innocentia numerantur, fi istis actionibus aliquoties læsisse constiterit (ut docetur postea) pro convictis habebuntur, totumque damnum compenfandum fuerit. Quod autem damnum scrupis datum nonnisi dimidio æstimetur, cum tamen id, quò refertur, gravius multetur; observa à regula communi hic exceptionem dari.
units.tr: {1} Although in the translation of the first clause I depart from the syntax of the Talmudists, the context sufficiently supports my rendering. Furthermore, so that all these matters and similar ones may be understood, and need not be repeated and pressed again and again, I now warn the reader more fully. In assessing the damage inflicted, one must carefully distinguish whether it proceeds from the animal in so far as it is convicted, that is, one that is accustomed to do such harm and is known for it, or whether it is inflicted by the same animal in so far as it does not usually harm in this way (or whether it causes some damage through an intervening medium), for the same animal often does harm in this manner, yet in this way it does harm only by chance and unexpectedly. As in the present case concerning the foot, it is established that it commonly tramples whatever lies in its path. But if perhaps an animal, walking, kicks loose pebbles from the pavement with its feet, because of their roundness and slipperiness, and these break some vessel, we shall say that this happens by chance. Therefore, a man must take care that he does not trample what lies in his path, and so damage caused by his carelessness is to be made good in full. But if pebbles thrown up by its walking break a glass that lies in the way, half the damage is to be repaid, because a man is not bound to take such anxious precautions against these accidents, since he cannot foresee chance events, nor can he always avert such mishaps by anxious care. If these points are applied to what follows, according to the diversity of the cases, everything will be plain. Add only this (of which something was also said above): animals are innocent with regard to this or that action, that is, they do not usually perform such actions, and therefore if in this way they cause damage, they oblige the owner to pay half the damage; but these same animals may be rendered convicted with regard to the same actions, that is, be regarded as those that usually harm in these ways. For a quadruped that kicks, if it is established to have done harm in this way several times, will then be held to be a kicker, and unless it is kept under guard, its owner will be liable for the whole damage. Thus, when an animal, or its tooth, foot, and so on, is counted among the innocent with respect to various actions, if it is established to have done harm by these actions several times (as will be taught later), it will be held to be convicted, and the whole damage must be made good. But that damage caused by pebbles is assessed at only half, although the matter to which it is referred is punished more severely, observe that here an exception is made to the general rule.

units.la: Secundum Maimon. t.4. l.1. c.2. §.2. כל קולדס כלא חוץ מזרות המכוון מתח רגלי הבהמה כשעת הילוכה, Omne consectarium leges principii (quò revocatur) sequitur: exceptis scrupis disjectis è vestigiis pecudis, quum incedit. Alias pede datum damnum in solidum præstatur. Modò quod Mifna dicit כדרכם, pro more suo, cum Maimon. duo continere statuamus. ut pecus ita agat, quomodo semper vel ut plurimum agere solet; ut etiam, fine interventu alicujus medii, ab illa proficiscatur actio. 2 In sequentibus autem mirari nolito, pecudem conculcantem (id est, iteratò calcantem) majori domini sui periculo obvia frangere, quam de gallo gallinaceo pedibus suis rei alicui infultante decernit Mifna: licet enim opera videantur similia, datum damnum ideo diversimodè compensatur, quia pecudis est pedibus conculcare; sed gallinaceus insilire quidem, at insultare non solet. Ideoque dominus illius ea in parte curam gerere debebat; quod in gallinaceo hac in re non requiritur, nisi hac in parte vitii convincatur, vel potius convictus fit. Non desunt tamen, qui סרו, insultantem esse negant; & Maimonides hic præit, qui inquit, מיפסור כרגלי כפר, qui exterit
units.tr: According to Maimonides, vol. 4, bk. 1, ch. 2, §2 [כל קולדס כלא חוץ מזרות המכוון מתח רגלי הבהמה כשעת הילוכה]: Every consequence follows the law of its principle (to which it is traced back), except stones scattered from the hoofprints of an animal as it walks. Otherwise, damage done by a foot is made good in full. Only, when the Mishnah says "according to their custom" [כדרכם], "in its usual way," we must hold that it contains two things, as Maimonides does: that the animal acts as it always or usually acts, and that the action proceeds from it without the intervention of any intermediary. 2 In what follows, however, do not be surprised that an animal that tramples (that is, treads again and again) breaks what lies in its way at greater peril to its owner than the Mishnah decides for a cock that kicks at something with its feet. For although the acts seem similar, the damage is compensated differently because it belongs to a beast to trample with its feet, whereas a cock usually leaps up but does not kick. Therefore its owner ought to take care in that respect, which is not required of the cock in this matter unless it is convicted, or rather becomes convicted, of this fault. Nevertheless, there are some who deny that the word [סרו], "kicking," applies, and Maimonides leads the way here, saying [מיפסור כרגלי כפר], "one who tramples."

units.la: 2 Maimon. t.4. l.1. c.2. §.2. terit sive effodit pedibus suis terram. Ita conspicua est inter illam pecudis, & hujus gallinacei actionem differentia: verum multa subsequens minor est, quam ut damno conveniat, quod ab eo datur, qui sic laedere consuevit: & sane hoc gallinaceorum omnium est, quod Maimonides describit.
units.tr: 2 Maimonides, vol. 4, bk. 1, ch. 2, §2: "one who tramples, or digs up the earth with his feet" [מיפסור כרגלי כפר]. Thus the difference between the action of that animal and this cock is clearly visible. Yet the many subsequent [actions] are too minor to count as the damage given by one who is accustomed to harm in this way, and indeed this is what Maimonides describes for all cocks.

units.la: Caeterum non in omnibus hanc Mishnam cum Romanis legibus convenire docet passim ff. Si quadrupes, & quae inde e l.1, §. 9. ad Mishnam primam produxi. Hactenus tamen conveniunt (de aliis actum in superioribus) quod non ea tantum quae primo laedunt multae subjiciantur; sed etiam quae alterius interventu damnum inferunt. Vt ff. Si quadrupes, l. 1. §. 8. Si alia quadrupes aliam concitavit, ut damnum daret, ejus quae concitavit nomine agendum est. quem paragraphum si quis cum jam memorato contulerit, latiorem convenientiam facile eruet. [Hebrew text, two columns, not transcribed in full]
units.tr: Moreover, that this Mishnah does not agree in all respects with the Roman laws, I show throughout the Digest, title Si quadrupes, and what follows from it, and I have brought it forward to the first Mishnah from law 1, §9. Nevertheless, in this they agree (I have treated the others above): that liability attaches not only to multiple [animals] that inflict the harm directly, but also to those that cause damage through the intervention of another. For example, Digest, title Si quadrupes, law 1, §8: If one quadruped sets on another so that it does damage, the action lies against the one that set it on. Anyone who compares this paragraph with the one already cited will easily discover a wider agreement. [Hebrew text, two columns, not transcribed in full]

units.la: §. 2. Qui dens convictus est, in eo quod sibi convenit comedendo? Pecus convicta est in edendis fructibus & herbis. Si ergo arrodat vestem aut vasa, dimidium damni praestatur. Quo casu haec intelligenda sunt? Si ea in fundo lapsi fiant; at si in loco publico, dominus liber est. Si bestia inde commodi percepit, redditur quantum commodi percepit. Quomodo redditur quantum commodi percepit? Si e media platea edit, quantum emolumenti percepit, redditur; si e platea lateribus, reependitur quantum damni intulit: si e projectura taberna, quantum emolumenti percepit: si ex ipsa taberna, quantum jactura intulit, rependitur.
units.tr: §2. What tooth is convicted? In that it eats what suits it. A beast is convicted of eating fruits and herbs. If therefore it gnaws a garment or vessels, half the damage is paid. In what case are these things understood? If they happen on private land; but if in a public place, the owner is free. If the beast gained some advantage from it, it pays back as much advantage as it gained. How is it paid back, as much as it gained? If it eats from the middle of the street, as much gain as it obtained is paid back; if from the side of the street, as much damage as it caused is paid; if from the projecting shop front, as much gain as it obtained; if from the shop itself, as much loss as it caused is paid back.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Hæc verba, si ea in fundo Læsi, non referuntur ad arrosas vestes, &c. sed ad priora: quia cum moris sit in publico vestes & vasa ad tempus certis de causis collocare, æquum non est ut ea lædens absolvatur. At fruges similiaque lædens, nonnisi in loco læsi tenetur; si nimirum istic læsa fuerint. nam (inquiunt) Exod. 22. 5. legimus, quod pascat in agro alterius: ubi alterius, non publico, reperitur. Nihilominus si bestia inde commodū percepit, restitutionem urgent: ita tamen ut hæc distinguant, quantum commodi sive emolumenti; & quantum damni. Exempli gratia, asinus comederit decem libras dactylorum, &c. ipsius dominus nonnisi quantum commodi percepit, rependere tenebitur, sive decem hordei aut dactylorum libras, vel potius eorum pretium: quia emolumentum e pabulo pecoris comedentis æstimatur. quinetiam pretium tertia parte minus, quam vulgò in foro decem istæ libræ venderentur, rependet. Si verò quantum damni dederat, solveret; decem dactylorum libras æquare deberet. Et quidem posteriori modo satisfaciet, quum bos suus e platea lateribus, ubi domus sint, quædam edulia decerpserit: nam latera ista ædibus contigua, veluti privatorum, quorum sunt ædes, loca censentur. quod enarrat Gemara, הכלב de jumento quod relicta platea progressum consistit in platea lateribus: sed quamvis caput etiam suum deflecteret ad latera, & in platea permanens e lateribus decerperet; non ita teneretur tamen dominus. Ut concludam hanc Misnam. Quicquid sit de reliquo, publicorum & privatorum locorum discrimen etiam aliquod facit l. Qui foveas. 28. D. Ad leg. Aquiliam: quamvis non eo modo, quem in Misna nostra vidimus.
units.tr: These words, if they fall into the field of the injured party, do not refer to the soiled garments, etc., but to what goes before. Since it is customary to set out garments and vessels in a public place for a time, for certain reasons, it is not fair that the one who causes the damage should be acquitted. But one who damages crops and the like is liable only in the place of the injured party, if the damage was in fact done there. For (they say) we read in Exod. 22.5 that it feeds in the field of another, where another's is found, not public. Nevertheless, if the beast has obtained a benefit from it, they insist on restitution, though they distinguish between the amount of the benefit or gain and the amount of the loss. For example, if a donkey has eaten ten pounds of dates, its owner will be bound to repay only the amount of benefit obtained, whether ten pounds of barley or dates, or rather their price, since the gain is valued from the fodder of the animal that eats it. Indeed he will repay the price at a third less than those ten pounds would commonly sell for in the market. If, however, he had to pay the amount of the damage, he would have to make up ten pounds of dates. He will satisfy in the latter manner when his ox has plucked some food from the side of the street where there are houses, for those sides adjoining the buildings, as belonging to the private persons whose houses they are, are counted as their places. The Gemara relates this of a beast [הכלב] which, having left the street, stands in the side of the street, but although it might also turn its head to the sides and, remaining in the street, pluck from the sides, the owner is not nevertheless bound. To conclude this Mishnah: whatever be the rest, the distinction between public and private places also makes some difference in l. Qui foveas, 28 D. Ad leg. Aquiliam, although not in the same way as we have seen in our Mishnah.

units.la: 1 Hæc verba, si ea in fundo Læsi, non referuntur ad arrosas vestes, &c.
units.tr: 1 These words, if they fall into the field of the injured party, do not refer to the soiled garments, etc.

units.la: {Hebrew block, left column; copied as printed:} הכלב והגרי שקפצו טלאש הגג וסכרו את הכלים משלם נוק שלם םפני םהן םוערין הכלב שנטל חורה והלך לגריש אכל חורה והוליק הגריש על החורה םשלם נוק שלם ועל הגריש םשלם חצי נוק ז
units.tr: The dog and the kid that jumped on the roof-ridge and broke the vessels pay full damages; the dog that took a beam and went to the goat, ate the beam and set the goat on fire, pays full damages, and for the goat half damages. [הכלב והגרי שקפצו טלאש הגג וסכרו את הכלים משלם נוק שלם םפני םהן םוערין הכלב שנטל חורה והלך לגריש אכל חורה והוליק הגריש על החורה םשלם נוק שלם ועל הגריש םשלם חצי נוק]

units.la: Si canis & hædus è tecti fastigio desilientes confringant vasa, totum damnum præstatur: quia convicti censentur. Si canis abrepta placenta tosta in segetum metâ ascendens, placentam comedat & metam incendat, ob placentam totum damnum reprenditur; ob metam dimidium damni præstatur.
units.tr: If a dog and a kid, leaping down from the ridge of a roof, break vessels, the whole damage is paid, because they are deemed to have been warned. If a dog, snatching a toasted cake, climbs onto a stack of grain, eats the cake and sets the stack on fire, it pays full damages for the cake and half damages for the stack.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Contestati censentur canis & hædus; quia omnes norunt eos saltare & rebus multis insilire: ideoque eos sub custodia habendos, omnibus etiam constat. Si ergo ita lædant, rependendum totum damnum: nam dominorum incuria datur. Consentit Plato de leg. l. 11. cum jubet, Ἐαὰν ὑπὸ ζύγον ἢ ἵππον ἢ κύων ἢ ὗ τῶν ἄλλων θρεμμάτων σὺν πῇ ὗ τῶν πλλας, ᾗ πῶς τὰ ἐκλυ-σαν τῷ βλάβλω, Si jumentum, velequus, vel canis, aut aliud ex iis quæ educantur rem proximi lædat, dominus pariter damnum rependat. Verum de sequentibus Mișnæ verbis dubitari potest, ubi placenta tosta metam incendere dicitur; quî hoc fieri queat? Respondeo è Maimon. quia primâ ipsi adhærent. Et deinde, quî major multa in placenta compensanda, quam in frugum meta constituatur: si quidem hic dimidii, ibi totius tenetur? Satisfacit Obadia de Bartenora: quia est veluti lapillus ejus: de quo constitutio tradit, dominum solvere dimidium damni. Sensus est, Quemadmodum si pecudis pede disjecti lapilli aliquid diffringant, dimidii obligatur dominus; quia id more consueto non fit, sed casu scrupi excutiuntur: sic canis quidem placentam edere solet, ideoq; id præcavendum; cavendum; sed meta casu accenditur, cum ignis scintilla placentæ adhæret, ut casus sit fortuitus, cujus satagere non solemus. Hæc causa est cur dimidium tantummodo exigatur; licet tantum damnum majori & seueriori pœna arcendum videri queat. Quod si jus civile Romanorum spectes, leges sunt mitiores si casu fortuito incendium excitetur: utpote quæ in locato & conducto dolum & negligentiam, non etiam casum fortuitum præstari jubeant. Ea de re videatur lex 28. C. de locato & conducto. In judicio tam locati, quam conducti, dolum & custodiam, non etiam casum, cui resisti non potest, venire constat. Et licet hic addat Accursius, Et hoc nisi ex pacto speciali; tamen aliam sententiam sibi quis deprehendere forte videatur, l. Si quis domum, §. 3. t. locati conducti, Digest. 1.19. Si colonis prædiorum lege locationis, ut innocentem ignem habeant, denunciatum sit: si quidem fortuitus casus incendii causam intulerit, non præstabit periculum locator. Verum hic disputare nolo, qui jurisconsulti conciliari debeant; dolum & negligentiam eos à casu fortuito distinxisse (etsi non eodem modo) nobis sufficiat. איזה הוא האם ואיזהו הוא מועד מועד כל שהעידו בו של שה ימים והם משיחזיר בו שלשה ימים רבוי רבייהו דרך רבי מאיר אומר מועד שהעידו בו שלשה פעמים והם כל שיהו החינוקות ממשמשין בו ואינו נוגח
units.tr: The dog and the kid are deemed to have been warned, since everyone knows that they leap and jump onto many things; that they must therefore be kept under guard is known to all. If, then, they damage in this way, the whole damage must be repaid, for it arises from the carelessness of the owners. Plato agrees in the Laws, book 11, where he orders: "If a yoke-ox, a horse, a dog, or any other of the animals that are reared damages the property of a neighbour, the owner likewise shall make good the damage" [ἐὰν ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ἢ ἵππον ἢ κύων ἢ τῶν ἄλλων θρεμμάτων τις τὸν πλησίον βλάπτῃ, ὁ κύριος ὁμοίως τὴν βλάβην ἀποτινέτω]. But a doubt may be raised about the following words of the Mishnah, where the toasted cake is said to set fire to the stack: how can this happen? I answer, following Maimonides, because it clings to it at first. Again, why is more to be compensated for the cake than for the stack of grain, since here half is owed and there the whole? Obadiah of Bertinoro satisfies this: because the cake is as it were a little stone of the beast's, concerning which the regulation says that the owner pays half the damage. The sense is this: just as, if small stones kicked up by the foot of a beast break something, the owner is bound for half, because this does not happen in the usual way but by chance, when sparks are knocked out, so the dog is accustomed to eat cakes, and so this must be guarded against; but the stack catches fire by chance, when a spark of fire clings to the cake, so that the accident is fortuitous, and we are not accustomed to take care of such things. This is why only half is required, though the damage might seem to be one to be averted by a greater and more severe penalty. If you look to the civil law of the Romans, the laws are milder if a fire breaks out by fortuitous chance, since in lease and hire they order that fraud and negligence, but not accidental chance, be made good. On this see the law 28 C. de locato et conducto: "In a lawsuit both of the lessee and of the hirer, it is agreed that fraud and custody, but not accident which cannot be resisted, come into play." And although Accursius adds here, "And this unless by special agreement," yet someone may perhaps find another opinion in himself, l. Si quis domum, §3, t. locati conducti, Digest 1.19: "If it has been announced to the tenants of farms under the terms of the lease that they are to keep fire harmless, and a fortuitous accident has caused the fire, the lessor will not bear the risk." But I do not wish to dispute here which jurists are to be reconciled; that they distinguished fraud and negligence from fortuitous chance (though not in the same way) is enough for us. [איזה הוא האם ואיזהו הוא מועד מועד כל שהעידו בו של שה ימים והם משיחזיר בו שלשה ימים רבוי רבייהו דרך רבי מאיר אומר מועד שהעידו בו שלשה פעמים והם כל שיהו החינוקות ממשמשין בו ואינו נוגח] Which is the innocent ox, and which the one that is habitually goring? Whatever has been testified against for three days, and they have again returned it for three days, the words of Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Meir says: habitual is what has been testified against three times, and whatever the children handle and it does not gore.

units.la: Quodnam est animal innocens; quodnam vero convictum? Convictum, adversus quodcunq; tres dies testimonia proferuntur; innocens autem habetur, quum per tres dies abstinuit: ut quidem sentit D. Iudas. Doctor Meir inquit, Convictum est, contra quod tribus vicibus testati sunt; innocens, quodcunque à pueris palpatum non ferit cornu.
units.tr: What is the innocent animal, and what the convicted one? The convicted one is that against which testimony is brought for three days; the innocent one is held to be that which has abstained for three days, as Rabbi Judah indeed thinks. Rabbi Meir says: convicted is that against which they have testified on three occasions; innocent is whatever the boys have handled and it does not gore with its horn.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ᾿ Tres dies continuos requirit; nec sufficit, si tribus diebus bovem petulcum fuisse, domino denuncient: ubi, exempli gratia, primo mensis die, & ultimo, ac deinde semel tertio mense cornu feriit. Illa sententia ex Abæi verbis liquet, [Hebrew], Heri semel, denuo nudiusfertius, & pridie tertio, nec asservavit eum dominus ejus; si perrexerint cornu ferire quarta vice: supple (nam oratio imperfecta est & obscura) tenebitur dominus. Abæus hic procul dubio ad ῾f.36. c.21. Exodi respexit; ubi habetur, [Hebrew], ab heri nudius-tertius: quæ verba multo melius Chaldæus enarravit, [Hebrew],inde ab hesterno die & retro.Sed Abæo [Hebrew] est heri, [Hebrew] nudiustertius, [Hebrew] pridie istius nudiustertius: idq; ut tres continuos dies designet, quibus singulis si semel aut bis aut sæpius ferierit, bos petulcus habeatur. Idem liquet è D. Simeonis verbis, quum ait, Sapientes [Hebrew], non dixerunt tres dies, nisi ob regressum: sensus est, ideo istorum dierum numerum exigi, quia bos [Hebrew], sua integritati restitutus & a vitio isto liberatus non censetur, nisi diebus istis elapsis, quibus cornu non ferierit. atqui videtur, bovem istum tum demum [Hebrew], integrum censeri, si tribus diebus continuis a isto vitio abstinuerit. Sententiam Simeonis non defendo: tantum [Hebrew] esse tres dies continuos,& hinc conjicimus.Præterea quæstio quæ in Gemara proponitur idem ostendit. [Hebrew] Quæsitum inter ipsos, Tres qui leguntur dies, num ad testandum de eo quod lex ait Exod.21.῾.36.(bovem petulcum fuisse ab heri & nudiustertius;) an vero ad solemniter denunciandum viro (bovem petulcum esse,requiruntur dies tres?) Quorsum per illam quæst.tenditur? Quum tres testium ordines uno die accedunt, si dicas, Ad testandum de eo quod lex ait(Exo.21.36.in Misna tres dies requiruntur,)testes testantur (per tres dies bovem cornu laesisse;) quod si dicas, Ad denunciandum viro adhibitis testibus (bovem petulcum esse, requiruntur dies tres, quia tribus distinctis diebus testes audiendi,) testium coetus non testatur (uno die, bovem tres dies obvia cornu laesisse.) Hinc constat Sapientes ad legem istam Exod. c.21. animum intendisse, quum trium dierum meminerunt: quos continuos esse nec intervalla admittere ipsi autumarunt, sicuti ex initio huius annotationis liquet.( quamvis legem non satis congruè exposuerint.) Porrò quod distinctionem generalem innocentis & convicti concernit; jam antea not.6.§.4.c.1. & hoc etiam c. de ea actum: verum hic tantum de bove cornupeta & non cornupeta.
units.tr: The Gemara requires three continuous days. It is not enough if the ox was goring on three days, and they report this to the owner, for example on the first day of the month and on the last, and then once in the third month. That opinion is clear from the words of Abaeus: Yesterday once, and again the day before yesterday, and the day before that, and his owner did not keep him; if he goes on goring a fourth time, supply (for the sentence is incomplete and obscure) that the owner will be liable. Abaeus here undoubtedly had in mind Exodus 21:36, where it reads from yesterday and the day before. The Chaldee paraphrast explained these words much better: from the previous day and back. But for Abaeus it is "yesterday," "the day before yesterday," and "the day before that," so that he designates three continuous days, and if on each of them the ox gored once, twice, or more often, it is regarded as a goring ox. The same is clear from the words of Rabbi Simeon, when he says: The Sages said "three days" only because of the return. The sense is that this number of days is required because the ox is not regarded as restored to its integrity and freed from this vice unless those days have passed in which it did not gore. Indeed it seems that the ox is then regarded as whole only if it has refrained from this vice for three continuous days. I do not defend Simeon's opinion, but it is clear that the three days must be continuous, and from this we conjecture so. Moreover, the question that is raised in the Gemara shows the same thing. It was asked among them: The three days that are read, are they required for testifying to what the law says (Exod. 21:36, that the ox was a goring ox from yesterday and the day before yesterday), or for solemnly declaring to the man (that the ox is goring, are three days required?). To what does that question tend? When three groups of witnesses come on one day, if you say, "For testifying to what the law says" (in the Mishnah three days are required, Exod. 21:36), the witnesses testify (that over three days the ox gored); but if you say, "For declaring to the man, with witnesses present" (that the ox is goring, three days are required, because the witnesses must be heard on three distinct days), the company of witnesses does not testify (that on one day the ox gored on three days). From this it is established that the Sages turned their attention to that law in Exodus 21 when they spoke of three days; they themselves held that these must be continuous and admit no intervals, as is clear from the beginning of this annotation, although they did not expound the law quite suitably. Furthermore, as to the general distinction between an innocent and a convicted animal, I have already noted it above, at note 6, §4, chapter 1, and treated it in that chapter; but here I speak only of the goring and non-goring ox.

units.la: 2 Majoris fortasse momenti (quandoquidem in superioribus prava scripturae expositio praestruitur) cum in Misna diversae Doctorum sententiae proponuntur, inquirere cujusnam obtineat: Id in Gemara definit Magister Nachman: in descriptione bovis convicti, sequendum D.Judam; bovis innocentis autem, Doctorem Meirum. Idque ob D. Jofes eatenus iis assentientis authoritate, vel potius rationes: quemadmodum subjungit, Mihi secundum D.Iofen videtur, nam D.Iofe rationes habet enim idem valet ac rationes & argumenta ejus: uti habet Glossa marginalis. De legibus Romanis, sub finem cap.1. annotationes consule.
units.tr: 2. Perhaps of greater importance (since in the preceding the faulty exposition of Scripture was set up), when different opinions of the teachers are set out in the Mishnah, is to inquire which of them prevails. The Gemara settles this: Master Nachman says that in the description of the convicted ox, Doctor Judah is to be followed, and for the innocent ox, Doctor Meir. And this is on account of the authority of Rabbi Jose, who agrees with them so far, or rather on account of his reasons, as the marginal Gloss adds: In my view, according to Rabbi Jose, for Rabbi Jose has reasons, for the word here means the same as his reasons and arguments. On the Roman laws, consult the annotations at the end of chapter 1.

units.la: Bos laedentis in fundo laesi, qui se habet? Si cornu feriat, impellat, mordeat, incubat, vel recalcitret, in loco publico; dimidium damni compensatur: at in fundo laesi, D.Tarphon exigit totius damni compensa-
units.tr: If an ox of a tenant of a damaged field gores, pushes, bites, lies down, or kicks, what is the position? If in a public place, half the damage is compensated; but in the damaged man's field, Doctor Tarphon requires full compensation of the whole damage; the sages wish half the damage to be made good.

units.la: אומרים חצי נזק אטר לחם רבי טרפון ופרה אם במקום שהקל על השן ועל הרגל ברשות הרבים שהוא פטור החמיר עליהם ברשות הניזק לשלם נזק טלם מקום ס שהחמיר על הקרן ברשות הרבים לשלם חצי נזק אינו דין שנחמיר עליה ברשות הניזק לשלם נזק שלם אמרו לו דיו לבא מן הדין להיות כנרן מה ברשות הרבים חצי נזק אף ברשות הניזק חצי נזק אמר להם אני לא אדון קרן מקרן אני אדון קרן סרגל ומה אם בקו' שהקל על השן ועל הרגל ברשות הרבים החמיר בקרן מקום שהחמיר על השן ועל הרגל ברשו' הניזוק אינו דין שנחמיר בקרן אמרו לו דיו לבא מן הדין להיות כנזון מה ברשות הרבים חצי נזק אף ברשות הניזק tionem ; sapientes vero dimidium damni praestari volunt. Quibus in hunc modum Doct. Tarphon, Quid quaeso? Si ubi lex mitior est pro dente & pede in loco publico, quum dominus liber est, contra eosdem durior sit in fundo lasi, ut totum damnum compensetur ; nonne ubi gravior est quod ad cornu in loco publico, ut damni dimidium compensetur ; aequum est ut quod ad ipsum graviores simus in fundo lasi, quo totius damni pretium solvatur ? Illi contra, Sufficit ei quod argumentando consequitur, ut sese habeat quemadmodum illud unde argumentamur. itaque uti in loco publico dimidium damni, ita etiam in loco lasi dimidium compensatur. Respondit illis, Ego non concludo illud de cornu e cornu; de cornu e pedis jure concludo. Quid quaeso? Si ubi lex in dentem & pedem mitior est in loco publico, in cornu est gravior; nonne ubi gravior est in dentem & pedem in fundo lasi, aequum est ut in cornu graviores simus? Regesserunt, Sufficit ei quod argumentando consequitur, ut sese habeat quemadmodum illud unde argumentamur. itaque uti in loco publico dimidium damni, ita etiam in loco lasi dimidium compensatur.
units.tr: compensated; but the sages want half the damage made good. To which Doctor Tarphon replied in this manner: What, I ask? If where the law is milder for tooth and foot in a public place, when the owner is free, against the same owner it is harsher in the damaged man's property, so that the whole damage is compensated; should it not be that where it is more severe regarding the horn in a public place, so that half the damage is compensated, it is fair that we should be more severe with it in the damaged man's property, so that the full price is paid? They replied to him: It suffices that he infers, that it should be as that from which we argue: so just as in a public place half the damage, so also in the damaged man's place half is compensated. He answered them: I do not conclude about horn from horn; I conclude about horn from tooth and foot. What, I ask? If where the law is milder for tooth and foot in a public place, it is harsher for horn; should it not be that where it is harsher for tooth and foot on the injured man's property, it is fair that we be harsher for horn? They replied: It suffices that he infers, that it should be as that from which we argue: so just as in a public place half the damage, so also in the injured man's place half is compensated.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Magni interest, quo quisque in loco noceat sive damnum inferat: ut ea propter tria loca distinguantur: locus publicus; locus privatus, qui duplex est, vel ejus cujus bos laedit; vel ejus cujus bona laeduntur. Itaque hic ventilatur injuria vel potius damnum quod quis in fundo suo ab alterius bove patitur: praemissa prius generali sententia de bove in loco publico laedente: idque ut quod hac de re c.1. Mishn.4. propositum erat, explicaretur plenius. ² Et cum hic de cornu aliisque agatur, in memoriam revocandum quod initio libri de damnorum fontibus, & eorum derivatis propositum fuit. Pariter enim in cornu se res habet: ubi damnum cornu datum vocatur אב sive fons & origo; quo deinde revocantur haec in hac Mishna recensita, impellere, mordere, incumbere, recalcitrare. De quibus observanda regula e libro praeceptorum magno ad praec. affirm. 66. Si pater (sive fons) convictus fit; derivata etiam convicta: si vero ille habeatur innocuus; generationes (sive quae inde derivantur eoq; referuntur) similiter se habent. Item, Omnis generatio ut pater suus (id est, derivatum fontis sui leges & jura in compensatione imitatur) exceptis scrupis, qui excutiuntur e vestigiis jumenti dum incedit. (de his consule c.2. Mishnam 1.) ³ At de fonte & derivatis in cornu non conveniunt doctores; siquidem D. Tarphon argumento ab impari caeteros impugnat. Haec ejus mens: si damnum dente & pede datum in privato alterius fundo, totum compensatur; ergo etiam damnum cornu ibidem datum. Ratio est, quia damnum dente & pede datum alibi, leviori legi subjicitur, quam si cornu laederet, (in loco enim publico ne dimidium quidem damni in ipso compensatur, ut constat e Mishn. 2.) atqui conveniens videtur, ut si quod alibi liberum est, in loco privato perfecta
units.tr: ¹ It matters greatly in what place a man harms or causes loss, so three places are distinguished: a public place; a private place, which is twofold, either that of the owner whose ox does the injury or that of the owner whose goods are harmed. Here, then, is discussed the wrong, or rather the loss, that someone suffers on his own land from another's ox. The general rule about an ox injuring in a public place is first set out, so that what was proposed on this matter in chapter 1, Mishnah 4, may be explained more fully. ² And since the discussion here concerns the horn and the other injuries, we must recall what was proposed at the beginning of the book about the sources of damages and their derivatives. The same holds for the horn: where damage done by the horn is called av [אב], that is, source and origin, and to it are referred the things listed in this Mishnah: to push, to bite, to lean on, to kick. For these the rule to be observed is from the great book of precepts, on positive precept 66: If the father (that is, the source) is convicted, the derivatives are convicted too; but if he is held innocent, the generations (that is, what derives from him and is referred to him) stand similarly. Likewise: every generation is like its father (that is, the derivative imitates the laws and rights of its source in compensation), except the scrapings, which are shaken off from the feet of a beast as it walks. (On these consult chapter 2, Mishnah 1.) ³ But the teachers do not agree about the source and derivatives in the case of the horn. For Rabbi Tarphon attacks the others with an argument from the lesser. His thought is this: if damage done by tooth and foot on another's private land is wholly compensated, then damage done there by the horn is too. The reason is that damage done by tooth and foot elsewhere is subject to a lighter law than if the horn had injured (for in a public place not even half the damage is compensated for that very thing, as appears from Mishnah 2). Yet it seems fitting that what is free elsewhere should, in a private place, be punished with full compensation, and what elsewhere is restrained by half compensation should, in the territory of another private owner, be punished by full compensation.

units.la: ¹ Magni interest … ² Et cum hic de cornu … ³ At de fonte … perfecta compensatione mulctatur; id quod alibi dimidia compensatione coercetur, in dioecesi alterius privati tota compensatione mulctetur. Sed excipiunt דין לבן מן כרין, Sufficit ei quod e judicio provenit, ut sit tanquam id quod in judicio praestitur. Hoc sibi volunt, in argumentando (judicare, judicium, &c. apud Judaeorum logicos ad argumenta & argumentationes transferuntur: ut palam fecimus in Halichoth Olam: quem librum Latine reddentes publici juris non ita pridem fecimus) sensus inquam est, in argumentando, sive in argumento a minori sufficere, ut vel gravissimum tantum quod in minori comparato invenitur, etiam in majori inveniatur: vel (quod hic locum habet) in comparato majori duorum membrorum, posterius membrum aequetur priori, unde vis argumenti profluit. Ita quum is, cujus bos in loco publico cornu ferit, dimidii damni teneatur; sufficere si cum respectu loci privati pari poena mulctemus. Nam hic in majori comparato duo sunt membra: quum bos cornu nocet in loco publico, dimidium damni rependitur; ita quoque cum in privato alterius loco damnum ea ratione dabit, altera comparationis pars etiam duo membra continet; quum bos dente damnum infert in loco publico, absolvitur; in loco privato idem si faciat, totum damnum compensatur. Sed quia etiam ex priori membro in superiori comparationis parte argumentatio dependet; ideo amplius non concludunt, quam ibi reperitur. Nihilo secius instat ille, se non concludere e cornu, quod cum ob cornu in loco publico dominus bovis dimidii damni obligetur, in privato loco gravior statuenda sit mulcta; sed suum argumentum a pede & dente procedere. Cui idem illud regerunt, Sufficit ei quod argumentando, &c. Etenim licet id non exprimatur; tamen cornu in loco publico nocens, est argumentationis fundamentum, atque hic spectatur inprimis. Ne quis ignorantiae Doctores istos insimulet, ac si non satisfacerent; sed ubi quo argumentum solverent non haberent, idem absque ullo fundamento occinerent: res penitius examinanda venit. קל ומר in levi & gravi: id est, in argumento ab impari (sive à minori, sive à majori ducatur ratio, ומר קל nuncupant) datur vulgò exceptio illa, quam in praecedentibus jam vidimus: sufficere ei quod concluditur, ut fundamento à quo argumentamur æquetur. Exceptionem e c.12. Num. confirmant. siquidem cum, postquā Maria peccasset, Deus à minori arcendam castris probaret, quod in antecedenti erat non auxit; sed idem istud temporis spatium exegit, ¥f. 14. Si pater ejus sputum insputuisset in faciem ejus (i. iratum se ei praebuisset) annon rubore suffusa esset (i. sese subduceret) septem dies? secluditor septem dies extra castra. Hic videtis, inquiunt, quamvis Deus patre terreno multo major sit; solos septem dies illius separationi designatos fuisse. Attamen de exceptione ista disputant, quando locum habeat. Sapientes, quos vocant, ubique ei locum esse arbitrantur: at D. Tarphon eo tantum casu, quum concludendum antea certum non fuit; si vero quod ab impari probandum est, jam satis in confesso sit, exceptionem non admittendam: etenim exceptio ספרך קל ומר, irritum faceret argumentum à minori. Ita hoc loco, quandoquidem constabat satis, dimidium damnum restituendum; quid attinebat argumento ab impari id ipsum confirmare? sic hoc argumentum plane supervacuum esset. Hoc ergo est quod sibi voluerunt Sapientes, quum exceptionem repeterent: q.d. Tu quidem hoc casu eam dari negas; at nos ubiq; eam admittendam censemus: ideoq; eam ingeminamus. Ex tota hac disputatione liquet, quanto conatu inter locum publicum & privatum in damnis distinguant. At Dig. l. 9. t. 1. §. 1. convenienter ultimis Misnæ verbis, lex generalis absque locorum distinctione proponitur. Si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicetur, actio ex lege duodecim tabularum descendit. quae lex voluit .... aut dari id quod nocuit, aut aestimationem noxiae offerri. ו׳ ו׳ אִם סוֹעֵר לְעוֹלָם בֵּין סוּעַ בֵּין מַזִּיק בֵּין עַר בֵּין יִשֵּׁן סִמְאֵ אֶת עֵין חֲבִירוֹ וּשְׁבַר אֶת הַכֵּלִים מְשֻׁלָּם נְזַק שָׁלֵם וּ
units.tr: ¹ It makes a great difference … ² And when here he speaks of the horn … ³ But as to the spring … he is fined the full compensation. What elsewhere is restrained by half compensation, on another private person's land is fined by full compensation. But they object: It suffices for him that it comes from judgment, so that it is as if it were given in judgment [דין לבן מן כרין]. What they mean by this, in argumentation (the words judge, judgment, and the like are used by the Jewish logicians of arguments and argumentations, as we made plain in the Halichoth Olam, which we lately made public by rendering it into Latin), is this, I say: in argumentation, or in an argument from the lesser, it suffices that whatever is found in the lesser compared case is also found in the greater; or (which is the point here) in a greater comparison of two members, the later member is made equal to the earlier, and from this the force of the argument flows. So when the owner of an ox that gores in a public place is liable for half the damage, it suffices that we fine him with the same penalty with respect to a private place. For here there are two members in the greater comparison: when an ox gores in a public place, half the damage is repaid; likewise when it does damage in another's private place by the same reasoning, the other part of the comparison also contains two members: when an ox inflicts damage with its teeth in a public place, it is acquitted; if it does the same in a private place, the whole damage is compensated. But since the argument also depends on the earlier member in the upper part of the comparison, they do not conclude more than is found there. Nevertheless, that opponent insists that he does not conclude from the horn that, since on account of the horn in a public place the owner of the ox is bound for half the damage, a heavier fine must be set in a private place; rather, that his argument proceeds from foot and tooth. To him they reply with the same thing: It suffices for him that by argument, &c. For although this is not expressed, nevertheless the ox that injures with its horn in a public place is the foundation of the argument, and this is chiefly what is regarded here. Let no one accuse these teachers of ignorance, as if they did not give satisfaction; but where they would not have had a way to resolve the matter, they would be repeating the same thing without any foundation: the matter has to be examined more deeply. In the rule [קל ומר] of light and heavy, that is, in an argument from the unequal (whether the reasoning is drawn from the lesser or from the greater, they call it קל ומר), that exception commonly given, which we have already seen in the preceding discussions, applies: it suffices for him that what is concluded is made equal to the foundation from which we argue. They confirm the exception from Numbers 12. For after Miriam had sinned, God, arguing from the lesser, proved that she should be shut out of the camp, and he did not enlarge what was in the preceding case, but required the same length of time: If her father had spat in her face (that is, had shown himself angry toward her) would she not be ashamed (that is, withdraw herself) for seven days? Let her be shut out of the camp for seven days. You see here, they say, that although God is much greater than an earthly father, only the seven days were appointed for her separation. Yet they dispute about this exception, as to when it applies. The wise men, as they are called, think it applies everywhere; but Rabbi Tarphon only in the case where the conclusion was not previously certain; but if what is to be proved from the unequal is already sufficiently granted, the exception is not to be admitted: for the exception [ספרך קל ומר] would make the argument from the lesser void. So here, since it was sufficiently established that half the damage must be restored, what was the point of confirming that very thing by an argument from the unequal? Thus this argument would be plainly superfluous. This, then, is what the wise men meant when they repeated the exception: as if to say, You indeed deny that it applies in this case; but we judge that it must be admitted everywhere, and therefore we repeat it. From this whole discussion it is clear with how much effort they distinguish between public and private place in matters of damage. But in Dig. 9.1.1, agreeing with the last words of the Mishnah, a general law is laid down without distinction of places: If a quadruped is said to have caused damage, the action arises from the law of the Twelve Tables, which wished either that what did the harm be given up, or that the estimated value of the harm be offered. [Mishnah: If a man, whether he be moving or stationary, whether awake or asleep, blinds the eye of his fellow and breaks his vessels, he pays full damages.] אִם סוֹעֵר לְעוֹלָם בֵּין סוּעַ בֵּין מַזִּיק בֵּין עַר בֵּין יִשֵּׁן סִמְאֵ אֶת עֵין חֲבִירוֹ וּשְׁבַר אֶת הַכֵּלִים מְשֻׁלָּם נְזַק שָׁלֵם

units.la: Homo semper contestatus ac convitius habetur; sive errore, sive destinata voluntate agat, sive denique vigilans, sive dormiens. Si excæcavit oculum socii sui, aut fregit vasa, totum damnum præstat.
units.tr: A man is always deemed to have been warned and is held liable, whether he acts through error or with settled intent, whether he is awake or asleep. If he blinds the eye of his companion or breaks his vessels, he makes full compensation for the whole loss.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Injustum quidem videtur, si error & scientia in damnis eodem loco habeantur. verum talis error hic consideratur, cujus culpa est penes eum qui damnum errore dedit. Nam si prohibere potuit quo minus errorem committeret, idem est ac si sciens peccasset. Quemadmodum colligitur è l.3.tit.4. lib.9. Digest. In omnibus noxalibus actionibus ubicunque scientia exigitur domini, sic accipienda est, si cum prohibere posset, non prohibuit. Ideoque Judæorum Magistri in Misna exponenda, cujus exemplo utuntur, qui secum cubantis oculum excæcavit dormiens. si quum alter dormiret ipse accesserit ut unà dormiret; quamvis in somno alterum læˈdat, tenetur: quia sese huic casui exponere non debuit. at si alteri posteaquam somno sopitus esset accedenti ut secum dormiret, oculum dormiens vitiet, non tenetur: ut qui alterius adventum in somno prævidere & præcavere non potuerit. Cæterum per מוּר, destinata voluntate agentem, quis designetur, docet oppositio, Exod.c.21. יףf.14. ubi מוּר opponitur casui fortuito, & explicatur vocc כשרמים, astu. unde liquet actionem isto verbo notatam patrari certo consilio & voluntate ac scientiâ. Unde Moses Albelda in c.21.Exod. in isto peccatore duo esse dicit: quod noverit quid agat; deinde pœnæ debitæ admoneatur. Similiter Isaac Karo requirit מחשבה, cogitationem; & מתן, moram. An admonitio requiratur, non disputabo; id constat, spectari in מוּר, ut non inopinato & incauto impetu peccet; sed sciens & præmeditatus.
units.tr: It seems unjust if error and knowledge are counted as equal in matters of damage. But the error considered here is one whose fault lies with the person who caused the damage through error. For if he could have prevented himself from making the mistake, it is the same as if he had sinned knowingly. This is gathered from Digest 9.4.3, In all noxal actions, wherever the knowledge of the owner is required, it is to be understood thus: if, when he could have prevented it, he did not prevent it. Accordingly, in explaining the Misnah, the Jewish masters, whose example they use, take the case of one who, while sleeping, blinds the eye of the man sleeping beside him. If he came to sleep beside the other while the other was asleep, he is liable, although he injures the other in his sleep, because he ought not to have exposed himself to this chance. But if, after the other had fallen asleep, he came to him to sleep beside him and in his sleep injured his eye, he is not liable, since he could not foresee and guard against the other's coming in his sleep. Moreover, what is meant by mur [מוּר], one acting with settled intent, the opposition shows in Exod. c.21. f.14, where mur is opposed to accidental chance, and is explained by the word kasherim [כשרמים], by guile. Whence it is clear that the action denoted by this word is done with deliberate purpose, will and knowledge. So Moses Albelda, on Exod. c.21, says that in such an offender there are two things: that he knew what he was doing, and then that he was warned of the penalty due. Similarly Isaac Karo requires mechashavah [מחשבה], thought, and matan [מתן], delay. Whether a warning is required, I shall not dispute; this much is agreed, that mur looks to whether a man sins not by a sudden and incautious impulse, but knowingly and with premeditation.
Chapter 36, Halakhah 1 [פרק ג״ו הלכי א.]
CHAP. III. §. I.

units.la: Si alicujus amphora loco publico deposita, veniat alius qui in eam impingens eandé frangat, liber ¹ est; & si eâ lædatur, istius cadi ² possessor, de ipsius læsione tenetur. Si frangatur cadus (sive amphora) in loco publico, alius autem ob aquæ lubricum ³ prolabatur, aut illius lædatur testis, possessor tenetur. D. Iudas inquit, Si ad ⁴ illa animum advertat, teneri; sin minus, liberum esse.
units.tr: If a jar of someone is placed in a public place, and another comes who, striking against it, breaks it, he is free; and if he is injured by it, the possessor of that jar is liable for the injury to him. If a jar is broken in a public place, and another slips on the slipperiness of the oil, or is hurt by the potsherds, the possessor is liable. Judah the Rabbi says: if he paid attention to these things, he is liable; but if not, he is free.
Notes

units.la: ¹ Liber est & absolvitur, qui vas confregit: cujus rationem his verbis exprimit Maimonides, [Hebrew text]. Hoc apud nos fundamenti instar est, non solere homines anxiè attendere ad vias: ideoque si veniens quispiam in eam (amphoram) impingat, liber est; nec dicemus, Attendere debebas, ubi tu incederes. ² Vas, de quo sermo est, primò vocatur כד, deinde חבית, cum tamen de eodem vase agatur: quemadmodum etiam Gemara כד & חבית ejusdem notionis esse annotat; & quæstionem insuper movet, quare idem diversis nominibus exprimatur. Gemaræ verba hæc sunt, [Hebrew text], Cadus est habith. i. amphora Attica. (cadum & amphoram latius hic accipio, quam ubi præcisè distinctam mensuram notant.) Quorsum inde tenditur? (id est, quare duo nomina ponuntur?) Idfit ob emptionem & venditionem. Hæc verba cum obscuriora sint, ex additamentis illustranda. Sic ergo additamenta marginalia: [Hebrew text]
units.tr: ¹ He who broke the jar is free and acquitted. Maimonides gives the reason for this in these words: With us this is in the nature of a principle: people are not accustomed to watch their paths anxiously, so if someone coming along strikes against that jar, he is free; and we will not say, "You ought to have paid attention where you were walking." ² The vessel in question is first called כד [kad], then חבית [havit], although the same vessel is meant. The Gemara likewise notes that כד and חבית have the same meaning, and it raises the further question why the same thing is expressed by different names. The Gemara's words are these: Cadus is habith, that is, an Attic amphora. (I take cadus and amphora here more broadly than where they denote a precisely defined measure.) To what does this lead? (that is, why are two names given?) It concerns buying and selling. Since these words are rather obscure, they must be clarified by the additions. The marginal additions read as follows:

units.la: ריכי שאם התנה לתת לו כד והקנה לו בסודר ונתחייב הלוקח לתת דמים יכול הלוקח לומר לו אתן לך דמים אם לא תתן לי תכית דקרי לויה לחבירתו כדי לפי סהוא מוחוק ולא תולין בתר רוכא ולא אם התנה לתת לו תכית וכתן הלוקח דמים יכול לומר לו ולא תולין כתר רוכא ולא אתן לך לא תתן לי תכית תבירת לכדי תבירת ולא תולין כתר רוכא. המוכר לא אתן לך דמים מכד דקרי לכרד Ambo sunt necessaria: nam si quis pactus fuit se alteri daturum cadum, cui acquisitus sit per alam vestimenti, ita ut emptor pretium solvere teneatur; emptor dicere potest, pretium non solvam, nisi mihi metretam Atticam dederis, (quia Attica metreta, sive magna amphora etiam cadus vocatur.) quandoquidem ipse in possessione est. nec multitudinem sequimur. Quod si pactus sit, se illi daturum Atticam metretam, & emptor pretium solverit; huic venditor dicere potest, Nonnisi cadum tibi dabo (quia cadus etiam metreta vocatur.) nec multitudinem sequimur. Antequâ pergam, ne obscura obscuris declarari videantur, paucula in istis additamentis breviter attingenda. Vbi cadus sudario acquiri dicitur, repetenda ex Eliæ Tisbi, quæ de ritu isto annotavit.
units.tr: Both are necessary. For if someone agreed to give another a jar, and it was acquired by him through the corner of a garment, and the buyer was bound to pay the price, the buyer may say, "I will not pay the price unless you give me an Attic metretes" (since the Attic metretes, or large amphora, is also called cadus), because the seller is already in possession. Nor do we follow the majority. But if he agreed to give him an Attic metretes, and the buyer has paid the price, the seller may say to him, "I will give you only a cadus" (since cadus is also called metretes). Nor do we follow the majority. Before I go on, so that obscure things are not seen to be explained by obscure things, a few points in these additions must be touched on briefly. Where it is said that a jar is acquired by a cloth, the rite should be explained from what Elijah of Tishbi noted about it.

units.la: לוקחים שני עדים ומבקרים לפניהם לקיים כל דבר כונעים כנפי כגדיהם וה נקרא קנין פורר נגדו והמקבלים עליהם לקיים דברי תנחיים וכל אחד מהעדים פותם כנף
units.tr: The contracting parties take two witnesses, in whose presence they set out their terms. Then each of the witnesses spreads out the wing of his garment (for they wore loose clothing). Those who bound themselves to uphold the words of the Sages touched the wings of one another's garments. This act is called the acquisition of the wing, and it is the sign of their pledge.

units.la: Contrahentes inter se duos testes capiunt, coram quibus conditiones suas exponunt. Deinde unusquisque testium extendit alam vestimenti sui (laxas enim vestes gerebant.) Itaque, qui in se recipiebant se rem quamcunque ratam habituros, attingebant alas vestimentorum ipsorum. Id vocatur Acquisitio alæ vestimenti. Præterea quum in Additamentis dicitur, Nec multitudinem sequimur, sensus est, Quamvis verba quibus Ebræis cadus & metreta notantur apud plerosque diversa significent, id non attendi; quia cum hic de pecunia agatur, quid dicant plerique sive major pars, non moramur. Quemadmodum Gemara docet, Quod dicere possis, Sequere multitudinem: jam edocti sumus, in pecuniaria causa multitudinem sequendam non esse. Denique quamvis כד cadus & חבית metreta Attica, sive amphora Attica, ejusdem quantitatis esse statuantur; nonnullum tamen Ebraeis vocibus discrimen notatur: nam ut inquit Salomon I. mensura חבת paulo major est, כר vero minor. Et licet כר saepe pro minori mensura accipiatur quam cadus, ut quum Rebecca, Gen.24. humeris כר gestare dicitur; quia tamen nomen Latinorum ab Ebraeo factum est, & in Mishnajoth saepe pro majori mensura venit, ideo cadi etiam nomen retinere visum fuit. Ut ergo ad priora Gem. & Addit. verba redeamus, id sibi auctor voluit, duo vocabula idcirco adhibita fuisse, quia licet nonnulla esset diversitas; in vendendo & emendo unam mensuram pro alia peteret vel traderet, qui in argenti possessione esset. 3 Caeterum Mishna alium casum suppeditat de aquae lubrico (ut voce utar, quam Tacitus frequenter adhibet.) Fit aliquando ut lubricum loci alicujus ex aqua aliove liquore ortum, labendi occasionem praebeat: quo casu is cujus amphora fracta fuerit tenetur, si eam in loco publico collocaverit; ex eaque effusus liquor viam lubricam fecerit: nempe quum praeteriens quis hac occasione cadit, aut laeditur testis, quas Mishna תרמיס nuncupat. quanquam in diversis editionibus legatur תרמית, quod licet calcis effossae genus significet, uti ex Aruch docuimus pag.158. Middoth; tamen de fictilium fragmentis etiam dicitur, quae significatio huic loco quadrat. 4 Sed in illo prolato casu D. Judas dissentit, si quis ad illa, i. aquam aliumve effusum liquorem & fragmenta testacea animum non advertat. D. Joseph fragmentorum tantum meminit: animum advertit ad obtinendum fragmina ejus; sc. amphorae. Exceptionis ratio: qui fragmina sibi servare vult, id quo alius laeditur suum agnoscit, & hac ratione se reum fatetur; at qui ista ut communia bona negligit, non magis datum damnum agnoscit, quam si quis ab iis quae publica & omnium sunt laesus fuisset. Novi quidem in posteriori Mishnae membro quosdam aliam sententiam excogitare; sed quae a verborum serie aberrat. Cum hac Mishna & initio sequentis optime convenit edictumPraetoris, quod extat l. 9. ff. sub inititium tit. 3. Unde in eum locum quo vulgo iter fiet, vel in quo consistetur, dejectum, vel effusum quid erit: quantum ex ea re damnum datum, factumve erit; in eum, qui habitaverit, in duplum judicium dabo. Vbi bene Accursius monet, verba ita construenda: in eum qui ibi inhabitaverit unde dejectum vel effusum quid erit in eum locum, &c. Videantur insuper caetera Praetoris verba quae ad rem faciunt; sed brevitati studens praetermitto, locum indicasse contentus.
units.tr: The contracting parties take two witnesses, in whose presence they state their conditions. Then each of the witnesses extends the wing of his garment (for they wore loose garments). Thus those who undertook to make any matter binding touched the wings of their garments. This is called the acquisition of the wing of a garment. Further, when the additions say Nor do we follow the majority, the meaning is this: although the words by which the Hebrews denote cadus and metreta mean different things among most people, this is not taken into account, because, since the matter here concerns money, we do not regard what most people, or the greater part, say. As the Gemara teaches: "You could say, follow the majority"; but we have been taught that in a monetary matter the majority is not to be followed. Finally, although כד [cadus] and חבית [metreta] Attica, that is, an Attic amphora, are held to be of the same quantity, nevertheless a certain difference is marked in the Hebrew words. For, as Solomon says in his commentary, the measure חבת is a little larger, while כר is smaller. And although כר is often taken for a smaller measure than cadus, as when Rebekah is said to have carried a כר on her shoulders (Gen. 24), yet because the Latin name is derived from the Hebrew, and in the Mishnayot it often stands for a larger measure, it seemed right to retain the name cadus as well. So to return to the earlier words of the Gemara and the additions: the author meant that the two terms were used because, although there was some difference, anyone who held silver in possession, in buying and selling, could demand or deliver one measure in place of the other. 3 Moreover, the Mishnah supplies another case, concerning a slippery place caused by water (to use the word which Tacitus often uses). It sometimes happens that a slippery spot, caused by water or some other liquid, offers an occasion for falling. In that case the man whose jar was broken is liable, if he set it down in a public place, and the liquid poured out from it made the path slippery; namely, when a passer-by falls on this occasion, or a shard injures him, which the Mishnah calls תרמיס [tarmis]. Although in different editions it is read as תרמית, which, though it denotes a kind of dug-up lime, as we showed from the Aruch at p. 158 of Middoth, yet is also said of fragments of pottery, a meaning which suits this place. 4 But in the case put forward, Rabbi Judah dissents, if someone does not pay attention to those things, that is, to the water or other poured liquid and the potsherds. Rabbi Joseph mentions only the fragments: he pays attention to keeping the pieces of it, that is, of the jar. The reason for the exception is this: whoever wants to keep the fragments for himself acknowledges that the thing by which another is injured is his own, and by this reasoning admits that he is at fault; but whoever neglects them as common goods does not acknowledge the damage done any more than if someone had been injured by things that belong to the public and to all. I know that some devise a different opinion in the latter part of the Mishnah, but it departs from the sequence of the words. The edict of the Praetor, which stands in l. 9 ff., sub initium tit. 3, agrees well with this Mishnah and the beginning of the following one: If anything is thrown down or poured out in a place where the public commonly passes, or where people stop, I will give a judgment for double the damage done or caused by that matter against the one who lived there. Here Accursius rightly advises that the words should be construed thus: against the one who lived there, from whose place something was thrown down or poured out into that place, etc. The other words of the Praetor which bear on the matter may be consulted as well; but, aiming at brevity, I omit them, content to have indicated the place.

units.la: השופך מים ברשות הרבים והוק כהן אחר חייב בנזקו הפצניע ארז הקוץ ואת הזכוכית והגודר ארז גדר בקוצים וגדר שנפל לרשות הרבים והוק בהן אחר חייב בנזקן׃
units.tr: He who pours water into a public place, so that another person is harmed, is liable for his damage. He who conceals a thorn or glass, and likewise he who builds a fence of thorns which falls into a public place, if another stumbles over them, is liable for the damage they cause.

units.la: {§}Effundens aquam in locum publicum, qua alius damnum patiatur, hujus damnum praestare tenetur. Occultans spinam aut vitrum, item suam saepem e spinis conficiens, cujus etiam saepes in publicum locum decidit; si alii per ista noceatur, damnum per ea illatum compensare tenetur.
units.tr: He who pours water into a public place, so that another suffers damage, is bound to make good that damage. Whoever conceals a thorn or glass, and likewise whoever builds his hedge of thorns, which also falls into a public place; if another is harmed by these, he is bound to compensate the damage done by them.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Saepe fit ut spinae similiaque amputentur, vitraque confringantur, & cum haec, tum illa loco quodam seponantur, abjiciantur, & occulto etiam loco à conspectu nostro removeantur. Hic eorum author reus peragitur, si quem ita spinarum aculeis, vel vitri fragmine laedi contingat. Modo, ut Hebraei observant, loco publico occultata laedant: etenim si quis ejusmodi in fundo proprio seponat, quamvis alius laedatur, ipse non tenetur. Ideoque חסידים פרושים סיו מנניעים קוצים וזכוכיות בתוך שדותיהם ומעמיקין לזן ג׳ טפחים כדי שלא יעבר המחרש רכ טפח סדי לזה בנורה רכ טפח סדי לזה כדגלת Pii isti antiqui seponebant spinas & vitra sua in agris suis, idque ad trium palmorum profunditatem, ne vomerem remorarentur. Magister Sefath ista in ignem projiciebat: Raba vero in Tigrin abjiciebat. Nam id operam dabant, ne sua culpa alius laederetur: quod plerique se facturos judicabant, si illa etiam in fundo suo collocarent ac seponerent. Quum ergo in sequentibus legitur, eum teneri qui suam sepem e spinis confecit, si inde praetereuntes damnum patiantur; id hac conditione obtinet, si rami in locum publicum excrescentes praetereuntem laedant: quandoquidem ni id fiat, hac in parte nemini in suo fundo leges praescribi possunt. In quam sententiam haec addit Gemara: הנ"ג ... Dixit D. Iohannes, Id nonnisi de excrescente sepe docuerunt; non vero de ea quae praecise intra limites continetur. Quae ratio, quare hoc casu liber fit? Respondit Magister Aha filius M. Ika, Quia non est consuetudo filiorum hominis, ut sese parietibus affricent. Sane si nihil quod nocere potest excrescat, ipse qui ad sepem propius accedit, sibi acceptum incommodum imputet. At si sepes suis quidem limitibus non egrediens, postea decidat in viam vel aream publicam, aliud judicium est: tum enim non spectatur cujusmodi antea fuerit; sed qui se jam habeat. Nisi quod ad idoneam & debitam structuram praecedentem ibi attendi, judicem ex eo quod R. Iom Tob f. Abrahami ad Maimonidae verba annotat; quae leguntur c. 13. constitutionum de damnis pecuniariis. [Hebrew] fi eum (loquitur de pariete) non exstruxit debito modo, tenetur. Quae posteriori Misnae membro proponuntur, ita se habent, Quemadmodum (ut cum Vlpiano loquar) si laqueos eo loci posuisset, quo jus ponendi non haberes, & pecus vicini in eos laqueos incidisset. ff. ad l. Aquil. l. 29. Sive enim laqueo, sive spinis vel ruderibus damnum in loco alieno vel publico detur, eodem res recidit. Quid vero hic juris sit, videre est loco citato.
units.tr: Often it happens that thorns and similar things are cut off, and broken glass is swept up, and these are set aside in some place, thrown away, and removed out of our sight into some hidden spot. Here the author of such things is prosecuted as liable if anyone happens to be hurt by the thorn-prickles or a fragment of glass. Only, as the Hebrews observe, if they injure people who have been hidden in a public place; for if anyone sets such things aside in his own field, he is not liable even if someone else is hurt. Hence the pious men of old used to place thorns and glass within their fields and sink them to a depth of three handbreadths, so that the plough would not be hindered [חסידים הפרושים היו מניחים קוצים וזכוכיות בתוך שדותיהם ומעמיקין להן ג׳ טפחים כדי שלא יעבור המחרש]. Those pious men of old set aside thorns and their glass in their fields, and this to a depth of three palms, so that they would not hinder the plough. Master Sefath used to throw these things into the fire; but Raba used to cast them into the Tigris. For they took pains that no one should be hurt through their fault, which most people judged they would do if they placed and set aside such things even on their own land. When, therefore, it is read in what follows that the one who has made his hedge of thorns is liable if passers-by suffer harm from it, this holds on the condition that the branches growing out into a public place hurt the passer-by; for unless this happens, laws cannot be prescribed to anyone in this matter within his own field. To this effect the Gemara adds this: Dixit D. Iohannes: They taught this only of a hedge that grows out; but not of one that is contained precisely within its boundaries. What is the reason that in this case it is free from liability? Master Aha son of Rabbi Ika answered: Because it is not the custom of the sons of men to rub themselves against walls. Certainly, if nothing that can cause harm grows out, the one who comes nearer to the hedge should impute the resulting injury to himself. But if the hedge, not going beyond its own boundaries, afterwards falls into a public road or open space, the judgment is different: for then one does not look at what it was before, but at what it now is. Except that I note here that a proper and due construction is required beforehand, as I judge from what Rabbi Iom Tob son of Abraham annotates on the words of Maimonides, which are read in chapter 13 of the Constitutions on pecuniary damages: If he (he speaks of a wall) did not build it in the due manner, he is liable. What is set forth in the latter part of the Mishnah is as follows: Just as (to speak with Ulpian) if you had set snares in a place where you had no right to set them, and a neighbour's cattle had fallen into those snares. Dig. ad l. Aquil., l. 29. For whether the damage is done in another's place or a public one by a snare, by thorns, or by rubble, the matter comes to the same thing. What the law is here may be seen in the place cited.

units.la: גיו המתיא את חבנו ואת קשו לרשות הרבי לזכלים והחק בהן אחר חייב בנזקו וכל הקורם בהן זכה ר׳ שמעון בן גמליאל אומר כל המקלקלין ברשות הרבים והזיקו חייבין לשלם וכל הקודי בהן זכה ההופך ארז הגלל ברשות הרבים והזק בהן אחר חייב בנזקו [?]
units.tr: If a man throws his jar [חבית] and his bow [קשת] into the public domain [רשות הרבים], and another person is injured by them, the one who threw them is liable for the damage. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel says: all who make a mess in the public domain and cause damage are liable to pay. Whoever stumbles over them is exempt. If a man overturns a dung-heap [גלל] in the public domain and another is injured by it, he is liable for the damage.

units.la: Qui stramen & paleam suam in locum publicum effert ad 'fimetum, ita ut iis damnum patiatur alius; hujus damnum praestare tenetur: & quicunque primus ipsa capit, acquirit. D. Simeon f. Gamalielis inquit, Omnes in loco publico aliquid inquinantes, damnum compensare tenentur: & quicunque primus hujusmodi intercipit, ea sibi acquirit. Qui stercus in locum publicum effundit, adeo ut eo damnum patiatur alius; hujus damnum compensare tenetur.
units.tr: Whoever carries his straw and chaff into a public place, to the dunghill, so that another suffers damage from them, is bound to make good the damage; and whoever first takes them up acquires them. Rabbi Simeon son of Gamaliel says: All who foul anything in a public place are bound to compensate the damage; and whoever first seizes such things acquires them. Whoever pours out dung into a public place, so that another suffers damage from it, is bound to compensate the damage.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Proprie ad fimos, id est, ut in fimum redigantur ad agros stercorandos: sicuti glossa enarrat, ויקח ונתנו וכו [?] לוכל מדות וכרמים Ut putrescant stramen & palea & in fimum redigantur ad stercorandos agros & vineta. secundum illud Plinii L.17. c. 9. Cato, stercus unde fiat, stramenta, lupinum, paleas, fabalia, ac frondes ilignas, quernasque, supple, capiendas. ² Ne autem hujusmodi rebus loca publica inquinarentur, occupantis esse voluerunt: sic enim קנסיהו רבנן ומקלקלין [?] multctarunt Magistri ipsos conspurcantes; ut loquitur R. Isaac Gabaeus. Imo etiamsi nonnunquam stercus foras efferre liceat, si damnum datum fit, tenentur authores. Ita Gemara, כל אלו שחמרו מזיקין [?] Omnes quibus veniam dederunt ut ita in loco publico aliquid inquinent; si noceant, tenentur. Atque ea de re non inconcinne etiam accipi posset, quod legimus Dig. l.9. t.3. leg.1. §.2. Semper ea loca, per qua vulgo iter solet fieri, eandem securitatem debent habere. Qui enim in vel per loca publica quid defert, ne damnum detur cavere debet.
units.tr: ¹ Properly to the dunghills, that is, to be rotted down into dung for manuring fields, as the gloss explains: [ויקח ונתנו וכו] that the straw and chaff may rot and be turned into dung for manuring fields and vineyards, according to that passage of Pliny, Book 17, ch. 9: Cato, on how dung is made: straw, lupine, chaff, bean-stalks, and holm-oak and oak leaves, namely, to be gathered. ² But lest public places be fouled by such things, they wished it to belong to whoever first occupied them: for so [קנסיהו רבנן ומקלקלין] the Masters fined those who fouled them, as R. Isaac Gabaeus says. Indeed, even if it is sometimes allowed to carry dung out, if damage is done, the authors are liable. So the Gemara: [כל אלו שחמרו מזיקין] All those to whom they gave permission to foul a public place in this way; if they do harm, they are liable. And on this matter what we read in Dig. l. 9, t. 3, leg. 1, §2 could be understood not inappropriately: Those places through which the public commonly makes its way should always have the same safety. For whoever carries something in or through public places must take care that no damage is caused.

units.la: ד׳ ו׳ שני קודין שהיו מהלכין זה אחר זה ונחקל הראשון ונפל ונחקל השני בראשון הראשון חייב בנזקי שני ו
units.tr: Two potters who were walking one after another: the first stumbled and fell, and the second stumbled over the first; the first is liable for the second's damage. [ד׳ ו׳ שני קודין שהיו מהלכין זה אחר זה ונחקל הראשון ונפל ונחקל השני בראשון הראשון חייב בנזקי שני]

units.la: Si duorum figulorum, qui alter post alterum incedunt, prior pingens cadat, impingatque secundus in priorem; prior de secundi lesione tenetur.
units.tr: If of two potters, who walk one after the other, the first, carrying his pots, falls, and the second stumbles into the first, the first is liable for the injury to the second.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Ita ut tamen in pedes stare & consistere possit: quod Gemara sic effert, cum stare poterat & non stetit, vel ut alius loquitur, modo stare potuerit. Id est, hoc pacto stabilitur Misna, quum tamdiu cunctatus est inter cadendum ut erigere se potuerit; nec tamen se erexit. Aliqui Doctores pronunciant, coactus fuit, ideoque absolvitur.
units.tr: ¹ Thus, however, he must be able to stand upright and remain on his feet. The Gemara puts it this way: when he could stand and did not stand, or, as another puts it, only if he could have stood. That is to say, the Mishnah is established in this sense: when he hesitated while falling for so long that he could have raised himself, and yet did not raise himself. Some teachers pronounce: he was forced, and so is acquitted.

units.la: ² Additur in Gemara alius casus, quem his verbis proponunt, si figulorum vel vitriariorum, qui alius post alium incedunt, primus impingat, & secundus in priorem procidat, tertiusque in secundum; primus de secundi damnis tenetur, similiter secundus tenetur de damnis tertii. quod si propter primum ceciderint, primus omnium damna praestare debet. Si vero alius alium monuerint, absolvuntur. Tandem in Gemara explicatur, quid sit, propter primum cadere: cum variare judicia possint, an primus in causa fuerit. Duae ergo proponuntur sententiae, quando cadere quis dicatur propter primum. Magister Papa inquit, Quum primus alterius viam praecidit instar mortticini; Magister Zebid ait, instar scipionis caecitatis. Sensus est, illum existimare, quod primus ille, si de damno teneatur, adeo viam obstruxerit, ac si cadaver transverse per viam jacuisset (ut glossa exponit:) hunc vero tantum impedimentum non exigere; sed ei sufficere, si primus ille se caeci instar habuerit, qui in sua caecitate scipionem adhibens, cum palpando ita per viam extendit, ut alius impingat. Qua utraque sententia ille tum demum teneri judicatur, si catenus secundo & tertio labendi occasionem dederit, ut cum alterutro, id est, morticino vel scipione per viam extenso quadantenus conferri queat. Cum hac Misna & posteriori casu conferri possit Alpheni responsum lib. Dig.9. t.2. leg. 52. §. In clivo: ubi de duobus plaustris quae mulae in clivo ducebant. Posterius plaustrum a priore percussum, retro redierat, & puerum cujusdam obtriverat. dominus pueri consulebat, cum quo se agere oporteret. Respondi, in causa jus esse positum. id est, exponente Accursio, ut ille teneatur qui causam mortis praebuit. Vti in superioribus tres homines in exemplum proferuntur, quorum tertius & secundus laedantur; sic producta lege, duo plaustra cum puero producuntur, ita ut prius plaustrum sit totius damni occasio. Quis vero causam praebuisse censeatur, cum plaustrum in plaustrum, & hoc plaustrum in puerum cecidit, videatur dicta lege: ubi cum distinctione respondetur.
units.tr: ² The Gemara adds another case, which they propose in these words: if of potters or glass-sellers, who walk one after another, the first strikes and the second falls on the first, and the third on the second, the first is liable for the losses of the second; likewise the second is liable for the losses of the third. But if they fell because of the first, the first must make good all the losses. If, however, one warned the other, they are acquitted. Finally, the Gemara explains what it means to fall because of the first, since opinions may differ as to whether the first was the cause. Two opinions are therefore put forward: when someone is said to fall because of the first. Rabbi Papa says: when the first cuts across another's path like a carcass; Rabbi Zebid says: like a staff of a blind man. The sense is this: the one holds that if that first man is to be liable for the damage, he must have blocked the way as completely as if a corpse had lain across the path (as the gloss explains); but the other holds that so great an obstruction is not required, and that it is enough if the first man was like a blind man who, using a staff in his blindness, feels his way along so that another strikes against him. Under either opinion, that man is judged liable only if he gave the second and third occasion to fall to such an extent that he can be compared, in some measure, with one or the other: that is, with the carcass or the staff laid across the path. With this Mishnah and the later case can be compared the opinion of Alphenus, in the Digest, book 9, title 2, law 52, §. In clivo, where two wagons drawn by mules were going down a slope. The rear wagon, struck by the front one, had run back and crushed a certain man's boy. The boy's master asked what action he should bring. I replied that the law is established in the case. That is, as Accursius explains, that he is liable who gave the cause of death.
