As in the above, three men are offered as an example, of whom the third and second are harmed; so, with the law brought forward, two wagons are brought forward with a boy, so that the first wagon is the occasion of all the damage. Who is deemed to have given the cause, when one wagon fell onto a wagon and this wagon onto the boy, may be seen in the cited law, where the answer is given with a distinction.

units.la: Si quum hic fert amphoram suam, & alter tignum suum, hujus amphora ad alterius tignum frangatur, alter liber est: quia cum huic, tum illi incedere licet. Si tignum gestans praecedat, & amphoram portans sequatur, amphora ad tignum fracta, tignum gestans liber est. at si tignum
units.tr: If, while this man carries his jar and the other carries his beam, the jar of the one is broken against the beam of the other, the other is free, because it is lawful for both of them to walk. If the man carrying the beam goes first and the man carrying the jar follows, and the jar is broken against the beam, the man carrying the beam is free. But if the beam

units.la: הקורה ואם עמר בעל הקורה חייב ואם אמר לבעל חביח עמור פטור היה בעל חביר ראשון ובעל קורה אחרון נשברה חביי בקורה חייב ואם עמר בעל חביח פטור ואם אמר לבעל קורה עמור חייב וכן זה בא בנרו וזה בפשתנו ׃
units.tr: הקורה ואם עמר בעל הקורה חייב ואם אמר לבעל חביח עמור פטור היה בעל חביר ראשון ובעל קורה אחרון נשברה חביי בקורה חייב ואם עמר בעל חביח פטור ואם אמר לבעל קורה עמור חייב וכן זה בא בנרו וזה בפשתנו ׃

units.la: tignum gestans restiterit, tenetur: sin amphorâ gestanti dixerit, Consiste; liber est. Si precedat amphoram portans & tignum gestans sequatur, fractâ ad tignum amphorâ, hic solvere tenetur. at fi amphoram portans restiterit, alter liber est: sin tignum gestanti dixerit, Consiste; ille tenetur. Similiter, ubi hic incedit cum lucerna sua; alter verò cum linofuo.
units.tr: If the jar-carrier goes first and the beam-carrier follows, and the jar is broken on the beam, the beam-carrier is liable. If the jar-carrier stops, he is exempt; but if he tells the beam-carrier, "Stop," the beam-carrier is liable. Likewise, where this man goes with his lamp and the other with his flax.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Quasi dicat, non est quod hic illum accuset, quandoquidem per viam & loca publica gradi licet: seipsum accuset, quod cum amphora sua impegerit. Hanc exceptionem, quod cuique incedere liceat, in Gemara ad alium casum ridiculum satis remotè extendunt; puta, si quis uxorem in concubitu laedat: quem tamen teneri concludunt. Sed hujusmodi nugas praetereamus: nullam enim utilitatem habent, nisi quod Judaeorum magnam caecitatem prodant: utpote qui ejusmodi casus tanta & tam operosa curiositate definiunt; interim de praecipuis religionis capitibus securi.
units.tr: It is as if he said: there is no reason for him to accuse this man, since it is lawful to walk along the road and public places; let him accuse himself, for striking into him with his jar. In the Gemara they extend this exception, that anyone may walk, rather far afield and absurdly, to another case: for instance, if someone injures a wife during intercourse; yet they conclude that he is liable. But let us pass over such trifles: they have no use, except to reveal the great blindness of the Jews, who define such cases with so much and so laborious curiosity, while being careless about the chief points of religion.

units.la: Caeterum incedens cum lucerna, hic assimilatur illi qui tignum gestabat; & linum ferens, illi qui amphoram portabat: adeo ut in dato damno, illorum jura ac leges hic similiter obtineant. Porrò cum videamus datum casu damnum etiam praestari, distinguendum, prout exempla superiora in Misna nostra exigunt, inter fortuitum casum ubi culpa non est; & eum cui se quis exponit: ut si tignum gestans restiterit & sequentem amphoram fortuitò fregerit. Sanè in fortuito casu diversitatem magnam agnoscunt Romanorum jurisconsulti. Nam si casus plane & omninò sit fortuitus, locum habet illud Dig. l. 40. t. 9. l. Julianus. Nec adventitii casus computandi sunt. Quum vero culpa accedit, secus loquuntur: ut Dig. l. 19. t. 2. leg. 11. §. 1. videre est. ubi casus fortuitus incendii proponitur. Si hoc in locatione convenit, Ignem ne habeto, & habuit; tenebitur etiamsi fortuitus casus admisit incendium: quia non debuit ignem habere. Unde generaliter jurisperitorum nonnemo concludit, Culpa precedens casum fortuitum, vel quando quis casui fortuito se commiserit, facit ut ex casu quoque quis teneatur, non aliter.
units.tr: Moreover, the one carrying a lamp is here likened to the one who carried the beam, and the one bearing flax to the one who carried the jar, so that in a given loss their rights and laws apply here in the same way. Furthermore, since we see that a loss caused by chance is also made good, we must distinguish, as the preceding examples in our Mishnah require, between a chance accident where there is no fault, and one to which a man exposes himself, as when the beam-bearer stands still and accidentally breaks the jar that follows. Certainly the Roman jurists recognise a great difference in a chance accident. For if the event is wholly and entirely accidental, that law applies, Digest, book 40, title 9, the law Julianus: Nor are accidental events to be reckoned. But where fault is present they speak otherwise, as may be seen in Digest, book 19, title 2, law 11, §. 1, where a chance fire is put forward: If it was agreed in the lease, "Do not keep fire," and he kept it, he will be liable even though a chance event admitted the fire, because he ought not to have kept fire. Hence some jurists conclude in general: A fault preceding a chance event, or when someone has exposed himself to a chance event, makes him liable even for what happens by chance, and not otherwise.

units.la: טנים שהיו מהלכין ברשות הרבים אחד ץ ואחר מהלך או שהיו שניהם רצים והזיקו זה את זה שניהם פטורין׃
units.tr: If two men walking in a public place, one runs and the other walks, or both run, and they injure one another, both are exempt. [טנים שהיו מהלכין ברשות הרבים אחד ץ ואחר מהלך או שהיו שניהם רצים והזיקו זה את זה שניהם פטורין׃]

units.la: Si duorum in loco publico euntium unus currat, alter incedat, aut uterque currat; ac alter alterum laedat, ambo liberi sunt.
units.tr: If, of two men going in a public place, one runs and the other walks, or both run, and one injures the other, both are free from liability.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Jam antea annotavimus, Misnas aliquando verborum quorundam defectu laborare, sive verba quaedam ad sententiam perficiendam esse supplenda: quod his verbis efferre solent, Misna deficiendo deficit. Hujusmodi defectum hoc loco agnoscit Gemara: quandoquidem si currens eum qui pedetentim incedit laedat, Judaeorum lege tenetur; in hac vero Misna absolvitur. Unde liquet addenda quaedam, ut haec constitutio cum aliis conveniat. Quod ita probat Gemara. ממלי מדקמני לו מסיו שנייםם רצים פטורים Unde colligitur defectus? Ex eo quod ἀδύνατοι, Aut si ambo currant, liberi sunt. Ecce denuo quorsum mihi jam ista adduntur? Cum si unus currat & alter incedat, ille laedens absolvitur; an de duobus currentibus quaeritur? Etenim si cum unus pedetentim incedit, ab altero currente impune laedatur, nec ullam in alterum actionem habeat; quanto minus habebit, si currens à currente lædatur? Ergo posterius membrum ex illa sententia & mente vacaret. Hinc patet in priori membro, כשרב תכת, in vespera sabbathi, aliaque similia addenda fuisse, in hanc sententiam: cum pridie sabbathi & diei festi currens lædit, eum non teneri; quia ad omnia præparanda in diem festum, cursum & festinationem laudant. Vt hæc sit completa oratio, אחד רן ולאחד מהלך כערבי סבתות וימים סוכים ושהיו סנייס' רתיס כסאר, ויומי הסנה סנייס פסוריס Si unus currat, alter incedat vesperis sabbathorum aut festorum dierum (pridie istorum dierum הסמטות כין, inter soles, id est, כין פערביס, inter duas vesperas) aut si ambo currant reliquis anni diebus, ambo lædentes liberi sunt. At si his diebus unus currens alterum pedetentim incedentem lædat, tenetur: quia פוזה ימסזוס, ipse à recepto more diversum facit. sin ambo currant, ambo à consueto eundi more abeunt: ideoque licet lædant, non tenentur,
units.tr: I have already noted that the Mishnah sometimes suffers from the lack of certain words, or that some words must be supplied to complete the sense; this they commonly express by the words The Mishnah fails by failing. The Gemara recognises such a defect here, since if the runner injures the one who walks slowly, he is held liable under Jewish law, yet in this Mishnah he is acquitted. It is clear, therefore, that some additions must be made so that this ruling agrees with the others. The Gemara proves this as follows: [מִמַּלִּי מִדְּקָמְנִי לוֹ מִסִּיּוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם רְצִים פְּטוּרִים]. Whence is the defect gathered? From the fact that it says, "Or if both run, they are free." Look, again, why are these words added to me? Since if one runs and the other walks, the one who injures is acquitted; is the question about two who run? For if one who walks slowly is injured with impunity by one who runs, and has no action against him, how much less will he have one if the runner is injured by a runner? Therefore the second clause would be empty of that ruling and meaning. Hence it is evident that in the first clause the words [כשרב תכת], on the eve of the Sabbath, and others like them, must be added with this sense: when on the day before the Sabbath or a festival a runner injures someone, he is not liable, because they praise running and haste in preparing everything for the festival day. So that the statement may be complete, it should read: [אחד רן ולאחד מהלך כערבי סבתות וימים סוכים ושהיו סנייס' רתיס כסאר, ויומי הסנה סנייס פסוריס] If one runs and the other walks on the eves of Sabbaths or festival days (that is, on the day before these days, [הסמטות כין], "between the suns," that is, [כין פערביס], "between the two evenings"), or if both run on the other days of the year, both who injure are free. But if on these days one who runs injures one who walks slowly, he is liable, because [פוזה ימסזוס], he himself acts contrary to the accepted custom. But if both run, both depart from the customary manner of walking, and therefore, although they injure, they are not liable.

units.la: Qui ligna findens in loco privato, alterum in loco publico lædit; vel findens in loco publico, lædit in loco privato; vel denique findens in loco privato, lædit in loco privato alterius, is tenetur.
units.tr: He who splits wood in a private place and injures someone in a public place; or who splits wood in a public place and injures someone in a private place; or, finally, who splits wood in a private place and injures another's private place, is liable.
Annotations.

units.la: Non omninò Judaïcum hoc statutum cum iis congruit, quæ ex Paulo jurisconsulto proferuntur ff. Ad l. Aq. l. 31. Quanquam enim casus idem non sit, analogicè tamen inde secus judicandum videtur de casu in Misna præsenti prolato. Illius verba sunt, Si putator ex arbore ramum cum dejiceret, vel machinarius, hominem prætereuntem occiderit; ita tenetur, si is in publicum decidat, nec ille proclamavit, ut casus ejus evitari posset. Sed Mucius etiam dixit, si in privato idem accidisset, posse de culpa agi.... Quod si nullum iter erit; dolum duntaxat praestare debet; ne immittat in eum, quem viderit transeuntem. Nam culpa ab eo exigenda non est; cum divinare non potuerit, an per eum locum aliquis transiturus sit.
units.tr: This Jewish statute does not entirely agree with what the jurist Paul sets out in ff. Ad l. Aq. l. 31. Although the case is not the same, it seems that by analogy one should judge the case put forward in this Mishnah differently. His words are: "If a pruner, while cutting a branch from a tree, or a workman with a machine, kills a passer-by, he is liable only if the branch fell into a public place and he did not shout a warning, so that the accident could have been avoided. But Mucius also said that if the same thing happened on private ground, an action for fault could lie... But if there is no public way, he owes only good faith, namely that he must not throw something at the one he sees passing. For fault cannot be required of him, since he could not foresee whether anyone would pass through that place."

units.la: שני שוורים תמים שחבלו זה את זה משלמים במוהר חצי נזק שניהם מועדים משלמים במוהר נזק שלם אחר הם ואחד מועד טועד בתם משלם במוהר נזק שלם הם במועד משלם במוהר חצי נזק וכן ב' אנשים שחבלו זה בזה משלמים במוהר נזק שלם אדם במועד ומועד באדם משלם במוהר נזק שלם אדם בתם וחם באדם אדם בתם משל' במוהר נזק שלם חם באדם משלם במוהר חצי נזק רבי עקיבא אומר אף תם שחבל באדם משלם במוהר נזק שלם ו
units.tr: If two innocent oxen injure one another, they pay half the damage from the common fund (mohar). If both are known to be dangerous (mu'ad), they pay full damage from the common fund. If one is innocent and the other known to be dangerous, the innocent one pays half the damage from the common fund, and the dangerous one pays full damage from the common fund; so too with two men who injure one another: they pay full damage from the common fund, and a man who injures a man... [the Hebrew continues with the parallel cases, ending:] [וכן ב' אנשים שחבלו זה בזה משלמים במוהר נזק שלם אדם במועד ומועד באדם משלם במוהר נזק שלם אדם בתם וחם באדם אדם בתם משל' במוהר נזק שלם חם באדם משלם במוהר חצי נזק רבי עקיבא אומר אף תם שחבל באדם משלם במוהר נזק שלם ו]

units.la: f. inaccurec[?] hominem, ... Si è duobus bobus innocentibus alter alterum vitiaverit; in t auctario, sive damni exuperantia, damni dimidium praestatur: si uterque convictus sit; totum damnum in auctario, sive residuo, compensatur. Si unus innocens, alter convictus sit, & convictus innocentem magis vitiet; quod ad residuum, praestatur totum damnum: si innocens, convictum; quoad residuum, damni dimidium praestatur. Pariter, si è duobus hominibus alter alterum vitiavit; in residuo, totum damnum compensatur. Si homo bestiam convictam, ita ut vicissim bestia convicta hominem vitiet; ex residuo praestatur totum damnum. Quum homo bestiam innocentem, & hac hominem vitiavit; si homo innocentem magis laesit, quod ad residuum, praestat damnum totum: [illegible, ~2 letters] innocens [?] hominem, ex residuo praestatur damni dimidium.
units.tr: ... if a man [injures] a man, ... If one of two innocent oxen injures the other, the damage in excess of the part borne by the owner is paid at half the damage; if both are convicted, the whole damage is compensated from the surplus or remainder. If one is innocent and the other convicted, and the convicted one injures the innocent one more, then as to the remainder the whole damage is paid; if the innocent one injures the convicted one, as to the remainder half the damage is paid. Likewise, if one of two men injures the other, the whole damage is compensated from the remainder. If a man injures a convicted beast, so that in turn the convicted beast injures the man, the whole damage is paid from the remainder. When a man injures an innocent beast and this one injures the man: if the man injured the beast more, then as to the remainder the whole damage is paid; [illegible] innocent [?] man, from the remainder half the damage is paid.

units.la: D. Akiba inquit, etiam quum innocens magis vitiavit hominem, quoad residuum praestatur damnum totum.
units.tr: Rabbi Akiba says that even when the innocent one injures the man more, as to the remainder the whole damage is paid.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Quò hæc distinctius percipiantur, in memoriam ea revocanda sunt, quæ c. I. §. 4. nota 8. dicta fuere. Siquidem hæc Misna ex illa compensationis diversitate dependet, qua nonnunquam damni dimidium, quandoq; totum damnum compensatur. Jam sæpe contingit, ut animalia sese mutuò lædant: sanè eo casu damnum damno, ubi pecora pariter vel convicta, vel mansueta censentur, opponendum; nec ulterius quid exigendum omnes Judæi fatentur: nimirum si solæ bestiæ lædantur. Verumenimvero in isto mutuo damno sæpissime aliud alio majus esse deprehendas: tum id quod excedit, יתר, residuum, sive auctarium, vel damni exuperantia illis dicitur. In quo residuo eadem illa superior distinctio redit: siquidem pro animalium conditione diversa, totum istud residuum, vel ejus solummodo dimidium compensandum venit. Idque eadem lege, qua satisfactio exigitur, si animal unum ita lædat alterum, ut vicissim nullum detrimentum patiatur. Sicuti enim si bos non petulcus alterum cornu feriat, dimidium damni debet; pariter cum vicissim ab eodem minus damnum patitur, in auctario quo alterum magis læsit, dimidium rependit: quoniam damnum damno, quatenus æqualia sunt, jam pensatum censetur. Quum verò animal lædens non vicissim læsum, de toto damno tenetur; si vicissim lædatur, relicto eo in quo conveniunt, de toto residuo, sive exuperantia, qua alterum magis læsit, tenetur. In similibus simile judicium esto, & cæteri casus patescent. Verum hic nullo modo præterundum, quod Maimonides Cod. de dam. pecuniariis sub finem c. 9. exemplo edocet: puta, in auctario damni compensando simul attente expendendum, quid in damno æquali (cui auctarium accedit) utraque pars debeat. idque in debito ex auctario promananti consideran-dum, quatenus mutuum debitum superat.
units.tr: ¹ To grasp this more clearly, we must recall what was said at c. I, §. 4, note 8. This Mishnah depends on that difference of compensation by which sometimes half the damage, and sometimes the whole damage, is made good. Now it often happens that animals injure one another. In that case, where both animals are considered either goring or tame, the damage done by each is set against the damage done by the other, and all Jews agree that nothing further is to be exacted, namely if only beasts have been injured. But in this mutual damage you will very often find that one harm is greater than the other. What exceeds the other is called יתר, the remainder or surplus, or the excess of the damage. In this remainder the same earlier distinction recurs: for according to the different condition of the animals, either the whole remainder or only half of it must be compensated. This is governed by the same law by which satisfaction is required when one animal injures another so that it suffers no harm in return. For just as, if an ox that is not goring strikes another with its horn, it owes half the damage, so when it in turn suffers less damage from the same animal, it makes up half in the surplus by which the other injured it more, since damage set against equal damage is considered already paid. But when the injuring animal is not itself injured in return, it is liable for the whole damage; if it is injured in return, then, leaving aside the part in which they agree, it is liable for the whole surplus by which it injured the other more. Let a like judgment hold in like cases, and the other cases will become clear. Yet here we must by no means pass over what Maimonides, in the Code of Pecuniary Damages near the end of c. 9, teaches by example: namely, that in compensating the surplus one must also carefully weigh what each party owes in the equal damage (to which the surplus is added). This is to be considered in the debt arising from the surplus, insofar as the mutual debt exceeds it.

units.la: Exempli gratia, prior bos in posteriori damnum dederit drachmarum centum, posterior vicissim, drachmarum quadraginta: prior cum bove convictus sit, posterior mansuetus; dominus prioris rependit octoginta: si prior mansuetus, & posterior convictus; dominus prioris rependit decem. Etenim in priori casu, unde posterior elucescit, dominus convicti bovis debet totam damni differentiam sexaginta drachmarum: & aequale damnum aequali pensatum non creditur; quia alter bovis mansueti nomine tantum debebat dimidium istarum quadraginta drachmarum. Itaque viginti per viginti compensantur: & a viginti ad centum usque, pretium damni prior solvere tenetur. 2 Sed de bestia quae hominem laedit (ut praetereaм quae Maimonides accurate distinguit in multa, Cod. Nizke Mammon c.7. §.3.) non eadem omnes sentiunt. Causa vero ut in diversas sententias abeant, est legis divinae diversimoda ad antecedens relatio: cum non omnes ad idem antecedens legem referant. Exodi 21.31. ita Deus sancit, Sive filium cornu petierit, sive filiam cornu petierit; secundum hoc jus fiat ei. Postrema verba, secundum hoc jus fiat ei, plerique Judaeorum Doctores sic accipiunt, ac si Deus dixisset, Ut in praecedentibus de bove innocente sive mansueto, & petulco actum fuit; similiter ubi filium vel filiam sive hominem cornu petit, distinctio ista boum attendenda: ut pro eorum diversitate medium vel totum damnum rependatur; secundum illam legem quae sub finem capitis hujus 21. fertur. D. Akiba secus: ut qui, secundum hoc jus fiat ei, in hunc sensum accipiat, Uti proxime de bove petulco lex lata fuit, ita etiam ubi filius vel filia, sive homo laeditur cornu, totum damnum rependendum: quemadmodum versu 36. in bove petulco alterum bovem laedente requiritur. Quam insulsa haec fuit! Comma 31. ad praecedentia quidem referunt, quatenus ibi de bove petulco, vel etiam innocente agitur; at in iis quæ in bòyes statuuntur, capitis finem respiciunt. cum in utrisque comma 31. ad præcedentia pertineat: filiusque & filia non commemorentur ad homines generatim designandos; sed quò filius & filia minores natu adultis æquentur, quorum sanguinem (non enim agitur de minori læsione) in superioribus sancitâ in hominem & bovem mortis pœnâ vindicaverat. Conserantur ff. Si quadrupes, & ff. Ad legem Aquil. non procul ab initio. Quod disparem mulctæ quantitatem concernit, magis hic in actione, quam in mulctæ quantitate discrimen ex jure Romano observare mihi videor. Consulatur l. Si quadrupes, §. 4. שור שור מנה סנגח שור שוה מאתים ואין הנבילה יפה כלום נוטל את השור שור שוה מאתים סנגח שור שוה מאתים ואין הנבילה יפה כלום אשר רבי מאיר על זה נאסר וסכרו את השור החי וחצי את כספו אשר לו רבי יהודה וכן הלכה קיימי וסכרו את השור החי וחצי את כספו ולא קייםה וגם את המת יחצון ואיוה זה שור שוה מאתים סנגח שור שוה מאתים והנבלה יפה חמשים זה שזה נוטל חצי החי וחצי
units.tr: For example, let the first ox do damage of one hundred drachmas to the second, and the second in turn do damage of forty drachmas: if the first ox is a gorer and the second tame, the owner of the first pays eighty; if the first is tame and the second a gorer, the owner of the first pays ten. For in the first case, from which the second follows, the owner of the goring ox must pay the whole difference of sixty drachmas; and equal damage is not regarded as settled by equal damage, because the owner of the tame ox owed only half of those forty drachmas on account of the tame ox. Thus twenty is set against twenty, and from twenty up to one hundred the first owner is bound to pay the price of the damage. ² But concerning a beast that injures a man (to pass over the distinctions Maimonides draws with care in many matters, Code of Nizke Mammon c. 7, §. 3), not everyone agrees. The cause of their holding different opinions is the various ways in which the divine law is related to its antecedent, since not all refer the law to the same antecedent. In Exodus 21:31 God thus ordains: Whether it has gored a son or gored a daughter, according to this law let it be done to it. Most of the Jewish teachers take the last words, according to this law let it be done to it, as if God had said: as was done in the preceding cases concerning an innocent or tame ox and a goring one, so similarly where it gores a son or a daughter, or a man, that distinction among oxen must be observed, so that the damage is made good as half or as whole according to their difference, in accordance with that law which is stated at the end of this chapter, 21. R. Akiba thinks otherwise, taking according to this law let it be done to it in this sense: just as the law was laid down immediately about a goring ox, so also where a son or daughter, or a man, is gored, the whole damage must be made good, just as in verse 36 the whole is required when a goring ox injures another ox. How foolish this is! They refer verse 31 indeed to what precedes, insofar as there the goring ox, or even the innocent one, is in question; but as for what is laid down about oxen, they look to the end of the chapter. In both cases verse 31 belongs to what precedes, and son and daughter are not mentioned to designate men generally, but so that sons and daughters, being minors, are placed on a level with adults, whose blood (for this is not a matter of a lesser injury) the death penalty sanctioned above for man and ox had avenged. Compare the Digest, Si quadrupes, and the Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam, not far from the beginning. As to the difference in the amount of the fine, I seem to observe here a distinction in the action rather than in the amount of the fine, according to Roman law. Let the law Si quadrupes, §. 4, be consulted. [Mishnah, in Hebrew: "If an ox worth a maneh gores an ox worth two hundred, and the carcass is worth nothing, he takes the live ox. If an ox worth two hundred gores an ox worth two hundred, and the carcass is worth nothing, R. Meir says it was said of this case (Ex. 21:35): then they shall sell the live ox and divide its price. R. Judah says..." — original: שור שוה מנה סנגח שור שוה מאתים ואין הנבילה יפה כלום נוטל את השור החי וחצי את כספו אשר רבי מאיר על זה נאמר וסכרו את השור החי וחצי את כספו אשר לו רבי יהודה וכן הלכה קיימא וסכרו את השור החי וחצי את כספו ולא קיימא וגם את המת יחצו ואיזה זה שור שוה מאתים סנגח שור שוה מאתים והנבלה יפה חמשים זה שזה נוטל חצי החי וחצי]

units.la: Si bos valens minam cornu feriat bovem 200 drachmarum, & cadaver nullius fit pretii, hujus possessor vivum bovem auferet. Si bos ducentarum drachmarum cornu feriat bovem ejusdem valoris, & cadaver nullius fit pretii, pronunciat D. Meir, de eo dictum fuisse (Ex. 21. 35.) Tum vendito vivo partientur pecuniam pretii ejus. Cui Doctor Judas, Ita quidem obtinet constitutio, & stabilis illud, Tum vendito vivo partientur pecuniam pretii ejus; sed non stabilis istud, Atq; etiam mortuum partientur. Quis ergo hic bos est? Quum bos ducentarum drachm. cornu feriit bovem 200 drachmarū, & cadaver valet 50 drachmas:
units.tr: If an ox worth a maneh gores an ox worth two hundred drachmas, and the carcass is worth nothing, the owner of the latter takes the live ox. If an ox worth two hundred drachmas gores an ox of the same value, and the carcass is worth nothing, R. Meir pronounces that this was said (Ex. 21:35): then they shall sell the live ox and divide its price. To him Doctor Judah replies: "Indeed this ordinance holds, and that statement stands: then they shall sell the live ox and divide its price; but this statement does not stand: and they shall also divide the dead one. Which ox, then, is this? It is an ox worth two hundred that gores an ox worth two hundred, and the carcass is worth fifty; thus each takes half of the live one and half of..." [Hebrew: וסכרו את השור החי וחצי את כספו ... ]

units.la: tum enim hic dimidium vivi & dimidium mortui; alter pariter dimidium vivi & mortui aufert.
units.tr: For here each takes half of the live ox and half of the dead one; the other likewise takes half of the live and of the dead.
Annotations.

units.la: ¹ Hæc etiam verba sunt D. Judæ: ne quis existimet, Mosis nam ipsam hoc porisma è præcedentibus deducere (licet approbet.) Hæc obscuriora sunt, quam ut sine enarratione prætermitti debeant: ideoque ad pleniorem dictorum intelligentiam, qui duo ultima Ex. 21. commata à Talmudistis accipiantur, paucis expendere operæpretium erit. Verba capitis ultima, mortuus (bos) ejus esto, ad læsum referunt sive eum qui damnum passus fuit: ejus futurum cadaver, non solum cum bos petulcus; sed etiam quum mansuetus occidit alterum. itaque ad penultimum comma etiam pertinere asserunt. Hujus vero mortui bovis pretio addi volunt ad dimidium usque damni dati valorem, si à mansueto occisus sit; sin à petulco, totum damni pretium insuper expleri. Verba autem ultima com. 35. Et similiter mortuum partientur, quidam generatim accipiunt; ut cum etiam casum complectantur, quum cadaveris valor post mortem, antequam judicio contendatur, excrevit; vel qui non erat ullus, postea esse deprehenditur. tum enim lucrum vel incrementum dividi jubent multi, ut D. Juda; & dimidio incremento tantum addi, donec debita multa compleatur, sive dimidium, sive totum damnum præstandum sit. (damnum æstimant, quanti bos aliaque per mortem depretiantur.) Alii tamen totum incrementum ei qui damnum passus est vendicant, nec quicquam præter pretium; quo mortis tempore æstimaretur, in rationem venire ajunt, ut D. Meïr; isti vero pretio reliquum ad compensandum damnum secundum præcedentem distinctionem & modum addi jubent. Itaque hi ista verba, mortuum partientur, eo modo accipiunt, ac si פתח mortuum partientur
units.tr: These are also the words of St Jude. Lest anyone think that this corollary is deduced from what precedes it (though he approves it), these matters are more obscure than they should be passed over without comment. So for a fuller understanding of the sayings, it will be worth our while to consider briefly how the Talmudists take the last two clauses of Exodus 21. The final words of the verse, mortuus (the ox) ejus esto, refer to the injured party, that is, the one who suffered the loss: the carcass becomes his not only when a goring ox kills another, but also when a gentle ox does so. Accordingly they say it applies also to the penultimate clause. They want the price of the dead ox added to the value of half the damage done if it was killed by a gentle ox, but if by a goring ox, the whole price of the damage to be made up in addition. As for the final words of verse 35, Et similiter mortuum partientur, some take them generally, so that they cover also the case where the value of the carcass rose after death, before the matter came to judgment, or where there was none and it is later found to exist. For then many order that the gain or increase be divided, as St Jude does, and that only half the increase be added until the fixed fine is paid, whether half or the whole damage is to be made good. (They estimate the damage as the amount by which the ox and other things lose value through death.) Others, however, claim the whole increase for the one who suffered the loss, and say that nothing is taken into account except the price at which it would have been valued at the time of death, as R. Meir does. But these order that what remains to compensate the damage be added to that price, according to the preceding distinction and method. So these latter understand the words mortuum partientur as if whatever, or however much, death had diminished were ordered to be divided.

units.la: [Hebrew line at foot right: מיקס] ꝑ, quicquid vel quantum mors imminuisset dividi juberetur. Hinc D. Judæ verba plana fiunt. Si modo hoc addas. Verba illa, Cadaver valet 50 drachmis, ita accipienda noris, ut (è D. Judæ sententia) auctum cadaveris pretium semper dividendum esse censeamus: non tantummodo quum cadaver mortis tempore nullius erat pretii, postea vero occasione quadam (quæ multiplex contingere poterit) 50 drachmas valere incipit (uti enim incrementum dividi volebat, si mortis tempore alicujus erat valoris; ita etiam totum pretium, si antea nullius erat: quia tum pretium totum est lucrum & incrementum;) sed etiam aliàs. licet in prioribus istis tantum à Doctore Meïro dissentiat, si restituendi quantitatem, non modum spectes. Ambo enim valoris imminutionem morte factam, dividi in partes æquales (si bos mansuetus lædat) autumant: & cadaver damnum passo cedere; cujus cadaveris valori illud pretium addi debeat, de quo digladiantur. Cæterum ut explicatè docet Maimonides in Nizke Mammon c.7. §.7. & seq. communiter verba legis, mortuum partientur, accipiunt de incremento pretii dividendo, atque exigunt, ut cadaver æstimetur, damnumque passo tradatur; cui tum quanti jumentum morte depretiatum fuerit, sic totum restituendum, vel ejus dimidium, prout pecus convicta, vel innocua censetur. Quod analogicè de minori damno quam morte datur, accipiendum. Adeo ut à verbis legis divinæ recedentes, hanc etiam analogicè non admittant sententiam, quâ exempli gratia in bove petulco, bovis occisi pretium cadaveris pretio addatur; nec qua totius bestiæ pretium exigatur, relicto tamen cadaveris valore, quod eodem recideret. Qui hæc cum legibus Romanis conveniant, liquet ex iis quæ sub finem c. 1. annotata sunt: & cum ibi casus proponatur, quum bos corrupeta damnum dedit; istinc analogicè de alio bove non petulco judicium facere possumus.
units.tr: [Hebrew catchword at foot right: מיקס] ꝑ: whatever, or however much, the death had diminished was ordered to be divided. From this the words of R. Judah become plain, if you add only this. The words The carcass is worth fifty drachmas are to be understood so that, in R. Judah's view, an increase in the carcass's value is always to be divided. This holds not only when the carcass had no value at the time of death and later, through some chance (which can happen in many ways), begins to be worth fifty drachmas. For just as he wanted an increase divided when the carcass had some value at the time of death, so too he wanted the whole price divided when it previously had none, because then the whole price is gain and increase. He also holds this in other cases. In these earlier cases he differs from R. Meïr only if you look at the amount to be restored and not the method. For both hold that the loss in value caused by death is to be divided into equal parts (if a tame ox injures), and that the carcass goes to the injured party. They dispute over which value that price should be added to. Moreover, as Maimonides explains clearly in Nizke Mammon ch. 7, §7 and following, the rabbis commonly take the words of the law, they shall divide the dead, to mean dividing the increase in price. They require that the carcass be valued and handed over to the injured party, and that the animal's value after its death in depreciation be restored to him in full, or half of it, according as the beast is judged a known gorer or harmless. This is to be understood by analogy for a lesser damage than death. So far do they depart from the words of the divine law that they do not even admit by analogy the view by which, for example, in the case of a butting ox, the price of the dead ox is added to the price of the carcass, nor the view by which the price of the whole beast is exacted while the value of the carcass is left out, which would come to the same thing. That these views agree with the Roman laws is clear from what is noted at the end of ch. 1. And since a case is proposed there in which an ox that has gored caused damage, from that we can by analogy form a judgment about another ox that is not a butter.
[illegible]

units.la: יש חייב על מעשה שורו ופטור על מעשה עצמו פטור על מעשה שורו וחייב על מעשה עצמו שורו שבייש פטור והוא שבייש חייב שורו שסימא את עין עבדו והפיל את שינו פטור׳ והוא שסימא את עין עבדו והפיל את שינו חייב שנרו שחבל באביו ואמו חייב והוא שחבל באביו ואמו פטור טורו שהרליק את הגדיש בשבת חייב והוא שהרליק את הגדיש בשב׳ פטור מפני שהוא כחחייב בנפשו׳
units.tr: There is one who is liable for the act of his ox but exempt for his own act, and one who is exempt for the act of his ox but liable for his own act. If his ox shamed someone, he is exempt; but if he himself shamed someone, he is liable. If his ox blinded his slave's eye and knocked out his tooth, he is exempt; but if he himself blinded his slave's eye and knocked out his tooth, he is liable. If his ox struck his father and mother, he is liable; but if he himself struck his father and mother, he is exempt. If his ox set fire to a stack of grain on the Sabbath, he is liable; but if he himself set fire to a stack of grain on the Sabbath, he is exempt, because he is like one who is liable for his own life.

units.la: Est qui tenetur ob factum bovis fui, qui tamen in sui ipsius facto liber est: & contra liber in facto bovis sui, qui tamen ob factum proprium teneatur. Bos alicujus qui hominem dedecorat, liber est; ipse si dedecoret, tenetur: bos qui servi alicujus oculum excaçat, & dentem excutit, liber est; ipse si servi sui oculum excaecet, aut dentem excutiat, tenetur. Si alicujus bos, vitiet patrem aut matrem ipsius, tenetur; ipse si vitiet patrem, aut matrem suam, liber est. Bos alicujus qui metam incendit sabbatho, tenetur; ipse si incendat metam frumenti in sabbatho, liber est. Quia ipse reus mortis peragitur.
units.tr: There is one who is liable for the act of his ox, yet is free in his own act; and conversely one who is free in the act of his ox, yet is liable for his own act. The ox of a man who shames another is free; he himself, if he shames, is liable. The ox of a man who blinds the eye of his slave and knocks out his tooth is free; he himself, if he blinds the eye of his slave or knocks out his tooth, is liable. If a man's ox injures his father or mother, he is liable; he himself, if he injures his father, or his mother, is free. The ox of a man who sets fire to a stack on the Sabbath is liable; he himself, if he sets fire to a stack of grain on the Sabbath, is free. Because he himself is tried as one liable to death.
ANNOTATIONES.

units.la: {2} Sensus est, idem si fiat à bove tuo & à teipso, pœnam aliquando bovis nomine debitam, à te non exigi: non quasi tui facti nomine non teneareris (quod omninò observandum;) sed quia hujus ordinis pœna vel mulĉta quæ hic consideratur, quamque bovis tui factum tibi imponit, non debetur: quamvis aliam quandoque longè graviorem subire tenearis. Quemadmodum sub Misnæ finem de incensa frumenti meta diserte annotatur. Nam si incendium à bove in sabbatho excitetur (uti simile quid de cane in præcedentibus etiam observatum fuit) bovis proprietarius de damno tenetur: at si ipse hoc peccatum committat, ut sabbatho incendium det, mortis ex Judæorum lege reus est. Qui vero morte afficiendus, ab alia pœna absolvitur: secundum vulgarem istam regulam, homo non afficitur morte & damnum simul rependere tenetur. 2 Cæterum bos si dedecore quodam afficiat hominem, bovis possessor absolvitur: כי המכניס נתגלו הוא אדם לא יהוייב כדין הכופת עד סיום מתכוון quia etiamsi dedecorans sit homo, dedecoris crimine non tenetur donec id intendat. At hujusmodi dedecorandi animum in bove reperire non est. Nihilominus Magister Papa hunc dedecorandi impetum bovi imputari vult, si læden e conetur: in Gemara dixisse fertur, נתכוון לכיים היכי מכסחת לה כגון סתכוון להזיק, ut intendat dedecus, quomodo invenis eum? quum lædere intendit. 3 Quod autem bos, id est, bovis dominus, si ille servi oculum excæcet &c. liber censeatur; id interpretes in hanc sententiam exponunt: dominum bovis sui nomine eam pœnam non subire, quæ ipsum si id patrasset manebat ex lege Ex. 21. 26. Quum percusserit quis oculum servi sui aut oculum ancillæ suæ, ita ut corruperit eum; in libertatem dimittito eum pro oculo ejus. Ab omni vero compensatione liberum non pronunciant; si a bove damnum datum fuerit. 4 Sed quod in Misna sequitur, alicui absurdum videri queat: eum qui lædit, vulnerat & aliquo modo vitiat patrem, insontem pronuntiari. Verum illud פטור, solutus sive liber, significat, eum liberum esse מיפטרמי מ, à compensatione damni; non vero ab omni pœna: nam morte tenetur, ut præcipiunt Judæi autoritate legis Exodi 21. 15. Qui percutit patrem suum aut matrem suam, omnino morte plectitor. 5 Quum in Misna de bove corpus humanum lædente vel metam incendente agitur, disputant in Gemara, cujusmodi bos designetur: nonnemo bovem כפס describi existimat. Ejus verba aliaque sequentia proferam & interpretabor, cum ut Judæorum indolem & vanitatem consideremus; tum etiam quod Judæos in illorum sensu reddendo hærere observaverim. לא פטרו הכא בתמי ממקיון כשור פקח שעלתה כסיכר
units.tr: The meaning is this: if the same thing is done by your ox and by you yourself, the penalty that is sometimes owed on account of the ox is not exacted from you. This is not because you would not be liable for your own act (which must be carefully noted), but because the penalty or fine considered here, which your ox's act imposes on you, is not owed. Yet you may sometimes be obliged to undergo another penalty, far more severe. This is stated expressly at the end of the Mishnah, concerning the burning of a field of grain. For if a fire is started by an ox on the Sabbath (as something similar was also observed about a dog in the preceding passages), the owner of the ox is liable for the damage. But if he himself commits this sin, by starting a fire on the Sabbath, he is liable to death under the law of the Jews. And the one who is to be put to death is released from any other penalty, according to this common rule: a man who is to be put to death is not also required to make restitution for the damage. [Hebrew: כי המכניס נתגלו הוא אדם לא יהוייב כדין הכופת עד סיום מתכוון] For even if a man injures by dedecoration, he is not liable for the crime of dedecoration unless he intends it. But an intention of this kind to dishonour cannot be found in an ox. Nevertheless, Master Papa wishes this impulse to dishonour to be imputed to the ox if it attempts to harm. It is said that in the Gemara he said [Hebrew: נתכוון לכיים היכי מכסחת לה כגון סתכוון להזיק] to intend dishonour, how do you find it? When he intends to harm.

units.la: נסיכה כנבו וקו כאי למיקלייה ולגנדר בקומתו ומכו ידעיון דלכתר דקלייה קמנגדר בקומתו ומי הינכו כי כלי גונכו לין הנסוו קורו דהוס כי רכ פנו דהוס כיכין ליה ןחינכיה ענל ופתקיה למייתן וסתי םיכר' ולייתקפי De quo hic agimus? de bove perspicace (S. J. sapiente) qui quum in tergo suo morsus obtigisset, & eum ustulare cuperet, devolvit se in cinerem. At unde novimus, Misnam respicere ad eum qui se ustulavit, devolvitque in cineres. Num est hujusmodi? Est. Nam ille bos qui in adibus Magistri Papae erat, quum ipsi dolerent gingivae dentium, ingressus detrusit operculum & siceram bibit: unde fanatus fuit. Caeterum quod totius Misnae summam concernit, tantum discrimen inter hunc cujus bos laesit, atque illum qui ipse laesit sua quadam actione, non constituunt leges Romanae. Siquidem de quadrupede haec leguntur ff. Si quadrupes l.3. Ex hac lege jam non dubitamus etiam liberarum personarum nomine agi posse: forte si patrem familias aut filium familias vulneravit quadrupes, scilicet ut non deformitatis ratio habeatur, cum liberum corpus aestimationem non recipiat: sed impensarum in curationem factarum & operarum amissarum, quasi amissurus quis esset, inutilis factus. At eadem pene de eo leguntur qui ipse effundendo vel dejiciendo ejusmodi injuria quempiam assicit, tit. De his qui effuderint vel dejecerint, l. ult. Cum liberi hominis corpus ex eo, quod dejectum effusumque quid erit, laesum fuerit: judex computat mercedes medicis praestitas, caeterasque impendia, qua in curatione facta sunt. praeterea operarum (vel, ut alii legunt, operas) quibus caruit, aut cariturus est ob id, quod inutilis factus est. Cicatricum autem, aut deformitatum nulla fit aestimatio: quia liberum corpus nullam recipit aestimationem.
units.tr: As for the statement that the ox, that is, the ox's owner, is deemed free if the ox blinds the eye of his servant, and so on, the commentators explain it to mean that the owner of the ox does not undergo, on account of his ox, the penalty which would have applied had he done it himself under the law of Exodus 21:26: When a man strikes the eye of his servant or the eye of his maidservant, so that he destroys it, he shall let him go free for his eye. But they do not declare him free from all compensation if damage has been done by an ox. What is it, then, that we are discussing here? A perceptive ox, (that is, a wise one), which, when it had been bitten on its back and wanted to burn it, rolled itself in ashes. But how do we know that the Mishnah refers to one who burned himself and rolled in ashes? Is it of this kind? It is. For that ox which belonged to Master Papa, when his gums were paining him, went in, pushed aside the lid and drank strong drink, and so became frenzied. As for the substance of the whole Mishnah, the Roman laws do not establish so great a distinction between this case, where the ox injured, and that case, where a man injured by some action of his own. For these things are read in the Digest about a quadruped: If a quadruped... From this law we no longer doubt that an action can also be brought in the name of free persons: perhaps if a quadruped has wounded a householder or a son under his authority, so that the reckoning of disfigurement is not taken into account, since a free body does not admit of valuation; rather the expenses incurred for treatment and the work lost, as if someone were about to lose it, and has been made unfit. Yet nearly the same things are read about one who injures someone by throwing or casting something down, title: On those who have poured out or cast down, last law: When the body of a free man has been injured by something that has been thrown down or poured out, the judge reckons the fees paid to physicians and the other expenses incurred in the cure; besides, the labour of which he has been deprived, or will be deprived, because he has been made unfit. But no valuation is made for scars or deformities, because a free body admits of no valuation.
§. II.

units.la: Si bos persequatur bovem alium qui laeditur, & hic dicat, Bos tuus laesit; alter vero, Nequaquam, sed ad petram impegit; ei qui a proximo
units.tr: If an ox attacks another ox and injures it, and the owner of the injured ox says, "Your ox injured mine," while the other says, "Not at all; it ran into a rock," the burden of proof falls on the one who claims the damages from his neighbour.

units.la: עליו הראיה היו שנים רודפים אחר אחר זה אומר שורך חזיק וזה אומר שורך הזיק שניהם פטורין אם היו שניהן של איש אחר שניהם חייבים היה אחר גדול ואחד קטן הניזק אומר גדול הזיק והמזיק אומר לא כי אלא קטן הזיק אחר הם ואחד מועד הניזק אומר מועד הזיק והמזיק אומר לא כי אלא הם הזיק המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה היו הניזוקין שנים אחד גדול ואחד קטן והמזיקים שנים אחד גדול ואחד קטן הניזק אומר גדול הזיק את הגדול. וקטן את הקטן והמזיק אומר לא כי אלא קטן את הגדול וגדול את הקטן אחד הם ואחד מועד הניזק אומר [?] ximo suo exigit, incumbit probatio. Si quum duo unum persecuti essent, hic dicat, bos tuus laesit, alter vero, bos tuus laesit, ambo liberi sunt: si ambo unius sint, ambo tenentur. Si quum unus fuisset magnus, alter parvus, proprietarius laesus dicat, Magnus laesit; laedens vero, Nequaquam, sed parvus laesit; aut si cum unus fuisset innocens, alter convictus, laesus dicat, Convictus laesit; laedens vero, Nequaquam, sed innocens laesit. ei qui a proximo suo exigit, incumbit probatio. Si duo boves laesi sint, unus magnus, alter parvus, similiter duo laedentes, unus magnus; alter parvus; & possessor laesus dicat, Magnus laesit magnum, & parvus parvum; laedens vero, Nequaquam, sed parvus laesit magnum, & magnus parvum; aut quum unus fuisset innocens, alter convictus, laesus dicat; Convictus laesit magnum, & innocens parvum; laedens vero dicat, Nequaquam, sed innocens laesit magnum, & convictus parvum: ei qui a proximo suo exigit probatio in numbit.
units.tr: If two oxen pursued one another, and one owner says, "Your ox injured," while the other says, "Your ox injured," both are free from liability. If both oxen belonged to another man, both are liable. If one ox was large and the other small, and the injured owner says, "The large one injured," while the one who did the injury says, "No, the small one injured," or the reverse; if one was accustomed to do such damage and the other was not, and the injured owner says, "The accustomed one injured," while the other says, "No, the innocent one injured," the burden of proof falls on the one who claims from his neighbour. If two oxen were injured, one large and one small, and two oxen did the injury, one large and one small, and the injured owner says, "The large injured the large, and the small the small," while the owner of the injuring oxen says, "No, the small injured the large, and the large the small," or, where one was innocent and the other convicted, and the injured owner says, "The convicted injured the large, and the innocent the small," while the injurer says, "No, the innocent injured the large, and the convicted the small," the burden of proof falls on the one who claims from his neighbour.
H ... Anno-

units.la: Passim in his libris, quum de bove aliisque irrationalibus dicitur ꝑ, reus est, sive tenetur, idem sensus ac si diceretur, dominos sive proprietarios eorum nomine teneri: quod enim pecudes patrant, possessoribus imputatur. Cum ergo de damno ejusve dimidio rependendo agitur, existimandum non est, ex Judaeorum lege pecora quae damnum dederunt vindicari posse, ut inde laeso satisfiat: sed conveniendus est dominus; adversus quem ex lege actio eo casu competit. In sequentibus dominorum contentionem istam merito quis prima fronte miretur, qua de bobus altercantes introducuntur; an bos magnus an parvus, petulcusne an mansuetus alterum laeserit: minimi enim vel nihil interesse videtur, quis ex ipsis laeserit, si de damno constet. At si quis penitius rem intueatur, magni saepe referre deprehendet, cui damnum imputetur: idque ob illam in superioribus explicatam rependendi differentiam, qua totum damnum praestandi modus ab eo discernitur, quo rependitur dimidium; praeterea quia petulcus & convictus totum, innocens sive mansuetus dimidium debet. Quocirca non levi cum ratione laesus, magnum bovem; laedens, bovem parvum dedisse damnum contendet: quippe hic, etsi bos parvus dimidium occisi bovis (quum dimidium compensandum est, ut si mansuetus occiderit) non aequabit, totum tradens bovem liber erit; quia e bovis corpore solutio praestatur, uti dictum ad cap. 1. sect. 4. nota 8. Ille vero, nisi magnus dedisse damnum statuatur, quum e corpore bovis restitutio fit, minus dimidio aliquando reportabit. Ita etiam merito laedens sive cujus bos laesit, mansuetum laesisse; laesus vero, petulcum laesisse contendet: quandoquidem illo casu dimidium; hoc vero totum damnum compensabit. Eadem ratione in exemplis sequentibus laesus & laedens altercantur, ubi quatuor sunt boves: duo lædentes, duo læsi. Etenim læso expedit, ut magnus magnum læsisse dicatur: siquidem dimidium saltem damni in magno dati facilius è magni pretio conficitur; ita ut parvi lædentis valor pro parvo læso refervetur: at lædenti conducit magis, ut suus bos parvus læserit magnum, & magnus parvum: quò si parvus forte bovis occisi dimidium non æquet, minus dimidio rependat; & cum dimidium omninò compensandum est, in parvo bove occiso id potius facere teneatur. Similiter læso, id est, cujus bos læsus vel occisus fuit, ei inquam expedit ut petulcus & convictus occiderit magnum; & innocens, sive mansuetus, parvum: quia eo casu magnus totus compensabitur; & cum in mansueto dimidium occisi pretium non invenitur, minus amittet si parvi, quam si magni dimidium omninò compensari nequeat. Contra lædenti magis probatur, ut innocès læserit magnum; quia tum magni dimidium tantummodo solvet: ita etiam, ut convictus parvum; quia hoc casu qui totus compensandus (utpote à petulco convicto occisus) is parvus est: itaque minori suo damno rependet, quam si magnus totus compensandus esset. Porrò Mišna autumat in istis altercationibus ac litibus ei probationem incumbere; qui ab altero quid exigit, id est, qui sibi alterum debere affirmat. Hac in parte consentit lex 2. ff. De probationibus, tit. 3. li. 22. Ei incumbit probatio, qui dicit; non qui negat. Cui convenientia leguntur verbal. 5. Ab ea parte quæ dicit adversarium suum ab aliquo jure prohibitum esse specialiter lege vel constitutione, id probari oportere. Et l. 22. quamvis quidam casus excipi dicantur; tamen id communis juris esse traditur. Prima fronte æquius videtur, ut petitor probet quod intendit: sed nimirum probationes quædam à reo exiguntur. Vide etiam Inst. de legatis §. 4. sub finem: Semper necessitas probandi incumbit illi, qui agit.
units.tr: Throughout these books, when it is said of an ox or other irrational animal that it is ꝑ, that it is liable, or held to answer, the sense is the same as if it were said that its owners or proprietors are held liable on its account, since what beasts do is imputed to their possessors. So when the question is of making good the damage, or half of it, one should not suppose that under the law of the Jews the animals that caused the damage can be seized so that the injured party may be satisfied from them. Rather the owner must be sued, and against him the action lies by law in that case. In the following passages one may rightly wonder, at first sight, at the dispute of the owners, in which the oxen are introduced quarrelling: whether the large ox or the small, the goring ox or the tame one, injured the other. For it seems to matter very little, or not at all, which of them did the injury, provided the damage is established. But if one looks into the matter more closely, one will find that it often matters greatly to whom the damage is imputed. This is because of the difference in making compensation explained above, by which the manner of paying the whole damage is distinguished from that by which half is paid; moreover, a goring ox that has been warned owes the whole, while an innocent or tame ox owes half. Accordingly, the injured party with good reason will contend that the large ox gave the damage, and the one causing it that the small ox did. For the small ox, though it does not equal half of the dead ox (since half is to be compensated, as when a tame ox has killed), when it hands over the whole ox is free; because satisfaction is made from the body of the ox, as was said at chapter 1, section 4, note 8. But the other party, unless the large ox is held to have done the injury, when restitution is made from the body of the ox, will sometimes recover less than half. So too the one causing the damage, or whose ox did the injury, will rightly contend that it was a tame ox that injured, while the injured party will contend that it was a goring ox, since in that case it compensates half, but in the latter case the whole damage. By the same reasoning, in the following examples the injured and the one causing the injury dispute where there are four oxen, two causing and two injured. For it is advantageous to the injured party that the large ox be said to have injured the large one, since at least half of the damage done to the large ox is more easily made up from the price of the large ox, so that the value of the small causing ox is kept for the small injured one. But it is more advantageous to the one causing the injury that his small ox injured the large, and the large the small; for if the small ox does not equal half of the dead ox, he pays less than half; and when half must be compensated in full, he is bound rather to do so for the small ox killed. Similarly, for the injured party, that is, the one whose ox was injured or killed, it is advantageous, I say, that a goring and warned ox killed the large one, and an innocent or tame one the small; because in that case the large one will be compensated in full; and since in a tame ox half the price of the dead ox is not found, he will lose less if half of the small is not made good than if half of the large cannot be compensated at all. On the other hand, it is more approved for the one causing the damage that an innocent ox injured the large one, since then he will pay only half of the large one's value; likewise that a warned ox injured the small one, since in this case the animal to be compensated in full (being killed by a warned, goring ox) is the small one; so he will make good with less loss than if the large one had to be compensated in full. Moreover, the Mishnah affirms that in these disputes and lawsuits the burden of proof lies on the one who demands something from another, that is, on the one who asserts that the other owes him. In this point the law agrees, D. 22.3.2, On Proofs: The burden of proof lies on him who asserts, not on him who denies. With this agree the words at 5: The party which says that its opponent is specifically forbidden by some law or constitution from some right must prove it. And at 22, although certain cases are said to be excepted, yet this is handed down as the common law: At first sight it seems fairer that the claimant prove what he asserts; but certain proofs are indeed required of the defendant. See also the Institutes, On Legacies, §4 at the end: The necessity of proving always rests on him who sues.

units.la: Quum bos cornu ferit quatuor aut quinq; boves alium post alium; compensandus eorum [?] postremus.
units.tr: When an ox gores four or five oxen, one after another, the last of them is compensated.

units.la: שור שנגח ארבע' והי שוורי זה אחר זה ישלם לאחרון שכהם ואם יש בו מוהר יחזיר לשלפניו ואם יש בו מוהר יחזיר לשלפני פניו והאחרון אחרון נשכר דברי רבי מאיר רבי שמעון אומר שור שוה מאתים שנגח שור שוה מאתים ואין הנבלה יפה כלום זה נוטל מנה וזה נוטל מנה חזר ונגח שור אחר שוה מאתים האחרון נוטל מנה ושלפניו זה נוטל חמשים זו וזה נוטל חמשים זו חזר ונגח שור אחר שוה מא זים האחרון נוטל מנה ושלפניו חמשים זו ושני' הראשונים דינר זהב: quod si ex isto quid superfit, hoc ad precedentem remittit; & si amplius quid restet, ad remotiorem pertinebit; atque ita remotissimus postremo compensandus, ut quidem statuit Doctor Meir. D. Simeon inquit, Si bos ducentarum drachmarum feriat bovem ejusdem pretii, & cadaver nullius sit pretii, hic minam; & alter similiter minam auferet: & si denuo ferierit alium bovem ducentarum drachmarum, possessor posterioris, minam auferet; & priorum, unus auferet 50 drachmas, & alter quinquaginta. Si denuò ferierit bovem alium ducentarum, postremi possessor minam auferet; antecedens verò, quinquaginta drachmas; duo verò primi habebunt singuli denarium aureum, id est, drachmas argenteas 25.
units.tr: If an ox gores four oxen one after another, they pay the last of them; and if there is any surplus in it, it returns to the one before, and if there is any surplus again, it returns to the one before that, and the last is compensated last. These are the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Simeon says: if an ox worth two hundred gores an ox worth two hundred, and the carcass is worth nothing, this one takes a mina and that one takes a mina. If it gores again another ox worth two hundred, the last takes a mina, and the one before it takes fifty, and the two first each take fifty. If it gores another ox worth two hundred, the last takes a mina, the one before fifty, and the first two have a gold denarius each, that is, twenty-five silver drachmas. [שור שנגח ארבע' והי שוורי זה אחר זה ישלם לאחרון שכהם ואם יש בו מוהר יחזיר לשלפניו ואם יש בו מוהר יחזיר לשלפני פניו והאחרון אחרון נשכר דברי רבי מאיר רבי שמעון אומר שור שוה מאתים שנגח שור שוה מאתים ואין הנבלה יפה כלום זה נוטל מנה וזה נוטל מנה חזר ונגח שור אחר שוה מאתים האחרון נוטל מנה ושלפניו זה נוטל חמשים זו וזה נוטל חמשים זו חזר ונגח שור אחר שוה מא זים האחרון נוטל מנה ושלפניו חמשים זו ושני' הראשונים דינר זהב]

units.la: Quod hic statuitur, iniquum videretur, puta quum pluribus damnum infertur, postremo tantum satisfieri: nisi Gemara casum plenius explicaret, הכל כמהי עסקינן כגון טפשטו גוין לגבות היזמו וכפשטה עלי כפוימר סכר לנוקין, Hic de quo agimus? Nempe quum prehendit eum lasus, ut ab eo exigat debitum, ideoque ejus respectu facti est veluti custos mercenarius, quod damna attinet. Hoc sibi volunt: priores damnum passos proprietario ipsius lædentis bovis adeo fieri similes, ut damnum postremo illatum ipsis imputetur; quum veriti ut proprietarius secundum legem ipsis satisfaciat, in bovem alius post alium manum injiciunt, quò de compensatione reddantur securi. Quo facto iis assimilantur, qui accepta mercede boves custodiunt; ideoque dato à bobus damno, culpæ tenentur. Similiter enim, quare primus cum læsus bovem in sua potestate habebat, negligentia sua præbebat secundo damno occasionem, & secundus similiter, adeo ut tandem postremus damnum pateretur? Sed objectionem in promptu esse video.
units.tr: This ruling would seem unjust, namely when damage is inflicted on several people and in the end the last one alone receives satisfaction, unless the Gemara explained the case more fully: "What are we dealing with here? Such as when the gentiles have seized it to collect the damage, and as the matter stands, it is a paid guard in respect of the damages" [הכל כמאי עסקינן כגון שטפשו גוים לגבות היזיקו וכפשטה על כופמר שכר לנוקין]. What is the case we are discussing? Clearly, when the injured party has seized the ox so as to exact what is owed to him; and so with respect to the act, he is like a paid guardian, so far as the damages are concerned. The meaning is this: the earlier victims of damage are so similar to the owner of the goring ox that the damage finally inflicted is imputed to them, since they fear that the owner will not satisfy them according to law. So they lay hands on the ox, one after another, so that they may be secure about compensation. By doing this they become like those who keep oxen for a wage, and therefore, when the ox causes damage, they are held liable. For why should the first, when he who was injured had the ox in his power, by his negligence provide the second with an occasion for damage, and the second likewise, so that at last the last one suffered the loss? But I see that an objection is ready to hand.

Quomodo igitur hic sequitur, si ex illo quid superfit &c.? sanè hæc, omnino de bove mansueto sive nondum saltem convicto sermonem esse, demonstrant: quia in damno per convictum dato, secundum Judæorum constitutiones non expendebatur an bos lædens ad compensationem sufficeret vel quid superesset; siquidem ꝓ̈ ꝓ̈ ꝓ̈, è præstantissimis facultatibus solutio urgebatur. Verumenimvero responsio facilis, Priora Mișnæ verba ideo non arguere, de convicto bove constitutionem intelligendam esse: quia nullo modo eum bovem Mișna describit qui ex intervallo cornu lædit alium; sed post bovem læsum, alias videns semel vel etiam aliquoties alios boves, lædere supersedet, nec eatenus à mansueto differt: adeo ut intervalla, quibus data licet occasione abstinet, cum mansuetis vel potius non convictis annumerari suadeant.3 Quum aliquid restare vel superesse dicitur, ita intelligas, quum possessor bovis non teneatur de damno, quod negligentia secundi & tertii læsi postea datum fuit, (quare non
units.tr: 2 For according to c. 2, Mishnah 4, an animal is judged convicted by repeated injury: for example, a goring ox that has often struck with its horn. So if, as at the beginning of the Mishnah, it gores a fifth time, it is no longer considered innocent or tame. How, then, does what follows, si ex illo quid superfit &c., fit in here? Surely these words show that the discussion concerns a tame ox, or at least one not yet convicted, because for damage done by a convicted ox, according to the Jewish regulations, it was not weighed whether the ox that did the harm would suffice for compensation or whether anything would be left over, since payment was demanded from the best of the owner's property. But the answer is easy: the preceding words of the Mishnah do not prove that the regulation must be understood of a convicted ox, for the Mishnah does not describe in any way an ox that gores another at intervals. Rather, after injuring one ox, it sees other oxen once or even several times and refrains from injuring them, and in this respect it does not differ from a tame ox. So the intervals during which it refrains, though it has the opportunity, suggest that it should be counted among tame oxen, or rather among those not convicted. When it is said that something remains or is left over, understand it thus: since the owner of the ox is not liable for the damage that was afterwards done through the negligence of the second and third injured oxen (for which reason they did not keep the ox upon which they had laid hands:)

Exempli gratia, bos duarum minarum occiderit alium ejusdem pretii; ubi possessori mina cedit: laesus prehensum bovem dimiserit, ut secundo alium bovem occidat unius minae; adeoque ei qui posterius laeditur, quinquaginta debeantur drachmae: quinquaginta drachmae restabunt, quas solas prior damnum passus reportabit; quum alias centum, id est minam acciperet. ⁴ Caeterum Doctor Simeon societatem illam & convenientiam superius expositam ita urget, ut e prioris laesi, postquam postremus dimidium ex lege accepit, altero dimidio suam singuli cum bovis laedentis proprietario partem auferant: siquidem deteriori loco esse nequeunt quam is cujus bos totius damni author fuerat: quin potius primis, cum multiplex fuerit damnum, minimam portionem ascribit. (verum istum casum considerat, ubi laesi priores manum in bovem non injecerint; si enim hoc fecerint, a priori non dissentit.) Sed postremo quia culpa omni caret semper, cum bos valet 200 drachmas, minam attribuit: mina autem est drachmarum centum; uti e quamplurimis horum librorum paragraphis observare licet. nec ulla dubitandi ratio se offert. ⁵ Aureus autem denarius vigintiquinque drachmis argenteis valet: quemadmodum interpretes communi consensu affirmant; & omnino e c. 4. Babae mediae in sequentibus constabit. Ab hac Misna non alienum est quod exstat ff. Si quadrupes, l. 1. §. 12. Et, cum etiam in quadrupedibus noxa caput sequitur, adversus dominum hac actio datur, non cujus fuerit quadrupes cum noceret; sed cujus nunc est. Ergo consequitur, si alicujus bos (uti Misna proponit) diversorum boves laeserit, & in priorum potestatem devenerit, adversus eos vel eum cujus postea fuerit, actionem dari: adeoque fieri quandoque posse, ut non solum proprietarius lædentis bovis teneatur, veluti si bovem retinuerit; sed etiam isti ordine, quorum alii boves ab eodem læsi fuerant antequam ultimus damnum pateretur: modo in bovem lædentem manus injecerint. Atque hoc est Misnæ fundamentum: quum priores bovem aliudve noxium animal occupaverint, postremo actionem in alios competere; ideoque debitam sibi ex lege divina multam consequi, relicto eo quod restat, prioribus. Simile quid de servo legitur Iust. l. 4. t. 8. §. 5. Omnis autem noxalis actio caput sequitur. Nam si servus tuus noxam commiserit, quandiu in tua potestate fit, tecum est actio. Si autem in alterius potestatem pervenerit, cum illo incipit actio esse.
units.tr: 2 Digitised text: the foot-note Hebrew and Greek phrases are copied as printed where legible; the Hebrew phrase aster "Judæorum" is illegible on the scan. did not keep the ox on which they laid hands) must bear its own half of the loss; the last to suffer loss likewise; and if anything is left over, the intermediate one or ones shall have it. For example, an ox worth two minas kills another of the same value; the owner pays one mina; the injured party, having seized the ox, releases it so that it kills a second ox worth one mina. So the one injured later is owed fifty drachmas. Fifty drachmas will remain, which the first who suffered loss alone will recover, whereas otherwise he would receive a hundred, that is, a mina. ⁴ Moreover, the Doctor Simeon presses that fellowship and agreement explained above in such a way that, after the last injured party has received half the loss by law, the individual earlier injured parties take from the other half their own share together with the owner of the harming ox, since they cannot be in a worse position than the one whose ox was the author of the whole loss. Indeed, he assigns the smallest portion to the first, when the loss is manifold. (But he considers that case where the earlier injured parties did not lay hands on the ox; for if they did, he does not dissent from the earlier view.) But for the last, since he is always free of all fault, when the ox is worth 200 drachmas, he assigns a mina. A mina, however, is worth one hundred drachmas, as may be observed from very many paragraphs of these books; nor does any ground for doubt present itself. ⁵ Now a gold denarius is worth twenty-five silver drachmas, as the interpreters affirm with common consent; and this will be altogether clear from chapter 4 of Baba Metzia below. Not foreign to this Mishnah is what stands in the Digest, Si quadrupes, law 1, §12: "And since in quadrupeds too liability follows the head, the action is given against the owner, not of whoever owned the quadruped when it did harm, but of whoever now owns it." It follows, then, that if one man's ox (as the Mishnah proposes) has harmed the oxen of several others, and has come into the power of the first, an action is given against them, or against him to whom it later passed; and so it may sometimes happen that not only the owner of the harming ox is liable, as when he has kept the ox, but also those in order, whose other oxen had been harmed by the same ox before the last suffered loss, provided they laid hands on the harming ox. And this is the foundation of the Mishnah: when the first have seized the ox, or another harmful animal, the action lies against others for the last; and therefore the last obtains the fine due to him by divine law, leaving to the first what remains. Something similar is read of a slave in Justinian's Institutes, book 4, title 8, §5: "Every noxal action follows the head. For if your slave has committed a wrong, as long as he is in your power, the action lies with you. But if he has come into another's power, the action begins to lie with that person."

units.la: Bos convictus respectu speciei suæ, nec convictus respectu aliarum specierum; convictus hominis respectu, nec bestiæ respectu convictus; convictus respectu minorum bestiarum, nec majorum respectu convictus: secundum quam speciem convictus est, præstatur damnum totum; & secundum quam speciem non est convictus, dimidium damni præstatur. Propositum fuerunt coram D. Iuda, Ecce secundum sabbatha; non vero dies profestos sit convictus. Ipsis respondit, Quoad sabbatha præstabitur totum damnum; quoad dies profestos præstabitur damni dimidium. Quando innocens censebitur? Quum ab eo abstinuerit tribus sabbathis.
units.tr: An ox is considered convicted with respect to its own species but not with respect to other species; convicted with respect to man, but not with respect to a beast; convicted with respect to smaller beasts, but not with respect to larger ones. For the species with respect to which it is convicted, the full damage is paid; for the species with respect to which it is not convicted, half the damage is paid. A case was put before Rabbi Judah: if it has gored on the Sabbath, is it convicted, but not if on weekdays? He answered: with respect to Sabbaths, the full damage is paid; with respect to weekdays, half the damage is paid. When is it deemed innocent? When it has abstained from goring for three Sabbaths.
