units.la: {1} Hic è Gemara spinosas quæstiones non repetam: sed id solum annoto, Etsi casus propositi forte inverti non possint, ut convictum respectu aliarum specierum non esse convictum respectu suæ speciei, &c. nihilominus contingere, ut bos, de quo denunciatum fuerit testibus adhibitis domino ejus (secundum Ex. 21. 29.) ipsum esse petulcum, in feriendo alio bove in specie sua; tamen in lædenda alia animantium specie ita convictus non sit: quod ad reliqua exempla extendendum. Etenim in his exemplis posterius membrum majus quid continet, quò non tam facile animal delabitur: nec ex minori audacia major consequitur. {2} Minora autem animalia in hac lege non censentur tantum oves & capræ ac similia; sed in majorum generibus etiam ea, quæ suam naturalem quantitatem nondum adepta sunt, ut juvencæ, equuleï atque id genus alia. {3} Et convictorum quidem animalium respectu damnum totum est refundendum: attamen si dubium fuerit, num respectu hujus vel illius animalis bos convictus haberi debeat, solum dimidium compensabitur. Itaque Maimonides quum Cod. de damnis pecuniariis c.6. varios casus dubios propositset, tandem subjicit, [illegible, ~20 letters] Et in omnibus ijs dubiis ac similibus non condemnant ledentem nisi in dimidium damni: quod si verò acceperit lasus perfectam damni compensationem, ex ipsius manu non repetunt.
units.tr: {1} I will not repeat the thorny questions from the Gemara here. I note only this: although the case as stated cannot perhaps be reversed, so that an animal convicted with respect to other species is not convicted with respect to its own species, etc., it can nevertheless happen that an ox, which has been declared, in the presence of witnesses, to its owner to be a gorer (according to Exod. 21:29), is convicted in striking another ox of its own species, yet is not convicted in injuring another kind of animal. The same is to be extended to the remaining examples, for in these examples the latter member contains something greater, by which an animal does not so easily slip, and from less boldness no greater boldness follows. {2} In this law, however, the smaller animals are not counted only as sheep and goats and the like, but within the kinds of larger animals also those that have not yet reached their natural size, such as heifers, colts, and the other animals of that sort. {3} For the damage done by convicted animals must be made good in full. Yet if it is doubtful whether an ox ought to be considered convicted with respect to this or that animal, only half the damage will be compensated. Accordingly, Maimonides, when in the treatise on pecuniary damages, chapter 6, he had set out various doubtful cases, finally adds: In all these doubtful and similar cases they condemn the one causing the injury only to half the damage; but if the injured party has received full compensation, they do not reclaim it from his hand.

units.la: {4} Sed quid sibi verba ista volunt? Si secundum sabbatha, non verò dies profestos sit convictus. An boves sabbathum ab aliis diebus distinguere solent? Sanè impossibile non est ut hoc die magis quam illo lædant, si alio modo habeantur. sicuti inquit Ifacides, in glossa, [illegible, ~25 letters] Convictus est respectu sabbathi, quia cum cessat ab opere suo, insolens in ipso indoles sua redditur. Addit R. Isaac Gabbæus, [illegible, ~3 letters] הזה בני אדם במלבוש צבעוני כאיש ולישון מכוון Aliquando bos intuetur hominum filios pulchris vestimentis indutos,nec eos agnoscit. Experientia docet rubrum colorem (quo pretiosiores vestes sæpe imbutas videmus) tauris ingratiorem, adeo ut ipso ad feritatem commoveantur. Huc ad aliaque similia forte ille respexit. 5 Hujusmodi autem bos, si cum sabbatho cornu ferire consueverit, postea ab isto vitio per tria sabbatha abstineat, innocens & mansuetus pronuntiabitur: idque analogicè è Misna 4. c. 2. ut enim tres dies convictum arguunt vel mansuetum; sic etiam tria sabbatha, licet non sint dies continui: modo alia sabbatha non intercesserint, quibus alios læserit. In Romanis legibus etiam inter quadrupedem quæ naturæ feritate commovetur, & eam quæ alia quadam de causa alteri nocet, discrimen innuitur: quum ff. Si quadrupes, l.1. §. 4. ita habetur, Tunc hæc actio (de qua legis initio) locum habet, cum commota feritate nocuit quadrupes: puta si equus calcitrosus calce percusserit; aut bos cornu petere solitus, petierit. Quò etiam refero ultima verba §.7. Si quum equum permulsisset quis, vel palpatus esset, calce eum percusserit; erit actioni locus. id enim signum habetur, quadrupedem istam jam efferatam fuisse. Quemadmodum contra mansuetus judicatur apud Judæos c. 2. Misna 4. bos ille, qui à pueris palpatus non ferit cornu. Neque in priori lege paragraphum 11. sententiæ nostræ officere existimo, ubi ita Vlpianus, Cum arietes, vel boves commisissent, & alter alterum occidit; Quintus Mucius distinxit, ut, si quidem is perisset, qui aggressus erat, cessaret actio, si is, qui non provocaverat, competeret actio. Quamobrem eum sibi aut noxam sarcire, aut in noxam dedere oportere. Namque hic etiam bos adgressus convenienter paragrapho quarto talis censetur qui feritate commotus fuerit: quod non ideo tantum constat, quia cum isto quarto paragrapho hic undecimus convenire debet; sed etiam quod adgressi & provocantis cõditio deterior constituatur, quam ejus qui non provocaverat. ideoque innocens & mansuetus habebatur. Fateor tamen inter hunc bovem, de quo leges Rom.isto titulo loquuntur,& eum quem Judæi in hoc codice מועד, testimonio convictum vocant, hanc esse differentiam. hujus vitium, exempli gratia quod petulcus sit bos, dominum quà vitio laborat non gravare,nisi id ipsi comprobatum fuerit; at secus in quadrupede in lege Si qu. memorata: siquidem admittantur quæ Gothofredus ad §. 4. ex Græc. schol.annotavit, illum casum sic accipiendum,quum dominus quadrupedis vitium ignoravit.
units.tr: {4} But what do those words mean? If it was convicted on the Sabbath, and not on working days. Do oxen customarily distinguish the Sabbath from the other days? Certainly it is not impossible that they injure more on this day than on that, if they are kept in another way, as Ifacides says in the gloss: It is convicted with respect to the Sabbath, because when it ceases from its work its disposition becomes unusually wild. R. Isaac Gabbai adds: [...] הזה בני אדם במלבוש צבעוני כאיש ולישון מכוון [...]; sometimes an ox looks at the sons of men dressed in many-coloured clothing and does not recognise them. Experience teaches that the colour red (in which we often see more costly garments dyed) is more unpleasant to bulls, so that they are roused to ferocity by it. Perhaps he had this and similar things in mind. {5} An ox of this sort, however, if it has been accustomed to gore with its horn on the Sabbath, and afterwards abstains from that vice for three Sabbaths, is pronounced innocent and gentle; and this is argued by analogy from Mishnah 4, chapter 2. For just as three days establish that an animal is convicted or gentle, so also three Sabbaths, even though they are not consecutive days, provided that no other Sabbaths have intervened in which it has injured others. In the Roman laws too a distinction is indicated between a quadruped which is stirred to ferocity by its wild nature and one which harms another for some other reason, since in the Digest, Si quadrupes, law 1, §4, it is stated: That action (of which the beginning of the law speaks) has its place when the quadruped has injured with its ferocity roused: for example, if a kicking horse has struck with its heel, or an ox accustomed to butt with its horn has butted. To this I also refer the final words of §7: If someone, after stroking a horse or having been caressed by it, has been struck by its heel, there will be room for the action. For this is taken as a sign that such a quadruped was already enraged. In the same way, among the Jews, that ox is judged gentle which, though handled by boys, does not gore with its horn (Mishnah 4, chapter 2). Nor do I think that paragraph 11 of the earlier law stands in the way of our opinion, where Ulpian says: When rams or oxen have fought, and one has killed the other, Quintus Mucius distinguished: if indeed the one that attacked had died, the action should cease; if the one that had not provoked the fight, the action should lie. Therefore the owner must either make good the damage or surrender the animal in noxal reparation. For here also the ox that attacked is, in agreement with the fourth paragraph, regarded as one that was roused to ferocity. This is clear not only because this eleventh paragraph ought to agree with that fourth paragraph, but also because the condition of the one who attacked and provoked is set down as worse than that of the one who had not provoked, and so the latter was regarded as innocent and gentle. I admit, however, that there is this difference between the ox about which the Roman laws speak under that title and the one which the Jews in this tractate call mu'ad [מועד], convicted by testimony: the fault of the latter, for example that the ox is a gorer, does not burden its owner, who suffers from the vice, unless this has been proved to him; but otherwise in the quadruped in the law Si quadrupes mentioned above, provided that what Godefroy noted at §4 from the Greek scholia is admitted, that this case is to be understood as when the owner of the quadruped was ignorant of the vice.

units.la: שור של ישראל שנגח שור של הקדש ושל הקדש שנגח שור של ישראל פטור שנאי שור רעהו ולא שור של הקדש שור של ישראל שנגח לשור של עובדי אלילים פטור ושל עובדי אלילים שנגח לשור של ישראל ביז חכם בין מועד משלם נזק שלם׃
units.tr: If an Israelite's ox gores a consecrated ox, or a consecrated ox gores an Israelite's ox, it is exempt, since the text says "his neighbour's ox" [שור רעהו] and not "a consecrated ox." If an Israelite's ox gores an idolater's ox, it is exempt; but if an idolater's ox gores an Israelite's ox, whether it is an innocent ox [תם] or one that has gored before [מועד], it pays full damages.

units.la: Si bos Israelita cornu petat bovem sacrum, aut bos sacer cornu petat bovem Israelita; possessor liber est, quia dicitur (Ex. 21. 35.) Bos proximi sui, non verò Bos sacer. Si bos Israelita cornu petat bovem Idololatra, possessor liber est; si verò bos Idololatra cornu petat bovem Israelita, sive innocens, sive convictus, totum damnum præstatur.
units.tr: If an Israelite's ox gores a sacred ox, or a sacred ox gores an Israelite's ox, the owner is free, because it is said (Ex. 21:35) "the ox of his neighbour," but not "the sacred ox." If an Israelite's ox gores an idolater's ox, the owner is free; but if an idolater's ox gores an Israelite's ox, whether innocent or convicted, full damage is paid.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Vt nihil de bove sacro & consecrato Jovæ dicam, sed eum suo loco relinquam; id sane ferri non potest, istos homines ita Dei legem in arctum cogere,ac si in hac causa gentiles impunè lædere, Israëlitis liceret. Nam quod Idololatrarum fiat mentio, ipsorum oculos in istos non defigit; sed quosvis gentiles,qui septem præcepta filiis Noæ tradita non observant,intendunt; sicuti è Gemara liquet. atqui ultimo præpraecepto Christianos non teneri censemus: itaque Christianos etiam impune expilare licebit. Etenim in Sanedrin f.56. p.1. circa sin. septimum continet interdictum, לא תאכלו, membrum de vivo animali, scilicet, comedendum non esse. Vt praeteream illic p. 2. subjungi, [Hebrew], Interdicta filiis Noachi animalium heterogeneorum admissio, & arboris insitio. at quibus haec apud nos prohibita sunt? Sed operaepretium est illius sententiae fundamentum examinare, quare gentilibus istis damna in facultatibus data compensanda non sint. Gemara ait, Deum gentilium, qui data Noachi filiis praecepta (quae recensent) non observant, bona proscripsisse & occupantis fecisse. licet alibi secus sentire videantur: ut Maim. de furto c. 1. §.1. & c.2. §.1. At perbellas rationes quibus istud fundamentum innititur expendamus. Producitur e Deut.33. 2. [Hebrew], illuxit Deus e monte Pharanis: unde concluditur in Gemara, [Hebrew], E Pharane publicavit eorum pecuniam, id est, bona Israelitis. quasi dicas, illustravit & ostendit eorum scilicet Ismaelitarum bona, eaque veluti ob oculos posuit Israelitis ut ea caperent. [Hebrew], pecuniam eorum manifestavit & publicavit. Verum haec altius repetenda sunt. Fingunt, Deum priusquam populo suo Israelitico legem daret, eam populis aliis obtulisse, puta Ismaelitis & Edomaeis: quod exprimit Salomon Isacides c. 33. Deut. circa initium: [Hebrew], Prius filiis Esavi proposuit ut legem acciperent; sed noluerunt: pergens ad Pharanis montem exhibuit eam filiis Ismaelis, ut ipsam acciperent; sed noluerunt: tandem ad Israelitas venit. At in commentariis ad Bavam 1. c. 4. latius hoc extendit: [Hebrew], circuivit & circumduxit legem ad omnes populos, qui eam non susceperunt. (Ideo additamenta ajunt, [Hebrew], Deum in Pharane Gentibus apparuisse.) Itaque eorum bona in publicum addixit. Sed quia hanc rationem non sufficere videbant, ei aliam è 3. capite Habakuk v. 6. adjunxerunt: verba Prophetæ sunt, Constitit & mensus est terram, vidit & יף diffurbavit gentes. Hæc ita in Gem. explicantur, רֹאשׁ י׳ מִנּוֹת סִקְבּוּ עָלָיו בְּנֵי נוֹחַ כְּיִן שְׁלֹשׁ קְיֵמוּ עֲמוֹד וּיִתֵּיר מִמּוּנוּם לִיִשְׂרָאֵל, Considerauit septem præcepta quæ in se susceperant filii Noæ: quandoquidem non præstiterant ea, constituit, proscripsit ac licitam fecit eorum pecuniam sive bona Israelitis. Ergo videmus Edomæorum bona etiam in ista proscriptione contineri. Quam hoc figmentum pulchrè convenit cum lege Dei Deut. 2. 5. Nec bellum miscete cum illis, non enim daturus sum vobis de terra eorum, vel vestigium plantæ pedis: nam hereditarium dedi Esavo montem Seiris. 6. Cibum comparate ab eis pecunia, quem comedatis; & similiter aquam emitote ab eis pecunia. Hæccine verba permittunt, ut eorum bona Israelitis data censeamus? Verumenimvero ut posteriorem locum scilicet Habakuk præteream, unde ex insulsa verbi יף expositione argumentantur; prior locus inspiciendus: hinc enim ansam erroris arripuerunt, quod cum non perciperent qui præsentiæ divinæ lux è Seïre & Pharane illuxisse dicatur, eò retulerint, quasi illuc Deus legem quandam tulerit vel Israëlitarum, vel aliorum filiorum Noæ futuram; quam cum hi neglexissent, in istam multam inciderint. Quomodo Deus è Sinai prodierit cum lege sua, & sua gratia, quâ deinde populum comitatus fuit, dubitat nemo. sed qui ortus è Seïre, illuxit è Pharane? Post Sinai ponitur Seïr (pro quo Habakuk 3.3. מדרום, meridies: quia erat ad meridiem Canaan) deinde Pharan: licet enim mons Paran secundo loco collocādus videretur, ut qui monti Sinai propior, prius ex Ægypto egredientibus occurreret, quam Sehir; tamen satis causæ fuit ut in verborum ordine postponeretur. Quia itineris ordinem quidem spectavit cum Moses, tum Habakuk; sed temporis seriem, non locorum situm expendens. Ita hoc iter divina providentia institutum fuit, ut per longas ambages Israelitæ in promissam regionem devenerint: ut qui Kadesbarneam, (Deut. 1. 19. cum c. 2. 1.) versus montem Sehiris assequuti, ob suam infidelitatem iter flectere jussi sint; adeo ut in extremo deserto quod Pharani adjacet tandem castrametati fuerint. Num. 33. 35. (Confer Ptolemaeum, qui illic Pharanem collocat; licet alius etiam mons Pharan videatur Num. 13. 1. 27. apud Chatserots Kades.) Mons Pharan autem potius, quam desertum, citatis supra locis commemoratur: quia Dei gratia cum solis ortu & ascensu ibi confertur; ut altiora potius quam depressiora produci debuerint, si phrases ab illis scriptoribus adhibitas spectemus. Duplex in hac descriptione fuit ratio, ob quam praeter Sinai montem, Sehiris & Pharanis meminisse authores nominati voluerint. Prior, ut quandoquidem ter veluti in istis anfractibus iter inter Aegyptum & Canaanem emensi sunt, terminos inflexi itineris notarent; quo Dei providentia in ipsis Israelitis per invia deserta ductitandis, ibique confervandis, & victu suppeditando ne ulla re egerent, suspiceretur. Primum, a Sinai digressi ad terminos terrae promissae circa montem Seiris pervenerunt; deinde retro iter flectentes longe remotius, quam mons Sinai esset, discesserunt ad Pharanis (de quo Ptolemaeus) montem; postea denuo conspectum ad Canaanem collimantes dictam regionem quidem petierunt, sed via ad orientem magis flexa, ita ut longo circuitu orientalem terrae promissae regionem ingressi sint. Altera causa est, quod accepto legis divinae in Sinai dono inestimabili, circa Sehirem & Pharanem montes singularem divinae benignitatis lucem ac ortum postea etiam experti sint. Etenim in conspectu Sehiris (ubi Edomaei a serpentibus icti; per serpentis aenei aspectum, qui Messiae a serpente diabolo sananistis typus erat, a morte praesentissima liberati fuere. Num. 21. 4. cum 9. In deserto denique (istud enim late patet) cui Pharan imminebat, insigne beneficium denuo perceperunt; dum Mosis ductu, iterum iter versus Canaan flectere jussi, ad illum locum recta tendere inciperent, quem in votis habebant. Qua divinae benignitatis luce, exorientis solis coruscatio potior non est. Porro licet à Judaeorum sententia discedere non liberet, potius Abrahami Peritsolidae sententia ab ipsis jam tum excogitanda fuisset. Is in Vichouah Hadath (quem librum contra Christianos conscriptum & nulli pene Christiano visum, ex Ebraeo jam transtuli, & in lucem edere paro: accepto manuscripto exemplari ab eximio & N.viro D. D. de Willem cognato meo, qui Illustrissimo Principi Auraico à consiliis ista studia tractare tamen non definit.) Ille Abraham c. 2.
units.tr: ¹ To say nothing of the sacred ox consecrated to Jove, which I shall leave in its place: it certainly cannot be tolerated that these men should so narrow God's law, as if in this case Israelites were allowed to injure gentiles with impunity. For the mention of idolaters does not fix their gaze on these people alone; it takes in any gentiles who do not observe the seven precepts given to the sons of Noah, as is clear from the Gemara. Yet we hold that Christians are not bound by the last of these precepts, and so it will be lawful to plunder Christians too with impunity. For in Sanhedrin f. 56, p. 1, near the end, the seventh prohibition is given as a limb cut from a living animal (לא תאכלו), that is, it is not to be eaten. I pass over the addition on p. 2 there: the sons of Noah are forbidden the admission of heterogeneous animals and the grafting of trees. But by what right are these things forbidden to us? It is worth examining the foundation of that opinion, why damages to the property of these gentiles need not be compensated. The Gemara says that God, because the gentiles who did not observe the precepts given to the sons of Noah (which they list) neglected them, proscribed their goods and made them the property of whoever seized them, although elsewhere they seem to think otherwise, as in Maimonides, On Theft, ch. 1, §1, and ch. 2, §1. But let us weigh the very fine reasons on which this foundation rests. They cite Deut. 33:2, "God shone forth from Mount Paran," whence the Gemara concludes: From Paran he published their money, that is, the goods of the Israelites. As if you said that he illuminated and displayed the goods of those Ishmaelites, and set them before the Israelites' eyes so that they might take them: he manifested and published their money. But these matters must be traced further back. They imagine that before giving the law to his Israelite people, God offered it to other peoples, namely the Ishmaelites and the Edomites. Solomon Isaaci expresses this in his commentary on Deut. ch. 33 near the beginning: First he offered the law to the sons of Esau that they might accept it, but they refused; going on to Mount Paran he presented it to the sons of Ishmael that they might accept it, but they refused; at last he came to the Israelites. But in the commentaries on Bava, 1, c. 4, he extends this more widely: he went round and led the law to all the peoples who did not accept it. (Hence the additions say, God appeared to the gentiles in Paran.) So he made their goods public property. But because they saw that this reason was not sufficient, they added another from the third chapter of Habakkuk, v. 6. The words of the prophet are, He stood and measured the earth, he saw and יף disturbed the nations. In the Gemara these are explained thus: [Hebrew], He considered the seven precepts which the sons of Noah had undertaken: since they had not fulfilled them, he established, proscribed and made lawful the money, that is, the goods, of the Israelites. So we see that the goods of the Edomites are also included in this proscription. How well this fiction agrees with God's law in Deut. 2:5–6: Do not wage war with them, for I will not give you so much as a footprint of their land, since I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his inheritance. You shall buy food from them for money, to eat, and likewise buy water from them for money. Do these words permit us to hold that their goods were given to the Israelites? Indeed, to pass over the latter passage, Habakkuk, from which they argue by a silly interpretation of the word יף, we must look at the former passage. For they seized on this as the source of their error: since they did not perceive that the light of the divine presence is said to have shone from Seir and Paran, they took it to mean that God had brought some law there, to be binding either on the Israelites or on the other sons of Noah; and when these neglected it, they fell into this penalty. That God came forth from Sinai with his law and his grace, with which he afterwards accompanied the people, nobody doubts. But how did he rise from Seir and shine from Paran? After Sinai comes Seir (for which Habakkuk 3:3 has מדרום, from the south, because it lay south of Canaan), then Paran. For although Mount Paran might seem to belong in second place, as being nearer Mount Sinai and so meeting those leaving Egypt before Seir, there was reason enough for it to be placed after in the order of words. For Moses and Habakkuk both had in view the order of the journey, not the sequence of time, weighing the position of the places rather than their chronology. So this journey was ordained by divine providence in such a way that the Israelites reached the promised land by long detours: having made their way toward Mount Seir from Kadesh-barnea (Deut. 1:19, with ch. 2:1), they were ordered, because of their unbelief, to turn their route, so that at last they encamped in the furthest part of the desert that borders on Paran (Num. 33:35). (Compare Ptolemy, who places Paran there, although another Mount Paran seems to appear at Num. 13:1, 27, near Kadesh in Chatserot.) But Mount Paran is mentioned in the places cited above rather than the desert, because God's grace is there conferred along with the rising and ascent of the sun; so if we consider the phrases used by those writers, the higher ground rather than the lower should have been brought forward. There were two reasons, in this description, why the authors named Seir and Paran besides Mount Sinai. The first was that, since they had thrice measured out the journey between Egypt and Canaan in these windings, they might mark the boundaries of the bent route, so that divine providence in leading the Israelites through trackless deserts, preserving them there, and supplying them with food, that they lacked nothing, might be recognised. First, setting out from Sinai, they came to the borders of the promised land near Mount Seir; then turning back along the route, they withdrew much further than Mount Sinai was, to Mount Paran (of which Ptolemy speaks); afterwards, again aiming at Canaan, they indeed sought that region, but by a way bent more toward the east, so that by a long circuit they entered the eastern region of the promised land. The other reason is that, having received the inestimable gift of the divine law at Sinai, they afterwards also experienced a singular light and rising of divine kindness near Mount Seir and Mount Paran. For in sight of Seir (where the Edomites were bitten by serpents), through looking at the bronze serpent, which was a type of the Messiah healing us from the serpent the devil, they were freed from imminent death (Num. 21:4, with 9). Finally, in the desert (for that stretches widely), which Paran overhangs, they again received an outstanding benefit, when under Moses' guidance, ordered to turn once more toward Canaan, they began to make straight for the place they had in mind. Compared with this light of divine kindness, the brightness of the rising sun is no greater. Moreover, although it is not right to depart from the Jewish opinion, Abraham Peritsolida's opinion ought to have been devised by them long ago. He, in the Vichouah Hadath (a book written against the Christians and seen by almost no Christian, which I have already translated from the Hebrew and am preparing to publish, having received a manuscript copy from the distinguished and noble Mr. D. de Willem, my kinsman, who still pursues these studies as adviser to the most illustrious Prince of Orange), that Abraham, in ch. 2…

units.la: Cum ita loquitur Deut.33. 2. Dixit ergo, Jova è Sinai prodiit, hoc sibi vult, Primò prodiit lex vera Israelitis è Sinai; qua lege ortus est ipsi Seiri, qui & Edom, quia illâ horum oculi aperti sunt, qui pro sua mente lucem in illa conspexerunt. Postea caelestis influentia etiam ex ista illuxit monti Paranis, qui est locus ubi Ismaelitae habitant, uti dictum est. Idcirco ibidem dicit, A dextera ejus ignis legis ipsis, num.pl. Hoc vult, à dextera ipsius Laudandi fuisse ignem edictalem; qui omnibus iis illucesceret. Hinc jam liquet ex illis locis istum Judaeorum errorem non stabiliri: cum omnino secus exponendi sint: itaque ad eorum explicationes, ejusmodi nugas excogitare necesse non est. Caeterum quò illam Judaeorum de damnis gentili illatis sententiam (cujus occasione huc delapsi sumus) plenius percipiamus, Maimonidae verba in hanc Misnam ascribere non pigebit: quibus Judaeorum animum non tantum in Gentilium etiam Christianorum bona; sed corpora quoque exprimit.
units.tr: When he speaks thus, Deut. 33:2, "The LORD came from Sinai," he means this: first, the true law came to the Israelites from Sinai, by which law Seir, that is Edom, was born, because by it the eyes of those were opened who saw light in it according to their own mind. Afterwards the heavenly influence also shone from it on Mount Paran, which is the place where the Ishmaelites live, as has been said. Therefore he says in the same place, "from his right hand went a fiery law for them." This means that the fire of the edict shone from the right hand of the one who was praised, for all those who would see it. From these passages it is now clear that this error of the Jews is not established, since they must be explained in an entirely different way; so there is no need to devise such trifles for the sake of their explanations. Moreover, so that we may grasp more fully that opinion of the Jews about the harm done to the Gentiles (the occasion for which we have wandered into this), it will not be tedious to set down the words of Maimonides on this Mishnah, in which he expresses the attitude of the Jews not only towards the goods of the Gentiles, including Christians, but also towards their bodies.

units.la: Quum Israelita controversia est cum Gentili, conditio litis inter ipsos talis est. Si nobis est in illorum juribus commodum aliquod, ipsos secundum jura sua judicabimus, isque dicemus, sic postulare ipsorum jura: quod si nobis in jure nostro appareat utilitas, judicabimus ipsos secundum jus nostrum, isque dicemus, sic postulare jus nostrum. Neque mireris hac de re, nec durum videatur in oculis tuis; sicuti dura sive crudelis tibi non videtur mactatio bestiarum, quamvis non peccaverint: quia cui non inest perfectio virtutum humanarum, inter homines non comprehenditur revera; sed finis essentia ipsius est ut hominis necessitati inserviat. Hinc jam facile judicium, quo loco nos habeant Judæi, nimirum bestiarum numero: adeò ut ipsis inservire & ipsorum commodo vivere vel mori debeamus, quod careamus virtutibus humanis. Et si corpora nostra ita ipsis addicta; quid de facultatibus dicendum? Atqui peregrinum amare jubentur, Lev. 19.34. Diliges eum sicut te. & ab eo opprimendo vel lædendo abstinere. imò (quod causæ nostræ magis directè inservit) Num. 15. 15. postquam peregrinum indigenæ in sacrificiis æquasset, in genere istam æqualitatem repetit ¶f. 16. Lex eadem & ratio eadem esto vobis; & peregrino qui peregrinatur apud vos. Sed respondent ea de proselyto intelligenda: ita author libri Hinnouch, ubi de judic. כמנאצו מלהנות סנר הפילו כדברים והוא אחר מן הפומות סנתנייר וככם כרתיו Interdictum est nobis agre facere peregrino, etiam solis verbis. is autem est unus ex gentibus qui proselytus factus accessit ad leges nostras. Hinc Maimonides codice de venditione c.14.f.15. & 16. opprimere peregrinum, peccatum esse dicit contra eam etiam legem qua proximum Hebræum quis opprimere prohibetur: nam cum peregrinum designari censet qui ad Judæorum castra concessit. Hæc restrictio levi fundamento nititur: Rabbini à גר, peregrinus, faciunt verbum in Hithpael גר, proselytus factus est: ac si vero, quia גר ipsis est proselytum fieri, hinc sequeretur גר esse proselytum; loca illa Scripturæ ad hunc proselytum restringunt. Licet alias nomen גר latius accipiant, etiam cum aliquatenus restringunt. ut quum non tantum agnoscunt גר תושב, peregrinum justitia sive justum, qui religione Judæus est; sed etiam גר תושב, peregrinum inquilinum, de quo Maimonides Cod. de Idololatria c. 10. sect. 6. [Hebrew], si (peregrinus) in se recepit septem præcepta filiis Noæ injuncta, ecce hic dicitur peregrinus inquilinus. Sed quorsum pluribus istum Judæorum in dato gentilibus damno errorem impugnare? ipsi in Gemara solidè sibi objiciunt ad cod. Bava Kama f. 38. p. 1. circa initium, [Hebrew]. Quid cogitas? Si dictum, Proximus ejus, præcise accipiatur, bos peregrini quum cornu ferit bovem Israelis, absolvendus est; sin vero, Proximus ejus, non præcise accipias, etiamsi bos Israelita feriat bovem peregrini, tenebitur. Quasi dicatur, Lex illa Exod. 21.35. Si ferierit bos viri bovem proximi ejus ita ut moriatur &c. quum præcisè accipitur de proximo ejus qui lædentis bovis dominus est, non interdicit quo minus bos peregrini interficiat bovem Israëlitæ: quandoquidem Israëlita non est proximus peregrini, cum peregrinus non sit proximus Israëlitæ; & propterea peregrinus lege illa ad restitutionem cogi non poterit. quod si latius accipias proximi vocem, ut etiam ad peregrinum extendatur, qui bove suo damnum bovi Israëlitæ infert; hic Israëlita proximus peregrini sit oportet, ideoque & hic illius proximus; & eapropter si ab Israëlita lædatur, ex illa lege in ipsum actionem habebit. Quæ sane objectio Talmudica hujusmodi est, ut eam dissolvere nequeant. Sane nisi רע, ὁ πλησίον, proximus, in dicta lege aliisque, ubi alter alteri injuriam facere prohibetur, latius accipiatur, quam pro Israëlita respectu alterius Israëlitæ; non vetatur injuria quam Gentilis Israë_ Israelitæ infert. Vt si in Decalogo, Ne concupiscito uxorem proximi tui, proximus Israelitæ intelligatur solummodo; Gentili licebit concupiscere uxorem Israelitæ: quia hic illi proximus non censebitur. Sin autem quum proximum lædere prohibentur homines, Israelita ab injuria defenditur; Israelita est proximus Gentilis alicujus. Ergo vice versa Gentilis est proximus Israelitæ: non enim possum tibi proximus censeri, nisi & tu vicissim mihi censearis talis. Vnde jam liquet in istiusmodi legibus proximum sive רע poni pro alter, quasi dicas, exempli gratia, Si bos unius, רעו alterius bovem ledat &c. Quidni etiam ita acciperetur, cum passim hic sit usus illius vocis in istiusmodi phrasibus: ut Gen. 11. 3. dicebat vir proximo suo, id est, alter alteri: nam Israelitæ nondum erant; hominum sese invicem promiscuè alloquentium sermo enarratur. similiter Deut. 22. 26. Cum vim fecerit quis puellæ in agro, hæc absolvitur: nam quemadmodum insurgens quis in proximum suum occidit cum, ita se habet hæc res. An non hoc exemplum indefinitum est de quovis qui alterum è medio tollit? num soli Judæi Judæis vitam eripiunt? Et quid manifestius commate secundo cap. 11. Exodi? Loquere nunc audiente hoc populo; ut petant quisque à proximo suo, & quaeque à proxima sua, instrumenta argentea, & instrumenta aurea. Quisnam hic est proximus & quænam proxima? profectò Gentiles & Israelitarum inimici Ægyptius & Ægyptia: uti exprimitur sequenti versu, & c. 3. v. 22. Petet unaquaeque à vicina sua & ab hospita domus sua instrumenta argentea... spoliabitis Ægyptum. Adullamæus etiam ille Gen. 38. 20. Judæ רע, proximus, dicitur: cum tamen Israelita non esset; sed socius & in via comes. Et quemadmodum istis locis proxima & proximus censentur cum quibus versatur quis, similiter Servator noster Luc. c. 10. 33. & seq. eum evincit alicujus esse πλησίον, proximum, qui alicui occurrit & cum quo est, versatur, & quicum ei res est. Quippe respicit ad vocis etymologiam, quatenus à רעה, adjociare sese & alteri adjungere significante, deducitur: unde quoque tam late accipitur, ut ad irrationalia etiam extendatur. nam Ef. 34.14. Concurrent fera animalia cum terrifico, & hirsutum proximo suo acclamabit. Imo ad inanimata extenditur Jobi 36.33. Annunciat eam pluviam proximus ipsius; id est, tonitru indicat simul imbrem secuturum. Sed ut Doctoris inter Judæos magnæ autoritatis testimonium proferam, qui præ aliis multis hac in parte sapit & in hac tota controversia; Davidis Kimchi verba notatu sunt dignissima: quia Servatoris nostri sententiam Luc. 10. sub finem de πλησίον, proximo, propositam omnino approbant. Cum majori judicio quam alii Judæi leges quasdam explicans, inter alia ita scribit ad Psal. 15. ‏ף‎ 3. ‏ל‎ ‏ט‎ ... socius (vel ut vulgo, proximus) ejus & propinquus ejus est cum quo intercedit illi (acceptio & datio, id est) commercium & conversatio, aut est vicinus ipsius. Præterea ibidem præceptum nonum explicans, subdit, ‏רע‎; proximum tuum, in ista lege exprimi, quia commercium & conversatio alicujus & negotia ejusdem cum ipso habentur. Itaque legem illam Levit. 19. 18. Diliges proximum tuum, sicut te; recte è ‏ף‎ 34. Servator noster Luc. c. 10. ‏ף‎ 27. & seq. adeo extendit, ut quemlibet, quicum nobis res est, spectare censeatur. Concludo itaque, cum in lege de quadrupede sine fundamento ‏רע‎, proximum, ad Judæos sive Israelitas restringant; nihil esse quo Mishnæ pars quam impugnamus defendi queat. ² Cæterum lex Dei Ex. 21. sub finem, non distinguit inter Gentilem & Israelitam: quo ergo fundamento in bove etiam mansueto ab illo totum damnum exigit Mishna? Hoc tandem subjiciam, nostros Imperatores longe æquiores erga Judæos in legibus suis fuisse, quam in superioribus Judæos Christianorum respectu observavimus. Legatur titulus 9. lib. 1. Codicis, ubi inter alia legitur leg. 8. Omnes Romanis legibus conferant & excipiant actiones. & 12. leg. NulNullus tanquam Iudaeus, (id est, ut Acc. ait. Ob hoc ipsum quod est Judæus) cum sit innocens, obteratur. At ipsi nos bestiarum numero habent, uti jam probavi; & arctius nos legibus quam seipsos constringunt.
units.tr: When an Israelite has a dispute with a Gentile, the terms of the suit between them are such: if we have some advantage in their laws, we shall judge them according to their laws, and we shall say that their laws require this; but if we see some advantage for us in our law, we shall judge them according to our law, and we shall say that our law requires this. Do not be surprised at this matter, nor let it seem harsh in your eyes, just as the slaughter of beasts does not seem harsh or cruel to you, although they have not sinned; for one who does not possess the perfection of human virtues is not truly counted among men, but the very end of his being is that he should serve the needs of man. From this it is easy to judge where the Jews place us, namely among the number of beasts, so that we ought to serve them and live or die for their advantage, because we lack human virtues. And if our bodies are thus given over to them, what is to be said of our goods? Yet they are commanded to love the stranger, Lev. 19:34, You shall love him as yourself, and to refrain from oppressing or harming him. Indeed (which serves our cause more directly), Num. 15:15–16, after making the stranger equal to the native in sacrifices, he repeats this equality in general terms: "The law and the custom shall be the same for you and for the stranger who sojourns among you." But they reply that these things are to be understood of the proselyte: so the author of the book Hinnouch, where he speaks of judgments, [Hebrew garbled in the scan], "It is forbidden for us to wrong the stranger, even by words alone. He is one of the nations who, having become a proselyte, came to our laws." Hence Maimonides, in the Code, Book of Sales, ch. 14, sections 15 and 16, says that to oppress the stranger is a sin against that law also by which one is forbidden to oppress a fellow Hebrew, for he judges that the stranger designated is one who has joined the camp of the Jews. This restriction rests on a slight foundation. The rabbis derive from ger, "stranger" [גר], the verb in the Hithpael, gar, "he has become a proselyte" [גר]: as if, indeed, because ger means "to become a proselyte" for them, it would follow that ger means a proselyte; and they restrict those passages of Scripture to this proselyte. Yet they otherwise take the term ger more broadly, even when they restrict it to some extent: for they recognise not only the ger toshav, the "stranger who is righteous" [גר תושב], or just stranger, who is a Jew by religion, but also the ger toshav, the "resident alien," of whom Maimonides speaks in the Code, Book of Idolatry, ch. 10, sect. 6: "if the stranger has accepted upon himself the seven precepts enjoined on the sons of Noah, behold, he is called a resident alien." But why should we attack this error of the Jews at such length, which is to the harm of the Gentiles? In the Gemara they themselves solidly object to it, on the tractate Bava Kamma, folio 38, page 1, near the beginning: "What do you think? If the words 'his neighbour' are taken strictly, then if the ox of a stranger gores the ox of an Israelite, he is to be acquitted; but if you do not take 'his neighbour' strictly, then even if an Israelite's ox gores the ox of a stranger, he will be liable." As if one were to say: that law of Exod. 21:35, "If one man's ox hurts another man's ox so that it dies," etc., when taken strictly of the neighbour who is the owner of the goring ox, does not forbid the stranger's ox from killing the ox of an Israelite, since the Israelite is not the neighbour of the stranger, as the stranger is not the neighbour of the Israelite; and therefore the stranger cannot be compelled to make restitution under that law. But if you take the word "neighbour" more broadly, so that it extends also to the stranger whose ox inflicts harm on the ox of an Israelite, then the Israelite must be the neighbour of the stranger, and therefore also the stranger is his neighbour; and consequently, if he is harmed by an Israelite, he will have an action against him under that law. This Talmudic objection is indeed of such a kind that they cannot dissolve it. Certainly, unless rea, ὁ πλησίον, "neighbour" [רע], in the said law and others, where one is forbidden to do an injury to another, is taken more broadly than for an Israelite with respect to another Israelite, the injury which a Gentile inflicts on an Israelite is not forbidden. For example, in the Decalogue, "You shall not covet your neighbour's wife": if the neighbour were understood only of an Israelite, a Gentile would be allowed to covet an Israelite's wife, since she would not be regarded as his neighbour. But if men are forbidden to harm their neighbour, and the Israelite is defended from injury, then the Israelite is the neighbour of some Gentile. Therefore, conversely, the Gentile is the neighbour of the Israelite; for I cannot be regarded as your neighbour unless you in turn are regarded as mine. From this it is now clear that in laws of this kind, "neighbour" or rea is used for "another," as if you were to say, for example, "If one man's ox hurts another man's [rea] ox," etc. Why should it not also be taken in this way, since everywhere in such phrases this word is so used: as Gen. 11:3, "each said to his neighbour," that is, one to another; for the Israelites did not yet exist, and the speech of men addressing one another indiscriminately is being recounted. Similarly Deut. 22:26: when a man has forced a girl in the field, she is acquitted: "for as when a man rises up against his neighbour and kills him, so is this matter." Is not this example indefinite, concerning anyone who takes another out of the way? Do only Jews take the lives of Jews? And what is clearer than verse 2 of chapter 11 of Exodus? "Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask every man of his neighbour, and every woman of her neighbour, jewels of silver and jewels of gold." Who, here, is the neighbour, and who is the neighbour woman? Surely the Gentiles, and the enemies of the Israelites, the Egyptian man and the Egyptian woman, as is expressed in the following verse, and in chapter 3, verse 22: "Every woman shall ask of her neighbour and of her who dwells in her house jewels of silver... and you shall spoil Egypt." That Adullamite too, Gen. 38:20, is called the rea, "neighbour," of Judah, although he was not an Israelite but a companion and fellow traveller. And just as in these passages those with whom one lives are called neighbour and neighbour woman, so likewise our Saviour, Luke 10:33ff., shows that he is the neighbour (πλησίον) of someone who meets him and is with him, has dealings with him and business with him. For he looks to the etymology of the word, as it is derived from ra'ah, meaning to associate oneself with another and join oneself to him; whence it is also taken so widely that it extends even to irrational creatures. For Isa. 34:14, "The wild beasts shall meet with the wolf, and the shaggy one shall call to his neighbour." Indeed it extends even to inanimate things, Job 36:33, "his neighbour declares the rain," that is, the thunder indicates at once that the shower will follow. But to bring forward the testimony of a teacher of great authority among the Jews, who in this respect and in this whole controversy is wiser than many others, the words of David Kimchi are most worthy of notice, because they entirely approve the sense of our Saviour's statement about the neighbour (πλησίον) set forth at the end of Luke 10. Explaining certain laws with greater judgement than other Jews, he writes among other things on Ps. 15:3: "his companion (or, as commonly, neighbour) and his kinsman is the one with whom he has dealings, that is, commerce and conversation, or who is his neighbour." Moreover, explaining the ninth precept there, he adds that "your neighbour" [רע] is expressed in that law "because commerce and conversation with someone and his affairs are had with him." Accordingly that law of Lev. 19:18, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself," rightly from Ps. 34, our Saviour in Luke 10:27ff. extends it so far that anyone with whom we have dealings is taken to be regarded as a neighbour. I conclude, therefore, that since in the law about the quadruped they restrict the word rea, "neighbour," to Jews or Israelites without foundation, there is nothing by which the part of the Mishnah which we are attacking can be defended. Besides, the law of God, Exod. 21 near the end, does not distinguish between Gentile and Israelite: on what foundation, then, does the Mishnah exact the whole damage even from a gentle ox? Finally I shall add this: our emperors were far fairer towards the Jews in their laws than we have observed the Jews to be towards Christians above. Let the title 9 of book 1 of the Code be read, where among other things we read in law 8, "Let all actions be brought and received under Roman laws," and in law 12, "No one, as a Jew" (that is, as Accius says, for this very reason, that he is a Jew), "since he is innocent, shall be oppressed." But they count us among the number of beasts, as I have now proved, and they bind us more tightly by their laws than they bind themselves.

units.tr: "If the ox of a man of sound mind gores the ox of a deaf-mute, an imbecile or a minor, he is liable; but if the ox of a deaf-mute, an imbecile or a minor gores the ox of a man of sound mind, they are exempt. If the ox of a deaf-mute, an imbecile or a minor gores [another ox], a guardian is appointed for them, and the owner is judged in the presence of the guardian. If the deaf-mute becomes sane, the imbecile becomes sane, or the minor comes of age, [the owner] must [again] keep watch over it." These are the words of R. Meir. R. Yose says: it remains in its former status. The ox of the ... is not liable; yet it is said, "if it gores" [Exod. 21], not "if they make it gore" [שור האטרין אינו חייב מיהו שנא' כי יגח ולא שיגיחוהו]

units.la: Si periti alicujus bos cornu feriat bovem surdi, stulti, aut pupilli, possessor tenetur; surdi vero, stulti, aut pupilli, si cornu feriat bovem periti, liber est. Si bos surdi, stulti, aut pupilli cornu feriat; judices his curatores praeficiunt, atque testes in ipsos testantur coram curatoribus. Si surdo aperiantur aures, respiscat fatuus, pupillus grandescat; bos in integrum restituitur, uti sentit D. Meir. R. Iose inquit, Ecce is in statu suo manet. Bos in theatro pugnans non fit mortis reus: quia dicitur, Quum cornu feriet; non vero, Quum adigent ipsum ut feriat.
units.tr: If the ox of a sane man gores the ox of a deaf-mute, a fool, or a minor, the owner is liable; but if the ox of a deaf-mute, a fool, or a minor gores the ox of a sane man, it is free. If the ox of a deaf-mute, a fool, or a minor gores, the judges appoint guardians over them, and witnesses testify against them before the guardians. If the deaf man's ears are opened, the fool comes to his senses, or the minor grows up, the ox is restored to its former state, as R. Meir holds. R. Yose says, Behold, it remains in its state. An ox fighting in the theatre does not become a capital case, because it is said, "when it gores"; not, "when they drive it to gore."
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: {1} Sed hoc loco strictius in Mishna nostra accipitur. sectionem recuperent & obtineant, bovem in integrum quorundam judicio restitui; ita in glossa explicantur: קסר רסות ... opinatur (scilicet ille cujus judicium profertur) dominium immutare bovem convictum; id est, quum hujus dominio subducitur & subjicitur potestati aliorum dominorum, dominium immutare jus illius obtestationis, sive potius testificationis. (testibus, petulcum esse, probari & denunciari solet.) Quorum verborum hic tft sensus, Quum, exempli gratia, pupilli bos petulcus est, ideoque coram illius tutoribus hunc eo vitio laborare probatur, tutores censeri bovis dominos, non pupillum; itaque quum pupillus sui juris est, tum demum haberi bovis proprietarium: quapropter bovem antea testimonio convictum, solummodo convictum judicari tutorum respectu; postquam autem veri proprietarii curae commissus est, testimonium praecedens ei non obesse, sed legibus de mansueto bove tantum subjectum, donec coram isto proprietario convincatur. 1 Sed alii qui D. Jofen sequuntur, secus sentiunt: utpote qui bovem במקפי, in robore vel potius statu suo esse vel manere afferant. Quid sit במקפי, non adeo notum; ideoque latius explicandum venit. verbum Hiphil מחזק in sacris literis significat, tenuit, prehendit, comprehendit: inde Talmudici formant ejus passivum מחזק ac si diceres, comprehensus, detentus fuit. atque de eo dicitur, qui detinetur veluti in facto quodam vel qualitate: id est, quem censent & judicant aliquid fecisse, vel aliqua dispositione, virtute, vel vitio praeditum; quibus obsideatur veluti & contineatur, ut in statu isto omnium judicio & sententia veluti cancellis constringatur; quia talem eum esse vulgo existimant. Ita in malam & bonam partem usurpatur: in bonam, ut quum Maimonides c. 2. de Phylacteriis, sect. 10. מחזק, vir ille (scilicet cujus phylacteria aliquot alter probavit ac examinavit) deprehenditur & tenetur, puta in sinceritate, id est, praesumitur sincerus, & reliqua ipsius phylacteria legitima esse censentur. Ita תפיל nomen inde derivatum, ex eadem significatione, robur quidem in Scr. sacris denotat; apud illos vero est praesumtio, qua quis hoc vel illud fecisse, hac vel illa qualitate praeditus judicatur. Vt in Baba tertia c. 1. sect. 4. מוחזק כמוחזק, in praesumptione quod dederit, id est, solvisse censetur. In malam partem accipitur cod. Maccoth f. 5. editionis Ven. p. 2. circa initium: החזקה, haec tenetur ac constringitur, scilicet judicio, id est, praesumitur, puta ut glossator inquit, ידוע עדים להביא עדים שקרים, producere testes falsos. Ita etiam nomen חזקה, praesumptio, hac Mishna quam enarramus, de bove petulco: quem D. Iose mutato etiam domino convictum habet; id est, quod etiamnunc petulcus esse praesumatur, & quidem testium testificatione id constare, affirmat.
units.tr: {1} But in this place it is taken more narrowly in our Mishnah. perfection, the ox is restored to its former state by the judgment of certain persons. This is explained in the gloss: קסר רסות ... he (namely the one whose judgment is pronounced) thinks that the ownership of a convicted ox is changed; that is, when it is withdrawn from his ownership and made subject to the power of other owners, the ownership changes the right of that warning, or rather of testimony (by which it is usually proved and declared, before witnesses, that the ox is goring). The sense of these words here is this: when, for example, a minor's ox is goring, and it is proved that it suffers from this defect in the presence of his guardians, the guardians are held to be the owners of the ox, not the minor. So when the minor is his own master, then at last he is regarded as the owner of the ox. Therefore the ox, once convicted by testimony, is judged convicted only with respect to the guardians; but after it is committed to the care of its true owner, the earlier testimony does not harm him, but remains subject only to the laws concerning a gentle ox, until it is convicted in the presence of that owner. 1 But others who follow D. Jofen think otherwise, for they assert that the ox is במקפי, "in its strength, or rather in its state, or remaining in it." What במקפי means is not very well known, so it must be explained at greater length. The Hiphil verb מחזק in the sacred writings means "he held, seized, took hold of"; from this the Talmudists form its passive מחזק, as if you said "he was held, detained". It is said of one who is detained, as it were, in some fact or quality; that is, one whom they judge to have done something, or to possess some disposition, virtue or vice, by which he is beset and contained, so that by the judgment and sentence of all he is bound, as it were, within the bars of that state, because commonly they think him to be such. It is used in a bad and in a good sense. In a good sense, as when Maimonides, chapter 2 on Phylacteries, section 10, says that mechazek, that man (namely whose phylacteries another has tested and examined) is held and retained in sincerity; that is, he is presumed sincere, and the rest of his phylacteries are judged lawful. Likewise the noun תפיל, derived from the same sense, indeed signifies strength in the sacred writings; but with them it is a presumption by which someone is judged to have done this or that, or to be endowed with this or that quality. As in Baba, third, chapter 1, section 4: מוחזק כמוחזק, on the presumption that he has given, that is, he is judged to have paid. In a bad sense it is taken in Maccoth, folio 5, Venice edition, page 2, near the beginning: החזקה, "he is held and bound", namely by judgment, that is, he is presumed, as the glossator says, "to produce false witnesses", ידוע עדים להביא עדים שקרים. So too the noun חזקה, "presumption", in this Mishnah we are expounding, concerning the goring ox, which R. Jose holds to have been convicted even after the owner was changed; that is, that it is still presumed to be goring, and indeed he affirms that this is established by the testimony of witnesses.

units.la: Denique bovem in theatro vel stadio &c. pugnantem (ista genera conjungo: quamvis enim theatra, stadia, circi, &c. propria sibique accommodata exercitia haberent; nihilominus eadem haec etiam quandoque sine discrimine peracta fuere) eum inquam vocant שור פרנסי, quasi dicas, bovem stadii σταδίων; id est, loci in quo homines bestiaeve currunt ac certant. nam voces Graecas & Latinas Talmudici etiam suas faciunt, uti in Middoth observavimus & expositimus. Maimonides ibi-lum esse dicit bovem quem assuefecerunt, ut dato vocis signo alium bovem aggrediatur, quo spectatores quis eorum vincat contemplentur. quam descriptionem ex Aruch habet, qui plene morem istum delineat his verbis: cum istum bovem esse dicit סמגדלין ... quem educant ut pramio de eo certent, itaque eum ad feriendum cornu assuefaciunt. tum (inquit) aliis bubus adductis qui cornibus cum ipso contendant, qui socium vincit, pramium de quo convenit reportat. Ultima fere Mishnae verba, non fit mortis reus, ita in transcursu R. Nathan in Aruch explicat, Si hominem interficiat, non fit mortis reus. Nam licet hic in praecedentibus de bobus inter se comparatis agatur; postremo hoc dicto ad hominem bos refertur: quandoquidem si bovem interficiat, nusquam mortis reus peragitur. Sed Misna tamen inprimis eo collimat, ut surdis, furiosis & pupillis subveniat. Quibus & consultum voluerunt leges Romanæ: ex iis enim quæ aliis in rebus statuerunt, analogicè diversi casus decidi queunt. Ne temerè quid in damnum suum agerent furiosi &c. ita Gajus Digest. 44.ti. 7. leg. 1. §. 12. & seq. Furiosum, sive stipuletur, sive promittat, nihil agere, natura manifestum est. Huic proximus est, qui ejus atatis est, ut nondum intelligat quid agatur. Sed quod ad hunc, benignius acceptum est. Nam qui loqui potest, creditur & stipulari & promittere recte posse. Mutum nihil pertinere ad obligationem verborum, manifestum est. Sed & de surdo idem dicitur.
units.tr: Finally, an ox fighting in a theatre or stadium, etc. (I join these kinds together, for although theatres, stadiums, circuses and the like had their own exercises suited to them, nevertheless these same events were sometimes carried on indiscriminately), this kind of ox they call שור פרנסי, as if you said "ox of the stadium", σταδίων [stadiōn]; that is, the place where men or beasts run and contend. For the Talmudists also make Greek and Latin words their own, as we observed and explained in Middoth. Maimonides says there that it is an ox which they have trained, so that at a given signal of the voice it attacks another ox, while spectators watch which of them prevails. He has this description from the Aruch, which sets out the custom fully in these words: this ox, he says, is one סמגדלין, "which they rear that they may contend for a prize with it, and so they train it to strike with the horn. Then (he says) other oxen are brought up which contend with it by their horns; whichever conquers his fellow carries off the prize agreed upon." The closing words of the Mishnah, "is not liable to death", R. Nathan explains in passing in the Aruch: "If it kills a man, it is not liable to death." For although the preceding discussion concerns oxen compared with one another, this last saying refers the ox to a man, since if it kills an ox it is never prosecuted as liable to death. But the Mishnah chiefly aims to help the deaf, the insane and minors. The Roman laws also provided for these, for by analogy different cases can be decided from what they laid down in other matters. Lest the insane, etc., act rashly to their own loss, so Gaius, Digest 44, title 7, law 1, sections 12 and following: "It is plain by nature that an insane person, whether he stipulates or promises, does nothing. Next to him is one of such an age that he does not yet understand what is being done. But in his case the view taken is more lenient. For one who can speak is believed to be able to stipulate and promise validly. That a mute person has no part in the obligation of words is plain. But the same is said of a deaf person."

units.la: שור שנגח את האדם ומת מועד משלם כופר והם פטור מן הכופר וזה וזה חייבים מיהה וכן בבן וכן בבת נגח עבר או אמה נותן שלשים סלעים בין שהוא יפה מאה מנה ובין שאינו יפה אלא דינר זהב ו
units.tr: "If an ox gores a man or a woman and they die, the owner pays a ransom; and if it is not the owner's fault, he is exempt from the ransom. In either case they are at least liable (to stoning)." [שור שנגח את האדם ומת מועד משלם כופר והם פטור מן הכופר וזה וזה חייבים מיהה וכן בבן וכן בבת נגח עבר או אמה נותן שלשים סלעים בין שהוא יפה מאה מנה ובין שאינו יפה אלא דינר זהב]

units.la: Quum bos cornu ferit hominem ita ut moriatur, si quidem convictus sit, λύτρον solvitur; si vero innocens sive mansuetus, possessor à λύτρῳ liber est: sed cum ipse, {1} tum ille morte tenentur. Pariter in filio {2} & filia se res habet. Si servum aut ancillam feriat, triginta sicli {3} pendentur: sive centum minas; sive tantum denarium aureum valeat.
units.tr: When an ox gores a man so that he dies, if it has indeed been proved to be a known danger, a ransom is paid (λύτρον); but if it is harmless or tame, the owner is free from the ransom. Yet in both cases the owner and the ox are liable to death. The same holds for a son or a daughter. If it gores a male or female slave, thirty shekels are paid, whether the slave is worth a hundred minas or only a golden denarius.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: {1} Bovem utrumque, puta nondum convictum, sed etiamnum ad illud factum usque omnium judicio innocentem; & istius pravitatis antea convictum, morte afficiendum ac lapidandum esse, lege docetur Exod. 21. ‎ vs. 28.29. quinetiam
units.tr: {1} That is, the ox, let us suppose not yet convicted but still, by the judgment of all, innocent up to that deed; and one previously convicted of such viciousness is taught by the law (Exod. 21.28, 29) to be put to death and stoned. Moreover

units.la: ejus dominum, si convictum non servaverit, quominus cædem committeret, mortis reum; saltem pretium redemtionis vitæ solvendum, ɣf.29. & 30. Verum ad bovem lapidandum & hoc modo morte afficiendum quod attinet, non temerè hic aliquid observat Maim. cod. Nizke Mammon, c. II.§. 10. נגמר דינו ואחר כך נתערב בתריום אפילו בלוֹ כולן נסקלים ונקברו ונשורין בתנאי, si absoluto judicio (bos) postea aliis immiscceatur, etiam mille; omnes lapidantur, & sepeliuntur, indeque lucrum percipere vetitum. alia spectemus. Præterea² è ɣf.31. c. 21. Ex. constat, perinde esse sive puer, sive adultus à bove interficiatur. Maimonides quoque recte legem ad alia pecora, ferasque etiam extendit, quin & ad aves ascendit. eadem enim omnium hac in parte est ratio. Sed licet hæc omnia ex lege Mosis satis plana videantur, merito tamen hic quæstionem movet, eamque suo more solvit memoratus Rabbi c.10.cod. de damnis pecuniariis, sect. 3. ותניא ומה Sed quandoquidem omne pecus, fera & avis, ubi hominem occidunt lapidantur; qui invenietur cædis convictus antequam domini λύτρον solvant? (ratio dubii, quia convincitur diversa & frequenti cæde: ergo ob primam cædem non solvendum λύτρον &c. docet ergo qui initio occidendus convinci queat:) veluti quum tres Samaritas interfecit, postea verò Israelitam. nam Samaritarum respectu convictus, ecce is etiam Israelitarum respectu convictus est. aut quod tres Israelitas jam laniatione (discerptos, ideoque alias etiam morituroc) interfecerit, postea verò vero sanum ac integrum interficiat: aut quum postquam post cedem aufugisset, deinde in quarto facinore deprehenditur (nam domini ad λύτρον non tenentur antequam bos lapidetur:) similiter si in periculum mortis tres hominum filios simul conjiciat: aut si tria pecora interfecerit. Ecce ille interficiendi convictus censetur, dominique pretium redemtionis sua persolvunt. Similiter si testes bovis proprietarium noverint, nec tamen noverint bovem prima vice, secunda & tertia; & quarta vice videant quidem bovem ipsum interficere, sed ignorent hiccine sit ille bos qui tribus prioribus vicibus interfecerat, an sit alius. quandoquidem coram testibus denunciatum fuerat domini, se in armento suo habere bovem qui ter eadem commiserit; observare omnia jumenta sua tenebantur, & quia non observarunt, λύτρον solvere tenentur. Quae plana sunt, nisi quod D. Jom Tob f. A. scrupulum moveat ad verba illa, quum tria pecora interfecit, occidendi convictus censetur: quia cum ipse Maimonides, tum alii afferant, bovem qui unius speciei respectu convictus est, non continuò alterius speciei respectu convictum censeri. Sed Josephus Karrus nodum hoc modo solvit: hoc loco in negotio Misna nostra propositio de bove non simpliciter laedente, sed interficiente hominem verba fieri; at aliis locis iis, qui scrupulum Doctori Jom Tob movebant, de solo damno in facultatibus & pecuniis similibusque dato sermonem esse. Verum majoris momenti merito censendum, quod ad legem qua Misna nostra nititur quammaximè spectat: nimirum an cujus bos cornupeta hominem liberum interfecit, is morte a magistratu plecti debeat: uti verba commat. 29. c. 21. Ex. exigere videntur. Sane Maimonides dicto capite, sect. 4. verba Mosis Ex. 21. &c. 29, 30. alternatim accipit, ut si pretium redemtionis solvat, ne quidem coram Deo mortis reus sit, nedum a magistratu morte plectendus. Verba ipsius haec sunt, Ad hoc quod lege
units.tr: its owner, if having been convicted he did not keep it from committing the slaughter, is liable to death; at least the ransom price of his life must be paid (Exod. 21.29, 30). But as to stoning the ox and putting it to death in this way, Maimonides has something to note here, not idly, in the Code, Nizke Mammon, ch. 2, §10: [נגמר דינו ואחר כך נתערב בתריום] [אפילו בלוֹ כולן נסקלים ונקברו ונשורין בתנאי] If its judgment has been concluded and afterwards it is mixed with others, even a thousand, all of them are stoned and buried, and it is forbidden to derive profit from them. Let us look at other matters. Moreover, from Exod. 21.31 it is plain that it makes no difference whether a child or an adult is killed by an ox. Maimonides also rightly extends the law to other cattle and wild beasts, and even ascends to birds, for the reasoning is the same in all of these cases. But although all these things seem quite plain from the law of Moses, the aforesaid Rabbi nonetheless rightly raises a question here and solves it in his own manner, in ch. 10 of the same Code, On Pecuniary Damages, sect. 3: [ותניא] [ומה] But since every beast, wild animal and bird that kills a man is stoned, who is found convicted of killing before the owners pay the ransom? (The reason for the doubt is that conviction comes from different and repeated killings. So it is taught that the ransom is not paid on account of the first killing, and so on, for one who should have been put to death at the start can be convicted in this way.) For example, if it has killed three Samaritans and afterwards an Israelite: with respect to the Samaritans it has been convicted, and behold, with respect to the Israelites it is convicted too. Or if it has already killed three Israelites by mangling them, so that they would die anyway, and afterwards kills a healthy and whole man; or if, after the killing, it has fled and is then caught in a fourth act of violence (for the owners are not liable for the ransom until the ox is stoned); likewise if it casts three sons of a man into mortal danger together; or if it has killed three animals. Behold, that animal is judged convicted of killing, and the owners pay the ransom for their own part. Likewise, if witnesses know the owner of an ox but do not know the ox in the first and second and third instances, and in the fourth instance they see the ox itself kill, but do not know whether this is that ox which killed in the three earlier instances or another; since it had been announced before witnesses that the owner had in his herd an ox which had committed the same thing three times, and he was bound to keep watch over all his beasts, and because he did not keep watch, he is bound to pay the ransom. These things are plain, except that Doctor Jom Tob (fol. A) raises a difficulty over those words, if it has killed three animals, it is judged convicted of killing, since Maimonides himself and others state that an ox which has been convicted with respect to one kind is not thereby judged convicted with respect to another kind. But Joseph Karo unties this knot as follows: in this passage our Mishnah speaks of an ox not simply causing harm but killing a man; in other places, those who raised Doctor Jom Tob's difficulty speak only of damage done to property, money and the like. Yet it must rightly be judged of greater weight that which our Mishnah is most concerned with, namely the law on which it rests: whether the owner of a goring ox that has killed a free man is to be punished with death by the magistrate, as the words of the commentary on Exod. 21.29 seem to require. Indeed Maimonides, in the aforesaid chapter, sect. 4, takes the words of Moses in Exod. 21, etc., 29, 30 alternately, so that if the owner pays the ransom, he is not even liable to death before God, much less to be put to death by the magistrate. His words are these: As to what is written in the law

units.la: L scriptum est, Etiamque dominus ejus morte plectitor; ex traditione discitur, hunc mortis reatum manum Dei respicere (id est, mortem hanc solius Dei, non magistratus opera subeundam:) & si λύτρον occisi solverit, illi reconciliari. Ut meam sententiam hic dicam, lex omninò casus distinguere mihi videtur, licet non explicitè, saltem implicitè: nam triplex poena proponitur, ut bos tantum lapidetur; homo unà occidatur; denique homo non plectatur morte, sed multa pecuniaria. Deinde considerandum venit, poenam supra bovis lapidati jacturam duabus de causis crescere, vel ex notitia quam de bove suo petulco dominus habuit, eique non respondente incuria, ut verba, Quamvis denunciatum fuerit testibus adhibitis, &c. edocent; vel etiam ex jure quodam quod interfecti familiares & amici sibi ex illa lata culpa acquirunt, quò spectat redemptionis pretium ipsis è comm. 30. solvendum. Itaque ¶f. 29. & 30. duos diversos à primo casus considerandos lex proponit: vel enim notitia, quam dominus habet, certa est, vel incerta, & incuria gravis vel levis; aut occisi ipsius amici jus strictissimum urgent, vel remittunt. Quod si scientia certa fuerit, incuria gravis, atque amici jus suum persequantur, reum morte plectendum verba & circumstantiæ ostendunt; sin scientia incerta, incuriave levior, vel amicorum animus remissior fuerit, comma 30. sequendum putarim. Adeoque Misnam eatenus aberrare censeo, quod in bove convicto semper λύτρα solutionem exigat; numquam domini mortem: quum utraque poena à Mose distinctè (casibus scilicet distinctis accommodanda) proponatur. Nimirum, cum Maimonide mortis poenam à magistratu irrogandam omninò excludit. Quemadmodum etiam alii: inter quos D. Isaac f. Aramæ, ad comma 23. c. 21. Ex. Dabis animam pro anima. Veniam dat ei qui hunc intendens, alium interfecit, ut seipsum redimat λύτρῳ anima sua. Idem juris est, quum dicit, ✠ f. 29. Etiamque dominus ejus morte plectitor. itaque eos excipit ab eo quod de completo homicida statuit, Num. 35. 31. Ne accipitote redemptionis pretium pro ullo occisore. Hæc ita simpliciter affirmat; sed Doctor Bechai in commentariis ad hunc locum, postquam hic ✠ f. 29. de morte à Deo, non judicibus irroganda agi præmisisset; subjungit quædam, ut objectionem quæ præter alias dictas circumstantias objici posset ex vocula of fi, ✠ f. 30. initio, dissolvat. quum enim redemptionis pretium designata illa quantitate solvendum præcipiatur, non absolute quoties petulcum bovem ex incuria nostra hominem occidere contigerit; sed tantum si ad redemptionis pretium deventum fuerit: sane hoc non semper fieri indicatur. Respondet ergo R. Bechai, פםק וה פםק יוח קוםכ ... Non est particula Si dubitationis; sed obligationis nota: quemadmodum Exodi 22. 25. Si pecuniam mutuam dederis. Verum hoc exemplum mihi astipulatur: ut enim hoc loco particula Si denotat, id non semper fieri ut pecuniam proximo mutues, sed tantum cum opus habet, uti textus addit, vel aliæ circumstantiæ id expedire ostendūt (multi enim nec habent, vel non sollicitantur; vel quædam impediunt quominus id fieri conveniat;) similiter, non semper λύτρον pro reo solvitur, sed quum illæ conditiones desunt, quæ mortis pœnam exigunt. Hanc itaque partieulam quum observaret Obadias Sephorno casum specialem definire, alium ✠ f. 29. fingit, כרינו ממיס חייב ... Petulci bovis qui hominem interfecit dominus judicio cœlesti tenetur, quum illic testes non sunt, quo ipsum judices ad λύτρον obligent: Si redemptionis pretium impositum fuerit ei, id est, si testentur testes eo modo, ut eum judices ad redemptionis pretium damnent. Eja: Deus inquit, reum morte teneri cum testes adsunt (nam quis non videt, Deum hic certitudinem rei definire, ideoque synecdochicè facti testes etiam comprehendi?) ille ŷf. 29. casum fingit, ubi nulli testes idonei; quò scilicet eo commate reum a morte eripiat, utpote qui sine testibus à magistratu mortis damnari non debeat. Abrabaniel ad hunc locum, quamvis Sapientum sententiam proponat; satis tamen se dissentire indicat: ut qui ŷf. 29. mortis reum peragi bovis dominum asserat; sed Deum versu sequenti de stricto jure remittere: quia non facto aliquo, verum בעלים ... per custodiam suam negligentiam (ut loquitur) ille occidit. quæ sententia cæteris tolerabilior. Sed tamen particulæ ꝺ locum non relinquit. Cum verò addit Sapientes suam sententiam ex eo confirmare, quod non dicatur Moriendo morietur; satis prodit quam sublesto argumento Scripturam depravent: quum infinitis locis in hac legislatione ista duplicatio non inveniatur. Quæ ex R. Mose Nachmane refert vix digna quæ repetantur: ut, ideo ŷf. 30. ꝺ, si, adhiberi, quia in ipsius rei arbitrio sit pretium redemptionis solvere, vel omnino abstinere. Quasi verò in legibus judicialibus non tradatur, ad quæ invitus reus à magistratu cogi debeat. Aben Ezra idem cum Abraban. sentit; Isaac Karo, Salomon Jarchi cum reliquis plurimis morte θηλαʹ ŷf.29. innui vel potius expresse designari autumant. Sed ad alia. ³ Siclos triginta definit Mishna in servo compensando (puta argenteos uti lex exprimit) sive centum minarum sit servus occisus; cum tamen mina centum drachmas contineat, & siclus communis duabus drachmis, sacer quatuor æstimetur: sive servus denario aureo valeat, cujus valor vigintiquinque drachmis taxatur, ut interpretes ad c. 4. Mis. primam observarunt. Licet inæqualitas magna videatur, & quæ pretium quandoque servo minime æquet; tamen Dei ipsius auctoritati obsecundandum existimarunt. Rationem divinæ legis hanc affert R. Isaac filius Aramæ, מחיר ... quod illud sit pretium servo quadrans ac conveniens,prout vulgo servi valent;& si in quo majus invenitur,ille in causa deprehendatur. Judaei quoque servos aliquando foeminis aequant: at foeminae aestimatio ab anno vigesimo ad sexagesimum erat etiam triginta siclorum, Lev. 27. 4. Huc referre lubet quandam Maim. observationem de isto redemptionis pretio c. 10. §. 11. Nizke Mammon אין שבלי מטלמיס את הכופר עד שתמיית בסמתן חוץ מרזותן הכל אם המית כרזות המיין אף אל פי סזוח כסקילה הכבלים פסורין מין הכופר Domini non solvunt λύτρον, donec eorum jumentum extra suum fundum eadem committat. sed si occidat in fundo ladentis; licet lapidandum sit, domini a λύτρῳ absolvuntur. Et quia varii casus diversi juris hic occurrunt, §. 13. cirta medium subjicit, נמצאת למר מסמופר שבשור שביןם כבכוס שיבין... Palam discis, quod bos convictus ubi cum intentione occidit, lapidetur; domini vero ad λύτρον teneantur: sin absque intentione occiderit, a morte absolvatur; domini vero ad redemptionis pretium teneantur: mansuetus autem qui occidit absque intentione, a morte & λύτρῳ absolvatur: quod si occidere intenderit, lapidandus sit; domini vero a redemptionis pretio, & similiter a multa fervi nomine, absolvantur. Porrò quod de bestiarum supplicio legis authoritate Mishna nostra statuit, quo homicidium Deo quammaxime abominabile magis detestari assuescamus; id non omnino ipsi Soloni praetermittendum in legibus suis visum fuit. Nam Plutarchus in ejus vita p. 167. edit. Henr. St. haec refert: ἐγεγψῃ ἢ καὶ βλάβης πεφαπώδων νόμου, ὃν ... Legem etiam scripsit de pauperie quadrupedum, in qua canem quoque qui momorderit noxa dari praecipit bojis (ut loquitur Plautus) quatuor cubitorum alligatum. Hoc quidem inventum scitum est ad securitatem. (quid sit κλοιὸς sive bojae, ostendit Xenophon Hellen. l. 3. cum inquit, διδιφῶσε L 3 Ἐ τὼ χαρὶς ἡ τὴν τεάχηλον ἐν κλοιῷ, illigatos bojis, quoad manus ac collum.) Ex dictis hoc etiam liquet, Plutarchum istud inventum approbasse ac utile censuisse, quò magis secuti degeremus. De solvendo pretio leges Romanæ dictis convenienter loquuntur: licet in quibusdam differant. Digest. lib. 21. tit. 1. l. 40. & seq. Ne quis canem, verrem, vel minorem aprum, lupum, ursum, pantheram, leonem, aliudve quod noceret animal, sive soluta sint, sive alligata, ut contineri vinculis quominus damnum inferant, non possint, quà vulgo iter fiet, ita habuisse velit, ut cuiquam nocere, damnumve dare possit. Si adversus ea factum erit, & homo liber ex ea re perierit, solidi ducenti prastabuntur. Antea quidem vidimus æstimationem hominis liberi ex legibus Rom. fieri non posse: sed ibi de propria æstimatione agitur; hic de impropria. Ad servos quod attinet, nec hic tacent leges Romanæ. ff. Ad leg. Aquil. l. 2. Qui servum servamve alienum alienamve, quadrupem vel pecudem injuria occiderit: quanti idin eo anno plurimi fuit, tantum æs dare domino damnas esto. Licet enim de bove occidente nō agatur; si tamen cum superiori lege hæc conferatur, servato servorum & liberarum personarum discrimine, bovis dominum teneri nemo dubitabit. Præterea semper in memoriam revocandum quod ff. Lege Corn. de sicar. l. 15. Vlpianus ait: Nihil interest, occidat quis, an causam mortis præbeat. Præbet autem mortis causam, qui bovem quem petulcum novit, non servat; sed liberum dimittit, ita ut is tandem alterius servum interficiat.
units.tr: It is written: "And if its owner too shall be put to death" (verse 29). From tradition it is learned that this guilt of death looks to the hand of God, that is, that this death is to be undergone by the act of God alone and not by the work of the magistrate, and "if he has paid the ransom [λύτρον] for the one killed, he is reconciled to him." To state my own opinion here: the law seems to me to distinguish the cases entirely, if not explicitly, at least implicitly. For three penalties are set out: that the ox alone be stoned; that the man be killed along with it; and finally that the man not be punished with death but with a money fine. Next it must be considered that the penalty beyond the loss of the stoned ox increases for two reasons: either from the knowledge the owner had of his wanton ox, and the carelessness that did not answer to it, as the words "although it has been declared with witnesses present," and so on, teach; or from a certain right which the family and friends of the one killed acquire from that serious fault, to which belongs the ransom price to be paid to them under verse 30. Thus verses 29 and 30 set out two cases to be considered apart from the first: for either the owner's knowledge is certain or uncertain, and the carelessness is grave or slight; or the dead man's friends press their right with the strictest justice or remit it. If the knowledge is certain, the carelessness grave, and the friends pursue their right, the words and circumstances show that the owner is to be punished with death; but if the knowledge is uncertain, or the carelessness slighter, or the friends' mind more lenient, I think verse 30 should be followed. Accordingly I judge that the Mishnah goes astray so far as it always requires a ransom for a convicted ox and never the owner's death, since Moses sets out both penalties distinctly, to be fitted to distinct cases. Certainly it wholly excludes, along with Maimonides, a death penalty imposed by the magistrate. So too do others, among whom Isaac son of Arama, on Exodus 21:23: "You shall give life for life." He grants pardon to the one who, intending this, killed another, so that he may redeem himself with the ransom of his life [λύτρῳ]. The same law applies when he says, "and the owner too shall be put to death" (verse 29); so he excepts them from what he decrees about the complete murderer (Num. 35:31): "You shall take no ransom for any murderer." He affirms this simply; but Doctor Bechai, in his commentary on this passage, after having premised that verse 29 speaks of death to be inflicted by God and not by judges, adds some points to dissolve an objection that could be raised from the little word if at the start of verse 30, besides the other circumstances mentioned. For since the ransom is ordered to be paid in that stated amount, it does not follow that whenever our carelessness allows a wanton ox to kill a man it must be paid; it is only so if the matter has come to a ransom price, and this, the text indicates, does not always happen. Bechai therefore answers: "It is not the particle 'if' of doubt, but the mark of obligation: as in Exodus 22:25, 'If you lend money.'" [פםק וה פםק יוח קוםכ ...] But this example supports my view. For just as in that place the particle if signifies that one does not always lend money to a neighbour, but only when he has need, as the text adds, or other circumstances show it to be expedient (for many neither have it nor are asked, or certain things prevent it from being fitting), so too a ransom is not always paid for the guilty party, but when those conditions are absent which require the penalty of death. Therefore, since Obadiah of Seforno observed this particle, he defines a special case and imagines another verse 29: "The owner of a wanton ox that has killed a man is liable to heavenly judgment, since there are no witnesses there by which the judges could bind him to a ransom; if the ransom price has been imposed on him, that is, if the witnesses testify in such a way that the judges condemn him to the ransom price." [כרינו ממיס חייב ...] Well then: God, he says, holds the guilty person liable to death when witnesses are present (for who does not see that God here defines the certainty of the case, and that by synecdoche the witnesses to the deed are also included?). That verse 29 imagines a case where there are no competent witnesses, so that by this verse he may rescue the guilty person from death, since without witnesses he should not be condemned to death by the magistrate. Abarbanel, on this passage, although he sets out the view of the Sages, nevertheless shows that he dissents enough: he asserts that the owner of the ox is guilty of death, but that God in the following verse remits the strict right, because it was not by some act but by his negligence in keeping [בעלים ... per custodiam suam negligentiam] (as he puts it) that the owner killed. This view is more tolerable than the others. Yet it leaves no room for the particle. When he adds that the Sages confirm their view from the fact that it is not said "dying he shall die," he sufficiently reveals with how flimsy an argument they distort Scripture, since in countless places in this legislation such a doubling is not found. What R. Moses Nachmanides reports is hardly worth repeating: that if in verse 30 is said to be applied because it lies in the owner's own choice to pay the ransom or to abstain altogether.
