As if in judicial laws it were not handed down by what means a reluctant defendant ought to be compelled by the magistrate! Aben Ezra agrees with Abraban; Isaac Karo and Solomon Jarchi, with most of the rest, think that death is implied, or rather expressly designated, in verse 29. But to other matters. The Mishnah fixes thirty shekels for compensation for a slave (namely, silver pieces, as the law expresses it), whether the slave killed weighs a hundred minas; yet a mina contains a hundred drachmas, and the common shekel is valued at two drachmas, the sacred at four; or the slave is worth a gold denarius, which is rated at twenty-five drachmas, as the commentators on the first chapter of the Mishnah have observed. Although the inequality appears great, and the price sometimes does not match the slave at all, they judged that the authority of God himself must be obeyed. R. Isaac son of Arama gives this reason for the divine law: [מחיר ...] that that is the price of a slave, fitting and suitable, as slaves commonly are worth; and if in any case a greater value is found, that is to be ascertained in the matter. The Jews also sometimes equate male slaves with women; but the valuation of a woman from twenty to sixty years was also thirty shekels (Lev. 27:4). I think it worth referring here to a certain observation of Maimonides on this redemption price, chapter 10, section 11, Nizke Mammon: [אין שבלי מטלמיס את הכופר עד שתמיית בסמתן חוץ מרזותן הכל אם המית כרזות המיין אף אל פי סזוח כסקילה הכבלים פסורין מין הכופר] The owners do not pay a ransom unless their animal kills outside its own field; but if it kills in the field of the one who is injured, although it is to be stoned, the owners are absolved from the ransom. And because various cases of different law arise here, in section 13 he adds a middle course: [נמצאת למד מסמופר שבשור שביןם כבכוס שיבין...] You learn plainly that an ox convicted, when it kills with intent, is stoned, but the owners are held liable for the ransom; but if it kills without intent, it is absolved from death; the owners, however, are liable for the redemption price. A gentle animal that kills without intent is absolved from death and from the ransom; but if it intended to kill, it is to be stoned, and its owners are absolved from the redemption price and likewise from the fine in the name of the slave. Further, what our Mishnah lays down by the authority of the law concerning the punishment of beasts, so that we may learn to detest homicide, which is most abominable to God, was not thought by Solon himself to be passed over in his laws. For Plutarch in his life, page 167 of the Henri Estienne edition, reports this: He also wrote a law concerning the mischief of quadrupeds, in which he orders that even a dog that has bitten be given up bound by the collar (as Plautus says) with a yoke of four cubits. This indeed is a shrewd invention for security. (What the κλοιός or collar is, Xenophon shows in Hellenica book 3, when he says that they were bound in the collar, fettered in the collar as to hands and neck.) From what has been said it is also clear that Plutarch approved this invention and judged it useful, so that we might live more carefully. Roman laws speak of paying the price in agreement with what has been said, although in some points they differ. Digest, book 21, title 1, law 40 and following: Let no one wish a dog, a boar or a smaller boar, a wolf, a bear, a panther, a lion, or any other animal that could do harm, whether loose or chained, so as to be unable to inflict damage by being held in chains, to be kept on the road where people commonly travel, so that it could harm or cause loss to anyone. If this is done contrary to that, and a free man perishes from that cause, two hundred solidi shall be paid. We saw earlier that the estimate of a free man cannot be made under Roman law; but there the proper estimate is in question, here the improper. As for slaves, Roman law is not silent here either: Digest, on the Aquilian law, law 2: Whoever wrongfully kills another's slave, male or female, or another's quadruped or cattle, shall pay its owner as much money as it was worth at its highest in that year. For although the killing of an ox is not in question, yet if this law is compared with the former law, the distinction between slaves and free persons being kept, no one will doubt that the owner of the ox is liable. Moreover, what Ulpian says in the Cornelian law on assassins, law 15, should always be recalled: It makes no difference whether someone kills or provides the cause of death. But he provides the cause of death who does not keep an ox that he knows to be wanton, but lets it go free, so that at last it kills another's slave.

units.la: לנפליםּ והרג בן קיּמא / פטור׃ dat; aut denique (ᵃ abortivum, & puerum stabilem, sive potius) apostatam, & fœderis filium ᵗ occidat; liber est possessor.
units.tr: [For abortions, and if he kills a viable child, he is exempt] (לנפלים והרג בן קיּמא פטור). Or finally, if he kills an abortion, and a child that is viable, or rather an apostate and a son of the covenant, the possessor is free.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Quid per idololatram intelligatur, arguit oppositum: siquidem ei opponitur Israëlita. ergo qui non est Israëlita, doctoribus istis idololatra habetur; nec hujusmodi hominis cædes tanti apud ipsos esse censetur, ut vel multa pecuniaria compensari debeat. Cum tamen lex divina, nullo inter Israëlitas & aliarum nationum homines discrimine, morte etiam in bovis occisoris dominum animadverti præcipiat, si sciens volens bovem petulcum liberum dimiserit; alias multam, quæcunque imposita fuerit, exigat: Exodi c.21.29.30. (Maimonides tamen cum aliis quibusdam Gemaricis doct. pretium redemptionis illo etiam casu exigit, uti antea observatum, si bos convictus sit.) Sed jam satis fontem illius Judæorum erroris hac in parte aperuimus ad Mishnam tertiam: nec quum omni ratione, qua suum statutum probare queant, vel speciose saltem palliare, destituantur; pluribus erroris isti immorandum existimo. Si autem quis excipiat, expressè in Mishna non definiri, quomodo cum eo agi conveniat cujus bos idololatram interfecerit; id satis perspicuè bona consequentia è constitutione hac deduci respondeo, si cum ratione sua conferatur. Non alia de causa, qui hominis idololatræ necem intendens, Israëlitam interficit, ab ipsis excusatur, quam quod bovis interfectoris intentio occidendi ad culpam requiratur: quasi dicas, morte teneri si Israëlitam interficere molitus sit ac interficiat. Vt Rab. Jom Tob ad Maimonidæ Nizke Mammon c.10. sect.9. inquit, [Hebrew text] Consequitur ex omnibus verbis Doctoris nostri, bovem si intendat interinterfícere Rubenem, & Simeonem interficiat, lapidandum: itaque in Gemara concludunt. Ergo qui Israëlitam alium intendit quam interficit, tenetur. Vbi videmus, animum interficiendi Israëlitam reatum mortis afferre. Vnde sequitur si alium præter Israëlitam occidere voluerit & occiderit, occisorem non teneri. Porrò intentionem in hoc facto ut totius negotii fundamentum spectari, docetur in Gemara. פיר קרף הסור יסקל ונס בעלין יומת כמיתת כעלים כך מיתת הסור מה בעלים עד דמיכוון ליה פ' סור כמי עד דמיכוון ליה, Ait Scriptura, Ex. 21. 29. Bos ille lapidator, etiamque dominus ejus morte plectitor. uti mors dominorum, ita se habet mors bovis: quemadmodum domini insontes sunt donec mortem intendant; ita etiam bos, donec eam intendat. Vbi bos abortivum interficere dicitur, vel idipsum intendere, hoc de fœtu accipiendum non est, qui ante pariendi tempus in lucem editus jam obiit, vel moritur; uti plerumque usurpatur: quemadmodum etiam Heb. פלא, de quo Eccl. 6. 5. Etiam solem non vidit, neque expertus est. Sed hujusmodi designatur abortivus, qui multo ante pariendi naturales terminos editus vivit quidem ad tempus; verum ex naturæ legibus brevi exspiraturus est. Ita אבר hic usurpari casus propositus evincit: utpote qui eum designari postulat, cujus vitam exstinguere bos quidam molìatur. Hoc addo ne quis Misnæ dictum absurditatis insimulet: quasi mortuum occidi statuat; quia Kimchius in libro radicum de אבר ita loquitur, est fœtus quem abortat mulier: & sic vocatur, quia excidit mortuus. Sed verba sequentia, filius Ἀπόστολος, (id est, qui non necessario moriturus, verum vitalis ac stabilis est, ut nonnemo Judæorum exponit) satis exponunt quis per אבר denotetur. Attamen ubi hanc phrasin maturius expendo & verba de Jeremia & ab ipso pronunciata Jerem. 37. 13. 14. confidero, secus de hoc membro judicare incipio. Vt à posteriori initium faciam: quum Jeremias Hierosolymis discedere moliretur ut ad Benjamitas jamitas se conferret, ita eum Jerias alloquebatur, [?] [Hebrew, illegible, ~12 letters] , Ad Chaldaeos cadis, id est, deficis: ubi D.K. [Hebrew, illegible, ~8 letters] conjungis te & auscultas ipsis. quomodo etiam Jonathan; & 70. ως σὺν Χαλδαίως οὐ Φέυγῃ, tu ad Chaldaeos transfugis. Vnde respondet Jeremias, [Hebrew, ~3 letters] , non cado, id est, Φέυγω. quibus locis i post deest: adeo ut in Mifna [Hebrew, ~3 letters], designent etsi i desit, transfugas, scil. ad aliam religionem, id est, apostatas; quemadmodum per ϰατα ἀιν redditur conjugatum verbum [Hebrew, ~3 letters] Job.31.22. licet significatione nonnihil diversa. Sed alibi de apostasia ad hostes verbum [Hebrew, ~3 letters] usurpari, exemplis prolatis docet R. D. Kimchi. Istam vocis [Hebrew, ~3 letters] significationem confirmat [Hebrew, ~3 letters], filius foederis: licet enim [Hebrew, ~3 letters], si etymon spectetur, sit tantum constantia sive permanentia & resurrectio; tamen passim a firmitate & stabilitate ita statutum & foedus nuncupantur. Vnde Ferrarius in Lexico Syriaco [Syriac, illegible, ~3 letters], fœdus. ut [Hebrew, ~3 letters] conveniat cum phrasi, qua Petrus utitur Act.3. sub finem, quum Israelitas (nempe si gratiam non rejiciant) υἱὸς τ' Αβραὰμ esse testatur, sive fœderis filios. Itaque in Mifna quam explicamus, apostatis opponuntur qui fœdere gratuito (uti sibi vendicant) Patri cœlesti adhærent. Verumenimvero quia [Hebrew, ~3 letters], ut [Syriac, illegible] & [Syriac, illegible], resurrectionem etiam significat, a [Hebrew, ~2 letters], surgere; nihil prohibet quin [Hebrew, ~3 letters] hic ponatur simili ratione ac Luc. 20.36. τ' ἀναστάσως υἱοὶ, filii resurrectionis: ubi Syrus eadem voce utitur, [Syriac, illegible], filii resurrectionis. Vbi per resurrectionem, beatam illam intelligi, qua ad beatitudinem resurgemus, vocis usu demonstrarunt alii. Hoc addam, phrasin etiam spectandam esse, nam filius hujus vel illius rei apud Hebræos dicitur, qui speciali quandam ad rem istam habet relationem; adeo ut licet aliis etiam competat, sibi speciali & proprio respectu conveniat. Vt Gen.15.3. Abraham negat se filium habere ; ideoque פִּנְפַּ בֶּן, filium domus, hæredem fore. Cum filius alicujus etiam domi nascatur; tamen verna filius domus dicitur : quia ipsi proprium est, ut quandiu servus manet, non alio loco sit quam si in familiæ istius bonum natus esset, ut speciali ratione domui isti & familiæ affixus maneat. Ita Pf. 102. 21. quamvis omnes homines mortem subire teneantur; non tamen omnes, sed certi ac designati quidam intelliguntur his Davidis verbis, Ad solvendum filios mortis: scilicet, קְרוֹבִים לְמוּת מָרוּב, vicini jam morti, ob adversitatum multitudinem, ut ait D. K. Et quum Saul 1 Sam. 20. 31. Davidem פִּנְפַּ בֶּן, filium mortis dicit, aliud sane vult, quam aliquando morte exstinguendum : hoc enim omnibus commune est. Pariter cum Servator pios statuit resurrectionis filios, eo aliis non denegatur resurrectio; sed speciali quadam ratione fidelibus obtingere intelligitur. & revera aliter nos, quam infideles resurgemus. Sane cum Servatori Luc. 16. 8. οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, filii hujus seculi, a filiis lucis distinguuntur; quis tam bardus, ut hinc filios lucis hoc seculo jam vivere neget? pariter quamvis resurrectionis filii ab aliis distinguantur; nemo reliquos resurrecturos negare poterit. Sed ut isti filii seculi specialem ad seculum hoc respectum habent; sic & hi resurrectionis filii, ad resurrectionem. Atque ut unde digressi sumus redeamus, בְּנֵי תְּחִיָּה, filius resurrectionis merito ex illa significatione opponitur apostatis. Quod etiam alia significatione & respectu a Judæorum doctoribus quibusdam fieri potuit: siquidem inter eos reperiuntur qui vel impiorum resurrectionem negant, vel in ulteriora tempora differunt, quam quidem justi resurgent. Sed de his alias, Deo dante, plegius. Denique quod leges Romanas attinet, nondum observavi, in iis ut in Misna nostra, ad bovis vel alterius quadrupedis intentionem spectari: imo cum injuria & sensus ipsis adimatur, istud discrimen quod ex intentione petitur potius negligi exististimem. mem. Si quadrupes, l. 1. §. 3. hæc occurrunt, Pauperies est damnum sine injuria facientis datum. Nec enim potest animal injuriam fecisse quod sensu caret. De pariete per jumentum in hominem everso sufficiunt, quæ ad primi capitis Mishnam primam è tit. Si quadrupes, l. 1. §. 9. deprompta fuere, Sive autem corpore suo pauperiem quadrupes dedit, sive per aliam rem quam tetigit, &c.
units.tr: ¹ The opposite of the term shows what is meant by an idolater, since the Israelite is set against him. So by these teachers' definition, one who is not an Israelite is regarded as an idolater, and the killing of such a man is not thought to be a matter serious enough to require even a monetary payment. Yet the divine law, making no distinction between Israelites and men of other nations, commands that the owner of an ox that gores be put to death if he knowingly let a dangerous ox run loose, and otherwise that he pay whatever fine is imposed (Exod. 21:29–30). (Maimonides, however, along with certain other Gemara authorities, requires the payment of a ransom even in that case, as noted earlier, if the ox has been proved dangerous.) But I have already sufficiently uncovered the source of this Jewish error on this point in my discussion of the third Mishnah. Nor do I think it necessary to dwell at length on this error, since they are not wholly lacking in every argument by which they might prove or at least speciously cover over their position. If anyone objects that the Mishnah does not expressly state how a man is to be dealt with whose ox has killed an idolater, I answer that this follows clearly enough by good inference from this rule, if it is compared with its rationale. The only reason the one who kills an idolater, intending to kill him, but kills an Israelite instead, is excused by them is that the intention of the ox's killer to kill is required for guilt, as if you were to say that he is liable to death if he has planned to kill an Israelite and does kill one. So Rabbi Jom Tob, on Maimonides' Nizke Mammon 10, sect. 9, says: It follows from all the words of our teacher that if an ox intends to kill Reuben and kills Simeon, it is to be stoned; and so they conclude in the Gemara. Therefore one who intends to kill one Israelite and kills another is liable. Here we see that the intention to kill an Israelite brings the guilt of death. From this it follows that if someone wishes to kill someone other than an Israelite and does so, the killer is not liable. Moreover, that intention in this act is to be considered the foundation of the whole matter, as is taught in the Gemara. Scripture says (Exod. 21:29): That ox shall be stoned, and its owner shall be put to death. As the death of the owners, so is the death of the ox: just as the owners are innocent until they intend death, so too the ox, until it intends it. Where the ox is said to kill an abortion, or to intend this, the word must not be taken to refer to a fetus which, already brought into the light before the time of birth, has died or is dying, as the term is commonly used. Likewise the Hebrew pela, of which Eccl. 6:5 says, nor has it seen the sun or known anything. Rather, this term designates an abortion which, born long before the natural limits of birth, lives for a time, but by the laws of nature is about to expire shortly. That the case proposed shows the word avar is used here in this sense: for it requires that the term designate one whose life a certain ox is planning to extinguish. I add this so that no one may accuse the saying of the Mishnah of absurdity, as if it required that a dead thing be killed. Kimchi, in his book of roots, speaks of avar in this way: it is the fetus that a woman aborts, and it is so called because it falls out dead. But the following words, son [of the covenant]—that is, one not necessarily destined to die, but living and stable, as some Jews explain it—sufficiently explain what is meant by avar. Yet when I weigh this phrase more carefully, and consider the words about Jeremiah, spoken by him and concerning him (Jer. 37:13–14), I begin to judge differently about this member. To begin from the later point: when Jeremiah was trying to leave Jerusalem to go over to the Benjamites, Jeriah addressed him thus: [Hebrew, illegible], You are going over to the Chaldeans, that is, you are deserting; where D.K. [Hebrew, illegible] you join yourself and listen to them. So also Jonathan, and the Seventy: ὡς σὺν Χαλδαίοις οὐ φεύγῃ [as you flee over to the Chaldeans]. Hence Jeremiah replies [Hebrew, ~3 letters], I am not going over, that is, I do not flee. In these passages the letter yod is missing afterward, so that in the Mishnah the words [Hebrew, ~3 letters] denote deserters, even though the yod is absent, namely to another religion, that is, apostates; just as the conjugated verb [Hebrew, ~3 letters] in Job 31:22 is rendered by κατὰ ἀνθρώπους, though with a somewhat different meaning. But R. D. Kimchi shows, by examples brought forward, that the verb [Hebrew, ~3 letters] is used elsewhere of apostasy to enemies. The phrase son of the covenant confirms this meaning of the word. For although, if the etymology is considered, [Hebrew, ~3 letters] signifies only constancy or permanence and resurrection, yet everywhere from firmness and stability both statutes and covenants are so named. Hence Ferrarius, in his Syriac lexicon, renders the Syriac word as covenant, so that it agrees with the phrase Peter uses at the end of Acts 3, when he testifies that the Israelites (namely, if they do not reject grace) are sons of Abraham [υἱοὶ τοῦ Ἀβραάμ], that is, sons of the covenant. Thus in the Mishnah which we are explaining, apostates are opposed to those who cling to the heavenly Father by a gratuitous covenant (as they claim for themselves). Indeed, since [Hebrew, ~3 letters], and the Syriac equivalents, also signify resurrection, and come from the verb to rise, nothing prevents [Hebrew, ~3 letters] from being used here in a manner similar to Luke 20:36, sons of the resurrection [τῆς ἀναστάσεως υἱοί]. There the Syriac uses the same word, meaning sons of the resurrection. Others have shown from the usage of the word that by resurrection there is understood that blessed resurrection by which we rise to blessedness. I will add this: the phrase must also be considered, for among the Hebrews one is called son of this or that thing if he has a special relation to that thing, so that although the term may also apply to others, it belongs to him in a special and proper respect. So in Gen. 15:3 Abraham denies that he has a son, and therefore ben bayit, son of the house, will be his heir. Although a son of someone is also born in the house, yet a home-born slave is called son of the house, because it is proper to him that, as long as he remains a slave, he is in no other place than if he had been born into the good of that household, so that he remains attached to that house and family by a special relation. So too in Ps. 102:21, although all men are bound to undergo death, yet not all, but certain designated persons, are understood by these words of David, to set free the sons of death: that is, קְרוֹבִים לְמוּת, those near to death because of the multitude of adversities, as D. K. says. And when Saul, in 1 Sam. 20:31, calls David son of death, he certainly means something other than that he is to be extinguished by death at some time, for this is common to all. Likewise, when the Saviour calls the godly sons of the resurrection, resurrection is not thereby denied to others; rather it is understood that a certain special ground attaches to the faithful, and indeed we shall rise in a different way from unbelievers. Indeed, when in Luke 16:8 the Saviour distinguishes the sons of this age [οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου] from the sons of light, who would be so harsh as to deny that the sons of light are already living in this age? Likewise, although the sons of the resurrection are distinguished from others, no one can deny that the rest will rise. But as those sons of this age have a special relation to this age, so also these sons of the resurrection have a relation to the resurrection. And to return to where we departed: ben tehiyah, son of the resurrection, is rightly opposed to apostates by that meaning. This could also be done by some Jewish teachers in another sense and respect, since among them are found those who either deny the resurrection of the wicked or postpone it to later times, when indeed the righteous will rise. But of these things elsewhere, God willing. Finally, as far as the Roman laws are concerned, I have not yet observed that in them, as in our Mishnah, the intention of an ox or other quadruped is considered; indeed, since injury and sense are taken away from them, I think that this distinction which is derived from intention should rather be disregarded. Si quadrupes, l. 1, §3: the following occur: Pauperies is damage given without injury by the one causing it. For an animal which lacks sense cannot commit an injury. Concerning a wall overturned by a beast onto a man, what has been drawn from the first Mishnah of the first chapter, under the title Si quadrupes, l. 1, §9, is sufficient: But whether the quadruped has caused damage by its body, or by some other thing which it touched, etc.

units.la: שור האשה שור היתומים שור האפוטרופוס שור ה הסרבר שור ההקדש שור הגר שמח ואין לו ירשין הרי אלו חייבים מיהה רבי יהודה אומר שור המרבר שור ההקדש שור הגר שמר ואין לו
units.tr: The ox of a married woman, the ox of orphans, the ox of a guardian, the wild ox, the consecrated ox, and the ox of a stranger who has died without heirs: behold, these are at least liable to death. Rabbi Judah says: the wild ox, the consecrated ox, and the ox of a stranger who has died without heirs are exempt from death, because they have no owners.

units.la: Bos mulieris, bos orphanorum, bos curatorum, bubalus, bos sacer, bos peregrini mortui cui non sunt haredes; ecce hi mortis rei sunt. Doctor Judas inquit, Bubalus, bos sacer, bos peregrini mortui cui non sunt haredes; a morte absolvuntur: quia dominos non habent.
units.tr: The woman's ox, the orphans' ox, the guardian's ox, the wild ox, the sacred ox, and the ox of a stranger who has died without heirs: behold, these are liable to death. The teacher Judah says: the wild ox, the sacred ox, and the ox of a stranger who has died without heirs are acquitted of death, since they have no owners.

units.la: ירשין פטורים מן המיתה לפי שאין להם בעלים:
units.tr: Heirs; they are exempt from death, because they have no owners. [ירשין פטורים מן המיתה לפי שאין להם בעלים]
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Vt hæc dextrè accipiantur, observa bovem orphanorum dici, quem orphani possident tutoribus destituti. Sic Bartenorius, שור לית אפוטרופוס, quibus non est procurator vel tutor. Etenim Mishna quarta pupilli non tenentur nisi coram curatoribus obtestatio de bove petulco facta fuerit. ² Sed ne sic quidem addita conditione curatorum coram quibus testatio fiat, cum ista Mishna, hæc conciliabitur: quia postea per שור יתומים, bovem curatoris, cum intelligunt qui sit שור אפוטרופוס לאמר, pupillorum; nisi quod tutoris sit eum custodire. Sane utut ad certum casum restringi posse videatur; si eorum bos, cum tutores habent, absolutè tenetur, ut hic dicitur, qui illic certo demum casu tenebatur? Verum illic de completo reatu, ubi ad λύτφοι & bovis occisoris lapidationem tenetur dominus; hic vero quoad pupillos de sola bovis lapidatione agitur. Ita sentit Maimonides de damnis pecuniariis c. 10. f. 6. [illegible, ~60 letters] buba-lus, bos sacer, & bos mortui extranei cui heredes non sunt, si occidit, ecce hic lapidatur: ejusque jus exercent, quamvis dominos non habeat. Similiter bos mulieris, & bos orphanorum, & curatorum, quum occiderunt, lapidantur; neq; tamen curatores λύτρον[?] persolvunt: quia λύτρον[?] est propitiatio; sed pupilli, surdi, vel fatui ita reatu non tenentur, ut propitiatione egeant. At cum hic & in Misna peregrinus describatur, cui non sunt haeredes; an sunt peregrini qui haeredes habeant? Ita est: nam in hoc casu qui haereditatem spectat, distinguunt peregrinos in eos qui religionem suam servaverint, & eos qui proselyti facti fuerint. Alii enim filios religionem Israeliticam prositentes vel potius conceptos natosque [illegible, ~5 letters], in religione Israelitica, relinquunt; alii tales superstites non habent. priores nullis quam haeredibus suis bona post mortem cedere coguntur; posteriorum vero bona occupantis fiunt.
units.tr: ¹ To understand these matters correctly, note that the ox of orphans means the ox that orphans own when they lack guardians. So Bartenora: the ox of one who has no guardian [שור לית אפוטרופוס], who has no procurator or tutor. For the fourth Mishnah says that minors are not liable unless the warning about the goring ox was given before the curators. ² But even with the added condition of the curators before whom the warning is given, this Mishnah cannot be reconciled with that one, since later they understand the ox of orphans to mean the ox of the curator [שור אפוטרופוס], that is, of the minors; except that it is the guardian's duty to keep it. Granted, it may seem that the rule can be restricted to a certain case: if the ox of minors, when they have guardians, is held liable absolutely, as is said here, why was it held liable only in a certain case there? But there the question concerns full guilt, where the owner is liable to a ransom [λύτρον] and to the stoning of the ox that killed; here, however, as regards minors, the matter concerns only the stoning of the ox. Maimonides holds this view concerning pecuniary damages, chapter 10, section 6: [illegible] The wild ox, the consecrated ox, and the ox of a dead stranger who has no heirs, if it kills, behold, it is stoned, and its right is exercised, although it has no owner. Likewise the ox of a woman, the ox of orphans, and of curators, when they kill, are stoned; yet the curators do not pay a ransom [λύτρον], because a ransom is an atonement; but minors, the deaf, and the simple are not so bound by guilt that they need atonement. But since here and in the Mishnah a stranger is described who has no heirs, are there strangers who do have heirs? Yes: in this matter, those who consider inheritance distinguish strangers into those who have kept their own religion and those who have become proselytes. For some leave sons who profess the Israelite religion, or rather who were conceived and born [illegible] in the Israelite religion; others have no such survivors. The former are compelled to surrender their goods after death to no one but their own heirs; but the goods of the latter become the property of whoever takes them.

units.la: Maimonides in hanc sententiam scribit codice de acquisitione & donatione c. 1. sect. 4. [illegible, ~45 letters] Peregrinus qui moritur nec genuit Israelitam postquam proselytus factus est, non habet haeredes; sed quicunque primus ejus facultates occupat, ipsas acquirit. Quanto minus ergo, si ne ipse quidem religionem istam susceperit, haeredes eodem illo casu habebit? Nonne haec pulchre conveniunt cum lege divina, Ex. 22. 21. Peregrino vim ne facito, nec opprimito eum: nam peregrini fuistis in terra Ægypti. Et ne haec verba detorqueantur, ut fieri solet; notanda Salomonis Jarchi expositio. vim ne facito, [illegible, ~15 letters] injuria verborum, gallice, controller: nec opprimito eum, [illegible, ~3 letters] facultates eripiendo: peregrino, homini qui in ista provincia natus non est; sed ex alia provincia venit ut ibi habitaret. Ne quis ergo ad eum referat, qui suam religionem deseruit, ut Abrabaniel ac alii nonnulli. 4 Sed ad rationem progrediamur, qua in Gemara utuntur, ad constitutionis suae confirmationem. Tradunt magistri, bovem septies repeti, ad includendum bovem mulieris & bovem pupillorum &c. sensus est, in sectione legis, septies bovem commemorari, semel pro se, ut ajunt, puta quod lex alioqui non intelligeretur; & praeterea sexies, ad includendos sex boves istos: quo peccantes reatu constringerentur. Sententiae vero R. Judae ratio in Misna exprimitur. Leges Romanae quam aequae sint in eos, quibus natura multa denegavit, vide ad finem Misnae quartae.
units.tr: Maimonides writes to this effect in the book on acquisition and gift, chapter 1, section 4: [illegible] A stranger who dies, and who did not beget an Israelite after he became a proselyte, has no heirs; but whoever first seizes his property acquires it. How much less, then, if he himself did not take up that religion, will he have heirs in that same case? Do not these things agree admirably with the divine law, Exodus 22:21: You shall not wrong a stranger, nor oppress him; for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. And lest these words be twisted, as is often done, consider the exposition of Solomon Jarchi: do not wrong [illegible] by injury of words, in French, control; nor oppress him [illegible] by taking away his goods; a stranger, a man who was not born in that province but came from another province to live there. Let no one therefore refer this to one who has deserted his religion, as Abarbanel and some others do. ⁴ But let us proceed to the reasoning which the Gemara uses to confirm its position. The masters teach that the ox is repeated seven times, to include the ox of a woman and the ox of minors, etc. The sense is that in the section of the law the ox is mentioned seven times: once for itself, as they say, that is, because otherwise the law would not be understood; and besides, six times, to include those six oxen, so that those who sin with them would be bound by guilt. The reason for R. Judah's opinion is expressed in the Mishnah. How fair the Roman laws are toward those whom nature has denied many things, see at the end of the fourth Mishnah.

units.la: Si bovem egressum ut lapidetur, consecret possessor, non censetur consecratus: si eum mactet, ejus caro illicita. Quod si eum, antequam peragatur judicium, consecret possessor, consecratus censetur: & si eum mactet, caro est licita.
units.tr: If the owner consecrates an ox that is going out to be stoned, it is not regarded as consecrated; if he slaughters it, its flesh is unlawful. But if the owner consecrates it before the judgment is carried out, it is regarded as consecrated; and if he slaughters it, its flesh is lawful.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: 1 Bos qui hominem ita feriisset, ut moreretur, lapidandus erat ex lege Exod. 21. 28. itaque educebatur foras ut, quod lege sanctum erat, executioni mandaretur. 2 Dubium ergo hic oritur, quum res sanctae violari nequeant, an proprietarius suum bovem consecrando liberare possit. Et quia certum erat, consecratum non posse lapidibus obrui, sed ad altare offerendum; ideo statuitur hujusmodi consecrationem legitimam non censeri. quod omnino (ex Judaeorum mente) sic accipiendum, fi lata sententia fuerit; sin minus, sequens membrum quid juris fit, expresse definit. Quod de carne ejusmodi bovis non comedenda subjicitur,id recte alii monent ad quamvis pecorum ac bestiarum carnem extendendum, quorum conditio in hujusmodi delicto aequalis est. Nam Scriptura inquiunt דבר ברגיל, loquitur de eo quod magis consuetum est: saepius bos necem cornibus perpetrat, quam caeterae pecudes occidunt. Verum hac de re nonnihil etiam in praecedentibus. Magis attendenda interdicti ratio, quam ita exprimunt alicubi, כדי לסכיים כדעתינו טבל מי טבח תקלה על ידי מרוחך וממנם עם אלוהים ותם הנשים וחכלו טוב כמו הכבמה פלא לא דעת וכל טבן מויר, Quod consentientes statuamus in animo nostro, cujufcunque opera scandalum datur, eum abominandum & rejectaneum esse coram Deo & hominibus; licet errantem (quemadmodum beftia quae mente destituitur) quanto magis contumacem. Cui rationi in eodem libro Hinnouch folio 28. admonitio subjungitur: וכתיבו דעתינו על דבר זה יביאו לאויר כרוב כבל מעשיהו עד שבת שלא תקלה מתחת ידיהו לאדם, Et quum advertemus animum nostrum ad hanc rem, id nos eo adducet, ut admodum cauti fimus in omnibus actionibus nostris, adeo ut nunquam opera nostra scandalum exoriatur. Quae notanda de legis illius usu autumavi, quod Servatoris nostri praeceptis sint convenientissima: quemadmodum cum alibi, tum Matt. 18.7. Va homini illi per quem offendiculum evenit. Ita etiam ejus discipuli, ut Paulus Rom. 14.13. Adhibete judicium, ut ne fratri proponatis quidpiam ad quod impingat vel offendat. Caeterum quum bovis occisoris carne interdicunt, cum designant qui inter latam fententiam & executionem mactatur, & bovem tum mactatum illicitum probant e verbis legis, Neque comeditor caro ejus. Quare enim, inquiunt, his opus fuisset: quum satis e praecedentibus constaret, bovem lapidatum non edendum esse? Ideo ergo ista verba adduntur, ut interdictum extendatur: quasi dicas, licet quis latâ jam sententiâ prævertat executionem; & bovem ad edendum mactet sive consecratum interea, sive minus; nullum inde fructum vel emolumentum hac in parte percipiet. Maimonides tamen alia de causa eaque magis generali verba ista addita censet: puta, ut interdiceretur quodvis commodum quo ex ejusmodi bove quis frui posset; sive edere, sive vendere, sive eo arare moliretur. quæ sententia non displicet: siquidem intentio & scopus legis in superioribus annotatus, quemvis fructum excludit. Secundam Misnæ partem probare nequeo. quid hoc enim aliud est, quam legi fraudem facere, ejusque sententiam circumvenire, quod hic permittunt Judæorum jurisconsulti? Cum Deus, quò nobis significet quam ab omni homicidio abhorreat, bovem etiam lapidari præcipiat, & carne ejus interdicat; an hoc in sensum communem cadere potest, eundem Deum ad suum altare tanquam acceptum sacrificium admittere hujusmodi bovem, ut carne etiam ejusdem tanquam gratæ victimæ vescamur? Hinc etiam liquet, quid de eo judicandum sit, quum in Gemara magistri permittunt ut simili casu vendatur; vel si in custodis manu læsit, ad dominum reducatur. Atque illicitam istam consecrationem non inconcinnè quis prohiberi dixerit Instit. l. 2. tit. 1. §. 8. Si quis autem authoritate sua quasi sacrum sibi constituerit, sacrum non est, sed profanum. Sane istiusmodi bovem quis authoritate sua, non Dei, consecraret: imo quin ista consecratio Deo displiceret, nullus dubito.
units.tr: 1 An ox that had struck a man so that he died was to be stoned under the law (Exod. 21.28), so it was led out of the city, so that what the law had made holy might be handed over to execution. 2 Here a doubt arises: since sacred things cannot be violated, can the owner free his ox by consecrating it? It was certain that a consecrated animal could not be stoned but had to be offered at the altar, so it is laid down that such a consecration is not regarded as lawful. This must be understood entirely (according to the mind of the Jews) as applying once sentence has been pronounced; if not, the following clause expressly defines what the law is. What is added about not eating the flesh of such an ox, others rightly remind us, extends to the flesh of any livestock and beasts, whose position in such a crime is the same. For Scripture, they say, "speaks of what is more usual" [דבר ברגיל]: an ox kills with its horns more often than other cattle kill. Yet something on this matter has also been said above. The reason for the prohibition deserves more attention, which they express somewhere thus: "That we resolve in our minds: by whose work a stumbling block is given, that man is abominable and rejected before God and men; and if he errs, like a beast deprived of mind, how much more if he is obstinate" [כדי לסכיים כדעתינו טבל מי טבח תקלה על ידי מרוחך וממנם עם אלוהים ותם הנשים וחכלו טוב כמו הכבמה פלא לא דעת וכל טבן מויר]. To this reason, in the same book, Hinnouch, folio 28, adds a warning: "And when we turn our minds to this matter, it will lead us to be very cautious in all our actions, so that our works never give rise to a stumbling block" [וכתיבו דעתינו על דבר זה יביאו לאויר כרוב כבל מעשיהו עד שבת שלא תקלה מתחת ידיהו לאדם]. These things I have thought worth noting about the use of that law, since they agree very well with the precepts of our Saviour, as elsewhere, so in Matt. 18.7: "Woe to that man through whom the offence comes." So too his disciples, as Paul in Rom. 14.13: "Take care not to put before your brother anything at which he may stumble or be offended." Moreover, when they forbid the flesh of the slayer ox, they mark out the animal that is killed between the pronouncing of sentence and its execution, and from the words of the law they prove that an ox killed then is unlawful: "Neither shall its flesh be eaten." Why, they ask, was this needed, since it was already clear from what precedes that a stoned ox is not to be eaten? Therefore these words are added so that the prohibition is extended: as if to say, even if someone, after sentence has been pronounced, anticipates the execution and kills the ox to eat, whether it has meanwhile been consecrated or not, he will gain no fruit or advantage from it in this respect. Maimonides, however, thinks these words were added for another reason, and a more general one: namely, that any benefit by which one might profit from such an ox should be forbidden, whether by eating it, selling it, or ploughing with it. This opinion does not displease me, since the intention and aim of the law noted above excludes every kind of gain. I cannot approve the second part of the Mishnah. For what else is this than to commit a fraud against the law and get around its meaning, which the Jewish jurists here allow? Since God, to show us how much he abhors all homicide, commands even an ox to be stoned and forbids its flesh, can it make sense that the same God would admit such an ox to his altar as an accepted sacrifice, so that we might feed on its flesh as a pleasing victim? From this too it is clear what is to be judged about the permission of the masters in the Gemara that in a similar case the ox be sold, or, if it has injured a keeper's hand, that it be returned to its owner. And that unlawful consecration may fittingly be forbidden, as one might say from Inst. 2.1.8: "If anyone by his own authority sets something apart as sacred, it is not sacred but profane." Surely whoever consecrated such an ox by his own authority, and not God's, would be doing so; indeed I have no doubt that such a consecration would displease God.

units.la: Quum bos traditur custodi gratuito, commodatario, mercenario, vel conducenti, hi in locum dominorum succedunt: itaq; si ille egressus damnum intulit, pro convicio totum
units.tr: When an ox is entrusted to a keeper who is unpaid, a borrower, a hired keeper, or a hirer, these take the place of the owners. So if the ox went out and did damage, the full damage is paid for a known (vicious) ox; for an innocent or tame ox half the damage is paid.

units.la: Hebrew text in the left column, not transcribed beyond the first lines: סמרו לשומר חנם ולשואל לנשא שכר ולשוכר נכנסו תחת הבעלים יצאו והזיק סוער שומ נוק שלם וחם משלם
units.tr: Those who keep for nothing, borrowers, paid keepers and hirers stand in the place of the owners; if [the ox] went out and did damage, [they pay] full damage [סמרו לשומר חנם ולשואל לנשא שכר ולשוכר נכנסו תחת הבעלים יצאו והזיק סוער שומ נוק שלם וחם משלם]
half damage; [if] it was tied by its owner with a rope [חצי נזק קשור בעליו בסורה]
and locked properly in its presence, and went out and did damage [ונעל בפניו כראוי ויצא והזיק]
whether a known (ox) or an unknown one, it is liable [אחר חכם ואחר מועד חייב]
These are the words of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah [דברי רבי מאיר רבי יהודה]
who say: a known (ox) is liable, and a guarded one is free [אומר חכם חייב וסועד פטור]
(Exod. 21.36: "and its owner did not keep it") [טנא' ולא ישתרנו בעליו]
and it is kept; and Rabbi Eliezer [ושמור היא ור' רבי אליעזר]
says: it has no keeping except [אומר אין לו שמירה אלא]
a knife [סכין ו]

units.la: totum damnum prastatur ; pro innocenti sive mansueto prastatur damni dimidium. Si eum dominus vinculo vinxerit & debitè conclu-serit, egressus tamen damnum intulerit ; sive innocens, sive convictus sit,³ prastanda culpa. uti sentit D. Meir. Doctor Iudas inquit, Innocens sive mansuetus tenetur ; ⁴ convictus verò liber est:quia (Ex. 21. 36.) dicitur⁵. Et non asservaverit eum dominus ejus: atqui hic asservatus fuerat. Doctor Eliezer inquit, Non aliter asservatur⁶, quam cultro.
units.tr: The whole damage is paid for a known ox; for an innocent or tame one half the damage is paid. If the owner has bound it with a chain and locked it up properly, yet it went out and did damage, then, whether it is innocent or convicted, the fault is to be paid for, as Rabbi Meir holds. Judah the teacher says: an innocent or tame ox is liable, but a convicted one is free, because (Exod. 21.36) it is said: And its owner did not keep it. Yet here it had been kept. Eliezer the teacher says: it is kept by nothing other than a knife.
Annotations.

units.la: {1} Quatuor isti hominum ordines, qui bovem à proprietario acceperunt, diversi sunt. Nam primus ac secundus à duobus reliquis differunt, quod nulla merces in illis intercedat; quemadmodum in his: primus à secundo, quod ille gratis operam suam impendat; hic gratis commodum percipiat:tertium denique à quarto distinguit diversa mercedis assignatio, hic enim mercede dat;ille accipit. {2} Hæc sequentia verba, Si egressus damnum dederit, non habentur in omnibus codicibus; sed quamvis in quibusdam desiderentur,satis è sequentibus liquet,subaudiri: siquidem nullum damnum, nisi datum fit, præstari debeat. Cæterum hanc Misnæ partem non absolutè ab omnibus admitti, ex ultima præcedetis Misnæ Gemara constat.{3} Cum vero præstanda culpa dicitur, cave (si verba Meïri ex vulgari sententia accipias) hic exigas æqualitatem:nam iis convenienter quæ hic præcedunt & in superioribus explicata sunt,pro bovis conditione diversa,dimidium vel totum damnum præstari volunt. Atq; ne verbis Mosaïcæ Mosaicæ legis refragari dicatur hic Doctor Meïr, Obadia de Bartenora hoc loco observavit, eum מיתה, de laxiori custodia locutum; quasi arctam custodiam proprietarium excusare, non vero laxiorem existimasset: cum tamen dixerit supra, vinculo vinxerit & debitè conclusserit. itaque non video, qui illa distinctione excusari queat: quandoquidem lex Mosis tum demum multam illam graviorem exigit in bove convicto, si non asservaverit eum. Itaque vel erravit Meïr; vel (quod mallem) præstanda culpa, indefinitè ab ipso accipitur. In hanc sententiam: bovem petulcum, si asservatus casu erumpat, damnumque inferat, de toto damno quidem non teneri; tanti tamen, quanti si mansuetus fuisset obligaretur. An hæc legis sub finem c. 21. Exodi sancitæ sit mens ac sententia, anxiè disputare nolo: ipsis tamen legis verbis convenientius existimo, ut si dominus debitè bovem asservaverit, de damno non teneatur. Quod si excipias, secundum istam expositionem, bovis petulci conditionem fore potiorem, quam bovis mansueti; cum hic de dimidio damno teneatur: respondeo, ex lege de petulco asservato consequi, nec mansuetum teneri ad damni dimidium, si custoditus; & asservatus, forte fortuna elapsus damnum dederit. Unicuique tamen suum judicium liberum esto. Doctoris Judæ sententia à vero alienior videtur, saltem prima fronte: mansuetum bovem, si asservatus casuq; elapsus damnum dederit, teneri; petulcum vero non teneri. Verum si bene verba ejus expendas, nihil dicit, quam legis Mosaicæ verba etiam suppeditare videntur; licet ipsa in superioribus aliter in priori membro acceperim & exposuerim. Nam quod lex de bove non petulco statuit, id obtinere censet, sive affervetur, sive relaxetur: & ubi idem R. Juda petulcum ac convictum liberum pronuntiat, hoc sibi vult, eo casu qui hic proponitur, si nempe bos asservatus erumpat, dominum de damno nulla parte teneri; quia lex inquit: Si non asservaverit eum. eum. Quo in membro posteriori, authori assentior; non vero in priori: uti jam dictum est. 5 Ad ea quae de custodia hujus bovis dicuntur, revoco illa Gemarae verba ... requiritur custodia excellens, id est, arcta & diligens: laxior enim non sufficit. 6 Denique R. Eliezer seccespita sive cultro quo boves jugulabant, custodiam perficiendam judicabat. Quam sententiam male judicat Rabba eum ex illis verbis, & non asservaverit eum, desumpsisse; acsi Eliezeri ista verba sonuissent, iterum ne huic custodia opus sit, ideoque occidatur. Ut cetera mittam, dextre illi Rabbae se opponit Abaus, cujus haec verba in Gemara citantur; ... Atqui hinc sequitur, illud commatis 33. Et non operuerit illum, etiam exponendum, iterum ne huic operculo opus sit. An dicis similiter etiam hoc accipiendum? Tamen vetus traditio ita habet, Si eum (scilicet puteum debite operuerit, posteaque in eum bos aut asinus incidens moriatur, liber est dominus. Liber tamen non esset, si eum replere & obthurare ac occludere debuisset; Itaque melius Abaus, Eliezerem ad traditionem D. Nathanis respexisse judicat, qui sic locutus fertur; ... Unde prohibetur, ne quis alat rabidum canem domi suae, nec erigat quassatam scalam domi suae? Quia interdicitur, Deut. 22. 8. Ne imponas reatum sanguinis domui tuae. Pariter bovem cornupetam re medio tollendum autumavit. Quatenus secundo Misnae membro reus peragitur dominus, si quadrupedem non rite asservaverit; convenientia docentur cum leg. 1. §. 5. ti. Si quadrupes. Si canis cum duceretur ab aliquo asperitate sua evaserit, & alicui damnum dederit: si contineri firmius ab alio poterit, vel si per eum locum induci non debuit, haec actio cessabit, & tenebitur qui canem tenebat. Prius vero membrum, quo damnum rependi praecipitur, licet quadrupes alteri commodata aliove modo tradita fuerit; congruit ultimis verbis leg. 8. tit. Ad l. Aqu. Idem juris est (mulionem impetum mularum non retinentem culpæ nomine teneri Gajus dixerat) in persona ejus, qui impetum equi quo vehebatur, propter imperitiam vel infirmitatem retinere non poterit. Agitur de bestiis quæ hominibus nocent, quod ab iis qui utuntur non retineantur. Vbi multo quivis, proprietarius non est; nec omnis equo vectus, equi dominus: attamen ex hac lege tenentur. Similiter in Mifna qui pecus ad tempus à proprietario accepit, de dato à pecore damno tenetur. Etiamsi enim in hac Judaica constitutione, quis teneatur, dominus ne an commodatarius &c. non exprimatur; tamen ex Maimonide de damnis pecun. c. 4. sect. 4. satis constat, quis reus constituatur. Vbi enim casum nostrum propositset, subjicit, Si leserit, tenetur custos. Custodis nomine veniunt omnes quorum in primo membro Mifna meminit, (secundo enim membro etiam de proprietario agitur:) quemadmodum Maimonidæ antecedentia verba edocent, quibus iidem illi recensentur.
units.tr: These four classes of men, who received the ox from its owner, differ from one another. The first and second differ from the other two in that no wage is involved in them, as in these: the first differs from the second in that the one lends his labour freely, and the other receives the benefit freely. Lastly, the third is distinguished from the fourth by the different assignment of wages, for this one gives the wage and that one receives it. {2} The following words, If it goes out and does damage, are not found in all manuscripts. But although they are missing in some, it is clear enough from what follows that they are to be understood, since no damage ought to be made good unless it was actually done. Moreover, that this part of the Mishnah is not absolutely accepted by everyone is evident from the last Gemara of the preceding Mishnah. {3} When it is said that the fault must be made good, beware (if you take Meïr's words in the common sense) of demanding equality here. For in agreement with what precedes here and has been explained above, they want half or all of the damage to be made good according to the differing condition of the ox. And lest it be said that Rabbi Meïr contradicts the words of the Mosaic law, Obadiah of Bertinoro observed in this place that he spoke of [מיתה] with reference to looser custody, as if he thought he excused the owner who kept the ox under close custody, not the one who kept it more loosely; yet he said above, he has bound it with a chain and shut it up properly. So I do not see how he can be excused by that distinction, since the law of Moses demands that heavier fine only in the case of an ox proved dangerous, if he has not kept it in custody. So either Meïr erred, or (which I would prefer) the fault to be made good is taken by him indefinitely. In this sense: if a goring ox, kept in custody, breaks loose by chance and does damage, the owner is not liable for the whole damage, but is bound to pay as much as he would have paid if the ox had been tame. Whether this is the intention and meaning of the law sanctioned at the end of chapter 21 of Exodus, I do not wish to dispute anxiously; yet I think it more agreeable to the very words of the law that if the owner has kept the ox properly, he is not liable for the damage. But if you object that, according to this explanation, the condition of a goring ox would be better than that of a tame ox, since the latter is liable for half the damage, I reply that it follows from the law about a goring ox that is kept in custody that a tame ox is not liable for half the damage either, if it was guarded, and, having been kept, by chance broke loose and did damage. Let each man, however, judge freely. The opinion of the teacher Judah seems rather far from the truth, at least at first sight: that a tame ox, if it broke loose by chance while kept and did damage, is liable, but a goring ox is not. Yet if you weigh his words carefully, he says nothing more than the words of the Mosaic law also seem to supply; although in the earlier part I have taken and explained the law differently. For what the law lays down about an ox that is not goring, he judges to hold whether it is kept or let loose; and where the same Rabbi Judah declares a goring and proven ox free, he means this: that in the case proposed here, if the kept ox breaks out, the owner is not liable for the damage in any part, because the law says: If he has not kept it. it. In the latter part I agree with the author, but not in the former, as has already been said. {5} To the things said about the custody of this ox, I recall those words of the Gemara: excellent custody is required, that is, close and diligent; for looser custody is not sufficient. {6} Lastly, Rabbi Eliezer judged that custody had to be carried out with a seccespita, or the knife with which they slaughtered oxen. Rabba judges this opinion wrongly, as if he had derived it from those words, and has not kept it; as if Eliezer's words had sounded like this: so that there is no need of custody again, and therefore it be killed. To pass over the rest, Abaye opposes Rabba squarely, and his words are cited in the Gemara: But from this it follows that the words of verse 33, and has not covered it, are also to be explained as so that there is no need of a covering again. Do you say that this too is to be understood in the same way? Yet the ancient tradition has it thus: if he has properly covered it (namely the pit), and afterwards an ox or an ass falls into it and dies, the owner is free. Yet he would not be free if he ought to have filled it up, stopped it and closed it. So Abaye rightly judges that Eliezer looked to the tradition of Rabbi Nathan, who is reported to have spoken thus: Whence is it forbidden that anyone keep a mad dog in his house, or set up a broken ladder in his house? Because it is forbidden, Deut. 22. 8, that you bring the guilt of blood upon your house. Likewise he judged that a goring ox must be removed from the midst. Insofar as, in the second part of the Mishnah, the owner is prosecuted as guilty if he has not properly kept a quadruped, things agreeing are taught by law 1, §. 5, tit. Si quadrupes: If a dog, while being led by someone, has got away from him through its fierceness and done damage to someone, if it could have been held more firmly by another, or if it ought not to have been led through that place, this action shall cease, and he who was holding the dog shall be liable. But the first part of the Mishnah, by which damage is ordered to be repaid, even if the quadruped was lent to another or handed over in some other way, agrees with the last words of law 8, tit. Ad l. Aqu.: It is the same law (Gaius had said that a muleteer who cannot restrain the rush of his mules is liable by reason of fault) in the case of one who, through inexperience or weakness, cannot restrain the rush of the horse on which he rides. It concerns beasts that harm men, which are not restrained by those who use them. Here the one who uses them is not necessarily the owner, nor is everyone who rides a horse its master; yet they are liable under this law. Similarly, in the Mishnah, one who has received livestock for a time from its owner is liable for damage done by the animal. For even though in this Jewish ordinance it is not stated who is liable, whether the owner or the borrower, etc., yet from Maimonides, On Damages to Property, chapter 4, section 4, it is quite clear who is made liable. For where he had proposed our case, he adds: If it has done injury, the keeper is liable. Under the name of keeper come all those whom the Mishnah mentions in the first part (for in the second part it is also a question of the owner), as the preceding words of Maimonides, in which the same persons are listed, make plain.

units.la: פרק היו הלכי א. שור שנגח את הפרה ונמצ' עוברה בצרה ואין ידוע אם עד שלא נגחה ילדה אם משנגחה ילדה משלם חצי נזק לפרה ודניץ נזק לולד וכן פרה שנגחה את השור ונמצא ולדה בצרה ואין ידוע אם עד שלא נגחה ילדה אם משנגחה ילדה משלם חצי נזק מן
units.tr: פרק היו הלכי א. שור שנגח את הפרה ונמצא עוברה בצרה ואין ידוע אם עד שלא נגחה ילדה אם משנגחה ילדה משלם חצי נזק לפרה ורביע נזק לולד וכן פרה שנגחה את השור ונמצא ולדה בצרה ואין ידוע אם עד שלא נגחה ילדה אם משנגחה ילדה משלם חצי נזק מן

units.la: Si bos vaccam cornu feriat, ad cujus latus inveniatur fœtus, nec liqueat an priusquam ille hanc feriisset hac peperit, an vero post quam feriisset peperit; damni dimidium quoad vaccam compensatur, & quarta pars quoad fœtum. Pariter quum vacca bovem feriit, & reperto ad illius latus fœtu non liqueat, num antequam feriret peperit, num vero postquam feriret peperit; damni dimidium compensatur. הפרה ורביע נוק מן הולד fatur è vacca, quarta verò damni pars è fœtu.
units.tr: If an ox gores a cow, and beside her side a fetus is found, and it is not clear whether she gave birth before he gored her or after he gored her, he pays half the damage for the cow and a quarter of the damage for the fetus. Likewise, when a cow gores an ox, and a calf is found beside its side, and it is not clear whether she gave birth before she gored or after she gored, he pays half the damage [הפרה ורביע נזק מן הולד] is paid from the cow, and the quarter part of the damage from the fetus.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Non quivis fœtus denotatur; sed abortu vitiatus: nam in sequentibus agitur de damno rependendo, quod abortu in hoc fœtu datum fuerit. Nec etiam ullo modo ad rem faceret, de fœtu quidpiam addere, nisi abortus spectaretur. Sed eò si collimemus, merito duplicem casum proponi judicabimus. Nam aut constat vaccam antequam à bove laederetur abortum fecisse, quo casu fœtus nullo modo compensatur; aut, postquam bos feriisset, vaccam abortum fecisse constat, quo casu dubium non est, quin bos fœtus respectu in dimidium, vel solidum teneatur, prout vel manuetus vel cornupeta fuerit. quamvis Misna mansuetum solummodo spectet ac consideret, unde quid de cornupeta statuendum è superioribus liquet. Ideo inquit, damni dimidium quoad vaccam compensatur: mansuetus enim in totum damnum non tenetur. Verum sæpe contingit, ut quo tempore ferierit bos, in incerto sit; adeoque ignoretur an quoad fœtum, qui obiit vel læsus sit, teneatur: hoc enim ex illa temporis observatione dependet. Itaque hac in re bipartiuntur: cum enim si fœtus è læsa vacca sensisset incommodum, bos teneretur; sin minus, innocens haberetur: loco dimidii, quadrantem exigunt. Idque ex illa R. Somcosi sententia qua pronuntiavit, Rem pecuniariam, quae in dubium trahitur, dividunt. cujus hæc mens, in iis quæ pecuniam & facultates tantum spectant, si oriatur de facto controversia, anxiè probationes non exigi: sed dimidium huic vendicari, qui actor est; cum alias totum obtineret. Itaque cum hoc casu, si de facto certò constaret, actor dimidium tantum obtineret; Misna quartam partem jam assignat; quia factum incertum est. Postea docetur quid juris sit, si vacca ipsa bovem ferierit & fœtum suum ediderit: ubi de fœtu compensando non quæritur; sed unde pretium, quod solvendum est, desumi debeat: an è vaccæ valore; an verò fœtus etiam in rationem veniat. si exempli gratia, vaccæ valor ad damnum compensandum non sufficiat; vel vacca amissa sit, aut perierit. 5 Ideo distinctio propònitur. vel enim bovè feriit postquam peperisset vitulum; quod ubi liquet, ut Judæi observant, vituli pretium nullo modo ad compensandum damnum bovi illatum concurrere constat: aut feriit antequam peperisset; qui casus si indubius fit, quum è vaccæ pretio satisfieri nequit, ad dimidium usque dati in bove damni, vituli pretium arripitur. quia cum in vulva esset dum vacca feriret, veluti vaccæ corpus censebatur. 6 Verum si de tempore disceptetur, ex illo pronuntiato R. Somcosi (de quo in superioribus) ubi è vacca compensari debito modo jactura nequit, ad vitulum remittitur actor: ut inde quartam damni partem recipiat; qui alioqui mediam partem ibi recuperaret, si vaccam feriisse antequam peperisset, judicibus innotecceret. Sed fundamentum illud à Somcoso jactum, à Judæorum quamplurimis magistris non approbatur: ideo que hic commune quoddam dictum locum habere contendunt, סמנין מתכאיו עלי סרוס Qui ab alio quid exigit, ei incumbit probatio. Quo non admittunt, ut quod in dubium vocatur, bipartito dividatur; sed actori probandi necessitatem imponunt. Vnde in proposito casu, quartam jacturæ partem à vitulo exigi nolunt; sed si probari queat, fœtum in vulva fuisse cum vacca feriret, dimidiam partem pro more exigi permittunt: & si illud probari non possit, ad nullam, ne quidem minimam partem teneri vitulum concedunt. Adeoque fundamentum suum magistri extollunt, ut in Gemara id hoc epitheto ornent, בין נדה יולא Insigne axioma in judicio. Sic etiam leges Romanæ exigunt ut judex probata sequatur, De officio Præf. l. Illicitas, §. Veritas. Præses provincia id id sequatur, quod convenit, eum, ex fide eorum quae probantur. Atque hujus rei in se exemplum nobis praebet A. Gellius Noct. Att. l. 14. c. 2. Petebatur (inquit) apud me pecunia, quae dicebatur data numerataque, sed qui petebat neque tabulis neque testibus id factum docebat, & argumentis admodum exilibus nitebatur, sed eum constabat virum esse fermè bonum, notaque & experta fidei, & vitae inculpatissimae: multaque & illustria exempla probitatis sinceritatisque ejus expromebantur. illum autem, unde petebatur, hominem esse non bonae fidei, vitaque turpi & sordida, convictumque vulgo in mendaciis, plenumque esse perfidiarum & fraudum ostendebatur. Subjungit tamen Gellius se magnorum etiam virorum autoritate induci non potuisse, ut judicium ferret, deficiente probatione. Improbata ergo illa Somcosi sententia, ut in re dubia ejus dimidium actori addiceretur, quod totum, si veritas constaret, obtineret.
units.tr: It is not any calf that is meant, but one lost through abortion. For what follows deals with making good the loss caused by abortion in this calf. Nor would it be relevant at all to add anything about the calf unless abortion were in view. If we keep that in view, we shall rightly judge that two cases are being put forward. For either it is agreed that the cow miscarried before the bull injured her, in which case the calf is in no way compensated; or it is agreed that the cow miscarried after the bull had gored her, in which case there is no doubt that the bull is liable for half or the whole of the calf's value, according as he was tame or a gorer. The Mishnah, however, considers and regards only the tame bull, and from the above it is clear what must be decided about the gorer. Therefore it says: half the loss is compensated for the cow, for a tame bull is not liable for the whole loss. But it often happens that the time at which the bull gored is uncertain, and so it is not known whether he is liable for the calf that died or was harmed, since this depends on that observation of time. Therefore they divide the matter: if the calf had suffered harm from the injured cow, the bull would be liable; if not, he would be held innocent. Instead of a half they exact a quarter. This follows from that opinion of R. Somcos, by which he pronounced, a money matter that is brought into doubt is divided. His meaning was this: in cases concerning only money and property, if a dispute arises about a fact, the proofs are not demanded anxiously; instead, half is awarded to the claimant, who would otherwise obtain the whole. So in this case, if the fact were certainly established, the claimant would obtain only half; the Mishnah now assigns a quarter, because the fact is uncertain. Next it is taught what the law is if the cow herself gores the bull and then bears her calf. Here the question is not about compensating for the calf, but about where the price to be paid must be taken from: from the value of the cow, or whether the calf too comes into the reckoning. For example, if the value of the cow is not enough to make good the loss, or the cow has been lost or has died. 5 Therefore a distinction is put forward. Either the bull was gored after the cow had borne the calf; and where this is clear, as the Jews observe, it is agreed that the price of the calf in no way contributes to compensating the bull for the loss inflicted on him. Or he was gored before she bore it; and if this case is undoubted, then when satisfaction cannot be made from the price of the cow, the price of the calf is taken to make up half of the loss suffered by the bull. For while the calf was in the womb when the cow gored, it was regarded as part of the cow's body. 6 But if the time is disputed, then by that saying of R. Somcos (mentioned above), when the loss cannot be properly compensated from the cow, the claimant is sent to the calf, so that he may receive from it a quarter of the loss; otherwise he would recover half there, if the judges learned that the cow had gored before she bore it. But that foundation laid down by Somcos is not approved by most of the Jewish masters. Therefore they contend that a common saying holds here: the one who demands something from another, on him lies the proof [המוציא מחברו עליו הראיה]. By this they do not allow what is called in doubt to be divided in two; instead they impose on the claimant the necessity of proof. Hence in the present case they are unwilling that a quarter of the loss be exacted from the calf; but if it can be proved that the calf was in the womb when the cow gored, they permit half to be exacted according to custom; and if that cannot be proved, they grant that the calf is liable for no part at all, not even the smallest. So the masters exalt their principle so highly that in the Gemara they adorn it with this epithet: [בין נדה יולא] a remarkable axiom in judgement. So too the Roman laws require that the judge follow what has been proved: On the Office of the Prefect, law Illicitas, §. Veritas: the governor of the province should follow that which agrees with the faith of what is proved. Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 14, chapter 2, provides us with an example of this matter. A sum of money was sought from me, he says, which was said to have been given and counted out; but the claimant proved the fact neither by documents nor by witnesses, and relied on very slight arguments. Yet it was clear that he was a man almost good, known and tested in faith, of most blameless life; and many illustrious examples of his integrity and sincerity were brought forward. But it was shown that the man from whom the money was sought was not of good faith, of a base and sordid life, convicted commonly of lies, and full of treachery and fraud. Gellius adds, however, that even the authority of great men could not induce him to give judgement when proof was lacking. Therefore that opinion of Somcos is rejected, namely that in a doubtful matter half should be awarded to the claimant, whereas if the truth were established he would obtain the whole.
Bin [בין]

units.la: הקוד שהכנים קדוחיו לחצר בעל הבית שלא ברשות ושברחן כהסתו של בעל הבית פטור ואם החקה בהן בעל הקדו׳ חייב׳ ואם הכנים ברשות בעל חצר חייב הכנים פירוהיו לחצ׳ בעל הבית שלא ברשות ואכלהן בהםתו של בעל הבית פטור ואם החקה בהן כעל הפירות חייב ואם הכנים ברשות בעל חצר חייב׳
units.tr: הקדרה שהכניס קדרותיו לחצר בעל הבית שלא ברשות ושברתן בהמתו של בעל הבית פטור, ואם החזיק בהן בעל הקדרה חייב. ואם הכניס ברשות בעל החצר חייב. הכניס פירותיו לחצר בעל הבית שלא ברשות ואכלתן בהמתו של בעל הבית פטור, ואם החזיק בהן כבעל הפירות חייב, ואם הכניס ברשות בעל החצר חייב. [הקוד שהכנים קדוחיו לחצר בעל הבית שלא ברשות ושברחן כהסתו של בעל הבית פטור ואם החקה בהן בעל הקדו׳ חייב׳ ואם הכנים ברשות בעל חצר חייב הכנים פירוהיו לחצ׳ בעל הבית שלא ברשות ואכלהן בהםתו של בעל הבית פטור ואם החקה בהן כעל הפירות חייב ואם הכנים ברשות בעל חצר חייב׳]

units.la: Quum ollas sine venia in aream patrisfamilias à figulo illatas, frangit pecus patrisfamilias; hic liber est: quod si pecus ipsius laedatur, ollarum {1} possessor tenetur. at quum intulit cum venia, possessor aream {2} tenetur. Si quis fructus suos in patrisfamilias aream sine venia inferat, quos deinde pecus patrisfamilias comedat; hic liber est: & si ipsius {3} laedatur, fructuum possessor tenetur. at si intulerit cum venia, possessor area tenetur.
units.tr: When a potter brings his pots without leave into the householder's courtyard, and the householder's beast breaks them, he is exempt; but if the beast of the householder is hurt, the owner of the pots {1} is liable. But when he brought them with leave, the owner of the courtyard {2} is liable. If anyone brings his fruits into the householder's courtyard without leave, and the householder's beast then eats them, this is exempt; and if its beast is hurt, {3} the owner of the fruits is liable. But if he brought them with leave, the owner of the courtyard is liable.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Meritò ollarum proprietarius tenetur, qui alterius fundum ingressus damni occasionem præbuit. quorsum alterius limites transgreditur? Ideo autem culpa tenetur, ut Gemara annotat, quia non impetrata venia res suas intulit. Nam alioqui non teneretur: ut concludit Gemara. Imò contra, loci dominus condemnatur, si ollæ illatæ ipsius pecore conterantur & conculcentur. Sed hic exurgit dubium: si enim post datam veniam, areæ dominus ollarum damnum præstare debet; annon vice versa istarum dominus damnum per eas pecori illatum rependere tenetur? Attamen figulus post impetratam ingrediendi veniam omninò absolvitur. Imo etiam areæ possessor sub finem sequentis Misnæ absolvitur, donec in se cautionem receperit. Hæc tria cohærere non videntur. Itaque Gemara postquam innocentiam figuli, cui inferendi concessa venia, asseruissel, de istis repugnantiis hæc subjungit; [Hebrew text illegible, ~40 letters] Cujus est? (sc. potior conditio patrisfamilias?) Ipsius Ribbi: qui ait, Quicunq; absolutè (sc. alteri dat veniam) in se non recipit cautionem. Verum dicam, At subjungitur, Quum intulit cum venia, possessor area tenetur. Hæc procedunt secundum magistros: qui affirmant, Quum absolute etiam loquitur, omnino in se cautionem recipit. Atqui iterum ait Ribbi, In istis omnibus non tenetur, donec in se paterfamilias cautionem recipiat. Verumenimverò principium & finis est ipsius Ribbi; medium est Magistrorum. E quibus liquet, Rabbi Judæ, qui Misnas collegit, primam & ultimam opinionem tribui; medio loco collocatam Magistris ascribi. Ideoque subjicit D. Zera, Est ita solvendum: qui hoc docuit, alterum non docuit. Raba tamen censet, omnia è placito sapientum dici: & quod de cautionis cura suscipienda dicitur, secundum Misnæ verba esse accommodandum, & pertinere ad quemvis patremfamilias cujus venia res in aream suam inferuntur. 3 Porrò quum fructuum proprietarius ejus jacturæ reus peragitur, quam paterfamilias in pecore suo fructibus læso passus est; magistri distinctionem adhibent, quam Rabi verbis concisè proponit Gemara, ﬠﬡ ﬢ ﬣ ﬤ ﬥ ﬦ ﬧ ﬨ, Non tradunt (magistri, quæ hic de reatu dicuntur,) nisi quum illis (fructibus pecus) lubricâ factâ viâ labitur; verum si comedat (plusquam par est,) liber est (fructuum dominus.) Quæ est ratio? Poterat pecus non comedere.
units.tr: Rightly is the owner of the pots held liable, since he, having entered another's field, gave the occasion for the damage. Why does he cross another's boundaries? The Gemara notes that he is held liable for fault because he brought in his goods without first obtaining permission. For otherwise he would not be liable, as the Gemara concludes. On the contrary, the owner of the place is condemned if the pots brought in are crushed and trampled by his cattle. But here a doubt arises. If, after permission has been given, the owner of the courtyard must make good the damage to the pots, must not the owner of the pots in turn make good the damage they did to the cattle? Yet the potter, once permission to enter has been obtained, is wholly acquitted. Indeed the possessor of the courtyard too is acquitted at the end of the following Mishnah, until he has taken a bond upon himself. These three points do not seem to cohere. So the Gemara, having asserted the innocence of the potter, to whom entry was granted, adds this about these contradictions: [Hebrew text illegible]. "Whose is it?" (that is, the better position of the householder?) "It is Rabbi's, who says: whoever gives permission absolutely (that is, to another) does not take a bond upon himself. But I will say," the text continues, "'When he brought it in with permission, the possessor of the courtyard is liable.' These things hold according to the masters, who affirm that when he speaks absolutely he indeed takes a bond upon himself. Yet again Rabbi says: in all these cases he is not liable until the householder takes a bond upon himself. The beginning and end are Rabbi's own; the middle is the masters'." From these words it is clear that the first and last opinions are attributed to Rabbi Judah, who collected the Mishnayot, while the opinion placed in the middle is ascribed to the masters. So D. Zera adds: "It is to be resolved thus: he who taught this did not teach the other." Raba, however, holds that everything is said by the consent of the sages, and that what is said about taking up the care of a bond should be applied according to the words of the Mishnah, and pertains to any householder whose goods are brought into his courtyard with his permission. 3 Furthermore, when the owner of the fruits is prosecuted for the loss which the householder has suffered in his cattle, injured by the fruits, the masters make a distinction, which the Gemara briefly sets out in Rabbi's words: [Hebrew text illegible]. "They do not hand down (the masters, concerning what is said here about guilt) unless the beast slips when the way has been made slippery by them (the fruits); but if it eats (more than is fitting), it is free (the owner of the fruits)." "What is the reason? The beast could have not eaten."

units.la: Jumentum aliquod, vel minus animal, exempli gratia canis, si ex illatis fructibus tantum voret, ut inde male habeat; fructuum proprietarium, licet sine patrisfamilias venia intraverit, absolvunt: quia totum damnum ex illa canis voracitate exortum. at si fructibus horariis ut cerasis, cornis, aliisve pavimentum reddatur lubricum, atque hac occasione jumentum lapsum lædatur; fructuum dominum teneri censent: quia tota culpa in ipso solo deprehenditur. Nec hic ex illorum sententia, subsistendum; sed de similibus similiter vel analogicè judicandum. Itaque ibidem de alio casu simili, שּׂ אַ אָ אּ בּ גּ דּ הּ, At dicam, Quid si sopitum jumentum obdormiat? Rabus inquit, Sequenda ista constitutio traditionis exotica, Quicunque collocat venenum lethiferum coram jumento proximi, liber est à condemnatione humana; sed tenetur judicio cœlesti. Solvitur dubium prolata traditione de veneno lethifico, vel concludendo à majori ad minus; vel à specie ad genus. Si enim is non teneatur qui venenum pecudi objecit, quanto minus, si cibum vel pabulum aliquod, quo sopiatur? vel si quis edulium venenatum objiciens non peragatur reus, sanè nec si alia eduliorum genera præbeat, quibus pecus præter modum vescens domino ad tempus inutile reddatur, datur, vel moriatur (nam מוֹת Talmud. ut Chaldæis mori etiam sonat.) Atque hæc est verborum istorum mens, cum inquiunt, יוֹמָן דְּאִיתִי מָטָא דְאִיתִי נָמֵי מִיתָה סָם מָוֶת וְהַשָּׁבַעַי Atque ecce constitutum nobis est, Quin etiam ob venenum lethiferum, quod factum non est ut cibus sit, reus tantum est in judicio cælesti. Vel si mavis dicam, venenum etiam lethiferum esse in ancipitum genere quæ sunt fructus. Hic duplex argumentum est, quorum prius ita enarratur in additamentis, Quia non docuit nos de reliquis fructibus, ad extendendum sumpsit venenum lethale, quasi dicas, quamvis absolute exterminet ex hoc mundo, nihilo secius author in humano judicio absolvitur. Posteriori argumento qui procedatur ut intelligamus, consideranda vox פִּתְרוֹנֵי, quæ hic adhibetur: de hac ita S. Jarchi, Herba quæ ad cibum creata est, sed est venenum mortiferum jumento. Ideo in versione voce anceps usus fui, quia de eo dicitur quod cum prodest, tum etiam nocet: his alimentum est; illis detrimentum & venenum. Est enim à פָּרַשׂ in Hiphil Talmudicis significante dilatare: nam illa latum & differentem usum habet, & à se invicem longissime distantem. Itaque à פָּרָז Judæi quidam פְּרָזוֹת, pagos deducunt, quod laxior & latior ibi sit habitatio. Sed ad rem ipsam. Quum is qui in alterius aream aliquid importavit, quo damnum infertur, condemnatur; id jure fieri omnino censendum est: quandoquidem qui in publica via, quæ tamen omnium est, hujusmodi occasionem damni præbet, damni tenetur; uti edocet totus titulus, De his qui effuderint vel dejecerint. ubi observanda verba leg. 1. §. 2. Parvi autem interesse debet, utrum publicus locus sit, an vero privatus: dummodo per eum vulgo iter fiat. Quibus verbis edictum Prætoris, cujus initio mentionem fecerat, extendit. Quid ergo de iis statuendum locis, ubi nullum tibi iter conceditur?
units.tr: If a beast of burden, or a smaller animal such as a dog, eats so much of the fruit that has been brought in that it is made ill, they acquit the owner of the fruit, even though it entered without the householder's permission, because the whole loss arises from the dog's voracity. But if the ground is made slippery by fruits that ripen at a particular season, such as cherries, cornelberries or others, and the beast falls and is injured on that occasion, they judge that the owner of the fruit is liable, because the whole fault is found in the ground itself. Nor should we stop at their opinion here, but judge similar cases similarly or by analogy. So in the same place, concerning another similar case, the Gemara says: But I will say, what if a beast of burden falls asleep? Rabbi says: that tradition of foreign origin must be followed: whoever places deadly poison before his neighbour's beast is free from human condemnation, but is held to the heavenly judgement [שּׂ אַ אָ אּ בּ גּ דּ הּ]. The doubt raised about deadly poison is resolved either by arguing from the greater to the lesser, or from the species to the genus. For if he who offers poison to a beast is not liable, how much less is he liable if he offers food or fodder by which it is put to sleep? Or if one who offers poisoned food is not prosecuted as guilty, surely neither is one who provides other kinds of food, by which an animal that eats beyond measure is rendered useless to its owner for a time, or dies (for the Talmud's word for death [מוֹת] also means to die in Chaldee). And this is the sense of those words when they say: Behold, it has been established for us: even for deadly poison, which is not made to be food, one is guilty only in the heavenly judgement. Or, if you prefer, I will say that deadly poison also belongs to the class of things that are ambiguous, which are fruits. Here there is a double argument. The first is explained in the additions thus: Because he has not taught us about the remaining fruits, he took up deadly poison to extend the rule, as if to say: although it utterly destroys a man in this world, nonetheless the author is acquitted in human judgement. To understand how the second argument proceeds, the word פִּתְרוֹנֵי used here must be considered. Of this, S. Jarchi says: an herb which was created for food, but is deadly poison to a beast. So in my version I have used the word ambiguous, because it is said of that which both benefits and harms: to some it is nourishment, to others loss and poison. For it comes from פָּרַשׂ in the Hiphil, which in Talmudic usage means to spread out, since that word has a broad and differing use, very far apart from itself. Hence some Jews derive פְּרָזוֹת, villages, from פָּרָז, because dwelling there is looser and wider. But to the matter itself. When one who has brought something into another's courtyard, by which damage is caused, is condemned, it must wholly be judged that this is done rightly, since he who in a public way, which nevertheless belongs to all, provides such an occasion of damage, is liable for the damage; as the whole title On those who have poured out or thrown down teaches. Here the words of law 1, §2 must be observed: It makes little difference whether the place is public or private, provided that by it a way is commonly used. By these words he extends the praetor's edict, of which he made mention at the beginning. What then must be decided about those places where no way is granted to you?

units.la: הכנים סורו לחצר בעל הבית שלא ברשות ונגחו סורו
units.tr: If a man's ox enters without permission the courtyard of the owner and gores, or the owner's ox or the owner's dog bites, he is exempt.

units.la: של בעל הבית או שנשכו כלבו של בעל הבית פטור
units.tr: If the ox of the owner gores, he is liable. If it falls into his pit, and the one who brought it in is liable...

units.la: נגח הוא סורו של בעל הבית חייב נפל לבורו והבאי מיפיו
units.tr: If it was the father or the son [of the owner] who was liable for the goring, he pays the ransom (kopher).

units.la: חייב היה אביו או בנו לזכו משלם ארז הכופר ואם
units.tr: But if they entered with the permission of the owner of the courtyard, he is liable. Rabbi says: in all these cases he is not liable

units.la: הכנים ברשות בעל החצר חייב רבי אומר בכולן אינו
units.tr: until the owner of the house accepts upon himself the duty of keeping them.

units.la: חייב עד שיקבל עליו בעל הבית לשמור׃
units.tr: (Concluding the Mishnah's statement that the owner is not liable until he undertakes to keep the animals.)
