units.la: Si postquam bovem suum quis introduxit sine venia in aream patrisfamilias, eum deinde cornu feriat bos patrisfamilias, aut canis ejusdem mordeat, hic liber est: si illius bos feriat bovem patrisfamilias, ille tenetur. Si in ejus foveam vel puteum cadat & considerceat ejus aquam, tenetur: quod si ejus pater aut filius in puteo fuerit, solvit λύτρον. Sin cum venia introduxerit, area possessor tenetur. Sed Ribbi inquit, In istis omnibus non tenetur, donec in se recipiat area possessor cautionem.
units.tr: If, after someone introduced his ox without permission into the householder's courtyard, the householder's ox gores it, or the householder's dog bites it, he is free. If the other's ox gores the householder's ox, that one is liable. If it falls into his pit or well and fouls its water, he is liable; but if the householder's father or son was in the well, he pays the ransom. But if he introduced it with permission, the possessor of the courtyard is liable. Yet Rabbi says that in all these cases he is not liable until the possessor of the courtyard takes a bond upon himself.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Hic casus satis perspicuus est: sed in Gemara alius admodum dubius profertur, de quo ex sententia Doctoris Tarphonis respondetur, ipsius admissa hypothesi. הכנים סורו לחצר בעל הבית שלא ברשות ונגחו סורו ... Introduxerit quis bovem suum in aream patrisfamilias absque ejus venia, atque aliunde ingressus alius priorem bovem feriat; (dominus bovis) non tenetur: at si cum venia introduxerit, tenetur. In hac ipsa quæstionis decisione dubia quædam superfunt. Quum enim dicitur חייב, tenetur, dubium est quis teneri dicatur: ad bovis tamen lædentis proprietarium hoc retuli; quia sic ibidem subjungitur. ... Quis innocens, & quis reus? annon liber est loci dominus, & reus loci dominus? Nequaquam. quaritur an bovis dominus liber, an reus sit. Verum hinc alia emergit quæstio: nam si de boum exterorum dominis, non de patrefamilias hic dubitetur, quorsum ea quæ veniam ingrediendi concernunt? siquidem ista bovem introducendi copia inter bovis dominum & patremfamilias spectatur. [illegible, ~60 letters] Si ita fit (inquiunt) quid sibi vult, Cum venia? & quid, Absque venia? Sunt qui ita dicant, Ista constitutio ex cujus mente est? Doctoris Tarphonis: qui ait, Alia est ipsius cornu conditio in area læsi, ubi totum damnum ejus nomine præstatur. Illi, quum dicitur, Cum venia, idem est ac, Cornu in area læsi, ideoque totum damnum rependitur; at quum dicitur, Absque venia, idem est ac, Cornu in loco publico, & nonnisi damni dimidium præstatur. Mens hæc est, in illo superiori casu non quæri, an quis omnino liber sit, an vero totius damni teneatur; sed an totum, an vero dimidium rependere teneatur: adeo ut ממור sit liber ab altero damni dimidio; ייחם, reus totius. deinde id juris hic servari, quod in cornu, si bos cornu feriat in loco privato ipsius læsi; vel in loco publico. itaque veniam illam spectari posse inter duos boum proprietarios, quorum area, in qua damnum datur, non sit. Idque in hunc modum: Si tuus & meus bos Titii aream ingrediatur, & meus ibi tuum, quem absque domini arexe consensu introduxisti, cornu feriat; ego non teneor: quia cum absque venia tuum introduxeris, ille locus non censetur tuus ullo modo; sed communis nobis, in quo nihil plus juris quam ego habeas. itaque nihil solvo, nisi quod deberem si bos meus in loco publico damnum intulisset, id est, dimidium. at si impetrata venia introduxeris bovem, de toto damno teneor: quia idem est ac si bos meus in ipsius læsi ditione damnum dedisset; siquidem venia & permissus patrisfamilias effecit, (quemadmodum Tarphon censet) ut locus ille quodammodo tuus fit, saltem ipso usu. Quocirca licet venia ista à patrefamilias petenda sit, jus tamen in causa nostra immutat, atque ad nostri utrumque certa quadam ratione referTur. Sed cum in posteriori loco legitur, Sunt qui ita dicant; merito quæri posset, an hæc verba causam dubiam non relinquant: siquidem alii secus sentire ex ista phrasi videntur. Verum in libro Halichoth Olam (quem latine versum, jam consulere potes) bene observatur, ista phrasi in Gemara communem sententiam notari. Accepimus, ubicunque in Gemara occurrit, Sunt qui dicant, ita esse ipsam constitutionem. ubi etiam improbatur alterius Doctoris sententia, qui secus autumabat. Ad sequentiam Isaac Gabæus e Gemara annotat, Idem jus in caeteris servatur; sed viam rei sumpsit: id est, hoc exemplum in similibus sequendum, quod in patre & filio patrisfamilias proponitur: ideo autem hoc potius quam aliud assumptum fuisse, quia Mishna viam rei, sive eam rem quæ veluti per viam plerumque incedit; id est, quæ plerumque vel magis frequenter contingit, in exemplum sumere solet. Factum est hujusmodi, Cum bos alienus aream alicujus viri ingressus, ubi pabulum forte conspicit in fovea & depresso ac excavato loco, eo se demittit & viri istius patrem aut filium opprimit. Tales enim boves esse qui id facere soleant, notat Maimonides. Salomon Jarchi tamen hoc secus accipit, puta quum videns viriditatem, id est, herbam ad oram putei, accedit ad vescendum, & incidit. Existimat Gemara de bove convicto, qui pabulum ita quærens sæpius in foveam incidere soleat, sermonem esse: quia alioqui ad λύτρον non teneretur. Morte vero hujusmodi bove afficiendum negant, quia ad eum casum non collimavit. Vbi vero subjicitur, arex dominum teneri, si alter cum permissu pecus introduxerit, id non refertur ad proxime præcedentia; sed ad remotiora, si cum feriat bos patrisfamilias, vel canis mordeat, scilicet hospi-
units.tr: This case is quite clear. But in the Gemara another case is put forward, a rather doubtful one, and it is answered according to the opinion of Doctor Tarphon, granting the hypothesis he has admitted: הכנים סורו לחצר בעל הבית שלא ברשות ונגחו סורו ... If a man brings his ox into the courtyard of a householder without the householder's permission, and another ox, coming in from elsewhere, gores the first ox, (the owner of the ox) is not liable; but if he brought it in with permission, he is liable. In this very decision of the question some doubts remain. For when it is said tenetur [חייב, "is liable"], it is unclear who is said to be liable. I have referred this, however, to the owner of the ox that does the injury, since the text goes on in the same place: ... Who is innocent, and who guilty? Is not the owner of the place free, and the owner of the place guilty? By no means. The question is whether the owner of the ox is free or guilty. But from this another question arises. For if the doubt concerns the owners of the foreign oxen, and not the householder, why are those things that concern permission to enter included? For this right to bring in an ox is considered between the owner of the ox and the householder. If that is so (they say), what does "with permission" mean? And what does "without permission" mean? Some say this: whose opinion is this ruling? It is Doctor Tarphon's, who says: "The ox's condition is different when it is in the courtyard of the one harmed, where the whole damage is paid on its account. When it is said 'with permission', it is the same as saying 'the ox is in the courtyard of the one harmed', and so the whole damage is repaid; but when it is said 'without permission', it is the same as saying 'the ox is in a public place', and only half the damage is paid." The sense is this: in that earlier case the question is not whether someone is wholly free, or whether he must pay the whole of the damage; it is whether he must pay the whole or only half. So the one who is free (מזור) is free from the other half of the damage, and the one who is liable (חייב) is liable for the whole. Then the law here is the same as for the horn: if an ox gores with its horn in the private place of the one harmed, or in a public place. Thus that permission can be considered between two owners of oxen, of whom the courtyard in which the damage is done is not one. And this is how: if your ox and mine enter Titius's courtyard, and my ox gores yours there, which you brought in without the consent of the owner of the courtyard, I am not liable; for since you brought it in without permission, that place is not considered yours in any way, but common to us, where you have no more right than I do. So I pay nothing, except what I would owe if my ox had done the damage in a public place, that is, half. But if you brought in the ox with permission obtained, I am liable for the whole damage, because it is the same as if my ox had done the damage within the domain of the one harmed; for the permission and consent of the householder make that place somewhat yours (as Tarphon thinks), at least by its use. Therefore, although that permission must be sought from the householder, it nevertheless changes the law in our case, and is referred to each of us in a certain fixed way. But since in the later passage we read Some say this, one might fairly ask whether these words leave the case doubtful, since from this phrase others seem to think otherwise. However, in the book Halichoth Olam (which you can consult now that it has been translated into Latin) it is well observed that by this phrase in the Gemara the common opinion is marked. We have received that, wherever in the Gemara it occurs, "Some say", the ruling itself is so. There too the opinion of another doctor, who thought otherwise, is rejected. As to what follows, Isaac Gabaeus notes from the Gemara: The same law is kept in the other cases, but he took the example of the thing: that is, this example is to be followed in similar cases, which is put forward in the case of the householder's father and son. The reason this example was chosen rather than another is that the Mishnah is accustomed to take as its example the case of the way, that is, a thing which for the most part goes along the way; that is, one which most often or more frequently happens. The case is of this kind: when another man's ox has entered the courtyard of someone, and sees fodder by chance in a pit, in a sunken and hollowed place, it lowers itself into it and crushes the father or the son of that man. Maimonides notes that such oxen are those which are accustomed to do this. Solomon Jarchi, however, understands it otherwise, namely, when, seeing greenness, that is, grass at the edge of a well, it approaches to feed, and falls in. The Gemara thinks the reference is to an ox already convicted, which, seeking fodder in this way, is often accustomed to fall into the pit; because otherwise it would not be liable for the ransom. They deny, however, that such an ox should be put to death, because it did not aim at that case. But where it is added that the householder is liable if another has brought in livestock with permission, this is not referred to the immediately preceding cases, but to the more remote ones: if the ox of the householder gores, or the dog bites, namely the guest's ox. This is clear from comparing this Mishnah with the preceding one. But although the owner of the courtyard is said to be liable for the damage that his animal inflicts on another's animal which he had admitted, Ribbi denies that he is liable. Ribbi is Doctor Judah; and Maimonides and Bartenora observe that the rule or custom holds according to the opinion of Ribbi, so that we may know what is to be followed in this disagreement. Indeed, that by Roman law one who has let an animal into another's land and done damage there is liable, the law Si quadrupes and other similar laws do not let us doubt. But conversely (as is also put forward here), does one who suffers damage there have an action against the owner? It seems so, if he had the same action for what he did there. For so at the end of the title Si quadrupes: When a groom was leading a horse into an inn, the horse smelled a mule; the mule kicked back and broke the groom's leg. It was asked whether an action could be brought against the mule's owner, because the mule had caused the injury. I answered that it could.

units.la: [Hebrew and Greek phrases in the original are not reproduced here; see notes.] hospitis bovem. Hoc liquet ex collatione hujus Mifnæ cum præcedenti. Sed licet areæ possessor teneri dicatur de damno, quod à pecore suo infertur alterius pecori quod admiserat; Ribbi teneri negat. Ribbi est Doctor Judas: & observant Maimonides & Bartenorius, constitutionem vel consuetudinem obtinere ex mente Ribbi; ut sciamus quid in hac discrepantia sequendum sit. Quin ex jure Romano tenecatur, qui jumento in alterius fundum immisso ibi damnum dedit, dubitare nos non finit lex Si quadrupes, & similes aliæ. Sed vice versa (ut hic etiam proponitur) an si damnum ibi patiatur, actionem in dominum habet? Hoc videtur, si modo quod illic ageret, habuerit. Ita enim sub finem tituli, Si quadrupes. Agaso cum in tabernam equum deduceret, mulam equus olfecit. mula calcem rejecit, & crus agasoni fregit. consulebatur, possetne cum domino mula agi, quod ea pauperiem fecisset. Respondi, posse.
units.tr: [Hebrew and Greek phrases in the original are not reproduced here; see notes.] the guest's ox. This is clear from comparing this Mishnah with the preceding one. But although the owner of the courtyard is said to be liable for damage that his animal inflicts on the animal of another which he had admitted, Ribbi denies that he is liable. Ribbi is Doctor Judah; and Maimonides and Bartenora observe that the rule or custom holds according to the opinion of Ribbi, so that we may know what is to be followed in this disagreement. Indeed, that by Roman law one who has let an animal into another's land and done damage there is liable, the law Si quadrupes and other similar laws do not let us doubt. But conversely (as is also put forward here), does one who suffers damage there have an action against the owner? It seems so, if he had the same action for what he did there. For so at the end of the title Si quadrupes: When a groom was leading a horse into an inn, the horse smelled a mule; the mule kicked back and broke the groom's leg. It was asked whether an action could be brought against the mule's owner, because the mule had caused the injury. I answered that it could.

units.la: Si bos comparem suum intendens, mulierem ita feriat, ut ejus fœtus expellantur; dominus pretium fœtuum solvere non tenetur. Si homo proximum suum intendens, ita mulierem percutiat, ut fœtus ejiciantur; fœtuum pretium solvit. Qui fœtuum pretium solvit? Æstimant mulierem, quanti valuerit antequam peperisset, & quanti valeat post partum. Excipit D. Sim. f. Gamalielis, Si ita fit, postquam mulier peperit, prestantior est. Sed æstimant natos, quanti valent; idque marito datur.
units.tr: If an ox, aiming at its fellow, strikes a woman so that her unborn young are expelled, its owner is not bound to pay for the unborn young. If a man, aiming at his neighbour, strikes a woman so that the unborn young are expelled, he pays the value of the unborn young. How is the value of the unborn young paid? They assess the woman's worth before she gave birth and her worth after the delivery. Rabbi Simeon son of Gamaliel objects to this: if it is so, after the woman has given birth she is more valuable. But they assess the children at what they are worth, and this is given to the husband.
