units.tr: ונתן לבעל ואם אין לה בעל [illegible, about 20 letters] ונתן ליורשיו היתה שפחה [illegible, about 20 letters] ונשחררה או גיורה פטור׃ [It shall be given to the husband; but if she has no husband ... it shall be given to her heirs; if she was a maidservant ... and was freed or converted, he is exempt.]

units.la: tur: quod si vidua fit, illius haredibus traditur. Si vero fuerit ancilla jam manu missa, aut peregrina; alter ille non tenetur.
units.tr: It must be given to her husband; but if she is a widow, it is handed over to her heirs. If, however, she was a maidservant already set free, or a foreigner, that other man is not bound.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Ne quidem si mulierem intenderit, teneri volunt. Qua ergò de causa hunc casum distinctè proponit auctor? Huic dubio in Gemara respondetur. [Hebrew text, ~2 lines] Quandoquidem voluit proponere sequens membrum, Homo proximum suum intendens &c. quomodo Scriptura loquitur; docet primò etiam, Bos comparem suum intendens &c. Sensus est, hic quidem nulla distinctione in bovis facto opus fuisse; quandoquidem neutro modo bos teneretur, sive cum intentione, sive absque ista illud fecisset: nihilominus hic solum modo proponi quod absque intentione fit, quia hunc casum in homine alterum laedente examinare animus erat.
units.tr: ¹ They hold that he is not bound even if he aimed at the woman. Why, then, does the author set out this case separately? The Gemara answers this question. [Hebrew text, about two lines.] Since he wished to set out the following clause, "A man aiming at his neighbour, etc.", as Scripture speaks, he first teaches "An ox aiming at its fellow, etc." The meaning is this: there was no need for a distinction in the case of the ox, since in neither way would the ox be bound, whether it did this with intent or without it; yet here only the case done without intent is set out, because the author meant to examine the case of one man injuring another.

units.la: ² Hanc de satisfactione decisionem ex illa lege Ex. 21.22.23. depromunt, Certantibus hominibus, si percusserit unus illorum mulierem gravidam, ita ut ejiciatur fetus ejus.... si exitium fit, tum reddes vitam pro vita. ubi rectè Salomo Jarchi ad priora legis verba, Certantibus hominibus, [Hebrew] altero cum altero, ita ut collimans ad proximum suum percutiendum, percutiat mulierem. Cujusmodi factum in Mishna exhibetur. Poenam deinde lege Dei sancitam idem Sal. J. ad Mishnae constitutionem accommodat, dum subjicit; [Hebrew] solvit haredibus illius (scilicet mariti mulieris), pretium fetus, quanti in foro vendi posset. Quae expositio eo nititur, quod foetum illum è medio tollere molitus non fuerit; sed alteri tantummodo damnum concertando intenderit.³ Aestimationem mulieris explicat glossa Gemarae: [Hebrew text, ~2 lines] Æstimant mulierem quanti mulier valuerit ob fœtum ipsos antequam parieret, & quanti jam valeat quum exonerata est, eiusque pretium imminutum: atque hoc marito solvitur. Mulier cum fœtu pluris ducitur, quam ubi fœtum edidit: quia fœtus ipsius pretium, mulieris pretium augebat. Hac ratione quanti depretiaretur post partum mulier, tantum pro infortunio mulieris marito, hujusve hæredibus solvi jubent.4 Verum adversus hanc æstimandi rationem Simeon f. Gamalielis excipit, Postquam mulier peperit, præstantior sive carior est. quasi dicas; Si quanti depretiatur, solvendum sit; nihil debebitur: nam alio respectu pluris habenda uxor post partum, quam si fœtum in utero adhuc gerat; quandoquidem (ut ait R. Isaac Gabæus,) antea versabatur in periculo mortis, ob partus dolorem & angustias. Ideoque ut Gemara docet, in ea saltem quæ antea nunquam peperat, ideoque magis periclitatur, fœtum in se spectari & æstimari contendebant.
units.tr: ² They draw this ruling on compensation from that law, Exodus 21:22-23: "When men strive together, and one of them strikes a pregnant woman, so that her offspring is expelled ... if there is harm, then you shall give life for life." Rightly Solomon Jarchi, on the first words of the law, "When men strive together", [Hebrew] "one with another, so that, aiming to strike his neighbour, he strikes the woman." Such an act is exhibited in the Mishnah. Solomon Jarchi then applies the penalty laid down by the law of God to the Mishnaic ruling when he adds: [Hebrew] "he pays to her heirs (that is, the woman's husband) the value of the offspring, as much as it could be sold for in the market." This explanation rests on the fact that the man did not set out to remove the offspring, but only intended harm to another in the struggle.³ The gloss on the Gemara explains the assessment of the woman: [Hebrew text, about two lines.] "They assess the woman, how much the woman was worth on account of the offspring before she gave birth, and how much she is now worth when she has been delivered, and the diminution of her value; and this is paid to the husband." The woman with her offspring is valued more highly than when she has brought forth the offspring, because the offspring increased the woman's value. By this reasoning they order that as much as the woman is depreciated after the birth is paid to the husband, or to his heirs, for the woman's misfortune.⁴ But against this method of assessment Simeon son of Gamaliel objects: "After the woman has given birth, she is more valuable or dearer." As if you said: if the payment is to be made for the depreciation, nothing will be owed; for after the birth the wife is to be valued more highly in another respect than when she still bears the offspring in her womb, since (as Rabbi Isaac Gabaeus says) she was previously in danger of death, on account of the pain and straits of childbirth. Therefore, as the Gemara teaches, they contended that the offspring should be regarded and valued in itself, at least in the case of a woman who had never given birth before and was therefore in greater peril.

units.la: 5 Quid per peregrinam & ancillam manumissam, ut verba textus sonant, significetur, omnino attendendum: non enim verba simpliciter accipienda; sed cum restrictione, utpote quæ synecdochice accipiantur. Nam, uti observat Bartenorius, ancilla hujusmodi designatur quæ post manumissionem nupsit peregrino aut liberto: similiter peregrina de qua hic agitur ea est, quæ alterutri matrimonio juncta est. Præterea quum in hac Misna subjicitur, Alter ille non tenetur (quod tamen cum lege Dei jam producta pugnat, ut quæ nullam exceptionem admittat,) id simpliciter accipiendum non est: sed eo casu, si mulier ista ex marito nondum proselyto gravida, damnumq; illud passa, maritum amiserit; vel post mariti mortem demum ita lædatur. Nam ex Judæorum hypothesi, qua peregrinus nullos hæredes habere statuitur, si ex ipso uxor nonnisi ante suscep tam ab eo religionem Judaicam conceperit, marito in gentilismo ante illatum damnum vel solutum pretium defuncto, alter ille saepe non tenetur: ut qui neminem, cui multam persolvat, habere censeatur. Ideoque ad hanc Misnam in Gemara dictum citatur ab omnibus fermè jam receptum, Si illa viro nupta sit, acquirendi jus ei, scilicet marito, tribuit D. Misericors; sin ipsa nupta viro non sit, non tribuit. quasi dicant, Totum multam petendi jus à marito dependet, eique hoc jus, vel ejus haeredibus competit: itaque marito mortuo uxor superstes nihil petere poterit; sed tantum in haeredes jus transit. uxor vero mariti haeres non est, ut in Baba bathra c. 8. sect. 1. sancitur. Nec liberi alicujus peregrini haeredes agnoscuntur, nisi dum conciperentur pater jam proselytus esset. Quod legis hujus in hac Misna contentae summam concernit, ea aliunde quoque stabiliri posset, si multam spectes, quae excussi foetus nomine deberi statuitur. Digest. li. 9. tit. 2. leg. 27. par. 22. Si mulier pugno, vel equa ictu a te percussa, ejecerit, Brutus ait, Aquilia teneri, quasi rupto vel ut vulg. de rupto. Vbi de muliere praegnante & ejecto partu verba fieri observat Glossa: adeo ut casus idem utrobique spectetur. Denique quum dicitur teneri quasi rupto, secundum legis Aquiliae caput spectari autumo, quod hac lege §. 5. exstat, Caeterarum rerum, praeter hominem & pecudem occisos, si quis alteri damnum fecit, quidve ustulerit, fregerit, ruperit injuria: quanti ea res erit in diebus triginta proximis, tantum as domino dare damnas esto.
units.tr: ⁵ What is meant by "foreigner" and "maidservant set free", as the words of the text sound, must be considered with care. The words are not to be taken simply, but with a restriction, since they are taken by synecdoche. For, as Bartenorius observes, a maidservant of this kind is one who after manumission married a foreigner or a freedman; likewise the foreign woman here in question is one who has been joined in marriage to either kind of man. Moreover, when in this Mishnah it is added, "that other man is not bound" (which nevertheless conflicts with the law of God already cited, since it admits no exception), this is not to be taken simply, but in the case where the woman, pregnant by a husband who was not yet a proselyte, suffered that harm and lost her husband, or where she was injured in this way only after the husband's death. For on the Jewish hypothesis, by which a foreigner is held to have no heirs, if the wife conceived by him only before she had accepted the Jewish religion from him, and the husband who had been the cause of the harm or had paid the fine died in his heathenism, that other man is often not bound, since he is regarded as having no one to whom he could pay the fine. Therefore, in the Gemara, to this Mishnah is cited a saying now almost universally accepted: "If she is married to a husband, the right to claim belongs to him, that is, to the husband; the merciful master grants this; but if she is not married to a husband, he does not grant it." As if they said: the whole right to claim the fine depends on the husband, and this right belongs to him or to his heirs; so, when the husband is dead, the surviving wife can claim nothing, but the right passes only to the heirs; for the wife is not an heir of her husband, as is laid down in Baba Bathra, chapter 8, section 1. Nor are the children of any foreigner acknowledged as heirs, unless the father was already a proselyte when they were conceived. The substance of this law contained in this Mishnah could also be established from elsewhere, if you consider the fine that is laid down as owed on account of the expelled offspring. Digest, book 9, title 2, law 27, paragraph 22: "If a woman struck by you with a fist, or a mare with a blow, has miscarried, Brutus says you are liable under the Aquilian law, as for a broken thing" (or, as the Vulgate has it, "for the broken thing"). Here the gloss observes that words are spoken about a pregnant woman and an expelled birth, so that the same case is considered on both sides. Finally, when it is said "liable as for a broken thing", I hold that the chapter of the Aquilian law is being considered, which stands in this law at paragraph 5: "If anyone has caused harm to another in respect of other things, apart from a slain man or beast, or has burned, broken or shattered something unlawfully, the damages shall be whatever that thing will be worth within the next thirty days, and he shall give that sum to the owner."

units.la: [Hebrew text, three lines, in Hebrew letters: החופר בור ברשות היחיד ופתחו לרשות הרבים או ברשות הרבים ופתחו לרשות היחיד ברשות היחיד ופתחו לרשות היחיד אחר]
units.tr: [He who digs a pit in a private domain and opens it onto the public domain, or in the public domain and opens it onto a private domain, or in a private domain and opens it onto another private domain. (Hebrew original, three lines: החופר בור ברשות היחיד ופתחו לרשות הרבים או ברשות הרבים ופתחו לרשות היחיד ברשות היחיד ופתחו לרשות היחיד אחר)]

units.la: Qui puteum fodit in loco privato, cujus os obvertatur loco publico, sive ibi aperiatur; aut in loco publico, cujus os aperiatur in loco privato; in loco privato, cujus os aperiatur in loco privato alterius: tene-
units.tr: He who digs a pit in a private place, whose mouth faces a public place, whether it opens there; or in a public place, whose mouth opens onto a private place; or in a private place, whose mouth opens onto another's private place: tene-

units.la: tenetur. Si quis puteum fodiat in loco publico, & in eum bos aut asinus incidens moriatur; tenetur. sive fodiat puteum3, sive scrobem, sive cryptam aut cisternam, sive lapicidinas, sive fossas; tenetur. Si ita est, quare dicitur puteus? Quemadmodum puteus dicitur, in quo sufficiunt ad occidendum 4 decem palmi; sic quodlibet comprehenditur, in quo ad occidendum sufficit decem palmorum profunditas. Si minus profunda fuerint quam ad decem palmos, & in eorum aliquod bos aut asinus cadens moriatur; liber est possessor5. si pecus eo ladatur, tenetur.
units.tr: He is liable. If anyone digs a pit in a public place, and an ox or donkey falls into it and dies, he is liable. Whether he digs a well, a trench, a vault or cistern, a quarry, or a ditch, he is liable. If that is so, why is it called a pit (puteus)? Just as a pit is so called when ten handbreadths of depth suffice to kill, so anything is included in which a depth of ten handbreadths suffices to kill. If the hollows are shallower than ten handbreadths, and an ox or donkey falls into one and dies, the owner is free of liability. If livestock is injured in it, he is liable.
Annotations.

units.la: 1 רשות, potestas, licentia, ut alias observatum fuit, de loco dicitur: ut רשות היחיד, licentia unici, sit locus, in quem privatus potestatem habet; רשות הרבים, licentia multorum, locus publicus, in quem omnibus aequale jus competit. itaque his formulis in hac Misna locus privatus & publicus denotatur. De priori autem legis parte annotatur in תוספות, Additionibus, כללו דמלתא ככל ךך שמתעי בור כתר פתח חולין דנחשב כאלו הוא במקום שהפתח שם, Summa sermonis in tota hac doctrina; in puteo, nos secundum os ipsius procedere: quia existimatur ac si eo loco esset, ubi apertura ipsius est. Unde consequitur in hac lege, לרשות, ad locum, sive obvertitur loco, ita accipiendum esse, ut putei os ibi esse intelligatur, cui loco obversum dicitur. Atque si apertio putei eo spatio reperitur, ubi puteum fodere tibi non licet, de damno teneris.2 Constitutio autem depromta e lege divina Exodi 21. 33. Quum retexerit quis puteum, aut quum foderit quis puteum, deinde non operuerit illum; itaque ceciderit illuc bos aut asinus: 33. Dominus ille putei rependito.qui paragraphus in Gemara hujus Misnæ varië in argumentando adhibetur; neque ista omnia, quum intellectu difficilia non sint, huc producenda exi-
units.tr: Reshut [רשות], meaning power or licence, as observed elsewhere, is said of a place. Reshut ha-yachid [רשות היחיד], the licence of one, is a place over which a private person has power. Reshut ha-rabim [רשות הרבים], the licence of many, is a public place, in which an equal right belongs to everyone. So in this Mishnah the private and the public place are designated by these formulas. But on the first part of the law, a note in the Tosafot [תוספות] reads: "The sum of the whole teaching is this: in a pit, we proceed according to its mouth [כללו דמלתא ככל ךך שמתעי בור כתר פתח חולין], because it is reckoned as if it were in the place where its opening is." Hence it follows that in this law, ad locum, or obvertitur loco [לרשות], is to be understood so that the mouth of the pit is taken to be there, and the place is said to face it. And if the opening of the pit is found in the space where you are not permitted to dig a pit, you are liable for the damage. The rule is drawn from the divine law of Exodus 21. 33: "When someone uncovers a pit, or digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or an ass falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restitution." This paragraph is used in various ways in arguing in the Gemara of this Mishnah; since not all of these are difficult to understand, I have not thought it necessary to bring them in here.

units.la: stimavi. Sed quod de putei ore in loco privato observant, præterequndum non est. Quin in suo fundo cuivis puteum aperire liceat, negandum non censent: itaque illic per locum privatum solummodo cum designari censent, quem privatus publici juris fecit, servato suo in puteum jure: ut docet Maim. Cod. de damnis pec. c. 12. §. 1.
units.tr: But what they observe about the mouth of a pit in a private place must not be passed over. They do not deny that anyone may open a pit on his own ground. Accordingly they think that a private place is mentioned there only as a place that the private owner has made public, his right over the pit being preserved, as Maimonides teaches in the Code, on damages caused by animals, chapter 12, §1.

units.la: Ita etiam Talmudis Glossa marginalis de puteo cujus aperitio in loco privati alicujus, ejus nomine damni dati dominum teneri [Hebrew], quum habet puteum in loco privato, & locum suum publici juris fecit; ut nequeat dicere quid quaeritur in loco meo? Similiter paulo post: [Hebrew], reus est, sed solummodo, si illum locum suum fecerit publicum, in cujus spatio os putei conspicitur. ³ Cæterum putei non tantum ratio habetur; sed etiam cujuscunque profunditatis similis: unde quatuor genera subjungunt distinctis nominibus expressa, quæ explicanda veniunt. Postquam Misna de [Hebrew], puteo angusto & rotundo egisset, subjicit [Hebrew], scrobem, quæ definiente Gemara est [Hebrew], longa & angusta; deinde [Hebrew] cryptam sive cisternam, quæ ejusdem authoritate ejusmodi statuitur ut sit [Hebrew], quadrata & obtecta, nempe solo ore excepto; tertiò [Hebrew], lapicidinas, quæ similiter quadratæ, sed ut Gemara inquit, [Hebrew], non sunt obtecta, nec ibi latiora spatia superiora quam inferiora; denique adjicit [Hebrew], vulgares fossas, quæ sunt [Hebrew], latiores supra quam infra, sicuti eos facere videmus qui sine magna cura foveam excavant, siquidem inferius spatium superiori angustius deprehenditur. Igitur quicunque damnum inferunt in aliqua fovea è propositis generibus, hac lege æquantur, pariterque rei peraguntur. Quod si minus profunda fuerint quam decem palmos, damni author absolvitur, si pecus mortuum fuerit: quia Ex. 21.33.34. mors spectatur; & puteus, uti censent, decem saltem palmorum. itaque si pecus in puteo minoris profunditatis moriatur, nulla sequitur eorum judicio multa. Sed si tantum lædatur, ex alia lege de damno tenebitur, qui ejus causa fuerit. Huc denique omnia redeunt, ne quis hujusmodi loco qui ab aliis etiam frequentari solet, foveam ea profunditate excavet, ut alterius pecora inde lædantur. Cum quo interdicto conferatur ff. Ad legem Aqu. lex 28. Qui foveas ursorum, cervorumque capiendorum causa faciunt, si in itineribus fecerunt, eoque aliquid decidit, factumque deterius est, lege Aquilia obligati sunt. at si in aliis locis, ubi fieri solent, secerunt, nihil tenentur. Hæc tamen actio ex causa danda est: id est, si neque denuntiatum est, neque scierit, aut prævidere potuerit.
units.tr: Likewise the marginal gloss of the Talmud, on a pit whose opening is in someone's private place: the owner is liable for the damage done in his name, "when he has a pit in a private place and has made his place public, so that he cannot say, what is sought in my place?" Similarly a little later: "He is liable, but only if he has made that place public, in whose space the mouth of the pit is seen." Moreover, the Mishnah takes account not only of a pit but of any similar depth. So they add four kinds, expressed by distinct names, which must be explained. After the Mishnah has treated of a narrow and round pit, it adds a scrobs [שקע]; the Gemara defines this as "long and narrow." Then a crypt or cistern [מערה], which by the same authority is set up to be "square and covered," except for the mouth alone. Third, quarries [מחצבה], which are likewise square, but, as the Gemara says, "are not covered," nor are their upper spaces wider than the lower. Last it adds common ditches [שיחה], which are "wider above than below," as we see those make who dig a trench without great care, since the lower space is found to be narrower than the upper. Therefore whoever causes damage in any pit of the kinds listed is bound by this law, and is pursued in the same way. But if they are less deep than ten handbreadths, the author of the damage is acquitted, if the animal has died; because Exodus 21:33–34 looks to death, and, as they hold, a pit must be at least ten handbreadths deep. So if an animal dies in a pit of less depth, by their judgement no fine follows. But if it is only hurt, the one who caused it will be liable for damage under another law. In short, everything comes back to this: no one may dig, in a place of this kind which others also commonly use, a trench of such depth that other people's cattle are injured by it. With this prohibition compare the Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam, law 28: "Those who make pits for catching bears and stags, if they made them on roads, and something falls into them and is made worse, are bound by the Aquilian law. But if they made them in other places where such things are usually done, they are not liable. Yet this action is to be granted for the case: that is, if neither warning was given nor did they know, or could they foresee it."

units.la: Si puteum duorum sociorum, eorum prior transfeat, nec tegat, item posterior, nec tegat eum; secundus tenetur. texerit eum prior, veniensque secundus & apertum deprehendens eum non tegat; secundus tenetur. Texerit eum uti oportet, & in eum bos aut asinus incidens moriatur; liber est: non texerit eum uti oportet, & in eum bos aut
units.tr: If two partners own a pit, and the first passes by it and does not cover it, and likewise the second does not cover it, the second is liable. If the first covered it, and the second, coming and finding it uncovered, does not cover it, the second is liable. If he covered it as it ought to be, and an ox or an ass falls into it and dies, he is free; if he did not cover it as it ought to be, and an ox or an ass falls into it and dies, he is liable; and so on.

units.la: בור של שחי טוחפין עבר עליו הראשון ולא כסהו והשני ולא כסהו השני חייב כסהו הראשון ובא השני ומצאו סגולה ולא כסהו השני חייב כסהו כראוי ונפל לחוכו שור או חסור וסח פטור לא כסהו כראוי ונפל לחוכו שור או חטו וסח חייב נפל לפניו סקול הכרייה חייב לאחריו סקול הכרייד פטור נפל להוכו שור וכליו ונשחברו חמור וכליו ונחקרעו חייב על הבהמה ופטור על הכלים נפל להוכו שור חרש שוטה וקטן חייב בן או בח עבד או אמה פטור ׃
units.tr: If a pit belongs to two partners, and the first passes by it and does not cover it, and the second likewise passes by and does not cover it, the second is liable. If the first covered it, and the second comes and finds it uncovered and does not cover it, the second is liable. If it was covered properly and an ox or an ass falls into it and dies, he is free. If it was not covered properly and an ox or an ass falls into it and dies, he is liable. If it falls in front of him, he is liable for an ox that is stoned; if behind him, he is free from an ox that is stoned. If an ox falls into it along with its utensils and they are broken, or an ass along with its utensils and they are torn, he is liable for the animal and free from the utensils. If an ox falls into it belonging to a deaf man, an imbecile, or a minor, he is liable. If it belongs to a son or daughter, a male servant or a female servant, he is free.

units.la: aut asinus incidens moriatur; tenetur. Si cadat pronus ² pra fossionis stridore, tenetur; supinus pra fossionis stridore, liber est. Si in eum incidat bos cum suis instrumentis ³ quae franguntur, asinus cum suis instrumentis quae lacerantur; ille quoad jumenta tenetur, ⁴ quoad instrumenta liber est. Si in eum incidat bos surdus, rabidus, parvulus sive juvencus; ⁵ tenetur: filius aut filia, servus aut ancilla ⁶; liber est.
units.tr: Or if a donkey falls into it and dies, he is liable. If it falls face down, because of the noise of the pit's opening, he is liable; if it falls on its back, because of the noise of the pit's opening, he is free. If an ox falls into it with its gear, which is broken, or a donkey with its gear, which is torn, the owner is liable for the animals but free from liability for the gear. If a deaf, mad, young or grown ox falls in, he is liable; for a son or daughter, a manservant or maidservant, he is free.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Quomodo prior non teneatur, sed posterior, licet uterque puteum apertum reliquerit, docetur in Gemara: מני מר ... Cujus sententia obtinet? unus ait, tum absolvi quum ipsum posteriorem reliquit puteo utentem; alter inquit, quum posteriori tradiderit illius situlam. & concluditur priorem in judicio absolvi, si posteriori situlam putei tradiderit, quo puteo uteretur. ² Bovis, qui putei occasione cadit, discrimen facit Misna: nam vel pronus procidit in puteum; vel supinus (hac voce latius sumta) in putei marginem, aut pede ad puteum offenso titubare incipiens in circumjacens spatium aliquod decidit. ita enim post longiorem disputationem concluditur, per לפני priorem; per לאחריו posteriorem designari casum: ita quidem ut bos priori in puteum; posteriori apud puteum decidat. idque stridore consternatus, quem in putei fundo à fossore excitatum percipit. Quod si vero supinus in puteum ipsum decidat, alter ille tenetur: utpote quum Dei lex generalis sit Ex. 21.33. Ceciderit illuc bos &c. Si in puteum cadat, quomodocunque id fiat, solvenda multa. ³ Quae bovi imposita sunt vel adhærent frangi; quæ asino incumbunt lacerari dicuntur: quia bovi jugum imponitur, & aratrum trahit, quæ franguntur; & asino clitellas aliaque incumbere, quæ lacerari queunt, Gabæus annotat. 4 Istorum vero instrumentorum nomine nullam ex illa producta lege deberi multam colligunt: quia lex ait, Ceciderit illuc bos aut asinus; nullam autem aliarum rerum mentionem facit. Maim. autem in Nizke Mamm. quia verbis nimis mordicus inhæret, injustam sententiam c.12. §. finali profert, Si in eum, qui puteum fodit in loco publico, incidat bos qui eum occidat; dominus bovis liber est: quod si bos moriatur, dominus bovis pretium bovis sui ab hæredibus domini ipsius putei reportat. Membra inter se collata impediunt, quominus ista regula excusari queat. 5 Atque male legem restringunt, ubi tum demum multam deberi contendunt, quum bos aut asinus deprehenditur furdus, rabidus, aut tenellæ ætatis sive parvulus. Etenim ubi lex non distinguit, nec nobis distinguendum sive excipiendum est. Quocirca Maimonidæ verba legi Divinæ adversari existimo, quum constitutionis posteriora verba in hunc modum enarrat, Nec etiam reus erit jumenti nomine, nisi hoc fuerit furdum, rabidum, aut parvulum sive novellum: at bovis nomine, qui justæ statura & providus sit, nihil ille debet; quia alter excipere potest, Incumbebat ipsi bovi ut prospiceret & prateriret. 6 Denique ubi author filioli, filiolæ, servi ac ancillæ casum excipit, & licet in puteum decidant, adeoque moriantur (de hujusmodi enim casu agitur,) eum qui puteum aperuit à reatu eximit; id sano sensu accipiendum: etenim qui causam præbuit, non omnino à reatu absolvendus; sed aliis legibus analogicè, atque ex ἀνθρωποκτονία condemnandus, quibus homicidii pœna sancitur. Verum interpretes contendunt, Misnæ verba proproprie & strictè accipienda: adeo ut manifesta injustitia contineatur. Leges Romanæ omnem lædendi occasionem præcidunt & interdicunt: quemadmodum enim in hac constitutione interdicitur, ne quis vel negligentia, dum puteum non tegit, vel stridore fossionis, dum hac ratione pecus consternatur, damni occasionem præbeat; alioquin multandum ac si damnum fecisset: similiter generali sententia ff. Ad l. Aqu. l. 30. §. 3. hujusmodi occasioni occurritur; quandoquidem Paulus scriptum reliquit, Qui occasionem præstat, damnum fecisse videtur.
units.tr: ¹ That the former is not liable, but the latter is, although both left the well open, is taught in the Gemara: מני מר [Whose opinion prevails?]. One says that he is acquitted only when he has left the well in the hands of the latter, who is using it; the other says, when he has handed over to the latter the bucket of that well. And it is concluded that the former is acquitted at law if he handed over to the latter the bucket of the well, so that he might use the well. ² The Mishnah distinguishes the case of an ox that falls because of a well: for either it falls headlong into the well, or it falls supine (taking this word more broadly) into the rim of the well, or, stumbling on its foot against the well, it begins to totter and falls into some space around it. For after a rather long discussion it is concluded that by לפני [before] the former case is meant, and by לאחריו [after it] the latter, so that the ox falls in the former case into the well, in the latter beside the well; and this happens because it is startled by the noise which the digger raises at the bottom of the well and which it perceives. But if, supine, it falls into the well itself, the other man is liable, since God's general law is in Ex. 21.33: If an ox or ass falls into it, etc. If it falls into the well, however it happens, a fine is to be paid. ³ The things laid on an ox or adhering to it are said to be broken; those lying on an ass are said to be torn, because a yoke is laid on an ox and it draws the plough, which things can be broken; and Gabaeus notes that packsaddles and other things lying on an ass can be torn. ⁴ Now from the mention of these instruments they gather that no fine is owed for them under the law just cited, because the law says, If an ox or ass falls into it, and makes no mention of other things. But Maimonides, in Nizke Mamm., because he clings too stubbornly to the words, gives an unjust ruling in ch. 12, final §: If an ox falls upon him who digs a well in a public place and kills him, the owner of the ox is free; but if the ox dies, the owner of the ox recovers the price of his ox from the heirs of the owner of the well. The parts, compared with one another, prevent that rule from being excused. ⁵ And they wrongly restrict the law, contending that a fine is owed only when the ox or ass is found to be deaf, mad, or of tender age or a young calf. For where the law makes no distinction, neither must we make one or except anything. Wherefore I judge that the words of Maimonides are contrary to the Divine law, since he explains the later words of the enactment in this way: Nor shall the owner be liable for a beast unless it was deaf, mad, or a young or unbroken one; but for an ox of just stature and prudent, he owes nothing; because he may except this: it was incumbent on the ox itself to look out and avoid. ⁶ Finally, where the author excepts the case of a little son, a little daughter, a male servant and a female servant, and although they fall into the well and so die (for it is of such a case that we are speaking), he frees from guilt the one who opened the well; this must be taken in a sound sense: for he who furnished the occasion is not wholly to be acquitted of guilt, but by analogy with other laws, and from ἀνθρωποκτονία [manslaughter], is to be condemned, by those laws under which the penalty for homicide is sanctioned. But the interpreters contend that the words of the Mishnah must be taken strictly and properly, so that a manifest injustice is contained in them. The Roman laws cut off and forbid every occasion of harm: for as in this enactment it is forbidden that anyone, either by negligence in not covering a well, or by the noise of digging when the cattle are startled in this way, should furnish an occasion of harm, and otherwise he is to be fined as if he had done the damage; similarly, by the general sentence of the Digest, Ad l. Aquil., l. 30, §3, such an occasion is met; since Paul has left it written: He who furnishes the occasion seems to have done the damage.

units.la: אחד טור ואחד כל בהמה לנפילת הבור ולהפרשת הר סיני ולהשלומי כפל ולהשבת אבודה לפריקה לחסיםה לכלאים ולשבח וכן חיה ועוף כיוצא בהן אם כן לםה נאמר שור או חסור אלא טרבר חכחוב בהוורה ו
units.tr: "One ox and one every beast" [אחד טור ואחד כל בהמה] applies to falling into the pit, to the separation from Mount Sinai, to double restitution, to the return of lost property, to unloading, to muzzling, to mixed kinds, and to praise; and likewise beast and fowl and the like. If so, why is it said "ox or ass" [שור או חמור]? But rather the Scripture speaks in the Torah [בהורה]...

units.la: Perinde se res habet, sive bos, sive aliud sit pecus, quum in puteum cadit, item quod ad segregationem à monte Sinai; & in solvendo duplo; atque restitutione rei perditæ; attollendis oneribus; non obthurando ore bovis; promiscuo pecudum congressu; & denique sabbatho. ita etiam fera & avis illis sunt similes. Si ita sit, quare dicitur (Ex. 21. 33.) bos aut asinus? Nonnisi quia Scriptura de eo, quod utplurimum contingit, loquitur.
units.tr: The case is the same whether it is an ox or another kind of livestock that falls into a pit; likewise with the separation from Mount Sinai; with paying double; with restoring a lost thing; with lifting burdens; with not muzzling the ox; with the mixed mating of animals; and finally with the Sabbath. So too a wild beast and a bird are like these. If so, why does it say (Ex. 21. 33.) "ox or ass"? Only because Scripture speaks of what usually happens.
Annotations.

units.la: ¹ Perquam rationi legis convenienter, quod de bove & asino dicitur ad alia etiam animalia bruta extenditur: & hac occasione qua de asino & bove in puteum cadentibus dicta ulterius extenduntur; ad alia pergitur: in quibus cum bos & asinus tum in genere pecora in exemplum quidem adducuntur; sed aliæ similiter bestiæ ipsis æquantur. Itaq; primò, interdictum Ex. 19. 19. quamvis bestiam concernere observatur. Deus leges populo suo laturus, ne montem in quo se exhiberet Mosi, tangeret quisquam, interdicit: ideoque expresse mortis poenam transgressori statuens addit, Sive pecus, sive homo fuerit: ubi in Hebraeo, בהמה או אדם. Hic Judaei, interdictum extendentes, Ferasub pecore continetur; particula או sive inservit auxesi, ut comprehendantur aves. Huc spectant autoris nostri verba, Sive bos, sive aliud pecus, quoad segregationem a monte Sinai: atque ad pecus aves reducendas arbitratur.2 Pariter legem Ex. 22. 9. de restitutione dupli, licet distincta bovis, asini, & parvae pecudis fiat mentio; generaliter accipientes, ad omnes bestias extendunt: idque e primis commatis verbis concludunt. Sic Deut. 22. 1. bovis ac parvae pecudis exempla in restituendis perditis extendunt: quia ‎ו״ף 3. sequitur, Ita facito omni rei amissae fratris tui.3 Nostrer etiam legem Ex. 23. 5. quamvis asinus inimici solummodo memoretur, de quovis jumento accipiendam subjungit.4 Atque in instituto pergens interdictum Deut. 25. 4. Ne capistrato bovem triturantem, generaliter intelligendum docet. Quo id fiat argumento, annotat Ob. de Bartenora, discimus per bovem, & bovem, e Sabbatho. Formula admodum obscura: ideoque quo eam explicem, libentius in medium profero. Rabbini quum a comparatis argumentantur, saepissime ejusdem vocis iterationem spectant: ut si eadem vox duobus locis occurrat, rei quae uno loco adjungitur ea tribuant, quae altero loco alteri rei iterata voce designatae competunt. Ut exempli gratia in hoc negotio, bos Deut. 25. 4. occurrit; eademque vox Deut. 5. 14. in quarto praecepto invenitur, ubi jumentum adjungitur: ideoque jumento tribuunt quod bovi, non quidem eodem loco; sed alio, puta Deut. 25. 4. competit. quasi dicant, quandoquidem Deut. 5. bos & jumentum conjunguntur; idcirco quod alibi interdicitur ne capistretur bos, id quodvis jumentum concernere censetur. Itaque discere per bovem è Sabbatho, idem est ac discere ex iterata bovis voce, quæ in præcepto sabbathi cum jumento conjungitur, atque alibi iteratur. Ad hunc modum similes phrases exponendæ. Sequitur in textu ʘɧɮ, heterogenea: de quibus Lev. 19. 19. Iumentorum tuorum ne finito coire duo genera &c. Sed interpretes Heterogeneorum conjunctionem aliam etiam spectant: nimirum quæ interdicitur Deut. 22. 10. Ne arato bove & asino simul. Licet vero interdicto hoc nonnisi conjunctionem bestiæ mundæ & immundæ in arando vetari asserant; ulterius tamen à Sapientibus suis ad majorem cautionem ita interdictum extendi tradunt, ut sive mundæ sive immundæ sint bestiæ, hujusmodi consortium illicitum habeatur. Quod de sabbatho subjicitur, è Deut. 5. 14. lucem mutuatur: ubi cujusvis jumenti usus interdicitur, ne quis illis sabbatho utatur. Denique feras reliquis æquiparant; quia sub ɔɴɔɔ eas comprehendunt: aves etiam cæteris annumerant, quia notas quibus sententia extenditur, aves respicere volunt, quo ista una intelligantur. ut quod de ɔɴɔɔ dicitur, ad aves & feras spectare in propositis casibus censeatur. Quod autem in legibus ac interdictis sæpissimè bovis & asini mentio fiat, causam hujus rei exprimit Misna; quia ... Scriptura loquitur de præsenti: ubi ɔɴɔ non tam existens & præsens designat, ut alibi sæpe; quam, ut Glossa explicat, rem quæ consuevit esse. Sensus est, in serendis legibus, eorum synecdochicè fieri mentionem, quæ utplurimum usu veniunt; quamvis alia non minus indigentur. Voces juris Romani huc quadrant, Titius, Sejus, &c. nam multi passim casus in jure sub illis nominibus exprimuntur, qui tamen ad quosvis pari conditione præditos promiscuè spectant. Atque ut bovis & asini voces in lege Mosis extendendæ; sic tit. de verborum significatione, multa vocabula latius accipienda docetur; ut quum numero 195. legimus,
units.tr: ¹ Quite in keeping with the reason of the law, what is said of ox and ass is extended also to other brute animals. On this occasion, the things said of an ass and an ox falling into a pit are extended further, and the discussion moves on to other cases. In these, although ox and ass, and cattle in general, are brought forward as examples, other beasts are likewise made equal to them. First, the prohibition of Exod. 19:19 is observed to concern even a beast. When God was about to give laws to his people, he forbade anyone to touch the mountain on which he showed himself to Moses. Setting the penalty of death expressly for the transgressor, he adds, "whether beast or man," where the Hebrew reads [בהמה או אדם]. Here the Jews, extending the prohibition, hold that the beast is included under cattle, and that the particle "or" serves as an amplification so that birds are also comprehended. To this refer the words of our author, "whether ox or other cattle, as to separation from Mount Sinai," and he thinks birds are brought back under cattle. ² Likewise the law of Exod. 22:9 on double restitution: although ox, ass, and small cattle are mentioned separately, they take it generally, extending it to all beasts, and they conclude this from the first words of the verse. So at Deut. 22:1 they extend the examples of ox and small cattle to the restoring of lost things, because the verse continues, "So you shall do with every lost thing of your brother." ³ Our author also holds that the law of Exod. 23:5, though only the enemy's ass is mentioned, is to be understood of any beast of burden. ⁴ Proceeding with the matter, he teaches that the prohibition of Deut. 25:4, "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the corn," is to be understood generally. Ob. de Bartenora notes the argument by which this is done: "we learn from ox and ox, from the Sabbath." It is a very obscure formula, so I will bring it forward more willingly in order to explain it. When the rabbis argue from comparisons, they most often look to the repetition of the same word. If the same word occurs in two places, they assign to the thing joined in one place what belongs, in the other place, to the thing designated by the repeated word. For example, in this matter, "ox" occurs at Deut. 25:4, and the same word is found at Deut. 5:14 in the fourth commandment, where a beast of burden is joined to it. So they assign to the beast of burden what belongs to the ox, not in the same place but in another, namely Deut. 25:4. It is as if they said: since in Deut. 5 ox and beast of burden are joined together, what is forbidden elsewhere, that the ox be muzzled, is judged to concern any beast of burden. Thus "to learn from ox from the Sabbath" is the same as to learn from the repeated word "ox," which in the commandment of the Sabbath is joined with the beast of burden and is repeated elsewhere. Similar phrases are to be explained in this way. Next in the text comes the word for heterogeneous things [כלאים], concerning which Lev. 19:19 says, "You shall not let your cattle gender with a diverse kind," etc. But the interpreters also look to another joining of heterogeneous things, namely that forbidden at Deut. 22:10: "You shall not plough with ox and ass together." Although they assert that this prohibition forbids only the yoking of a clean and an unclean beast in ploughing, yet by their Sages they hand down that, for greater caution, the prohibition is extended so that, whether the beasts are clean or unclean, such an unlawful association is held to be forbidden. What is added concerning the Sabbath borrows its light from Deut. 5:14, where the use of any beast of burden is forbidden on the Sabbath. Finally, they make wild beasts equal to the rest, because they comprehend them under cattle. They also count birds among the others, because they wish the signs by which the sentence is extended to refer to birds, so that these are understood together, and so that what is said of cattle is judged to apply to birds in the cases proposed. Now, why mention of ox and ass is so very often made in the laws and prohibitions, the Mishnah states the cause: "Scripture speaks of the present." Here [the word] does not so much designate "existing and present," as it often does elsewhere, but, as the Gloss explains, "a thing which is customarily so." The sense is that in framing laws, mention is made by synecdoche of those things which most commonly come into use, although others are no less in need of regulation. Roman legal names fit here, Titius, Seius, and so on; for many cases are expressed everywhere in law under those names, yet they pertain indiscriminately to whoever is in the same condition. And just as the words ox and ass in the law of Moses are to be extended, so the title on the meaning of words teaches that many words are to be taken more broadly, as when at number 195 we read:

units.la: Pronuntiatio sermonis in sexu masculino ad utrumque sexum pertinet, ut in multis aliisque plurima. Sed ne speciali bus dictis inhaereamus, generalem Juliani sententiam habemus l. 12. ff. De legibus: qua ut in hac Misna speciales de quibusdam pecoribus leges ad alias bestias, etiam feras & aves dilatantur; sic ubique ad similia procedere jubemur: ubi & hujus rei causa ac ratio praemittitur. Non possunt omnes articuli singulatim aut legibus, aut senatusconsultis comprehendi: sed cum in aliqua causa sententia eorum manifesta est, is qui jurisdictioni praeest, ad similia procedere, atque ita jus dicere debet. Hujusmodi extensionis exemplum legitur in verbis Ulpiani D. De jurisdictione l. 7. §. 2. ubi cum esset sancita multa in eos qui jam antea in albo &c. propositi corrupissent, alius casus additur ad quem edictum praecedens porrigitur. Quod si dum proponitur, vel ante propositionem quis corruperit, edicti quidem verba cessabunt. Pomponius autem ait sententiam edicti porrigendam esse ad haec. Verumtamen si quid singulari ratione certis tantum in personis contra rationem juris communis receptum sit, hoc jus ad similia produci leges vetant. ff. De legibus l. 14. & seq. Quod vero contra rationem juris receptum est, non est producendum ad consequentias. 15. In his quae contra rationem juris constituta sunt, non possumus sequi regulam juris. In aliis vero servanda lex praecedens 13: quae cum Misna nostra optime convenit. Quoties lege aliquid unum vel alterum introductum est, bona occasio est, cetera quae tendunt ad eandem utilitatem vel interpretationem, vel certe jurisdictione suppleri.
units.tr: "The pronunciation of speech in the masculine gender applies to both sexes, as in very many other cases." But, not to cling to particular sayings, we have the general opinion of Julian, law 12 of the Digest, De legibus, by which, just as in this Mishnah the special laws about certain cattle are extended to other beasts, even wild beasts and birds, so we are everywhere ordered to proceed to similar cases; and the cause and reason of this matter is also set out there: "Not all articles can be comprehended one by one either in laws or in senatus-consults; but when in some case their meaning is plain, the one who presides over jurisdiction ought to proceed to similar cases, and so declare the law." An example of this kind of extension is read in the words of Ulpian, Digest, De iurisdictione, law 7 §2, where, since many penalties had been enacted against those who had already corrupted, etc., another case is added to which the preceding edict is extended: "But if someone corrupts while it is being posted, or before it is posted, the words of the edict indeed will cease; yet Pomponius says the sense of the edict is to be extended to these cases." Nevertheless, if something has been received against the reason of common law by a special reason only in certain persons, the laws forbid this right to be carried over to similar cases (Digest, De legibus, law 14 and following): "What is received against the reason of law is not to be carried over to consequences." (15) "In those things which are established against the reason of law, we cannot follow the rule of law." In other cases the preceding law is to be observed (13), which agrees very well with our Mishnah: "Whenever one or another thing has been introduced by law, there is a good occasion for the other things which tend to the same usefulness to be supplied, either by interpretation or certainly by jurisdiction."
CHAPTER VI. §. I.

units.la: Si ubi quis pecudem in caulam introduxit, eamque conclusit ut convenit, ipsa egressa damnum intulerit; liber est: si cum eam non conclusit; והזיקה חייב נפרצי כלילהאו שפרצוה ליסטי ויצאוהזיקה פטור הוציאוּלסטים חייבים ו fit uti convenit, egressa damnum intulerit, tenetur. Si noctu ejus paries effractus fuerit, aut eum latrones effregerint, ita ut ista egressa damnum intulerit; ille liber est. Si eam eduxerint latrones, latrones tenentur.
units.tr: If a man has brought a beast into a fold and shut it in as agreed, and the beast then goes out and does damage, he is free. If he did not shut it in as agreed, and it goes out and does damage, he is liable. If its wall was broken through at night, or robbers broke through it, so that the beast went out and did damage, he is free. If robbers led it out, the robbers are liable.
Annotations.

units.la: ¹ Qui pecus satis conclusa censeatur, in Gemara docetur: חייבו כרקוי ונחשבו שלא כרקוי דלת סיכולם לעמוד כרוח מנויים זהו כרקוי חייבו כרקוי ונחשבו שלא כרקוי, Quid hoc, Vti convenit? & quid etiam, Non uti convenit? Si sit janua, qua consistere possit contra ventum ordinarium, tum uti convenit, concluditur; si janua, qua ventum ordinarium sustinere nequeat, tum non concluditur pecus ut oportet. ² Quod de effractura additur, diversi quid continet: nam prioribus verbis de janua egerat, quam ventus vel pecus aperuerat; jam verò ulterius quaeritur, quid juris sit, quum effodiendo, pecus dejicit parietem: vel simili ratione paries effractus noctu fuit. Hic etiam excusatur qui eam concluserat; nisi paries ruinosus fuerit. Porrò sic Misnæ verba accipienda esse, quemadmodum explicamus, docent Maimonidæ verba Cod. de dam. pec. c. 4. §. 1. ubi ad דיר, caulam subintelligit מחיצה in Misna nostra. Ideo inquit, si maceria sive paries firmus fuerit, & effringatur noctu, aut eum effringant latrones. ³ In תוספות, Additionibus, additur ratio, quare haec verba, aut eum latrones effregerunt, subjiciantur: necesse erat hoc proponere; quia etiam latrones absolvuntur, quum pecudem non eduxerunt. tenentur quidem alio nomine ubi caulam effringunt; sed ob pecudem quae egressa damnum dederit nihil debere hic statuuntur, donec eduxerint armenta. ⁴ Educere autem quid hoc loco significet, docetur his Gemarae verbis, קהו לא כאשר [?] stant ipsi in conspectu ejus. Sensus est, non esse dubium, latrones si pecudes eduxerint, de damno per eas dato teneri; sed etiam ejusdem criminis reos esse, si ita coram pecude steterint, ut ab ullo latere evadere nequeat, ideoque se proripiat e caula, posteaque damnum inferat. Romanæ leges convenienter huic Misnæ, occasionem damni reatum afferre censent: nam ut hic condemnatur, cujus negligentia vel facto occasio præbetur, qua pecus damnum infert; similiter sub finem sect. 6. cap. 5. hanc sententiam ex jure Rom. percepimus, Qui occasionem præstat, damnum fecisse videtur.
units.tr: ¹ That an animal is sufficiently shut in is taught in the Gemara: "They are held liable if it was shut as it ought to be, and they are reckoned as not shut as it ought to be, if the door cannot stand against the ordinary wind" [חייבו כרקוי ונחשבו שלא כרקוי דלת סיכולם לעמוד כרוח מנויים זהו כרקוי חייבו כרקוי ונחשבו שלא כרקוי]. What is meant by "as it ought to be," and what by "not as it ought to be"? If there is a door able to stand against the ordinary wind, then the animal is shut in as it ought to be; if a door cannot withstand the ordinary wind, then the animal is not shut in as it ought to be. ² What is added about the breach contains something different. For the earlier words dealt with a door which the wind or the animal had opened; but now it is asked further what the law is when the animal, by digging, knocks down the wall, or when the wall was breached in the night in a similar way. Here too the one who had shut the animal in is excused, unless the wall was ruinous. Moreover, the words of the Mishnah must be understood as we explain them, as the words of Maimonides in the Code, Laws of Damage by Animals, ch. 4, §1, show. There, at "pen" [דיר], he understands a partition [מחיצה] in our Mishnah. Therefore he says: "if the wall or fence is firm and is breached at night, or the thieves breach it." ³ In the Tosafot, the Additions, the reason is given why these words, "or the thieves breached it," are added: it was necessary to propose this, because thieves are also acquitted when they have not led the animal out. They are indeed liable on another count where they break into the pen; but for the animal which went out and caused damage they are here held to owe nothing, until they have led the cattle out. ⁴ What to lead out means here is shown by these words of the Gemara, "they stand before her" [קהו לא כאשר [?]]. They stand in her sight. The sense is that there is no doubt that if thieves lead the animals out they are liable for the damage done by them; but they are also guilty of the same offence if they have stood before the animal in such a way that she cannot escape from any side, and so she rushes out of the pen and afterwards does damage. Roman laws, agreeing with this Mishnah, hold that an occasion of damage brings guilt: just as one is condemned whose negligence or deed provides the occasion by which an animal does damage, so too, near the end of section 6 of chapter 5, we have taken this opinion from Roman law: one who provides the occasion is seen to have caused the damage.

units.la: הניחה בחמש או שסטרה לחרש שוטה וקטן ויצאה והזיקה חייב מסרה לרועה נכגם רועה תחתיו נפלה לגינה ונהניית משלם מה שנהני' ירדה כורכח והזיקה משלם מה שהזיקה כיצד משלם מה שהזיקה שמין בית סאה באוהה שדה כמה היתה יפה וכמה היא יפה רבי שמעון אומר אכלה פירות גמורים משלם פירוה גמורים אם סאה סאה אם סאיתם סאיתם ;
units.tr: If one left it out in the sun, or struck it, or handed it over to a deaf-mute, a fool or a minor, and it went out and did damage, he is liable. If he handed it to a herdsman, and another herdsman took his place, [the second herdsman is liable]. If it fell into a garden and got benefit from it, he pays for the benefit. If it went down into a field [כורכר] and did damage, he pays for the damage. How so? He pays for the damage: they estimate the field of a se'ah [בית סאה], how beautiful it was and how beautiful it is now. Rabbi Shimon says: if it ate whole fruit, he pays for whole fruit; [if it ate] se'ah [for se'ah], he pays se'ah [for se'ah]; [if it ate] se'ayim, he pays se'ayim.

units.la: Si cum eam in sole{1} collocavit, aut surdo, stulto, pupillo commendavit, egressa damnum fecerit; tenebitur: si tradiderit pastori, pastor{2} ipsius loco succedet. Si in hortum delapsa{3} emolumentum percepit, satisfaciendum erit pro emolumento percepto: si aliquo descendens{4} more suo damnum intulerit, reddetur quantum damni intulerit. Quomodo redditur quantum damni intulit? Æstimant fundum una sea consitum,{5} quanti in isto agro valuerit, & quanti jam valeat. D. Simeon inquit, Si comederit fructus maturos,{6} reddentur fructus maturi; sea pro sea, aut dua sea pro duabus.
units.tr: If, when she has placed it in the sun{1}, or has entrusted it to a deaf person, a fool, or a minor, and it goes out and does damage, she shall be liable. If she has handed it over to a herdsman, the herdsman shall take her place{2}. If it slips into a garden{3} and gets some benefit, she must make satisfaction for the benefit it received. If it goes down into a field{4} in its usual way and does damage, she shall repay as much as the damage it caused. How is the damage it caused repaid? They estimate a field sown with one seah{5}: what it was worth in that field, and what it is now worth. Rabbi Simeon says: if it has eaten ripe fruits, ripe fruits shall be repaid{6}; a seah for a seah, or two seahs for two seahs.
Annotations.

units.la: {4} Ardoris impatiens pecus nonnunquam erumpit & aliis nocet:quod ubi fit,licet caulam clauserit pastor;nihilominus teneri eum arbitratur Gloffator, qui Mifnam extendit. 2 Primarius pastor, quia plerumque inferioribus pecoris curam committere solet, absolvitur; atque idcirco de damno inferiorem pastorem teneri statuunt. Et licet custos custodi rem commendans teneatur; hic secus fe res habet: דאורייתא דורשי לְמִימֵר לְכְרוֹזְיֵי, quia consuetudo pastoris est,ut tradat gregem discipulo suo, id est, vicario pastori qui suo imperio paret. 3 Duobus autem modis fieri contingit, ut pecus in alterius horto fructus edat: vel enim נִפְלָה, illabitur, quod in hunc modum S. Jarchi enarrat, נִפְלָה לְגִינָה בְּחֶצֶר מִכָּאן... רמזין... incidit in hortum per vim è tecto domini fui quod contiguum est horto proximi ejus;aut è loco publico qui altior fit ipso horto delabitur. Maimonides vero hoc pacto enarrat, וְאִם נִפְלָה... quod ad lapfum attinet, ita fe habet, ut cum in lapidem aut lignum impingens procidit. Si ea occasione fructus decerpat,quicquid emolumenti ex ista depastione percipit, tantundem proprietarius rependere tenetur. 4 Alter modus est, quum in hortum יָרַד כְּדַרְכּוֹ, descendit more suo, id est, quum non coacta in consitum locum progreditur; quemadmodum alias sua sponte incedere solet. Tum major mulcta manet: quia vis nulla vel casus fortuitus obtendi potest. Itaque non percepti emolumenti; sed dati damni quantitas spectabitur, ut totum damnum restituatur: quo pacto plus rependetur, quam fi utilitas quam pecus percepit solummodo in compensatione examinaretur. Etenim pecus semper fere alienum agrum vel consitum hortum depascens, plus damni infert, quam utilitatis inde percipit; multa pedibus atterit, dentibus arrodit, corpore evertit, aliave ratione corrumpit; cum pauciora ore decerpens in alimentum convertat. Verum ratio ac modus expendendus, quo damnum æstimatur. 5 Si comederit (exempli gratia) areolæ unius legumina, rationem incunt, quanti hortus sexaginta areolarum (semper enim hac in re hanc multiplicationem servant) æstimaretur; deinde quanti post depastam sexagesimam partem valeat: differentiæ autem summam, multæ loco pecudis possessori imponunt. Qua ratione ipsi reo se consulere testantur: quandoquidem si areola per se æstimaretur, pluris fieret quam est differentia commemorata: quum totum agrum emens, tanti sexagesimam partem in toto agro simul sumto non faciat; quam quidem ille, cui illam solam portionem emere animus esset. Itaque partem seorsim non considerant; sed quicunque fructus comestus sit, quantum depastum est per sexaginta multiplicantes, dictam rationem observant. De qua re distincte Maimonides Cod. Nizke Mammon c. 4. §. 13. 14. Et hæc quidem in fructibus & segetibus nondum maturitatem adeptis: at in maturis secus se rem habere D. Simeon existimavit; cujus sententia obtinet. Nam cum maturæ fruges ipso agro amplius non egeant, per se ac si jam messæ aut decerptæ essent, considerantur: ideoque eadem ratio, quæ in demessis frugibus, hic etiam observanda videtur. Quoniam hac Misna depastio agrorum vel hortorum interdicitur, jure cum ea conferri potest C. De lege Aqu. l. ult. De his quæ per injuriam depasta contendis, ex sententia legis Aquilia agere minime prohiberis.
units.tr: {4} A beast that cannot endure its heat sometimes breaks out and harms others. When this happens, the Glossator who extends the Mishnah holds that the owner is liable even though the shepherd has shut the fold. (2) The chief shepherd is usually released, since he is accustomed to entrust the care of the flock to his inferiors, and so they rule that the lower shepherd is liable for the damage. Although a keeper who entrusts a thing to a keeper is himself liable, here the case is otherwise: because it is the custom of a shepherd to hand over the flock to his disciple, that is, to his deputy shepherd, who obeys his command [דאורייתא דורשי לְמִימֵר לְכְרוֹזְיֵי]. (3) There are two ways in which it may happen that an animal eats fruit in another man's garden. Either it falls [נִפְלָה], it slips down, as S. Jarchi explains it in this way: [נִפְלָה לְגִינָה בְּחֶצֶר מִכָּאן... רמזין...] it falls into the garden by force from the roof of its owner's house, which adjoins the garden of his neighbour; or it slips down from a public place which is higher than the garden itself. Maimonides, however, explains it this way: [וְאִם נִפְלָה...] as far as the fall is concerned, it is as when it falls after striking a stone or a piece of wood. If on that occasion it picks the fruit, the owner is bound to make good whatever profit it gains from that grazing. (4) The other way is when it goes down into the garden [יָרַד כְּדַרְכּוֹ], it goes down as is its way, that is, when it goes forward unforced into the planted place, as it is accustomed to wander of its own accord at other times. Then the heavier penalty applies, because no force or chance accident can be pleaded. Therefore it is not the amount of profit obtained that is considered, but the amount of the damage done, so that the whole loss is made good. In this way more is repaid than if only the advantage the animal gained were assessed in compensation. For an animal grazing on another's field or planted garden almost always does more harm than it gets profit from it: it tramples much with its feet, gnaws with its teeth, overturns with its body, and corrupts in other ways, while it converts into food only what it has nipped with its mouth. But one must weigh the method and manner by which the damage is valued. (5) If it has eaten (for example) the pulse of one small bed, they reckon what a garden of sixty beds would be worth (for in this matter they always keep this multiplication), and then what it is worth after the sixtieth part has been grazed; the sum of the difference they impose on the owner of the animal as a fine. By this method they profess to take care of the accused himself, since if the small bed were valued by itself, it would come to more than the difference mentioned; for a man buying the whole field would not put so high a value on the sixtieth part of the whole field taken together, as he would who intended to buy that portion alone. Therefore they do not consider the part separately, but whatever fruit has been eaten, they apply the said reckoning by multiplying by sixty as much as has been grazed. On this matter Maimonides speaks distinctly in Cod. Nizke Mammon c. 4 §§ 13, 14. And these things hold for fruits and crops not yet ripe; but for ripe produce, S. Simeon thought the matter stands otherwise, and his opinion prevails. For since ripe crops no longer need the field itself, they are considered in themselves, as if they had already been reaped or picked; so the same reckoning that applies to harvested crops seems to be observed here too. Since this Mishnah forbids the grazing of fields or gardens, it can justly be compared with C. De lege Aquilia, last law: Concerning those things which you say were grazed through injury, you are by no means forbidden to bring suit according to the provision of the Aquilian law.

units.la: Quum sine venia metam quis colligit in agro proximi fui, quam comedat pecus domini ipsius agri; hic liber est: si per illam ledatur, meta dominus tenetur: quod si impetrata venia metam colligat, agri dominus tenetur.
units.tr: When someone gathers a stack without permission in the field of his neighbour, and the owner's cattle eat it, the owner of the field is free; but if the owner of the stack holds them back, he is liable. If, however, he gathers the stack with permission, the owner of the field is liable.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Quò hæc plenius percipiantur, attendendum est, moris olim fuisse inter Israelitas, ut cum plurium segetes in valle quadam crescerent, singuli areas non haberent, quò segetes suas in metas colligerent: itaque in unius alicujus aream conveniebant, deleêto sæpius communi custode, qui metas ab injuria bestiarum defenderet & custodiret. Vbi ergo segetum meta ibi conficeretur fine expressa proprietarii venia, hic de damno non tenebatur. Sed contra, fi proprietarii pecus vel gallinæ &c. inde læderentur, alter cujus effent segetes ad restitutionem obligabatur: puta fi forte meta eversa gallinam oppressisset, aliove modo nocuisset. Verum quia ultima pars de proprietario accepta cum Mifna 3. cap. 5. pugnare censetur, ubi ne quidem concessa venia, areæ dominus damnum rependere dicitur, antequam in fe cautionem receperit; ideo Gemara ultimo saltem hujus Mifnæ membro de communi illo custode verba fieri censet. Hæc enim in explicatione: Hic de custode arearum agimus, quod posteaquam dixit alteri, Ingredere & metam confice, idem fit ac fi dixisset, Ingredere, & tibi custos ero. Quum veniam dat custos, idem esse censetur, ac fi cautionem in fe reciperet: ideoq; quemadmodum proprietarius cautione recepta tenetur; pariter & custos concessâ venia: siquidem hic venia data pro recepta cautione reputatur. Quia de eo agitur quod in alterius possessione damnum patitur, conferatur D. De præscriptis verbis l. 14. §. 3. Si glans ex arbore tua in meum fundum cadat, eamque ego immisso pecore depascam, Arifto scribit non sibi occurrere legitimam actionem, qua experiri possim. nam neque ex lege duodecim tabularum de pastu pecoris, quia non in tuo pascitur: neque de pauperie, neque damni injuria agi posse. in factum itaque erit agendum.
units.tr: That these matters may be understood more fully, it must be noted that it was once the custom among the Israelites, when the crops of several men grew in a certain valley, for the individuals to have no threshing floors on which to gather their sheaves into stacks. So they came together to the threshing floor of one man, and the common guard, who was often hired, defended and watched the stacks against injury from beasts. Therefore, where a stack of grain was built on the threshing floor without the express permission of the owner, the owner was not liable for any damage. On the contrary, if the owner's cattle or hens, etc., were harmed thereby, the other man, whose crops they were, was bound to make restitution: for example, if the stack had fallen over and crushed a hen or otherwise harmed it. But because this last part, understood as concerning the owner, is thought to conflict with Mishnah 3, chapter 5, where the owner of the threshing floor is said to make good the damage, even when permission was not granted, before he has taken a guarantee upon himself, the Gemara therefore holds that at least in the last clause of this Mishnah the words refer to that common guard. For it says in its explanation: Here we are dealing with the guardian of the threshing floors, for after he said to the other, "Go in and build the stack," it is the same as if he had said, "Go in, and I will be your guardian." When the guardian gives permission, it is considered the same as if he had taken a guarantee upon himself; therefore, just as the owner is bound once a guarantee has been received, so too is the guardian once permission has been given, since here the permission given is reckoned as a guarantee received. Because the case concerns one who suffers damage on another's property, compare D. De praescriptis verbis l. 14 §3: If an acorn falls from your tree onto my field, and I graze it by letting in my herd, Aristo writes that no legitimate action occurs to him by which I could be sued: for neither can it be brought under the law of the Twelve Tables concerning the pasturing of cattle, because it is not pastured on your land, nor concerning pauperies, nor for wrongful damage. Therefore the action will have to be brought in factum.

units.tr: "If a man sends fire by the hand of a deaf-mute, an imbecile or a minor, he is exempt by human law but liable by the law of heaven [השולח את הבערה ביד חרש שוטה וקטן פטור בדיני אדם וחייב בדיני שמים]. If he sends it by the hand of a sane adult, that adult is liable. If one man brought the fire and another afterwards brought the wood, the one who brought the wood is liable; if one brought the wood and another afterwards brought the fire, the one who brought the fire is liable. If another came and blew on it, the one who blew is liable; if the wind blew it, all are exempt. If a man sends fire and it consumes wood, stones or earth, he is liable, as it is said: 'If fire break out and catch in thorns, so that the stacked grain, or the standing corn, or the field is consumed, he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution' [כי תצא אש ומצאה קוצים ונאכל גדיש או הקמה או חשדה שלם ישלם]. If a man kindles fire and it spreads, he is exempt if there is a fence four cubits high, or a public road, or a river between."
ANNOTATIONS

units.la: Qui incendium immittit per ministerium furdi, stulti, aut pupilli, humano judicio non tenetur; at tenetur judicio cœlesti: si immittit periti sive providi alicujus operâ, providus tenetur. Si unus ferat ignem, deinde alter ligna; ferens ligna tenetur: si unus ligna, alter deinde ignem ferat; ignem gestans tenetur: si postea accedens alius ignem suscitet, hic tenetur: si ventus ignem suscitet, illi omnes liberi sunt. Qui ita immittit incendium ut absumat ligna, aut lapides, aut pulverem; tenetur: quia legitur (Ex.22.6.) Quum egressus ignis invenit spinas, absumiturq; meta, aut ipsa seges, aut ager; omnino rependito is qui fecit ut incendium fit. Si incendium transiliat sepem quatuor cubitis altam, aut viam publicam, aut flumen; ille liber est.
units.tr: One who sets fire through the agency of a deaf person, a fool, or a minor is not liable by human judgment, but is liable by heavenly judgment. If he sets it through the agency of a skilled or prudent person, the prudent person is liable. If one carries the fire and then another carries the wood, the one carrying the wood is liable; if one carries the wood and then another carries the fire, the one carrying the fire is liable; if afterwards another comes and kindles the fire, he is liable; if the wind kindles the fire, all of them are free. One who sets a fire so that it consumes wood, stones, or dust is liable, because it is written (Exod. 22:6). When the escaped fire finds thorns, and the stack, or the crop itself, or the field is consumed, the one who caused the fire must in every case make restitution. If the fire leaps over a fence four cubits high, or over a public road, or a river, he is free.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Cód. in Gemara, alii insuper qualesti teneri statuuntur. הרבה רבריס העושה חיתן פסר מדיני חדם וחייב כריני טמיס חבירו ומכופף קמתו של חבירו בסני הדליקה והסquatuor aliquod patrans, humano judicio cœlesti. ifti sunt: qui effringit sepem
units.tr: The Gemara and others also lay down that certain other persons are liable. [הרבה דברים העושה חייבין ... פטור בדיני אדם וחייב בדיני שמים ... חבירו ומכופף קמתו של חבירו בשעת הדליקה] Four who commit something are liable by heavenly judgment but not by human judgment. These are: one who breaks through a fence

units.la: {1} Hebrew and Greek lines of the note are printed here as they stand on the scan. sepem in conspeƈtu pecoris proximi sui, puta ut ita pecus ausugere contingat ; qui incurvat metam proximi sui apud incendium,nimirum si comburatur;qui mercede conducit testes&falsos ad testandum, scilicet pro alio, nam qui sibi conducit, humano judicio tenetur ; qui solus denique testimonium novit pro proximo suo, nec ipsi tamen testimonium perhibet. Hic autem præcedentibus adjungitur qui incendium innocentium opera facit: cujusmodi surdus, stultus, pupillus. Itaque præcedentia Rabbi Josuæ (ipsi enim accepta feruntur) verba eo. modo intelligenda non sunt, quasi ista tantum quatuor peccatorum genera à solo Deo punirentur. Cæterum legem hanc restringit Maim. Cod. de dam. pecun. c.14. §. 5. [illegible, ~12 letters] De quo casu hæc dicuntur? Quum tradidit ipsis carbonem, qui candescit: quia hæc est carbonis indoles, ut sponte extinguatur priusquam progressus incendium faciat. Verum si ipsis flammam tradat; tenetur: quandoquidem ejus opera in causa sunt. Illud, qui candescit, non legitur in viri nobilissimi ac doctissimi Ludovici Gerardi à Renesse antiquissimo exemplari, Maimónidæ coævo: neque admodum requiri videtur; utpote quum legis verba id satis contineant.
