Vnde Ef. 42. 20. [illegible, ~3 letters] aperire aures, de iis qui corporeis auribus audiunt; licet alioquin surdos se in spiritualibus præbeant. Ergo in Misna nostra [illegible, ~3 letters] est qui audit, sapit, & adolevit. Cum plures causæ ad incendium quandoque concurrant, postrema reatum inducit ; si huic constitutioni adhæreamus. Vt cum lignum prius assertur, postea
units.tr: {1} The Hebrew and Greek lines of the note are printed here as they stand on the scan. a fence in sight of his neighbour's flock, that is, so that the flock may happen to graze on it; one who bends over his neighbour's stack at a fire, namely if it is burned; one who hires false witnesses to testify, namely for another, for one who hires them for himself is liable by human judgment; and finally one who alone knows the testimony for his neighbour, yet does not himself give testimony. Here, however, to the preceding is added one who causes a fire through the agency of innocent persons, of which kind are the deaf, the fool, and the minor. Therefore the preceding words of Rabbi Joshua (for these are reported to him) are not to be understood in such a way as if only these four kinds of wrongdoing were punished by God alone. Moreover, Maimonides, Code, On Damages to Property, chapter 14, section 5, restricts this law: "To what case do these words refer? When he hands over to them a coal that is glowing, because this is the nature of a coal, that it goes out of its own accord before it makes the fire spread. But if he hands them a flame, he is liable, since his action is the cause." The phrase "that is glowing" is not found in the most ancient copy of the most noble and learned Ludovicus Gerardus à Renesse, which is contemporary with Maimonides; nor does it seem altogether needed, since the words of the law contain it sufficiently. [illegible] is often opposed in the Talmudic rulings to the deaf, the fool, and the minor, although properly it means one who sees; but as "providus" (prudent) is derived from seeing, and also refers to a suitable disposition of mind, so [illegible] is opposed to the stupid, the foolish, and the inexperienced boy. And just as seeing is used for hearing in Exodus 20:18, by the same reasoning [illegible] "seeing" includes one endowed with hearing. Hence Isaiah 42:20, "opening the ears," refers to those who hear with bodily ears, although otherwise they show themselves deaf in spiritual things. Therefore in our Mishnah he is one who hears, is wise, and has grown up. Since several causes sometimes concur in a fire, the last one incurs guilt, if we adhere to this rule: as when the wood is brought first and afterwards

units.la: {2} Hebrew word, cf. the text above. vero ignis; vel prius ignis, postea lignum; vel denique post allatum lignum & ignem, hic ab alio suscitatur: illic ignem ferens; istic lignum gestans; hic denique ignem suscitans condemnatur. Ideoque si ventus ignem suscitet, priores absolvuntur. Hæc est autoris mens: quapropter in textu particulas deinde & postea inserui; cum alioquin sententia sibi non constaret. 4 Quod de lapidibus & pulvere sancitur, è cap. 22. Exod. ℣. 6. colligunt. quo modo, vel è qua voce, explicatur inGemara, Quare mihi ager nominatur? ad includendum quum lambitur ejus novale, & lapides adduruntur. Deus spinarum, metæ, & segetis distinctam mentionem faciens, tandem agrum etiam commemorat: quia is non solum reus peragitur, qui priora incendit; sed etiam qui ignem excitat, quo lambente ipse ager licet segetibus vacuus (quem vocant ניר, id est, teste Glossatore, vervactum nondum consitum) leviter ustulatur ac corrumpitur: cui hac in parte lapides exæquant; quos etiam ab igne tutos esse volunt. Viterius observa è Maimonida de damnis pecuniariis c. 14. sect. ultima, quod de igne depascente statuitur, ad similia extendendum esse. [Hebrew text] Omnes ignis propagines ita se habent ut ignis. Quomodo? Si quis lapidem, aut cultrum, aut sarcinam in summo suo tecto reliquerit, eaque ordinario vento decidentia damnum dederint; totum damnum rependere tenetur: quia ista omnia ac similia, incendii consequentia sunt. sive, horum jura ex eo definiuntur, quod lex Mosis de igne constituit. Similiter in objecto non tantum ager quæque in eo sunt segetes; sed etiam homo spectandus. unde Maimon. ibidem sect. 15. [Hebrew text] si ignis urat & ladat hominem, cumque vitiet; ecce incendens tenetur damni, & de cessatione illius, curatione, dolore, & igno& ignominia; ac si eum sua manu laesisset. 5 Tandem spatium definitur, ultra quod si ignis serpat aut exiliat, author non teneatur: nam certi limites statuendi, ne innocens pro nocente multetur. Et hac quidem Misna, quia raro communis ignis ultra quatuor cubitos ascendens alienum agrum petere solet, aut viam publicam quae lata esse consuevit, vel flumen ita transilire, ut in alieno obvia comburat; ideo qui hoc eventu ignem accendit, absolvitur. sed ea de re plenius Misna sequenti: tantum de via publica hoc addam, eam in Gem. definiri, [?], sedecim cubitis; de flumine vero discrepantem esse sententiam: hic flumen ipsum designari existimat; alius autem, [?], rivum irrigationis, sive e quo agros irrigant. Sed conciliatio sequitur: [?] [?], secundum eum qui intelligit justum flumen, absolvitur reus, licet nulla sit aqua: secundum eum qui rivum irrigationis intelligit, si in eo aqua sit, ita, id est, absolvitur; sed si in eo non sit aqua, secus. Digest. li. 47. t. 9. l. 9. incendia etiam prohibentur.
units.tr: {2} Hebrew word; see the text above. the fire; or the fire first and afterwards the wood; or finally, after the wood and fire have been brought, another kindles it: the one carrying the fire is liable there, the one carrying the wood here, and here finally the one kindling the fire is condemned. Therefore if the wind kindles the fire, the earlier parties are acquitted. This is the author's meaning, which is why I have inserted the particles then and afterwards in the text, since otherwise the sense would not hold together. (4) What is laid down about stones and dust, they gather from chapter 22 of Exodus, verse 6. How, or from what word, this is explained in the Gemara: "Why is the field named to me? To include the case when its fallow ground is licked and the stones are burned up." God, making a distinct mention of the thorns, the stack, and the crop, finally also mentions the field, because not only is he prosecuted who first set the fire, but also he who kindles the blaze, by whose licking flame the field itself, though empty of crops (which they call nir, that is, according to the Glossator, "fallow not yet sown"), is lightly scorched and spoiled; to which, in this respect, stones are equated, which they also want to be safe from fire. Further, observe from Maimonides on Pecuniary Damages, chapter 14, last section, that what is laid down about a fire that spreads is to be extended to similar cases. [Hebrew text] "All the offshoots of a fire are in the same state as the fire. How so? If someone leaves a stone, or a knife, or a load on the top of his roof, and these fall in the ordinary wind and cause damage, he is bound to make good the whole damage, because all these things and similar ones are consequences of the fire." That is, their rights are defined by what the law of Moses lays down about fire. Similarly, in the object, not only the field and the crops in it but also the human being is to be considered. Hence Maimonides in the same place, section 15: [Hebrew text] "If fire burns and injures a man and damages him, behold, the one who set it is liable for the loss, and for the cessation of his work, the cost of his cure, his pain, his shame and disgrace, as if he had injured him with his own hand." (5) Finally the distance is defined, beyond which, if the fire creeps or leaps, the author is not liable; for certain limits must be fixed, lest an innocent person be fined in place of a guilty one. And indeed this Mishnah, because a common fire rising above four cubits rarely tends to reach another's field, or a public road, which is customarily broad, or to leap a river in such a way that it burns what lies in the way on the other side, therefore whoever kindles a fire in such an event is acquitted. But the Mishnah will treat this matter more fully in what follows. I will add only this about the public road: in the Gemara it is defined as sixteen cubits; but about the river the opinion differs. One holds that the river itself is meant here; another, however, holds that it is an irrigation channel, or one from which they irrigate their fields. But a reconciliation follows: according to the one who understands a true river, the accused is acquitted even though there is no water; according to the one who understands an irrigation channel, if there is water in it, he is acquitted; but if there is no water in it, otherwise. Digest, book 47, title 9, law 9: fires are also forbidden.

units.la: Qui aedes, acervumve frumenti juxta domum positum combusserit, vinctus verberatus igni necari jubetur: si modo sciens prudensque id commiserit. Si vero casu, id est negligentia: aut noxam sarcire jubetur; aut si minus idoneus sit, levius castigatur. Appellatione autem aedium omnes species aedificii continentur.
units.tr: Whoever sets fire to a house or a heap of grain placed beside a house is ordered to be bound, beaten, and put to death by fire, provided he did it knowingly and deliberately. If he did it by chance, that is, through negligence, he is ordered either to make good the damage or, if he is not able to do so, to be punished more lightly. The term "houses" includes every kind of building.
They were [היו]

units.la: הסליק כחוך שלו ער כמה העבור הדליקה רבי אלעזר בן עזריה אומר ראין אותה באלו היא באמצע בית כור רבי אליעזר אומר שש עשרה אמות כדך רשות חרבים רבי עקיבא אומר נ׳ אמרה
units.tr: If a thread ... how high does the flame reach? Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah says: we see it where it is in the middle of the house of the cor measure. Rabbi Eliezer says: sixteen cubits, like a well, the public domain. Rabbi Akiva says: fifty.

units.la: Si quis ignem accendat in fundo suo, quousque hoc incendium pertingere censetur? D. Eleazarus filius Azaria inquit, Ita incendium considerant, ac si esset in medio fundo cori mensura consito; D. Eliezer 16 cubitos assignat, pro spacio loci publici; D. Akiba 50 cubitos requi-
units.tr: If anyone kindles a fire on his land, how far is the conflagration judged to reach? Rabbi Eleazar son of Azariah says: reckon the fire as if it were in the middle of a field sown with a cor measure. Rabbi Eliezer assigns sixteen cubits, for the width of the public way. Rabbi Akiba

units.la: רבי שמעון אומר שלם ישלם הסבעיר את הבערה הכל לפי הוליקו הטוליק את הגריש והיו בו כליום וולקו רבייהודה אומר ישלם מה שבחוכו וחכמים אומרים אינו משלם אלא גריש של חטין או של שעורים היה גרי כפות לו ועבר סמיך לו ונשרף עסו חייב עבר כפות לו הגרי סמיך לו ונשרף עסו פטור וםודים חכמים לרבי יהודה בטוליק את הבורה שהוא משלם כל מה שבחוכה שכן דרך בני אדם להניח כבחים׃
units.tr: "Rabbi Simeon says: he must pay in full. He who sets the blaze pays for everything, in proportion to how far the fire spread. If he set fire to a stack and there were utensils in it, and they burned too, Rabbi Judah says he must pay for whatever was inside it. The Sages say he pays only for the stack of wheat or barley. If a goat was tied to a stack, and a servant stood beside it and was burned with it, the owner is liable. If the servant was tied to the stack, and a goat stood beside it and was burned, the owner is free." [רבי שמעון אומר שלם ישלם הסבעיר את הבערה הכל לפי הוליקו הטוליק את הגריש והיו בו כליום וולקו רבייהודה אומר ישלם מה שבחוכו וחכמים אומרים אינו משלם אלא גריש של חטין או של שעורים היה גרי כפות לו ועבר סמיך לו ונשרף עסו חייב עבר כפות לו הגרי סמיך לו ונשרף עסו פטור]

units.la: requirit; D. Simeon inquit, Omnino qui facit ut incendium fit, omnia rependet pro incendii ratione. Vbi quis metam frumenti incendit, in qua sint instrumenta quae una conflagrant, D. Iudas exigit ut compenset quod in ea continebatur; at Sapientes statuunt, ut nihil compenset, quam tritici aut hordei metam. Si haedus illi alligatus sit, cui servus assiet qui una cum eo comburatur; author tenetur: si servus illi meta alligatus sit, cui assiet haedus qui cum eo comburatur; author liber est. Porro Sapientes D. Iudae assentiuntur, quod incendentem aedes concernit; hunc compensare quicquid iis continebatur: quia ita homines in aedibus sua deponere consueverint.
units.tr: demands; Rabbi Simeon says that whoever causes the fire to spread at all must make restitution for everything, in proportion to the extent of the fire. Where someone sets fire to a stack of grain in which there are implements that burn together with it, Rabbi Judah requires him to make good what was contained in it; but the Sages hold that he makes good nothing but the stack of wheat or barley. If a goat tied to him, next to which a servant stands, burns with him, the author is liable; if a servant tied to the stack, next to whom a goat stands that burns with him, the author is free. Moreover, the Sages agree with Rabbi Judah in the case of one who sets fire to a house: he must make good whatever was contained in it, because this is how people are accustomed to store their goods in houses.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Quandoquidem unicuique in fundo suo ignem sumere licet, ignisque in alienum agrum serpens segetes aliaq; comburere potest; quam procul ab alterius possessione ignis excitari debeat, ut culpa non imputetur, quaeritur: adeo ut תעבור הלין, transfibit incendium, non sit simpliciter transfire & pertingere; sed ita aliquo pertingere, ut igne serpente ulterius, crimine vaces.² R. Eleazarus ignem tam remotè à vicini tui possessione collocandum censet, quam si cum agrum habes qui sementem cori capiat, in medio ignem suscitares. Itaque quantitas huiusmodi agri spectanda: quam glossa Salomonis Jarchi describit in Baba Bathra octonarii » folio octavo edit. Constant. circa medium. Ibi é spatio atrii, quod cingens tabernaculum in longitudinem centum cubita, in latitudinem quinquaginta patebat; quantitatem de qua loquimur concludit. quandoquidem atrii spatium, communi consensu erat [illegible, ~4 letters] locus searum duarum sementem capiens. Seas tres continet Epha, quæ ejusdem capacitatis est cum Bato; Batos decem capit Corus: ergo corus est searum triginta; ita ut duas seas quindecies contineat. Vnde jam habemus, si ager duarum searum (sive qui duarum searum semine conseritur) quantum erat atrii tabernaculi spatium, 100 cubit. in longitudinem, & 50 in latitudinem patebat; agrum cori sive qui coro conseritur continere septuaginta quinque cubitorum millia. quæ in quadraturam dispositæ in unumquodque latus paulo amplius quam 270 cubita relinquunt: cujus ferme medium ex Eleazari sententia est spatium quo ab alterius possessione remotus ignis tuto accendi potest, ita ut si forte casu quodam nocumentum inferat, accendens non teneatur. Nec tamen existimandum, hujusmodi agros vulgò conseri; sed ille R. exemplo ostendere voluit, quanto spatio distans ignis, licet damnum det, neminem reum faciat. Alius sedecim cubitorum distantiam sufficere arbitratur: quia ut in præcedentibus dictum fuit, si ignis viam publicam transiliat, atque aliena comburat, crimen nullum est; via autem publica sedecim saltem cubitos lata est. Verumtamen communis Doctorum sententia à D. Simeone non discedit: qui incendii rationem ac modum controversiam decidere arbitrabatur. Ardoris vehementiam spectari volebat: exempli gratia, si accensus ignis via ac modo usitato ac vulgari ad viginti tantum cubitos pertingere posset, quicquid intra hoc spatium comburetur, rependi debebat; sin vento quodam singulari & rarissimo ulterius delatus ignis aliena læsisset, ex ipsius mente damnum compensari non debebat. Quemadmodum autem Judæi caute in hac materia distinguunt; sic & Romani : uti videre est ff. Ad leg. Aqu. l. 30. §. 3. Si quis in stipulam suam, vel spinam comburenda ejus causa, ignem immiserit; & ulterius evagatus & progressus ignis, alienam segetem vel vineam laserit: requiramus, num imperitia ejus, aut negligentia id accidit. nam si die ventoso id fecit, culpa reus est. & paulo post: In eodem crimine est, & qui non observavit, ne ignis longius procederet. At si omnia, quae oportuit, observavit, vel subita vis venti longius ignem produxit, caret culpa. 5 Hic dubium occurrit in rebus, quae cum meta comburitur, in meta delitescunt. eas Sapientes compensari nolunt, uti hic legitur: verum Judaei observant distinctionem adhibendam. Nam Sapientes res istas eximunt, quia earum locus non est meta: itaque de vomere, falce ac similibus aliis quae illic reponi solent, diversum est judicium; utpote quum eorum cum ipsa meta eandem esse rationem, Doctori Judae assentiantur. Haec etiam causa est; cur sub finem hujus constitutionis, quaecunque in aedibus comburuntur compensari, statuitur: quia consuetudo fert, ut quaevis in aedibus asserventur. Caeterum licet cum meta quae exuritur, res contentae non compensentur; attamen quia spatium occupant, tantum frugum rependi volunt, quantum res contentae spatii occupant. Exempli gratia, lectus illic sepositus conflagret: is quidem non rependitur; sed si meta tritici fuerit, tantum tritici restituendum, quam lecti spatio contineri potuisset, quia totus ille acervus pro tritici meta habetur. 6 Quum, si servus astans comburatur, reus condemnatur; si servus alligatus comburatur, absolvitur: id ex Judaeorum mente acceptum nihil absurdi continet. Id enim haedi etiam respectu dicitur: hoc sensu, ut incendiarius tantum propter metam & haedum alligatum & combustum teneatur, quia servus fugere poterat; si vero haedus astans comburatur cum servo alligato, absolvitur: non ratione ac respectu servi; sed haedi, cujus nomine nihil debeat. Etenim regula juris Judaici omnino in hisce constitutionibus semper ob oculos versari debet, nisi in multas absurdas opiniones incidere velimus: quae hujusmodi est, קיס ליך כדרכם מיכיס [?], statuë ipsi secundum quod ipsius maximum exigit. Quasi dicant, Si quis in peccato quodam plura deliquit, majoris culpae poena subeunda; minoris vero omittenda est. Quemadmodum in hoc exemplo: incendiarius metam cum haedo & alligato servo combusserit; hominis necem luere tenebitur, metae & haedi exusti poena alia non irrogabitur. De incendiariis ex jure Rom. jam actum est.
units.tr: ¹ Since everyone is permitted to take fire on his own land, and fire creeping onto another's field can burn the crops and other things, the question is how far from another's property a fire must be kindled so that the blame is not imputed. The phrase it shall pass over the fire [תעבור הלין] does not simply mean to pass over and reach; it means to reach some point in such a way that, with the fire creeping further, one is free of guilt. ² Rabbi Eleazar holds that the fire must be placed as far from your neighbour's property as if you had a field that takes a kor of seed, and you kindled the fire in its middle. The size of such a field is therefore to be considered. The gloss of Solomon Jarchi describes it in Baba Bathra, eighth chapter, folio eight, Constantinople edition, about the middle. There, from the space of the court that surrounded the tabernacle, which was one hundred cubits long and fifty wide, he works out the quantity we are discussing; for the court's space, by common agreement, was the place of two seahs [of seed]. An ephah contains three seahs, which is the same capacity as a bath; a kor holds ten baths; so a kor is thirty seahs, and therefore it contains fifteen times two seahs. Hence we now have: if a field of two seahs (that is, one sown with the seed of two seahs) covers the court's space of the tabernacle, which measured one hundred cubits in length and fifty in breadth, then a field that takes a kor contains seventy-five thousand cubits. Arranged as a square, this leaves a little over 270 cubits on each side; roughly the middle of that, according to Eleazar's opinion, is the distance at which a fire, removed from another's property, may safely be lit, so that if by some chance it does harm, the one who lit it is not liable. Yet one should not suppose that such fields were commonly sown; the rabbi wished rather to show by example how great a distance separates a fire which, even if it causes damage, makes no one guilty. Another thinks a distance of sixteen cubits is enough, because, as was said above, if a fire leaps across the public way and burns another's property, there is no crime, and a public way is at least sixteen cubits wide. Nevertheless the common opinion of the teachers does not depart from that of Rabbi Simeon, who thought the reasoning and manner of the blaze would settle the controversy. He wished the intensity of the heat to be considered: for example, if a fire, lit in the usual and ordinary way, could reach only twenty cubits, whatever burned within that space must be made good; but if a fire carried further by some unusual and very rare wind had harmed another's property, in his view the damage ought not to be compensated. Just as the Jews distinguish carefully in this matter, so do the Romans, as may be seen in the Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam, law 30, §3: If anyone has set fire to his stubble or thorns for the purpose of burning them, and the fire, spreading and advancing further, has damaged another's crop or vineyard, we inquire whether this happened through his inexperience or his negligence; for if he did it on a windy day, he is guilty of fault. And a little later: He is in the same guilt who did not take care that the fire should not proceed further. But if he observed everything that ought to be observed, or a sudden violence of the wind carried the fire further, he is free from fault. ⁵ Here a doubt arises about things which, when the stack is burned, lie hidden within it. The Sages do not wish these to be compensated, as is read here; but the Jews observe that a distinction must be applied. For the Sages exempt those things because their place is not the stack; so the judgment about ploughshares, sickles and similar tools, which are customarily stored there, is different, since they agree with Rabbi Judah that these have the same status as the stack itself. This is also the reason why, near the end of this rule, it is laid down that whatever is burned in a house must be compensated: custom has it that all sorts of things are kept in houses. Moreover, although the contents of a burned stack are not compensated, nevertheless, because they occupy space, they wish that as much grain be repaid as the space occupied by the contents would hold. For example, if a bed stored there is burned, it is not repaid; but if the stack was of wheat, as much wheat must be restored as the space of the bed could have held, since that whole heap is regarded as a stack of wheat. ⁶ That, when a servant standing by is burned, the offender is condemned, but when a servant tied up is burned, he is acquitted: this, received in the mind of the Jews, contains nothing absurd. For it is also said with respect to the kid: in this sense, that the arsonist is liable only on account of the stack and the tied kid that was burned, since the servant could have fled; but if the kid standing free is burned with the servant tied up, he is acquitted, not with respect to the servant, but with respect to the kid, for whose sake he owes nothing. For indeed, the rule of Jewish law must always be kept before our eyes in these regulations, unless we wish to fall into many absurd opinions. It runs thus: set for him according to what is greatest [קיס ליך כדרכם מיכיס], as if they said: if someone has committed several offences in one sin, the penalty of the greater fault must be undergone, and that of the lesser omitted. Just so in this example: if an arsonist has burned a stack together with a kid and a tied servant, he will be bound to pay the penalty for the killing of the man, and no other penalty will be imposed for the stack and the burned kid. Concerning arsonists under Roman law, we have already treated.

units.la: גן שיצא מחחר הפטישוהזיק חייב גמל שחיה טעןפשחן ועבר בֹרה ונכנס' פפשחנו לחוך החנית ודלקהבנרו של חנוני והדליק אשהבירה בעל הגמל חייב הניחחנוני נרו סבחוך החנוני חייברבי יהודה אומר בנר חנוכהפטור ז
units.tr: A garden [wall] that issued from a smith's hammer and caused damage: the one who made it is liable. A camel that was carrying flax passed through a public place, and the flax went into a shop and was set alight by the shopkeeper's lamp and burned the house: the owner of the camel is liable. But if the shopkeeper set his lamp down outside, the shopkeeper is liable. Rabbi Judah says: concerning a Hanukkah lamp he is exempt.

units.la: Stricture{1} à malleis fabrilibus dissiliente & dissiliendo damnum inferente, author tenetur. Si camelus lino onustus per locum publicum transfeat, linumque in tabernam irrepens & instito-ris lucernâ conflagrans aedes incendat; cameli dominus tenetur: verum si instito-r lucernam suam foris depo-suit, ipse instito-r tenetur. D. Judas inquit, eum quod ad{2} encaniorum lucernam, liberum esse.
units.tr: Stricture{1} from smiths' hammers, flying off and causing damage, the author is liable. If a camel loaded with flax passes through a public place, and the flax creeping into a shop and set alight by the shopkeeper's lamp burns the house, the camel's owner is liable; but if the shopkeeper has set his lamp outside, the shopkeeper himself is liable. Rabbi Judah says that concerning the lamp of the dedication (Hanukkah) he is free.{2}
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: {1} In originali est רן, qua voce quid significetur docetur in Aruch: ubi R. Nathan hunc locum explicans ait, פיזין מתחת הפסים כמכה על הכרזל טכסדן קרוין ניתין, ista scintilla quae prosiliunt ab inferiori mallei parte, quum tundit ferrum quod in incude est, vocantur ניתין. ergo רן omnino per stricturam vertendum: nam Latini hujusmodi scintillam, qualem describit R.Nathan, proprie strictturam dicunt. Hanc, licet nullam culpam arguere videatur, Judæi in incendio authorem obligare tradunt. 2 Sed sequens casus minus culpæ habere meritò censeatur. Nam omninò fortuitum est, linum, quod ubi asino, &c. imponitur in arctum comprimitur, quò minus spatium occupet ideoque facilius gestetur, ante tabernam quodammodo dissolvi & sese dilatare, vel longitudine sua protuberare; adeo ut sarcinæ pars quædam protuberans inque tabernam extensa, ibidem à lucerna accendatur; quo deinde fiat ut toto lino conflagrante, ædes institoris flammam concipiant. Sanè hujusmodi fortuitum casum Romanorum leges excusarent: utpote quæ generatim incendium fortuitò factum absolvant. ff. li. 47. t. 9. le. 11. Si fortuitò incendium factum fit, venia indiget: nisi tam lata culpa fuit, ut luxuria aut dolo fit proxima. Nec repugnat quod l. 9. qui casu combussit, noxam sarcire jubetur: nam casu ibidem exponitur negligentia. Etenim triplex differentia hic locum habet: incendium fortuitum est; vel culpâ factum; vel denique consilio patratum. in primo genere damnum non sarcitur, ut jam probatum; in secundo castigatio & damni restitutio obtinet; in tertium capitali pœna animadvertitur, ut ex Rom. jure ad Misnam quartam probavimus. 3 Denique sub finem capitis, R. Judas producitur, qui institorem è taberna lucernam proferentem, licet hoc modo lini incendendi occasionem in via publica præbeat, in encæniis culpa vacare pronuntiat. Idque ad hunc modum exponit Gemara, ut lege præceptum dicat, lucernam eo die in publico accendere, quò homines videnda videre queant; idque non altius decem cubitis. alioqui excipi posset, tam altè accendendam lucem ne asini sarcina eò pertingere queat; verum ista solemnitate id non licet, ob ea quæ distinctè videri debent. Quocirca si ea ratione incendium fortuitum contingat, non tenebitur; secundum legem Si vendita, D. l. 18. t. 6. qua in insula vendita easque combusta venditor absolvitur, si ipsius respectu incendium fortuitum fuerit. Ibi quidem incendium sine culpa fieri non posse, initio dicitur: attamen quod pertinet ad damni restitutionem servanda lex quæ supra è Dig. 47.tit.9. producta fuit. Cui consentit l. 6. li.4. Cod. tit. 24. Quæ fortuitis casibus accidunt, cum prævideri non potuerint… nullo bonæ fidei judicio præstantur: & l. Contractus, De reg. Juris: Animalium casus, mortes, quaque sine culpa accidunt, fuga servorum qui custodiri non solent, rapina, tumultus, incendia, aquarum magnitudines, impetus prædonum à nullo præstantur.
units.tr: {1} In the original it is רן, a word which Aruch explains: there R. Nathan, explaining this passage, says that the sparks which leap from the lower part of the hammer when it strikes the iron lying on the anvil are called ניתין. So רן must be rendered altogether as stricture, for the Latins properly call such a spark of the kind R. Nathan describes a stricture. The Jews hand down that the author is bound for the fire by this, although it seems to prove no fault. 2 But the following case may rightly be judged to involve less fault. For it is entirely accidental that the flax, which is packed tightly when it is loaded on a donkey, etc., loosens somewhat in front of the shop, so that it may occupy less space and be more easily carried, or it bulges out by its own length; so that some part of the load, bulging and stretched out into the shop, is set alight there by the lamp, with the result that, the whole flax then burning, the shopkeeper's house catches fire. Certainly the Roman laws would excuse such an accidental case, since they generally absolve an accidentally caused fire. Dig. bk. 47, tit. 9, law 11: If a fire is caused by chance, it needs pardon, unless the fault was so gross that it approaches wantonness or fraud. Nor does it conflict that law 9 orders the one who burned by chance to make good the loss; for chance is there explained as negligence. Indeed a threefold distinction applies here: a fire is either accidental, or caused by fault, or finally carried out by design. In the first kind the damage is not made good, as has now been shown; in the second, punishment and restitution of the damage apply; for the third, capital punishment is inflicted, as we have shown from Roman law at the fourth Mishnah. 3 Finally, at the end of the chapter, R. Judah is brought forward, who declares that the shopkeeper who carries a lamp out of his shop is free from fault at the encaenia, although in this way he provides an occasion for the flax to catch fire in the public way. The Gemara explains this so that the law says that on that day the lamp is to be lit in public, so that people can see what they need to see; and not higher than ten cubits. Otherwise one might object that the light must be lit so high that the donkey's load cannot reach it; but on that solemn day this is not permitted, because of the things that must be seen clearly. Therefore if a fire happens accidentally in this way, he will not be liable; according to the law Si vendita, Dig. bk. 18, tit. 6, in which a seller of an island and its buildings is absolved if a fire happened by chance in relation to him. There it is said at the outset that a fire cannot occur without fault; yet as regards the restitution of damage, the law produced above from Dig. 47, tit. 9, must be observed. With this agrees Cod. bk. 4, tit. 24, law 6: Things that happen by chance, since they could not be foreseen… are not made good by any judgment of good faith; and the law Contractus, De reg. iuris: The accidents of animals, deaths, and whatever happens without fault, the flight of slaves who are not usually guarded, robbery, tumults, fires, floods of waters, and the attacks of pirates, are made good by no one.
CHAPTER 7, HALAKHAH 1

units.la: סרוכה סרח חשלומי כפל סמורח חשלומי ארבעה וחמשה שטרח חשלומי כפל נוהגת בין בדבר שיש בו רוח חיים ובין בדבר שאין בו רוח חיים ומרח חשלומי ארבע׳ וחמשה אינה נוהגת אלא בשור ושה בלבד שנאמר כי יגנוב איש שור או שה וטבחו או מכרו וגומר אין הגונב אחר הגנב משלם חשלומי כפל ולא הטובח ולא המוכר אחר הגנב משלם חשלומי ארבע׳ וחמשה׃
units.tr: A double payment is made for a thing that is stolen and sold or slaughtered, and a fourfold and fivefold payment; the double payment applies both to a thing that has living breath and to one that has no living breath, but the fourfold and fivefold payment applies only to ox and sheep, as it is said: If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, etc. The one who steals from a thief pays double; but neither the slaughterer nor the seller who is not the thief pays fourfold or fivefold. [סרוכה ... ארבעה וחמשה ... בשור ושה בלבד שנאמר כי יגנוב איש שור או שה וטבחו או מכרו וגומר אין הגונב אחר הגנב משלם כפל ולא הטובח ולא המוכר אחר הגנב משלם ארבעה וחמשה]
CHAPTER VII, §. I.

units.la: Modus duplum rependendi frequentior est modo rependendi quadruplum aut quintuplum: quia modus duplum restituendi usitatus est cum in iis' quæ animata sunt, tum in iis quæ vitali spiritu carent; at modus rependendi quadruplum & quintuplum non est in usu, nisi in bove & parva pecude tantummodo. Nam (Exodi 22. 1.) dicitur, Quum quis furatus bovem aut parvam pecudem mactavit aut vendidit eam, &c. Qui furatur' à fure, non rependit duplum; nec qui mactat aut vendit furi furreptum, rependit quadruplum aut quintuplum.
units.tr: The double restitution is more frequent than the restitution of fourfold or fivefold, because the mode of restoring double is customary both for things that are animate and for things that lack vital breath; but the mode of restoring fourfold and fivefold is not in use, except only for ox and small cattle. For it is said (Exodus 22:1): When anyone has stolen an ox or a small beast and slaughtered it or sold it, etc. One who steals from a thief does not restore double; nor does one who slaughters or sells what was stolen from the thief restore fourfold or fivefold.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ' Ex. 22. 9. de iis quæ alteri concredita (exceptis personis: de plagiariis enim alia sancitur pœna) vel amittuntur, vel intervertuntur, generalis extat regula: quam sequentia ibidem distinctius exponunt. Verba legis, De omni re interversa, de bove, de asino, de parva pecude, de vestimento; de omni re amissa, quum dixerit, illum ipsum esse; ad ipsos magistratus venito negotium amborum: quem condemnabunt magistratus, rependito duplum proximo suo. Hinc Talmudici, in omnibus rebus poenam dupli, in solis bubus & parvis pecudibus poenam quadrupli & quintupli obtinere concludunt. nam duplum & quadruplum in ejusdem rei furto exigi potest, pro diverso furandi modo. Concredita enim, quaecunque sint, duplo rependuntur; at bos & parva pecus si non concredantur, sed surripiantur, bos quintuplo, parva pecus quadruplo compensatur. Nisi istae bestiae etiamnum integrae in furis manibus deprehendantur: eo enim casu duplum sufficit, uti legimus Ex. 22. 4. Quia autem hoc ῾f. 4. asinus etiam commemoratur, nimis a Judaeis comm. 1. coartari existimo: quum 1 & 4 inter se collata, quaevis pecora intelligenda esse suadeant, quae in pascuis relinqui solent. Haec enim videtur augendi poenam ratio, quod ista animalia furandi occasio semper in promtu sit: quapropter ne, quorum tantus est usus & necessitas (quae altera ratio est,) temere & frequenter, quia facta facile sit, furto auferantur vel abducantur, tanta sancita fuit multa. Ideo enim ῾f. 9. duplum tantum exigitur: quia tale furtum praecaveri potest, puta si alteri pecora non concredamus. de hoc enim ibi sermo est. Deinde usum & utilitatem istarum bestiarum etiam spectari inde liquet, quod si bos vel ovis &c. adhuc vivi in furis potestate sint, nonnisi ad duplum teneatur ῾f. 4. quandoquidem eo modo dominus nullum damnum in istius pecoris corpore percipit. quare etiam bos quintuplo rependitur: quia ejus usus major. Haec igitur duplex ratio spectanda. Unde de similibus simile judicium ferendum est. Verumenimvero ut alia loca concilientur, distinguendum autumo inter eum, qui invitus deprehenditur, & culpam agnoscere cogitur; & eum qui sponte poenitentia ductus culpam fatetur & deprecatur. Levit. c. 6. ꝑ f. 4. ita legitur, Restituet rapinam ipsam quam rapuit, aut ipsam rem dolo interversam, aut depositum ipsum quod apud se depositum fuerat: aut ipsam rem amissam quam invenit: ꝑ f. 24. aut de quocunque juraverit mendaciter, rependet illud quanti fuerit, & quintam ejus superaddet ei. Hic multa minor injungitur, quam Ex. 22. cum tamen furtum ibi 1. & ꝑ f. 9. descriptum, hic inter alia contineatur. Sed ex adjuncta expiatione, ad quam arietem afferre dicitur ꝑ f. 6. de poenitentia agente agi, constare judico. Quem enim facti poenitet idcoque expiationem quaerit, minus lex condemnat, quam pertinacem furem, qui nonnisi convictus vi ad restitutionem cogitur. Quod de poenitentia dixi, e Num. 5. 7. magis confirmatur: siquidem in haec verba Deus loquitur. Si confitebuntur quisque peccatum suum quod fecerunt; tum restituens reatum suum quanti est, quintam ejus superaddet ei; dabitque ei in quem reus est. Vbi initio, per Si commode redditur: quemadmodum Num. 12. 14. פר פרה, ubi recte Graeci LXX. εἰ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῆς πλὺων ἐπέπληξεν, &c. Si pater ejus spuendo inspuisset, &c. Similiter c. 5. ꝑ f. 7. ויתודו, si confitebuntur. Num. autem 5.7. conferendum cum Lev. 6.4. quis non videt? Quod si mutuo sese explicant, ista solius summae cum quinta parte restitutio ad quosvis non pertinebit; sed eos tantum, qui poenitentia ducti sponte aliena bona restituunt. Unde nulla amplius legum pugna apparet. Hoc addo, Lev. 6.4. de consitente reo qui sponte sua alteri suum restituit agi, ex eo etiam constare, quod אשם eum quandoque denotare videatur, qui culpam per se agnoscit; eademque vox illic eodem commate inveniatur, ואשם כי יאשם, erit autem cum peccato admisso culpam ex se agnoverit. Ita omnino accipiendum c. 4. ꝑ f. 22. 23. si commodum sensum eruere velis. verba haec sunt de Principe qui errore peccaverit, ואשם אם, si se reum agnoverit, aut indicatum ei fuerit peccatum ejus. Quum ϭϭϭ vertitur per reum esse, non vero reatum suum per se agnoscere; nullus est locus enunciationi disjunctivæ, quam indicat particula ϭ, aut. Etenim reum esse, & reatum alicui indicari, disjunctive non opponuntur; sed per se sive ex se culpam agnoscere, & ab alio eam indicari ita opponuntur, ut segregativam propositionem constituere queant. Nec Hebraeis insuetum est, ut vocabula non tam rem, quam ejus agnitionem & professionem denotent: quod adeo verum, ut nuda professio, licet rei non quadret, quandoque significetur. exempli gratia, Ef. c. 58. ϡ 2. volunt, vel delectantur, hunc habere sensum ac si diceretur, profitentur se delectari, agnovit Chaldæus, dum verteret, ac si vellent sive delectarentur. Ideo David Kimchi id enarrans inquit, ore, non animo nec opere. Nihil ergo impedit, quo minus Levit. 6.4. ubi rei veritas verbis subest, ϭϭϭ de eo dicatur, qui verbis ex animo & sponte suum reatum profitetur. Sane Hos. 5.15. rei erunt, Chal. reddit agnoscent se reos esse: & plerique Rabbinorum de peccati consessione & agnitione hoc accipiunt. Ut D. Kimchi ad illum Hos. locum, A. Ezra & Sal. Jarchi: cujus verba, habebunt seipsos pro reis, confitendo reatum suum. Hanc illarum legum conciliationem retinens donec quis convenientiorem ostenderit, pergo. Romanæ leges convenienter jam dictis, furtum quoddam duplo, quoddam quadruplo multant. Inst. l. 4. t. 1. §. 5. Pœna manifesti furti, quadrupli est, tam ex servi, quam ex liberi persona; nec manifesti, dupli. Quis fur manifestus, quis nec manifestus, docet Paulus jurisconsultus libro sententiarum sub titulo de furibus. Manifestus fur est, qui in faciendo deprehensus est, & intra terminos ejus loci unde furatus est, comprehensus est, vel antequam ad eum locum quo destinaverat, pervenerit. Nec manifestus est fur, qui in rapiendo comprehensus non est, sed eum fecisse fecisse negari non poterit. Distinctio quidem multæ convenit; sed applicatio diversa: uti conferenti liquet.2 Quod de fure subjungitur, qui ab alio fure furatur, plenius à Maimon. c. 1. sect. 17. Codicis de furto enarratur: ubi rationem his verbis apponit, יגנוב ממנו אחר ... [Hebrew]
units.tr: Ex. 22. 9. Concerning things entrusted to another (excepting persons, for kidnappers are punished under a different penalty) that are either lost or misappropriated, there stands a general rule, which the following verses set out more distinctly. The words of the law: Concerning every thing misappropriated, concerning an ox, concerning an ass, concerning a small animal, concerning a garment; concerning every thing lost, when he says that it is his; the cause of both shall come before the magistrates themselves: whom the magistrates condemn, let him repay double to his neighbour. Hence the Talmudists conclude that the penalty of double applies in all things, while the penalty of fourfold and fivefold applies only to oxen and small animals. For double and fourfold may be exacted for theft of the same thing, according to the different manner of stealing. If the things entrusted are whatever they may be, they are repaid double; but if an ox or a small animal is not entrusted but stolen, the ox is repaid fivefold and the small animal fourfold. Unless these beasts are still found intact in the thief's hands; in that case double suffices, as we read in Ex. 22. 4. But since the ass is also mentioned in this verse 4, I think the Jews restrict it too narrowly, since verses 1 and 4 compared together suggest that any livestock is meant, which are usually left in the pastures. For this seems to be the reason for increasing the penalty: because the opportunity of stealing these animals is always at hand, and so, lest those things whose use and necessity are so great (which is the other reason) should be carried off or led away lightly and frequently, because the deed is easy to do, such a heavy fine was enacted. For the reason the penalty is only double in verse 9 is that such a theft can be guarded against, for instance if we do not entrust livestock to another; for it is of this that the passage speaks. Further, that the use and usefulness of these beasts are also taken into account is clear from this: that if an ox or a sheep and so on are still alive in the thief's power, he is liable only for double, since in that way the owner suffers no loss in the body of that animal. Hence the ox too is repaid fivefold, because its use is greater. This double reason, then, is to be considered. Therefore a similar judgment must be passed in similar cases. But in truth, to reconcile the other passages, I think one must distinguish between the man who is caught against his will and is forced to acknowledge his guilt, and the man who, moved by repentance of his own accord, confesses and deprecates his fault. Lev. 6. 4. reads thus: He shall restore the robbery itself which he took, or the thing itself misappropriated by fraud, or the deposit itself which had been deposited with him, or the lost thing itself which he found: verse 24: or concerning whatever he has sworn falsely, he shall repay it at its full value, and add a fifth part to it. Here a much smaller fine is imposed than in Ex. 22, though theft is described there in verse 1 and verse 9, and here it is included among other things. But I judge it clear from the added atonement, for which a ram is said to be brought in verse 6, that this concerns a man who repents. For the law condemns less the one who regrets his deed and therefore seeks atonement, than the obstinate thief, who is compelled to restitution by force only once convicted. What I have said about repentance is further confirmed by Num. 5. 7., for God speaks in these words: If they shall confess each his sin which they have committed; then he shall restore his guilt in full, and add a fifth part of it to him, and give it to him against whom he is guilty. Where at the beginning If is fitly rendered by si, as in Num. 12. 14., a father [פר פרה, where the Greek Seventy rightly render: εἰ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῆς πλὺων ἐπέπληξεν, etc.], If her father had spat in her face, etc. Similarly in chapter 5, verse 7, vitvadu [ויתודו] means if they shall confess. But who does not see that Num. 5. 7. must be compared with Lev. 6. 4.? If they explain each other mutually, this restitution of the sum with a fifth part alone will not pertain to all, but only to those who, moved by repentance, voluntarily restore the goods of another. Hence no further conflict between the laws appears. I add this: that Lev. 6. 4. concerns the guilty party who, of his own accord, restores to another what is his, is also shown by this, that the word asham [אשם] seems sometimes to denote one who acknowledges his fault by himself; and the same word is found there in the same verse: and he shall be guilty, when he shall have acknowledged his fault of himself [ואשם כי יאשם]. So too chapter 4, verses 22 and 23, must be understood in this way, if you wish to draw out a suitable sense. The words concern a prince who has sinned through error: and he shall be guilty, if he shall have acknowledged himself guilty, or his sin shall have been pointed out to him [ואשם אם]. When asham [ϭϭϭ] is rendered to be guilty, and not to acknowledge one's guilt by oneself, there is no place for the disjunctive proposition which the particle or indicates. For to be guilty and to have one's guilt pointed out to one are not opposed disjunctively; but to acknowledge one's fault by oneself, or from oneself, and to have it pointed out by another, are opposed in such a way that they can form a segregative proposition. Nor is it unusual for the Hebrews that words denote not so much the thing as its acknowledgment and profession; so true is this that a bare profession, even when the thing does not match it, is sometimes meant. For example, Isa. 58. 2. they desire, or they delight, has the sense as if it were said they profess that they delight; the Chaldean recognised this when he rendered it as if they desired or delighted. Hence David Kimchi, explaining it, says: with the mouth, not the mind nor the deed. Nothing therefore prevents Lev. 6. 4., where the truth of the matter underlies the words, from saying asham [ϭϭϭ] of the one who professes his guilt in words, from his heart and voluntarily. Indeed at Hos. 5. 15. they shall be guilty, the Chaldean renders they shall acknowledge that they are guilty; and most of the rabbis take this of confession and acknowledgment of sin: as David Kimchi on that passage of Hosea, and Abraham Ezra and Solomon Jarchi, whose words are: they shall hold themselves guilty, by confessing their guilt. Keeping this reconciliation of those laws until someone shows a more fitting one, I proceed. The Roman laws, agreeing with what has been said, punish one kind of theft with double and another with fourfold. Inst. l. 4. t. 1. §. 5.: The penalty for manifest theft is fourfold, whether in the person of a slave or of a freeman; and for non-manifest theft, double. Who is a manifest thief and who is not manifest, Paulus the jurist teaches in his book of Sentences under the title on thieves: A manifest thief is one who is caught in the act, and is seized within the bounds of the place from which he stole, or before he has reached the place to which he had determined to go. Nor is a thief non-manifest who was not caught in the act of seizing, but whose deed cannot be denied. The distinction is indeed much the same, but the application is different, as comparing the two makes plain. What is added concerning the thief who steals from another thief is explained more fully by Maimonides, ch. 1, sect. 17, of the Code on theft, where he gives the reason in these words: he who steals from him, another [יגנוב ממנו אחר ...]

units.la: Qui furatur à fure alio, licet proprietarii recuperandi spem abjecerint, non rependit duplum; nec si macta-vit aut vendidit, quadruplum aut quintuplum rependit: furi enim priori non rependit, quia jus & conditio istius bestiæ est, ut ea ipsa ad proprietarios redeat, nec eam fur acquisivit; proprietarius autem nec duplum, nec quadruplum aut quintuplum rependit, quia ex ipsorum potestate non surripuit. Ratio duobus membris constat: vel furi, vel proprietario debitum solvendum, id est, pœna furti subeunda: non illud, quia furi nullum jus in istam bestiam competebat, siquidem ipsius possessio jure ad proprietarium redibat; non alterum, quia multa ista lege divina ei injungitur, qui proprietario propriam bestiam eripuit, atqui fur furi eripuerat. Cogitur tamen bestiam vel pretium restituere. Ita quidem Judæorum magistri, f. 68. Bab. Kam. Cæterum quod Maimonides dicat, Licet spem non abjecerint; eorum sententiam respicit, qui furem priorem rei ereptæ possessionem sibi acquisivisse statuunt, post desperationem, sive quum jam proprietarius recuperandi spem abjecit; ideoque posteriorem furem priori veluti proprietario rem auferre. Id ergo negat Maimonides. Lex quidem Dei hunc casum non definit; Judæorum tamen magistri à graviori ista multa secundum furem eximunt, autoritate Exod. 22.7. Licet enim aliud furtum quam fur. consideretur; quia tamen simile est, illius multam ex hujus conditione spectandam censent. Ideoque hæc verba expendentes, Si id furto ablatum fuerit è domo viri illius (scilicet apud quem depositum tum erat) ad furtum in genere hoc modo applicant: quum non dicatur è domo furis, sed è domo illius viri; poena etiam furti eum spectat,qui è domo illius depositarii &c. non vero è domo furis abstulit. Denique Maimonides capite citato par. ultimo, casum proponit, quo fur secundus priori, cui rem furto ablatam vicissim abstulerat, satisfacere tenetur: puta si aliquo modo (ut Maim. existimat) rem acquisiverit. Simile quid legere est l. 6. Pand. t. 2. sub finem: uti quidem censet Jurisconsultorum nonnemo, cujus haec sunt verba, Prædo etiam restituendus & fur. hoc tamen intelligendum, quando spoliatus est ab alio quam à domino, à quo subtracta res est; exemplo publiciana actionis l. penult. & sin. de Publ. in rem actione. Sed Publiciana actio bonam fidem requirit, quæ in fure non deprehenditur.
units.tr: He who steals from another thief, even though the owners have given up hope of recovering it, does not repay double; nor, if he has slaughtered or sold it, does he repay fourfold or fivefold: for he does not repay the first thief, because it is the right and condition of that beast that it returns to its owners, and the thief did not acquire it; but the owner does not repay double, nor fourfold or fivefold, because it was not stolen from their power. The reasoning consists of two parts: that the debt must be paid either to the thief or to the owner, that is, the penalty for theft must be undergone; not to the thief, because no right to that beast belonged to the thief, since its possession by right returned to the owner; not to the owner, because the multiple fine laid down by this divine law applies to one who has snatched a beast from its owner, whereas the thief snatched it from a thief. Nevertheless he is compelled to restore the beast or its price. So indeed the masters of the Jews, folio 68, Bab. Kam. But as to what Maimonides says, though they have not given up hope, he refers to those who hold that the earlier thief acquired possession of the thing taken away, after despair, that is, when the owner has already given up hope of recovering it; and therefore the later thief, as if he were the owner, takes the thing from the earlier one. Maimonides denies this. The law of God indeed does not define this case; yet the masters of the Jews exempt the second thief from this heavier fine, on the authority of Ex. 22. 7. For although another kind of theft than that of the thief is considered there, since nevertheless it is similar, they think its fine should be judged from the condition of the latter. Hence, weighing these words, If it be stolen from the house of that man (namely, with whom the deposit then was), they apply it in this way to theft in general: since it is not said from the house of the thief, but from the house of that man, the penalty for theft concerns also the one who has taken it from the house of that depositary etc., and not one who has taken it from the house of the thief. Finally, Maimonides, in the last paragraph of the chapter cited, sets out a case in which a second thief is bound to make satisfaction to the first, from whom he in turn had taken the stolen thing: for instance, if he has acquired it in some way (as Maimonides thinks). Something similar is found in l. 6. Pand. t. 2. near the end, where one of the jurists, whose words these are, is of the opinion: A robber is also to be restored, and a thief. This, however, must be understood when he has been despoiled by someone other than the owner from whom the thing was taken; by the example of the Publician action. But the Publician action requires good faith, which is not found in a thief.

units.tr: "If a thief slaughters or sells (the stolen animal) before two witnesses [גנב על פי שנים וטבח], ..." The Hebrew continues to "the peace-offering" [השלומי], in the rabbinic text that the Latin notes that follow set out: the thief who has slaughtered or sold before two witnesses, or before two others, pays four or five times the value.

units.tr: Whoever steals and slaughters or sells an animal in the presence of two witnesses, before the same witnesses or two others, repays fourfold or fivefold. Whoever steals and sells on the Sabbath; whoever steals and sells for idolatry; whoever steals and slaughters or sells on the Day of Atonement; whoever steals from his father and slaughters or sells, so that the father dies only afterwards; whoever steals, slaughters, and afterwards consecrates the animal: each of these repays fourfold or fivefold.
