units.la: ארבעה וחמשה רבי שמעון / פוטר בשני אלו ׃ rependit quadruplum aut quintuplum. D. Simeon in his duobus absolvit.
units.tr: Arba'ah vechamishah, Rabbi Shimon / poter beshnei eylu [ארבעה וחמשה רבי שמעון / פוטר בשני אלו]: he repays fourfold or fivefold. Rabbi Simeon acquits him in these two cases.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ In his & similibus copulativa particula, pro disjunctiva accipitur; ut Ex. 22. 15. Percutiens patrem & matrem omninò moriatur, id est, patrem aut matrem: non enim tum demum mortis reus est, si ambos percusserit; sed etiamsi patrem tantum, aut solam matrem verberaverit. Similiter non ille solum tenetur, qui mactavit & vendidit; sed etiam qui tantum mactavit, vel tantum vendidit ablatam pecudem. ² Attendendum, hic non dici mactavit; sed vendidit: nam qui mactavit in sabbatho, mortis poenam incurrit; qui vero morte multatur, a quadrupli compensatione absolvitur. Idque secundum generalem regulam, subsistit sibi in maximo sui peccati. (sic enim hoc pronunciatum etiam reddi potest.) cujus sensus, Si in uno facto duo peccata, quae poenam diversam requirunt, concurrant; reo sufficit si maximum luat: ut in hoc exemplo, Sabbatho operans lapidandus ex lege Num. 15. 36. at qui mactat, opus servile facit; idcoque lapidandus. Idem tamen si alienum pecus mactet, quadrupli tenetur. Quid ergo hic faciendum? Quandoquidem Sabbathi violatio furto atrocior est; idcirco illud peccatum morte punitur; hoc vero negligitur, ejusque poena magistratorum judicio in illa morte contineri censetur. ³ Sic aliena pecora vendens idolis, sive ad idololatriam; furti gravioris tenetur, adeoque quadruplum & quintuplum rependere debet: sed Misna non addit mactavit. Nam ut priori casu; sic hoc sequenti, venditionis poena in idololatriae poena absorberetur: siquidem gravior idololatriae (quae mactando exercetur) poena incumbit, secundum legem Ex. 22. 19. Qui sacrificat diis aliis, ut anathema perditor. ⁴ Quis sit expiationis dies, è Levit. c. 16. ℣. 29. satis liquet, cum inquit Deus, Mense septimo, die decimo illius mensis affligitote animas vestras...30, quia isto die expiationem faciet, &c. Iam expendamus, quare fur cum die sabbathico mactans pecudem, quadruplum non rependat, sed moriatur; hoc die mactans rependat, nec morte afficiatur. Gemara manifeste in illo rationem reddit, quæ supra fuit annotata; in hoc verò posteriori casu distinguendum putant, nec semper eum qui die expiationis mactat pecudem quam furatus sit, ad quadruplum teneri. Verum non præmonitus id fecerit; vel (ut alii putant) per alium id peregerit; ad compensationem istam obligabitur: si per se, sive suis manibus mactavit, aut præmonitus non desisterit; vapulabit, nec quadruplum reddet. Nam ut ait Maimonides de furto c. 3. פמוטם עבירה מנתחייב מלקות ותשלומין לוקה ואינו משלם, Qui legem transgressus, ideo verberum & restitutionis reus est; vapulat, nec rependit. Quandoquidem major pœna (casibus quibusdam exceptis) minorem absorbet; ad quadrupli restitutionem non tenentur, qui plagis luunt. Hæc est Maimonidæ in isto dicto mens ac sententia. confer ibidem finem sectionis secundæ, ubi Maim. regulam applicat. Qui furatus pecudem nec mactavit, nec vendidit, ad duplum tantum tenetur Ex. 22. 4. Quid ergo, si filius patri pecudem auferat, nec mactet, aut vendat; nisi patre jam vita functo? Patre mortuo pecus filio cedit: itaque cum antea furatus, post patris mortem mactat, suam pecudem mactat: quocirca lege Exod. 22. 1. non tenetur. Hæc est causa, quare Misnæ author ita factum circumscribat, ut nonnisi patre vivo filium bovem vel ovem &c. mactantem aut vendentem ad quadruplum vel quintuplum obliget. Si fur pecudem furto ablatam mactet, posteaque Deo consecret, nihilominus ad quadruplum obligatur: si vero antequam furtivam pecudem mactavit, aut vendidit, eam consecraverit, rependet duplum; non quadruplum aut quintuplum:
units.tr: ¹ In these and similar passages the copulative particle is taken as disjunctive, as in Exod. 21:15: Whoever strikes his father and mother shall surely die, that is, his father or his mother. For he is not liable to death only if he has struck both, but even if he has struck only the father or only the mother. Similarly, the one who has slaughtered and sold is not the only one bound by the law. The one who has merely slaughtered, or merely sold the stolen animal, is bound too. ² Note that here it is not said slaughtered, but sold. For whoever slaughters on the sabbath incurs the penalty of death, and whoever is punished with death is released from the fourfold compensation. This follows the general rule, it stands on its own in the greatest of its sins. (The saying can also be rendered this way.) Its meaning is this: if in one act two sins that demand different penalties coincide, it is enough for the guilty person to pay the greatest. Take this example: one who works on the sabbath is to be stoned by the law of Num. 15:36, and one who slaughters is doing servile work, and so is to be stoned. Yet if he slaughters another's flock, he is liable to fourfold restitution. What, then, is to be done here? Since the violation of the sabbath is a more heinous theft, that sin is punished with death, while the other is set aside, and its penalty is considered to be contained in that death by the judgment of the magistrates. ³ Likewise, one who sells another's flock to idols, or for idolatry, is liable to the heavier theft, and so must make fourfold or fivefold restitution. But the Mishnah does not add slaughtered. For as in the earlier case, so in this later one, the penalty for selling is absorbed into the penalty for idolatry, since the heavier penalty for idolatry (which is carried out by slaughtering) falls upon him, according to the law of Exod. 22:19: He who sacrifices to other gods, shall be utterly destroyed. ⁴ What the day of atonement is, is quite clear from Lev. 16:29, where God says: In the seventh month, on the tenth day of that month, you shall afflict your souls ... 30, for on that day he shall make atonement, and so on. Now let us consider why a thief who slaughters an animal on a sabbath day does not make fourfold restitution but dies, whereas one who slaughters on the day of atonement makes restitution and is not put to death. The Gemara clearly gives the reason noted above for the first case. But in this latter case they think a distinction must be made. The one who slaughters on the day of atonement the animal he has stolen is not always bound to fourfold restitution. Yet if he did it without warning, or (as others think) had it done through another, he will be bound to that compensation. If he slaughtered it himself, with his own hands, or did not desist after being warned, he will be flogged and will not pay fourfold. For, as Maimonides says in the treatise on theft, chapter 3: One who has transgressed the law is therefore liable to lashes and to restitution; he is flogged and does not pay. Since the greater penalty (apart from certain exceptions) absorbs the lesser, those who pay with stripes are not bound to fourfold restitution. This is the mind and opinion of Maimonides in that passage. Compare the end of the second section of the same chapter, where Maimonides applies the rule. One who stole an animal and neither slaughtered nor sold it is bound only to double restitution, Exod. 22:4. What then if a son takes his father's animal, and neither slaughters nor sells it, until the father has already died? When the father dies, the flock passes to the son, so if he slaughters it after the father's death, having stolen it before, he slaughters his own animal, and is therefore not bound by the law of Exod. 22:1. This is why the author of the Mishnah frames the case as he does: only while the father is alive does he bind the son who slaughters or sells an ox or sheep, and so on, to fourfold or fivefold restitution. If a thief slaughters a stolen animal and afterwards consecrates it to God, he is nonetheless bound to fourfold restitution. But if before slaughtering or selling the stolen animal he consecrates it, he makes restitution of double, not fourfold or fivefold,

units.la: plum: uti quidem expresse cum aliis Maimonides c. 2. de furto, sect. sexta. Etenim rei sanctificatio post commissum peccatum, non minuit culpam: sed antequam quod in furto gravius est, puta vendere aut mactare rem furtivam, peractum fit, rei consecrationem sive sanctificationem poenam minuere Ebræi statuunt. Idque hac ratione. Vt simplex furtum duplo luitur, & si pecus furtiva vendatur, aut occidatur, quadruplo; ita si pecus furtiva fit sacra, tantum rependi volunt; si vero eadem deinde vendita aut mactata fuerit, duplum exigunt. Quæ ex eo dependent, quod in rei consecratæ furtum leviori multa animadvertant, quam si profana & privata fuerit. Idque Maimonides Talmudicos secutus, è cap. 22. Ex. ꝭf. 9. rependito duplum proximo suo. (inquit Maim.) proximo suo; non sanctificato. Quia isto commate de furto agitur, ideo priores leges de furto ita accipiunt, ut quadrupli restitutio & quintupli, ad proximi quidem bona referantur; non vero ad rem consecratam. Atqui considerandum erat, sub proximo quemvis contineri, cui bona eriperentur; ideoque legem de quadruplo &c. in sacris etiam locum habere, ut eis restituantur & compensentur, quibus Deus res consecratas cedere voluit: de quibus c. 18. Num. & c. 5. ꝭf. 9. Non enim consentaneum est, cum minori periculo & damno sacra, quam privata bona furto auferri. Legimus quidem Lev. 5. 16. Quod peccavit minuens è re sacra, rependito, & quintam partem ejus super addito ei, quam det Sacerdoti: verum non magis hinc multam istius furti minuent; quam cujuscunque & omnis injustitiæ, è cap. ejusdem libri 6. ꝭf. 2. & seq. item Num. 5. 7. ubi eadem multæ quantitas; licet de aliis furtis & injuriis ibi agatur. Itaque istis locis observandum quod jam antea monui, multam illius definiri qui pœnitentia ductus sua sponte rem furtivam restituit: uti è circumstantiis demonstravi. Qua in reipsum Maimonidem non admodum reluctantem habeo, si verba c. 1. sect. c. 1. sect. 6. de furto expendas, [Hebrew: נכ סהורים מעמו מגנב מטלם ית הקרן] ופסור מן הכסף מנחמר אשר ירמיע' אלהים ישלם שנים ולא המרמיע ית מעמו מטלם [Hebrew: ממס והוא ידין לכל הקכנסו סהמודב כהן פסור] fur qui sua sponte furtum faetetur, solam fortem restituit, & liber est à dupli restitutione: quia dicitur Exod. 22. 9. Quem condemnabunt magistratus, rependito duplum proximo suo; non vero dicitur, qui condemnat seipsum, rependit duplum. idem jus in omnibus civilibus injuriis, ut qui eas confitetur, illo modo evadat. Quapropter, male ex illa lege, qua in consecratis sola quinta pars sorti superadditur, concluderetur, nihil à quoquam in sacris amplius esse exigendum: vidimus enim eam esse omnium surum conditionem communem, ut solam ferme rem furtivam restituant; quod tamen simpliciter nemo admittet. Qui ergo? Si poenitentia ductus sponte restituat quod abstulit. Ita ergo in rebus consecratis, qui sponte sua rem restituit, quintam partem solummodo superaddit; alii vero dupli, quadrupli, quintupli poena tenentur, pro circumstantiarum diversitate. 7 Quod de canibus & medicina additur, magistrorum sententiam respicit, qui in furto lucri & commodi rationem spectant: ideoque cum alimento canum parum furi accedere videretur, nec medicina alat, de isto casu dubitari poterat. idcirco quadruplum & quintuplum hic etiam exigunt. 8 Hac eadem de causa disceptum hic considerant: quum enim fur hinc nullum emolumentum rite percipere queat, ut quod edere ipsi non liceat; nec furti poena ipsum manere videtur. ideoque ne quis dubitet, poena sancitur: nec R. Simeonis, qui secus statuit, sententia admittitur. Ut occasio legis, adeoque ipsa lex intelligatur plenius, expendenda veniunt Dei verba, quae Ex. 22. ÿf. ultimo leguntur, Carnem in agro discerptam ne comeditote. Pro discerpta in originali est, [Hebrew: טריפה]: quam vocem bene explicat Moses Mikkotsi in interdicto 134. [Hebrew: טריפה היא אשר הוציא ממנה ...] Quam discerpsit (vel laceravit aliquatenus) fera, quamq. contri-
units.tr: double: as Maimonides expressly says, along with others, in chapter 2 on theft, section 6. For the consecration of a thing after the sin has been committed does not lessen the guilt. But the Hebrews hold that if, before the more serious act is done, that is, before the stolen thing is sold or slaughtered, its consecration or sanctification lessens the penalty. And they reason thus. Just as simple theft is repaid double, and if the stolen flock is sold or killed, fourfold, so if a stolen flock is made sacred, they want only the simple restitution. But if it is afterwards sold or slaughtered, they require double. These rulings depend on the fact that they regard theft of a consecrated thing as punished more lightly than theft of a profane and private thing. Maimonides, following the Talmudists, takes this from Exod. 22:9: he shall pay double to his neighbour (he says): to his neighbour, not to the holy. Because that verse deals with theft, the earlier laws on theft are understood so that the restitution of fourfold and fivefold applies to the goods of a neighbour, not to a consecrated thing. Yet it had to be considered that under neighbour anyone is included from whom goods are taken away. So the law about fourfold, and so on, has its place also in sacred matters, that these things be restored and compensated to those to whom God wished consecrated things to belong. Concerning these see Num. 18 and Exod. 22:9. For it is not consistent that sacred property should be taken with less risk and loss than private goods. We read indeed in Lev. 5:16: He who has sinned by diminishing the holy thing shall make restitution, and add a fifth part of it, and give it to the priest. Yet from this they do not derive the penalty for that theft any more than for any and every injustice, from chapter 6 of the same book, verse 2 and following, and likewise Num. 5:7, where the same amount of penalty appears, although other thefts and injuries are dealt with there. So in these passages one must observe what I have already said before, that the penalty is fixed for one who, moved by repentance, restores the stolen thing of his own accord, as I have shown from the circumstances. I find Maimonides himself not very opposed to this, if you weigh his words in chapter 1, section 6, on theft: [Hebrew: נכ סהורים מעמו מגנב מטלם ית הקרן ופסור מן הכסף מנחמר אשר ירמיע' אלהים ישלם שנים ולא המרמיע ית מעמו מטלם ממס והוא ידין לכל הקכנסו סהמודב כהן פסור]: A thief who confesses his theft of his own accord restores only the principal and is free from the double restitution, because it is said (Exod. 22:9): whom the judges condemn, he shall pay double to his neighbour; but it is not said, one who condemns himself pays double. The same law holds in all civil injuries: whoever confesses them escapes in that way. Therefore it would be wrong to conclude from that law, in which only a fifth part is added to the principal for consecrated things, that nothing more is to be exacted from anyone in sacred matters. For we have seen that it is the common condition of all thieves that they generally restore only the stolen thing, which nonetheless no one will simply admit. What then? If moved by repentance they restore of their own accord what they took. So in consecrated things, one who restores of his own accord adds only a fifth part; others are bound to double, fourfold, or fivefold penalty, according to the diversity of circumstances. ⁷ What is added about dogs and medicine refers to the opinion of those masters who consider the matter of gain and advantage in theft. Since the feeding of dogs seemed to bring the thief little gain, and medicine does not nourish, doubt could arise about that case. Therefore they require fourfold and fivefold here too. ⁸ For this same reason they discuss here: since a thief can gain nothing lawfully from it, as he may not eat it himself, the penalty of theft does not seem to apply to him. So, lest anyone doubt it, the penalty is ordained, and the view of R. Simeon, who holds otherwise, is not admitted. So that the occasion of the law, and thus the law itself, may be understood more fully, we must weigh the words of God that are read at the very end of Exod. 22: You shall not eat flesh torn in the field. For torn the original has [Hebrew: טריפה], which Moses Mikkotsi explains well in precept 134: [Hebrew: טריפה היא אשר הוציא ממנה ...]: that which a beast has torn, or mangled to some extent, and has been crushed, so that it tends toward death but is not yet dead.

units.la: {1} Hebrew marginal and interlinear glosses as printed. contrivit, ut ad mortem quidem vergat, nondum tamen mortua fit. Si enim mortua fit, vocatur כנלה, morticina: siquidem non solum נכלה, morticina dicitur, si per se moriatur; sed etiam פכה אותה כסיף והמיתה או טברס לרי והמיתה, si quis eam telo impetens confodiat, aut leo laniando occidat. Quemadmodum etiam טרפה, lacerata sive discerpta habetur, non solum quam laniavit fera; sed etiam quae alio modo male affecta morti vicina est. כין טנפלה מן פנג ונטברו רוב נלטוניה, Sive cum è tecto decidit pleraque costa frangantur; כין טנפלה ונתרסקו רוב היכריה, sive cum decidit, pleraque membra conterantur; כין סורק מן ויקב לכס או רויתה, sive emissa sagitta ipsius cor aut pulmo impetatur; כין טבף לה חולי, מהמת מנמס וניקב לכס או רויתה, sive morbus eam ex se invadat, quo cor ipsius, aut pulmo gravius afficiatur. Modo ex ejusmodi infortunio mors sequuntur demum fit, טרפה ab Ebraeis nuncupatur. Si quis interroget, quodnam sit temporis spatium, intra quod bestia ex hujusmodi casu mori censeatur: quidam contractum tempus annotant; sed magistrorum aliquot annuum tempus assignant. Fieri ergo saepe potest, ut quis pecora macet, quae discerpta esse, vel aliqua ratione lethaliter laesa ignoraverit. Atque huc respicit Misna, quam explicamus.
units.tr: {1} Hebrew marginal and interlinear glosses as printed. It has been crushed so that it tends towards death, but is not yet dead. For if it dies, it is called nebela [נכלה], a carcass. A beast is called a carcass not only if it dies of itself, but also if someone strikes it with a weapon and kills it, or a lion mauls it to death [פכה אותה כסיף והמיתה או טברס לרי והמיתה]. In the same way, tereifa [טרפה], torn or lacerated, is applied not only to what a beast has mauled, but also to what, otherwise injured, is close to death: if it falls from a roof and most of its ribs are broken [כין טנפלה מן פנג ונטברו רוב נלטוניה]; if, when it falls, most of its limbs are crushed [כין טנפלה ונתרסקו רוב היכריה]; if an arrow shot at it strikes its heart or lungs [כין סורק מן ויקב לכס או רויתה]; if a disease attacks it, by which its heart or lungs are more seriously affected [כין טבף לה חולי, מהמת מנמס וניקב לכס או רויתה]. Only when death follows from such a misfortune is the animal called tereifa by the Hebrews. If someone asks what length of time a beast may live after such an accident and still be considered to have died from it, some write of a short period, but several of the teachers assign a full year. So it can often happen that someone eats an animal which he did not know was torn or otherwise mortally injured. It is to this that the Mishnah, which we are explaining, refers.

units.la: ' Quae tandem de profanis in atrio mactatis subjiciuntur, interdictum spectant, quod occurrit in Gemara Cod. Kiddoufschin f. 57. p. 2. edit. Sabionetensis. ubi Deus in haec verba loquens introducitur, מה טלי כתוך אתור סד טלך כתוך אתור, Quemadmodum meum in tuo fundo mactatum, est interdictum; ita etiam tuum in meo fundo mactatum, interdictum est. Hoc sibi volebat R. Meïr: quemadmodum edere non licet pecudis carnem, quae Deo consecrata extra locum sanctum mactatur; ita edere carnem profanam pecudis in loco sancto mactatae, nemini licere: imo nec emolumentum aliud inde percipere. Itaque quum, uti antea dictum fuit, illi in furto emolumentum considerent; an fur ob tale furtum ad quadruplum & quintuplum teneretur, dubitari poterat: quandoquidem ista caro esset שחוטה נבלה, interdicta quoad utilitatem quæ inde perciperetur. Nihilominus, quia ob istam illicitam mactationem, ex interdicto sapientum de percipienda utilitate fur ad tantam pœnam non tenebatur, quæ furti pœnam absorberet, à consueta multa non liberabatur: quicquid R. Simeon statuerit. Cæterum illud atrium, עזרה, in quo profana mactari prohibebantur, synecdochicè forte accipiunt pro illo etiam loco, ubi ante templum coram altari victimario ista saltem pecora mactari solebant, quæ usui sanctiori destinata erant, dicebanturque קדשי קדשים, sanctitates sanctitatum. Cujusmodi erant holocausta, victimæ pro reatu & peccato, nec non eucharistica totius cœtus. De isto loco in Talmude Cod. Middoth c. 3. sect. 5. ומכעות היו לצפון של מזבח, annuli erant ad Septentrionem altaris; & paulò post, טבעות שחטו בהן קדשים, ad quos mactabant victimas. Diversa quidem ante ædem sacram erant spatia quæ isto nomine עזרות veniebant, quemadmodum ostendi ad Cod. Middoth p. 173. ac alibi: sed rationem non video quare his locis suas pecudes mactare vellent; at illum annulorum locum non sine causa ad privatam etiam mactationem quærere potuerunt. Nam qui vocantur annuli, erant dimidiata annulorum segmenta, quorum una extremitas pavimento affixa erat; altera, immisso jam animalis collo, pavimento jungebatur. Hinc tanta commoditas ut vel unus mactationi par esset. Quod leges Romanas concernit, jam supra ad sectionem secundam ostendi, iis etiam pœnam quadrupli sancitam fuisse; quemadmodum Judæi hac præsenti Misna quadruplum & quintuplum stabiliunt. Verum diversa respiciunt: nam Judæi ex lege Ex. 22. 1. illam pœnam tantummodo exigunt, si fur parvam pecudem vel bovem mactaverit, vel vendiderit; alibi duplo contenti: Romani ad res quasvis in genere extendunt, eoque oculos intendunt, an fur manifestus sit; an minus: ibi quadruplum; hic duplum exigentes. Unde subinde contingit, ut qui lege Dei ad duplum; plum; lege Romana ad quadruplum teneatur. Exempli gratia Exodi 22. 4. si bos in furis manibus deprehendatur, dupli tenetur; at quicunque in faciendo deprehenfus eft, & intra terminos ejus loci unde furatus eft, comprehenfus, lege Romana quadruplum debet: utpote fur manifestus. Inst. l.4. tit.1.
units.tr: What is finally added about profane animals slaughtered in the court belongs to a rule which occurs in the Gemara of the Kiddushin tractate, folio 57, page 2, Sabbionetta edition, where God is introduced speaking in these words: "Just as my [animal] slaughtered in your field is forbidden, so your [animal] slaughtered in my field is forbidden" [מה טלי כתוך אתור סד טלך כתוך אתור]. This is what R. Meir meant: just as it is not lawful to eat the flesh of an animal consecrated to God that is slaughtered outside the holy place, so it is lawful for no one to eat the profane flesh of an animal slaughtered in the holy place; indeed, no other benefit may be derived from it. Therefore, since, as was said before, they considered the benefit in theft, it could be doubted whether a thief who stole in this way was liable to a fourfold or fivefold penalty, since that flesh would be "forbidden as to the benefit" [שחוטה נבלה] derived from it. Nevertheless, because on account of that unlawful slaughter the thief was not bound, by the rule of the sages concerning the enjoyment of benefit, to a penalty so great that it would absorb the penalty for theft, he was not freed from the customary fine, whatever R. Simeon decided. Moreover, that "court" [עזרה], in which profane animals were forbidden to be slaughtered, they perhaps take by synecdoche to mean also that place before the temple, before the altar, where the sacrificer used to slaughter those animals at least which were destined for a more holy use and were called "holies of holies" [קדשי קדשים]. Such were the burnt offerings, the sin and trespass offerings, and the thank offerings of the whole assembly. Concerning this place, in the Middoth tractate, chapter 3, section 5, it is said: "There were rings [טבעות] on the north side of the altar," and a little later: "rings to which they tied the holy animals for slaughter" [טבעות שחטו בהן קדשים]. There were indeed various open spaces before the sacred house which bore this name of azarot, as I showed on the Middoth tractate, page 173, and elsewhere; but I do not see why they would wish to slaughter their own animals in those places. The place of those rings, however, they could seek, not without reason, even for private slaughter. For what are called rings were half-circles of rings, one end of which was fixed to the pavement; when the animal's neck was put in, the other end was joined to the pavement. Hence such convenience that one man alone could manage the slaughter. As for the Roman laws, I have already shown above, in the second section, that they too decreed a fourfold penalty; and the Jews, in this present Mishnah, establish a fourfold and fivefold penalty. But they differ in what they cover: the Jews, under the law of Exodus 22.1, exact that penalty only if the thief has slaughtered or sold a small animal or an ox, and elsewhere they are content with double; the Romans extend it to things of any kind, and look to whether the thief was caught in the act or not: there they exact fourfold, here double. Hence it sometimes happens that one who is bound to double under God's law is bound to fourfold under Roman law. For example, Exodus 22.4: if an ox is found in the thief's hands, he owes double; "but whoever is caught in the act of stealing, and seized within the bounds of the place from which he stole," owes fourfold under Roman law, as a manifest thief. Inst. l.4, tit.1.

units.la: גנב על פי שנים וטבח וסכר על פיהם ונמצאו וזמסין משלסין הכל גנב על פי שנים וטבח וסכר על פי שנים אחריום אלו ואלו נמצאו וזמסין הראשונים משלמין חשלומי כפל והאחרונים משלמין חשלומי שלשה נמצאו אחרונים וזמסין הוא משלם השלומי כפל והן משלמין השלומי שלשה אחר מן האחרונים זומם בטלה עורת שניה אחר מן הראשונים זומם בטלה כל העדות שאם אין גניבה אין טביחה ואין סכירה ו
units.tr: If a man stole on the testimony of two witnesses, and slaughtered or sold, and on their testimony the witnesses were found to be false [זוממין], they all pay. If one stole on the testimony of two, and one slaughtered or sold on the testimony of two, and afterwards these and those were found to be false witnesses, the first pay double restitution and the latter pay triple restitution. If the latter were found to be false witnesses, the thief pays double restitution and they pay triple restitution. If one of the latter is a false witness, the testimony of the second is void. If one of the first is a false witness, all the testimony is void, because if there is no theft there is no slaughtering and no selling [אם אין גניבה אין טביחה ואין סכירה].
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ' Videndum quinam dicantur ווממים, incongrui: hi enim non sunt מוכחתים, falsitatis convicti, ut putatur; sed ab iis re ipsa distinguuntur, licet personae eaedem ad utrumque ordinem subinde pertineant, quia duo crimina in eundem cadere possunt. Itaque ווממים, incongrui censentur, qui sive verum quoad causam principalem, sive falsum dicant, idonei testes non sunt: quia ubi quod testantur factum fuit, præsto non erant; sed alibi fuisse convincuntur. Quam descriptionem vocis usus comprobat, & verba Gemaræ Cod. Maccoth, f. 5. p. 1. quæ ita habent, Illud Deut. 19. 16. Ad testandum contra eum aversionem, accipiendum, quasi dicas, Donec diverso ac alio loco fuerit corpus testium; scilicet non censentur testes incongrui. Male quidem פרו pro radice ponitur; tamen hæc est Talmudistarum mens, quam expressit S. Jacum annotaret, quia inde remoti sunt. Hinc apparet testes eos dici, quos ambos aliorum testimonio constat, ab illo loco remotos fuisse, ubi factum quod investigatur, contigit. Dico ambos: quia si unus tantum ibi non fuisse deprehendatur, dicitur & convictus falsi. Non dubito quin is, cui Misnæ & Maimonidæ quoddam dictum alio sensu prolatum videbatur, omnibus expensis sententiam meam approbaturus sit. Testes vero simpliciter mendaces dicuntur falsarii sive falsitatis convicti. Unde Nathan in Aruch, Si testes posteriores contra priores testentur, occisorem vel occisum eo tempore secum fuisse; priores non erunt, sed. Unde jam liquet, quamvis iidem possint esse falsarii & ob absentiam incongrui, diversam rationem & modum icтis duabus vocibus significari: nam utrique quidem mentiuntur; sed in rebus diversis. incongrui in eo mentiri deprehenduntur, quod se suis oculis rem vidisse vel auribus audivisse asserant; quod circa idem factum aliis modis à veritate abierint, in quibus falsi arguuntur. ² Quæ in sequentibus de istis incongruis testibus sanciuntur, ad quosvis mendaces testes pro circumstantiarum differentiis applicanda & extendenda esse, rationi congruit. Itaque sequentia expendamus: ubi varietas magna deprehenditur. Sed quo omnia dextrè accipiantur, unum inprimis attendendum: in tota hac Misna illud in casibus proponendis spectari furtum, quod in bove committitur: siquidem passim ad quintuplum collimatur, cujus ille tenetur, qui bovem vel saltem æquale pecus furatus eò progressus fuit, ut vel vendiderit, vel mactaverit. Nihilominus hæ leges servata proportione in aliis quoque furtis locum habent, quorum nomine fures nonnisi ad duplum tenentur. Cum hæc ita se habeant, author postquam hujusmodi factum expendisset, ubi iidem testes de furto simul & rei furtivæ mactatione vel venditione testati, deprehendebantur incongrui, eosque ad eam pœnam damnasset, quam fur luere debuisset, idque secundum legem Deut. 19.19. Omnino facietis ei, quemadmodum molitus fuerat facere fratri suo: quum inquam hunc casum propositisset; alium subjecit, ubi furti testes, & venditionis, diversi sunt. Tum simul totam pœnam, nimirum quintupli, sustinent; & quidem convenienter legi jam productæ: adeo ut priores testes, qui proximum furti insimulabant, dupli tantum obligentur; licet de bove agatur. Ratio est, quia fur, quamvis bovem furatus, si nondum mactaverit, aut vendiderit; sed etiamnunc penes furem res furtiva deprehendatur; nonnisi dupli teneatur ex lege Exod. 22.4. ideoque nec incongrui & falsi testes ulterius obligantur. 3 At testes posteriores, qui furem rem furtivam vendidisse, vel mactasse asserunt, triplum, cum de bove agitur, rependunt: quandoquidem fur, si bovem furto ablatum mactasset, vel vendidisset, tanto plura rependere debebat, puta, cum furti nomine duplum deberet; venditionis, vel mactationis nomine debebat triplum: siquidem in universum quintupli tenebatur, secundum legem Ex. 22.1. Antequam ad alia pergamus, id etiam minime prætereundum, cum posteriores testes in triplum condemnantur, id fieri, quando convincuntur ante priores. etenim quid opus est, posteriores testes examinare, si priores falsò de commisso furto testati sunt? Si furatus non est, mactare & vendere licet. quorsum de venditione agitur, ubi rem sibi venditam vel alio modo suam vendidisse vel mactasse potuit? Verum retrò examen merito instituitur: ut cum de venditione constat, ad furtum pergatur, inque istud inquiratur. Quo ordine servato contingit quandoque, ut posteriores sive qui de posteriori facto testantur, & priores qui de furto testimonium perhibent, omnino falsi convincantur, vel ea non vidisse, quæ tamen sibi visa profitentur. 4 Quod si hoc in posterioribus tantum deprehendatur, & priores idonei testes sint, fur solummodo, si bovem furatus sit, duplum solvit; falsi testes triplum. Hac quidem de causa, quia tota pœna est quintupli, si bos mactatus vel venditus fuerit; sin tantum abductus penes surem superfit, dupli, uti in superioribus jam aliquoties oftensum fuit. Unde sequitur, ut quum testes de furto veraces sunt, fur simplicis furti pœnam luat, id est, duplum rependat; posteriores testes de ulteriori delicto, cujus nomine fur triplum addere debuisset; contra veritatem testantes, triplum solvant: utpote qui debeant pati, quod proximo moliti fuerant.5 Contingit autem quandoque, ut alter testium, qui de venditione rei furtivæ testati sunt, falsi arguatur: hoc modo testimonium secundum habetur irritum; quia legimus Deuter.19.15. Non stabit testis unus in quenquam, pro ulla iniquitate. Nihilominus, ut bene observat Glossator, ipse fur duplum solvit; quandoquidem, licet posterioris criminis nomine non teneatur, ut quod uno teste solummodo affirmetur; prioris, puta, furti nomine, dupli tenetur, utpote quod idoneis testibus probatum sit. Verumenimvero si in prioris facti, id est, furti testimonio, testium alter minus idoneus deprehendatur; non solum prioris, sed etiam posterioris criminis testimonium irritum fit. Ut enim subjicit author,6 nisi furtum sit, non est illicita mactatio aut venditio. Autoris verba sano sensu accipienda: infinita quidem pecora absque furto mactari & vendi contingit; sed cum hic de crimine agitur, fieri non posse, ut nisi furto bos alicui ereptus sit, in mactatione aut venditione crimen sive culpam mactanti, aut vendenti adscribamus. unicuiq; enim in rebus suis quod vult facere licet. Si suum bovem mactet, quid peccat? Hic dubium aliquod occurrit, si incongrui testes, qui non viderunt, quod se vidisse affirmant, de eo convicti, ipsi ad eam multam tenentur, quam reus sustinuisset; quum unus testis isto crimine tenetur, dimidiam saltem multam debere videtur. Attamen regulam hanc observant Judæi, [Hebrew] testes pecuniam non rependunt, donec incongrui deprehendantur ambo. Cæterum de pœna quadrupli è legibus Rom. antea dictum fuit, Judæorum sententiæ, qua testes duos saltem hic requirunt, concinit Imp. Constantini sanctio Cod.l. 4. t. 20. l. 9. Nunc manifeste sancimus, ut unius omnino testis responsio non audiatur, etiamsi praclara curia honore praefulgeat. Porrò quod incongruos & falsos testes eo modo multant Judæi, quo reus testimonio vero convictus excipi debuisset; in eo non minus rigidi fuere Romani. Hinc Cod. l. 4. t. 20. l. 13. Si velit falso testimonio condemnatus civiliter agere contra eum qui falso testatus est, ab ipso omne quod sustinuit damnum recipiet, praterquam quod ille legibus definitam poenam sustinebit.
units.tr: It must be considered who are called zomemin, that is, the incongruous. These are not the convicted of falsehood, as is commonly supposed, but are distinguished from them in fact, although the same persons may at times belong to both classes, since two charges can fall on the same man. The zomemin, or incongruous, are therefore those who, whether they say what is true or what is false about the principal matter, are not competent witnesses, because when the thing they attest was done they were not present, but are proved to have been elsewhere. This description is confirmed by ordinary usage and by the words of the Gemara, tractate Makkot, folio 5, page 1, which read: "That verse, Deuteronomy 19:16, to testify against him a wrongdoing, is to be understood as if you said, until the body of witnesses is in a different and other place"; that is, they are not counted as incongruous witnesses. The Gemara certainly puts paru in the place of the root, but this is the mind of the Talmudists, which S. Jacum expressed in his note, because they have been removed from there. From this it appears that they are called witnesses whom the testimony of others shows to have been removed from the place where the act under investigation took place. I say both, because if only one is found not to have been there, he too is said to be convicted of falsehood. I do not doubt that the one who thought a certain saying of the Mishnah and of Maimonides had been uttered in another sense will, on weighing everything, approve my opinion. Witnesses who are simply lying, however, are called falsarii, or convicted of falsehood. Hence Nathan in the Aruch: if later witnesses testify against earlier ones that the killer or the killed was with them at that time, the earlier ones are not to be believed. From this it is now clear that, although the same persons may be both forgers and, through absence, incongruous, the two words signify different reasons and manners, for both groups do lie, but about different things. The incongrui are caught lying in this, that they assert they saw the thing with their own eyes or heard it with their own ears; the forgers depart from the truth about the same deed in other ways, for which they are convicted of falsehood. Reason agrees that what is laid down in what follows about these incongruous witnesses is to be applied and extended to any lying witnesses, according to the differences of circumstances. So let us weigh what follows, where great variety is found. But so that everything may be rightly understood, one thing must be attended to above all: in the whole of this Mishnah, in the cases proposed, the theft in view is that committed against an ox. For everywhere the penalty aimed at is the fivefold one, which falls on him who, having stolen an ox or at least an equal beast, went so far as to sell it or slaughter it. Nevertheless these laws, with the proportion kept, hold also in other thefts, for which thieves are liable only to double. Since matters stand so, the author, after weighing such a case, where the same witnesses, testifying to the theft and to the slaughter or sale of the stolen thing at once, were found incongruous, condemned them to the penalty the thief ought to have paid, and this according to Deuteronomy 19:19, You shall do to him as he had thought to do to his brother. Having proposed this case, I say, he then added another, where the witnesses to the theft and those to the sale are different. Then they bear the whole penalty, that is, the fivefold, and indeed this agrees with the law just cited, so that the earlier witnesses, who accused the neighbour of theft, are bound only to double, although the matter concerns an ox. The reason is that the thief, though he stole the ox, if he has not yet slaughtered or sold it, but the stolen thing is still found in the thief's possession, is liable only to double by the law of Exodus 22:4, and so the incongruous and false witnesses are not bound further. But the later witnesses, who assert that the thief sold or slaughtered the stolen thing, pay back triple, when the matter concerns an ox, since if the thief had slaughtered or sold the ox taken by theft, he ought to repay more: for example, when on account of theft he owed double, on account of sale or slaughter he owed triple, since in general he was liable to fivefold by the law of Exodus 22:1. Before we go on, this too must not be passed over: when later witnesses are condemned to triple, this happens when they are convicted before the earlier ones. For what need is there to examine the later witnesses if the earlier ones have falsely testified to the theft committed? If he did not steal, he may slaughter and sell. Why is there a question of sale, when he could have sold or slaughtered a thing that was his own, sold to him or otherwise his? But the reverse examination is rightly instituted, so that when the sale is established, one proceeds to the theft and inquires into that. When this order is kept, it sometimes happens that the later witnesses, or those who testify to the later act, and the earlier ones who bear witness to the theft, are both convicted of falsehood, or of not having seen what they profess to have seen. 4 But if this is found only in the later witnesses, and the earlier ones are competent, the thief alone, if he stole an ox, pays double; the false witnesses pay triple. This is because the whole penalty is fivefold if the ox was slaughtered or sold; if it was only led away and remains in the thief's hands, the penalty is double, as has been shown several times above. Hence it follows that when the witnesses to the theft are truthful, the thief bears the penalty for simple theft, that is, repays double; the later witnesses, who testify to a further offence, for which the thief ought to have added the triple, and who testify against the truth, pay triple, since they ought to suffer what they had plotted against their neighbour. 5 It sometimes happens, however, that one of the witnesses who testified to the sale of the stolen thing is convicted of falsehood. In this way the testimony is held to be void as a whole, because we read in Deuteronomy 19:15, One witness shall not stand against anyone for any iniquity. Nevertheless, as the Glossator rightly observes, the thief himself pays double; since, although he is not liable for the later offence, because it is affirmed by only one witness, he is liable for the earlier one, namely the theft, because it has been proved by competent witnesses. But if in the testimony to the earlier act, that is, the theft, one of the witnesses is found less competent, the testimony not only to the earlier crime but also to the later one is void. For, as the author adds, 6 unless there was theft, the slaughter or sale is not unlawful. The author's words must be taken in a sound sense: it often happens that countless animals are slaughtered and sold without theft; but since here the crime is in question, we cannot assign guilt or fault in the slaughter or sale to the one who slaughters or sells, unless the ox was taken from someone by theft. For to each person it is lawful to do what he wishes with his own things. If he slaughters his own ox, what sin does he commit? Here a doubt arises: if incongruous witnesses, who did not see what they affirm they saw, are convicted of this, are they themselves liable to the fine the accused would have borne? Since one witness is liable for that crime, he seems to owe at least half the fine. Yet the Jews keep this rule, [the Hebrew phrase for] witnesses do not repay the money until both incongruous witnesses are detected. Moreover, concerning the penalty of fourfold from the Roman laws, something was said earlier. The opinion of the Jews, which here requires at least two witnesses, agrees with the sanction of the Emperor Constantine, Code book 4, title 20, law 9: We now plainly decree that the testimony of one witness is not to be heard at all, even if he shines with the honour of a distinguished court. Furthermore, that the Jews fine incongruous and false witnesses in the same way as the accused would have been excused by true testimony, the Romans were no less strict in this. Hence Code book 4, title 20, law 13: If a man condemned on false testimony wishes to act civilly against the one who testified falsely, he shall recover from him all the loss he has sustained, except that the other shall suffer the penalty fixed by law.

A thief who slaughtered on the Sabbath, a thief who slaughtered for idolatry, and a thief who stole from his father pay [גנב על פי שנים וטבח ומכר על פי עד אחד או על פי עצמו משלם תשלומי כפל ואינו משלם תשלושי ארבעה וחמשה גנב וטבח בשבת גנב וטבח לעבודה אלילים גנב משלם אביו] ## §. 4.
