units.la: postquam pater obiit mactavit & vendidit; furatus sanctificavit & postea mactavit aut vendidit: singuli duplum rependunt; nec rependunt quadruplum aut quintuplum. D. Simeon statuit, sancta, pro quibus desideratu homo alia substituere tenetur, quadruplo aut quintuplo compensari; pro quibus vero alia substituere non tenetur, ibi reum absolvi.
units.tr: after the father has died, slaughters and sells; a thief who consecrates and afterwards slaughters or sells: each pays double; they do not pay fourfold or fivefold. Rabbi Simeon determines that for sacred things, for which the man is obliged to substitute another, he is compensated fourfold or fivefold; but for those for which he is not obliged to substitute another, the accused is acquitted there.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Hæc Misna sive constitutio respondet secundæ hujus capitis sectioni: ideoque ex ista explicanda est. ut ibi in similibus factis, conditionum & circumstantiarum intuitu, exigitur quadruplum & quintuplum; ita hic ob illarum diversitatem duplum tantummodo deberi statuitur. Primò, quia illic de mactato bove testabantur testes duo, quintuplum exigebatur; hic quoniam id factum fuerat uno teste conscio, ultra duplum non procedituir. Ideo autem additur, aut se tantum conscio & teste, quia reus culpam fassus pro uno tantum teste habetur: præterea quod fassus injuriam liber fit. Quod tamen posterius dictum restrictione eget, Quum fatetur antequam testes præsto sunt, liber est. modo furtum fateatur, non tantum se pecudem mactasse vel vendidisse. Alioquin quilibet reus absolvi facile posset: utpote qui simulac se convictum animadverteret, culpam lubens fateretur, quo poenam effugeret; & sine ulla difficultate mactationem omnes fatentur, modo furtivam rem mactatam esse non constaret. Cæterum fur ille qui postquam furatus est, de mactatione uno tantum teste convincitur, vel ipse culpam istam fatetur; quamvis recepto more ob mactamactatum bovem non puniatur, nihilominus ob commissam furti culpam rependere duplum tenetur. Nam licet etiam tempestivè furtum fassus fit (quo casu rem furtivam tantum rependit, sive quanti est; & si Dei legem spectemus, quintam superaddit;) nihilominus ob mactationem, vel venditionem poena ferme duplicanda videri queat. Nam ut furti convictus duplum solvit, & si mactaverit quadruplum vel quintuplum; ita quum furti culpam fassus simplum restituat, si mactaverit quoque vel vendiderit, sc fatente, duplum non male exigetur. 2 Mactans pecudem furtivam in sabbatho, vel ad idololatriam, ad duplum hujus Misnæ constitutione damnatur; à quadruplo absolvitur: quum tamen cæteris gravius peccet qui sabbathum violat, vel idolis inservit. Verum ideo absolvitur à quadruplo & quintuplo, quia graviorem poenam incurrit: nam uti nota 2. & 3. sect. 2. dictum fuit, mortis poena in tales transgressores sancitur. Quandoquidem autem gravior poena minorem secundum magistrorum sententiam includit vel potius absorbet; hinc fit, ut capitale supplicium istam multam hic auferat, quæ mactationis nomine irroganda fuisset. Etenim furtum nihilominus plectitur, adeoque duplum rependitur: sed augmentum quod in quadruplo & quintuplo invenitur, id est alterum duplum vel triplum, non exigitur: quoniam id mactationis nomine exigendum esset; mactatio autem quia in sabbatho, vel ad idolorum cultum peracta fuit, morte luenda. Qui morte punitur quia mactavit, non vero quia furatus est; is judicibus satisfecisse censetur, ut ad quadruplum vel quintuplum ob mactationis crimen procedere non debeant. 3 Qui mactavit aut vendidit post obitum patris, à quadruplo & quintuplo liber est: quia res furtiva postquam patris morte hæres est filius, istum titulum simpliciter non sustinet: siquidem cum fratribus &c. hæreditatem participans filius, in illam rem juris aliquid habet. Ita fit ut cum furti saltem teneatur ante patris mortem, simplicis furti poenam debeat, quæ est dupli; ulterius verò non obligetur: quia nec mactatio, nec venditio erat istius rei, quæ omninò alterius esset. * De re sanctificata hic convenienter sectioni secundæ judicatur: ibi sanctificatio mactationem subsequens, à communi multa sanctificantem non liberabat, quia res consecrata non mactabatur; hic multa minuitur, quod consecratio mactationem vel venditionem præcedat, adeo ut res consecrata sit quæ mactatur aut venditur. Ita quidem magistris placet, qui duplum tamen à fure exigunt; licet ulteriori poena supersedeant: quia præter alia, ut res sacra si furto auferatur, tota saltem compensari, addita quinta parte debet; sic si insuper mactetur vel alienetur, duplum ejus tantum reddendum putant. quemadmodum alias quod duplo compensari debet, si tantum furto auferatur; insuper mactatum, quadruplum saltem exigit. Sed de ista constitutione, quà isto fundamento innititur, nihil addam: quandoquidem ad sectionis secundæ notam sextam, ipsum ἀπέωπν ψιυδ@ aperui & refelli. ' Subjicitur tandem R. Simeonis sententia, quasi cum magistrorum judicio non conveniret, in iis quæ hic dicuntur. Verumtamen authoris mens alia fuit; nimirum ut R. Simeonem alia in re reliquis opponeret: non quidem in hujusmodi facto, siquis rem furtivam postea consecraret, ac deinde mactaret; verum si quis rem consecratam furatus, eandem mactaret. Sapientes eum qui consecratam pecudem furatus esset, posteaque mactasset, ad quadruplum non obligabant: quia Ex. 22.7. legatur, Furto ablatum fuerit è domo viri; non enim dici, ... è domo rei consecrata. At R. Simeon hic distinguit: quandoquidem bona consecrata deprehenduntur, quibus amissis vel perditis consecrans ulterius non obligatur. Exempli gratia, in ... spontaneis sacrificiis, si quis ita dixerit, hanc ovem Deo immolandam consecro; si pecus ista forte deperdita fuerit, aliam substituere non tenebitur: in aliis vero quamplurimis, novam illius loco offerre debet. Itaque distinguit R. Simeon: illas pecudes si fures auferant, & mactent, quadruplum, & in bove quintuplum rependi non vult; in his vero posterioris generis gravem istam multam omnino exigit. Si modo rite quoad alias circumstantias munda pecus offeratur: ut si in loco sacro, sine macula a fure offerenda curetur; sin immunda, alibi &c. etenim mactationem contra leges factam, utpote quae legitima mactatio dici nequeat, istum reatum inducere non censet. Caeterum illius sententiae fundamentum, quum solitae poenae reos facit, qui pecudes alienas quarum evictio dominis incumbit, mactant, ejusmodi est. Quandoquidem proprietarius ad earum evictionem tenetur, quum mactat, id quod domini pecudis istius est, id mactat. Sensus est, Quoniam fur ad gravem istam multam tenetur, si privati alicujus pecudem (non sacram, ut illi sentiunt) mactavit; idcirco is qui pecudem ab alio consecratam mactat, poenae illius reus est, si dominus ad aliam substituendam, quae Deo offeratur, obligatus sit: nam eo casu fur non tam consecratam mactat, quam quae est domini; siquidem dominus aliam consecrare debet. Leges Romanae severius in ista peccata animadvertunt: ut quae istos fures, qui privata etiam sacra tentarunt, pro sacrilegis quidem non habeant; severius tamen quam alios fures tractandos censeant. Libro Digest. 48. t. 13. l. 9. Qui privata sacra vel adiculas incustoditas tentaverunt, amplius quam fures; minus quam sacrilegi, merentur.
units.tr: This Mishnah, or rule, corresponds to the second section of this chapter, and so must be explained in light of it. There, in similar deeds, the fourfold and fivefold are demanded in view of the conditions and circumstances; so here, because of their difference, it is laid down that only double is owed. First, because there two witnesses testified to the slaughtered ox, a fivefold payment was demanded; here, since the deed was done with one witness aware of it, it does not go beyond double. The phrase aut se tantum conscio & teste is added because the accused, having confessed his fault, is held to count as one witness; besides which, one who confesses wrongdoing is set free. This latter statement, however, needs a qualification: When he confesses before the witnesses are present, he is free, provided he confesses to the theft and not merely to having slaughtered or sold an animal. Otherwise any accused person could easily be acquitted: as soon as he saw himself convicted, he would gladly confess the fault in order to escape the penalty; and everyone without any difficulty admits the slaughter, provided it is not established that the stolen thing was slaughtered. Moreover, the thief who, after he has stolen, is convicted of slaughtering by one witness alone, or confesses that fault himself, although by accepted custom he is not punished for slaughtering the ox, is nonetheless bound to make restitution of double for the fault of theft committed. For even if he confessed the theft in good time (in which case he makes restitution only of the thing stolen, that is, its value, and, if we look to the law of God, adds a fifth), nevertheless, on account of the slaughter or sale, the penalty may seem almost to have to be doubled. For just as one convicted of theft pays double, and if he has slaughtered, fourfold or fivefold; so when one who confessed the theft restores the single amount, and has also slaughtered or sold, with his confession, double may not unreasonably be exacted. 2 A man who slaughters a stolen animal on the Sabbath, or for idolatry, is condemned by the decree of this Mishnah to double; he is acquitted of the fourfold, although he sins more gravely than others who violate the Sabbath or serve idols. Indeed he is acquitted of the fourfold and fivefold because he incurs a heavier penalty: for, as was said in notes 2 and 3 of section 2, the penalty of death is decreed against such transgressors. Since, however, a heavier penalty includes, or rather absorbs, a lesser one according to the opinion of the teachers, it follows that capital punishment here removes that fine which would have been imposed in the name of slaughter. For theft is nonetheless punished, and so double is restored; but the increase found in the fourfold and fivefold, that is, the second double or triple, is not exacted, since that would be demanded in the name of slaughter; and the slaughter, because it was carried out on the Sabbath or for the worship of idols, is to be atoned for by death. He who is punished with death because he slaughtered, and not because he stole, is considered to have satisfied the judges, so that they need not proceed to the fourfold or fivefold on account of the crime of slaughter. 3 He who slaughters or sells after his father's death is free from the fourfold and fivefold: because, after the father's death, the thing stolen is inherited by the son, and the son does not simply hold that title; for a son who shares the inheritance with his brothers etc. has some right in that property. Thus it comes about that, since he is bound at least for the theft before his father's death, he owes the penalty for simple theft, which is double; but he is not further obligated, because neither the slaughter nor the sale was of that thing, which wholly belonged to another. * Concerning a consecrated thing, the rule here agrees with the second section: there, consecration following the slaughter did not free from the common fine, because a consecrated thing was not slaughtered; here the fine is reduced, because the consecration precedes the slaughter or sale, so that the consecrated thing is what is slaughtered or sold. The teachers indeed hold this, yet they exact double from the thief, although they forgo a further penalty; for, besides other things, if a sacred thing is taken by theft, the whole must be restored at least, with a fifth part added; so if it is further slaughtered or alienated, they think only its double is to be repaid, just as elsewhere what must be repaid double if merely stolen, if it is also slaughtered, requires at least the fourfold. But concerning this rule, on which it rests, I will add nothing, since at note 6 of section 2 I have set out and refuted that false [Greek word, garbled in the scan]. Finally, the opinion of R. Simeon is appended, as if it did not agree with the judgement of the teachers in what is said here. Yet the author's mind was otherwise: namely, to set R. Simeon against the rest in another matter: not indeed in the case of someone who first consecrates a stolen thing and then slaughters it, but if someone steals a consecrated thing and slaughters that same thing. The sages did not bind one who stole a consecrated animal and afterwards slaughtered it to the fourfold, because it is read in Ex. 22.7, taken by theft out of the man's house; for it is not said, out of the house of a consecrated thing. But R. Simeon here distinguishes: since consecrated goods are deposited, and when they are lost or perished the consecrator is no longer bound. For example, in voluntary sacrifices, if someone says, "I consecrate this sheep to be offered to God"; if that animal is perhaps lost, he will not be obliged to substitute another; but in very many other cases he must offer a new one in its place. So R. Simeon distinguishes: he does not want those animals, if thieves take them and slaughter them, to be repaid fourfold, and fivefold for an ox; but for the latter kind he altogether exacts this heavy fine. Provided that the animal is offered rightly in respect of the other circumstances, as when, in a holy place, it is brought without blemish by one who is to offer it; but if it is unclean, elsewhere, etc. For he does not hold that a slaughter made contrary to the laws, which cannot be called a lawful slaughter, induces that guilt. Moreover, the foundation of that opinion, since it makes the usual penalties apply to those who slaughter the animals of others whose eviction falls upon the owners, is of this kind: Since the proprietor is bound to their eviction, when he slaughters what belongs to the owner of the animal, he slaughters it. The sense is this: since a thief is liable to this heavy fine if he has slaughtered a private person's animal (not a sacred one, as they hold), therefore he who slaughters an animal consecrated by another is liable to that penalty, if the owner is bound to substitute another to be offered to God; for in that case the thief does not so much slaughter a consecrated animal as one which belongs to the owner, since the owner must consecrate another. The Roman laws punish these sins more severely: so that they do not indeed regard as sacrilegious those thieves who have attempted private sacred things, yet think they should be treated more severely than other thieves. Digest, book 48, title 13, law 9: Those who have attempted private sacred things or unguarded shrines deserve more than thieves, but less than sacrilegious persons.

units.la: Qui vendidit totum excepta veluti parte ejus centesima 1; aut si in ea partem habuit; qui ita mactat ut in manu sua morticini conditionem mactatum induat; discerpens 2; evellens 3: singuli rependunt duplum; היו מכרו חץ מאחר מסאר שבו או שהחיה לו בו שוחפות השוחט ותחנבלה בירו הנוחר והמעקר משלם תשלומי כפל
units.tr: He who has sold the whole of it, except for, as it were, a hundredth part 1, or if he had a share in it; he who slaughters it so that the slaughtered animal takes on the condition of carrion in his hand; tearing it apart 2; tearing out 3: each pays double. [היו מכרו חץ מאחר מסאר שבו או שהחיה לו בו שוחפות השוחט ותחנבלה בירו הנוחר והמעקר משלם תשלומי כפל]

units.la: 1 Hebrew and Latin notes as printed in the foot-of-page columns. ואינו משלם חשלומי ארבעה וחמשה גנב ברשות הבעלים וטבח ומכר חוץ מרשותם או שגנב חוץ מרשותם וטבח ומכר ברשותם או שגנב וטבח ומכר חוץ מרשותם משלם חשלומי ארבעה; וחמש׳ אבל גנב וטבח ומכר ברשותם פטור ׃
units.tr: 1 Hebrew and Latin notes as printed in the foot-of-page columns. He does not pay the payment of four or five. If he stole in the owners' possession and slaughtered and sold outside their possession, or stole outside their possession and slaughtered and sold in their possession, or stole and slaughtered and sold outside their possession, he pays the payment of four or five; but if he stole, slaughtered and sold in their possession, he is exempt. [ואינו משלם חשלומי ארבעה וחמשה גנב ברשות הבעלים וטבח ומכר חוץ מרשותם או שגנב חוץ מרשותם וטבח ומכר ברשותם או שגנב וטבח ומכר חוץ מרשותם משלם חשלומי ארבעה; וחמש׳ אבל גנב וטבח ומכר ברשותם פטור]

units.la: duplum ; nec rependunt quadruplum aut quintuplum.Si furatus in dominorum fundo , extra eorum fundum mactavit,& vendidit;aut furatus extra eorum fundum, mactavit & vendidit in fundo ; aut furatus est, mactavit & vendidit extra eorum fundum : solvit quadruplum aut quintuplum. at si furatus est, mactavit & vendidit in eorum ditione¹ ; liber est.
units.tr: duplum; nor do they pay fourfold or fivefold. If he stole in the field of the owners, and slaughtered and sold outside their field; or stole outside their field, and slaughtered and sold in the field; or stole, slaughtered and sold outside their field: he pays fourfold or fivefold. But if he stole, slaughtered and sold within their control, he is free.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Sanè mira est Judæorum indoles ac ingenium. Aliquando Scripturam ita extendunt, adeoque late accipiunt & interpretantur, ut à mente Scripturæ alienissima ex ipsius verbis eruere non erubescant: aliàs hoc pluribus ostendi; jam uno exemplo contenti simus. In Berachoth Talm. sol.8.p.1. תניא נמי הכי תשע מיתות וטלטט מיני מיתה נכרתו כעולם טנאמר ולמות תונחות תונחות כנגימטריא הכי היו, Traditio etiam ita habet, Nongenta & tria mortis genera creata sunt in hoc mundo: quia dicitur Psal. 68.21.Ipsi morti exitus sunt (id est, Deus è morte liberat.) Exitus enim per Geometriam (quam pro Arithmetica improprie accipiunt) eum numerum reddit. Aliquando, cum lubet, ita mordicus verbis adhærent, ut nullam consequentiam Logicam admittant. Vti hujus Misnæ initium indicio est: ubi à quadruplo & quintuplo cum absolvunt, qui ovem vel bovem furatus, etiam vendidit; modo centesimam partem ejus non vendiderit. Etenim, inquiunt, lex c. 22. Exodi ita loquitur, Si quis furatus bovem aut parvam pecudem mactaverit aut vendiderit eam, quinque boves rependito &c. Iam ergo, ut dicitur in Gemara, in dicto Aut vendiderit eam, totam ipsam requirimus: quasi dicas; Lex de ea pecude agit quam vendiderit: si ergo aliquam portionem non vendiderit, ista lege fur non tenetur. Adeo ut in Gemara pronunciet Rab,illam centesimam esse דכר ונקיר ... בכתיב rem quamvis, qua cum pecude in mactatione dissolvitur: cujusmodi est, quælibet etiam carnis portiuncula, quā non vendita, à pœnæ gravitate secundum illius sententiam fur absolvetur. Imo ulterius progreditur Levi in eadem Gemara, ut modo fur נוקיר, vellera pecudis non vendiderit, quadruplum vel quintuplum non exigat. Nonne hoc est legi illudere? Quid? Annon recta ratio suadet, ut proportione saltem inter venditum & quod venditum non est servata, lex vigorem suum retineat? Sed nugacem illam exceptionem omittamus.2 quod sequitur examinandum venit: quare qui pecus post ejus furtum mactat, cum alibi ad quadruplum &c. obligetur; in morticini conditionem induente, ea pœna non teneatur. Legimus Deut. 14. 21. Ne comeditote ullum morticinum. Hinc & è locis similibus eliciunt, hujusmodi mactationem legitimam non esse: adeoq; nullam ex isto cibo utilitatem in edendo percipere Israëlitas, si pecus cum mactatur eo modo dispositum sit, vel tractetur ut morticini quædam conditio in eo deprehendatur. veluti si contra legitimum modum mactetur, vel aliunde vulneratum interea per se moriatur &c. (de quibus in præcepto negativo 134 lib. præceptorum maj.) Quia ergo, quam fur utilitatem percipiat, quodque inde damnum patiatur proprietarius, expendunt, multique censent, מחויב מחויב ... mactationem incongruentem non censeri mactationem; istiusmodi mactationem ad legem Ex. 22. ubi dicitur, Pecudem mactaverit, referendam negant: adeoque à quadruplo reum absolvunt. Ita legem Dei, quam diversis verbis expressit, quaq; in hujusmodi furtum gravi multa in aliorum exemplum animadverti voluit, quæcunque esset pecudis conditio; istam inquam legem coarctant.3 Eadem ferme ratione, qua eum excusant, qui dilaniat pecudem: ut qui istam mactationem non admittant, nec pro mactatione habeant. Sed primo videndum quid sit נוקר, discerpens. Nomen נקורים Hebræis sonat nares: unde in Misna & Gemara verbum נקר, quasi dicas, fecit quid ad nares pertinens. id Glossator enarrat, קורעו מנחיריו עד לבו, discerpit eam (bestiam) naribus ejus usq; ad pectus ipsius. Hoc in agnellis & avibus factu facile est, ut prehensa superiori mandibula manu hac, inferiori vero altera; vel inferiori & superiori parte rostri in avibus, guttur ad imam colli partem & ulterius dilanietur. Vel נקר est ita jugulare ut jugulum non transversum, sed rectum ab ore ad pectus disseces. Inter Judæos nonnemo suffocationem hic designari existimavit: quasi pro קורת in glossa S. Jarchi legeretur כורת, idque transitivè in hunc sensum acciperetur, nares ad pectus deductas ita obthurari, ne pecus respirare possit, adeoque halitus defectu extinguatur. Sed altera illa lectio indubia est: utpote quam Bartenora, commentator Alphefi, & Caph nachat constanter exprimant. (licet ipse S.J. de eadem re agens ad חולין c. 6. sect. 2. נוקר per חנק, id est, strangulans, exponat.) Deinde in suffocatione sanguis retinetur, at in ista actione profluit: quemadmodum cum aliunde; tum hisce verbis omninò liquet quæ leguntur codice כריתות c. 5. sect. 1. Sanguis discerptionis, sanguis evulsionis, sanguis venæsectionis, quicum anima expiratur; horum inquam nomine rei sunt, scilicet qui hujusmodi in alimentum adhibent, ac assumunt. Itaque in נקרים sanguis effunditur. Cum נוקר conjungitur is, qui eo modo pecudem occidit ut œsaphagum & asperam arteriam evellat & diffringat. Hunc cum præcedenti à quadruplo & quintuplo absolvunt; licet hi istas pecudes furati sint. Idque ex hac hypothesi, quod illa nullo modo sit mactatio. quocirca quam pœnam Deus furi pecudem occidenti irrogat, illos non tenere autumant. Quasi verò legislator certum tantum modum mactandi, non verò quamlibet interficiendi rationem indigitasset. 5 Quod tandem subjungitur, furem si rem furtivâ etiam mactaverit vel vendiderit in proprietarii fundo, non teneri; hac ratione stabilire volunt: in proprio domini loco furem non censeri talem, sive pro fure haberi, nisi vel attollat ac elevet rem; vel eduxerit: alioqui enim non ϙιρ, acquirere sibique sumere. Solum attactum, vel eductionem imperfectam illic non sufficere autumant: licet extra domini fundum attactus rei alienæ, vel potius attractio furem constituat, ut qui ea sibi rem furtivam ϙιρ, vendicare velle censeatur. Quod priores aliquot hujus Misnæ casus attinet jam examinatos, Romani tam inepti non fuere ut iis parallelas leges sanciverint: postremum etiam hunc cum Judæis non definiunt; sed potius contra statuunt. Tantum enim abest, ut fures iistos in ipso proprietarii fundo deprehensos minus puniant vel absolvant; ut contra graviorem poenam irrogent: utpote qui sint fures manifesti, sive ἐπαυλοφῶρω. uti jam aliquoties occasion data observatum fuit. Præterea contrectatio ubique apu Romanos furtum constituit, nempe fraudulosa, lucrifaciendi gratia, vel ipsius rei, vel etiam usus ejus, possessionisve. ff. De furtis, non procul ab initio. Nedum ut eum excusent & absolvant, qui alterius pecudem in proprietarii fundo non solum contrectat, sed etiam mactat aut vendit; ut præter & contra Dei legem facit Misnæ author.
units.tr: Truly remarkable is the character and cleverness of the Jews. Sometimes they stretch Scripture so far, and take and interpret it so broadly, that they are not ashamed to draw from its very words meanings most alien to its intent. I have shown this in several instances elsewhere; now let one example suffice. In the Talmud, Berachoth, page 8, side 1, [תניא נמי הכי תשע מיתות וטלטט מיני מיתה נכרתו כעולם טנאמר ולמות תונחות תונחות כנגימטריא הכי היו] the tradition also says this: nine hundred and three kinds of death were created in this world, because it is said, Psalm 68:21, "To God the Lord belong the issues from death" (that is, God delivers from death). For "issues" by Geometry (which they improperly take for Arithmetic) yields that number. Sometimes, when it suits them, they cling so stubbornly to words that they admit no logical consequence. The beginning of this Mishnah is evidence of this: there they acquit of the fourfold and fivefold payment one who has stolen a sheep or an ox and also sold it, provided he has not sold its hundredth part. For, they say, Exodus 22 speaks thus: "If anyone steals an ox or a small beast and slaughters or sells it, he shall restore five oxen," etc. Now, as is said in the Gemara on the words "or sells it", we require the whole of that very animal: as if you said, the law speaks of that beast which he has sold; so if he has not sold some portion, the thief is not bound by this law. So much so that in the Gemara Rab pronounces that the hundredth part, [דכר ונקיר ... בכתיב] whatever thing it is, which is dissolved together with the beast in slaughter, such as any little portion of flesh not sold, by his judgment frees the thief from the severity of the penalty. Levi goes further still in the same Gemara: if the thief has not sold [נוקיר] the fleeces of the beast, he does not exact fourfold or fivefold. Is this not to mock the law? What then? Does not sound reason suggest that the law should retain its force, at least in proportion, between what was sold and what was not sold? But let us set aside that trifling exception. What follows must be examined: why one who after the theft slaughters the animal, although elsewhere he is bound to fourfold etc., is not held to that penalty when he brings the animal into the condition of carrion. We read in Deuteronomy 14:21, "You shall not eat any carrion." From this and from similar passages they infer that such slaughter is not lawful, and that the Israelites therefore gain no benefit from eating that food if the animal, when slaughtered, has been so disposed or handled that some condition of carrion is found in it, as if it were slaughtered contrary to the lawful manner, or had otherwise been wounded and died of itself in the meantime, etc. (on which matters see the negative precept 134 in the greater Book of Precepts). Because they weigh what benefit the thief gains and what loss the owner suffers, and many think that [מחויב מחויב ...] an unfitting slaughter is not to be counted as slaughter, they deny that such slaughter falls under the law of Exodus 22, where it says "he has slaughtered the beast," and so they acquit the guilty man of the fourfold payment. Thus they narrow the law of God, which expressed in different words and which wished such a grave fine for theft of this kind to be exacted as an example to others, whatever the condition of the beast. Almost by the same reasoning they excuse the one who tears the beast apart, so that they do not admit this as slaughter nor regard it as slaughter. But first we must consider what [נוקר], "tearing apart", means. The noun [נקורים] in Hebrew means nostrils, whence in the Mishnah and Gemara the verb [נקר] is used, as if you said did something pertaining to the nostrils. The Glossator explains it: he tears it (the beast) by its nostrils down to its breast. This is easily done with lambs and birds: the upper jaw is seized with one hand and the lower with the other, or, in birds, the upper and lower parts of the beak, and the throat is torn further down to the base of the neck. Or [נקר] means to cut the throat not across but straight from the mouth down to the breast. Some Jews have thought that suffocation is meant here, as if for [קורת] in the gloss of S. Jarchi one should read [כורת], and this were taken transitively in the sense that the nostrils, drawn down to the breast, are so blocked that the beast cannot breathe, and so is killed by lack of breath. But that other reading is certain, since Bartenora, the commentator on Alfasi, and the Caph Nachat consistently express it so (although S. Jarchi himself, treating the same matter at Chullin 6, section 2, explains [נוקר] by [חנק], that is, strangling). Moreover, in suffocation the blood is retained, but in this action it flows out; this is clear both from elsewhere and from these words read in the book Keritot, chapter 5, section 1: "The blood of tearing, the blood of evulsion, the blood of venesection, with which the life is breathed out"; those who use such animals as food or take them into their use are guilty of the blood of these things. Thus in [נקרים] the blood is poured out. He who kills the animal in such a way as to tear out the gullet and the windpipe is joined with the one who tears it. These two they acquit of the fourfold and fivefold payment, even though they have stolen these animals; and they do so on this supposition, that such a thing is in no way slaughter. Hence they claim that the penalty which God imposes on the thief who kills the animal does not bind them. As if the lawgiver had specified only a certain manner of slaughtering, and not any manner of killing at all. Finally, as to what is added, that if a thief has even slaughtered or sold the stolen thing on the owner's land, he is not bound: they wish to establish this by the reasoning that a thief is not regarded or held to be such on the owner's own ground, unless he lifts up and raises the thing, or has drawn it out; for otherwise it is not [לקח], to acquire or take to oneself. They maintain that mere touching or an imperfect drawing out is not enough there, although outside the owner's field the touching of another's property, or rather the drawing of it, makes a thief, since one who is thought to wish to claim the stolen thing for himself [לקח]. As for the earlier cases of this Mishnah already examined, the Romans were not so foolish as to enact parallel laws for them; but this last case they do not define with the Jews, and indeed they lay down the opposite. For it is far from the case that the Romans punish or acquit less those thieves caught on the very ground of the owner; rather they impose a graver penalty, since they are manifest thieves, or [ἐπαυλοφῶρω] (thieves caught on the farm), as has been observed several times when occasion was given. Moreover, contrectation everywhere among the Romans constitutes theft, namely fraudulent handling, for the sake of gain, of the thing itself, or even of its use or possession. Digest, On Thefts, not far from the beginning. Far from excusing and acquitting one who not only handles but also slaughters or sells another's beast on the owner's ground, as the author of the Mishnah does, contrary to and against the law of God.

units.la: Si traxit animal ut exiret, & moriatur in dominorum fundo; liber est: si id elevavit, aut eduxit è dominorum fundo, & moriatur; tenetur. Quum id dedit in primogeniti sui redemptionem, aut creditori suo, custodi gratuito, mutuanti,
units.tr: If he dragged the animal so that it went out and died in the owners' field, he is free. If he lifted it up or led it out of the owners' field and it died, he is liable. This applies when he gave it as the redemption of his firstborn, or to his creditor, to an unpaid keeper, to a borrower,

units.la: tuanti, mercenario, conducenti; si id trahat & in dominorum fundo moriatur, liber est: si id elevavit, aut è dominorum fundo eduxit, itaque mortuum est, tenetur.
units.tr: to the keeper, the hired man, or the renter: if he draws it along and it dies in the owners' field, he is free; but if he lifted it up, or led it out of the owners' field, so that it died, he is liable.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Hæc aliquo modo è præcedentibus liquent: sed quò penitus percipiantur, quædam è codice Kiddoufchin repetenda, ubi modus res vel pecora acquirendi definitur. Quandiu quis aliena bona alteri relinquit, nec ad se transfert, sibique acquirere & vendicare studet; furti insimulari nequit: ideoque constare debet, quî quave ratione ac modo hujus bona ad alterum transeant, ipsíque sive jure, sive contra jus acquirantur: ut ista voce cum Hebræis, qui קנה in hac materia adhibent, latius utamur. Itaque in isto cod. c. 1. sect. 4. magnum pecus traditione acquiritur; parva pecus elevatione &c. & postea ex Sapientum sententia, parva pecus attractione acquiritur. Tribus modis ergo pecus ad alterum transit, traditione; elevatione; attractione: de quibus variè disputantes, tandem concludunt, utrumque animalis genus attractione & elevatione comparari. Traditionem omitto, quia in furto nullum locum habet. Iam ulterius expendendum, ubi attractio, ubi elevatio suas vires exerit: hæc enim in parte est magna differentia. Bartenora ad citatum locum Kiddoufchin in hæc verba scribit, elevatio ubique acquirit, id est, ubicunque fiat. attractio acquirit in semita, & in amborum scilicet amittentis & accipientis atrio. Quid sit מיחה docet S. Jarchi f. 25. Kidd: circa finem, extremitas apud locum publicum, quæ nec locus publicus, nec privatus censetur. Sed quid est attractio, & elevatio? Elevatio animalis alicujus,
units.tr: These points are partly clear from what has gone before, but to understand them fully some passages must be repeated from the tractate Kiddushin, where the mode of acquiring goods or cattle is defined. As long as someone leaves another's goods with the owner and does not transfer them to himself, seeking to acquire and claim them for himself, he cannot be accused of theft. It must therefore be settled how, and by what means, such goods pass to another, and whether they are acquired lawfully or unlawfully. Here, with the Hebrews, who use the word קנה [qanah] in this matter, we will use the term more broadly. Accordingly, in that tractate, chapter 1, section 4: a large animal is acquired by delivery; a small animal by lifting, and so on; and afterwards, according to the opinion of the sages: a small animal is acquired by drawing. So an animal passes to another in three ways: by delivery, by lifting, and by drawing. Disputing these variously, they finally conclude that either kind of animal may be acquired by drawing or by lifting. I set aside delivery, since it has no place in theft. Now we must examine further where drawing and where lifting exerts its force, for this is a great difference in the matter. Bartenora, on the passage of Kiddushin cited, writes in these words: lifting acquires everywhere, that is, wherever it is done; drawing acquires in the path, and in the courtyard of both, namely of the one who loses and of the one who receives. What מיחה [mikhah, i.e. the public way] is, Rabbi Jarchi teaches on Kiddushin, folio 25, near the end: an extremity near a public place, which is considered neither a public nor a private place. But what are drawing and lifting? The lifting of any animal, by which it is raised from the ground, is not in doubt, except that the height must at least be observed, which Rabbi Jarchi on Kiddushin, folio 26, near the beginning, fixes at three palms. But drawing may be called into question. Therefore I shall add the words of Maimonides, On Sales, chapter 2, section 6.

units.la: X cujus, quâ è terra attollitur, dubia non est, nisi quod observanda sit saltem altitudo, quam S. J. Kiddoufchin f. 26. circa initium tribus palmis definit; sed attractio in dubium vocari potest. ideo Maimonidæ verba c. 2. de venditione, sect. 6. subjiciam. כיצד קנין את הבהמה במשיכה הין לא מטה והלכה או מרכב עליה והלכה כו טקנה ולא ילקח קרא לה וכלה או טהכיסה במקל ודחפה בפניו כיון שנקרה יד ורגל קנאה, Quomodo acquirunt pecudem attractione? Non opus est hæc dicere, si eam ita trahat ut progrediatur, aut si in ea progrediente equitet; ipsum ea ratione istam sibi sumere; verù etiamsi eam ita tantum vocaverit ut sequatur, aut baculo percusserit ut præcurrat; quandoquidem ipsa anteriores & posteriores pedes loco movit, hanc ille sibi sumsit & acquisivit. Idem Maimonides ad c. 7. Bav. Kam. hæc, in illa quæ jam explicatur Mifna, expendenda annotat. Nam author Mifnæ ita inquit, Si traxit animal ut exiret, & mortuum sit in fundo domini; liber est: ubi furem etiam absolvit à restitutione dupli; nedum quadrupli: idque eo fundamento, quod (uti jam dictum & explicatum est) attractione in domini fundo pecus non acquiratur; sed illa tantum in semita (de qua dictum est) & communi amborum atrio locum habeat. Itaque Maimonides annotat, פגנב לא יקרא גנב עד שיביא את הגנוב מרשות הניקח, fur non vocatur fur donec eduxerit rem furtivam à domini ditione, & acquisiverit eam quodam ex iis modis, quibus mobilia acquiruntur. Adeo ut trahere & abducere non sufficiat; sed ut furti agas, necesse est ut eum jam extra tuum fundum pecudem eduxisse noveris: nec exire, ut loquitur Mifna, rem facit, sed exivisse; videlicet si trahendo jam eduxerit, reus est. At si vel elevaverit tantum, inquit Mifna, jam tenetur: quia, sicuti in superioribus intelleximus, Elevatio in omni loco acquirit. Itaque in fundo domini, cujus est pecus, si alius ad tres palmos è terra extulerit parvam pecudem, capram vel ovem, jam istam furatus censetur: adeoque hac in parte attractio & elevatio diversæ sunt conditionis.
units.tr: How does one acquire an animal by drawing? It is not necessary to say this, if he draws it so that it goes forward, or if, while it is going forward, he rides upon it; for by that means he takes it to himself. But even if he merely calls it so that it follows, or strikes it with a stick so that it runs ahead, since it has moved its front and hind feet, he has taken it to himself and acquired it. [כיצד קונה את הבהמה במשיכה? אין צריך לומר שימשוך אותה והולכת, או שירכב עליה בהליכתה; אלא אפילו קראה והלכה אחריו, או הכהו במקל ודחפה לפניו, כיון שהזיזה יד ורגל קנאה.] The same Maimonides, on chapter 7 of Bava Kamma, notes that the Mishnah which is now being explained must be weighed in this way. For the author of the Mishnah says: If he drew the animal so that it went out, and it died in the owner's field, he is free: where he also absolves the thief from restitution of double, let alone quadruple; and this on the ground that (as has already been said and explained) an animal is not acquired by drawing in the owner's field, but that drawing has its place only in the path (of which it was spoken) and in the common courtyard of both. Therefore Maimonides notes: [פגנב לא יקרא גנב עד שיביא את הגנוב מרשות הניקח] a thief is not called a thief until he has brought the stolen thing out of the ditione of the one who is robbed, and has acquired it by one of those modes by which movable things are acquired. So drawing and leading away is not enough; but for a charge of theft to lie, it is necessary that you know he has already led the animal out beyond your field. And it is not the word exire (to go out) that makes the thing, as the Mishnah speaks, but exivisse (to have gone out); that is, if by drawing he has already led it out, he is liable. But if he has merely lifted it, the Mishnah says, he is already liable: because, as we have understood above, lifting acquires in every place. Accordingly, if someone lifts a small animal, a goat or a sheep, three palms from the ground in the field of the owner to whom it belongs, he is already deemed to have stolen it; and so in this respect drawing and lifting are in different conditions.

units.la: Ex aliis tamen circumstantiis colligendū, an furandi animo, id fecerit. ³ Primogeniti redemptio, quæ inter alias species subjicitur, è c. 13. Exod. illustranda. Ibi commate 13. Deus in hæc verba loquitur, Omnem primogenitum humanum ex filiis tuis redimito: pretium definitur Numerorum 18.16. Redimendos eorum à nato unum mensem redimi jubeto secundum æstimationem tuam, argenti quinque siclis, prout est siclus sanctuarii: viginti obolorum est. Hunc itaque casum proponit author, si pater pro siclis quinque, quos primogeniti nomine debet, pecudem quandam sacerdoti conferat, quam inscio sacerdote cujus sit fundus, an furis an alterius, in proprietarii fundo largiatur. Sed obiter expendamus, quare cum primogenitos Deo debeant, passim filius unius mensis commemoratur: ab ipsa enim nativitate primogenitus redimendus videtur. Unde in memoriam revocanda lex Num. 3. 40. qua primogeniti inde à filiis mensis (ut cum Scriptura loquar) & deinceps recenseri jubentur. Hoc mandatum cum altero conferatur Lev. 12. 6. ubi mater si peperisset marem, præter septem dies separationis, triginta tres dies subsistere jubebatur, antequam ad sanctuarium accederet: ubi puerum Deo sistendum fuisse constat. Adeo ut Deus primogenitos filios post mensem suos agnosceret. Itaque cum Servator noster absoluta demum Mariæ purgatione Hierosolymam adduceretur; id legi convenienter factum fuit: quandoquidem mense majores tantum exigebat Deus. Vbi tamen distinguendum inter tempus quo primogeniti debitum incipiebat; & alterum quo offerebant redemptionis pretium: hoc posterius quidem ob dictam in puerpera causam differebatur; sed pater simul ac filius mensem unum egisset, obligationem ad eum redimendum contrahebat. Hoc videre est apud Maimonidem c. 11. Biccourim, sect. 17. [Hebrew] A quo tempore redemptionis debitum sustinei? Quum triginta dies absolvit. Ideoque addit, [Hebrew] [Greek] X 2 [Hebrew] Si filius intra triginta dies moriatur, imo ipso die tricesimo, ille pater quinque siclos non debet; quod si anticipavit, & sacerdoti dedit, hic illi redemtionis pretium restituet. Cæterum ex sententia magistrorum istud redemtionis pretium non necessario siclis constat; quod tamen lex Num. 18. 16. omninò exigit: sed æquivalens (licet non quodvis) etiam admittunt. Vnde in Talmude Cod. Bechoroth c. 8. sect. 7. [Hebrew] quinque siclì primogeniti compensantur eo quod argento æquivalet. Sed Maimonides clarius loco superius citato sect. 6. redemptionem illam his rebus fieri observat, [Hebrew] sive argento, sive re æquipollente è mobilibus, quorum substantia facile pecunia conficitur. Atque huc Mișna nostra, quæ jam explicatur, respicit: quum fur pecudem in primogeniti redemptionem sacerdoti tradens introducitur.
units.tr: Yet from other circumstances it must be gathered whether he did it with intent to steal. The redemption of the firstborn, which is treated among the other kinds, is to be explained from Exodus 13. There, in verse 13, God speaks in these words: Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem. The price is fixed at Numbers 18:16: Those to be redeemed from a month old you shall redeem, according to your valuation, for five shekels of silver, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs. The author therefore sets out this case: if a father gives over to a priest, in payment of the five shekels which he owes on account of the firstborn, a certain animal, which the priest, not knowing whose field it is, whether a thief's or another's, has received in the field of its owner. But let us examine in passing why, although they owe their firstborn to God, a son of one month is commonly mentioned: for the firstborn seems to be redeemable from the very moment of birth. Hence the law of Numbers 3:40 must be recalled, by which the firstborn are ordered to be counted from the sons of a month old (to speak with Scripture) and onward. This command should be compared with another, Leviticus 12:6, where, if a mother had borne a male child, she was commanded, after seven days of separation, to remain thirty-three days more before she approached the sanctuary: from which it is clear that the boy was to be presented to God. So God acknowledged the firstborn sons as his after a month. Therefore, when our Saviour was brought up to Jerusalem only after Mary's purification was complete, this was done in accordance with the law, since God required only those of a month. Yet we must distinguish between the time at which the obligation of the firstborn began and the other time at which they offered the price of redemption: the latter was indeed deferred, for the reason mentioned concerning the woman in childbed; but as soon as the father and son had completed one month, he incurred the obligation to redeem him. This may be seen in Maimonides, On Firstlings, chapter 11, section 17: [...] From what time does the debt of redemption arise? When he has completed thirty days. Therefore he adds: [...] If the son dies within thirty days, or indeed on the thirtieth day itself, that father does not owe the five shekels; but if he has paid in advance and given it to the priest, the priest shall restore the price of redemption to him. Moreover, according to the opinion of the masters, that price of redemption does not necessarily consist of shekels, which the law of Numbers 18:16 nevertheless wholly requires; but they also admit an equivalent (though not just any). Hence in the Talmud, tractate Bekhorot, chapter 8, section 7: [...] five shekels of the firstborn are made up by that which is equivalent to silver. But Maimonides, in the passage cited above, section 6, more clearly observes that this redemption is made either with silver, or with a thing of equal value among movables, whose substance is easily turned into money. And our Mishnah, which is now being explained, looks to this, when the thief is introduced handing over the animal to the priest in redemption of the firstborn.

units.la: * Vbi, quemadmodum etiam in sequentibus personis annotandum, quum dicitur, si id trahat, ut postea, si id elevavit, ea ipsum sacerdotem aliosque commemoratos concernere; quum vero continuo subjicitur liber est, item tenetur, hæc ad furem pertinere. Idque in hunc sensum, Si sacerdos datam à fure pecudem trahat & ducat, vel id faciat creditor, custos aliive sequentes, atque interea dum etiamnum in proprietarii fundo sunt, pecus moriatur, furem non teneri; sin vero iidem illi traditam pecudem elevaverint aut eduxerint, mortua pecude furem culpæ teneri. Quæ ampliori commentario non illustrabo, quandoquidem è superioribus fundamentis penitus pernosci queunt. Romani has ineptas distinctiones ignorantes, inter attractionem & elevationem, item educere & eduxisse, tantam differentiam non constituunt, ut attrahentem in privato proprietarii loco & etiamnum educentem absolvant: quippe qui contrectando sape furtum fieri agnoscant ff. De furtis l. 6. Imo generalis est sententia l. 5. ff. eod. Sive igitur in publico, sive in privato deprehendatur antequam ad locum destinatum rem perferret: in ea causa est, ut fur manifestus sit, si cum re furtiva deprehendatur.
units.tr: * Here, as is also to be noted in what follows, when it is said if he draws it, and afterwards if he lifted it, these refer to the priest and the other persons mentioned; but when it is immediately added he is free, and likewise he is liable, these pertain to the thief. And this is the sense: if the priest, or a creditor, a keeper, or others who follow, draw and lead an animal given by the thief, and meanwhile, while they are still in the owner's field, the animal dies, the thief is not liable; but if the same persons have lifted or led out the animal delivered to them, then, the animal having died, the thief is liable for the fault. I shall not illustrate this with a longer commentary, since it can be fully learned from the foundations set out above. The Romans, ignorant of these foolish distinctions between drawing and lifting, and likewise between leading out and having led out, did not make so great a difference as to acquit one who draws in the private place of the owner and is still leading out; for they recognise that theft is often committed by handling, Digest, On Thefts, law 6. Indeed the general opinion is in Digest, same title, law 5: Whether therefore he is caught in a public or a private place before he has carried the thing to the destined place, the case is such that the thief is manifest if he is caught with the stolen thing.
Chapter 7, section 6 [זי ו]

units.la: Minuta animalia non educant in terra Israelitica; sed in Syria, & in deserti terra Israelitica: nec gallinaceos Hierosolymis educant; propter consecrata; nec ipsi sacerdotes per terram Israeliticam, propter puritates. Nec Israelita porcos ullo loco educabit. Nemo canem educabit, nisi catena ligetur. Nec retia columbis expandunt , nisi id fiat procul à loco habitato ad triginta stadia.
units.tr: They shall not pasture small cattle in the land of Israel, but in Syria and in the desert of the land of Israel. Nor shall they keep fowl in Jerusalem, on account of the holy things; nor shall the priests themselves keep them through the land of Israel, on account of their purity. Nor shall an Israelite pasture pigs in any place. No one shall keep a dog unless it is tied with a chain. Nor shall they spread nets for doves, unless this is done at a distance of thirty stadia from an inhabited place.

units.la: פורסין ניסבין לוונים אלא אם כן היה רחוק מן היסוב שלשים ריס
units.tr: They spread nets for doves only if it is thirty ris (stadia) from the inhabited area [פורסין ניסבין לוונים אלא אם כן היה רחוק מן היסוב שלשים ריס].
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Judæorum antiquissimi in id summopere incubuerunt, ne Israelitæ alii ab aliis injuria afficerentur: quo cum collimarent, inter alias constitutiones hanc etiam promulgavere, ne quis oves, capras, cuniculos, vel etiam vulpes (ut observat) aliasve minores bestias iis locis aleret, ubi vicini agro damna inferre possent. Imo Josuam in terræ distributione cum suo synedrio inter decem sanctiones & hanc sanxisse ajunt, qua priora Misnæ nostræ verba illustrantur. His interdicitur, ne quis minuta animalia in terra culta, ubi segetes vel vineta aut oliveta similiave reperiuntur, alat ac educet; in desertis, & ex Gemaræ enarratione in sylvis id permittitur. Josuam autem in posteriori membro distinctionem adhibuisse ferunt. Unde Maimonides Cod. de damnis pecuniariis c. 5. sect. 7. Josua בְּתוֹךְ הַמִּדְבָּר דָּקַר כִּי־יָשַׁרְתָּ אֶת־הַחָכְמָה הַזֹּאת Stipulatus est, ut quidem minuta pecora in sylvis pascerent ubi crassiores essent arbores; verum ibi magna pecora non pascerent. וּבְכָל־אִישׁ לֹא־יִשְׂרָאֵל מִבְּנֵי־יְהוּדָה Caeterum in sylva, cujus arbores tenellae essent, non pascerent nec magnum, nec parvum pecus, nisi consentiret dominus.
units.tr: The most ancient Jews took great pains to ensure that Israelites did not wrong one another. With this aim they published, among their other regulations, this one: no one should keep sheep, goats, rabbits, or even foxes (as one observer notes) or other small beasts in places where they could do damage to a neighbour's field. They also say that Joshua, in the distribution of the land, together with his Sanhedrin, enacted this among ten ordinances, and that this illustrates the earlier words of our Mishnah. By this rule it is forbidden to keep and feed small animals in cultivated land, where crops, vineyards, olive groves or the like are found; in the desert, and, according to the explanation of the Gemara, in the woods, it is permitted. They say that Joshua made a distinction in the latter clause. Hence Maimonides, in the Code, on pecuniary damages, chapter 5, section 7: Joshua stipulated that small cattle might graze in the woods where the trees were thick, but that large cattle should not graze there [בְּתוֹךְ הַמִּדְבָּר דָּקַר כִּי־יָשַׁרְתָּ אֶת־הַחָכְמָה הַזֹּאת]. But in a wood whose trees were young, neither large nor small cattle should graze, unless the owner consented [וּבְכָל־אִישׁ לֹא־יִשְׂרָאֵל מִבְּנֵי־יְהוּדָה].

units.la: Hic videmus quanta sollicitudine veteres caverint, ne quadrupes paupertiem faceret. Huc enim Mishnae author, aliique respexere, cum minora illa pecora ab illa regione arcerent, ubi damnum darent. Ideoque in Choschen Hammischpat (quem librum mihi suppeditavit vir spectatissimus Abrahamus Heidanus magni viri filius haud degener; sed qui praeter alias dotes eruditione & eloquentia inter praecipuos nostri seculi pastores eminet:) in illo inquam libro, quum illud interdictum ab authore tractatur, hujusmodi ratio in haec verba additur, Quia minutum pecus depascere solet aliena agros, ejusque damnum est frequens, constituere Sapientes, ne quis illud educaret ubi agri & vineta essent. Neque solum lege, sed etiam exemplis istam aequitatem populo persuadere conati sunt: imo ad ineptam usque superstitionem. Cujus e Talmude specimen aliquod subjiciendum existimavi, quod Judaeorum ingenium, nobis manifeste aperiet: qui non contemnendas alioqui leges suis minutiis & ineptiis depravant, & alio detorquent, quam earum primum institutum ferebat. Cod. Bava Kam. f. 81. p. 1. narratur, בְּחַיֵּי הָרֵי הַסְּפָרִים הַחֲדָשִׁים narratur inquam, de pio quodam, cui, cum tabifica pectoris tussi laboraret, medicique consulerentur, responderunt, nullam fore sanitatis restitutionem, donec lat fervidum unoquoque mane fugeret. Itaque adductam ei capram lecti fulcris alligarunt, unde singulis matutinis sugebat. Postea evenit ut socii ipsius ipsum invisendi gratia adirent: qui cum iflam capram lecti fulcris alligatam viderent, retroceffere, ita fati; Latro in hujus adibus educatur, nosne ad eum ingrediemur? Consedere ac inquisivere; sed nihil in eo deprehenderunt praeter iflam iniquitatem iflius capra. Ipse etiam hora mortis pronunciabat, Novi in me nullam esse iniquitatem praeter iniquitatem iflius capra: quod sociorum meorum mandata transgressus sim. Sane legenti merito mirum videri queat, quod viri isti illo interdicto capram, quae lecto alligata esset in aedibus, interdici censuerint: quandoquidem scopus & finis, quem supra e Chofchen Mifchpat expressi, hic locum habere nequit. quid enim damni ab hujusmodi asservata capra metuendum? Quinetiam similes casus isti magistri excipiunt: nam in Bav. Kathi f. 79. p. 2. Ita ajunt: [Hebrew text]. Quamvis statuant, parvam bestiam alendam non esse; tamen homini eam triginta dies ante festum asservare licet; & triginta dies ante filii nuptias. Nam mactanda animalia statim haberi nequeunt: ideoque mature conquirenda, & interea asservanda, donec festum, vel convivii tempus instet. Verumenimvero rationem audiamus, quare hic majora pecora admittant, minora excludant: ut illa regiones frugiferae capiant; haec vero arceant: quemadmodum constitutionis nostrae verba ostendunt. Causam reddit Gemara, [Hebrew text]. Educant magna pecora, sed passim in regione Israelitica, quia non decernunt statutum in coetum, nisi maxima populi pars in eo persistere possit. quasi dicas; vulgo ista animalia ad usum necessaria sunt, & praesto esse debent, puta [Hebrew text], ad portandum & arandum: ideoque nunquam iis carere possumus. At parvae pecudes, quoties iis opus habemus, peregrè addu-ci possunt. Ita quidem illi; nos ad sequentia pergamus. * Vbi Syriæ idcirco fit mentio, ut regiones, quas extra terram Chanaan acquisiverant & debellaverant Israëlitæ, synecdochicè denotarentur: nam quicquid hostibus eripuerant, in Syria magna ex parte situm erat. Deinde per Syriam potius reliquas terras etiam innuere voluerunt, quia ad Davidis victoriam, quam de Syris reportaverat, utpote sibi admodum gloriosam, lectorem oculos intendere voluerunt. Ideo interpres S. J. Syriam esse dicit Aram Tsobæ, quam subjugaverat David. Victoria 2 Sam. 8. vf. 3. & 4. narratur: nec ista tantum, sed alia etiam, quam de aliis Syris, puta Damascenis obtinuit; quemadmodum sequentia enarrant. Verum hac de causa potius Syriæ Tsobæ, quam alterius meminit S. Jarchi, quod posterior pugna prioris cladis, quam Syri passi erant, occasione subsecuta sit, quum Damasceni Tsobanis opem ferre conarentur. Syria Tsobæa quo loco fuerit, docet Josephus Antiq. L. 7. c. 5. quum de ista expeditione ad hunc modum scribit, Ἐπὶ Ἀδραζαρον τ᾽ Ἀ ἐμὶ ὁ ᾿ ὁν, Βασιλέα τ᾽ Σωφηνῆς ἱσράλον, Contra Adrazarum (Hader Ezerem Scriptura 1 Chr. 18. vocat) Araï filium, Sophenes regem, expeditionem fuscepit. Quam Scriptura Tsobam nuncupat, Josephus Sophenem dixit: eumque sequuntur alii. Sed cum bona aliorum venia liberè profiteor, hanc sententiam non facile mihi probandam videri. Etenim Ptolemæus l. 5. c. 13. Sophenem ultra Euphratem ad orientem collocat: atque si sacram historiam 2 Samuelis 8. & 1 Chron. 18. expendas, Tsobam Damasco vicinam (ut cui ideirco Damasceni succurrere moliren-tur) atq; inter Terram sanctam & Euphratem sitam suisse animadvertes. Hamathæ rex & rex Tsobæ ut vicini bella inter se gessisse leguntur; Hamath autem Canaani, vicina erat. Et omnino attendendum com. 3. c. 8. l. 2. Sam. cum expeditionis occasio exprimitur, hæc adhiberi verba, Quum iret & re-
units.tr: Here we see with what great care the ancients guarded against four-footed animals causing poverty. For the author of the Mishnah and others had this in view when they kept those small animals away from the region where they would do damage. Therefore in the Choschen Hammischpat (a book supplied to me by the most distinguished Abraham Heidanus, a worthy son of a great father, who, besides his other gifts, is eminent for learning and eloquence among the chief ministers of our age), when that prohibition is treated by the author, this reason is added in these words: Because small cattle are accustomed to feed on other people's fields, and the damage they cause is frequent, the wise men decreed that no one should keep them where there are fields and vineyards. Nor did they try to persuade the people of this fairness by law alone, but also by examples, even to the point of absurd superstition. I have thought fit to add one specimen of this from the Talmud, which will clearly reveal to us the Jewish mind, which corrupts laws not to be despised in themselves by its petty and foolish details, and twists them to another purpose than their original institution intended. In the Bava Kama tractate, folio 81, page 1, it is related, [Hebrew text] it is related, I say, of a certain pious man, who, suffering from a consumptive cough of the chest, consulted physicians; they replied that there would be no restoration of health unless he drove away the goat that sucked on him every morning. So they tied the goat that had been brought to him to the legs of his bed, from which it sucked every morning. Afterwards it happened that his companions came to visit him, and when they saw the goat tied to the legs of the bed, they drew back, saying: "A thief is kept in this man's house; shall we go in to him?" They sat down and inquired, but found nothing in him except that iniquity of the goat. He himself, at the hour of death, declared: "I know of no iniquity in me except the iniquity of that goat, in that I transgressed the commands of my companions." Surely a reader may justly wonder why these men judged that a goat tied to a bed in a house should be forbidden under that prohibition, since the aim and purpose I have set out above from the Choschen Mishpat cannot apply here. For what harm is to be feared from a goat kept in this way? Indeed these masters make similar exceptions: for in the Bava Kathi, folio 79, page 2, they say as follows: [Hebrew text]. Although they lay down that a small beast is not to be fed, nevertheless it is lawful for a man to keep it for thirty days before a festival, and for thirty days before his son's wedding. For animals meant for slaughter cannot be had at once; therefore they must be sought out in good time and kept meanwhile, until the feast or the time of the banquet is at hand. But let us hear the reason why they admit larger cattle and exclude smaller ones, so that the fruitful regions may hold the former but keep out the latter, as the words of our regulation show. The Gemara gives the reason: [Hebrew text]. They may keep large cattle, but everywhere in the land of Israel, because they do not decree a rule for the community unless the greater part of the people can persist in it. As if to say: these animals are commonly necessary for use and ought to be at hand, that is, [Hebrew text] for carrying and ploughing; therefore we can never do without them. But small cattle, whenever we need them, can be brought in from abroad. So far they; let us now go on to what follows. * Syria is mentioned here so that the regions which the Israelites had acquired and subdued outside the land of Canaan might be indicated by synecdoche, for whatever they had snatched from their enemies lay for the most part in Syria. Next, they wished by "Syria" rather to point also to the remaining lands, because they wanted the reader to fix his eyes on David's victory over the Syrians, which was very glorious to him. Hence the commentator S. J. says that the Syria meant is Aram-Zobah, which David had subdued. The victory is narrated in 2 Sam. 8.3–4; and not only that, but also another he won over other Syrians, namely the Damascenes, as the following verses relate. But for this reason Jarchi mentions Zobah rather than another place: the later battle followed on the occasion of the earlier defeat that the Syrians had suffered, when the Damascenes tried to bring help to the Zobaites. Josephus, Antiquities book 7, chapter 5, shows where Syria Zobah was, when he writes thus about that expedition: Against Adrazar (whom Scripture calls Hadad-ezer, 1 Chr. 18) son of Arai, king of Sophene, he undertook an expedition [Ἐπὶ Ἀδραζαρον τὸν Ἀραΐου, Βασιλέα τῆς Σωφηνῆς, ἐστράτευσε]. What Scripture calls Zobah, Josephus called Sophene, and others follow him. But with all due respect to others, I freely declare that this opinion does not seem easy for me to approve. For Ptolemy, book 5, chapter 13, places Sophene beyond the Euphrates to the east; and if you examine the sacred history in 2 Samuel 8 and 1 Chronicles 18, you will notice that Zobah was near Damascus (since the Damascenes were therefore striving to help it) and lay between the Holy Land and the Euphrates. The king of Hamath and the king of Zobah are read of as waging war against each other as neighbours; and Hamath was near Canaan. And one must note, in general, that in 2 Samuel 8.3, when the occasion of the expedition is stated, these words are used, when he went to restore his hand to the river Euphrates, and in 1 Chr. 18.3, instead of "to restore", it is written "to establish". Compared together, these clearly indicate that his intention was to extend his dominion again to the Euphrates. Therefore, whether these words refer to David or to Hadad-ezer, it is clear that Zobah lay between the Holy Land and the Euphrates. For if David, when he set out there, fought with the king of Zobah in battle, it is established that he was in that tract; but if Hadad-ezer, setting out thither, that is, to the Euphrates, met David as an enemy on the road, we must place him on this side of the Euphrates too. For what right had David beyond the Euphrates over the kings of that region? The right granted by God extended as far as the Euphrates, Gen. 15.18. What if we say it was Palmyrene? Those skilled in these matters may judge; I for my part judge thus. Before we leave the history we have brought forward, we must see briefly whether verse 4 of chapter 8 of book 2 of Samuel agrees with 1 Chronicles 18.4: for there we read that David took seven hundred horsemen in battle, but here seven thousand horsemen; so that the numbers do not seem to agree, since seven hundred is far from seven thousand. Holy Scripture was written for those who study it (as the Psalmist says, Ps. 1.2) day and night; such people, being accustomed to its phrases, will easily get out of difficulties of this kind. First, from the comparison itself it is plain that there is an ellipsis: for in the former place only thousand is said, but in the latter, that is, in Chronicles, chariots is added, so that by thousand

units.la: * Vbi Syriæ idcirco fit mentio: haec nota marginalis non legitur; nota ad sinistram tantum punctum. ut reduceret manum suam ad flumen Euphratis, & 1 Chr. 18.3. pro reduceret, scribi stabiliret. quæ inter se collata, id animi fuisse ut dominium iterum ad Euphratem extenderet, omnino indicant. Itaque sive hæc ad Davidem, sive ad Adar-Ezerem referantur, Tsobam inter terram sanctam & Euphratem suisse liquet. Nam si David quum proficisceretur eò, cum rege Tsobæ acie certavit, hunc in isto tractu fuisse constat: si vero Adar-Ezer eò, scilicet ad Euphratem proficiscens, Davidem in via hostem offendit, etiam cis Euphratem eum collocemus oportet. quid enim juris Davidi ultra Euphratem in istius regionis reges? usque ad Euphratem sese extendit jus à Deo concessum Gen. 15.18. Quid si igitur Palmyrenam suisse dicamus? Harum rerum periti judicent; ego jam quidem ita judico. Antequam productam historiam relinquamus, paucis videndum, an comma 4. cap. 8. lib. 2. Sam. cum 1 Chronic. 18.4. conveniat: si quidem illic Davidem in prælio septingentos equites; hic vero septies mille equites cepisse legimus: adeo ut numeri convenire non videantur; cum septingenti à septies mille longè absint. Scriptura sacra pro iis conscripta fuit, qui eam (ut ait Psaltes Ps. 1.2.) interdiu & noctu expendunt: hi ipsius phrasibus assuefacti ex hujusmodi difficultatibus sese facile expedient. Primò ex ipsa collatione liquet esse ellipsin: nam priori loco tantum dicitur, mille, posteriori verò, sive in Chron. additur, currus: ut per mille
