units.tr: 1. It is forbidden to defile this offering within the Israelite territory, as also the other holy things; nor is anyone to bring it into danger of uncleanness. For this reason the priests did not rear fowls, lest unclean reptiles, or their particles scratched up with the claws, should fall into the holy firstfruits and defile them. But these offerings were eaten by priests throughout the whole land of Canaan; hence in all those places fowls were removed from the priests' houses. 5 But for the Israelites, it was forbidden everywhere to rear pigs. The reason for this prohibition is given in the Gemara, which, so that it may be better understood, must be drawn from Josephus, books 13 and 14, where it is related that after their father's death a contest over the kingdom arose between Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. So in Antiquities 14, ch. 1, the author writes this way, after narrating Aristobulus' victory in a certain battle: Hyrcanus flees into the citadel, where it happened that Aristobulus' wife was also seized [Φεύγει εἰς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν Ὑρκανός, ἔνθα συνέβαινε καὶ ἁρπάζειν τὴν Ἀριστοβούλης γυναῖκα]; he shows in the last chapter of book 13 that this citadel was in Jerusalem. Hence it is clear that Hyrcanus was inside the city and Aristobulus outside it, at least during the last phase of that difficult time. Therefore the Gemara doctors relate: When the Hasmoneans attacked one another, Hyrcanus was inside the city and Aristobulus outside it. Every day they let down denarii in a chest by chains to each other, and in turn they hoisted up the victims of the continual sacrifice. But when there was an old man there, skilled in Greek wisdom, he said to the besiegers: "As long as they are occupied in their worship, they will not be handed over into your hand. Tomorrow they will let down denarii in a chest by chain; then send them a pig." When it had been raised to the middle of the wall, it fixed its hooves in the wall; whereupon the land of Israel was shaken for four hundred parasangs on every side, and at that hour they pronounced: Cursed is the man who rears pigs, and cursed is the man who teaches his son Greek wisdom. And since an exception was ready at hand, namely that it is not permitted to eat them, yet their lard and fat are much used for anointing and rubbing; if pigs were not forbidden for this purpose, perhaps they were forbidden for this reason too. So D. Ascher, a man of great authority among the Jews, annotates the words of the Mishnah, An Israelite shall rear pigs in no place, that not even may skins be anointed with them. Indeed he adds that pigs may not be reared even to be sold to others, to whom they are not forbidden. Nor do the Jews excuse themselves if they rear pigs somewhere in order to carry on trade. The Mishnah of the Code Shebiit supports Ascher: where in chapter 7, section 3 (or according to the division of the Jerusalem Talmud, 6), we read: They do not carry on trade in carrion, nor in torn animals, nor in abominable things, nor in reptiles. Here they prohibit beasts whose eating was forbidden to Israelites, and the Mishnah of Levit. ch. 11 teaches us that swine and pigs are included in this class. There, to be sure, it is not forbidden to sell these beasts; but the Jerusalem Gemara, at the end of chapter 7 of Baba prima, tries to elicit this from the very words of that chapter, where it says: It is written (several times in Lev. 11) "They are unclean to you." What then does the teaching add, "And they shall be unclean to you"? It teaches that the prohibition of eating and the prohibition of profit agree (that is, that it is not lawful to eat them, nor to gain any other profit from them, such as a price in selling). But in whatever matter of those things the teachers forbid, it is lawful to carry on trade. If the eating of some thing is forbidden by the Law, they want its trade forbidden too; and therefore they do not admit even the sale of pigs, since they are contained in that kind. Here is the objection which Doctor Simeon raises for us in his notes on chapter 7 of Shebiit: Yet behold, the ass is raised for its work, and behold, the camel is raised for its work; and they do not forbid trade in them. I answer: that matter concerns only those things which are fit for eating; not those which are used for bearing burdens or similar work. But swine and pigs have no use except to supply food. Whence, then, the pigs mentioned in Matt. 8. 30? At least the authority of the teachers forbade feeding them. If someone should reply that only Benjamin and Judah returned, together with the Levites, while the remaining tribes stayed in captivity, and that therefore whatever lay outside Judea and the territory of Benjamin was occupied by other nations, to whom pigs were not forbidden, this reason will not satisfy those who weigh the whole matter more carefully. For I cannot grant that those other places were inhabited only by Gentiles. This can be refuted first from the words of our Saviour in Matt. 15. 24: I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, namely to proclaim the gospel by my mouth and to perform miracles now; yet he preached the gospel everywhere outside the tribes of Benjamin and Judah, and confirmed it by miracles. Therefore Israelites must have had their dwellings everywhere there. This, in my judgment, is beyond doubt, both for the reason stated and also because Christ enjoined his disciples not to go into the way of the Gentiles, Matt. 10. 5; yet they went through the individual villages, Luke 9. 6, that is, where Christ used to walk, as is clear if one compares Luke 10. 1, where it is narrated that other disciples were sent into every city and place where he himself was about to come. I seem to be right in concluding that Israelites lived there, who could be constituted at least as a double group: those returning from the Babylonian captivity, and, besides, some of their descendants who had been carried off by Shalmaneser. For Neh. 8. 1 says that all the Israelites (those returning) dwelt in their cities. It is true that Judah, along with Benjamin and the Levites, was led away into captivity, and that it is chiefly of them that the passage speaks; but what must not be neglected is that

units.la: 2 Chr. 10. 17. legitur, Israëlitas à Judæis descivisse, verum super filios Israëlis qui habitabant inter civitates Iuda regnasse Salomonis filium. & c.11.16. quum Levitas se ad Judæos contulisse narrasset autor, subjecit, Et sequuti illos ex omnibus tribubus Israëlis, qui dedebant animum suum ad requirendum Iovam: quod amplius sub piis regibus qui subinde excitabantur factum. Adeo ut inter Judæos alii Israëlitæ vixerint, qui ut cum ipsis abducti; sic reduces cum iis loca sua & possessiones avitas occuparunt. Neh. 8.1. Deinde à Salmanassare in reliquis Israëlitarum tribubus multos relictos fuisse satis manifestè è 2 Chron. 34. colligitur. nam Josuæ temporibus jam Israëlitæ in Assyriam abducti fuerant; attamen 6. & 9. ac 33. versibus regiones Ephraimitarum &c. ad verum Dei cultum, imo quemlibet in Israële inventum ille ad colendum Jovam perduxisse legitur: cum novi isti coloni è Babylonia aliisque locis additi in idololatria sua perseverasse legantur, 2 Reg. 17. Qui Israëlitæ vel remanserunt cum reliqui abducerentur; vel saltem redierant cum sacerdote, quum feris Deus regionem adeo puniret, ut aliquo saltem modo Deum revereri cogerentur? quemadmodum eodem capite narratur. Etiam prædictum per Jeremiam non tantum Judæos; sed etiam alios tribules redituros, Jer. c. 50. 4. Venient filii Israëlis, ipsi cum filiis Iuda unà. ubi de solutione captivitatis Babylonicæ sermo est. Zacharias etiam c. 8. v. 13. in hunc modum loquitur, Eritque ut quemadmodum fuistis maledictioni in gentibus, O domus Iehuda, & domus Israëlis, ita servem vos & sitis benedictioni. Et sane secus factum non fuisse, omninò suadet monarchiæ Persicæ conditio: quandoquidem enim Cyrus & sequentes monarchæ regiones illas occupaverant in quas Israëlitæ abducti fuerant (unde Ezr. 1. 2. Cyrus inquit, Omnia regna terræ tradidit mihi Iova,)& redeundi potestatem omnibus faciebant (Ezr. 1. cap.) quis Israëlitarum nullos hanc gratiam amplexos, sed solos Judæos ac Benj. credat? Fateor quidem multos, imo illorum plerosque istam Dei benignitatem contempsisse: nam ut Ezr. 1. 5. ex Judaeis, Benjamitis & Levitis ii tantum rediisse dicuntur, quorum Deus excitaverat spiritum; ita in reliquis tribubus factum fuit, ubi hanc Dei gratiam rariorem fuisse agnosco.Ex iis tamen multos rediisse docetur 1 Chr. 9. 3. ubi etiam Jerosolymam quidam Ephrajimitarum & Menassensium incoluisse narrantur.Quid ergo dicendum ad comma 6. cap. 1. Hoseae, Non pergam amplius misereri domus Israelis? Hujusmodi de maxima eorum parte sunt intelligenda. Quomodo etiam accipio Josephi verba Antiq. l. 11. c. 5. αἱ δέκα φυλαὶ, πέραν τοῦ Εὐφράτου τὴν ἄνω χώραν ἔχουσι, Decem tribus, ultra Euphratem degunt hactenus. Nec quisquam credo negabit, multa de gente dici quae singulis hominibus in ista gente non competunt.Si quis tam bardus ut neget, vel a puero refelletur. Itaque hinc factum ut iis locis, ubi docuit Servator noster, passim Israelitas offenderit: licet quamplurimi diversis locis alienigenae habitaverint. adeo ut Matt. c. 10. v. 5. duodecim discipulis dixerit Christus, In urbem Samaritanorum ne ingrediamini. Sed alienigenae inprimis transjordanenses regiones incolebant: ubi inter alios Gadareni, & Gergeseni, qui porcos pascebant, quorum mentio Matt. 8. Quapropter nihil miri, si contra Judaeorum ac Israelitarum statuta sues habuerint: nam Gezara & Gadara a lacu Genezareth remotiores; loca ubi Christus ultra lacum inter suos docebat & miracula edebat, Capernaumo & lacui viciniora erant, ut Chorazin & Dalmanutha.Licet Gadareni ad lacus australiorem partem porcorum pastores dimitterent: qui tamen μακρὰν, procul a Christo ejusque discipulis aberant.Ista loca remotiora ultra Jordanē & lacum a multis Judaeis vel Israelitis habitata fuisse non videntur; sed nonnulli tamen ut alibi, sic istis locis inter istos commorabantur gentiles, qui magistrorum placitis se astringi passi non sunt. Clarissimus Beza Josephi quendam paragraphum citat, quo illa loca alienigenarum fuisse constat. stat. Libro 2. de bello c. 33. secundum Lat. 19. quum Judæorum in Syros excursiones describit, hæc inter alia habet, ϳαδαρois ἐ ἴπποω ἡ τῇ γαυλανιτ-ιδι ϖεϱιϖεσόντες, In Gadaram, Hippon & Gaulanitidem irruentes, &c. Adeo ut Gadareni plerique Syri, non Israëlitæ fuerint; ideoque horum de porcis interdictum Gadarenos non constrinxerit; Judæique inter ipsos commorantes id ferre debuerint. Inter quos, illos dæmoniacos per Christum liberatos, fuisse ex historia ab Evangelistis descripta liquet. Nec enim Israëlitas ab alienigenarū urbibus abstinuisse, Josephus indicat; quum Α'λώσ. l. 2. c. 34. inter eos qui Judæos in sua urbe degentes duriter tractabant, Gadarenses collocat, Γ'πτωλοοί τ ἢ καὶ ϳαδαρᾶς ὁμοίως, οὐν' μὲν ϑεραπεύσαντο, οὐν' ἡ φοβερᾶς Δἰ ϕυλακῶν ἔχον, Hippeni quoque & Gadarenses similiter, audaciores quidem è medio sustulerunt, formidandos autem carcere detinebant. Atque sic per occasionem Euangelica historia ea ratione illustrata fuit; ut ea Misnam, quam tractamus, non everti, simul ostensum sit. Cæterum illud de porcis interdictum Maimonides annotationibus ad hanc Misnam ulterius extendit. [Hebrew] Idem ju-ris est in reliquis rebus interdictis quoad esum: sed loquitur de suibus, quia notissimum est, eas educari posse. Quod judicium si sequamur, alia animalia, quorum carne vesci non licet, nisi ad opera & onera subeunda alantur, habere non licet. Hujus vero speciei mentio injecta, quia inquit Maimonides omnibus notum est, istàm bestiam educari posse: nam aliæ etiam interdictæ quarum natura & feritas hoc non permittit; ideoque si in exemplum propositæ fuissent, frustra de iis suscepta cura videretur. ⁶ Sed quare canem etiam specialiter hic considerat author? Quia cum ejus usus extra cibum magnus sit, ipsoque carere commodè non possimus, promiscue tamen admittendus non sit; sed circumspectè conditiones quædam sint considerandæ. Itaque Misna hanc conditionem exigit, ut catenis ligetur. R. Joseph Karo se in exemplari correcto haec addita invenisse testatur, ipsius ferri, id est, catenis ferreis: ideoque R. Jacob cum hanc in Choschen Mischpat constitutione repetit, pro cane, habet canem malignum; quia vulgares canes ferreis catenis non coercentur. Verum ubi rationes expenduntur, quae in subjuncta Gemara occurrunt; & si canem catenis licet ferreis ligent, non sufficere apparebit. Duae rationes proponuntur: una quod canis mordeat; altera quod latret, & latrando mulieres gravidas ita consternet, ut abortiendi periculum imminet. Priori quidem rationi illa cautione satisfit; sed posterior remanet. Itaque hac de causa magnus R. Eliezer dixisse videretur, Qui educat canes est illi par, qui educat sues: ut sicut hoc omnino prohibetur; pariter & illud, sed subjuncta verba, aliam illius fuisse mentem edocent, cum haec adduntur: Quo inde pergitur? (id est, quid ex illa comparatione discitur?) Ad aggrediendum ipsum cum maledicto. sensus est, ut quemadmodum antea maledictio stringebatur in eum qui porcos aleret; sic etiam maledictioni subjiciatur is qui canes alit: nisi illa conditione, quam Misna postulat. Deinde, in exoticis, ut vocant, traditionibus, aliam hac in re cautionem adhibent: Homo canem alit in civitate littori sive confinio vicina: ubi eum ligat interdiu; & noctu solvit. Quamvis alibi solutos canes habere non liceat; tamen ad limites regionum licet: ut finitima & extrema loca per ipsos a praedonibus tutiora esse queant. Atque hoc jus in Babylonia etiam obtinuisse nonnulli existimant: cum multi Judaei illic degerent. Unde in Gem. Pronuntiavit Magister Nahman, Babel ut civitas quae limiti adjacet esse videtur, in eaque designari dixit (videlicet M. Joseph, qui Nahmanis sententiam refert) Nehardeam. Quia in Babylonia multi erant Judaei, & ad tempus illic fixam veluti sedem habuerunt; ipsam hac in parte R. Nahman terræ Canaan æquavit, ut eo modo in portubus & regionis limitibus (nam יסם late accipiunt Talmudistæ) canes alere & noctu solutos habere liceret: quemadmodum in terra sancta. Babel autem regionis & civitatis nomen esse constat: sed cum Nahman Babyloniæ meminit, aliam civitatem in Babylonica regione designare voluit, puta Nehardeam: quæ ut inquit Glossa, in confinio erat; ideoque illo gaudebat privilegio: Etenim ad Euphratem conditam ferunt (ut Josephus aliique observarunt) ubi Babylonicæ regionis terminus ac limes. Denique, ne columbæ Israëlitarum caperentur, legibus cautum fuit: adeoque retia nonnisi triginta stadiis à יסם, loco habitato tendere permittitur. Vbi per locum habitatum designant urbem. Neque tamen permissio hæc, qua ultra stadia triginta permittunt ut tendantur retia, adeo generalis est, ut exceptiones non admittat. Duobus enim locis id prohibetur, licet stadia illa intercurrant. Si vineta vel ad centum milliaria circum urbem, vel ab uno ejus latere extendantur, ibi reti columbas capere interdictum: quod columbæ de vineto ad vinetum transvolent; atque sic quam longissimè à civitate, quam Israëlitæ incolunt, recedant. Præterea si columbaria non ita procul à se invicem disposita per centum milliaria extendantur, ibi retia expandere vetitum: quia similiter columbæ etiam Israëlitarum per diversa columbaria tandem longissimè avolant. Ideoque in Gemara de utroque succinctè veterem traditionem legimus: תניא כיצד In exoticis dicitur, Etiamsi centum milliaria intercedant, non expandet; Magister Josephus inquit, in loco vitibus confito id servari; Rabba addit, etiam in loco columbariis occupato. Sed excipies (sive non existimabis) id propter columbaria ipsa dici. Prioribus verbis utrumque prohiberi; non vero diversas tantum recenseri sententias oftendunt cum Choschen Mispat, tum Jad Chazaka, ubi idem interdictum repetitur. Posteriora verba hoc sibi volunt,non quidem ipsa columbaria hoc impedire, quasi contra jus ipsum veniret qui inter columbaria sua (nam & eò interdictum extendunt) retia tenderet; sed ut pacis servanda modi servarentur, id interdixisse Judæos. Verum objectio solvenda, quæ ex inspecta Misna oboritur: nam triginta stadiorum distantiam exigit, ut rete tendatur; cum tamen quinquaginta tantum cubitis à columbariis suis discedere censeantur columbæ, Cod. Bab. Bathr. c. 2. sect. 5. Columbarium à civitate 50 cubitis arcent: hunc nempe in finem, ne istic terræ proventum lædant. Cur ergo triginta stadia exigit Misna? Verum in Gemara brevibus hæc difficultas tollitur: Abæus enim respondet, Vagando vagantur admodum, sed ingluvies earum intra quinquaginta cubitos expletur: vagatio autem triginta stadiis procedit, non ultrius. Ac si dixisset, columbas quidem quinquaginta tantum cubitis à columbariis ad pastum discedere, atque illo spatio quod sibi sufficit invenire: ulterius tamen volitare, ad longe remotiora loca; ideoque quod capturam attinet, extra stadia triginta eam demum licitam esse, ne fratrum suorum columbas capiant, quæ eò usque nonnunquam avolare solent. Romanis etiam legibus,sicuti præcedentibus constitutionibus (licet diverso modo) nociva animalia prohibita fuere: cujus rei exemplum habemus,lib. 21. dig. tit. 1. leg. 11. 12. & 13. Nequis canem, verrem, (vel minorem aprum) lupum, ursum, pantheram, leonem, aliudve quod noceret animal, sive soluta sint, sive alligata, ut contineri vinculis quominus damnum inferant, non possint, quà vulgo iter fiet, ita habuisse velit, ut cuiquam nocere, damnumve dare possit. Hac lege vel expresse præcedentia Misnæ membra; vel deducendo aliud ex alio κατ' ἀναλογίαν probari possent, quatenus in iis æquitas quædam invenitur: longius enim in iis Judæos progredi, quam recta ratio suadet, saniores lectores judicabunt. Postremum membrum de columbis illustratur lege Naturalem, §.cervos, ff. De acquirendo rerum dominio. Vbi hujusmodi animalia semper occupantium non fieri docetur: unde sequitur eo casu occupantem furtum committere, adeoque id ne faciat prohiberi. In his animalibus quae consuetudine abire & redire solent, talis regula comprobata est, ut eousque nostra esse intelligantur, donec revertendi animum habeant: quod si desierint revertendi animum habere, desinant nostra esse, & fiant occupantium. Ergo quandiu columbae ad columbaria redire solent, non fiunt occupantium; ideoque interea eas aucupare non licet.
units.tr: 2 Chr. 10. 17 reads that the Israelites revolted from the Judaeans, but over the sons of Israel who dwelt among the cities of Judah, the son of Solomon reigned. And at c. 11. 16, after the author has said that the Levites went over to the Judaeans, he adds: And those from all the tribes of Israel who set their heart on seeking Jehovah followed them. This happened more often under the pious kings who were raised up from time to time. So there were Israelites living among the Judaeans who were carried off with them and who, on their return, occupied their own places and ancestral possessions (Neh. 8. 1). Further, that Shalmaneser left many in the remaining tribes of Israel is clear enough from 2 Chron. 34. For although the Israelites had already been carried off to Assyria in Joshua's time, yet at verses 6, 9 and 33 we read that the regions of the Ephraimites and others were brought to the true worship of God, and that he led to the worship of Jehovah everyone found in Israel. Those newcomers who had been brought in from Babylon and other places are read to have persisted in their idolatry (2 Kings 17). Did those Israelites either remain when the rest were carried away, or at least return with the priest, since God punished the land with wild beasts so severely that they were forced in some way to revere God? This is what the same chapter relates. Jeremiah also foretold that not only the Judaeans but also the other tribes would return (Jer. 50. 4): The sons of Israel shall come, they and the sons of Judah together, where he speaks of the release from the Babylonian captivity. Zechariah too says at 8. 13: And it shall come to pass that as you were a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you and you shall be a blessing. Indeed the condition of the Persian monarchy strongly suggests that it did not happen otherwise. For since Cyrus and his successors held the regions into which the Israelites had been carried, and gave everyone the power to return (Ezra 1. 2 and the whole of Ezra 1), who can believe that none of the Israelites embraced this grace, but only the Judaeans and Benjaminites? I grant that many, indeed most of them, despised this kindness of God. For as Ezra 1. 5 says that only those from Judah, Benjamin and Levi returned, whose spirit God had stirred up, so it was in the other tribes, where, I admit, this grace of God was rarer. Yet we are told that many of them did return (1 Chron. 9. 3), where some of the Ephraimites and Manassites are also said to have dwelt in Jerusalem. What then is to be said of Hos. 1. 6: I will no more have mercy on the house of Israel? Such words must be understood of the greater part of them. I also take in this way the words of Josephus, Antiq. bk. 11, ch. 5: The ten tribes live beyond the Euphrates in the upper country [αἱ δέκα φυλαὶ, πέραν τοῦ Εὐφράτου τὴν ἄνω χώραν ἔχουσι], that is, the ten tribes, so far, dwell beyond the Euphrates. Nor do I think anyone will deny that many things are said of a nation which do not apply to every individual in that nation. If anyone is so dull as to deny it, he would be refuted even by a boy. Hence it came about that in those places where our Saviour taught, he found Israelites everywhere, although very many foreigners lived in various places. So Christ said to the twelve disciples in Matt. 10. 5: Do not enter a city of the Samaritans. But foreigners lived chiefly in the regions beyond the Jordan, among whom were the Gadarenes and Gergesenes, who kept swine, of whom Matt. 8 speaks. Therefore it is no wonder if, against the statutes of the Judaeans and Israelites, they kept swine. For Gezara and Gadara were more remote from the Lake of Gennesaret, while the places where Christ taught among his own people beyond the lake and worked miracles were nearer to Capernaum and the lake, as Chorazin and Dalmanutha were. Although the Gadarenes kept their swineherds on the southern side of the lake, they were nonetheless far away [μακρὰν, procul a] from Christ and his disciples. These more remote places beyond the Jordan and the lake do not seem to have been inhabited by many Judaeans or Israelites; but, as elsewhere, so in these places some Gentiles lived among them, who did not allow themselves to be bound by the decrees of the teachers. The most distinguished Beza cites a passage of Josephus which shows that those places belonged to foreigners. In Bk. 2 of the War, ch. 33 (according to the Latin, 19), where he describes the raids of the Judaeans against the Syrians, he has among other things: falling upon Gadara, Hippos and Gaulanitis [ϳαδαρois ... ἱππω ... γαυλανιτιδι, In Gadaram, Hippon & Gaulanitidem irruentes]. So most of the Gadarenes were Syrians, not Israelites, and therefore the prohibition on swine did not bind the Gadarenes; and the Judaeans who lived among them had to put up with it. From the history described by the Evangelists it is clear that among them were those demoniacs freed by Christ. Nor did the Israelites, Josephus shows, keep away from the cities of foreigners, since in Bk. 2 of the Antiquities, ch. 34 (the Greek title is not clear), he places the Gadarenes among those who treated harshly the Judaeans living in their city: The Hippeni and Gadarenes likewise: they put to death the bolder ones, but kept the fearful ones in prison [Γ'πτωλοοί ... ἡ ... Δἰ ... ἔχον]. In this way the evangelical history was, by the way, illustrated, and it was at the same time shown that the Mishnah we are discussing is not overturned. Moreover, Maimonides, in his notes on this Mishnah, extends the prohibition on swine further: The same law applies to the other things forbidden as to eating, but he speaks of swine because it is well known that they can be reared. If we follow this opinion, we may not keep other animals whose flesh may not be eaten, unless they are fed for work and burdens. But the mention of this kind was introduced because, as Maimonides says, it is known to all that this beast can be reared. For other forbidden animals, whose nature and ferocity do not allow this, would, if they had been proposed as examples, have given care to them in vain. But why does the author here consider the dog in particular? Because although its use beyond food is great, and we cannot conveniently do without it, it is nonetheless not to be admitted indiscriminately, but certain conditions must be carefully considered. So the Mishnah requires this condition, that it be tied with chains. R. Joseph Karo testifies that he found these words added in a corrected copy: of iron itself, that is, with iron chains. Therefore R. Jacob, when he repeats this regulation in Choschen Mishpat, has, instead of dog, a malignant dog [canem malignum], because ordinary dogs are not restrained by iron chains. But when the reasons are weighed which occur in the Gemara that follows, it will appear that even if they tie the dog with iron chains, this is not enough. Two reasons are offered: one, that the dog bites; the other, that it barks, and by barking so terrifies pregnant women that there is danger of miscarriage. The first reason is indeed met by that precaution, but the second remains. For this reason, it seems, the great R. Eliezer said: He who rears dogs is like him who rears swine, so that just as the one is wholly forbidden, so is the other. But the words added show that his meaning was different, since these are added: What follows from this? (that is, what is learned from that comparison?) To attack him with a curse. The sense is that, just as previously a curse was pronounced against the one who reared swine, so also the one who rears dogs is subject to the curse, unless he observes the condition the Mishnah demands. Then, in what they call the foreign traditions, they apply a different precaution in this matter: A man may rear a dog in a city on the shore or near a border; he ties it by day and lets it loose by night. Although it is not allowed to keep dogs loose elsewhere, yet it is allowed at the borders of regions, so that the neighbouring and outlying places may be safer from robbers. Some think this right also held in Babylonia, where many Judaeans lived. Hence in the Gemara: Master Nahman pronounced that Babel seems to be a city adjoining the border, and he said that Nehardea is designated in it (namely Master Joseph, who reports Nahman's opinion). Because there were many Judaeans in Babylonia, and they had for a time a settled seat there, R. Nahman in this respect equated it with the land of Canaan, so that in this way, in the ports and borders of the region (for the Talmudists take the word yishuv [יסם] widely), it would be lawful to keep dogs and let them loose at night, as in the Holy Land. But Babel is known to be the name of both a region and a city. When Nahman mentioned Babylonia, he wished to designate another city in the Babylonian region, namely Nehardea, which, as the Gloss says, was on the border, and therefore enjoyed that privilege. For they report that it was founded on the Euphrates (as Josephus and others have noted), where is the boundary and limit of the Babylonian region. Finally, lest the doves of the Israelites be caught, the laws provided against it, and so nets are permitted to be set only thirty stadia from a yishuv [יסם], that is, an inhabited place. By an inhabited place they mean a city. Nor is this permission, by which they allow nets to be set beyond thirty stadia, so general that it admits no exceptions. For there are two places where it is forbidden, even though those stadia lie between. If vineyards extend a hundred miles around the city, or from one side of it, it is forbidden to catch doves there with a net, because the doves fly from vineyard to vineyard and so withdraw as far as possible from the city which the Israelites inhabit. Also, if dovecotes set not far from one another extend over a hundred miles, it is forbidden to spread nets there, because likewise the doves of the Israelites, passing among the various dovecotes, at last fly off very far. Therefore in the Gemara we read a short old tradition about both: It is taught, how so? [תניא כיצד]. It is said in the foreign traditions: Even if a hundred miles intervene, he shall not spread [nets]. Master Joseph says this holds in a place planted with vines; Rabba adds, even in a place occupied by dovecotes. But you will except (or you will not think) that this is said on account of the dovecotes themselves. The earlier words show that both are forbidden; but the later words show that not merely different opinions are recorded, both in the Choschen Mishpat and in the Jad Chazaka, where the same prohibition is repeated. The later words mean that it is not the dovecotes themselves which cause this, as if it were against right for someone to set nets among his own dovecotes (for they extend the prohibition to that too); but that the Judaeans forbade it so that the measure of peace might be kept. But an objection arising from the Mishnah must be answered: for it requires a distance of thirty stadia for a net to be set, whereas doves are reckoned to withdraw from their dovecotes only fifty cubits, Cod. Bab. Bathr. ch. 2, sect. 5: They keep the dovecote fifty cubits from the city, namely for this purpose, that they may not harm the produce of the land there. Why then does the Mishnah require thirty stadia? But the difficulty is briefly removed in the Gemara: Abaye replies, They wander about very much, but their crop is filled within fifty cubits; their wandering however extends thirty stadia, and no further. As if he had said: the doves indeed withdraw only fifty cubits from the dovecotes to feed, and within that space they find what suffices for them; but beyond that they fly to much more distant places. Therefore, as far as the catching is concerned, it is lawful only beyond thirty stadia, lest they catch the doves of their brothers, which are accustomed sometimes to fly off as far as that. Under Roman law too, as under the preceding constitutions (though in a different way), harmful animals were forbidden. We have an example of this in Bk. 21, Dig. tit. 1, laws 11, 12 and 13: Let no one wish to have a dog, a boar (or a smaller wild boar), a wolf, a bear, a panther, a lion, or any other animal which could do harm, whether loose or tied, so that they cannot be restrained by chains from causing damage, in a place where the road is commonly used, so that it can harm or do damage to anyone. By this law the preceding clauses of the Mishnah could either be proved expressly, or by deducing one thing from another by analogy [κατ' ἀναλογίαν], insofar as some fairness is found in them; for more judicious readers will judge that the Judaeans went further in these matters than right reason suggests. The last clause, about doves, is illustrated by the law Naturalem, §cervos, Dig., On acquiring the ownership of things, where it is taught that animals of this kind do not become the property of whoever seizes them. In the case of animals which are accustomed to go away and return, this rule has been approved: that they are understood to be ours as long as they have the intention of returning; but if they cease to have the intention of returning, they cease to be ours and become the property of whoever seizes them. Therefore, as long as doves are accustomed to return to their dovecotes, they do not become the property of whoever seizes them; and so meanwhile it is not lawful to catch them.
Chapter 8, Halakhah 1 [פרק ח הלכה א]

units.la: החובל בחבירו חייב עליו שומם חמש' דברים בנזק בצער ברפו' בשבת ובבושת בנזק כיצר מיסא ארז עינו קטע את ידו שיבר את רגלו רואין אותו כאלו הוא עבר נסכר בשוק ושטין כסח היה יפר וכמה הוא יפה צער כואו בשפוד או בסספר ואפילו על ציפורנו מקום שאינו עושה חבורה א אומרין כסה ארם כיוצא בזה רוצה ליטול להיו' מצטער כך רפוי הכהו חייב
units.tr: One who wounds his fellow is liable to him for five things: for the damage [נזק], for the pain [צער], for the healing [רפוי], for the loss of time [שבת], and for the shame [בושת]. How is the damage assessed? If he blinded his eye, cut off his hand, or broke his leg, they regard him as if he were a slave being sold in the market, and assess how much he was worth before and how much he is worth after. How is the pain assessed? If he pricked him with a spear or a needle, even on his fingernail, in a place that does not make a wound, they ask how much a man would want to be paid to suffer in this way. The healing: whoever struck him is liable for his cure.
Chapter 8, §1.

units.la: Qui proximum ladit, in eo multis, id est, quinque nominibus tenetur: damni nomine, doloris, curationis, cessationis, & ignominiae. In damno, quomodo? Si illius oculum excaecavit, manum amputavit, pedem fregit; eum considerant, ac si servus esset in foro vendendus: atque aestimant quanti antea valebat; & quanti jam valet. In dolore vero ita fit: exempli gratia, hominem adusserit quis veru aut clavo, etiam in ejus ungue, ubi non fit vibex; tum expendunt, quantum homo istius conditionis reportare vellet, ut tanto dolore afficeretur. Quod curationem attinet; si alium percussit, ad curationem tenetur. Quum
units.tr: Whoever harms his neighbour is liable for him on five counts: the name of damage, of pain, of healing, of cessation (loss of work), and of shame. As to damage, how is it assessed? If he blinded his eye, amputated his hand, or broke his foot, they consider him as though he were a slave to be sold in the market, and they estimate what he was worth before and what he is worth now. As to pain, it is done thus: for example, if someone burned a man with a spit or a nail, even on his fingernail where no blister forms, they then estimate how much a man of that condition would wish to be paid to be subjected to such pain. As to healing, if he struck another, he is liable for the cost of healing.

units.la: לרפאותו עלו בו צמחיום אם מחסרת הסכה חייב שלא מחסת הסכה פטור חיתרה ונסתררה חיתרה ונסתררה חייב לרפאותו חיית' כל צרכה אינו חיו' לרפאותו שכרת רואין איתו כאלו הוא שוסר קישואין שכבר נהן לו רמי ידו ורמי רגלו בשת הכל לפי הסכיו' והמתבייש הסבייש את הערום הסבייש את הסום' והמבייש את חיטין חייב ויטן שבייש פטור נפל כן הגג והזקן ובייש חייב על הנזק ופטור על הבושת שנאמר ושלחה ידה והחזיקה במבושיו אינו חייב על הבושת עד שיהא מהכוין ׃ ex inflicta plaga id fiat, tenetur; si non ex inflicta plaga, liber est. Si subinde plaga sanetur & recrudescat, ille ad curationem ejus tenetur; si in solidum semel sanetur, non amplius tenetur ad ejus curationem. Quoad cessationem, eum considerant ac si cucumeres custodiret: nam antea ipsi dedit pretium manus pretiumque pedis ipsius. In ignominia compensanda, omnia pro conditione ejus qui eam inurit, & patitur. Qui ignominia afficit nudum, aut caecum, aut dormientem, tenetur; dormiens qui ignominia afficit, liber est. Si de tecto decidens ladat & ignominia afficiat, tenetur damni nomine; & in ignominia liber est: quia dicitur Deut. 25. v. 11. Et extendens manum suam apprehendat pudenda ejus. Non tenetur de ignominia, donec animum eo intendat.
units.tr: to heal him, the physicians are called in. If the wound is one that heals, he is liable; if it is not one that heals, he is free. If the wound heals and then breaks open again, he is liable for its healing; if it heals completely once, he is no longer liable for its cure. As to cessation, they consider him as though he were a guard of cucumbers, for previously he had given him the price of his hand and the price of his foot. In compensating for shame, everything is judged by the condition of the one who inflicts it and of the one who suffers it. He who shames a naked man, or a blind man, or a sleeping man, is liable; a sleeping man who shames another is free. If a man falling from a roof injures and shames someone, he is liable for the damage, and free as to the shame, because it is said (Deut. 25. 11), "and stretches out her hand and seizes his private parts." He is not liable for the shame unless he intended it. [Hebrew: ...לרפאותו עלו בו צמחיום אם מחסרת הסכה חייב שלא מחסת הסכה פטור חיתרה ונסתררה חיתרה ונסתררה חייב לרפאותו חיית' כל צרכה אינו חיו' לרפאותו שכרת רואין איתו כאלו הוא שוסר קישואין שכבר נהן לו רמי ידו ורמי רגלו בשת הכל לפי הסכיו' והמתבייש הסבייש את הערום הסבייש את הסום' והמבייש את חיטין חייב ויטן שבייש פטור נפל כן הגג והזקן ובייש חייב על הנזק ופטור על הבושת שנאמר ושלחה ידה והחזיקה במבושיו אינו חייב על הבושת עד שיהא מהכוין]
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Si quis alium laeserit, quinque praestare tenetur, ut alteri satisfaciat. Puta si corpus alicujus laeserit; ut vulnus inflixerit, vel membrum aliquod fregerit, vel amputaverit, vel simile fecerit. Atque singula illa quinque sacrarum literarum autoritate probare nituntur. Exempli gratia, omnium primo, ut damnum ac laesio ipsa compensetur, exigunt; idque autoritate legis Ex. 21. 23. & seq. Sin autem exitium sit, tum reddes vitam pro vita. Oculum pro oculo, &c. item Levit. 24. 20. Fractura esto pro fractura, oculus pro oculo, dens pro dente: prout intulerit corporis vitium homini, ita infertor ei. Hæc verba ubi secundum simplicem sensum accipiuntur, simile vitium lædentis corpori infligi postulant: nimirum ubi quis alterius lacertum fregit, lædentis similiter lacertum frangi; ubi manum vulneravit, vulnerantis manum simili vulnere deformari; atque eodem modo ac ratione in reliquis vitiis alterius corpori illatis. Exemplum Deut. 19. 19, simplicem etiam sensum suadet: hæc enim verba, Si ecce testis falsus est testis ille, falsum testatus est contra fratrem suum; omninò facietis ei, quemadmodum molitus fuerat facere fratri suo: hæc inquam Judæorum magistri in eum sensum accipiunt, ut falsus ille testis eam pœnam luat; quam alteri non ipso facto, sed conamine molitus fuerat. Atqui Lev. 24. & Ex. 21. etiam similitudo, sive potius æqualitas in pœna exigitur: ut quod vitium quis alteri intulerit, idem reum maneat. Cur hic à simplici sensu abeunt? Illic Deut. 19. conatus nocendi, eandem pœnam meretur: hic Ex. 21. ipsum factum & vitium corpori illatum diversam & minorem miseriam mereri dicemus; cum utrobique æqualitas præcipiatur? Nihilominus Judæorum magistris secus placuit. Multorum instar est Maimonides, qui c. 1. Codicis Chobel Oumaffik Judæorum mentem non tantum expressit; sed etiam defendere conatus fuit: Primum indicium, quare istis verbis, oculum pro oculo, multa pecuniaria intelligenda sit, in voce pro, constituitur: [Hebrew] Traditione acceperunt, id [Hebrew] pro vel vice, quod hic scribitur, ad rependendam pecuniam spectare. Atqui in præcedentibus, quum dicitur, Reddes vitam pro vita, eadem vox [Hebrew], pro vel vice, occurrit: quum tamen homicidam morte; non pretio quodam mulctandum censeant omnes. Postea objectionem diluere conatus, ad verba Levit. 24. 20: prout intulerit corporis vitium homini, ita infertor ei, sensum esse respondet, מסוח רתוי למסרו תכר פו למכול כו כסתר פעם, ipsum dignum esse ut ei membrum auferatur, aut eo corporis vitio afficiatur, quo affecit alium: ideoque compensandum damnum.Nihil hic regero: nam hæc expositio cum textu pugnat manifestè. Aliam deinde rationem subjicit, quia Num. 35. 31. legimus, Ne accipitote redemptionis pretium pro ullo occisore. subjicit ergo, לחנם כלבר פוח טתין כו כופר פכל לחסרין, אפרים פו למכלוק יט כו כופר, Pro occisore tantum interdicitur redemptionis pretium; sed propter membrum defectum, aut corporis vitia pretium accipere licet. Quasi verò quod Deus propter homicidii atrocitatem magis inculcat, id in aliis contra leges suas præteriri & negligi permittat.Non est insolens, ut quod multis commune est, in specie quadam expressius urgeatur, si id in ipsa omnium maximè attendi debeat. Quin etiam in vitio corporibus illato idem expresse repetitur Deut. 19. 21. Ne igitur parcito oculus tuus: vita pro vita, oculus pro oculo, dens pro dente, manus pro manu, pes pro pede esto. Vti illic redemptionis pretium expresse excluditur; ita hoc loco, quum dicitur, ne parcito oculus tuus: ubi nullum effugium admittitur; sed oculus pro oculo, dens pro dente, &c. exiguntur. Licet Maimonides sine ullo indicio textus, istud ad numerorum solutionem restringat; in qua nemini à judice parci permittit. Verum ratio quam ultimo loco profert, præcipua est & speciosa: ut quum in hunc modum loquitur Deus Exod. 21. 18. & 19. Quum percusserit unus alterum lapide aut pugno, ita ut mortuus non fit, sed decumbat in lecto; si surgens ambulaverit foras nixus scipione suo, tum impunis erit percussor: tantummodo cessationem ejus reddito, & plenam curationem ejus præstato: cum hac lege confert verba commatis 25. tumicem pro tumice. Quasi dicat, Lex talionis illustratur exemplo tumicis. atqui quum alter alterum percutit, ut inde decumbat, id sine tumice non fit: tamen quum quis alterum ita percutit ut decumbat, tantummodo cessationem ejus reddit, & curationem præstat ÿ f.19. nec ulterior pœna postulatur. At si quis paulo attentius locum expendat, nonne statim animadvertet, eadem ratione pecuniariam multam excludi, quam ante curationis mercedem &c. exigunt magistri; quum ÿ f. 19. quo totum argumentum nititur, ne quidem istius multæ fiat mentio? Nisi ergo isti doctores seipsos refellant, suamque sententiam qua pecuniam exigunt evertant, verba commatis 19. secus exponant necesse est. Series ipsius contextus abundè Legislatoris mentem nobis indicat. De altercantibus agitur, qui sæpe cædes jurgiis immiscent: itaque quandoquidem inter altercandum acceptis vulneribus & tumicibus non raro decumbunt, iterumque eousque convalescunt ut foras prodeant; voluntatem hic suam exprimit Legislator: licet vulneratus postea moriatur, quia eousque convaluit ut prodierit in publicum, alterum morte plectendum non esse. Atque hoc sibi inprimis hac lege Deus propositum habuit, ut reum à morte absolveret: ideoque ait, impunis erit percuffor. Sed quia absurdum videbatur, reum omninò ab omni pœna ac multa excusari, idcirco subjicitur, pɼ, Verum, cessationem &c. atque aliam pœnam quæ aliis delictis erat communis in comma 23. & sequentia differt, ut una eademque opera omnes istas lædendi species simili pœna involvat. Interea ÿ f. 19. quod isti facto specialiter conveniebat, expressit, ut reus decumbentis cessationem & curationem præstaret. Nam voculam pɼ quod attinet, ea non solum significat tantummodò, sed etiam verum vel sane, aut similia: ut Pf.32.6. Oraturus est te ... quo tempore obvenerit malum: pɼ, verum (vel sane) in inundatione etiam aquarum multarum, ad eum non pertingent. Imo etiamsi pɼ pro tantummodò accipias Ex.21.19. tantum ista vocula mortem excludit: alioqui ipsa pecuniaria multa quam supra cessationem & curationem exigunt Judæi excluderetur; quod sane non admittent. Denique nec hoc reticebo: non absonum fore, si Ex. 21. 23. & seq. de isto
units.tr: If anyone injures another, he is bound to make good five things to the other party. Suppose he has injured a person's body: he has inflicted a wound, or broken a limb, or cut one off, or done something similar. The rabbis strive to prove each of these five from the authority of sacred letters. For example, first of all they demand that the damage and the injury itself be made good, and they base this on the authority of Exod. 21. 23 and following: "But if there be any harm, then thou shalt give life for life, eye for eye," etc. Likewise Lev. 24. 20: "Breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him." When these words are taken according to their plain sense, they require that a like injury be inflicted on the one who injured: namely, if someone broke another's arm, the injurer's arm is broken in the same way; if he wounded a hand, the wounder's hand is disfigured by a like wound; and likewise in the other injuries done to another's body. Deut. 19. 19 also suggests the plain sense: "If the false witness be a false witness, and have testified falsely against his brother, then shall ye do to him as he had thought to have done unto his brother." The masters of the Jews, I say, take these words to mean that the false witness suffers the penalty that he had planned to inflict on another, not by the deed itself but by the attempt. Yet in Lev. 24 and Exod. 21 also a likeness, or rather an equality, in the penalty is required, so that the one who has inflicted a given injury on another remains liable to the same. Why do they depart here from the plain sense? In Deut. 19 the attempt to harm deserves the same penalty; here in Exod. 21, shall we say that the deed itself and the injury done to the body deserve a different and smaller misery, when equality is commanded in both places? Nevertheless it pleased the masters of the Jews otherwise. Maimonides is the representative of many, who in chapter 1 of the Code Chobel Oumaffik not only expressed the opinion of the Jews but also tried to defend it. His first indication that by the words "eye for eye" a monetary fine must be understood lies in the word "for" (Hebrew: tachat): [Hebrew] "They received by tradition that this 'for' or 'instead of,' written here, refers to repaying money." But in the preceding verses, where it says "life for life," the same word, "for" or "instead of," occurs, yet all agree that a murderer is to be punished by death, not mulcted by some payment. Afterwards he tries to dispel the objection regarding the words of Lev. 24. 20, "as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him," answering that the sense is: [Hebrew] that he himself is worthy to have a limb removed from him, or to be afflicted with the same bodily defect with which he afflicted another; and therefore the damage is to be compensated. I say nothing here, for this explanation clearly conflicts with the text. He then offers another reason: because we read in Num. 35. 31, "Ye shall take no satisfaction (ransom price) for the life of a murderer," he therefore adds: [Hebrew] "A ransom is forbidden only for the murderer; but on account of a missing limb or a bodily defect, a payment may be accepted." As if God, who inculcates a thing more emphatically on account of the atrocity of murder, would permit it to be passed over and neglected in other cases contrary to his laws. It is not unusual that what is common to many is urged more expressly in a particular species, if it ought to be most attended to in that very case. Indeed, the same is expressly repeated for bodily injuries in Deut. 19. 21: "Thine eye shall not pity; life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot." Just as there the ransom price is expressly excluded, so here, when it is said "thine eye shall not pity," where no escape is admitted, but eye for eye, tooth for tooth, etc., are demanded. Although Maimonides, without any indication in the text, restricts this to the payment of numbers, in which no one is spared by the judge. But the reason he gives last is the chief and the plausible one: when God speaks in this way in Exod. 21. 18 and 19, "If men strive together, and one smite the other with a stone, or with his fist, and he die not, but keepeth his bed; if he rise again and walk abroad upon his staff, then shall he that smote him be quit: only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed," he compares with this law the words of verse 25, "stripe for stripe." As if he should say: the law of retaliation is illustrated by the example of the stripe. But when one strikes another so that he falls to bed, this does not happen without a stripe; yet when someone so strikes another that he is laid up, he pays only for the loss of time and provides for the cure (verse 19), and no further penalty is demanded. But if anyone weighs the passage a little more attentively, will he not at once notice that by the same reasoning the monetary fine, which the masters demand before the wage of healing, etc., is excluded, since in verse 19, on which the whole argument rests, not even mention of such a fine is made? Unless therefore those teachers refute themselves and overturn their own opinion by which they demand payment, they must interpret the words of verse 19 otherwise. The sequence of the context sufficiently indicates the Lawgiver's intention to us. It concerns those who quarrel, who often mix killings into their brawls; so, since in the course of quarrelling they often receive wounds and stripes and lie down, and then recover again so far that they come out of doors, the Lawgiver here expresses his will: even if the wounded man afterwards dies, because he had recovered so far that he went out in public, the one who struck him is not to be punished with death. And God intended above all by this law to acquit the accused of death; therefore he says, "he shall be quit." But because it seemed absurd that the accused should be wholly excused from all penalty and fine, it is therefore added, "only," "but," (Hebrew raq), "he shall pay for the loss of time," etc., and in verses 23 and following he sets out a different penalty, which was common to other offences, so that by one and the same work he might include all these species of harming under a like penalty. Meanwhile, in verse 19 he expressed what was specially suited to this deed, namely that the one who struck should pay for the cessation and the cure of the man who lay down. For as to the little word raq, it signifies not only "only," but also "truly" or "surely," or similar things: as in Ps. 32. 6, "for this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: surely (raq) in the floods of great waters they shall not come nigh unto him." Moreover, even if you take raq to mean "only" in Exod. 21. 19, that little word excludes only death; otherwise the monetary fine which the Jews demand above the cessation and the cure would be excluded too, which they certainly will not admit. Finally, I shall not pass over this: it would not be absurd, if we said that Exod. 21. 23 and following deal with an injury that is not cured, so that a deformity remains; but verse 19 refers to the case in which a complete cure is seen, so that we seem able to demand nothing beyond the cure and the cessation. Therefore, since the case is different, this reasoning of Maimonides proves nothing. Indeed...

units.la: vitio agi dicamus quod non curatur, quin deformitas maneat; at s. 19. eum spectari casum, in quo curatio perfecta conspicitur: ut nihil præter curationem & cessationem exigere posse videamur. Itaque cum diversus sit casus, nihil probat hæc Maimonidæ ratio. Verumenimvero hoc agnosco: licet lex talionis ita intelligenda, uti dictum est, tamen penes judicem fuisse, ut pœnam corporalem in pecuniariam pro circumstantiarum conditione mutaret: idque argumento legis quæ Ex. 21. 29. & 30. datur, ubi alternatio pœnæ etiam gravioris admittitur. sed de eo postea. Verum jam videamus, qua ratione, quove modo illam multam definiant. Si conditionis diversitas attenderetur, nulla esset certa æstimandi ratio: in singulis vitæ generibus, & personarum statu diversissimo, semper quidpiam proferret læsus, cujus nomine damnum vel vitium corporis admodum extenderet, ejusque compensationem augeri postularet. Itaque omnes læsos pro servis hac in parte censeri volunt: quorum pretium ignorari non poterat. atque etiam istis temporibus usitatum erat, ut liberæ personæ necessitate quadam urgente seipsas in servos venderent. Quapropter utrumque statum & conditionem expendunt: quanti vendi persona posset, antequam (exempli gratia) manus abscissa fuisset; quantique jam valere posset, postquam abscissa est: reus solvit imminutionem, qua illius valorem imminuit. ut si antea so siclis æstimatus, postea quadraginta tantum siclis vendi queat; læsdens quanti læsus depretiatus fuerit, rependet: puta siclos decem. Multi hic casus expendi possent, quibus læsdens damni nomine non tencatur; sed curationis vel cessationis &c. quos ob eorum multitudinem præterco. Si quis omnes expendere velit, legat in Chofchen Mischpat sect. 420. circa initium: ubi distincte proponuntur. Iam ad leges apud Romanos receptas veniamus; quæ olim idem cum lege divina præcipiebant. Vnde in legibus 12. Tab. talio stabilitur: Si membrum rupit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto. Cum hac convenit dictum l. sin. t. 2. l. 9. Cod. Nec impunitam fore noverit licentiam mentiendi, cum calumniantes ad vindictam poscat similitudo supplicii. Sed ut ait Imperator Inst. l. 4. t. 4. poenam talionis clementia juris praetorii postea revocavit. ita enim legimus §. Poena autem; Sed poena quidem injuria, quae ex lege 12. Tabularum introducta est, in desuetudinem abiit: quam autem Praetores introduxerunt (quae etiam honoraria appellatur) in judiciis frequentatur. Imo dum talio vigeret, quemadmodum apud Judaeos in pecuniariam multam saepissime mutabatur; sic in aliis tribunalibus pecuniae multa eadem mansuetudine admittebatur. Gellius Noct. Att. l. 20. c. 1. ubi multa de lege talionis in utramque partem disputantur ejusque aequitas defenditur, haec inter alia habet verba, quae Sexto Caecilio tribuit; Quae ista acerbitas est, si idem fiat in te quod tute in alio feceris: praesertim quum habeas facultatem paciscendi: & non necesse sit pati talionem, nisi eam tu elegeris? quod edictum autem praetorium de aestimandis injuriis probabilius esse potest? Nolo hoc ignores, hanc quoque ipsam talionem ad aestimationem judicis redigi necessario solitam. Nam si reus, qui depacisci noluerat, judici talionem imperanti non parebat; aestimata lite judex hominem pecunia damnabat. Atque ita, si reo pastio gravis & acerba talio visa fuerat, severitas legis ad pecuniae multam redibat. Non erit à ratione alienum, si in foro Judaico eundem procedendi modum ac viam servatam fuisse dicamus. Vt talio etiam jure exigeretur, si laedens minus atrociter peccasset, aut depacisci nollet; multa tamen pecuniaria saepè reus satisfacere posset, vel alia quadam ratione, cui laesus acquiesceret. Nam si (quemadmodum jam antea innui) Ex. 21. 30. morte dignus eaque plestendus id juris habebat, ut certo casu, pretio vitam redimendi facultas esset; quidni idipsum in leviori crimine admittatur? Legislator hac de causa utramque legem eodem loco proposuisse videtur, illam Yf. 25. hanc verò Yf. 30. ut posterior prioris essct explicatio. Non tamen Judæis assentior, qui legem priorem mordicus de pecuniaria multa accipiendam contendunt: non enim magis illa lege pecunia exigitur, quam Yf. 29. ubi dicitur, Dominus ejus morte plectitor. verum uti hic redemptio vitæ permittitur commate sequenti; pariter illic, membri &c. redemptionem argumento posterioris legis (Yf. 30.) non denegandam autumo.
units.tr: we may say the injury is treated as not healed, so that the deformity remains; but s. 19. refers to a case in which a complete cure is evident, so that it seems he can demand only the cure and the cessation of work. Therefore, since the case is different, this argument of Maimonides proves nothing. Yet I admit this: although the law of retaliation must be understood as stated above, it rested with the judge to change the bodily penalty into a monetary one according to the circumstances of the case. This is shown by the law given in Ex. 21. 29 and 30, where a choice of even a heavier penalty is allowed. But more on that later. Let us now see by what reasoning, and in what manner, they fix that fine. If the difference of condition were taken into account, there would be no fixed rule of valuation: in the many kinds of life and the very different states of persons, the injured party would always put forward something, and on account of it would enlarge the damage or the bodily defect and demand a greater compensation. Therefore they wish all the injured to be counted as slaves in this respect, since their price could be known. Indeed, in those times it was also customary for free persons, under some pressing necessity, to sell themselves into slavery. Hence they weigh both states and conditions: what price a person could fetch before (for example) a hand had been cut off, and what he could now fetch after it was cut off: the wrongdoer pays the diminution by which he has lessened the value of the other. So if he was valued at sixty shekels before, and can now be sold for only forty, the one who injured him pays the amount by which the injured man has been depreciated, say ten shekels. Many cases here could be weighed in which the one who injured is not bound to pay damages, but only the cost of cure, or of cessation of work, and so on; these I pass over because of their number. If anyone wishes to weigh them all, let him read in the Choshen Mishpat, sect. 420, near the beginning, where they are set out clearly. Now let us come to the laws received among the Romans, which once prescribed the same as the divine law. Hence in the Twelve Tables retaliation is established: If he has broken a limb, and does not come to terms with him, let there be retaliation. With this agrees the saying in l. sin. t. 2, l. 9, Cod.: Nor let him know that the license of lying will go unpunished, since the likeness of punishment calls the slanderers to vengeance. But as the Emperor says in Inst. l. 4, t. 4, the clemency of the praetorian law later revoked the penalty of retaliation. For thus we read in §. Poena autem: But the penalty for injury which was introduced by the law of the Twelve Tables has fallen into disuse; whereas that which the praetors introduced (which is also called honorary) is frequently used in the courts. Indeed, while retaliation was in force, just as among the Jews it was very often changed into a monetary fine, so in other courts a fine of money was admitted with the same mildness. Gellius, Noct. Att. l. 20, c. 1, where much about the law of retaliation is disputed on both sides and its equity is defended, has among other things these words, which he attributes to Sextus Caecilius: What harshness is this, if the same is done to you that you yourself have done to another; especially since you have the power of coming to terms, and it is not necessary to suffer retaliation unless you yourself have chosen it? What praetorian edict concerning the assessment of injuries can be more reasonable? I would not have you ignore this, that retaliation itself was necessarily customarily reduced to the judge's assessment. For if the defendant, who had refused to come to terms, did not obey the judge who ordered retaliation, the judge, having assessed the case, condemned the man to pay money. And so, if the sentence of retaliation seemed too severe and harsh to the defendant, the rigour of the law came back to a fine of money. It will not be out of reason if we say that the same procedure and method was observed in the Jewish court. So that retaliation might also be enforced by law if the one who injured had sinned less atrociously, or was unwilling to come to terms, yet the defendant could often make satisfaction by a monetary fine, or by some other arrangement to which the injured party would consent. For if (as was hinted above) he who deserved death, and was to be punished by it, had in a certain case the right that he might redeem his life by a price (Ex. 21. 30), why should not the same be allowed in a lighter crime? For this reason the lawgiver seems to have set out both laws in the same place, the former at Ex. 21. 25 and the latter at Ex. 21. 30, so that the later might be an explanation of the earlier. Yet I do not agree with the Jews who stubbornly insist that the former law must be understood of a monetary fine: for money is no more exacted by that law than by Ex. 21. 29, where it is said, his owner shall be put to death. But just as redemption of life is permitted here in the following verse, so there, I maintain, redemption of a limb and the like is not to be denied, on the argument of the later law (Ex. 21. 30).

units.la: ³ Verum crure fracto, vulnere inflicto &c. non tantum integritatem corporis redimendam; sed etiam pro aliis satisfaciendum esse Misna asserit. Itaque secundò dolorem compensari vult; ejusq; exemplum in adusto proponit, cujus unguis tantum candenti ferro leviter ustuletur: ubi merito conditione personarum spectari præcipit. Nam & Maimonides tractatu in superioribus citato c.2. sect.10. observat, Hominem divitem & delicatulum invenias qui grandi pecunia, ut dolorem remissum sustineat, adduci non poterit; vicissim robustum quendam pauperem laboribusque assuetum deprehendas vel pro uno denario magnum non detrectare dolorem. Hominum ergò conditio & indoles spectanda: quod quidem in exemplo ab authore Misnæ propósito, atque etiam similibus, magnam difficultatem non habet. Verum quandoquidem ipsius mens ac intentio hæc est, ut conveniens pretium pro illo etiam dolore rependatur, quem quis ex amputata manu, aliisve membris sustinet; quo modo iste dolor æstimari queat, expendamus. Maimonidæ tantum verba è sect. 11. dicti capitis ascribam. [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] Quum manum ejus aut digitum amputavit; expendunt quantum issius conditionis homo dare vellet, ut potius quam sibi hoc membrum gladio præcideretur, id medicinà tolleretur, si de ipso rex constituisset, manum vel pedem amputandum. tum quanti sit utrinsque differentia æstimant, idque ladens persolvit. Sanè ut inquit Gemara, pecuniam nemo חיוב ... accipiet ut in seipsum eum dolorem admittat. Sed si manus ob delictum & peccatum contra majestatem regiam admissum amputanda magno cum cruciatu; æstimari potest dolor, quantum reus iste expendere vellet, si leni medicina manus tolli posset, idq; rex admitteret. Verumenimvero unde doloris compensationem probant? In Gemara verba illa Ex. 21.25. Vstionem pro ustione.... tumicem pro tumice, pro fundamento sternuntur; licet satis obscurè: ideo verba ascribere & addita versione explicare non gravabor. רבי ... Ribbi censet simplicem ustionem esse quae prius memoratur: ut qui existimet, ustionem quae tumicem continet proprie quidem illa voce designari; sed misericordem D. postea subjecisse tumicem, quo ustionem illam declararet, eam intelligi quae tumice careat. Ac si dixisset R. Judas, (Ribbi dictus) Vstio commatis initio, similesque laesiones designantur, quae oculis etiam expositae non sunt; ut quidem tumices & vulnera; ideoq; horum postea demum fit mentio: quapropter dolor simplex etiam compensandus, licet grave vitium corpori illatum non fit. nam dicitur ustio pro ustione, quasi dicat, Levissima etiam laesio dolorem afferens, compensanda. quanto ergo magis, si dolor iste in vulneribus, tumice, amputata manu &c. inveniatur? Haec est verborum illorum sententia. Maimonides verò è Deut. 22. 29. idem confirmari existimat. ubi de eo qui vi virgini vitium offert lex praecipit, Dabit vir ille qui concubuit cum ea, patri puellae quinquaginta siclos argenteos &c. quod compresserit eam: eadem inquit ille, est omnium ratio qui alterius corpus vitiarunt, scilicet ut animi vel corporis dolorem compensent. Legibus etiam Romanis hujusmodi compensationis habitam fuisse rationem constat è Dig. li. 47. tit. 10. ubi le. 5. Lex Cornelia de injuriis competit ei qui injuriarum agere volet ob eam rem, quod se pulsatum, verberatumve, domumve suam vi introitam esse dicat. Quæ verba prima quidem fronte quod intendo probare non videntur: sed cum iis conferendus paragraphus sequens,Inter pulsationem & verberationem hoc interest, ut Ofilius scribit, verberare, est cum dolore cædere; pulsare, sine dolore. Si propter pulsationem & verberationem ut res diversas agere injuriarum licet, & pulsationem verberatio solo dolore superat; quis non videt legibus Romanis ob illatum dolorem læso actionem in lædentem dari, quod Misna nostra stabilitur? Laurentium Vallam li. 6. elegant. istam differentiam improbantem jam prætereo: etenim in ista scupulosius inquirere animus non est. Porro in curatione sumptus vulneranti sive lædenti ascribendos esse manifeste docetur Ex. 21. 19. Plenam curationem ejus præstato: verum inde primo intuitu non liquet,an si pustulæ in læsa cute succrescant, aliave incommoda oborian-tur, eorum curationem reus præstare teneatur. Misnæ author affirmat; sed adhibita distinctione: nam hujusmodi tubercula, aliave vitia, vel aliunde casu fortuito eodem tempore accidunt; vel eorum causa est inflicta plaga. si fortuitò hoc malum concurrat, reus non tenetur; at si causa in ipsa plaga deprehendatur, ad curationem obligatur. Nec ad curationem tantum; sed etiam cessationem compensandam, uti in Gemara explicatur: fit enim sæpe,ut ex fortuito hujusmodi malo ulterius ac diutius ab opere suo prohibeatur vulneratus. Ratio qua præcedentem distinctionem in Gemara confirmant hisce verbis exprimitur: [Hebrew] magistri, voculam [Hebrew] ad ea quæ ex plaga non proveniunt excludenda venire sive præmitti, censent. Quia [Hebrew] etiam excludendi particula est,ideo Vf.19. exprimi autumant, ut plagæ ejusque quod ex plaga provenit curatio & plagam istam consequens cessatio solummodo intelligatur, non vero si accidentarium illud malum ex inflicta plaga non oriatur. Qui autem aliunde etiam procedat, in Gemara additur: ubi [Hebrew] pustulas paulo aliter Abæus exponit, quam solent Ebræi. [illegible, ~40 letters] Qui se res habet, quum è plaga non provenit? quemadmodum traditione accepimus, Ecce quando medici verba neglexit, & mel, ullave dulciariorum genera edit: quia mellis genera, omniumque dulciariorum, plaga infesta sunt, adeo ut plaga proferat. Deinde postrema hæc vox explicatur: [illegible, ~20 letters] Quid est? respondet Abaus, caro mortua. Glossa Salomonis exponit caro mortua: puta, quæ in parte læsa excrescens fit sensus expers. Cæterum in vulneris & similium curatione aliud etiam expendendum venit. Contingit non raro, ut morbus vel vulnus ac plaga recrudescat, & male affectus veluti recidivam patiatur. Misna quidem in genere reum condemnat, si læsus à malo suo nondum plane sanatus fuisset; at si post recuperatam valetudinem, læsus iterum male habere incipiat, recidivi mali alterum non teneri censent. Attamen Gemara cum in genere excusat, si sua culpa, non plagæ vi ac conditione pejus habere læsus coeperit; quemadmodum in carnis pustulis, sive in excrescente carne jam antea observatum fuit. Ita etiam R. Jacob autor Choschen Mischpat & Maimonides sentire videntur: licet eorum verba varie construi, aliumque sensum habere queant.
units.tr: ³ But if a leg is broken, or a wound inflicted, and so on, the Mishnah asserts that not only the body's soundness must be made good, but also that compensation must be paid for the other losses. Second, it therefore wants the pain to be compensated, and it offers as an example a burnt man whose nail alone is slightly scorched with a red-hot iron. Here it rightly directs that the condition of the persons be considered. For Maimonides, in the treatise cited above, ch. 2, sect. 10, observes: you may find a rich and delicate man who cannot be persuaded to endure a slight pain for a large sum of money; conversely, you may find a poor man, hardened by labour, who does not shrink from great pain even for a single denarius. The condition and temperament of the people must therefore be considered. In the example proposed by the author of the Mishnah, and in similar ones, this presents no great difficulty. But since his mind and intention is that a fitting price be paid also for that pain which someone suffers from the amputation of a hand or other limbs, let us consider how that pain may be estimated. I shall set down only Maimonides' words from sect. 11 of the same chapter: When he has cut off his hand or finger, they estimate how much a man of that condition would be willing to pay so that, rather than having this limb cut off by the sword, it might be removed by medicine, supposing the king had decreed that the hand or foot be amputated. Then they estimate the difference between the two, and the one who caused the injury pays that. Certainly, as the Gemara says, nobody will accept [חיוב] payment in order to subject himself to that pain. But if the hand is to be amputated with great torment on account of a crime and an offence against royal majesty, the pain can be estimated: how much the guilty man would be willing to spend if the hand could be removed by a gentle medicine, and the king would allow it. But on what do they base the compensation for pain? In the Gemara those words of Ex. 21.25 are laid down as the foundation: burning for burning... stripe for stripe; though very obscurely. So I shall not hesitate to set down the words and explain them with an added version. [Hebrew] Rabbi Ribbi thinks that the simple burn is the one mentioned first: as if someone should think that the burn which contains a weal is properly designated by that word; but that the merciful God afterwards added the weal, to declare that burn, so that it is understood as one lacking a weal. And it is as if R. Judah (called Ribbi) had said: the burn at the beginning of the verse, and similar injuries which are not even exposed to the eyes, are designated, such as weals and wounds; therefore mention of these comes only afterwards. Hence even simple pain is to be compensated, though no grave defect has been inflicted on the body. For it is said burning for burning, as if to say: even the slightest injury causing pain is to be compensated. How much more, then, if that pain is found in wounds, weals, an amputated hand, and so on? This is the sense of those words. Maimonides, however, thinks the same is confirmed from Deut. 22.29, where the law, concerning one who violates a virgin by force, commands: the man who lay with her shall give to the girl's father fifty shekels of silver, etc., because he has ravished her. The same, he says, is the principle for all who have injured another's body, namely that they should compensate for the pain of mind or body. It is also clear from Roman law that a reckoning of this kind of compensation was made, from Dig. bk. 47, tit. 10, law 5: The Cornelian law concerning injuries is available to one who wishes to bring an action for injuries because he says he has been struck, beaten, or his house entered by force. At first sight these words do not seem to prove what I intend. But the following paragraph should be compared with them: Between striking and beating there is this difference, as Ofilius writes: to beat is to strike with pain; to strike is without pain. If it is permitted to bring an action for injuries on account of striking and beating as different matters, and beating surpasses striking by pain alone, who does not see that Roman law grants an action against the one who injures, on account of the pain inflicted on the injured party, which our Mishnah establishes? I pass over Laurentius Valla, who in book 6 of his Elegantiae disapproves of this distinction; for I have no intention of inquiring too scrupulously into it. Moreover, it is clearly taught that the expenses of treatment are to be charged to the one who wounds or injures, Ex. 21.19: Provide for his complete cure. But from this, at first sight, it is not clear whether, if pustules or other troubles grow up in the injured skin, the wrongdoer is bound to provide their cure. The author of the Mishnah affirms it, but with a distinction: for such tubercles or other defects either happen by chance at the same time from another cause, or their cause is the inflicted blow. If this evil happens by accident, the wrongdoer is not bound; but if the cause is found in the blow itself, he is obliged to the cure. And he is obliged not only to the cure but also to compensate for the loss of work, as is explained in the Gemara: for it often happens that the injured man is hindered from his work for longer and more lengthily because of such an accidental evil. The reason by which they confirm the preceding distinction in the Gemara is expressed in these words: [Hebrew] the masters think the little word [Hebrew] comes in, or is placed first, to exclude those things which do not arise from the blow. Because [Hebrew] is also a particle of exclusion, they therefore maintain that Ex. 21.19 is to be understood so that only the cure of the blow, and the cessation of work following the blow, are meant, and not if that accidental evil does not arise from the inflicted blow. But that it proceeds also from another cause is added in the Gemara, where [Hebrew] pustules is explained by Abaeus somewhat differently from the way the Hebrews usually do: [illegible] How is the matter when it does not arise from the blow? As we have received by tradition: behold, when the injured man has neglected the physician's words and eaten honey or any kind of sweetmeats, since honey and all sweetmeats are hostile to a wound, so that the wound worsens. Then this last word is explained: [illegible] What is it? Abaeus answers: dead flesh. The Gloss of Solomon explains dead flesh as: that is, flesh which grows up in the injured part and becomes without feeling. Moreover, another point must be weighed in the treatment of wounds and similar injuries. It not infrequently happens that a disease or wound or blow breaks out again, and the ill-affected part suffers a sort of relapse. The Mishnah in general condemns the wrongdoer if the injured man was not yet fully healed of his injury; but if, after his health was recovered, the injured man begins to be unwell again, they hold that the wrongdoer is not liable for the second, relapsing evil. Yet the Gemara, while generally excusing this, does so only if the injured man has begun to be worse through his own fault and not by the force and condition of the blow, as was observed before in the case of pustules of flesh or in proud flesh. So also R. Jacob, the author of the Choschen Mischpat, and Maimonides seem to think; although their words can be construed variously and may bear another sense.

units.la: ⁶ Pergit Misna ad cessationem: nam qui inflicto vulnere impeditur, quo minus opus suum peragere possit, magnum inde etiam damnum percipit; quod præstare vulneris author lege tenetur, Ex. 21. v. 19. Verum quæstio oritur, qui, quave ratione ac modo illa cessatio æstimanda sit. Doctores læsi conditionem exactè considerant: eum vi ac vigore præcedentium constitutionum, pro corporis vitio, nec non pro exantlato dolore, pecuniariam mulctam à lædente accepisse. itaque (exempli gratia) quid pede vel manu mutilatus, si manum vel pedem retinuisset, lucraretur, spectandum non esse
units.tr: ⁶ The Mishnah goes on to loss of work: for the one who, because of an inflicted wound, is prevented from being able to carry out his work, also suffers great loss thereby; and the author of the wound is bound by law to make this good, Ex. 21.19. But the question arises as to who, and in what way and manner, that loss of work is to be estimated. The teachers carefully consider the condition of the injured man: that by the force and strength of the preceding enactments, according to the defect of the body and also according to the pain endured, he has received a monetary fine from the one who injured him. Thus (for example) they maintain that what a man mutilated in foot or hand would have gained, had he kept his hand or foot, ought not to be considered; but since satisfaction has already been made for the hand and foot, they wish that what he suffers in loss during the continuing sickness, with respect to the work which the mutilated man, although maimed, would nevertheless have done while sound, be weighed. Therefore they think that the mutilated man may experience that price for each day of the illness, which…

units.la: [illegible, ~10 letters] esse contendunt; sed quia jam pro manu & pede satisfactum est, quid damni durante morbo patiatur, operis respectu quod licet mutilatus tamen sanus faceret, expendi volunt. Idcirco mutilatum, illud pretium singulis morbi diebus experi posse censent, quod è servato cucumerario quotidie reportaret. Sed quia perinde non est, sive pede, sive manu privatus sit, nam ad diversa deinde opera idoneus est; nec etiam perinde se res habet, sive vulneratus ad tempus decumbat, posteaque sine ullo vitio sanitatem recuperet, sive membrum aliquod amittat: propterea cessatio ab opere æqualiter æstimari potis non est. Vnde varios respectus hic admittendos esse constat: adeo ut Maimonidæ distinctiones merito adjiciendæ videantur, qui propositis diversis casibus, ex illis reliquos judicandos censet.
units.tr: [illegible] they maintain; but since satisfaction has already been made for the hand and the foot, they want the loss suffered during the illness to be reckoned in terms of the work which the maimed man, though mutilated, would still have done had he been healthy. They therefore think the maimed man can have each day of illness valued at that wage which he would daily earn from a guarded cucumber bed. But since it makes no difference whether he has been deprived of a foot or of a hand, for he is then fit for different kinds of work; and the matter is not the same whether he is wounded and lies ill for a time and afterwards recovers his health without any defect, or whether he loses some limb: therefore the loss of work cannot be assessed in one way for all. Whence it is clear that various considerations must be admitted here, so that the distinctions of Maimonides rightly seem to be added, who, having proposed different cases, judges the rest from them.

units.la: Si membrum ejus mutilatum non sit, sed agrotet & in lecto decumbat, aut ita tumeat manus, ut tandem convalescat, alter ipsi cessationem uniuscujusque diei reddet, pro ratione opificis, qui ab eo opere cessat, à quo ille abstinet. Sin ladens eum membro mutilaverit, aut manum amputaverit, reddito manus valore (scilicet damno pretio,) quoad cessationem eum ut cucumerum custodem considerant: atque expendunt, quanta sit hujusmodi custodis merces quotidiana, quotque dies agrotaverit supputant, tantumque ipsi rependitur. similiter si pedem ipsius abscidit, eum ac si ad portas civitatis custodem ageret, considerant. excaecaverit oculum ipsius; ac si in mola moleret. similiterque similes æstimant. Quod proponit Maimonides, quæque in superioribus de curatione dicta fuere, non male cum Dig. l. 9. t. 3. leg. sin. conveniunt: ubi secundum legem Dei Ex. 21. 19. cessationem & curationem Gajus exigit. Cum liberi hominis corpus ex eo, quòd dejectum effusumve quid erit, lafum fuerit: judex computat mercedes medicis præstitas, cateraque impendia, qua in curatione facta sunt. præterea operas quibus caruit, aut cariturus est ob id, quod inutilus factus est. Casus non sunt plane iidem; sed similium simile est judicium. 7 Denique luenda est ignominia, qua quis alterum afficit: sed hic cum agentis, tum patientis status ac conditio spectanda; alioqui multa peccato non responderet. Quis quaeso hæc æqualem mereri pœnam dicat, si bajulus alapam prætori impingat, & vili mendico? Merito hac in re, ignominiam patientis & inferentis conditionem spectare præcipit Misna. Rationem D. Jacob in libro aliquoties jam citato reddidit: hanc fermè, quod longe major sit ignominia, si quis à plebeio infimæ sortis eam excipere cogatur, quam ubi ab illustri viro in gradu sublimi collocato infertur. Vicissim, inquit, indignius est virum honoratum in magna dignitate constitutum probro & dedecore affici, quam ubi quis ex infima plebe in simile opprobrium incurrit. 8 Verum quæ causa, ut expresse is reus peragatur qui nudum probro affecerit? nam ipsa etiam nuditas alterum excusare videtur: quem enim non pudet ut corpus suum denudet, leges in hac causa merito negligere videntur. Itaque observa non quemvis nudum hic spectari; sed eum hic speciatim ab ignominia defendi, cui casu quodam contingit ut exterior vestis elevetur.
