In oriente vestes talares Judæis in usu erant, quas ita subduci ut corpus videretur, ignominiosum habebatur. quapropter gradibus ad altare ascendere vetitum: ne sublatis pedibus laciniæ & vestis alæ attollerentur, adeoque femora conspicerentur, Ex. 20. 26. qua de re alibi in Middoth pluribus egi. Ne ergo, si ventus alam attollat, alterius nuditatem quis augeat, vestemque amplius subducat, hic interdicitur: alioqui ignominiæ illatæ nomine quicunque id fecerit multam soluturum. (nam qui sacerdotes non erant femoralibus sæpe caruisse videntur Deut. 25. 11.) Inde in Gemara legimus: מהי פרוס דאתא ורקא ... Quid est quod dicitur, Nudus? Quum irruente vento qui sursum inflectit ipsas vestes, accedens quis eas magis sursum subducit, ipsumque dedecore afficit. Cæterum cæci & dormientis mentionem injicit Misnæ author; quia cum ignominia illata ab ipsis non animadvertatur, impunè reum hoc laturum, facilè putaretur. ideo multam isti reo irrogat. Contrà, dormiens quia ignorans peccat, ignominiæ illatæ non tenetur, quod similiter de cæco statuendum esse, suadet ratio. Adeoque scientia, animiq; intentio in dedecore alicui inferendo spectatur: ut licet damni teneatur qui de tecto invitus decidit, ignominiæ nomine qua hoc casu aliquem forte afficeret (ut si eum fortuito isto impetu in lutum detruderet) nihil debere censeatur. Idque è Deut. 25. 11. magistri eruunt, ubi mulierem, quæ contendentibus viris, alterius pudenda prehendit, quo eum retineat ne maritum percutiat; manu multandam docemur: quem locum ita Talmudici accipiunt, quasi solam ignominiam viro inde inustam lex spectaret. Atque hinc in omni dedecore, lædentis animum & voluntatem attendendam eliciunt: quod de ista muliere lex dicat, extendens manum suam; manum verò nemo nisi volens extendat, ut quidpiam assequatur. Aben-Ezra autem periculum etiam considerari à legislatore autumat, quum ita inquit, adhac locus ille periculosus est: quasi dicas, Verendis apprehensus vir ac in excandescentia sua vi retentus, facile obnitendi violentia lædituc. Porrò quod pœnam subjunctam concernit, Amputabis manum illius, eodem modo exponunt atque illud, Ex. 21. 24. Oculus pro oculo: ubi æstimandum oculum contendunt, & pretium æquale solvendum. Sed melius Aben-Ezra, qui in hanc sententiam scribit, Ut oculus pro oculo; si eam manum non redimat amputabis. Vbi idem simile quidem accipit; sed alio sensu: non quod pecuniaria multa directè illic præcipiatur; sed per Ϝπεικίαν sæpè permittatur. quod comparatio Exod. 21.30. omninò suadet: quemadmodum antea pluribus ea de re actum fuit. Apud Romanos ignominia, convitium, probrum ac similia legibus prohibebantur. Vnde Dig. l. 47. t. 10. l. c. 15. §. 27. Generaliter vetuit prætor quid ad infamiam alicujus fieri. Et quemadmodum supra è R. Jacobo intelleximus contumeliam ex eo crescere, quod persona inferioris sortis eam faciat; ita Vlpianus fere etiam loquitur, cujus verba producuntur eodem titulo, l. 17. §. 3. Quædam injuria à liberis hominibus facta, levis nonnullius momenti videntur: enimverò à servis, graves sunt. Crescit enim contumelia ex persona ejus qui contumeliam facit. Præterea quemadmodum apud Judæos intentio alium ignominia afficiendi, quam eum quem dedecore afficimus, non excusat; sic nec apud Romanos. Maimonides c. 1. Chobel Oumaffik sect. 14. המקכוין לכייס טעבד וכיוס לת כן חורין דמי כסתו של עבד, Qui animo concipit ut servum dedecore afficiat, & ingenuum pudore afficit; is ingenuo solvit, quanti probrum servi æstimatur. Similiter titulo in præcedentibus produ&to, lege 18. §. 3. Si injuria mihi fiat ab eo cui sim ignotus, aut si quis putet me Lucium Titium esse, cum sim Gajus Sejus; prævalet quod principale est, injuriam eum mihi facere velle: nam certus ego sum, licet ille putet me alium esse quam sum: & ideo injuriarum habeo.
units.tr: If his member is not mutilated, but he is sick and keeps to his bed, or his hand swells so that he finally recovers, the other shall give him, for each day of cessation, the wage of the workman who stops from that work from which he abstains. But if, striking him, he mutilates his member or cuts off his hand, then, once the value of the hand has been restored (namely the damage in money), they regard him with respect to cessation as a keeper of cucumbers. They weigh how great the daily wage of such a keeper is, count how many days he was ill, and that sum is repaid to him. Similarly, if he cuts off his foot, they regard him as if he were a guard at the city gates. If he blinds his eye, [they regard him] as if he were grinding at a mill. And they value similar cases similarly. What Maimonides sets out, and what was said above about cure, agrees well with Digest 9.3, the law sin, where Gaius requires cessation and cure according to the law of God, Exodus 21.19: When the body of a free man has been injured by something thrown down or poured out, the judge computes the fees paid to doctors and the other expenses incurred in the cure, and besides the services of which he has been deprived, or will be deprived, because he has been made useless. The cases are not altogether the same, but the judgment for like cases is alike. Finally, the disgrace which one man inflicts on another must be atoned for. But here the state and condition both of the agent and of the sufferer must be considered; otherwise many a wrong would not be matched by its penalty. Who, I ask you, would say that these deserve an equal penalty, if a porter struck a praetor with his palm, and a worthless beggar did the same? Rightly, in this matter, the Mishnah directs that the disgrace of the one who suffers and of the one who inflicts it be considered. Rabbi Jacob has given the reason in the book already cited several times: roughly, that it is far greater disgrace if a man is compelled to receive it from a commoner of the lowest rank, than when it is inflicted by an illustrious man placed in a high rank. Conversely, he says, it is more unworthy for an honoured man placed in great dignity to be afflicted with shame and dishonour than when someone from the lowest common people incurs such reproach. 8 But what is the reason that the defendant is to be prosecuted expressly when he has affronted a naked man? For nakedness itself seems to excuse the other: for who is not ashamed to bare his own body? In this matter the laws rightly seem to disregard it. So observe that it is not any naked man who is considered here, but the one who is specifically protected here from disgrace, to whom by some chance the outer garment is lifted. In the East the Jews used long garments reaching to the ankles, which, if drawn up so that the body could be seen, was regarded as shameful. For this reason it was forbidden to ascend to the altar by steps, lest, with the feet raised, the hems and the wings of the garment be lifted and the thighs thus be seen, Exodus 20.26; I have treated this matter at more length elsewhere in Middoth. So if the wind should lift a wing of someone's garment, and one should thereby increase another's nakedness, and draw the garment up further, this is forbidden here; otherwise whoever does it will pay a fine in the name of the disgrace inflicted. (For those who were not priests seem often to have lacked breeches, Deuteronomy 25.11.) Hence in the Gemara we read: מהי פרוס דאתא ורקא [What is meant by 'Nudus'?] When a wind rushes in and blows up the garments, and someone coming near draws them further up, and so affronts him. Moreover, the author of the Mishnah touches on the blind man and the sleeping man, because it might easily be supposed that, since the disgrace inflicted by them is not noticed, the defendant would bear it unpunished. Therefore he imposes a fine on that defendant. On the contrary, since the sleeper sins in ignorance, he is not liable for the disgrace inflicted, and reason suggests that the same must be decided about the blind man. Thus knowledge and intention to inflict dishonour are looked at: so that, although one who falls from a roof against his will is liable for the damage, he is deemed to owe nothing in the name of the disgrace which he might perhaps inflict on someone in that fall (as if by that chance rush he thrust him down into the mud). The teachers draw this from Deuteronomy 25.11, where a woman who, while men are fighting, seizes the private parts of one of them in order to hold him back from striking her husband, is taught to be fined in the hand. The Talmudists take this passage as if the law looked only to the disgrace inflicted on the husband thereby. And from this they draw that in every dishonour the mind and will of the one who injures must be attended to: which the law expresses in saying of this woman, stretching out her hand; but no one stretches out a hand unless willingly, in order to achieve something. Aben-Ezra, however, asserts that the lawgiver considers also the danger, when he says: Moreover that place is dangerous; as if you said that a man seized by the private parts, and held back by force in his excitement, easily injures by the violence of his resistance. Further, as to the penalty appended, You shall cut off her hand, they expound it in the same way as that at Exodus 21.24, Eye for eye, where they contend that the eye is to be valued and an equal price paid. But Aben-Ezra is better, who writes to this effect: As eye for eye; if she does not redeem that hand, you shall cut it off. There he takes the same thing, but in another sense: not that a monetary fine is directly commanded there, but that by ἐπιείκεια [epieikeia] it is often permitted. The comparison with Exodus 21.30 altogether suggests this, as was discussed at more length on that matter earlier. Among the Romans, disgrace, insult, reproach and the like were forbidden by law. Hence Digest 47.10, law 15, §27: The praetor has in general forbidden anything to be done to the infamy of anyone. And as above we have learned from Rabbi Jacob that the insult grows from the fact that a person of inferior rank inflicts it, so Ulpian also speaks almost in the same way, whose words are cited under the same title, law 17, §3: Certain injuries done by free men seem of slight importance; but when done by slaves they are grave. For the insult grows from the person of the one who inflicts it. Besides, just as among the Jews the intention to inflict disgrace on another does not excuse one who afflicts someone else than the one he dishonours, so neither among the Romans. Maimonides, chapter 1, Chobel Oumaffik, section 14: המקכוין לכייס טעבד וכיוס לת כן חורין דמי כסתו של עבד [He who intends to dishonour a servant and dishonours a freeman], he who conceives in his mind to dishonour a servant, and afflicts a freeman with shame, shall pay the freeman as much as the servant's disgrace is valued. Similarly, under the title cited above, law 18, §3: If an injury is done to me by one who does not know me, or if someone thinks I am Lucius Titius when I am Gaius Seius, what is principal prevails, namely that he wishes to do an injury to me: for I am certain, even though he thinks I am other than I am, and therefore I have an action for injury.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Multam ob ejectum fœtum impositam lege Dei confirmant, quum ad hunc modum Ex. 21. 22. loquitur Legislator, Certantibus hominibus, si percusserit unus illorum mulierem gravidam, ita ut ejiciatur fœtus ejus, nec tamen sit exitium; omnino multator prout imposuerit ei maritus ipse mulieris, & per judices dato. Quam legem in hanc sententiam enarrant Judæorum Doctores, Si fœtus ejiciatur vel abortivus, sive qui ex intempestiva nativitate postea moriatur, sive etiam ejectus maneat superstes; multam quam maritus ex æquitate imposuerit, per judices imperandam esse: adeoque illa verba, Nec tamen sit exitium, mulierem ipsam concernere asseverant; mulierisque exitium intelligi, sive vitam, sive aliquod ipsius membrum perdiderit. Nostri autem Theologi cum fœtus, tum mulieris exitium intelligendum asserunt. Judæorum tamen sententia ratione destitui non videtur. Nam qui casu hujusmodi fortuito fœtum, cujus exitium non intendebat, perdit, eum pari cum eo pœna qui sciens volens alterum adultum hominem interfecit affici, durius vulgò judicatur. Differentiam duplicem ponunt, uti ex Abrabaniele ad hunc locum apparet: non tantum in priori causa hominem non perfectum interimi (quod tamen magno crimine non caret, quia ni interfectus fuisset, in perfectum hominem evasisset;) sed etiam illic fortuitam esse cædem duplici modo. animus non erat, ut fœtum læderet, nedum interficeret; præterea nec illam ullo malo afficere volebat, qua læsa fœtus ejectus fuit: agitur enim de eo qui cum alterum percutere vellet, ictum invitus in mulierem declinavit. ergò non nisi remota cædis causa est; & quidem præter animi intentionem. Quapropter hoc sibi legislator voluisse videtur, si fœtus ante tempus ejiciatur, nec exitium in muliere deprehendatur, reum pecunia multandum esse; sin verò mulier vel interficiatur, vel membrum amittat, aut vulneretur, aut aliud incommodum percipiat, talionem servandam. Vbi Judæi in hoc membro; reddes animam pro anima, sive vitam pro vita, inter se disputant, an vita reo eripienda; an vero pecuniaria multa irrogANDA sit. Sanè non video, quare à verborum proprietate recedendum sit: nam cum in sequentibus, oculum pro oculo, &c. verbis adhærendum sit; ut jam antea probatum fuit; quidni in primo membro hoc retineamus? hanc enim de homicidio legem passim inculcavit Deus; adeoque statim à diluvio hominibus, antequam denuò multiplicati fuissent, expresse lata fuit, Gen. 9. 6. & Deus verbis disertis & perspicuis multam pecuniariam in hoc crimine exclusit, Num. 35. 31. Itaque licet per Exod. 21. in oculi, dentis &c. interitu, pecuniariam multam ex ipsius legislatoris simili lege v.f. 30. admittam; in adempta vita eam hic non admitto: quia vitam pro vita exigens Deus, multam pecuniariam totidem verbis alibi excludit. Atq; Judæorum fundamentum ruit: posteriora enim verba assumunt, ubi dens pro dente, manus pro manu &c. postulantur. Atqui & hic omnia proprie accipienda contendo (quæ de re in superioribus) & dentem pro dente exigit lege divina; sed quemadmodum v.f. 30. permittitur pretii solutio, pariter eam in dente &c. permittendam dico, nec dentem erundum, vel manum amputandam; nisi reus atrociter id fecerit, aut pretium dando satisfacere detrectet. Vrgere solent incommodum talionis, contingere enim aliquando ut in talione æqualitas servari nequeat: nam si quis ob illatum vulnus vulneretur, vulneris æqualitas non facile servabitur; & si oculus eruatur, periculum erit ne mors subsequatur. Nihil hic eorum repetam quæ antea ad nostræ sententiæ confirmationem è legibus Dei protuli; sed patris respondeo, ut præteream certis modis occurri illis incommodis posse, ut experientia testatus, esse quod sibi reus ille omnia incommoda imputet: ut qui illius pœnæ gravitatem perspectam habens, nihilominus contra expressum Dei interdictum venerit. Insuper si dissimilia incommoda, quæ utrobique deprehendi queant, ad pœnam immutandam admittas, ne quidem in spontaneo homicidio pœnam à Deo inculcatam observare poteris. Paterfamilias, cui multi sint liberi, qui ipsius opera ad vitam sustinendam omnino egeant, cujusq; operâ respublica non mediocriter opus habeat, hic inquam occiderit cælibem, eumque privatum, qui tantum fruges consumere natus sit; in hoc exemplo, si ex lege Dei manifestissima homicidium morte puniatur, magna incommoda homicidæ supplicium sequentur, quæ in altero non erunt: nam respublica magnum patietur detrimentum; illiusque liberi ferme una interibunt, qui illius solius opera sustentabantur. An ob ista incommoda legem Dei rescindemus? Est quod rei accusentur hac in parte, quod ista incommoda excitarint. Denique nec istud prætereundum, qui dentem excussisset, manum amputasset; hanc sæpe alterius legis comparatione, pœnæ mitigationem impetrasse, uti redimere talionem potuerit. quod tamen priorem legem non evertit. Ut verò ad ejecti fœtus pœnam redeamus, cum ea convenit quod in legibus Salicis ti. 28. De homic. §. f. legitur, Qui infantem in utero matris occiderit, 8000 denariorum, qui faciunt solidos 200. scilicet culpabilis judicatur (hæc verba è par. 4. adjicienda.) At qui dolo malo mulieri per verbera abortiendi causa est, si partus animatus sit, lege civili capite plectitur: quod à pari probatur le. 38. de pœnis §. 5. Qui abortionis aut amatorium poculum dant, etsi dolo non faciant, tamen quia mali exempli res est, humiliores in metallum, honestiores in insulam amissa parte bonorum relegantur. quod si eo mulier aut homo perierit, summo supplicio afficiuntur. Ad Misnam redeamus, ubi cum damno dato, homo ad quinque præstanda sæpe obligetur; si per bovem simileve jumentum datum fuerit, solius damni repetitio conceditur: neque si ejecti fœtus jumentum causa fuerit, actio datur. Utrumque Talmudistæ duobus S. Scripturæ paragraphis statuminant. In damno per bovem dato omnia illa quinque non exigi eliciunt è c. 24. Levit. ῾f. 19. Quod si quis intulerit corporis vitium proximo suo: ubi pro quis in Ebraeo ish, homo. Atqui inquiunt, homo proximo, ait legislator; non vero, bos proximo: ergo homo laedens proximum ad illa omnia tenetur; non vero bovis laedentis nomine eadem praestare debet. Et licet de illis omnibus isto loco expresse non agatur, legem istam cum altera Ex. 21.19. comparant, eique similem agnoscunt. Alterum vero illud de abortu, sive potius abortivo, è commate 22. hujus 21, c. Exodi: ubi dicitur, Certantibus hominibus, si percusserit unus illorum mulierem gravidam &c. non dicitur, ajunt, certantibus bobus, quasi cum hujus feritate abortit foemina, fœtus compensari debeat. Haec est Judaeorum in legibus explicandis ratio ac modus, ut quaedam dilatent, quaedam coarctent levi de causa, imo plane nulla. Sane analogia legum, quae Ex. 21. ῾f. 28. &seq. ad finem usque capitis proponuntur, ut pauperiem per quadrupedes factam acrius persequamur, postulat. Si bovis occisoris nomine, ubi petulcum fuisse constat, proprietarius mortis reus peragatur, ῾f. 39. quidni si mulieri causa abortiendi fuerit, proprietarius fœtum compensare teneatur? Praeterea si ab ejusmodi petulco bove datum in altero bove damnum (῾f. ult.) totum compensandum sit; an homo à bove laesus, damnum suum quod ex plaga, curationis sumptibus, & cessatione patitur, repetere non poterit? deteriorne hominis, quam bovis erit conditio? Fateor tamen si bos petulcus non sit, minus exigendum: idque ex analogia legum; quae sub finem cap. 21. Exod. feruntur. Ideoque Judaeorum constitutionibus hac in parte jurisconsultorum Romanorum placita sunt praeferenda: quae habes lege, Si quadrupes: ubi in omni pauperie (ut loquuntur) aut animal quod nocuit, aut noxiæ æstimatio postulatur.
units.tr: They uphold the fine imposed for an expelled foetus by the law of God, since the Lawgiver speaks in this manner in Exod. 21. 22: If men strive together, and one of them strikes a pregnant woman so that her fetus is expelled, but there is no harm, he shall surely be fined, as the woman's husband shall lay upon him, and it shall be given through the judges. The Jewish doctors explain this law to this effect: if the fetus is expelled, whether it is premature or dies later from an untimely birth, or remains alive after being expelled, the fine which the husband imposes in fairness is to be exacted through the judges. Accordingly they maintain that the words but there is no harm concern the woman herself, and that harm to the woman is understood whether she loses her life or some limb. Our theologians, however, hold that harm must be understood both to the fetus and to the woman. The opinion of the Jews, nevertheless, does not seem to lack reason. For one who by such an accident loses a fetus he did not intend to harm is commonly judged to deserve a heavier penalty than one who knowingly and willingly kills another adult. They lay down a twofold difference, as appears from Abrabanel on this passage: first, in the former case the person killed is not yet a complete human being (which nevertheless is no slight crime, because had he not been killed he would have grown into a complete human being); but also, in that case the killing is accidental in two ways. The intention was not to harm the fetus, much less to kill it; moreover, he did not wish to inflict the injury by which the fetus was expelled: the case concerns one who, wishing to strike another, unwillingly struck the woman instead. Therefore the cause of the killing is only remote, and indeed beyond the intention of the mind. Wherefore the lawgiver seems to have meant this: if the fetus is expelled before its time and no harm is found in the woman, the guilty party is to be fined in money; but if the woman is killed, or loses a limb, or is wounded, or suffers some other injury, the law of retaliation is to be kept. Here the Jews dispute among themselves, on the words you shall give life for life, whether the guilty man's life is to be taken, or whether a fine of money is to be imposed. Certainly I cannot see why we should depart from the proper meaning of the words. For since in what follows we must adhere to the words eye for eye, etc., as has already been shown above, why should we not retain this in the first clause? For God repeatedly impressed this law concerning homicide; and so it was expressly given to men immediately after the Flood, before they had multiplied again (Gen. 9. 6), and God, in plain and clear words, excluded a money fine for this crime (Num. 35. 31). Therefore, although through Exod. 21 I admit a money fine in the case of the loss of an eye, a tooth, etc., by the similar law of the same Lawgiver at v. 30, in the case of the taking of life I do not admit it here, because God, who demands life for life, excludes a money fine in so many words elsewhere. And so the Jewish foundation collapses: for they take the later words, where tooth for tooth, hand for hand, etc., are demanded. But here too I maintain that everything must be taken in its proper sense (as concerning this matter I have said above), and the divine law demands tooth for tooth; yet just as at v. 30 the payment of a price is permitted, so I say that in the case of a tooth, etc., it is likewise to be permitted, and that a tooth need not be knocked out or a hand cut off, unless the offender has done it atrociously or refuses to make satisfaction by giving the price. They are accustomed to press the inconvenience of retaliation, for it sometimes happens that equality cannot be preserved in retaliation: for if someone is wounded in return for a wound inflicted, equality of wound will not easily be kept; and if an eye is torn out, there will be danger that death follows. I will not here repeat what I have previously brought forward from the laws of God to confirm our view; but I answer, to pass over the fact that these inconveniences can be met in certain ways, as experience attests, that the offender may impute to himself all the inconveniences, since he, having a clear view of the severity of that penalty, nevertheless came against the express prohibition of God. Moreover, if you admit dissimilar inconveniences, which may be found on either side, as grounds for changing the penalty, you will not be able to observe even the penalty God impressed for voluntary homicide. Suppose a father of a family, who has many children, who absolutely needs his labour to sustain life, and by whose labour the commonwealth has no small need, kills an unmarried man, and one private, who was born only to consume fruits: in this example, if by the most manifest law of God homicide is punished by death, great inconveniences will follow the killer's punishment which will not follow in the other case; for the commonwealth will suffer great loss, and his children will almost all perish together, who were sustained by his labour alone. Shall we, on account of these inconveniences, rescind the law of God? Are the accused to be blamed in this respect, that they brought about these inconveniences? Finally, this too must not be passed over: he who knocked out a tooth or cut off a hand has often obtained a mitigation of the penalty by comparison with another law, so that he could redeem the retaliation. Yet this does not overturn the former law. But to return to the penalty for an expelled fetus: it agrees with what is read in the Salic laws, title 28, On Homicide, §. f.: Whoever kills an infant in its mother's womb shall be judged culpable for 8000 denarii, which make 200 solidi (these words are to be added from par. 4). But whoever by evil design causes a woman, by blows, to abort, if the birth was animate, is punished by capital penalty under civil law; which is proved by the like law, 38, On Penalties, §. 5: Those who give a potion of abortion or of love, even if they do not do it with evil intent, nevertheless, because it is a matter of bad example, are relegated, the humbler to the mines, the more honourable to an island, with the loss of part of their goods. But if a woman or a man has died from it, they are subjected to the highest punishment. Let us return to the Mishnah, where when damage has been done by a man, he is often bound to make restitution of five things; if it was done through an ox or similar beast, only the restitution of the damage itself is granted; nor, if the cause was a beast which expelled the fetus, is an action given. The Talmudists support both views by two paragraphs of Holy Scripture. They infer that in damage done by an ox all those five are not to be exacted from Lev. 24, v. 19: If anyone inflicts a bodily defect on his neighbour: where for anyone the Hebrew has ish, man. Yet, they say, the lawgiver says man to neighbour; not ox to neighbour: therefore a man who injures his neighbour is bound to all those things; but on account of an injuring ox he ought not to furnish the same things. And although all those things are not expressly treated in that place, they compare this law with the other at Exod. 21. 19, and acknowledge it to be similar. But that other passage concerning abortion, or rather an abortive, from verse 22 of this same chapter 21 of Exodus, where it is said: If men strive together, and one of them strikes a pregnant woman etc., does not say, they claim, if oxen strive together, as if with the ferocity of such a beast the woman miscarries and the fetus ought to be compensated. This is the Jewish manner and method in explaining the laws: they extend some things and restrict others for slight reason, indeed for no reason at all. Surely the analogy of the laws, which are set forth in Exod. 21 from verse 28 to the end of the chapter, requires that damage done by quadrupeds be pursued more sharply. If the owner of a goring ox, where it is established that it was accustomed to gore, is prosecuted as guilty of death on account of the ox's killing (v. 39), why should not the owner be bound to compensate the fetus if the woman was caused to abort? Moreover, if the damage done by such a goring ox to another ox is to be compensated in full (v. ult.), will a man injured by an ox not be able to recover his damage, which he suffers from the wound, the costs of cure, and loss of work? Will the condition of a man be worse than that of an ox? I admit, however, that if the ox is not goring, less is to be exacted, and this from the analogy of the laws which are set out at the end of Exod. 21. Therefore in this matter the decisions of the Roman jurists are to be preferred to the constitutions of the Jews: which you have in the law, If a four-footed beast, where in every case of damage (as they say) either the animal that did the harm or the estimate of the harm is demanded.

units.la: המכה אביו ואת אמו ולא עשה בהם חבורה והחובל בחבירו ביום הכפורי חייב בכולן. החובל בעבר עברי חייב בכולן חוץ מן השבת בזמן שהוא שלו החובל בעבד כנעני של אחרים חייב בכולן רבי יהודה אומר אין לעברים נושא׃
units.tr: He who strikes his father or his mother, but does not leave a wound on them, and he who wounds his fellow on the Day of Atonement, is liable for all of them. He who wounds a Hebrew bondservant is liable for all of them, except for the loss of time, while the servant is his own. He who wounds the Canaanite slave of another is liable for all of them. Rabbi Judah says: Hebrew slaves have no [נושא].

units.la: Percutiens patrem aut matrem suam, nec in iis tamen vibicem excitans; vitians proximum suum expiationis die, ad illa omnia tenetur. Qui servum Hebræum vitiat, ad omnia illa tenetur; excepta cessatione, quàdiu ipsius est servus. Vitians aliorum servum Cananæum, ad omnia illa tenetur. D. Iudas asserit, in servos non cadere ignominiam.
units.tr: Whoever strikes his father or his mother without, however, raising a wale on them, and whoever wounds his neighbour on the Day of Atonement, is liable for all of those penalties. Whoever wounds a Hebrew servant is liable for all of them, except for the loss of work, for as long as he is the servant's master. Whoever wounds the Canaanite servant of another is liable for all of them. Rabbi Judah asserts that disgrace does not fall upon servants.
ANNOTATIONES.

units.la: ¹ R. Jacob in Choschen Mischpat pro vibice sanguinem habet, atque loco horum verborum, nec in iis tamen vibicem excitans, alia collocat, נלא הויאה מסם רס, nec tamen ex iis cruorem expresserit. Autor Misnæ, R. Jacob, Maimonides, Moses Mikkotfi in libro præceptorum; in eo conveniunt, filium qui parentes verberando vibicem non excitaverit, vel sanguinem expresserit, mortis reum non esse: sed sufficere, si quinque illa (de quibus supra actum fuit) præstet, quæ vulnerantes præstare tenentur. Hac ratione cum lege Dei pugnant: nam Ex.21.15. ita sancivit Deus, Qui percutit patrem suum, aut matrem suam, omnino morte plectitor. An hic distinguit legislator? nonne ut omnes potius exceptiones rejiceret, gemino vocabulo pœnam sancivit: מות יומת, moriendo morti detur? Vera expositio ‡f. 17. confirmatur: ubi qui verbis tantum parentes impetit, morti adjudicatur; nedum ut filius ulla verbera patri infligens mortis pœnam effugere possit. Et quod mirandum, R. Jacob, Maimonides & Moses Mikkotsi, cum mansuetudinis patroni esse velint; in eadem causa sævitiæ patrocinantur: dum eum morte afficiendum contendunt, qui patrem errore quodam occiderit. Quo casu tamen Deus sine ulla distinctione reum à morte absolvit; ut & alii legislatores. In aliis verò superstitiosi admodum sunt, ut à sanguine effundendo quammaximè abhorrere Judæi videantur: veluti quum metu ne filius patri sanguinem emittat, venam ipsi secare (aliaque nonnulla præstare, ut spinam educere & ulcus aperire, ne forte sanguis sequatur) non permittunt. quemadmodum in Choschen Mischpat numero 424. in principio videre est. Verum hæc missa faciamus.
units.tr: ¹ Rabbi Jacob, in the Choschen Mischpat, takes "vibex" to mean blood, and in place of these words, "nor yet does he raise a bruise on them," he puts another phrase, "nor has he drawn blood from them" [לא הוציאה מהם דם]. The author of the Mishnah, Rabbi Jacob, Maimonides and Moses Mikkotsi in the book of precepts agree that a son who beats his parents without raising a bruise or drawing blood is not liable to death; it is enough that he perform those five things (of which we spoke above) which those who wound are bound to perform. This view conflicts with the law of God. For in Exodus 21:15 God decreed thus: "He who strikes his father or his mother shall certainly be put to death." Does the lawgiver here make any distinction? Rather, in order to reject all exceptions, did he not decree the penalty with a double expression: [מות יומת], "let him be put to death by dying"? The true interpretation is confirmed by the case in which one who attacks his parents only with words is condemned to death; how much less could a son who inflicts any blows on his father escape the penalty of death. And what is remarkable: Rabbi Jacob, Maimonides and Moses Mikkotsi, though they wish to be advocates of mildness, in the same case play the advocate of cruelty, since they contend that he is to be put to death who killed his father by some mistake. Yet in that case God absolved the guilty party from death without any distinction, as did other lawgivers. In other matters, however, they are excessively superstitious, so that the Jews seem to shrink as far as possible from shedding blood: for example, for fear that a son might draw blood from his father, they do not permit a vein to be cut for him (nor some other things, such as removing a thorn or opening an ulcer, lest blood perhaps follow). This may be seen in the Choschen Mischpat, number 424, at the beginning. But let us set these matters aside.

units.la: Dubium hic oboritur de eo qui corporis vitium intulerit proximo expiationis die, an curationem, cessationem &c. compensare cogatur; an vero verberibus luere teneatur: verbera enim à cæteris pœnis reum liberant. Ratio quare plagis obnoxius videatur, ex illa lege Talm. profluit, qua Cod. Maccoth c. 3. sect. 2. eum qui opus facit die expiationis, plagis cædendum judicant. atqui legimus Cod. Cethouboth f. 32. p. 2. [illegible, ~12 letters] Vbicunque (id est, in quocunque crimine) multa pecuniaria & flagellatio merita est, atque reum obtestati sunt; is vapulando vapulat, pecuniam non pendit. Itaque à multa absolvendus videtur. Nihilominus Misna nostra solas plagas quadraginta una minus non exigit: cujus hanc reddunt rationem in Cethouboth f. 32. [illegible, ~10 letters] qui multam solvit, non vapulat; sed [illegible, ~12 letters] intendens lex sermonem in eo qui vitiat proximum, ad compensationem pecuniariam obligat. Ibidemque citatur sententia Levit. 24. 19. Quemadmodum fecit, sic fiat ei, & paulo post ⁊ f. 20. Prout intulerit corporis vitium homini, ita infertor ei. In Hebræo occurrit verbum [illegible, ~6 letters] dedit pro intulit. unde quærit Gemara, [illegible, ~12 letters] Quorsum mihi proponitur res, quæ dari potest, & quænam ista est? deinde respondet, pnn, pecunia. quasi dicat, Scriptura idem duplici sententia exprimens, posteriori verbum dandi adhibet, quo nos doceat illam multam in dando consistere, adeoque dandam esse pecuniam qua pro illato vitio satisfiat. De firmitate illius argumenti non disputo; quid illi sentiant jam perspectum habemus. Leges autem Romanæ nihil de speciali isto facto statuunt, si quis die expiationis alterum vulneret. Qui corporis vitium servo suo, eiq; Ebræo intulerit, ad curationem, damni compensationem &c. hic astringitur, excepta cessatione: quia quod ab opere cessat ipsi domino obest, totaque jactura ipsum concernit. Hæc ita constituunt: quia legem Ex. 21. 26. Quum percusserit quis oculum servi sui &c. in libertatem dimittito eum &c. ad servum Cananæum cum nostrorum quibusdam referunt. Verum non video, quid impediat quominus hæc verba de servis in genere intelligantur: qui quidem aliis in rebus pares non sunt; nihilominus in corporis detrimento æquantur, ut libertate ob oculum corruptum &c. donentur. Adeo ut lex illa Levit. 24. 19. liberas personas tantum concernat. quod melius patet è comparatione Lev. 24. 17. cum Exod. 21. 21. Quocirca Maimonides mihi non persuadet, quod de servo Cananæo è Misna quinta decernit: Qui vitium infert servo suo Cananæo, liber est, (scilicet ab illis quinque;) quasi idem in servo Israelita non obtineret. Per Cananæum quemvis designat qui Israelita non sit: Ebræo enim sive Israelitæ eum opponit. Magis placet alterum ipsius, quod Alphes & R. Chananeel similiter affirmant: Si quis alterius servo Ebræo manum amputasset, similemve injuriam intulisset, eum læso fundum daturum; cujus fructum dominus ipsius servi percipiat, donec manumissus fundum cum reditibus auferat. Atque hoc modo observabitur analogia legis Ex. 21. 7. Ne exito ut isti servi exeunt: ut quidem illam accipit S. Jarchi, qui diversas conditiones vulneratorum servorum hic innui existimat. Quæ Mifna in eum statuit,qui alterius servum Cananæum læsisset, non pugnant cum eo, quod ad Num. 3. è verbis Ex. 21. 26. confirmavi, omnes fervos ob vitiata membra manumittendos: nam illic de lædentis fervo agebatur; hic verò de fervo alterius. Tandem privata Judæ sententia de ignominia fervi profertur, quasi fervis inusta ignominiæ nota compensanda non fit. Verum ut Maimonides & Obadia de Bartenora observant, ipsius sententia non recipitur: sublesto enim argumento nititur,quod è comm. 11. c. 25. Deut. depromitur: ubi ignominia alicui illata vindicatur. ibi cum fratris fiat mentio,servum ab ignominia non defendi putabat: quasi verò vir cum fratre, phrafi Hebræa non significaret,alter cum altero;nec fervi Ebræi fratres censerentur. Hac sectione ne manus parentibus inferantur cavetur: sed magis id præstat Vlpianus: uti est le. 1. li.37. Dig. §.2. Si filius matrem aut patrem quos venerari oportet,contumeliis adficit, vel impias manus eis infert; prafectus urbis delictum ad publicam pietatem pertinens, pro modo ejus vindicat. De fervis etiam, quos hæc Mifna ab injuria defendit, Divus Pius ad Ælium Marcianum ff. De his qui fui vel alieni juris, l. 2. Si vel durius habitos (scilicet servos) quam æquum est, vel infami injuria affectos cognoveris, venire jube; ita ut in potestatem domini non revertantur. & postea,Divus etiam Hadrianus Vmbriciam quandam matronam in quinquennium relegavit, quod ex levissimis causis ancillas atrocissime tractaffet.Denique de aliorum fervis non lædendis, vel saltem injuria compensanda ff. Ad legem Aquiliam, l.45. §.1. Lege Aquilia agi potest, & fanato vulnerato, fervo fc. ut habet glofla, ratione expensarum & operarum. Vide & alia dicta eodem titulo.
units.tr: A doubt arises here about one who has inflicted a bodily injury on his neighbour on the day of atonement, whether he is compelled to make compensation for the healing, the cessation of work, and so on, or whether he is bound to atone with stripes; for stripes free the guilty party from other penalties. The reason why he seems liable to blows arises from that law of the Talmud by which, in the tractate Makkoth, chapter 3, section 2, they judge that one who does work on the day of atonement is to be beaten with stripes. Yet we read in the tractate Kethuboth, folio 32, page 2: Wherever (that is, in whatever crime) a fine and flogging are deserved, and the guilty party has been called upon to answer, he who is flogged does not pay the money. Therefore he seems to be freed from the fine. Nevertheless our Mishnah demands only forty stripes less one, and they give this reason in Kethuboth, folio 32: "He who pays the fine is not flogged; but the law, directing its speech to him who injures his neighbour, binds him to pecuniary compensation." In the same place is cited the sentence of Leviticus 24:19: "As he has done, so shall it be done to him," and shortly after, folio 20: "As he has inflicted a bodily injury on a man, so shall it be inflicted on him." In the Hebrew there occurs the verb [נתן], "gave," in place of "inflicted," whence the Gemara asks: "Why is a matter set before me that can be given, and what is that?" Then it answers: money [כסף], as if to say that Scripture, expressing the same thing in a double form, uses the verb "to give" in the second place, to teach us that the fine consists in giving, and that therefore money must be given by which satisfaction is made for the injury inflicted. I do not dispute the firmness of that argument; we already understand what they think. But the Roman laws say nothing about this special case, that if someone wounds another on the day of atonement. For one who inflicts a bodily injury on his slave, who is a Hebrew, is bound to pay for the healing, compensation for the loss and so on, except for the cessation of work, because what ceases from work harms the master himself, and the whole loss concerns him. They lay this down because they refer the law of Exodus 21:26, "When a man strikes the eye of his servant, etc., he shall let him go free, etc.," to a Canaanite slave, with some of our people. But I do not see what prevents these words from being understood of slaves in general; who indeed are not equal in other respects, yet in bodily harm they are made equal, so that they are given freedom on account of an injured eye and so on. So that law of Leviticus 24:19 concerns only free persons. This is more clearly seen from comparing Leviticus 24:17 with Exodus 21:21. Therefore Maimonides does not persuade me in what he decides from the fifth Mishnah about a Canaanite slave: "He who inflicts a bodily injury on his Canaanite slave is free" (namely from those five penalties), as if the same did not hold for an Israelite slave. By "Canaanite" he means anyone who is not an Israelite; for he sets him against the Hebrew or Israelite. The other view of his pleases me more, which Alphes and Rabbi Chananeel similarly affirm: if anyone had cut off the hand of another's Hebrew slave, or inflicted a similar injury, he is to give the injured man a field, whose produce the slave's master may receive until the slave, set free, takes away the field with its revenues. And in this way the analogy of the law of Exodus 21:7, "they shall not go out as male servants go out," will be observed, as indeed Rashi understood it, who thinks that different conditions of wounded slaves are hinted at here. What the Mishnah lays down against one who had injured another's Canaanite slave does not conflict with what I argued at Numbers 3 from the words of Exodus 21:26, that all slaves are to be set free because of injured limbs; for there the case was of a slave belonging to the one who inflicts the injury, but here it is of a slave belonging to another. Finally, the private opinion of Judah about the disgrace of slaves is put forward, as if the mark of disgrace inflicted on slaves were not to be made good. But as Maimonides and Obadiah of Bertinoro observe, his opinion is not accepted: for it rests on a weak argument drawn from Deuteronomy 25:11, where disgrace inflicted on someone is avenged. There, since mention is made of a brother, he thought a slave was not protected from disgrace; as if the Hebrew phrase "a man with his brother" did not mean "one with another," nor were Hebrew slaves counted as brothers. This section provides against hands being laid on parents; but Ulpian provides this more strongly, as in law 1, book 37 of the Digest, §2: "If a son insults his mother or father, whom he ought to revere, or lays impious hands on them, the prefect of the city punishes the offence, which pertains to public piety, according to its measure." Concerning slaves also, whom this Mishnah protects from injury, the Divine Pius, writing to Aelius Marcianus, in the Digest, On those who are under their own or another's power, law 2: "If you learn that slaves have been treated more harshly than is fair, or have been subjected to shameful injury, order them to be sold, so that they do not return to the power of their master." And afterwards: "The Divine Hadrian also banished a certain matron, Umbricia, for five years, because she had treated her maidservants most atrociously for very slight causes." Finally, concerning not injuring the slaves of others, or at least making good the injury, in the Digest, On the Lex Aquilia, law 45, §1: "An action may be brought under the Lex Aquilia, both for a healthy slave and for a wounded one", namely, as the gloss has it, "by reckoning the expenses and the labour." See also other sayings under the same title.

units.la: חרש שוטה וקטן פגיעתן רעה החובל בהן חייב Surdi, stulti, & pupilli occursus infelix est: quia eos vitians, tenetur;
units.tr: The deaf, the imbecile and the minor: their encounter is evil; whoever injures them is liable. The deaf, the fool and the child: their meeting is unlucky, since whoever injures them is liable. [חרש שוטה וקטן פגיעתן רעה החובל בהן חייב]
But they, when they injure others, are exempt. [והם שחבלו באחרים פטורין]
"The slave and the woman: their injury is evil" [העבד והאשה פגיעתן רעה]
The one who wounds them is liable, and they who have wounded [החובל בהן חייב והם שחבלו]
In other cases they are exempt, but they pay [באחרים פטורין אבל משלמין]
after a time, when the wife is divorced [לאחר זמן נתגרשו האשה]
or the servant is set free: they are liable to pay. [נשתחרר העבד חייבין לשלם]

units.la: tur ; quum ipsi alios vitiant, liberi sunt. Servi & marita occursus infelix est : eos vitians tenetur ; quum ipsi alios vitiant, liberi sunt; verum postea repudiant: marita quum ei repudium mittitur ; servus quum libertate donatur, rependere debent.
units.tr: ...tur; when they themselves injure others, they are free. The servant and the married woman: their encounter is evil; whoever injures them is liable; when they themselves injure others, they are free; but afterwards, when the wife is divorced or the servant is set free, they must make restitution.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Duplex est lectio: quidam & plerique codices habent פגיעתן רעה, occursus infelix est; Basileensis tamen editio eorum loco haec ponit verba, non expedit cum ipsis sociari. ac si dicat, si cui cum ipsis negotium sit, ipsorum conditio potior: ideoque illa conversatio utilis non est. Atque in sensu nulla differentia; licet verba discrepent. Talmud autem Hierosolymitanum priorem lectionem confirmat.
units.tr: There are two readings. Some and most manuscripts have "their encounter is evil" (פגיעתן רעה), but the Basel edition puts in their place the words "it is not advantageous to associate with them": that is, if anyone has dealings with them, their position is the stronger, and so that association is not useful. The sense is no different, though the words differ. The Jerusalem Talmud confirms the first reading.

units.la: Porro surdus, fatuus, pupillus idcirco absolvuntur, quod naturae vitia, vel aetatis imbecillitas idoneos esse non sinunt, ut sibi caveant, ne alios damno ullo afficiant. Hoc sibi vult Maimonides, cum illos ad compensationem teneri negat; licet stultus resipiscat, surdus auditum recuperet, pupillus adolescat: quod dum peccarent, scientia carerent.
units.tr: Moreover, the deaf, the fool and the minor are acquitted for this reason: a natural defect or the weakness of age does not allow them to be competent to take care that they do no harm to anyone. This is what Maimonides means when he denies that they are bound to make compensation; even if the fool comes to his senses, the deaf man recovers his hearing, or the minor grows up, they lacked knowledge at the time when they did wrong.

units.la: Verum maritae & servi ratio diversa est: licet enim absolvantur, dum maritus uxorem, & dominus servum retinet; nihilominus tenentur, quum uxor repudiata, servusque manumissus est. Fundamentum in obligatione praecedenti: nam utrq; dum peccaret reatu implicabatur; sed quod uterque nihil haberet, nihil etiam exigebatur. Illi vero ob naturalem defectum non obligabantur: ideoque ab iis licet immutatis, nihil exigere fas est. At objici posset, quare maritata nihil habere dicatur: quum tamen ipsi attribuatur, est dos quam inferre solet, quamque maritus decoquere non poterat: ideoq; Glolla
units.tr: But the case of the wife and the servant is different. For although they are acquitted while the husband keeps the wife and the master keeps the servant, nevertheless they are liable when the wife is divorced and the servant is manumitted. The ground lies in the earlier obligation: for each, while doing wrong, was bound by guilt; but since each had nothing, nothing was demanded either. The others, however, were not bound because of their natural defect; therefore, though they are changed, it is not right to demand anything from them. But someone might object: why is the married woman said to have nothing, since property is attributed to her, namely the dowry she usually brings in, which the husband could not squander? And so the Gloss

units.la: Glossa in Baba Bathra c. 9. נכסים הנקנסין ויוצאין ממה הייכו נכסי מלוג, bona quae unà cum ipsa veniunt & discedunt, vocantur bona מלוג propria, quae ipsi accidunt è paterna familia, quorumque ipsi evictio competit. Nonne ergo uxor facultatem solvendi debita habere creditur, cum istiusmodi bona possideat? Tamen iis uti non potest: quia dum marito conjungitur, maritus illorum bonorum fructus percipit; & ipsa sors, nisi repudium interveniat, ipsi marito מתועבר לירושה, subjecta manet ad haereditatem. ut si uxor moriatur, maritus illam haereditate acquirat, vel filii post patris obitum eam accipiant. Quam benignè de surdo, furioso & pupillo leges Romanæ judicent, jam antea sub finem notarum ad c. 4. sect. 4. è Jure civili ostensum fuit: unde quid de hoc casu statuerent, constare potest. Servus verò si delinquat, secus quam Judæi faciunt, Romanæ leges imperant. Ut ff. De noxalibus actionibus, pr. Noxales actiones appellantur, quae non ex contractu, sed ex noxa, atque maleficio servorum adversus nos instituuntur. quarum actionum vis & potestas haec est; ut, si damnati fuerimus, liceat nobis deditione ipsius corporis, quod deliquerit, evitare litis aestimationem. Id tamen cum lege Judaica convenit, quod habetur l. ejusdem tituli 6. Sed & servus ipse manumissus tenetur: puta nisi antea satisfactum fuerit. Tandem, uxoribus illud privilegium concedere non videntur Romani, ut quandiu cum marito vivit, conveniri de illato corporis vitio (puta si oculum eruerit &c.) non possit. Nam ad Cod. li. 9. t. 4. ex Authent. adjicitur, Si pro fiscali aut privato debito pulsetur, per virum suum, aut quem alium legitimè respondeat. Quod si noluerit vel respondere, vel persequi litem suam: legitimè in rebus suis executio procedat. Illud autem à Misna nostra alienum non est, quod Jurisconsulti observant, maritatam, cum utplurimum sine mariti autoritate contrahere non possit; ut debitum ex ejusmodi contractu ortum dissolvat, obligari, quum matrimonium solvitur.
units.tr: Gloss on Baba Bathra ch. 9: the goods that are brought in and carried out [נכסים הנקנסין ויוצאין] are the goods of the wife's own property [נכסי מלוג]. Goods which come and go together with her are called her own goods, which fall to her from her father's household, and for which she has the right of recovery. Does it not follow, then, that the wife is believed to have the means to pay her debts, since she possesses such goods? Yet she cannot use them, because while she is joined to her husband, the husband receives the fruits of those goods; and the principal itself, unless divorce intervenes, remains subject to inheritance for the husband [מתועבר לירושה], so that if the wife dies, the husband acquires it by inheritance, or the sons receive it after their father's death. How kindly the Roman laws judge the deaf, the insane and the minor was shown earlier, at the end of the notes on ch. 4, sect. 4, from the civil law; so it can be established what they decided in this case. But if a slave commits an offence, the Roman laws order otherwise than the Jews do. So the Digest, On Noxal Actions, pr.: Noxal actions are those which are brought against us not from a contract but from the harm and wrong of slaves. The force and power of these actions is this: that if we are condemned, we may, by surrendering the body that did the wrong, avoid the assessment of the lawsuit. That agrees, however, with the Jewish law, which is found in law 6 of the same title: But the slave himself, even when manumitted, is liable, namely unless satisfaction was made beforehand. Finally, the Romans do not seem to grant wives the privilege that, as long as she lives with her husband, she cannot be sued for bodily injury inflicted (for example, if she gouged out an eye, etc.). For in Code book 9, title 4, from the Authentic, it is added: If she is sued for a debt to the treasury or a private debt, let her answer through her husband or some other lawful representative. But if she is unwilling either to answer or to pursue her suit, let execution proceed lawfully against her property. Nor is it foreign to our Mishnah that the jurists observe that a married woman, since she usually cannot contract without her husband's authority, is bound by a debt arising from such a contract only when the marriage is dissolved.

units.la: הי הטכה אביו ואמו ועשה כהן חבורה והחובל בחבריו בשברת פטור מכולן מפני שהוא נרון בנפשו והחובל בעבר כנעני שלו פטור מכולן ו
units.tr: He who strikes his father and his mother, or who makes a priestly wound, and one who injures his fellow with a fracture, is exempt from all of these, because he is condemned in his own person; and one who injures his Canaanite slave is exempt from all of them.

units.la: Percutiens patrem suum & matrem suam, ita ut in iis vibicem excitet ', & vitians proximum suum ² in sabbatho, ab omnibus illis liber est; quia ipse morte damnatur: etiam vitians servum suum Cananeum, ³ ab omnibus illis liber est.
units.tr: Whoever strikes his father and his mother so as to raise a welt on them,¹ and whoever injures his neighbour² on the sabbath, is free from all those [charges], because he is condemned to death; whoever injures his Canaanite slave³ is free from all of them.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Antea percutiens patrem aut matrem absque vibice, vel sine sanguinis effusione aut expressione, condemnabatur, ut cicatricem, dolorem, curationem, cessationem & ignominiam compensaret; jam vero quia vibicem excitat, ab iis quidem absolvitur: sed ideo quia gravior poena irrogatur, puta mortis; nam capitale supplicium pecuniariam multam delet. Capitis vero poena Ex. 21.15. sancitur. Quae cum alibi, tum in libro Chinnouch dicitur fuisse ṗṅṅ, strangulatio: mortem enim illic sancitam autor in eo consistere ait, ut percutiens patrem laqueo suffocetur. Et quamvis vox in sacris literis adhibita marem proprie concernat; optime in eodem libro ex legislatoris mente ad feminas extenditur: quibus non minus tantum scelus interdictum fuisse docet recta ratio; quae scopum interdicti, & utriusque rei aequalitatem expendit. Romanos severe in hujusmodi homines animadvertisse, in superioribus observatum fuit. ² Hoc loco a quinque illis, quibus tenebatur iste qui proximum vitiaret, idem absolvitur si id sabbatho faciat: quia morte tenetur authoritate sanctionis, Num. 15.35. Verumenimvero Talmudistae scrupulum hic movent: siquidem ṗḥṗ, corrumpens & vitians aliquid die sabbathi apud ipsos mortis reus non habeatur; sed qui efficit aliquid & parat sive adaptat. Respondet secundum ipsorum conclusiones & placita Maimonides, הוא"ל ותפס כחת רוח לזרו הוא בית מחכל כחכירו הרי הוא כמתקן ונמצ' פון מיתס Quandoquidem conficit animi placationem prava sua indoli, dum proximum suum vitiat; ecce habetur instar illius qui aptat, adeoque peccatum mortale deprehenditur. ac si diceret, ille quidem potius destruit, quam ut aliquid novi faciat; tamen quia hoc efficit ut concitatus animus vindicta subsidat, & naturalis illa pravitas suavitatem quandam ex alieno malo percipiat, aliquid novi efficere censetur. Denique servum Cananaeum vitians ab omni poena pecuniaria absolvitur: nimirum quod libertatem laesus acquirat; quae sufficiens sit compensatio. Sed ad Num. 3. sect. 3. ostendi, haec ad servum Cananaeum restringenda non esse; verum latissime, uti voces sonant, legislatoris verba Ex. 21. 26. accipienda: ut omnes servos cujuscunque conditionis complectantur. Istamque Dei clementiam ab Imperatoribus simili quadam lenitate comprobatam sub finem sectionis dedi.
units.tr: Formerly, a man who struck his father or mother without leaving a bruise, or without drawing blood or causing a wound, was condemned to pay for the scar, the pain, the cost of the cure, the loss of work and the disgrace. Now, however, because he has raised a bruise, he is acquitted of that payment, but only because a heavier penalty is imposed on him, namely death, since capital punishment cancels a fine in money. The death penalty is laid down in Exod. 21.15. The book Chinnouch says that this penalty was strangulation [ḥnq], and the author there holds that the death decreed consists in the one who struck his father being choked with a noose. Although the word used in Holy Scripture properly concerns men, the same book rightly extends it, from the mind of the lawgiver, to women as well, since right reason teaches that no less a crime is forbidden to them, and it weighs both the purpose of the prohibition and the equality of the two cases. It has been noted above how severely the Romans punished people of this kind. At this point, the one who injures his neighbour is acquitted of those five penalties if he does it on the sabbath, because he is liable to death by the authority of the decree in Num. 15.35. Yet the Talmudists raise a scruple here: for among them, one who corrupts [ḥbl] or injures something on the sabbath is not held liable to death, but one who makes something and prepares or adapts it is. Maimonides answers according to their own conclusions and opinions: since he produces an appeasement of his spirit by his perverse disposition, while he injures his neighbour; behold, he is held to be like one who adapts, and so a mortal sin is detected [הוא"ל ותפס כחת רוח לזרו הוא בית מחכל כחכירו הרי הוא כמתקן ונמצ' פון מיתס]. It is as if he were saying that the man rather destroys than makes anything new; yet, because by this he brings it about that his aroused spirit subsides, and that natural wickedness perceives a certain sweetness from another's harm, he is judged to have produced something new. Finally, one who injures a Canaanite slave is acquitted of every pecuniary penalty, namely because the injured slave gains his freedom, which is a sufficient compensation. But in Num. 3, sect. 3, I showed that these words are not to be restricted to the Canaanite slave; rather, the lawgiver's words in Exod. 21.26 must be taken very broadly, as the words sound, so that they embrace all slaves of whatever condition. At the end of the section I also set out how the Emperors approved this clemency of God with a similar mildness.

units.la: החוקע לחכירו נוחן לו סלע רבי יהודה אומר סשום רבי זמי הגלילי סנה סטרו נותן לו מאתים זו לאחר ידו נותן לו ארבע מאות זו צרם באזנו חלש בסערו רקק והגיע בו רוקו העביר טליחו מסנו פרע ראש האשה בשוק נותן ארבעמאות זו הכל לפיכבודו אלו עקיבא אפילו עניים שבישראל רואין אותם כאלו הם בני חורין שירדו
units.tr: Whoever wounds his neighbour pays him a sela. R. Judah says in the name of R. Zemi of Galilee: if he struck him with the palm of his hand, he pays him two hundred zuz; if with the back of his hand, four hundred zuz; if he wounded his ear, or slapped him, or spat and the spittle reached him, or removed his cloak, or uncovered the head of a woman in the market, he pays four hundred zuz. All these are assessed according to his honour. So R. Akiva. Even the poor of Israel are to be regarded as free men who have fallen into poverty.

units.la: Impingens socio colaphum, ei siclum pendit. D. Iudas nomine D. Iosés Galilei minam statuit. Si ei alapam impegit, ducentas drachmas ipsi pendit; si id fecit inversa manu, quadringentas drachmas solvit. Si ejus aures vulsit, evulsit ejus capillos, excreans eum conspuit, pallium ei detraxit, denudavit mulieris caput palam, quadringentas drachmas rependit. Omnia pro ipsius dignitate. D. Akiba statuit, Israelitarum pauperrimos considerari ac si essent nobiles, qui bonis suis
units.tr: Whoever strikes his fellow with a blow must pay him a shekel. Rabbi Judas, in the name of Rabbi Jose the Galilean, fixed a mina. If he struck him with the palm, he pays him two hundred drachmas; if he did it with the back of the hand, he pays four hundred drachmas. If he tore his ears, pulled out his hair, spat at him, stripped off his cloak, or uncovered a woman's head in public, he repays four hundred drachmas. All this is according to the dignity of the injured person. Rabbi Akiba ruled that the poorest of the Israelites should be considered as if they were nobles, who

units.la: סנכסיהם שהם בני אברהם יצחק ויעקב ומעשה באחר שפרע ראש האשה בשוק ובארת לפני לע וחייכו ליחז להארבע מאות זוז אל ר' חז לי זסן ונחן לו זסן שפרה עוסרת על פתח חצר' ושכר את הפך בפניה ובו כאיסר שמן גילחת את ראשה והיהה סטפחת וסנחח ידה על ראשה העמיר עליה עדים ובא לפני ר' עקיבא אסר לו רבי לזו אני נוחן ארבע מאות זוז אסר לו לא אמרת כלום שהחובל בעצמו אף על פי שאינו רשאי פטור אחרים שחבלו בו חייבין הקרוץ נטיעותין אף על פי שאינו רשאי פטור אחרים שקצצו את נטיעותיו חייבים ; suis excidissent: quia sunt Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi posteri. Exemplum habemus cuiusdam, à quo cum mulieris caput palam denudatum fuisset, ipsa convenit D. Akibam: qui illum condemnavit ut ipsi quadringentas drachmas penderet. Cui ille, mi doctor, concede mihi tempus. Itaque concesso tempore, cum ipsam astantem ostio atrii sui observaret, confregit in ejus conspectu lenticulam, cui inerat oleum fermè dimidii λεπτὸν. Hîc cum nudato capite ipsa manus comploderet, manusque capiti imponeret, ei testes appesuit. Deinde ad D. Akibam accedens ei dixit, mi Doctor, huicne ego quadringentas drachmas persolvam? Cui ille, nihil est quod dicis: quia seipsum vitians, quamvis id non conveniat, liber est; alii qui ipsum vitiarunt, tenentur: precidens plantas suas, quamvis id indecens sit, liber est; alii qui ejus plantas praciderunt, tenentur.
units.tr: their property, since they are the sons of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And there was a case of a man who uncovered a woman's head in the marketplace, and she came before Rabbi Akiba. He ruled that he must pay her four hundred zuz. He said to him, "Rabbi, let me have time." So when she was standing at the door of her courtyard, he broke a little pot in her sight, which held about a quarter-log of oil. He shaved her head, she became bald, and he laid his hand on her head. He brought witnesses against her. Then he came before Rabbi Akiba, and said to him, "Rabbi, am I to pay her four hundred zuz?" Rabbi Akiba said to him, "You have said nothing. One who injures himself, though he has no right to do so, is exempt; others who injure him are liable. One who cuts down his own plantings, though he has no right to do so, is exempt; others who cut down his plantings are liable." Since they are children of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. We have an example of a certain man who uncovered a woman's head in public; she brought the matter to Rabbi Akiba, who condemned him to pay her four hundred drachmas. He said, "My teacher, grant me time." So, with time granted, while she was standing at the door of her courtyard, he broke in her sight a little pot which held about half a litra of oil. Then, when she was bare-headed and clapped her hands and laid her hand on her head, he hanged witnesses on her. Then, approaching Rabbi Akiba, he said to him, "My teacher, am I to pay her four hundred drachmas?" He replied, "You have said nothing: one who injures himself, though it is not proper, is free; others who injured him are liable. One who cuts off his own plants, though it is indecent, is free; others who cut off his plants are liable." [סנכסיהם שהם בני אברהם יצחק ויעקב ומעשה באחר שפרע ראש האשה בשוק ובארת לפני לע וחייכו ליחז להארבע מאות זוז אל ר' חז לי זסן ונחן לו זסן שפרה עוסרת על פתח חצר' ושכר את הפך בפניה ובו כאיסר שמן גילחת את ראשה והיהה סטפחת וסנחח ידה על ראשה העמיר עליה עדים ובא לפני ר' עקיבא אסר לו רבי לזו אני נוחן ארבע מאות זוז אסר לו לא אמרת כלום שהחובל בעצמו אף על פי שאינו רשאי פטור אחרים שחבלו בו חייבין הקרוץ נטיעותין אף על פי שאינו רשאי פטור אחרים שקצצו את נטיעותיו חייבים]
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Sequuntur jam aliarum injuriarum species: quarum damnum quidem, si corporis vitia spectes quae in superioribus expendebantur, magnum non est; sed omnes in dedecore inprimis quo alius afficitur, & quodam dolore, versantur. Itaque sicuti cum alterum manu quis verberat, id tribus modis plerumque fieri contingit, vel impacto colapho, vel alapa recta, vel eadem inversa; ita hoc loco singulis sua statuitur multa. Incipit à colapho, cum inquit, [Hebrew]: quæ verba variis modis ab enarratoribus Ebraeis explicantur. Hæc constitutio, ut [Hebrew] pendat siclum multis locis passim in Gemaris repetitur: ut Cod. Bechoroth sol. 50. p. 2. Vbi glossator, [Hebrew], qui proximum suum ad aurem verberat: quam sui præceptoris sententiam esse dicit; addítque aliam, [Hebrew], clangens proprie, qui ore suo in alterius auribus clanxit. quasi dicat, ut alibi tubâ clangere illa voce exprimitur; sic in hac constitutione maledicere significat: ubi quis palam maledictis veluti alterius aures ferit, cui scilicet maledicit. Eadem pene glossa in [Hebrew] f. 11. p. 2. & in Baba prima f.37. p.1. sub initium. Denique glossator ad hanc nostram Misnam. Maimonides Codice jam sæpius citato c. 3. sect. 8. quum ait [Hebrew], percusserit proximum suum volâ suâ, priorem explicationem approbat: non enim in genere hujusmodi verbera designat; sed quæ circa aurem infliguntur. qua de causa hanc Misnam explicans inquit, [Hebrew], ad cervicem ejus. Attamen in hac Misna explicanda cum Obadia de Bartenora, si nō omninò, saltem aliquatenus facere videtur. Hæc sunt ipsius verba, [Hebrew] qui cadit proximum suum, est, qui percutit proximi cervicem carpo manus clausa. vel, palmâ clausâ. Obadia de Bartenora, [Hebrew], qui digitos suos in manus suâ carpum vel, in volam, contrahit, & ipsum proximum pugno cædit. Docti expositores, cum hoc capite præcipuæ injuriæ corporibus illatæ multarentur, illam prætermissam non fuisse, qua colaphus proximo impingeretur, animadverterunt. Itaque quod alibi, puta sol. 27. Babæ postremæ p. 2. [Hebrew] quorundam judicio vocatur, id hoc loco designari autumarunt; nisi hanc differentiam addas, [Hebrew] latius ab iis exponi qui colaphũ significari volunt: nam cum Maimonides colaphum circa aures & cervicem impactum
units.tr: Now follow the other kinds of injury. As far as loss goes, if you look at bodily harms, which were weighed in the earlier passages, the loss is not great. But all of these consist chiefly in the disgrace that one person inflicts on another, and in a certain pain. So, just as when someone strikes another with the hand, this usually happens in one of three ways: with a fist-blow (colaphus), with a straight slap, or with the back of the hand, so here a fixed fine is set for each kind. The passage begins with the colaphus, when it says [הנכה בקורפוס]: words which the Hebrew commentators explain in various ways. This rule, that the offender pays a shekel [סלע], is repeated in many places throughout the Gemaras, for example Bechoroth fol. 50, p. 2, where the glossator says [who strikes his neighbour on the ear], which he says is his teacher's opinion; and he adds another, [clanging properly, one who has clanged with his mouth in another's ears]. As if to say: just as elsewhere the word expresses "to sound a trumpet," so in this rule it means to slander, where someone with insults strikes, as it were, the ears of the person he insults. Almost the same gloss appears in [Hebrew] fol. 11, p. 2, and in Baba prima fol. 37, p. 1, near the beginning. Finally, the glossator on this our Mishna. Maimonides, in the code already cited many times, ch. 3, sect. 8, when he says [he struck his neighbour with his palm], approves the former explanation. For he does not mean blows of this kind in general, but those inflicted about the ear. For this reason, in explaining this Mishna, he says [at his neck]. Yet in explaining this Mishna, Obadiah of Bertinoro seems to agree with him, if not altogether, at least in some measure. These are his own words: [he who falls upon his neighbour is one who strikes his neighbour's neck with the wrist of a closed hand], or with a closed palm. Obadiah of Bertinoro: [who draws his fingers into the palm of his hand, at the wrist] or into the palm, [and strikes his neighbour with a fist]. Learned expositors, when this chapter punished the chief injuries done to bodies, noticed that the blow by which a slap is struck on a neighbour had been passed over. So what elsewhere, for example Baba last, fol. 27, p. 2, is called by some the judgment [Hebrew], they thought was meant here, unless you add this difference: that the term is explained more broadly by those who want the colaphus to be meant. For while Maimonides wants a colaphus struck about the ears and neck to be marked by that word, these authors designate any blow.

units.la: illa voce notari velit; hac quemvis designant. Verumtamen in voce פנוקרת exponenda omnes non conveniunt. locus ita habet, לרכובפ שלש ולכניטיס חמש לפנוקרת שלש עבדים, Si quis genu trudat alium, tres sicli solvendi; si quis calcitret, quinque; si colaphizet, tredecim. Hic Rabbi Nathan in Aruch, secundò exponit, פכלאה בפגרוף יפת, percussio pugno facta loco manus. Tamen prius aliam expositionem propositerat: מתקורר היד פכסה בפנוי, obversa manu percussit faciem ipsius. Verum qui observationes marginales in Maimonidem conscripsit, nec colaphum, nec posteriorem hunc percutiendi modum significari per פנוקרת arbitratur; sed quod ibi Maimonides innuit, cum ita loquitur, תוקף פת חבירו בכמו פנוקרת, cedit proximum suum vola sua. ubi ex aliis verbis quibus alias species recenset, ita eum de cava manu agere liquet, ut nec alapa, nec colaphus, sed medium quid designetur.
units.tr: Yet not all agree on how the word פנוקרת is to be explained. The passage reads: [Si quis genu trudat alium, tres sicli solvendi; si quis calcitret, quinque; si colaphizet, tredecim] (that is, "If someone pushes another with the knee, three shekels are to be paid; if he kicks, five; if he strikes with a fist, thirteen"). Here Rabbi Nathan in the Aruch gives a second explanation: [a blow with a fist made in place of the hand]. Yet earlier he had put forward a different explanation: [the hand turned back struck his face]. But the author of the marginal observations on Maimonides holds that neither the colaphus nor this latter way of striking is meant by פנוקרת. What Maimonides hints at, when he speaks thus, [he strikes his neighbour with the palm of his hand], is that he means a blow with the hollow hand. From the other words by which he lists the other kinds, it is clear that he is speaking of the hollow hand, so that neither a slap nor a colaphus is meant, but something in between.

units.la: Deniq; Sal. J. ad פנוקרת hanc notam subjungit, asinariarum clitellarum pars anterior, qua proximum suum cædit. Variæ cum sint vocis פנוקרת expositiones, prima qua cum colapho confunditur, forte minus probabitur: siquidem istius multa tredecim sela'im, ; colaphi vero, uno שלה definitur. Nisi velis unum sela pro ignominia exigi (ut nonnulli existimant) tredecim verò pro ignominia, dolore &c. Quicquid sit, colaphum tam indignum visum fuisse Judæis videmus, ut ignominiam, dolorem, aliaque incommoda inde orta compensari certa lege præceperint. Et inprimis dedecoris notam hac ratione inustam Judæorum plerique hic considerant: unde liquet qua potissimum de causa Judæi Servatorem nostrum colaphis petierint. Hoc enim factum fuisse postquam à Synedrio condemnatus fuisset, testatur Mar. 14. 65. Caeperunt quidam insputare in eum, & obtegere faciem ejus, & colaphos ei infligere, & dicere ei Vaticinare. ubi circumstantiæ edocent ad ignominiam & dedecus collimasse Judæos. Eadem annotat Matt. 26.67. ubi Ebraica versio (quo magis actionem jam descriptam ex Ebraeorum scriptis, denotari scias) קְלִיךְ, & percusserunt eum pugnis, scilicet judices Judaei, de quibus locutus Matthaeus fuerat. 2 Quum pro colapho סלע decreverint, quid eo nomine veniat, expendendum venit. E textu Ebraeo & Chaldaeo inter se collatis satis liquet, סלע siclum & סלע, unum & idem esse: ut siclus sacer & communis dicatur סלע: licet Elias quatuor denarios singulis סלעין attribuat, quod de sacro accipiendum constat. Verumenimvero e multis Gemaris, סלע duo inter se valore admodum distantia significare docemur: (ut jam illam differentiam praeteream, qua סלע Judaicus duplum Galilaei valebat, ut est in Cethouboth f. 64.) duplex enim statuitur סלע, unus נורי, Tyrius; alter סלע מדינה, provincialis. Ille (si sacer) valebat drachmis quatuor; hic vero dimidia drachma. itaque hic erat illius pars octava. Singula, quia non satis perspecta, ex illorum Talmudistarum scriptis confirmabo. In Bechoroth f. 50. Ne dicas (in negotio nostro) siclum esse quatuor denariorum: sed dimidium denarii: nam homines siclum vocant dimidium denarii. & paulo ante, Omnis moneta argentea, quae determinatur & proponitur in lege, est moneta Tyria; at quae in illorum magistrorum verbis determinatur est moneta provincialis. Et quidem eo epitheto nuncupatur; quia, ut inquit Maimonides, eo tempore in Chanaan usitata erat. Hinc Glossa ad verba Gemarae f. 11. Kiddoufchin, siclus quatuor denariorum est siclus Tyrius; dimidium denarii est siclus provincialis. Forte dictus tamen siclus, quia quatuor ferme denarios aeneos continebat, ut alter ille argenteos: quemadmodum annotant. Addit Glossa istum סלע esse, octavam sicli Tyrii partem. Itaque non aberraret, qui Matth. 5. f. 26. Syriacum ..., octantem cum hoc סלע provinciali eundem faceret: quum hunc videamus octavam sacri sicli partem fuisse, puta dimidium denarium. Atque idcirco Matthæus κodράντης, quadrantem vocat; quia sicli communis pars quarta erat, licet octava sicli sacri. Quam bene Græcus & Syrus in Matthæi loco secundum hanc sententiam conveniunt? ubi aliàs operosè conciliationem quærunt etiam doctissimi. At dicat quis, nonne Marc. 12. 42. duo lepta, λεπτὰ, quadrantem constituere dicuntur? atqui λεπτὸν quinque chalcos esse docui Midd. p. 50. & e cap. 1. Schekalim sub finem confirmatur. ergo quadrans est tantum unus obolus. Verum hoc expendi velim, omnes quadrantes æquales non esse; sed diversos, prout ad totum quid referuntur. Quadrans sicli communis est siclus provincialis: id jam ostendi; nec æquus lector, uti spero, obnitetur. Quadrans verò ארבע, darma, sive drama tantum non est; sed obolus unicus, sive duo λεπτὰ, ut Servator noster apud Marcum loquitur. De drama ita se rem habere, ut credas, consule commentaria in Maimonidem Cod. Kele Hammikdas. c. 2. Præterea id attente considerandum est, quod in Gemara Kiddoufchin f. 11. p. 2. legimus. homines vocant, dimidium denarii, Ifliram. eadem ferme in Cethouboth f. 64. p. 1. quanti valet Afliram? dimidio denario. ubi Glossa, denario scilicet Tyrio, qui sex argenteos trefles continet. Hinc jam liquet, δοκάριον cujus Matt. c. 10. & Luc. 12. mentio fit, non rectè cum aftira vel iftira conferri, quasi eadem esset moneta: quod tamen facit vir Doctissimus D. Tremellius ad c. 12. Marci. id moneo ne viri autoritas, utpote Judæi ideoque in istis versatissimi, quemquam seducat. Aftir sive aftira, ut neminem, qui loca è Talmude producta expendit, latere potest, valet tribus trefsibus, sive dimidio denarii, qui denarius duplicatus siclum communem reddit. Ergo aftir est (imperialis pars circiter decimasexta, si πηχυλέρως numos æstimemus, in priori templo; sed) decimasexta coronati decem drachmis Æginæis æstimati, tempore templi secundi, cum Servator in terris degeret. quo pretio duos passeres in Judæa væniisse non est verisimile; sed multo minore. Verum alius nummus erat Judæis usitatissimus, adeo ut eo in legum decisionibus veluti notissimo uterentur: uti in Baba Metsia c. 4. sect. 5. Nomen non adeo dissimile, quod fortasse Tremellium aliosque fefellit: dicebatur םיפּ & םפּר, sive ut loquitur Matth. & Lucas, ἀσσάριον. valebat, teste Glossatore in illum Bab. M. paragraphum, partem tressis quartam: quod cum Misnæ & Gemaræ verbis sol. 2. Cod. קרוטן apprime convenit; quantum est minutum? octava pars issari Italici. Ad quem Misnæ paragraphum consulendus est Maimonides, qui assarum (si eum expendamus subducto calculo) quadragesimam octavam sicli communis partem esse docet. ergo assarus non λεπτὸν, sed ipsius dimidium: nam λεπτὸν quinque chalcis sive deutis Hollandicis æstimandum jam antea docui. Unde corrigendus Hesychius, si verum sit, quod nonnulli testantur (ipse nondum inveni) eum alicubi scripsisse, ἀσσάριον καὶ λεπτὸν ἐν ἀσι. Ita per occasionem quædam N. Testamenti numismata suo valore æstimavimus: neque aliunde id fieri melius posse quam ex Ebræorum scriptis, qui suam monetam noverant; mihi persuadere possum. quadrantes, octantes aliosque nummos ad nostratem potius, quam Judæorum monetam examinare, atque inquirere quis nummus apud nos quatuor vel octo partes contineat; id vero ab omni ratione alienum existimo: nomina enim illa à suis nummis, quorum partes erant, Judæi defumserunt. Redeamus ad Misnam, 3 quæ ad alapam pergit, eumque qui ipsam infringit ducentis drachmis multat: etenim multo indignius & cum longe majori dedecore conjunctum censent Judæi, ubi quis alapam, quam si colaphum impingat. Alapam autem designari, interpretes docent, quorum unus מטרי inquit ..., volam sua manus ipsius faci
units.tr: Finally, Salomon Jarchi, at פנוקרת, adds this note: "the front part of the donkey's pack-saddles, with which one strikes one's neighbour." Since there are various explanations of the word פנוקרת, the first, which confuses it with the colaphus, will perhaps be less acceptable. For the fine for it is thirteen sela'im, while for the colaphus it is fixed at one sela. Unless you want one sela to be exacted for the disgrace (as some think) and thirteen for disgrace, pain, and so on. Whatever the case, we see that the Jews regarded the colaphus as so shameful that they prescribed by a fixed rule that the disgrace, pain, and other harms arising from it should be compensated. And above all, most Jews here consider the mark of disgrace branded in this way; from this it is clear for what reason in particular the Jews struck our Saviour with blows. For that this was done after he had been condemned by the Sanhedrin, Mark 14:65 testifies: [Some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to strike him with fists, and to say to him, Prophesy.] There the circumstances show that the Jews aimed at disgrace and shame. Matthew 26:67 notes the same, where the Hebrew version (so that you may know that the action just described is denoted from Hebrew writings) has [and they struck him with fists], namely the Jewish judges, of whom Matthew had spoken. Since they fixed the colaphus at one סלע, we must consider what that term means. From the Hebrew and Chaldee texts compared with each other it is quite clear that סלע means the shekel, and that סלע is one and the same thing; so that the sacred and common shekel are both called סלע, although Elias assigns four denarii to each סלע, which must be understood of the sacred one. Yet from many Gemaras we are taught that סלע signifies two coins of very different value (to pass over that difference by which the Jewish סלע was worth double the Galilean, as is found in Ketubot fol. 64). For two kinds of סלע are set down: one, the נורי, the Tyrian; the other, the סלע מדינה, the provincial. The former (if sacred) was worth four drachmas; the latter only half a drachma. So this was the eighth part of that. I will confirm these points, which are not sufficiently known, from the writings of those Talmudists. In Bechoroth fol. 50: "Do not say" (in our matter) "that the shekel is of four denarii, but of half a denarius; for men call half a denarius a shekel." And a little before: "Every silver coin that is fixed and proposed in the law is Tyrian money; but what is fixed in the words of those teachers is provincial money." And indeed it is so named because, as Maimonides says, it was then in use in Canaan. Hence the gloss on the words of the Gemara, fol. 11, Kiddushin: "the shekel of four denarii is the Tyrian shekel; half a denarius is the provincial shekel." Perhaps the shekel was so called because it contained about four bronze denarii, just as that other one contained silver ones, as the commentators note. The gloss adds that this סלע is "the eighth part of the Tyrian shekel." So he would not go wrong who made the Syriac [octantem] of Matthew 5, fol. 26, the same as this provincial סלע; since we see that it was the eighth part of the sacred shekel, namely half a denarius. And for this reason Matthew calls it κοδράντης, [quadrans], because it was a quarter of the common shekel, though an eighth of the sacred shekel.
