How well the Greek and the Syriac agree in Matthew's passage on this view, where otherwise even very learned men labour to reconcile them! But someone may say: do not Mark 12:42 say that two lepta, λεπτά, make a quadrans? Yet I have shown in Middoth, p. 50, that λεπτόν is five chalci, and it is confirmed from ch. 1 of Shekalim near the end. Therefore a quadrans is only one obol. But I would have it considered that not all quadrantes are equal, but differ according as they are referred to a whole. The quadrans of the common shekel is the provincial shekel; this I have already shown, and I hope a fair reader will not resist. But the quadrans of ארבע, darma, or drama, is not a quadrans at all, but a single obol, or two lepta, as our Saviour speaks in Mark. That the drama stands as you should believe, consult the commentaries on Maimonides, Kele Hammikdas, ch. 2. Moreover, it must be carefully considered what we read in the Gemara Kiddushin, fol. 11, p. 2: "men call half a denarius an Ifliram." Almost the same in Ketubot fol. 64, p. 1: "what is an Asliram worth? Half a denarius," where the gloss means the Tyrian denarius, "which contains six silver trefles." From this it is now clear that the δοκάριον, which is mentioned in Matthew 10 and Luke 12, is not rightly compared with the astir or istira, as though it were the same coin; yet the most learned Mr. Tremellius does this on Mark 12. I give this warning, lest the authority of so great a man, being a Jew and therefore very versed in these matters, lead anyone astray. The astir or astira, as cannot be hidden from anyone who examines the passages drawn from the Talmud, is worth three trefles, or half a denarius; and a denarius doubled makes the common shekel. Therefore the astir is (in the first temple, by the imperial reckoning, about the sixteenth part, if we value the coins by πηχυλέρως; but) the sixteenth part of a crown valued at ten Aeginetan drachmas, in the time of the second temple, while the Saviour lived on earth. It is not likely that two sparrows were sold in Judaea for this price, but for much less. But there was another coin very much in use among the Jews, so that they used it in deciding laws as a very well-known standard, as in Baba Metzia, ch. 4, sect. 5. Its name is not so different, which perhaps misled Tremellius and others: it was called םיפּ and םפּר, or, as Matthew and Luke speak, ἀσσάριον. It was worth, according to the commentator on that paragraph of Baba Metzia, the fourth part of a trefle; and this agrees very well with the words of the Mishna and Gemara, in Shabbat fol. 2, under the name קרוטן: "what is the smallest coin? The eighth part of an Italian as." On this paragraph of the Mishna Maimonides should be consulted, who teaches that the as (if we reckon it by calculation) is the forty-eighth part of the common shekel. So the assarus is not the λεπτόν, but half of it; for I have already shown that λεπτόν is to be valued at five chalci or Dutch doits. Hence Hesychius should be corrected, if it is true, as some witness (I have not yet found it myself), that he somewhere wrote ἀσσάριον καὶ λεπτὸν ἐν ἀσι. Thus, by the way, I have valued certain coins of the New Testament by their worth; and I can persuade myself that this cannot be done better than from the writings of the Hebrews, who knew their own money. But that one should examine quadrantes, octantes, and other coins by our money rather than the Jews' money, and inquire which coin among us contains four or eight parts, I think entirely foreign to all reason: for the Jews took those names from their own coins, of which they were the parts. Let us return to the Mishna, [3] which proceeds to the slap and fines the one who strikes it two hundred drachmas. For the Jews consider it a much more shameful thing, and attended with far greater disgrace, when someone gives a slap than when he strikes with a colaphus. The commentators teach that a slap is meant, one of whom says [the palm of his own hand, with the hand itself] — [with the back of the hand, the hand] — volam sua manus ipsius faci

units.la: Ee cici ciei impingendo. Hanc injuriam quam adeo exaggerant Iudæi, ab ipsis Servator passus fuit, quum jam mortis damnatus esset, Matt. 26. 67. tote ἐῤῥάπισαν: quæ verba Ebræus interpres bene reddidit, מכו ידיו בו ויכו, alii autem manus impegerunt in faciem ipsius. alii, scilicet ut Mar. 14. 65. observat, οἱ ὑπηρέται, ministri præcedentium Iudicum. Imo in synedrio, cum ipsos ob voluntariam ignorantiam carperet, unus ministrorum ἔδωκε ῥάπισμα τῷ Ἰησοῦ, alapam impegit ipsi Iesu. Verbum ῥαπίζω cum conjugatis hanc ignominiæ significationem habere, Hesychius non ignoravit: qui non tantum per ῥάβδῳ πληγῇ, bacillo verberare, quem sensum Cl. Beza sequitur; sed etiam per χλευάζειν, irridere proprie cavillis, παίζειν, illudere, & generaliter τύπτειν, percutere reddidit: percutit autem etiam ille qui alapam impingit, maximeque illudit & ignominia afficit. quam sententiam urbis nostræ decus D. de Dieu in notis ad Matthæum ex interpretatione Syra defendit. Vir Amplissimus & Nobilissimus eorum qui scientiam quærunt coryphæus, Daniel Heinsius, quid sibi Euangelistæ voluerint præclarè nobis in Aristarcho suo aperuit: ubi pag. 495. in Esaiæ quodam dicto cum Euangelica historia conciliando occupatur. de quo hæc mea est sententia. Esa. c. 50. v. 6. Corpus meum expono percussoribus, & malas meas depilantibus. postrema vox in Ebraeo est מרטים. de qua ejusque conjugatis D.K. מנתפים, Eorum significatio, quum pili decidunt aut cutis ipsius carnis, vel cum avelluntur. Utrumq; proprie in Servatore nostro præstitum contendo: nam de cute nullum est dubium; quum ita flagellatus fuerit, ut solo intuitu Pilatus populum ad misericordiam commotum iri speraret. Genis vero pilos detractos fuisse satis innuunt Euangelistæ: Lucas quum c. 22. 63. de viris Iesum in domo summi sacerdotis servantibus, donec judices causam ipsius tractarent, εἰσὶν ... ὕβριζον, Illudebant ipsi, cædentes. exponit qua ratione ipsum ludibrio habuerint rint, nimirum non tam verbis, quam manibus ipsum impetendo: inter ludibria autem quæ in ipso facto consistunt non minimum est, barbam vellere pilosque detrahere. Quapropter Euangelista διφθ voce aptissima usus est; utpote quæ cutem ipsam nedum pilos avellere significet. Matthæus & Marcus idem innuerunt, cum colaphis & alapis ab hostibus inhumanis cæsum narrarunt: ea enim magna ferocia præstiterunt, ut illud subsecutum fuerit. Adde utrumque Euangelistam spineam coronam calamo capiti infixam, distincte enarrasse; adeo ut cruentatis temporibus corona illa sine adhærentibus pilis detracta non fuerit. tempora autem malarum superiores partes constituunt. Quocirca ubi Esaiæ prophetia impleta narretur, satis constare autumo: adeoque simplicem sensum servari posse, non est quod negemus. Quæ deinde in Mishna sequitur dictio ors, est dubiæ significationis: nam invenias qui exponunt תשך, trahere; sunt etiam qui ססג, incisionem quandam facere. idque cum duplici modo fiat, ors פשך, vulsit aurem, exponitur משכו ומשכו כו רוסם, compressit eam (scilicet unguibus) in eaque cicatricem impressit; vel ורשך וכהשכו כפין עקיד, torsit aurem ejus, eumque dolore affecit veluti evulsione quadam. Ideo inter alia R. Nathan פרץ, scidit. Tria igitur sunt interpretamenta, trahere, unguibus cicatricem imprimere, denique ita vellere & torquere ut aliquatenus à capite laceretur. Postremam interpretationem facile admitto; quia Cod. de sacrificiis sol. 25. p. 2. in Gemara, invenio, פשך, si quis vellat aurem vituli, posteaque sanguinem ejus excipiat; rejectaneus est vitulus. Hinc omnino constat grave vulnus ista ratione infligi: utpote cum vitulus istiusmodi rejiciatur, cui auris ita vitiata sit; quum ors, vitium idcirco in illo accidisse censeatur. Nam non solum cum mactatur; sed etiam quum sanguis ejus ad spargendum excipitur, vitio omni carere debet. In eadem hac Mishna Iudæi inter gravissima opprobria & dedecora (quæ in his inprimis attendi annotant) etiam collocant, ubi pili evelluntur, homo conspuitur, pallium detrahitur. Hæc tam indigna judicarunt, ut quadringentarum drachmarum multam decreverint. Atque hæc Servatori præstita fuisse, ex Euangelica historia constat: ut nihil fere omissum, quod ad ignominiam apud Judæos pertinet, animadvertamus. Luc.22.63. merito id ἐμπαιζὼν, illudere nuncupavit, quum Christo pilos evellerent: quod grave ludibrium apud Judæos haberetur. de quo antea. Iudæorum judices, & Pilati milites Iesum conspuisse, sacri illi historici narrant. Denique vestem subinde detractam & quidem magno cum ludibrio, apud eosdem invenies: cum antequam eum Pilatus morti addixisset, de quo initio c.19. Ioh. tum postquam condemnatus ab ipso suisset, uti alii Euangelistæ testantur. Tandem generalis cautio subjicitur: quam in hanc sententiam accipiunt interpretes, multas illas in eos quadrare qui honoratos viros ignominia affecissent; sed minuendam multam pro humiliori aliorum conditione. ut pro gradibus, quibus admodum honoratis cederent & inferiores essent; injuria ipsis illata leviori multa vindicaretur. Atque hæc regula apud Judæos ita recepta fuit, ut R. Akibæ sententiam de æqualitate rejecerint. Romanos sedulò cavisse ne quis ullo ignominiæ genere afficeretur, docet vel solus titulus de injuriis Dig. li. 47. ubi t.10. l.1. Injuriam autem fieri Labeo ait, aut re, aut verbis ... omnemque injuriam aut in corpus inferri; aut ad dignitatem, aut ad infamiam pertinere. In corpus fit, cum quis pulsatur. Ad dignitatem, cum comes matronæ abducitur. Ad infamiam, cum pudicitia attentatur. Deinde speciales leges subjiciuntur, ut l. 15. §. Generaliter. Quodcunque quis fecerit aut dixerit ut alium infamet, erit actio injuriarum. & notandus paragr. primus ejusdem legis, Si quis pulsatus quidem non est, verum manus adversus eum levata, & sape territus quasi vapulaturus, non tamen percussit, utili injuriarum actione tenetur. Similiter
units.tr: Ee cici by a blow with the palm of the hand. The Savior himself endured this insult, which the Jews so greatly magnify, when he was already condemned to death (Matt. 26. 67): then they struck [ἐῤῥάπισαν]. The Hebrew translator renders these words well, מכו ידיו בו ויכו, but others, that they struck him in the face with their hands. Others, namely, as Mark 14. 65 notes, the attendants [οἱ ὑπηρέται], the ministers of the judges who had gone before. Indeed, in the council, when he reproached them for their wilful ignorance, one of the attendants gave a blow [ἔδωκε ῥάπισμα τῷ Ἰησοῦ], and struck Jesus himself with the palm of his hand. Hesychius knew that the verb ῥαπίζω [to strike with the palm], in its inflected forms, carries this sense of disgrace. He rendered it not only as ῥάβδῳ πληγῇ [to beat with a rod], to beat with a stick, which is the sense Beza follows, but also as χλευάζειν [to mock], to jeer at, properly with taunts, as παίζειν [to play with, to make sport of], to mock, and generally as τύπτειν [to strike], to strike. Yet he who gives a blow with the palm also strikes, and above all mocks and puts to shame. Our city's glory, D. de Dieu, defends this view in his notes on Matthew from the Syriac translation. That most distinguished and noble chief of those who seek learning, Daniel Heinsius, has clearly shown us in his Aristarchus what the Evangelists meant. There, at p. 495, he is occupied with reconciling a certain saying of Isaiah with the Gospel narrative. On this matter my own opinion is as follows. Isa. 50. 6: I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked out the hair. The last word in Hebrew is מרטים. Concerning it and its inflected forms, D.K. [Kimchi] gives מנתפים, their meaning is when the hair falls off, or the skin of the flesh itself, or when they are torn away. I maintain that both were properly carried out upon our Savior. Concerning the skin there is no doubt, since he was so scourged that Pilate hoped the sight alone would move the people to pity. That the hair was plucked from his cheeks the Evangelists sufficiently suggest. Luke, when he says (22. 63) that the men who kept Jesus in the house of the high priest, until the judges should deal with his case, [εἰσὶν ... ὕβριζον] were mocking him, beating him, explains in what way they made him an object of ridicule: namely, by assailing him not so much with words as with their hands. Among mockeries that consist in the deed itself, it is no small one to tear out the beard and pluck the hair. Therefore the Evangelist used the word διφθ, most apt, since it signifies not only tearing out hair but tearing the very skin. Matthew and Mark indicate the same thing when they relate that he was struck with blows and slaps by inhuman enemies, for they showed such great savagery that this followed. Add that both Evangelists have plainly described the crown of thorns fixed to his head with a reed; so that, with the temples bloodied, the crown could not have been removed without the hair sticking to it. The temples, moreover, form the upper parts of the cheeks. Wherefore, when the prophecy of Isaiah is said to be fulfilled, I think it is sufficiently established; and that the plain sense can be preserved there is no reason for us to deny. The word ors that follows in the Mishnah is of doubtful meaning. For you will find some who explain תשך as to drag, and others who take ססג as to make a certain incision. Since this happens in two ways, ors פשך, he tore out the ear, is explained as משכו ומשכו כו רוסם, he pressed it (namely with the nails) and imprinted a scar upon it; or ורשך וכהשכו כפין עקיד, he twisted his ear and afflicted him with pain, as if by a kind of tearing out. Hence, among other interpretations, R. Nathan has פרץ, he tore. There are therefore three explanations: to drag, to imprint a scar with the nails, and finally to tear and twist in such a way that it is partly torn from the head. I readily accept the last interpretation, because I find in the Gemara on Tractate Sacrifices, sol. 25, p. 2: פשך, if anyone should tear out the ear of a calf, and afterwards collect its blood, the calf is rejected. From this it is certainly clear that a grave wound is inflicted in that way, since a calf is rejected when its ear has been so damaged; for ors, a defect, is deemed to have arisen in it for that reason. For it must be free of every defect not only when it is slaughtered but also when its blood is collected for sprinkling. In this same Mishnah the Jews also count among the gravest insults and disgraces (which, they note, must be especially attended to) the case where hair is plucked out, a man is spat upon, and his cloak is taken away. They judged these things so unworthy that they fixed a fine of four hundred drachmas. That these things were done to the Savior is clear from the Gospel history, so that we may notice almost nothing omitted that pertains to ignominy among the Jews. Luke 22. 63 rightly called it ἐμπαιζὼν, mocking, when they plucked out Christ's hair, which among the Jews was regarded as a grave mockery; of this I spoke above. Those sacred historians relate that the Jewish judges and Pilate's soldiers spat upon Jesus. Finally, you will find among the same people that his clothing was sometimes stripped off, and that with great mockery: both before Pilate condemned him to death, as I mentioned at the beginning of John 19, and after he had been condemned by him, as the other Evangelists attest. Lastly a general caution is added, which the commentators take to mean that those rules apply to those who have put honorable men to shame, but that the fine is to be reduced for the lower station of others: that the injury done to people of greater rank is to be punished by a lighter fine, in proportion to the degrees by which they were superior and of higher standing. This rule was so accepted among the Jews that they rejected the opinion of R. Akiba concerning equality. That the Romans took great care that no one should be subjected to any kind of ignominy is shown by the title on injuries in the Digest, book 47, title 10, law 1 alone: Labeo says that an injury is done either by deed or by words ... and that every injury either is inflicted on the body, or pertains to dignity, or to infamy. It is done to the body when someone is struck. To dignity, when a matron's companion is led away. To infamy, when chastity is assailed. Then specific laws are added, such as law 15, §. Generally: Whatever someone does or says in order to defame another, there will be an action for injury. And the first paragraph of the same law is to be noted: If someone has not indeed been struck, but has raised his hand against another, and has frightened him often as if about to be beaten, yet has not struck him, he is liable to the useful action for injury. Similarly

units.la: Maim. c. §. sect. 2. זכירו להנביא ידו על חבר ... הרשע רע רע מכלם שר וז רע רע. Etiam attollere manum contra proximum est interdictum, & quicunque manum elevat in proximum, etiamsi eum non percutiat, ecce is improbus est. Deinde cum generali cautione in Mishna nostra convenit quod §. 2.1.18. legimus. Quod sua cujusque injuria propriam aestimationem haberet. Reliqua prudens lector ipse conferat. locum notavi, omnia transscribere longum esset. זי ו אף על פי שהוא נותן לו אינו נסחל לו עד שיבקש מסנו שנאסר ועתה השב אשת וגו׳ וסנין שלא יהא המוחל (סא וסנין שאם לא מחל לו שהוא) אכורי שנאי ויתפלל אברהם אל האלהים וגומר האומר סםא ארת עיני קטע את ידי שכר את רגלי חייב על מנח לפטור חייב קרע את כסותי שכר ארת כרי חייב על מנרת לפטור פטור עשה כן לאיש פלוני על מנרת לפטור חייב בין בגופו בין בסםונו ז
units.tr: Maim. c. §. sect. 2. Remember that to lift up the hand against a neighbor is forbidden, and whoever raises his hand against his neighbor, even if he does not strike him, behold, he is wicked. Then the Mishnah agrees with the general caution that we read at §. 2.1.18: that each person's injury has its own estimate. The rest the prudent reader may compare himself; I have noted the passage, since transcribing everything would be tedious. זי ו אף על פי שהוא נותן לו אינו נסחל לו עד שיבקש מסנו שנאסר ועתה השב אשת וגו׳ וסנין שלא יהא המוחל (סא וסנין שאם לא מחל לו שהוא) אכורי שנאי ויתפלל אברהם אל האלהים וגומר האומר סםא ארת עיני קטע את ידי שכר את רגלי חייב על מנח לפטור חייב קרע את כסותי שכר ארת כרי חייב על מנרת לפטור פטור עשה כן לאיש פלוני על מנרת לפטור חייב בין בגופו בין בסםונו ז

units.la: §. 7. Quamvis hic illi rependat, peccatum huic non remittitur, donec id ab illo petat: quia dicitur (Genef. 20.) Nunc itaque restitue uxorem, &c. Caeterum unde constat, quod propitiandus se non auferrum prabere debeat? (vel, Si non remittat, aufersus sit.) Quia dicitur, Et oravit Abraham Deum, &c. Si quis dixerit, excaca oculum meum, amputa manum meam, frange pedem meum; alter tenetur: etiamsi ea conditione, ut liber fit, sive absolvatur; tenetur. Si dixerit, lacera vestem meam, frange amphoram meam; alter tenetur: si ea conditione ut liber fit; liber est. Si dixerit, Ita facito illi viro N. ea conditione ut liber fis; faciens tenetur: sive de corpore; sive de pecunia ipsius agatur.
units.tr: §. 7. Although the one repays him, the sin is not forgiven him until he asks it of the other; because it is said (Gen. 20): "Now therefore restore the man his wife," etc. Moreover, how is it established that the one who is to be appeased must not be made to suffer? (or, If he does not forgive, he is to be made to suffer.) Because it is said: "And Abraham prayed to God," etc. If someone says, "Blind my eye, cut off my hand, break my foot," the other is liable, even if on condition that he may go free or be acquitted; he is liable. If he says, "Tear my garment, break my jar," the other is liable; if on condition that he goes free, he is free. If he says, "Do this to that man N. on condition that you go free," the doer is liable, whether the matter concerns the body or his money.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Vt ignominiam sibi illatam doloremque ex ista ignominia minia conceptum læsus ex animo remittat, Iudæi exigunt submissam petitionem, qua lædens peccatum sibi ignosci precetur: idque è commate 7.cap. 20. Gen. confirmant;ubi Abimelec uxorem Abrahami restituere jubetur, Nunc itaque restitue uxorem illius viri, propheta enim est, ut oret pro te, tum vivito. quasi dicat, Propheta est, itaq; non succensebit tibi, uxorem enim intactam mansisse novit; non erit difficilis in admittenda reconciliatione, & mihi charus cujus preces exaudiam: itaque id operam da verbis ac muneribus, ut tibi placatus pro te intercedat. Unde ꝟf. 14. & 15. Abrahamum muneribus & blandis verbis excepisse legitur. Hoc exemplo recte ab omnibus, qui alios quosdam ex illis delictis offenderunt, ut præter satisfactionem à læso verbis veniam petant, exigunt. Quemadmodum Christus ipse non tantum pro nostris peccatis Deo sufficienti pœna satisfecit; sed etiam pro nobis à Patre veniam sua intercessione petiit & etiamnum petit. Sanè cum Magistrorum constitutione Doctoris nostri Christi sententia facit: qui ab omnibus sibi conscios, fratres merito sibi infensos esse, ut reconcilientur sollicite operam dari, postulat: Matt. 5. 24,25. Abi... Reconciliator fratri tuo.... Esto amicus adversario tuo cito. Non hoc tantum desiderat ut injuria compensetur (sanè si læsus desideret, negligi quo ipsi satisfiat non potest;) sed eousque nos progredi, omniaque peragere desiderat, donec animus ipsius placetur, & amicus reddatur. Quò pertinere blandam orationem, qua peccati venia expetitur, verba Christi edocent Luc. 17. 4. Si septies in die revertatur ad te, dicens, Resipui &c. Huc pertinet Gemara K. f. 92. [Hebrew] Etiamsi offerat omnes arietes Nabathaea qui in mundo reperiuntur, non remittitur ipsi, donec ab illo veniam petat. Ad [Hebrew] remittitur, scilicet, [Hebrew] iniquitas ipsius (ut alibi additur) Maimonides adjungit, [Hebrew] non propitiatur ipsi: puta, læsus ipsi lædenti. qua voce in conjugatione activa usus fuit interpres Ebræus Matt. 5. 24. quum exprimeret, υπαγε πρῶτον διαλλάγηθι τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου, ... abi prius ut propities aut places iratum vultum fratris tui. Id eo pertinet, ut veteris Judaicæ & Christianæ religionis consonantiam observemus. 2 Talis consensus in sequenti membro apparet: quemadmodum enim hic in remittendo facilitatem exigunt Judæi; pariter Servator noster. Nam omninò cum Judæorum magistris hac in parte facit. Conferamus verba totasque sententias. Servator Luc. 17. 3. 4. Si peccaverit in te frater tuus, objurga eum: & si respuerit, remitte ei. Et si septies in die peccaverit in te, & septies in die revertatur ad te, dicens, Resipui; remittas ei. Ita sentit Maimonides libro sæpius producto, scilicet in 'מ c. 5. sect. 10. ubi ad hunc modum scribit, [illegible, ~40 letters] Quandoquidem petit ab ipso lædens, & deprecatur semel atque iterum, adeo ut agnoscat lædentem à peccato suo se convertisse & pravitatis suæ pœnitentiam agere; ignoscet ipsi. & quicunque ad ignoscendum festinat, is laudandus, & sapientum animus ab ipso refocillatur. 3 Vbi subjungitur in textu nostro, si quis dixerit Amputa manum meam; &c. alterum teneri; sensus est, tantopere cavendum ne alterius corpus lædamus, ut etiamsi quispiam à nobis damnum in corpore suo accipere velit, non obtemperemus: quinetiam luendas pœnas si volentem hujusmodi injuria afficiamus. Judæi hanc rationem reddunt, [illegible, ~10 letters] quia nemo condonat, ubi de extremis membris agitur. quasi dicant, in aliis quidem facile nonnunquam peccandi veniam dat; nunquam verò ut adeo necessaria instrumenta eripiantur concedit: ideoque id seriò unquam præcipi, nimirum ut propria manus amputetur &c. verisimile non est. 4 Quapropter, licet quis alteri dicat, Frange pedem meum &c. & cum alter responderit, An ea conditione hoc præcipis ut me absolvas? dicat, Ita, (hæc enim eo modo resolvunt Talmudiftæ;) nihilominus, inquam, alterum qui vitium corpori infert, teneri pœnaq; obnoxium affirmant. Siquidem credendum non est, illud mandatum de pede frangendo &c. eo modo ac mente ista prolatum fuisse: nam inquit Gemara, ופ שמ כ״ם אט est ita quod instar non sc habeat. ut cum admiratione prolatum, Itane? an putas me hæc velle aut concedere? 5 Verum in bonis externis secus se rem habere agnoscunt: quandoquidem ratio quandoque subest, quare hujusmodi perdenda sint. Itaque in his, si jussō conditionem hanc stipulanti, ut id perpetrans absolvatur, alter respondeat, ופ non; istud Non affirmare asserit O. de Bartenora, ac si dixisset, Nonne dixi tibi quod tu quæris &c. 6 At in bonis alterius hoc minime admittitur: quid enim tibi juris in alterius facultates & supellectilem? nec eum qui damnum infert, stipulatio excusat, qua absolutionem stipulatus est: hanc enim nonnisi proprietarius spondere poterat.7 Et si in bonis alterius hoc obtinet, quanto magis in corpore: ut qui jussu alterius tertium quendam vulnerat, quicquid ab altero stipulatus sit, vulneris teneatur? Et licet malum perpetrans damnum præstare & luere debeat; alter qui jussit est רשע, improbus, inquit Maimonides: quia כפסיל עיור וחוק ידי עוברי עבירה, veluti cæcum impingere fecit, & confirmavit eorum manus qui legem transgrediuntur. Cujusmodi hominum malitiam magis quam aliorum culpat Apostolus Rom. 1. sub finem. Non solum ea faciunt, sed etiam facientibus consentiunt ultro. Peccare humanum est; sed alterius peccatum approbare, infirmitatis & imbecillitatis humanæ miseratione veniam non facile obtinet. quanto minus si quis alteri peccatorum author exstiterit, de quo in Mifna nostra agitur? Leges Romanæ similiter pœna & multa in hujusmodi factum ac peccatum censent animadvertendum, quod quis alterius jussu commisit. Imo etiam peccati approbationem, in eodem crimine censent. Unde ff. de diversis reg. juris, num. 152. Dejicit & qui mandat. In maleficio ratihabitio mandato comparatur. Sed in eo à Misna nostra dissident, quod eum qui injuriam fieri aut damnum dari jubet, eo loco habeant, ac si ipse faceret. Ita leg. 169. eod. tit. Is damnum dat qui jubet dare. ejus verò nulla culpa est, cui parere necesse sit. Judæi à faciente totam injuriam compensari volunt ac præcipiunt.
units.tr: So that the one who has been wronged may, from the heart, let go the disgrace done to him and the grief arising from it, the Jews require a humble petition by which the offender begs forgiveness for his sin. They confirm this from Genesis 20:7, where Abimelech is ordered to restore Abraham's wife: Now therefore restore the man's wife, for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for you, and you shall live. It is as if he said: he is a prophet, so he will not be angry with you, for he knows that his wife remained untouched. He will not be hard to reconcile, and I hold dear the one whose prayers I will hear. Therefore take pains, with words and gifts, to win his favour so that he will intercede for you. Hence in verses 14 and 15 we read that Abraham received him with gifts and kind words. From this example, everyone who has offended certain people in such ways rightly requires that, besides making satisfaction, they also ask pardon from the one wronged, in words. Christ himself did likewise: he not only satisfied the Father for our sins by a sufficient punishment, but also sought, and still seeks, pardon for us from the Father by his intercession. Indeed, the saying of our Teacher Christ agrees with the constitution of the Masters. He requires that everyone who knows he has a brother who is rightly hostile to him be earnestly urged to be reconciled: Matthew 5:24-25, Go... be reconciled to your brother... Agree with your adversary quickly. He does not desire only that the injury be made good (for if the one wronged wishes it, satisfaction cannot be neglected); he wants us to go further and do everything until his mind is appeased and he becomes a friend. Luke 17:4 teaches what the gentle entreaty by which forgiveness of sin is sought has to do with this: If he turns again to you seven times in a day, saying, I repent, etc. To this belongs the Gemara, K. f. 92: Even if he offers all the rams of Nabatea that are found in the world, it is not forgiven him until he asks pardon from him. On the words it is forgiven, namely his iniquity (as is added elsewhere), Maimonides adds: he is not propitiated, that is, the one wronged is not propitiated toward the one who wronged him. The Hebrew interpreter used this word in the active conjugation at Matthew 5:24, when he rendered ὑπαγε πρῶτον διαλλάγηθι τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου [ὑπαγε πρῶτον διαλλάγηθι τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου], that is, go first, and make propitiation or placate the angry face of your brother. This is to show that we observe the agreement of the old Jewish and the Christian religion. 2 Such agreement appears in the following clause. As the Jews require readiness to forgive here, so does our Saviour. For in this part he entirely agrees with the Jewish masters. Let us compare the words and the whole sentences. The Saviour says in Luke 17:3-4: If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to you, saying, I repent, you shall forgive him. Maimonides thinks the same, in the book often cited, namely in 'מ chapter 5, section 10, where he writes in this way: [illegible] Since the one who wronged him asks of him and entreats him once and again, so that he acknowledges that the wrongdoer has turned from his sin and is doing penance for his wickedness, he shall forgive him. And whoever hastens to forgive is to be praised, and the mind of the wise is refreshed by him. 3 Where our text adds, if someone says, Cut off my hand, etc., the other is bound; the sense is that we must be so careful not to harm another's body that, even if someone wishes to receive harm to his body from us, we should not comply; indeed, if we inflict such an injury on a willing person, we must pay penalties. The Jews give this reason: [illegible] because no one pardons when the extremities of the body are at issue. As if they said: in other matters he sometimes readily grants forgiveness of sin, but never does he concede that such necessary instruments be taken away; therefore it is not likely that this command, that one's own hand be cut off, etc., was ever seriously given. 4 Accordingly, although someone may say to another, Break my foot, etc., and the other replies, Do you order this on condition that you be absolved? and he says, Yes (for the Talmudists resolve these matters in this way), nevertheless, I say, they affirm that the one who inflicts bodily injury is bound and liable to punishment. For it is not to be believed that that command to break the foot, etc., was uttered in that manner and with that intention: for the Gemara says that the word so, which stands in place of not, is spoken with astonishment, as if to say: Is that so? Do you think I want these things or grant them? 5 But they acknowledge that the matter is otherwise with external goods, since there is sometimes a reason why such things must be destroyed. So if, when someone bargains with a command on this condition, that the one carrying it out be absolved, the other replies not, O. de Bartenora asserts that this Not is to be affirmed, as if he had said, Did I not tell you what you seek, etc.? 6 But in another's goods this is by no means allowed. For what right have you over another's property and household goods? Nor does the stipulation excuse the one who does the harm, the stipulation by which he has sought absolution; for only the owner could promise that, since it was the owner's to give. 7 And if this holds in another's goods, how much more in the body: that he who at another's command wounds a third person is liable for the wound, whatever he may have stipulated from the other? And although the one who commits the evil ought to make good the loss and pay for it, the one who gave the command is wicked, says Maimonides, improbus, because he has made a blind man stumble, as it were, and has strengthened the hands of those who transgress the law. The Apostle blames the malice of such men more than that of others, Romans 1 near the end: They not only do these things, but also readily consent with those who do them. To sin is human; but to approve another's sin does not easily obtain pardon through the compassion due to human frailty and weakness. How much less if someone has been the author of another's sins, which is what our Mishnah is about? The Roman laws likewise hold that the one who has committed such a deed or sin at another's command is to be punished with penalty and fine. Indeed, they also hold approval of a sin to be the same crime. Hence in the Digest, On Various Rules of Law, number 152: He who commands is also liable. In a wrong, ratification is equal to command. But they differ from our Mishnah in this: they regard the one who orders an injury to be done or damage to be given as if he did it himself. So in law 169 of the same title: He does the damage who orders it to be given; but the one who is bound to obey is not at fault. The Jews want, and command, that the whole injury be made good by the one who does it.
Chapter 9, Halakhah 1.

units.la: הגזל עצים ועשאן כלים צבר ועשאן בגרים משלם כשע' הגזלה גזל פרה םעוברת וילדה רחל טעונה וגזוה משלם דמי פרה העופדת לילד דמי רחל העופדה ליגז גזל פרה ונחעברה אצלו וילדה רחל ונטענה אצלו וגזוה משלם כשעת הגזלה זה הכלל כל הגזלנים משלמין כשעת הגזלה ו
units.tr: If someone robbed wood and made it into utensils, or robbed timber and made it into beams, he pays according to its value at the time of the robbery. If someone robbed a cow that was pregnant, and it gave birth, and he robbed a ewe that was laden, and it was shorn while in his possession, he pays the value of the cow at the time of the robbery for the calf, and the value of the ewe at the time of the robbery for the shearing. This is the general rule: all robbers pay according to the value at the time of the robbery.
CAP. IX. §. I.

units.la: Qui postquam ligna rapuit, ex iis instrumenta fecit; lanam, ex ea vestes fecit: is rependit secundum rapina tempus. Qui rapuit vaccam fœtam, quæ postea parit; ovem lanigeram, quam postea tondet: ut pretium vaccæ paritura, pretiumque ovis tondenda rependit. Qui rapuit vaccam, quæ apud se fœcunda ta fœtum edit; ovem, quam apud se factam lanigeram tondet: * pro temporis ipsius rapti ratione rependit. Hæc generalis regula est: omnes raptores rependere secundum rapiendi tempus.
units.tr: He who, after he has stolen wood and made tools from it, or wool and made garments from it, makes restitution according to the time of the robbery. He who has stolen a pregnant cow, which afterwards gives birth, or a woolly ewe, which afterwards is shorn: he makes restitution as the price of the cow at the time she was about to give birth, and the price of the ewe at the time she is to be shorn. He who has stolen a cow which, while in his possession, becomes pregnant and bears a calf, or a ewe which, while in his possession, becomes woolly and is shorn: makes restitution according to the value at the time of the robbery. This is the general rule: all robbers make restitution according to the time of robbing.
Annotations.

units.la: ¹ Ante omnia annotandum est discrimen, quo גניבה, furtum, à גזלה, rapina distinguitur. Maimonides c.1.Cod. Gezela sect. 3. לי וסו גזול וס הלוקח ממון םדס כמוקם, Quis dicitur raptor? Qui pecuniam (sive aliam rem, ut dicitur in sequentibus) hominis alicujus vi adhibita aufert. Et c.1. גניב sect. 3. לי וסו גנב וס הלוקח ממון םדס כסתר ונחן הכעליס יודעיס Quis censetur fur? Qui facultates alicujus clam insciis proprietariis aufert. Magnam esse differentiam inter utrumque nemo negare audet: sed hanc differentiam quam ponunt, in furto duplum & quadruplum; in rapina solum ferme simplum exigi, pernego. Nec Levit. 6. 4. 5. hujusmodi discrimen observari jubetur: nam (ut jam in superioribus ostendi) istic de fatente reo, qui sponte peccatum fatetur,verba fiunt.Ipsum vocabulum reus est. ꝟf. 4. hanc restrictionem confirmat: quid enim sibi volunt hæc verba? Erit quum peccaverit & reus fuerit &c. Num quis dubitat, an peccata tam gravia reum faciant? Verum hæc vera est interpretatio, Quum peccaverit istorum aliquid patrans, & reatum agnoverit. Quid quæso, an qui aperta vi alterius bona aufert mitius multabitur, quam is qui inscio quidpiam surripit? hic alteri resistere non audet; ille poffeffori etiam vim facit, nec ulla verecundia, reverentia, ullove timore ac metu ducitur. 2 De raptore dubium oboritur, an fi rem furtivam vel potius raptam immutaverit inque aliam formam redegerit, ut fi ex lana rapta vestes fecerit; dum rei pretium rependendum est (quia ipsa res ut fuerat restituí nequit,) solvendum fit rei pretium quæ ex rapta materia facta est. Doctores tempus spectare præcipiunt, quo materia rapta fuit. Idque ad hunc modum, ut quanti res tum efset quum raperetur æstimetur, atque hoc pretium proprietario reddatur. 3 Pariter in aliis rebus, nimirum in animantibus, omnia fe habent. vacca fœta abripiatur, dumque in raptoris potestate est fœtum edat: hæc minoris habetur ubi peperit, quam dum staret ad pariendum, id est, quum demum paritura effet: ut quæ una cum fœtu pluris fieret, quam fine fœtu. Itaque hoc casu qui rapuit, non temporis quo rependit; sed quo rapuerat rationem habebit, solvetque quanti erat vacca, cum fœta abduceretur: quo tempore pluris fiebat. Adeo ut hac ratione plus reddere teneatur, quam vacca inptæfentiarum valeat. 4 Sed ex eodem fundamento, minus solvit qui raptam vaccam, tam diu penes se habuit, ut foeta reddita fit vitulumque pariat. Quandoquidem enim rapiendi momentum considerandum est, atque postea in raptoris manibus valor ac pretium auctum; minus raptor pendit quam res rapta æstimetur: quia foetus deinde additus in rationem non venit; sed in rapti compensatione tantum detrahitur, quanti foetus habetur. Non aliter in ove lanigera fieri debet. Itaque conclusio generalis omnia rapta spectans subjicitur: compensationem secundum istud temporis momentum præstari, quo raptor rem ipsam rapuerat; non vero quo res rapta reperenditur. Apud Romanos in compensando damno sæpe tempus in rationem venit, quo ipso aut circiter damnum datum sit. unde Inst. l. 4. t. 3. §. Illud palam, Ex hoc tamen capite non quanti in eo anno, sed quanti in diebus triginta proximis res fuerit, obligatur is, qui damnum dederit. Verumenimvero in compensatione rapti longe aliter quam Judæi procedunt. Quod ex initio t. 2. l. 4. Inst. liquet, cujus verba notanda, quia superiorem Judæorum errorem refellunt eodem quo supra argumento usus sum. Qui vi res alienas rapit, tenetur quidem etiam furti: (quis enim magis alienam rem invito domino contrectat, quam qui vi rapit? ideoque rectè dictum est, eum improbum furem esse) sed tamen propriam actionem ejus delicti nomine Prator introduxit, qua appellatur, Vi bonorum raptorum: & est intra annum quadrupli; post annum, simpli. Qua actio utilis est, etiamsi quis unam rem, licet minimam, rapuerit. Quadruplum autem non totum pœna est, sicut in actione furti manifesti diximus: sed in quadruplo inest & rei persecutio: ut pœna tripli fit, sive comprehendatur raptor in ipso delicto, sive non. Ridiculum enim esset, levioris conditionis esse eum, qui vi rapit, quam qui clam amovet.
units.tr: ¹ Before all else, the distinction must be noted by which גניבה [ganevah], theft, is distinguished from גזלה [gezelah], robbery. Maimonides, ch. 1 of Hilkhot Gezelah, sect. 3: [לי וסו גזול וס הלוקח ממון םדס כמוקם] Who is called a robber? One who takes money (or another thing, as is said in what follows) of some person by force. And ch. 1 of Hilkhot Genevah, sect. 3: [לי וסו גנב וס הלוקח ממון םדס כסתר ונחן הכעליס יודעיס] Who is considered a thief? One who takes another's property secretly, without the owners knowing. No one dares deny that there is a great difference between the two; but I flatly deny that the difference they set down, namely that for theft a double or quadruple payment is exacted, while for robbery only about the simple amount is required, is valid. Nor is Lev. 6:4–5 commanded to observe a distinction of this kind: for (as I have already shown above) those verses speak of a guilty man who voluntarily confesses his sin. The very word is reus est. Verse 4 confirms this restriction: for what do these words mean? It shall be, when he has sinned and is guilty, etc. Does anyone doubt whether sins so grave make a man guilty? The true interpretation is this: when he has sinned by committing one of those things, and has acknowledged his guilt. I ask, will one who takes another's goods by open force be punished more leniently than one who secretly steals something? The latter does not dare to resist the owner; the former even uses violence against the possessor, and is restrained by no shame, reverence, or fear whatever. ² A doubt arises about a robber: if he has changed the stolen, or rather robbed, thing and reshaped it into another form, as when he makes garments from wool he has robbed, then, since the price of the thing must be repaid (because the thing cannot be restored as it was), the price of the thing made from the robbed material must be paid. The teachers direct us to look at the time when the material was robbed. And this in such a way that the worth the thing had at the time it was robbed is assessed, and that price is returned to the owner. ³ Similarly with other things, namely animals, all stands the same. If a pregnant cow is seized, and while in the robber's power she gives birth: she is valued lower after she has calved than while she was standing to give birth, that is, when she was about to calve; for with her calf she was worth more than without it. So in this case the robber will reckon not the time of repayment but the time of the robbery, and will pay what the cow was worth when she was carried off pregnant, at which time she was worth more. So by this reckoning he is bound to give back more than the cow is currently worth. ⁴ But on the same principle, he who has kept the robbed cow so long that she is returned pregnant and bears a calf pays less. For since the moment of the robbing must be considered, and afterwards the value and price increased in the robber's hands, the robber pays less than the robbed thing is valued at, because the offspring added afterwards does not enter the reckoning; rather, only the worth of the offspring is deducted from the compensation for what was robbed. It should be no different with a woolly ewe. Thus a general conclusion covering all robbed things is laid down: compensation is to be made according to the moment at which the robber robbed the thing itself, not the time at which the robbed thing is returned. Among the Romans, in compensating for damage, the time at which the damage was done, or about then, often came into account; whence Inst. 4.3, §. "Illud palam": From this chapter, however, he who has caused the damage is bound not for what the thing was worth in that year, but for what it was worth in the thirty days nearest to it. But in compensation for robbery the Jews proceed quite differently. This is clear from the beginning of Inst. 4.2, whose words are to be noted, because they refute the earlier error of the Jews by the same argument I have used above. He who takes another's goods by force is indeed liable also for theft (for who handles another's property against the owner's will more than one who seizes it by force? and so it is rightly said that he is a wicked thief); yet the Praetor introduced a special action for this wrong, called the action "for goods taken by force," which is for four times the value within a year, and for simple value after a year. This action is available even if someone has taken a single thing, however small. The quadruple, moreover, is not wholly a penalty, as we said in the action for manifest theft; rather, the quadruple includes also the recovery of the thing, so that the penalty is threefold, whether the robber is caught in the very act or not. For it would be absurd for one who seizes by force to be in a lighter position than one who removes secretly.

units.la: Qui rapuit bestiam quam postea educauit, servos ' qui postea adoleverunt; secundum rapinæ tempus compensat. At D. Meir inquit, Ille quod ad servos alteri dicit, Ecce tibi quod tuum est. Qui rapuit numum, qui postea ² dissecatur; fructus, qui postea putrescunt; vinum, quod deinde accessit: is pro raptus tempore compensat. Qui rapuit monetam, postea improbatam; primulas oblationes, postea ³ contaminatas; fermentum, deinde ultra pascha servatum; bestiam, quâ postea sceleus comittitur, aut ab altari repudienda judicatur, aut denique ut lapidetur, egreditur: is alteri dicit, ecce tibi tuum.
units.tr: If someone stole an animal that afterwards bore young, or slaves who afterwards grew up, he makes compensation according to the time of the theft. But Rabbi Meir says: he says to the other, "Behold, what is yours is yours." If someone stole money that afterwards was cut up, fruits that afterwards rotted, or wine that afterwards turned sour, he makes compensation according to the time of the theft. If someone stole coin that was afterwards declared invalid, first-fruit offerings that were afterwards defiled, or leaven that was kept beyond the Passover, or an animal with which a crime was afterwards committed, or which is judged unfit to be offered on the altar, or which finally goes out to be stoned, he says to the other, "Behold, yours is yours."
Annotations.

units.la: ¹ In restituendis servis omnes non conveniunt: quidam ut in præcedentibus, pretium è raptus tempore æstimant, atque id solum restitui volunt; alii qui D. Meïrum sequuntur, siquis servum parvulum rapiat, eumque ad multos annos secum retinebat, servum adultum reddendum censent. Vtraque sententia suum habet fundamentum, vel potius se habere putat. Hi istud pro fundamento sumunt, servos fundi instar se habere, adeoque in dominorum potestate remanere. id lege Lev. 25.46. statuminant, ubi de servis alienigenis, Constituetis vos possessores illorum, cum filiis vestris post vos, obtinendo hereditario jure possessionem. Quemadmodum fundos suos possidebant, ita inquiunt possessio erat servorum: ideoq; servi rapti non acquirebantur raptoribus, ut postea eorum pretio satisfacere possent. Illi secus judicabant, nimirum עבדים כמטלטלי דמי, servos mobilium bonorum instar se habere. De mobilibus autem quid statuant docet Maimonides c.2.גזלה sect.1. אם נתפס כיד הגזלן ..., Si res mutata sit in raptoris manu, licet ejus proprietarii nondum spem abjecerint, illa immutatione rem acquirit (raptor) ejusque pretium solvit pro raptus tempore. Ita censent illi, servos, quia immutati, quippe grandiores facti sunt, in potestatem & dominium raptorum transisse: ideoque si pretium, quo raptus tempore vendi poterant, solverent, nihil restare quod proprietarii repetere possent. Quod ad legem Levit. attinet, nonnemo ita censet, דורשי לכל מילי דהוריתא quod procul dubio in omnibus rebus quae lege praecipiuntur, servus habeatur instar fundi; sed ubi cum mobilibus conferetur, de rebus per magistros statutis sermonem esse. 2 De voce כסף, scinditur, in Gemara dissentiunt, atque diversa ratione explicant. Unus proprie vocem accipiendam contendit; alter latius eandem extendendam censet: quocirca sequentia, rapuit monetam postea improbatam sive סלע, pro illa diversitate non eodem modo enarrant. Numismata quae non amplius recipiuntur, saepe secantur in partes; vel facta ex parte & aliquousque sectione, inutilia in commerciis redduntur: utplurimum, tantum proclamando publicove diplomate numi improbantur. Illud si fiat, numus כסף, sectus dicitur; cum vero hoc posteriori modo numus exauctoratur, proprie usurpatur dictio, סלע, improbatur. Haec sunt significationes propriissimae; a quibus R. Judas propter ipsum utriusque membri jus diversum recedit: utpote qui omnem improbatum numum, modo absolute & universim rejiciatur, etiam כסף, sectum dici arbitratur: non quidem proprie,
units.tr: ¹ Authorities do not agree on the restitution of slaves. Some, as in the preceding cases, value the slave at the price he had at the time of the theft and want only that sum restored. Others, who follow R. Meir, hold that if someone steals a young slave and keeps him with him for many years, the adult slave must be returned. Each opinion has its own foundation, or at least thinks it has one. The first group takes as its foundation that slaves are like land and so remain in the power of their masters. They support this from Lev. 25:46, where concerning foreign slaves it is said: "You shall make them your possession, and they shall be an inheritance for your children after you, to hold as a possession by hereditary right." Just as they possessed their fields, they say, so possession of slaves was the same. Therefore stolen slaves did not become the thieves' property, so that the thieves could later make satisfaction by paying their price. The others judged otherwise, since slaves are regarded as movable goods (עבדים כמטלטלי דמי). On what the rules say about movable goods, Maimonides teaches (Hilkhot Gezelah, ch. 2, sect. 1): "If the thing has been changed in the hand of the robber, though its owners have not yet given up hope, the robber acquires it by that change and pays its price at the time of the robbery." So these men hold that slaves, who have been changed because they have grown older, passed into the power and ownership of the thieves; so if the thieves paid the price for which they could have been sold at the time of the theft, nothing would remain that the owners could reclaim. As for the law in Leviticus, some hold that the interpreters of the Law (דורשי לכל מילי דהוריתא) take it that in all matters commanded by the law a slave is held to be like land; but where slaves are compared with movables, the rule concerns things fixed by the teachers. 2 As to the word כסף, "cut," the Gemara disagrees and explains it in different ways. One insists that the word must be taken in its proper sense; the other thinks it should be extended more widely. Hence they do not explain the phrase "he stole money that was afterwards rejected," that is, סלע, in the same way, given that difference. Coins that are no longer accepted are often cut into pieces, or, once partly cut, become useless in trade; most often coins are rejected only by public proclamation or an official decree. If the first happens, the coin is called כסף, "cut"; when a coin is withdrawn in the second way, the word סלע, "rejected," is properly used. These are the most proper meanings, but R. Judah departs from them, holding that for both members of the phrase the rule is different. He thinks that any rejected coin, if it is rejected absolutely and in general, is also called כסף, "cut"; not indeed in the proper sense,

units.la: sed tropicè. Nam ut numisma in partes dissectum pro numo non admittitur; ita etiam cum regio diplomate numi exauctorantur, non amplius recipiuntur. Idcirco ait R. Judas, [Hebrew: פסקי מלכות נמי סיינו כסף] si eum improbaverit regnum, tum etiam pro [Hebrew: כסף] discisso habetur. quasi dicat, si rex cujus latissimum sit dominium, improbatum numum promulgeт; tum etiam ad [Hebrew: כסף] refertur: quia ut numisma dissectum non amplius commerciale & receptum est; pariter nec illud quod monarcha vel rex latissimè dominans, universim improbaverit. (Eodem modo quum fructus recensèt putrescentes, omnes & universim putrescentes intelligit: nam si partim putruerunt, ipse fructus redditur.) Hisce convenienter in sequentibus [Hebrew: כסף] ipsi non est quævis improbata pecunia: sed quæ [Hebrew: כסף], improbatur in hac provincia; in alia probatur. Verum M. Houna [Hebrew: כסף] nonnisi de numismate secto accipit; & [Hebrew: כסף], improbatum à rege vel monarcha esse asserit, quod in toto regno, non tantum civitate quadam vel provincia rejicitur. Istius Hounæ sententia rejecta; illius Judæ vulgò recepta est. Quia numorum mentio injecta est, quod Gemara de Jerosolymitano observat, negligendum non videtur; quo istos numos dignoscere queamus. [Hebrew: שטרות מטבע של ירושלים דור ושלמה מצד אחד וירושלם מצד אחר] (ut habet glossa) Quodnam est numisma Ierosolymitanum? Vbi nomina David & Salomon expressa ab uno latere; ab altero latere exaratum, Jerusalem, civitas Sancta. ita hæc Glossator enarrat. Postea nonnulla (inter quæ etiam oblatio [Hebrew: תרומה], quæ hic strictius accepta, ut sequentia docent, oblationem pentecostes festo sacerdotibus offerédam, vel etiam decimas à Levitis sacerdotibus pro more conferédas designat) nonnulla inquam, quibus uti & frui ob contractum vitium non licet, restituenda judicantur: quod judicium iniquum videtur. Nam si meam rem tam diu retinuisti, ut ob legem quandam ceremonialem &c. tractu temporis inepta & inutilis vel minus utilis mihi facta sit; potius pro raptus tempore (ut in aliis loquitur Mifna)id est quanti erat cum illam raperes,rependendam æquitas decernit:ut pretium potius,quam rem inutilem recipiam. Verum magistri in furto & rápina compensanda hoc etiam expendunt, an fur aut raptor utilitatem quandam inde percipiat: cujus utilitatis nomine pretium solvere teneatur. atqui illæ res raptori etiam inutiles redduntur. Tamen in Gemara distinctio quædam adhibetur:quâ à bove de quo agitur ad alias res extensâ,proprietarii commodum attenderetur. antequam res plane judicata sit, affirmatur (scilicet restituendam rem;) postquam plane judicata est, negatur. Ita proprietario consuli videtur:ut si causa decisa nondum fit,adeoque res judicio nondum improbetur, ejusq; conditio talis nondum judicetur, quod vitio laborat; ex ipsa utilitatem percipiat: sin vero judicio rejectanea facta sit; pro ea à raptore pretium recipiat proprietarius. Qui hoc in fermento reservato locum habeat non videmus: quandoquidem sine ullo judicio, ex elapso paschate fermentum rejectaneum factum constat. Qui raptum ex legibus Romanis compensetur, ad præcedentem Misnam satis prolixè annotatum fuit.
units.tr: but figuratively. For just as a coin cut into pieces is not admitted as money, so too when coins are withdrawn by royal decree they are no longer accepted. Hence R. Judah says: "[Hebrew: פסקי מלכות נמי סיינו כסף] If the kingdom has rejected it, then it too is regarded as cut money (כסף)." As if to say: if a king whose dominion is very wide issues a decree rejecting a coin, then it too is referred to as כסף, because just as a coin cut into pieces is no longer current and accepted in trade, so is a coin which a monarch or a king ruling very widely has rejected in general. (In the same way, when he speaks of rotting fruit he means all fruit that has rotted in general; for if only part has rotted, the fruit itself is returned.) In keeping with this, in what follows, כסף does not mean any rejected money, but money which is "rejected" in this province and accepted in another. But M. Houna understands כסף only of a coin that has been cut, and holds that "rejected" means rejected by a king or monarch, since it is refused throughout the whole realm and not just in one city or province. Houna's opinion has been rejected, and Judah's is generally accepted. Since mention of coins has been made, it does not seem to be neglected what the Gemara notes about the Jerusalem coin, by which we may recognise those coins. [Hebrew: שטרות מטבע של ירושלים דור ושלמה מצד אחד וירושלם מצד אחר] (as the gloss has it): "What is the Jerusalem coin? Where the names David and Solomon are expressed on one side, and on the other side is written Jerusalem, the holy city." So the Glossator explains it. Afterwards some things (among which is the offering [Hebrew: תרומה], which here is taken more narrowly, as what follows shows, designating the offering to be made to the priests at the feast of Pentecost, or also the tithes which by custom are to be paid by the Levites to the priests) some things, I say, which it is not lawful to use or enjoy because of the defect they have contracted, are judged to be restored; and this judgment seems unfair. For if you have kept my property so long that, because of some ceremonial law, through lapse of time it has become useless or less useful to me, justice decides that I should be repaid the price it had at the time you took it (as the Mishnah says elsewhere), that is, the amount it was worth when you seized it, so that I receive the price rather than the useless thing. But the teachers in cases of theft and robbery also consider this: whether the thief or robber derives some benefit from it, for which benefit he is bound to pay. Yet those things become useless even to the robber. Still, the Gemara applies a certain distinction, by which the owner's advantage is considered when the case is extended from the ox in question to other things: "Before the matter has been fully decided, it is affirmed (namely, that the thing must be restored); after it has been fully decided, it is denied." Thus the owner seems to be protected: if the case is not yet decided, and so the thing has not yet been condemned by judgment, and its condition as defective has not yet been judged, he may take the benefit from it; but if it has been declared rejected by judgment, the owner receives the price from the robber in its place. We do not see how this applies to leavened bread kept past Passover, since it is evident that the leaven became rejected after Passover without any judgment. How this is compensated under Roman law has been noted quite fully on the preceding Mishnah.

units.la: Hebrew text (right-to-left, verse-like lines in the left column), printed as a block: נתן לאופנין להקן וקילקלו חייבים לשלם נתן לחרס שירה חבה ומגרל להקן וקלקל חייב לשלם הבנאי שקבל עליו לסחור את הכוהל ושבר את האבנים או שהזיק חייב לשלם היה סוחר מצר זה ונפל מצר אחר פטור ואם מחמה הסכה חייב.
units.tr: Mishnah (Hebrew text, verse-like lines): [Hebrew: נתן לאופנין להקן וקילקלו חייבים לשלם נתן לחרש שירה חבה ומגרל להקן וקלקל חייב לשלם הבנאי שקבל עליו לסחור את הכותל ושבר את האבנים או שהזיק חייב לשלם היה סוחר מצד זה ונפל מצד אחר פטור ואם מחמה הסכה חייב.] If someone gave potters something to make and they spoiled it, they are liable to pay. If someone gave a craftsman a beam or a tower to make and he spoiled it, he is liable to pay. The builder who undertook to rebuild the wall and broke the stones or caused damage, is liable to pay. If a merchant was on one side and fell to the other side, he is exempt; but if it was from the heat of the sun, he is liable.

units.la: * Si ubi quis fabris aliquid ad parandum dedit, hi corrumpant; ad compensationem tenetur. Si ubi fabro pilentum, arcam, aviarium ad reparandum dedit, is corrumpat; compensare tenetur. Architectus qui cū in se recepit parietem destruere, lapides frangit aut quem vitiat; rependere tenetur. Si ipso ab uno latere destruente, ab alio latere paries concidat; liber est: at si id ictus impetu fiat, tenetur.
units.tr: * If someone gave something to smiths to prepare, and they spoil it, he is bound to make compensation. If he gave a carriage, a chest, or an aviary to a wheelwright to repair, and he spoils it, he must make compensation. An architect who has undertaken to pull down a wall and breaks stones or damages something, is bound to make restitution. If, while the wall is being pulled down from one side, the wall falls on the other side, he is free; but if it happens by the force of a blow, he is liable.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: םיק in hoc & sequenti dicto occurrit; sed significatione & sensu diverso. Verbum ipsum duo significat, quidpiam certa mensura rectaque dispositione perficere; vel quod depravatum & corruptum est ad pristinam rectamque formam revocare. Prius, inquiunt Talmudistæ, in primo membro locum habet, quum dicitur, Si ubi quis fabris aliquid ad parandum dedit, hi corrumpant, compensare tenentur. Etenim si hic de reparatione ageretur, sequens dictum esset superfluum: namque ubi in genere aliquid dicitur, id sufficit, nec species addere necesse est; nisi specialis quædam dubitandi ratio subsit. itaque si faber prima sententia, in reparando ad compensationem damnatur, quorsum de pilento, arca, alveario, seorsum præciperetur, cum teneri si hæc corrumpat? Quapropter legitur in Gemara hujus Misnæ, מכלל דריסא conclusio est, prima sententia de ligno agi, atque tum etiam ad compensandum teneri. Quasi dicas, Secundo dicto exigitur, ut faber lignarius arcam & alveariūm aliave ad reficiendum accepta rependat, si ista inter reparandum corruperit vel fregerit: ergo initio Misnæ de vasis jam confectis sermo non est; sed de ligno: quod ubi fabro lignario traditum est ut inde pilentum aliave conficiat; si pilentum, exempli gratia, casu quodam frangat, faber pilenti pretium dare tenetur. Nam de laboris mercede pactus erat: itaque pactum servans, pilentum acceptis lignis aliisque necessariis præstare debet: nisi faciat, pretium pilenti ob præcedens pactum exigitur. Hinc Maimonides codice c.10.sect.4. Dederit fabro ligna ut ex iis pilentum, arcam, aut aviarium paret, deinde frangi contingat, postquam illa confecta fuissent; illi (qui materiam suppeditaverat) pretium pilenti, arca, & aviarii rependet; quia faber per vasis praestantiam nihil acquirit. Vltimorum verborum haec mens: per rei immutationem, saepe transfire ipsam (uti in superioribus intelleximus) in possidentis dominium, ut solo pretio rei refundendo, quanti scilicet res esset cum illam in manus suas acciperet, absolveretur; verum artificem licet lignum in pilentum &c. immutet, ipsorum non fieri dominum; sed cum de mercede pactus est, ipsum pilentum dandum, ejusve pretium solvendum esse.2 Frequenter in Talmudicis constitutionibus haec dictio מגדל occurrit: quam aviarium reddidi; licet turrim significet. Quia aviaria oblonga erant &c, quemadmodum multae olim turres, ex ligno, idcirco cavea qua aves servabantur ac alebantur dicta Talmudistis מגדל. Locus minime dubius occurrit in Gemara Codicis כינד sol. 24. p. 1. Qui venando avem in aviarium & capreolum in domu agit, tenetur. Vbi מגדל aviarium notat; uti & R. Nathan in Aruch observat, & Glossa S. J. attestatur: licet etiam alvearium denotet. 3 Tandem in Misna excusatur, qui destruit parietem, si paries ab altero latere concidat; quia ipse id prohibere non potest, si vetustate ruinosus paries decidat. Illum tamen architectum condemnant, si ictu ipsius paries, quem demoliendum sumserat, ab alio latere cadat & hoc modo lapides frangantur, aut laedatur aliquis. Maimonides Cod. פיוי c. 6. sect. 11. hanc subjungit rationem, Quia est veluti qui sagittam jacit, eaque damnum infert. Cavendum erat ne tantopere ictum vibraret, ut altera & aversa parietis pars inde labefactaretur: alioqui sicuti sagitta alium petens & jaculans, si laedat, culpam luere debet; pariter qui nimio impetu parietem tractans vel lapides in alia parte cadentes frangit, vel etiam praetereuntes laedit, satisfacere tenetur. Tota hac Misna locatori consulitur, ut damnum datum sit conductoris qui opus faciendum conduxit. Similiter lex Rom. locatori favet, ff. l. 19. t. 2. leg. 51. §. 1. Locavi opus faciendum ita, ut pro opere redemptori certam mercedem in dies singulos darem. opus vitiosum factum est. an ex locato agere possum? Respondit: si ita opus locasti, ut bonitas ejus tibi à conductore approbaretur: tametsi convenit ut in singulas operas certa pecunia daretur, praestari tamen tibi à conductore debet, si id opus vitiosum factum est. Non enim quicquam interest, utrum uno pretio opus, an in singulas operas collocatur, si modo universitas consummationis ad conductorem pertinuit. id est, si universum opus perficere debuit. Sed quemadmodum hic excusatur architectus, cujus culpa parietis ab altera parte ruentis lapides franguntur; similiter Gajus, uti extat ff. eod. leg. 25. §. 7.
units.tr: [םיק] occurs in this and the following saying, but with a different meaning and sense. The verb itself has two senses: to make something complete by a fixed measure and proper arrangement, or to restore what has been spoiled and corrupted to its former and right form. The Talmudists say the first sense applies in the first clause, where it is said: If anyone has given something to craftsmen to prepare, and they spoil it, they are bound to compensate. For if this clause were about repair, the following saying would be superfluous. When something is said in general, that is enough, and there is no need to add a particular case unless some special ground for doubt lies behind it. So if the craftsman, by the first sentence, is condemned to compensate for damage in preparing the goods, why would the cart, the chest and the beehive be singled out separately, when he is bound to pay if he spoils them? Therefore it is read in the Gemara on this Mishnah: [מכלל דריסא] by inference, the first sentence concerns wood, and then he is also bound to compensate. As if you were to say: by the second saying it is required that the wood-craftsman make good the chest, the beehive, or other things received for repair, if he spoils or breaks them in the repairing. Therefore the beginning of the Mishnah is not about vessels already finished, but about wood. When wood is handed over to a wood-craftsman to make a cart or some other thing from it, and the cart, for example, breaks by some accident, the craftsman is bound to pay the price of the cart. For he had agreed on a wage for his labour, and so, keeping to the agreement, he must supply a cart from the wood and the other necessary materials he received. If he does not, the price of the cart is exacted on account of the earlier agreement. Hence Maimonides, in his Code, chapter 10, section 4: If he gave wood to a craftsman so that he might make from it a cart, a chest, or an aviary, and then it happened to be broken after those things had been made, he (who supplied the material) shall repay the price of the cart, the chest and the aviary, because the craftsman gains nothing from the excellence of the vessel. The meaning of these last words is this: by the change of a thing, the thing often passes (as we have seen above) into the ownership of the possessor, so that he is released by repaying only the price of the thing, namely what it was worth when he received it into his hands. But although the craftsman changes the wood into a cart and so on, he does not become its owner. Rather, since he agreed on a wage, the cart itself must be given, or its price paid. In the Talmudic regulations the word [מגדל] frequently occurs, which I have rendered aviary, although it means a tower. Because aviaries were long, like many towers of old, made of wood, the cage in which birds were kept and fed was called [מגדל] by the Talmudists. A quite unambiguous passage occurs in the Gemara of the Code [כינד], folio 24, page 1: He who hunts a bird and carries it into an aviary, or a roe-deer into a house, is bound to pay. Here [מגדל] means an aviary, as R. Nathan observes in the Aruch, and the Gloss of S. J. attests; although it may also denote a beehive. 3 Finally, the Mishnah excuses the man who pulls down a wall if the wall falls from the other side, because he cannot prevent it if the wall collapses through age and decay. Yet the builder is condemned if, by a blow of his own, the wall he had undertaken to demolish falls from the other side, and in this way stones are broken or someone is hurt. Maimonides, in his Code [פיוי], chapter 6, section 11, adds this reason: Because he is like one who shoots an arrow and does damage with it. He ought to have taken care not to strike so hard that the other and far side of the wall was thereby weakened. Otherwise, just as one who shoots an arrow at another and wounds him must pay for the harm, so likewise one who, handling a wall with too great force, breaks stones falling on the other side, or even hurts passers-by, is bound to make amends. This whole Mishnah takes the side of the one who lets the work, so that the damage is borne by the contractor who undertook the work. In a similar way the Roman law favours the lessor, Dig. 19.2, law 51, §1: I let out a work to be done so that I should give the contractor a fixed wage for each day's work. The work was done faultily. Can I sue on the lease? He replied: if you let out the work so that its goodness was to be approved by you by the contractor; although it was agreed that a fixed sum be given for each day's work, nevertheless the contractor must make good to you, if the work was done faultily. For it makes no difference whether the work is let out for one price or for individual days' labour, provided the whole completion of the work pertains to the contractor, that is, if he was bound to finish the whole work. But just as the builder is excused here, whose fault is that the stones fall and are broken when the wall gives way on the other side, so too Gaius, as it stands in the same title, law 25, §7: He who undertook to carry a column, if it is broken while it is being lifted, carried or set down, is liable for that risk only if it happened through his own fault or the fault of those whose labour he used. There is no fault if everything was done that the most diligent man would have observed. The same we shall understand if someone undertook to transport jars or wood; and the same can be transferred to other things.

units.la: Qui columnam transportandam conduxit, si ea dum tollitur, aut portatur, aut reponitur, fracta sit; ita id periculum praestat, si qua ipsius, eorumque quorum opera uteretur, culpa acciderit. Culpa autem abest, si omnia facta sunt quae diligentissimus quisque observaturus suisset. Idem scilicet intelligemus & si dolia, vel lignum transportandum aliquis conduxerit: idemque etiam ad cateras res transferri potest.
units.tr: He who has hired a column to be carried, if it is broken while being raised, carried or set down, bears the risk only if the fault was his own or that of those whose labour he used. There is no fault, however, if everything was done that the most diligent person would have observed. We shall understand the same if someone has hired casks or timber to be transported; and the same can also be applied to other things.

units.la: [ד ו] הנותן צמר לצבע והקדיחו יורה נותן לו רמי צמרו צבעו כאור אם השבח יחר על היציאה נותן לו ארת היציאה ואם היציאה יחירה על השבח נותן לו ארם השבח לצבוע לו ארום וצבעו שחור שחור וצבעו ארום רבי מאיר אומר נותן לו רמי צמרו רבי
units.tr: If someone gives wool to a dyer and it is burned, the owner gives the dyer the value of the wool. If he dyed it red, the owner gives him the value of the wool dyed, and if the dyeing came out with the wrong colour, the owner gives him the dye costs when the added value exceeds the outlay, and the added value when the outlay exceeds it. If he ordered it dyed red and it came out black, or ordered it dyed black and it came out red, R. Meir says that he gives him the value of his wool.

units.la: Si ubi quis lanam infectori tradidit, eam adurat ' cortina, infector ipsi suae lanae pretium persolvit. Quum eam ² fusco, &c. colore foedavit, si pretii auctarium, sive exuperantia ³ excedat sumptus, ille huic sumptus reddit; sin sumptus exuperantiam excedant, exuperantiam compensat. Si cum ad inficiendum rubedine tradidit, ille nigredine infecit; ad inficiendum nigredine, infecit rubedine: D. Meir alteri {*}pretium lana solvi jubet. Doctor Iudas
units.tr: If, when someone has handed wool to a dyer, the kiln scorches it, the dyer pays the wool's price to its owner. If the dyer has spoiled it with a dusky or other colour, and the increase in value exceeds the cost, the dyer restores the cost to the owner; but if the cost exceeds the increase, he makes up the increase. If he handed it over to be dyed red and he dyed it black, or handed it over to be dyed black and he dyed it red, Rabbi Meir orders that the price of the wool be paid to the other party. Doctor Judas

units.la: יהוה אוטר אם השבת יחר על היציאה נותן לו את היציאה ואם היציאה יחרה על השבת נותן לו את השבת׃
units.tr: Judah says: if the increase in value exceeds the outlay, he gives him the outlay; and if the outlay exceeds the increase, he gives him the increase. [יהודה אומר אם השבח יתר על היציאה נותן לו את היציאה ואם היציאה יתרה על השבח נותן לו את השבח]

units.la: Iudas ita statuit¹, Si exuperantia sumptus excedat, sumptus esse restituendos; & si sumptus excedat exuperantiam, pretii auctarium, sive exuperantiam compensandam esse.
units.tr: Judah thus decided: if the surplus exceeds the cost, the cost is to be restored; and if the cost exceeds the surplus, the increase in price, or surplus, is to be compensated.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ יורה hoc loco est vas tinctorium, quod igni subjecto calefit, ut in ipsum conjectus pannus vel lana colorem infecti liquoris, calore omnino imbibat. id Latini cortinam nuncupant. Hac fervefacta praeter modum lana saepe aduritur, inutilisque redditur: quod cum insector praecavere debuerit, fit ut ex hypothesi in superioribus aliquoties admissa, proprietario suae lanae pretium rependat. Quippe cum res deterior facta sit, nihil restat aliud, quam ut temporis istius habita ratione, quo lanam acceperit, quanti tunc fiebat, restituatur. ² At si eam כפור, eo casu distinctio adhibenda. Distinguenda autem prius duplex vocis כפור significatio, quam diversa Doctorum opinio ipsi attribuit. Quidam כפור idem esse cum כפור fœdo, sive deformi judicant, adeoque inprimis quendam colorem fuscum denotare, qui ad eum reduci nequeat, quem proprietarius desiderat. nec fuscum tantum, sed fuscum & fœdum eo nomine venire; saltem fœdum qui ad alium converti non possit, autumant. Eapropter totum membrum reddidi; Quum eam fusco colore fœdavit, Attamen ubi Gemaram expendo, alia notio se offert, quae fortassis convenientior ac magis idonea judicabitur. Haec sunt Gem. verba, מלי כפור לחר רב נחמן ... Quid est fœdum?(quo explicatur כפור.) respondit M. Nahman ex sententia R. f. Bar Anna, Eluvies. Quid est Eluvies? respondit Rabba filius Samuelis, Proluvies cortina. Hoc sibi volunt, esse reliquias tinctura quibus tinctoria vasa eluuntur & purgantur. Itaque כפור positum fuerit pro ככפור, & vertendum כבשו כפור, Quum eam tinctura reliquiis infecerit. Fieri etiam potest, ut כלבים & כברת דורי in istis Gemarae verbis pro penicillo tinctorio ponantur, quo cortina intus abstergi folet, cujusmodi penicillus diversis coloribus imbutus appareret. Qua significatione admissa, כפור vertendum fuerit, ac fi pro כפור scriberetur, Quum eam infecerit instar mantilis tinctorii ejusque versicoloris. Quomodocunque reddatur, vitium exprimitur, quo lana isto eleganti colore privatur, quem desiderabat, qui tingendam dederat. 3 Id fi eveniat, infectoris conditio semper est deterior, quod Talmudici dicunt, ידו על כפור, manus ipsius est loco infimo. Namque fi נסר, exuperantia five praftantia ac eminentia five pretii lanae autarium deprehendatur, quod ipsos tinctura sumptus fuperet, id est, fi valor quo tincta lana puram excedit, major fit quam sumptus quos in inficiendo tinctor fecit; huic sumptus solummodo refundentur, atque istud lucrum proprietario accrescet. quia hic cum illo pactus erat, ut lanam eleganti colore inficeret; quod tamen neglexerat, imo lanam foedaverat. Sin vero sumptus excedant, majorisque sint valoris, quam augmentum quo lana tincta puram omnique colore destitutam superat (non enim foedus ille color ita accipitur, quasi eo lana deprecietur; sed qui proprietario ingratus est, & minus elegans, & alterius coloris respectu deformis, denotatur:) tum inquam ex eodem fundamento tinctor illud solum augmentum accipit. ut tinctor id amittat quo sumptus augmentum excedit, augmentum scilicet valoris inter lanam tinctam & puram diversi, cum tinctura valorem augeat. Haec est Maimonidae expositio: sed in Chofchen Mifpat alia sententia exprimitur, quae inepta mihi videtur. * Caeterum nonnunquam fit, ut insector alterius mente non satis percepta, colorem diversum licet oculis gratum adhibeat. Quid hoc casu agendum est? Meir alteri, nimirum proprietario, qui lanam tradiderat, ejus pretium reddendum censet: quandoquidem insector (ut ipse quidem arbitratur) ϙᵽ, acquisivit lanam suamque fecit, dum alium quam alter volebat colorem induit. de qua ratione jam aliquoties actum. At D. Judæ sententia obtinet, qui potius פנים לים לבפי רמיים, multatat eum, quia mutavit colorem: unde eodem modo hic agendum censet, atq; in praecedenti facto, ubi foedum colorem induentis conditio deterior semper censebatur.3 Quare si expensae, quas fecit tinctor, majores sint, quam praestantia aestimatur, qua lanam nullo colore imbutam excedit atque exuperat lana colore isto tincta; ne quidem suas expensas omnes recipiet: sed istius inter utramque lanam differentiae valorem refundet qui lanam tradiderat. Porro Maimonides addit in פכירות c. 10. sect. 4. אם יאמר פשעון כפ לך דמי נמרך ולך אין מומין לו מאין פשעון קונס כסנם כלי מעשה, Si dicat artifex, Ecce pretium lanae tuae, abi; non parent ipsi: quia artifex ex eo quod res praestantior facta fit, eam non facit suam. Licet lana grato colore tincta reddatur praestantior, & immutetur, immutatio autem alibi rem alienet; hic ob pactum praecedens lanam restituere debet tinctam, nec eam certo pretio retinere infectori licet. Hac Judaeorum constitutione exigitur, ut conductor locatori praestet de quo inter ipsos convenit. Similiter ff. Loc. conducti, Paulus l. 24. init. Si in lege locationis comprehensum fit, ut arbitratu domini opus adprobetur; perinde habetur ac si viri boni arbitrium comprehensum fuisset. Idemque servatur si alterius cujuslibet arbitrium comprehensum sit. Nam fides bona exigit, ut arbitrium tale praestetur, quale viro bono convenit: idque arbitrium ad qualitatem operis, non ad prorogandum tempus quod lege finitum sit, pertinet. lege, id est, pacto. Confer. ff. Pro socio. l. 77 Ita. l. 3. Inst. t. 25. §. 5. Conductor autem omnia secundum legem conductionis facere debet: & si quid in lege praetermissum fuerit, id ex bono & aequo praestare. Per legem iterum pactum intelligit. הנזל ארת חבירו טור פרוטה ונשבע לו יוליבנו אחריו אפילו למרי לא יהן לא לבנו ולא לשלוחו אכל נוחן לשליח בירת דין ואכ סרת יחזיר ליורשיו׃
units.tr: ¹ Here יורה [yoreh] means a dyeing vat, which is heated by a fire placed under it, so that cloth or wool put into it soaks up the colour of the dye-liquor entirely through the heat. The Latins call it a cortina. When it has been overheated, the wool is often scorched beyond measure and rendered useless. The dyer ought to have guarded against this, so on the hypothesis admitted several times above, he repays the owner of the wool its price. Indeed, since the thing has become worse, nothing remains but that it be restored at what it was worth at the time when he received the wool. ² But if the wool is כפור [kafor], a distinction must be applied in that case. First the twofold meaning of the word כפור must be distinguished, to which the teachers ascribe different opinions. Some judge that כפור is the same as כפור, foul or deformed, and so denotes chiefly a dark colour that cannot be brought to the colour the owner desires. They hold that the word means not merely dark but dark and foul, at least foul in a way that cannot be converted into another colour. For this reason I rendered the whole clause: When she has defiled it with a dark colour, But when I examine the Gemara, another sense presents itself, which will perhaps be judged more suitable and apt. These are the words of the Gemara: מלי כפור [What is kafor?] (by which כפור is explained). Rabbi Nahman replied, following R. Bar Anna, Eluvies. What is Eluvies? Rabbah son of Samuel replied, the washing-out of the cortina. This means the remnants of the dye with which dyeing vessels are rinsed and cleansed. So כפור is to be taken for ככפור, and the clause rendered: כבשו כפור [when he has dyed it with kafor], When he has stained it with the remnants of the dye. It is also possible that כלבים and כברת דורי in these words of the Gemara denote the dyer's brush, with which the cortina is commonly wiped clean inside, a brush which would appear dyed with various colours. On this sense, כפור should be rendered as if the text were written כפור, When he has dyed it like a dyer's cloth, and of many colours.
