However it is rendered, a fault is expressed, by which the wool is deprived of the elegant colour that the one who gave it to be dyed desired. ³ If this happens, the dyer's position is always the worse, as the Talmudists say: ידו על כפור [his hand is in the lowest place]. For if the נסר [nesar], the excess, that is the surplus or advantage, or the increase in value of the wool, is found to exceed the cost of the dye, that is, if the value by which the dyed wool surpasses the pure wool is greater than the expenses the dyer incurred in dyeing, then only those expenses are refunded to him, and that gain accrues to the owner, because the owner had agreed with him that he would dye the wool a fine colour, which he had neglected, indeed had defiled the wool. But if the expenses exceed, and are of greater value than the increase by which the dyed wool surpasses the pure wool stripped of all colour (for that foul colour is not understood as meaning that the wool is depreciated by it, but denotes what is unwelcome to the owner, less elegant, and deformed in comparison with another colour), then, I say, on the same ground the dyer receives only that increase, so that he loses the amount by which his expenses exceed the increase, namely the difference in value between the dyed and the pure wool, since the dye raises the value. This is the exposition of Maimonides, but in the Choshen Mishpat another opinion is expressed, which seems to me absurd. * Otherwise it sometimes happens that the dyer, not having understood the other's mind well enough, uses a different colour, though pleasing to the eye. What is to be done in this case? Meir holds that the price must be paid to the other, namely the owner who handed over the wool, since the dyer (as he himself thinks) has acquired the wool and made it his own, by putting on a colour other than the other wished. We have already treated this reasoning several times. But the opinion of R. Judah prevails, who rather fines him, because he has changed the colour; hence he judges that the matter is to be handled here in the same way as in the preceding case, where the position of one who puts on a foul colour was always regarded as the worse. Therefore, if the expenses the dyer incurred are greater than the advantage by which wool dyed in that colour exceeds and surpasses wool not dyed in any colour, he will not recover all his expenses, but will refund to the one who handed over the wool the value of the difference between the two kinds of wool. Further, Maimonides adds, in Sales, ch. 10, sect. 4: אם יאמר פשעון כפ לך דמי נמרך ולך [If the craftsman says, here is the price of your wool, go away; they do not obey him, because the craftsman, by the fact that the thing has become more valuable, does not make it his own]. Although wool dyed in a pleasing colour becomes more valuable and is changed, and change elsewhere alienates a thing, here, because of the prior agreement, he must return the wool dyed, nor is the dyer permitted to keep it for a fixed price. By this constitution of the Jews, the lessee is required to perform to the lessor what was agreed between them. Similarly, in the Digest, Locati conducti, Paulus, l. 24 init.: If it is included in the terms of the letting that the work is to be approved at the discretion of the owner, it is held just as if the discretion of a good man had been included. And the same is observed if the discretion of any other person is included. For good faith requires that such discretion be exercised as befits a good man, and that discretion relates to the quality of the work, not to extending the time fixed by the contract. By lex, he means agreement. Compare Digest, Pro socio, l. 77 Ita; Institutes, l. 3, t. 25, §5: The lessee must do everything according to the terms of the lease; and if anything has been left out of the terms, he must make it good according to what is good and fair. Again by lex he means the agreement. הנזל ארת חבירו טור פרוטה ונשבע לו יוליבנו אחריו אפילו למרי לא יהן לא לבנו ולא לשלוחו אכל נוחן לשליח בירת דין ואכ סרת יחזיר ליורשיו [If a man robs his fellow of a penny and swears to him, he shall not be liable even to his heirs; he shall not give it to his son or his agent; but if he gives it to an agent, it is a matter for the court, and he shall return it to his heirs].

units.la: Qui surripuit proximo valorem minuti, eique pejeravit; illum ad eum deferet etiam in Mediam. non dabit ejus filio, nec ejus institutori vel parario; sed curiæ recuperatori: si ille moriatur, ipsius hæredibus restituet.
units.tr: He who steals from his neighbour the value of a minutia and swears falsely to him, shall bring it back to him even to Media. He shall not give it to his son, nor to his agent or factor, but to the recoverer of the court. If that man dies, he shall restore it to his heirs.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: In textu originali est פרוטה. minutum vel minutia reddi potest, quia est minimus Ebræorum numus. Ad c. 8. sect. 6. Num. 2. de hoc numismate jam actum fuit: ubi octavam dorageis sive חֵלֶק partem fuisse, testimonium illic productum evincit. חֵלֶק autem ibidem, S. Jarchi teste, quartam tressis partem, sive duos chalcos cum dimidio, id est, λεπτὸν dimidium continebat: unde exigui valoris fuisse constat. Nihilominus si quis istum numulum rapiat, & post rapinam, non rapuisse juratus, culpam agnoscat; istam minutiam proprietario licet in remoto loco habitanti deferre tenetur. Quod Judæi se ex hoc commate 5.cap.6.Levit. probare autumant, Aut de quocunque juraverit mendaciter, (inter varias species, com. præcedenti rapinam recensuerat,) rependat illud quanti fuerit, & quintam ejus superaddito ei: ei cujus est dato illud, quo die reatum agnoverit. Adeo ut ultimam vocem אשם, reatus, argumento com.4. ubi אשם est reatum agnovit, pro reatus agnitione accipiant: ut qui utrobique idem designari observaverint. Et quia, ei cujus est dato, istic legitur, ipsi proprietario reddi præcipiunt, nec alium admittunt qui proprietarii nomine raptum recipiat. שבע etiam in Mischna esse pejeravit contextus edocet: quandoquidem exprimere voluit author illa verba comm. 3. juraverit de mendacio, id est, juramento mendacium suum confirmare voluerit; item Sic ellipsis in Mifnico textu agnoscitur, ut ישבע, juravit, fit תפ ישבע, juravit mendaciter, sive perjeravit. Hoc comma quintum cum paucis praecedentibus gravia & horrenda delicta continet: nihilominus sequentia duo commata expiationem ariete peragi edocent. Adeo ut Socinianorum error de levioribus tantum peccatis per sacrificia expiatis hic corruat. nonne enim haec gravia sunt flagitia, rem apud se depositam negare, quidpiam rapere raptumque negare, rem ab alio amissam detinere, omniaque haec peccata ac similia falso juramento occultare velle?4 Sed quod ad rem praesentem facit, ex illo testimonio nequidem raptum ויקח, ei qui ab illo proprietario missus est reddi posse contendunt. Magistrorum mens non est, eum qui minutiam abreptam recepturus est, quendam ablegare, qui numuli valorem recepturus sit. (licet id in rebus majoris momenti, ut si ingens pecuniae summa, aliaque recipienda sint, locum habeat: nam eo casu בעל דין שהשביעו בית דין, recuperator quem is constituit adhibitis testibus cui res erepta fuit, habetur pro recuperatore; ut in Gemara f.104. docetur. ideoque huic rem ereptam reddi posse statuunt Maimonides & R. Jacob. hic tamen de hujusmodi delegato non agitur.) sed שליח vocatur, quem Latini pararium dicunt, cujus opera inter venditorem & emptorem intervenit; cujusque interventu commercia habentur. vel etiam institor non male redditur, qui negotiationi quaestuariae a mercatoribus praeponi solet, ut in tabernis, vel alibi merces vendat. Ne quidem raptori permittunt, ut si mercator peregre profectus in longinqua loca pararium vel institorem reliquerit, ei ablatum numulum reddat. quo mordicus legis vocabulis adhaerent: quum tamen initio sequentis Mifnae ab ista longa profectione raptorem excusent, qui fortem solvit nec quintam addidit; licet quinta ista saepe multo major sit illa minutia. tiâ. atqui Deus Levit. 6. 5. quintam cum forte proprietario reddendam sancit. Nec est in affixo ו, cum dicitur, יתנך, dabit illud, quo ista sententia defendi queat: quandoquidem cum praecedunt nomina diversi generis, masculinum ut dignius ad utrumque praecedens referri non est inusitatum. Quis non videt ultima verba, ei cujus est dato illud &c. ad utrumque referri, puta ad summam principalem, & quintam ejus partem quae addenda erat? Hoc modo Judaei solent, vel scrupulose coarctare leges; vel dilatare ubi commodum videtur. Evestigio tamen, licet interdictum praecedens illo commate statuminent, vel pallient; totum revocant, dum ipsi יד בית שלום raptum reddi concedunt, quo is proprietario restituat. Quemadmodum שליח ציבור, legatus coetus dicitur qui legem publico nomine in coetu praelegit, vel concionatur, aut etiam sacerdotis munere in benedicendo fungitur, (uti notis ad Benjaminem docui;) sic etiam fieri potest, ut חזן vel praesidem senatus qui senatorum nomine multa dicit agitque; vel senatus & curiae statorem notet, quo in citandis personis aliisque ministeriis senatus uti consuevit, modo publico senatorum nomine sua negotia peragat. Attamen hoc loco שליח בית דין est delegatus per ipsum senatum, quo raptum accipiat, postea proprietario reddendum. Id cum aliunde liqueat, tum etiam notis Josephi Karo ad Chofchen Mifchpat confirmatur, qui num. 367. lit. ב scribit, Quod vero dicit (R. Jacob in Chofchen Mifchpat) Similiter, si postquam constituit senatus recuperatorem, huic raptor reddit, liber est; id ibi in Mifna legitur, Sed ipse tradit recuperatori senatus. Hinc satis apparet eundem esse recuperatorem senatus cum eo, quem senatus ad eam rem recuperatorem constituit. Karo enim Rabbi Jacobi sententiam in Mifna aliis tantum verbis exprimi affirmat. Hunc שליח בית דין per quandam similitudinem recuperatorem dici posse existimo: quia hic de privatis rebus per injuriam extortis ex delegatione cognoscebat; ita ille מלית à senatu delegabatur, quò raptum reciperet, quod sine rei cognitione fieri non poterat. Non errabit forte, qui è Cicerone Coactorem dixerit: cujus erat numos cogere & exigere; quod illi מלית כד competebat. Caeterum ubi Misnæ author, aliique recentiores id raptori permittunt, ut huic coactori solvat, cum ipsum proprietarium omninò compellandum antea decernant; non satis cohæret. Idcirco priori decreto convenientius in Gemara hoc posterius restringitur: הס סיקס סיתיס יתיר על הקרן מטלס קרן וחומס לבית דין, Si expensa sortem excedant, sortem cum ejus quinta parte Senatui reddit. Nam si mina consumenda esset in itinere, quò minutiam proprietario redderet; nonne multo æquius ut alicui solveret debitum, qui minori sumtu proprietario id restituere alia quadam ratione posset? Ideo Scriptura sacra nihil definit: tantum summam cum quinta parte restituendam docet; si sponte reus suam culpam agnoscat & deprecetur. Romanæ leges pœnitentiæ statum hac in re non considerant; sed actionem qua proprietarius rem suam persequitur. atque istam pœnam exigunt, cujus supra facta mentio. Imo si quis rem suam se putaret rapere, duplum saltem rependere debebat. Inst. l. 4. t. 2. circa medium, Sin autem aliena res fit (quam suam putabat) post restitutionem ejus, etiam æstimationem ejusdem rei præstare. Quod non solum in mobilibus rebus, quæ rapi possunt, Constitutiones obtinere censuerunt; sed etiam in invasionibus, quæ circa res soli fiunt, ut ex hac causa ab omni rapina homines abstineant.
units.tr: The original text has פרוטה [peruta]. It can be rendered "minutum" or "minutia", because it is the smallest Hebrew coin. I have already discussed this coin at chapter 8, section 6, note 2, where the testimony produced there shows that it was the eighth part of a dorageis, or חֵלֶק [heleq]. According to S. Jarchi, a heleq contained a quarter of a tressis, that is, two and a half chalcoi, or half a λεπτόν [lepton]. It is clear, then, that it was of very small value. Nevertheless, if someone takes this little coin, and after the theft, having sworn that he did not steal it, acknowledges his guilt, he is bound to bring the minutia to the owner, even if the owner lives in a distant place. The Jews claim that they prove this from the fifth verse of Leviticus 6, "Or in anything about which he has sworn falsely" (among the various kinds of offence, which the preceding verse had listed as robbery), "he shall restore it in full, and add a fifth part to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs, on the day he acknowledges his guilt." They take the last word, אשם [asham], "guilt", in the sense of the acknowledgement of guilt, by the argument of verse 4, where אשם means "he acknowledged his guilt", so that in both places the same thing is meant. And because the text reads "give it to him to whom it belongs", they order that it be returned to the owner himself, and do not admit anyone who would receive the stolen goods in the owner's name. That שבע [shava] means "swore falsely" in the Mishnah is shown by the context: the author wished to express by those words the phrase of verse 3, "swears about a lie", that is, he wishes to confirm his lie by an oath. Likewise, in the Mishnaic text an ellipsis is recognised, so that ישבע, "he swore", becomes תפ ישבע, "he swore falsely", or "perjured himself". This fifth verse, together with the few preceding ones, deals with serious and dreadful offences. Yet the following two verses teach that atonement is made by a ram. So the error of the Socinians, that only lighter sins are expiated by sacrifices, collapses here. For are these not grave crimes: to deny a deposit held by another, to steal something and then deny the theft, to keep back a thing lost by another, and to want to conceal all these sins and similar ones by a false oath? But as far as the present matter goes, from that testimony they contend that the stolen goods cannot even be returned by "ויקח" [vayiqach], "someone who has been sent by that owner" (as in "to him who is sent by him"). It is not the mind of the masters that the one who is about to receive the stolen minutia should send someone else to receive the value of the coin. (This may hold in matters of greater importance, where a large sum of money or other things are to be recovered; in that case, "a party to a suit whom the court has made swear, the recoverer whom he appoints, with witnesses present, is regarded as a recoverer", as is taught in the Gemara, folio 104. Therefore Maimonides and R. Jacob hold that the stolen thing may be returned to such a recoverer; but here we are not concerned with such a deputy.) But the one called שליח [shaliach] is what the Latins call a pararius, through whose agency a transaction is conducted between seller and buyer, and through whose intervention commerce is carried on. It may also be fairly rendered institor, the man who is usually placed over a retail trade by merchants, to sell wares in a shop or elsewhere. They do not even permit the thief, if a merchant, having gone abroad to distant places, has left a pararius or institor, to return to him the stolen coin. In this they cling stubbornly to the words of the law, although at the beginning of the following Mishnah they excuse, on account of that long journey, a thief who pays the principal and does not add the fifth part, even though that fifth part is often much greater than the minutia itself. And yet God in Leviticus 6:5 orders that the fifth part be returned with the principal to the owner. Nor does the suffix ו in יתנך [yitnekha], "he shall give it", allow this opinion to be defended, since when nouns of different gender precede, it is not unusual for the masculine to be referred to both preceding nouns, as the more worthy. Who does not see that the final words, "he shall give it to him to whom it belongs", etc., refer to both: to the principal sum, and to the fifth part that had to be added? In this way the Jews are accustomed either to restrict laws scrupulously, or to stretch them wherever it seems convenient. Immediately, however, although they set up or soften the prohibition expressed in the preceding verse, they revoke the whole, while they concede that the stolen thing may be given to יד בית שלום [yad beit shalom], so that he may restore it to the owner. Just as שליח ציבור [shaliach tzibbur] is the term for the one who reads the law aloud in the assembly on behalf of the public, or preaches, or even performs the priestly function of blessing (as I showed in my notes on Benjamin), so it may also be that חזן [chazzan] denotes the president of the senate who says and does many things in the name of the senators, or the usher of the senate and the court, whom the senate customarily uses for summoning persons and other services, provided he conducts his business in the public name of the senators. Yet in this passage שליח בית דין [shaliach beit din] is a deputy appointed by the senate itself, to receive the stolen thing so that it may afterwards be returned to the owner. This is clear from elsewhere, and it is confirmed also by the notes of Joseph Karo on the Choshen Mishpat, who writes at number 367, letter ב: "As for what he says (R. Jacob in Choshen Mishpat), 'Likewise, if after the senate has appointed a recoverer, the thief gives it to him, he is free' — this is what is read in the Mishnah there: 'But he himself hands it over to the senate's recoverer.'" From this it is clear enough that the senate's recoverer is the same as the one whom the senate appoints as recoverer for that matter. For Karo asserts that R. Jacob's opinion is expressed in the Mishnah only in different words. I think this שליח בית דין can be called a recoverer by a certain similarity: because the latter dealt with private goods taken by violence, by delegation from the court, so that the former was delegated by the senate to receive the stolen goods, which could not be done without a hearing of the case. Perhaps he will not be wrong who, from Cicero, calls him a coactor, whose task was to collect and exact money, which corresponds to the כד [kad] of that office. Besides, where the author of the Mishnah and other more recent writers permit the thief to pay this collector, although they had earlier decreed that the owner himself must be fully approached, it does not agree well. Therefore, in the Gemara, the later decision is restricted in line with the earlier one: "If the expenses exceed the principal, he gives back the principal with its fifth part to the senate" (הס סיקס סיתיס יתיר על הקרן מטלס קרן וחומס לבית דין). For if a mina were to be spent on the journey in order to return the minutia to the owner, would it not be much fairer that he pay the debt to someone who could restore it to the owner by some other means at less expense? Therefore Holy Scripture settles nothing, but teaches only that the sum with its fifth part must be restored, if the offender voluntarily acknowledges and deplores his fault. The Roman laws do not consider the state of repentance in this matter, but the action by which the owner pursues his property; and they exact that penalty of which mention was made above. Indeed, if someone were to think that he was stealing his own property, he ought at least to return double. Inst. book 4, title 2, near the middle: "But if the thing is someone else's (which he thought was his own), after its restitution he must also pay its estimated value. This the constitutions have decided holds not only for movable things, which can be taken away, but also for invasions that concern immovable property, so that men may refrain from every kind of robbery for this reason."
