units.la: Quintam à Deo præceptam non tanto rigore exigunt, quam rem surreptam: quasi verba Levit. 6. 5. Ei cujus est dato illud, non ad proximum, Quintam ejus superaddito ei; sed remotius de restituendo rapto præceptum pertinerent. unde hæc distinctio eorum ortum ducit. Si rapto פרוס minutum defit, quod adhuc debeatur, in longinquis locis proprietarium quærendum docent; quinta rapti pars si solvenda restet, quamvis isto minuto major, proficiscendi molestiam raptori remittunt. Illa tamen verba è Levit. producta ad utrumq; membrum præcedens spectare, series ostendit. Hac de causa Ebræi qui legem in Græcum sermonem transtulerunt, viri summi, legisque peritissimi, quum sententiam illam utramque respicere cognoscerent, istud relativum ײ in יתננו non expresserunt, ne quis alterutrum tantum intelligi existimaret; verum ellipsi sua, non alió quam ad præcedentia referendam voculam, significarunt dum verterent, ὅν ᾧ ἐστι, αὐτῷ δώσει, cujus est, ei dabit. Quod antea dixi jam confirmo, pronomen masculinum vocibus ita quandoque assigi, ut nomini masculino & fœminino respondeat, quia masculinum dignius est. Gen. 2. 19. Omnem bestiam agri omnemque volucrem cæli adduxisset ad Adamum ut videret qui vocaret eum. םיִח, bestia Ebraeis fœminini est generis, קִּו, volucris, masculini: hisce subjungitur ִּי, eum: ubi affixum ı masculinum adhibetur, quod utrumque nomen præcedens respicit. Pariter Levit.6. 5. ıı in ּיִּנָּ dabit illud, cum remotius ּיִנִּח, ipsum raptum in sua sorte, sive quanti est; tum proximum ּםִיִנֵּח, quintam, complexu suo ambit. Cum hæc ita se habeant, quid causæ cur in ipsa sorte ad proprietarium ipsum deferenda ultimam ųsque minutiam non prætermittant; quintam vero minutia majorem quovis loco & cuivis pararios rependi sinunt? 2 Propterea licet in ipsa sorte reddenda םיִּח, minutum nondum solutum, ad iter suscipiendum, quo dominum adeas, obligare contendant; at 'ּיִּחִּםֶּםָּ םיִח,minus valore minuti non obligare docent: ut si cui tota summa quam rapuit, excepto isto minutulo, remissa fit, ad iter non teneatur. Id sibi volunt hæc verba, Ille gratificatus est utramque excepto minimo, quod םיִח, minuto in ipsa sorte nondum æquivalet; hic illum sequi non tenetur. Quasi dicatur, defectus minoris in rapto valoris, quam םיִח,non obligat. At si ipsum םיִח adhuc debeas, ut ipsum proprietarium adeas necesse est. 3 Nimirum si םיִח, minutum in sorte sive ipsa summa rei rapta, (non in addenda quinta quæ tota non obligat,) desideretur: vel quod eo excepto reliquam sortem solveris; vel etiam, si alter totam ista portiuncula excepta remiserit. Romani in suis legibus non ita κυμινοπ: ideoque non est, quod parallelam distinctionem in rapto ad dominum perserendo anxiè investigemus. Hoc solum subjiciam, quemadmodum in superioribus Deum Levit.6. de fatente reo ultroque culpam deprecante agere docui, ideoque non cujusvis rapti pœnam ac multam ibidem exprimi; sed in genere nisi sponte fateatur, si non extendendam, saltem æquandam esse furti pœnæ, rationi videri consentaneum: simile etiam in Corpore Canonico haberi judicium. Causa 14. q. 5. c. 13. ex Aug. (ubi extare putant) producunt Canonistæ: Pœnale est occulte auferre: multo majoris pœna est visibiliter eripere. Mifnicos Doctores in alia potius distinctione occupari præstitisset, qua raptoris testibus convicti; & sponte culpam agnoscentis, mulctas esse diversas ostenderetur. זי ו §. 7.
units.tr: They do not demand the fifth commanded by God with such rigour as they demand the thing seized. It is as though the words of Lev. 6. 5, To him whose it is, he shall give it, did not refer to the neighbour, and he shall add its fifth to it, but pertained more remotely to the restoring of what was taken by robbery; and from this their distinction arises. If a minim [פרוס] of the principal is still owed, they teach that the owner must be sought out in distant places; but if the fifth part of what was taken is still to be paid, however much greater than that minim, they release the robber from the trouble of the journey. That those words from Leviticus refer to both the preceding members, the sequence shows. For this reason the Hebrews who translated the law into Greek, men of the highest rank and most skilled in the law, when they recognised that the sentence referred to both, did not express the relative ײ in יתננו, lest anyone suppose that only one of the two was meant. Instead, by their ellipsis, by which the little word is referred to what precedes, they signified it in their translation: ὃν ᾧ ἐστι, αὐτῷ δώσει, to whom it belongs, to him he shall give it. What I said before I now confirm: the masculine pronoun is sometimes attached to words in such a way that it agrees with a masculine or feminine noun, because the masculine is the more worthy. Gen. 2. 19: He brought every beast of the field and every bird of the air to Adam, to see what he would call it. The word for beast [חַיָּה] is feminine, the word for bird [עוֹף] masculine; and the pronoun it [אֹתוֹ] is joined to them, where the attached masculine ending is used, referring to both preceding nouns. Likewise in Lev. 6. 5 the pronoun in he shall give it [יִתְּנֶנּוּ] refers to the raptum itself in its principal, that is, to the full amount, more remotely; and the nearer fifth [חֲמִישִׁתוֹ] it embraces in the same construction. Since these things stand thus, what reason is there why they should not omit the last smallest fraction in restoring the principal to the owner himself, yet allow the fifth, if it is smaller than the minim, to be paid at any place and to any person? Therefore, although they contend that the minim [חִסָּר] still unpaid in the restoring of the principal obliges one to undertake the journey to find the owner, they teach that a deficiency less than the value of a minim [פחות משוה פרוטה] does not oblige, so that if the whole sum he took, except that tiny fraction, is remitted to someone, he is not bound to travel. This is what these words mean: He forgave him both, except the least, which in the principal is not yet equal to a minim; he is not bound to follow him. As if to say, a shortfall in the value of the thing taken that is less than a minim does not oblige. But if you still owe the minim itself, it is necessary to go to the owner himself. 3 Namely, if a minim [מִנִּי] is wanting in the principal, that is, in the sum of the thing seized (not in the added fifth, which altogether does not oblige), either because you paid the rest of the principal except that amount, or because the other party remitted the whole of that small portion except it. The Romans in their laws did not put it so; therefore there is no need for us to inquire anxiously after a parallel distinction in carrying the stolen goods back to the owner. I will add only this: as I showed above, Lev. 6 deals with the accused who confesses and voluntarily pleads for pardon, and therefore that passage does not express the penalty or fine for every kind of robbery; but in general it seems reasonable that, unless he confesses of his own accord, the penalty should, if not be extended, at least be made equal to that for theft. The Canonists also cite a similar judgment in the Canon Law: Causa 14, q. 5, c. 13, from Augustine (where they think it is found): The penalty for secretly taking is a penalty; the penalty for seizing openly is much greater. It would have been better for the Mifnic teachers to occupy themselves with another distinction, by which it would be shown that fines differ when the robber is convicted by witnesses and when he acknowledges his guilt of his own accord. §. 7

units.la: נתן לו ארץ הקרן ונשבע | Si illi summam reddidit, & de quinta pejeravit; ecce hic insuper quintam partem de quinta persolvet, donec sors reddatur minor valore minuti. Ita se res habet sive depositum sit, sive mutuum, sive raptum, aut cum fraudavit proxi-mum suum, aut rem perditam invenit de qua mentitus est: si pejeravit, ecce is solvit sortem cū quinta & sacrificium reatus. (Quum proprietarius) Vbi est depositum meum; (depositarius) ei respondet, Amissum est: (proprietarius) Adjurote; respondet ille, Amen: & testes contra eum testantur, eum istud consumpsisse. tum rependit sortem. Si sua sponte fatetur; sortem, quintam & reatum rependit.
units.tr: If he restored the principal to him and swore falsely about the fifth, then behold, he shall pay the fifth part of the fifth in addition, until the principal is returned less than the value of a minim [נתן לו ארץ הקרן ונשבע]. So the matter stands whether it was a deposit, a loan, or a seizure, or when he has defrauded his neighbour, or has found a lost thing about which he has lied: if he has sworn falsely, behold, he pays the principal with the fifth and the sacrifice for his guilt. (When the owner asks) "Where is my deposit?" (the depositary) answers him, "It has been lost." (The owner) "I adjure you"; he answers, "Amen"; and witnesses testify against him that he has consumed it. Then he repays the principal. If he confesses of his own accord, he repays the principal, the fifth and the guilt.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ Evenire potest ut, qui sortem ipsam in rapto refudit, quintam cujus ob falsum juramentum reus est retinere cupiens, hanc inquam se solvisse pejeret.Hoc casu istam quintam ꝑp sive sortem fieri ac censeri tradunt: quo fit ut legi Levit. 6. convenienter, non solum quintam istam, ubi peccatum agnoscitur; sed etiam istius quintæ quintam debeat. Etenim perjurus, illa lege, quod perjurio sibi ex alienis bonis retinere voluit, restituere jubetur; atque praterea quinta pars (quam magistri quartam esse volunt, & cum quatuor rapti &c. partibus quintam censeri putant) exigitur: unde consequitur, si quintam alienæ rei perjurio detinere moliatur, ut illam quintam, quippe alteri debitam, restituere; quintamque istius quintæ, quippe ordinariam multam, superaddere teneatur. 2 Verumenimvero, ne ista res in infinitum abeat, cautionem adjecerunt, qua ubi quinta multæ loco addenda minor minuto פרוטה evaderet; licet de ea pejeraverit, ipsa tantum postularetur. Vbi non possum quin Maimonidæ sphalma annotem, eumque Talmudistarum authoritate refellam. Hic in commentariis adMisnajoth, exemplo hanc exceptionem explicat: quod hujusmodi est. Rapuerit quis quatuor denarios, hic solvere quinque tenetur: si ergo postquam quatuor persolvit, de quinto pejeret; quintum denarium & quartam ejus partem debebit: si denuò soluto jam denario, de quarta parte pejeret; insuper quartam debebit: si ulterius soluta ista quarta, de quarta falsò juret, nonnisi quartam istam solvere tenebitur; quia minuti valore sive פרוטה minor est (hic quartam pro quinta in lege expressa exigit.) denarium vocat מ: ita R. Nathan in Aruch מ״ו; drachma & denarius non differunt. & in siclo sacro quatuor esse denarios adjicit. At quid ista ergo sibi volunt? an quarta pars quartæ partis, sive decimasexta pars denarii sive dimidii sicli communis, minoris est valoris quam minutum sive פרוטה? atqui hoc Maim. affirmare videtur. In præcedentibus cum de moneta ageretur, minutum esse octavam assari partem ostensum fuit. issarus autem oboli est quadrans: ut ibidem annotatum. oboli quadrans duos chalcos sive vulgares æreolos cum dimidio ferme aut præcisè continet. Decimasexta denarii pars sub posteriori templo ferme quatuor chalcis sive æreolis valebat: & minutum ne quidem ad dimidii chalci valorem ascendebat. Quis itaque numum vel valorem quatuor chalcorum minuto superari affirmabit, fi modo ad rem attendat? Itaque ut magis de errore constet, glossam S. Jarchi ad pag. 2. f. 10. Codicis Cerithouth adjiciendam duxi, quam ex initio Kiddoufchin & Gemara Cerithouth aliusque locis deprompsit. Ita legitur, מעה סתי מונדיונן ופונדיון סתי היסרין ולסר כ' ממסין מסם סני קונטרקין קונסרק סתי פרוסות דקייכו לכ פרוסות לסעה ולמעה וחני סיוח רוכב דינר היו מ"ח פרוסות Obolus duos femiobolos continet; femiobolus duo ἀσσάρια; ἀσσάριον duos ferme teruncios; teruncius duos parvos areolos; areolus duo minuta, quorum sunt triginta duo in obolo, (quam vocem ut notiorem latius accipio pro treffe;) obolo vero sive treffi cum dimidio, qui est denarii quadrans, insunt minuta quadraginta octo. Hinc quæ nuper de numismatibus, iterumque hoc loco affirmavi confirmantur, materiaque alioqui dubia certior redditur: nec dubito quin loca aliquam multa hinc lucem nancisci queant, cum omnia ad denarium quartam sacri sicli partem revocentur. ³ In sequentibus plerique Codices quædam ante sive depositum sit, legunt: hoc modo, In deposito: quemadmodum dicitur (Levit. 6. 2.) Sive depositum sit &c. ut hoc orationis membro tantum ex professo depositum expendatur; reliquæ verò species solum producantur, quia in illo testimonio, unde depositum hac ratione restituendum probatur, unà occurrunt. Verum cur secundum hanc lectionem וו, aut, sive, ante פקדון; depositum insereretur? quandoquidem in textu sacro non habetur.⁴ Majoris momenti est interpretum diversitas in enarratione verborum, תקומת יד, positio manus. Obadia de Bartenora reddit מלוה, mutuum; ubi quis mutuum sibi concessum postea se accepisse negat, & mendacium juramento stabilire conatur. expositionemque istam proferens etiam Abrabaniel, designari numorum mutuationem; rationem innuit quare hæc manus positio dicatur: ממסמים מיד ליד, qui numi sic ponuntur de manu in manum. qui alteri pecuniam mutuat, plerumque manu sua in alterius manum illam transfert: unde per יד תמורת illam mutuationem signari, existimant. AbenEzra vero secus: ut qui arbitretur designari תמורת ידו אם סוחר, societatem, qua quis manum suam cum altero componit. Quod sequitur Cl. Junius: qui & Jer. 50. 15. dare manum (dare enim in sacris literis saepe pro ponere usurpatur) de societate & iuncto foedere accipiendum censet: quae expositio e Gal. 2. 9. Syriaco, ubi voces eadem, confirmatur. Et sane quum ex ipsa depositi conditione, hac in parte satis constare posse quid in mutuata pecunia servari oporteat; aliud quid per יד תמורת denotari facile crediderim. nimirum casum hunc proponit legislator, quum post initam societatem, communia bona ita curantur, ut unus sociorum ea, eorumve partem, intervertat. id si postea a se factum pejeret, eodem modo uti in reliquis satisfacere hic iubetur. Porro תמורת in eo quod sequitur, fraudavit proximum suum, quid proprie significare videatur, a quibusdam annotatum. Meam ut sententiam proferam, generale esse vocabulum autumo opprimere significans, quoquo modo oppressio fiat: tamen quandoque vi alterius bona, vel personas etiam detinere notat. atque hoc sibi voluit D. K. in radicum libro, qui inter תמורת & תמורה hoc discrimen non statuit, quasi illud fraudare esset, hoc vero vi rapere; sed quod illud vi retinere, hoc vero per vim rapere quod nondum habes denotet. Unde fit ut תמורת nonnunquam ad mercedem, quae a locatore per vim contra iustitiam detinetur, relatum videamus. Quemadmodum Deut. 24. 14. לא תעשק שכיר עני, Ne vi retineas quod est mercenarii pauperis &c. sed clarius Mal. 3. 5. בכחש שכר שכיר, contra vi detinentes mercedem mercenarii. Unde ad locum Levit. in hac Mishna prolatum notat S. J. שכר שכיר הוא, est merces mercenarii. quasi diceret, hoc תמורת est mercedem mercenarii iniuste retinere; quod ubi fieri negatur & quidem cum perjurio; si culpa deinde agnoscatur, reum ad quintam etiam superaddendam obligat. Et cum ab aliis injustitiæ speciebus hæc distinguatur, non repugno, quin S.J. sententia approbetur. Contingit autem in hoc casu ut fraus concurrat. nam qui alteri mercedem postulanti, se non daturum respondet, posteaque citatus se dedisse jurat; vi & fraude alterum opprimit: licet id totum voce πεν proprie non denotetur. sicuti in aliis injustitiæ speciebus adjunctis liquet: quibus passim fraus in perjurio subsequente accidit; quum tamen fraus reliquis vocibus proprie non exprimatur. Negare tamen nolim fraudandi notionem specialiter aliquando in hac voce reperiri: sed loca quæ id omninò suadeant nondum reperi; licet satis concinnè diversis locis illam quadrare agnoscam. Quapropter cum Judæos quosdam ita sentire deprehendam, & quia cui merces detinetur mercede fraudari non inconcinnè dicetur; fraudandi verbum usurpavi: præsertim cum de eo agatur, cui fraus deinde conjungitur. Itaque Abrabaniel, per vim (scilicet oppresserit) aut quod deceperit eum in computatione sua: adeo ut πεν utrumque denotare existimaverit. Quod ad com.14.c.3.Lucæ attinet, ubi occurrit pro μηδὲ συκοφαντήσῃς; non necesse videtur ut omninò ab opprimendi significatu recedamus. Συκοφαντεῖν satis latè accipitur: adeoq; quovis modo bona extorquere, etiam sub latiori notione continetur. Hinc συκοφάντρια in genere de muliere mala, quæ ita alios injuria afficit ut vitam miserrimam, id est, gravem pœnam mereatur, dici videtur in Aristophanis Pluto: ubi act. 4. sc. 4. quum anus conquesta dixisset vitam miserrimam ago, respondet Chorus, Τί δ' ἐστιν, ἡ πᾶς ἐοὐ συκοφάντρια Ἐν τῆς γυναιξὶν ἡδα.
units.tr: It may happen that someone who has handed back the principal of the stolen goods, but wishes to keep back the fifth for which he is liable because of the false oath, should swear that he has paid this fifth as well. In that case they teach that this fifth is treated and counted as the principal. Hence, in accordance with Leviticus 6, it follows that the person who has sworn falsely must restore not only this fifth, where the sin is acknowledged, but also a fifth of that fifth. For by that law the perjurer, who wanted to keep for himself what he had taken from another's goods by perjury, is ordered to restore it; and besides, a fifth part (which the teachers hold to be a fourth, and which they think is counted as a fifth together with the four parts of the stolen goods, and so on) is exacted. From this it follows that if someone attempts by perjury to withhold the fifth of another's property, he is bound to restore that fifth, which is owed to another, and to add a fifth of that fifth as the ordinary fine. But so that this matter should not go on to infinity, they added a safeguard: when the fifth to be added as a fine would fall below a minute [פרוטה], then, even if he has sworn falsely about it, only that amount is to be demanded. Here I cannot refrain from noting a slip of Maimonides and refuting it on the authority of the Talmudists. Here, in the commentaries on the Mishnah, he explains this exception by an example, which runs as follows. Suppose someone has stolen four denarii; he is bound to pay back five. If, then, after he has paid the four, he swears falsely about the fifth, he will owe the fifth denarius and a fourth part of it. If again, when a denarius has been paid, he swears falsely about the fourth part, he will owe in addition a fourth part. If further, when this fourth part has been paid, he swears falsely about a fourth, he will be bound to pay only that fourth, since it is less in value than a minute [פרוטה] (here he demands a fourth in place of the fifth expressed in the law). He calls the denarius מ: so R. Nathan in the Aruch מ״ו; a drachma and a denarius do not differ. He also adds that there are four denarii in the holy shekel. But what do these things mean? Is a fourth part of a fourth part, that is, a sixteenth part of a denarius or of half a common shekel, of less value than a minute [פרוטה]? Yet Maimonides seems to affirm exactly this. In the preceding discussion, when we dealt with coinage, it was shown that a minute is the eighth assarius part. Now the issarus is a quarter of an obol, as noted in the same place. A quarter of an obol contains about two and a half common brass coins, or exactly so. In the later temple a sixteenth part of a denarius was worth about four brass coins, and a minute did not even reach the value of half a brass coin. Who, then, if he attends to the matter at all, will affirm that a coin or the value of four brass coins is exceeded by a minute? So that the error may be more clearly established, I have thought fit to add the gloss of S. Jarchi on page 2, folio 10, of the Codex Cerithouth, which he drew from the beginning of Kiddushin, the Gemara of Cerithouth, and other places. It reads thus: מעה סתי מונדיונן ופונדיון סתי היסרין ולסר כ' ממסין מסם סני קונטרקין קונסרק סתי פרוסות דקייכו לכ פרוסות לסעה ולמעה וחני סיוח רוכב דינר היו מ"ח פרוסות An obolus contains two half-obols; a half-obol contains two assaria; an assarium about two teruncii; a teruncius two small brass coins; a brass coin two minutes, of which there are thirty-two in an obol (which word, as better known, I take more broadly to mean a treffe); but in an obol or treffe with a half, which is the quarter of a denarius, there are forty-eight minutes. From this, what I have recently said about coins, and again here, is confirmed, and a matter otherwise doubtful is made more certain; nor do I doubt that many passages may gain some light from this, since everything is referred back to the denarius, the fourth part of the holy shekel. In what follows, most codices read some words before whether a deposit is involved: thus, In a deposit: as it is said (Lev. 6:2) Whether a deposit &c. so that only the deposit is treated expressly in this clause of the sentence, while the other kinds are merely mentioned, because they occur together in that testimony from which it is proved that a deposit must be restored in this way. But why should the particle וו, or, whether, be inserted before פקדון, deposit, according to this reading, since it is not found in the sacred text? The difference among the interpreters in explaining the words תקומת יד, the laying on of the hand, is of greater importance. Obadiah of Bertinoro renders it מלוה, a loan, where a man denies that he has received a loan made to him and tries to confirm the lie by oath. Abrabanel, offering this explanation too, says that the lending of money is meant, and he hints at the reason why this laying on of the hand is so called: ממסמים מיד ליד, coins are thus placed from hand to hand. He who lends money to another usually transfers it with his own hand into the other's hand; hence they think that the loan is signified by the phrase יד תמורת. Aben Ezra, however, thinks otherwise, holding that what is meant is תמורת ידו אם סוחר, partnership, by which someone joins his hand with another's. The distinguished Junius follows this; he also takes Jeremiah 50:15, to give the hand (for in sacred letters "to give" is often used for "to place"), as referring to partnership and a joined covenant. This explanation is confirmed by the Syriac version of Galatians 2:9, where the same words occur. And indeed, since from the very terms of a deposit it can be sufficiently established in this part what ought to be kept in a loaned sum, I would readily believe that something else is denoted by יד תמורת. Surely the lawgiver is proposing the case in which, after a partnership has been entered into, the common goods are so managed that one of the partners embezzles them, or part of them. If he later swears that he has not done so, he is here ordered to make restitution in the same way as in the other cases. Further, what תמורת seems properly to signify in the phrase that follows, he has defrauded his neighbour, has been noted by some people. To give my own opinion: I think it is a general word meaning to oppress, whatever way the oppression is made; yet at times it denotes the holding back of another's goods or even of persons by force. This was also the meaning of D. K. in his book of roots, who does not distinguish between תמורת and תמורה as if the former meant to defraud and the latter to seize by force; rather, that the former denotes holding back by force, and the latter taking by force what you do not yet have. Hence it happens that תמורת is sometimes applied to wages which are unjustly withheld by force by the employer. Compare Deuteronomy 24:14, לא תעשק שכיר עני, You shall not hold back by force what belongs to a poor hired servant, &c.; but more clearly Malachi 3:5, בכחש שכר שכיר, those who hold back the wages of the hired labourer by force. Hence, on the passage of Leviticus cited in this Mishnah, S. J. notes שכר שכיר הוא, it is the wage of the hired labourer, as if to say that this תמורת means unjustly withholding the wages of a hired labourer; and where this is denied, and indeed with perjury, if the fault is afterwards acknowledged, it binds the guilty party to add a fifth as well. And since this is distinguished from other kinds of injustice, I do not object to S. J.'s view being approved. In this case, however, it happens that fraud is also involved. For he who, when another asks for wages, answers that he will not pay, and afterwards, when summoned, swears that he has paid, oppresses the other by force and by fraud; although the whole of this is not properly expressed by the word פֵן. This is clear also in other kinds of injustice that are attended by such circumstances, in which fraud often accompanies the perjury that follows, although fraud is not properly expressed by the other words. Yet I would not deny that the notion of defrauding is sometimes found specifically in this word; but I have not yet found passages that wholly support it, although I recognise that it fits quite neatly in various places. Therefore, since I find that certain Jews think so, and because one from whom wages are withheld may fittingly be said to be defrauded of them, I have used the verb to defraud, especially since the matter concerns someone to whom fraud is subsequently joined. So Abrabanel: by force (that is, he has oppressed) or because he has deceived him in his reckoning: so that he thought the word signifies both. As for Luke 14:3, where it occurs for μηδὲ συκοφαντήσῃς, it does not seem necessary that we should entirely depart from the sense of oppressing. συκοφαντεῖν is taken fairly broadly, and so to extort goods by any means is included under its wider meaning. Hence συκοφάντρια seems to be used in general of a wicked woman who so injures others that she deserves a most wretched life, that is, a severe punishment, in Aristophanes' Plutus: where, in act 4, scene 4, when the old woman has complained that I lead a most wretched life, the Chorus replies, Τί δ' ἐστιν, ἡ πᾶς ἐοὐ συκοφάντρια Ἐν τῆς γυναιξὶν ἡδα [What is it? Surely you were not also a sycophantress among the women?].

units.la: Quid est? num forte & tu sycophantria inter mulieres eras? Ad quem locum scholia Græca, ἆρα χ' οὐ ἐν τῆς γυναιξὶ πονηρά, Num etiam tu inter mulieres flagitiosa es? Hic sycophantriam triam & valdè pravam ac improbam (gradum istum poenæ gravitas ostendit) eandë esse vides. Origine quidem sua vox συκοφάντης strictius accipitur, atque ad accusatores designandos qui temere accusant usurpatur: unde Scholia Græca in eundem authorem eandemq;comœdiam id nomen τὴς ἐπωσθὲν μάτλω ἐχκαλύσαν, iis qui quocunque modo temerè ac sine causa accusant, attribui docet. Verum hæc in verbis Johannis apud Lucam locum non habent: milites potius sine judicio forensi rapiunt ac spoliant, quam ut accusandi onus suscipiant. Sed media significatio, qua nec temerè accusantes, nec quivis improbi & injurii; verum vafritie ac dolosis actionibus opprimentes & lædentes significantur, satis commodè in illo Lucæ paragrapho admittitur. Nam ut Scholia Gr. in act. 1. sc. 1. observant, inde vox ista profluxit, quod cum ex Attico agro ficus exportare non liceret, quidam sagacitate quadam iis qui exportarent deprehensis, ad magistratum eos deferebant. Ἐκαλοῦντο συκοφάντης ὡς τὰ σύκα φαίνοντες. ἐπιχειρήσαν αὐτὸ ἐξ ἐκείνης τῆς ὁμοια τῶν πάλαι τοῦ ὡσαύτως. Vocabantur sycophanta, utpote ficus prodentes ac indicantes. Inde ergo hoc nomen invaluit & promonavit ad omnes vafros & versipelles. Itaque vel hæc fuit Johannis mens, Vos milites, neminem vexetis; neque spolietis: id est, neque molestias verbis vel verberibus exhibete; neque aliis bona sua eripite. vel ita ut priori membro aperta vis; posteriori conjuncta fraus ac dolus prohibeatur. quemadmodum ψευδ (cujus conjugato verbo hic Syrus utitur) à Chaldæo alicubi per ψευδ, falsitatem, exprimitur: licet D. K. fraudis ac falsitatis non meminerit. ⁶ Quum perjurio in recensitis factis crimen suum hic reus aggravavit, ex lege Dei eum ad hæc præstanda, quorum meminit Misnæ author, obligari fatemur. Verum addendum, quemadmodum jam antea observatum fuit, quod eadem lex nos monitos voluit, ουδὲ, quum reatum agnoverit: nam si ultro culpam deprecatum non veniret, peccatumque sponte fateretur, hisce non defungebatur; sed poenam furti saltem luebat, nisi etiam graviorem. rapina enim sub furto comprehenditur, & magis congruè reliquæ istæ injustitiæ speciès eodem reducuntur. Hoc sensu Maimonides rectè scripserit Cod. גלה c. 7. sect. 8. אין הנשבע על כפירת ממון ממלם חומם פר סלורה מענמי אבל אם כהו פרים והוא עומר בכפירתו ממלם הקרן בלבד על פי עדים והינו ממלם את החומש שהחומש עם הקרן לכפרה םם כהים והינו מביאים אשם על פי מצמוי
units.tr: What is it? Perhaps you too were a sycophantess among the women? On this line the Greek scholia read: Are you not also wicked among the women? [ἆρα χ' οὐ ἐν τῆς γυναιξὶ πονηρά]. Here you see that a sycophantess is the same as a very wicked and depraved woman (the severity of the punishment shows this degree). By its origin the word συκοφάντης [sykophantes] is taken more strictly and is used for those who accuse rashly, and so the Greek scholia on the same author and comedy teach that this name was given to those who accuse rashly and without cause, by whatever means [τὴς ἐπωσθὲν μάτλω ἐχκαλύσαν]. But this meaning has no place in John's words in Luke: the soldiers seize and plunder without any legal hearing, rather than take on the burden of accusing. Yet the middle meaning, which denotes neither rash accusers nor anyone at all who is wicked and unjust, but those who oppress and harm by trickery and deceitful acts, fits quite well in that passage of Luke. For, as the Greek scholia on Act 1, scene 1 observe, the word arose from this: since it was not lawful to export figs from Attic territory, certain men with a kind of cunning used to denounce to the magistrate those whom they caught exporting them. They were called sycophants, as those who revealed and informed on figs [Ἐκαλοῦντο συκοφάντης ὡς τὰ σύκα φαίνοντες. ἐπιχειρήσαν αὐτὸ ἐξ ἐκείνης τῆς ὁμοια τῶν πάλαι τοῦ ὡσαύτως]. Hence the name took hold and was extended to all crafty and wily people. So either this was John's meaning, You soldiers, harass no one, and plunder no one: that is, do not vex people with words or blows, and do not snatch their goods from them; or else, in such a way that open force is forbidden in the first part and, in the second, joined fraud and deceit. In the same way ψευδ (whose verbal cognate the Syriac uses here) is rendered somewhere by the Chaldee as ψευδ, falsehood, although D. K. makes no mention of fraud or falsehood. ⁶ Since the defendant here has aggravated his crime by perjury in the deeds recounted, we grant that he is bound by the law of God to make restitution of the things the author of the Mishnah mentions. But it must be added, as was observed earlier, that the same law wishes us to be warned [that it applies] even when he has acknowledged his guilt: for if he did not come forward and voluntarily confess the fault and admit the sin of his own accord, he was not discharged by these means, but paid only the penalty for theft, or even a heavier one. For robbery is included under theft, and those other kinds of injustice are more fittingly reduced to the same head. In this sense Maimonides wrote correctly in Cod. Gelah c. 7 sect. 8: [Hebrew: One who swears falsely about denying money does not pay the fifth part unless he confesses of his own accord; but if witnesses come forward and he persists in his denial, he repays only the principal on the testimony of the witnesses, and not the fifth; and the fifth together with the principal is for the expiation of the sin, and they bring a guilt offering on the testimony of the witnesses.]

units.la: Falsò juratus de negata pecunia non rependit quintam, donec sponte ultrò fateatur: sed si accedentibus testibus ipse in negando perfistat, fortem solam refundit ex ore testium; quintam verò non superaddit. Siquidem quinta cum oblatione ad expiationem pertineat: itaq; ista non nisi secundum ultroneam confessionem suam affert. Verum si hæc in eum sensum acciperentur, quasi minoris teneretur perjurus & injurius pertinacia crimen aggravans, quam ille cujus pœnitentia facto probatur; meritò istius magistri sententia rejiceretur auctoritate legis divinæ Ex. 22.9. 7 Atqui è subjunctis Misnæ verbis malè etiam sensisse Maimonides videtur. Procedendi modus duobus casibus iisque duplicibus exhibetur: ubi personæ colloquentes introducuntur, licet id ubique non exprimatur, cujus personæ verba sint, quæ proponuntur. Qui loquendi & scribendi modus in Prophetarum scriptis ac orationibus sæpe occurrit: ut cum Dei & Prophetæ verba esse constet, tamen nonnisi è sensu & circumstantiis liqueat, à quo hic vel ille sermo habeatur. Exemplo nobis sit canticum à Mose exhibitum Deut. 32. Vbi Deus proximè loquutus fuisset, Moses sermonem habet ࿐ f. 29,30,31,32,33. Iterum verò Deus loquitur ࿐ f. 34. & 35. In Cant. Cantic. quam crebrò personæ variant? puta in sponsæ & sponsi colloquio. Non ideo ad nutum personæ loquentes sunt inducendæ: sed cum de diversis loquentibus constat, non semper diserte quis loquatur exprimi dico: quia hoc emphasin sermonum tam arctè conjunctorum vitiaret; & crebra illa repetitio nec non supervacanea, ingrata effet auribus. Illam scribendi formulam Gemarici authores adeo inconcinnè affectarunt, ut magnæ obscuritatis quæ in Gemara occurrit causa sit ac origo. Similiter in hac & seq. Misna, personarum loquentium indicium & nota quandoque prætermissa fuit: ideoque ubi oratio obscurior reddebatur, illas inserui. Prior casus est duplex: cum convincitur; vel ubi ultro culpam fatetur. Et quia à convicto sola sors sive summa principalis postulatur, sequenti verò Misna in altero casu à convicto fure sive depositario duplum saltem exigitur; ex illa collatione casuum, quibus totum non explicant, liquet, Judæos in consumpto depósito & reliquis enumeratis injustitiæ speciebus, excepto furto, minorem multam, imo solam sæpè sortis restitutionem exigere. quod ni alia pœna corrigatur, iniquum est. In hac Misna depositi & quintæ restitutio urgetur: ita Digest. l.16. t.3. §.1. lex in depositarium animadvertit, sed diversimodè. Prætor ait; Quod neque tumultus, neque incendii, neque ruina, neque naufragii causa depositum fit, in simplum: ex earum autem rerum, quæ supra comprehensa sunt, in ipsum, in duplum: in hæredem ejus, quod dolo malo ejus factum esse dicetur, qui mortuus fit, in simplum: quod ipsius, in duplum, judicium dabo. Similiter de rapto, si hæres demum fateatur patris &c. peccatum l. cit. Maimonides, c.7. sect. 6. [Hebrew] , Rapuerit & pejeraverit, mortuusque fit; hæres cum fatetur culpam, fortem solam reprendit: & cum hoc, tum illo casu (quum pater ante mortem fatetur culpam) hæres à reatu offerendo absolvitur. Rapti autem & depositi rationem eandem esse tradunt Misnici. In mutuo hoc considerandum, sub [Hebrew] una cum mutuo comprehendi commodatum: itaque si alterutrum contra æquitatem & justitiam detineatur, eandem multam hoc casu in præcedentibus descripto magistri exigunt. Lex tamen Divina in hujusmodi communiter duplum exigit Ex.22. 9. De omni negotio rerum amotarum de bove, de asino, &c. ad ipsos magistratus venito negotium amborum : quem condemnabunt magistratus, rependito duplum proximo suo. De mutuo ita sancitur Inst. l. 4. t. 6. §. 22. In simplum agitur: veluti ex stipulatione, ex mutui datione, &c. De commodato detento vide Titulum 6. li. 13. ff. Ait Prætor : Quod quis commodasse dicetur, de eo judicium dabo. scilicet, ei qui commodavit adversus eum qui accepit. Vide multa eodem tit. quæ huc spectant, ut commodatum restituatur. Sequitur mercedis solutio: cujus sategisse Romanos vel unicus §. 9. legis 20. Loc. conduc. edocet. Cum quidam exceptor operas suas locasset, deinde is qui eas conduxerat decessisset, Imperator Antoninus cum divo Severo rescripsit ad libellum exceptoris in hac verba: cum per te non stetisse proponas quo minus locatas operas Antonio Aquilia solvereres; si eodem anno mercedes ab alio non accepisti, fidem contractus impleri æquum est. Simile occurrit paragr. 10. Denique ab eo, qui rem perditam invenit, ipsam repeti posse, ostendit quæ tum datur furti actio: unde & poena innotescit. ff. de furtis l. 43. §. 4. Qui alienum quid jacens lucri faciendi causa sustulit, furti obstringitur: sive scit cujus sit, sive ignoravit. Nihil enim ad furtum minuendum facit, quod cujus sit ignoret. Quia vero in Misna hujusmodi casus proponitur, quo reus perjurio peccatum tegere annititur, perjurii poenam ex jure Rom. civili apponamus. Disputari quidem, an perjurus humana poena puniendus sit, cum satis Deum ultorem habeat, non ignoro: nihilominus legibus ista sententia confirmatur, quæ poenam ab hominibus inferendam, hujusmodi flagitioso homini irrogat. Dig. l. 12. t. 2. le. 13. §. 6. Si quis juraverit in re pecuniaria per genium principis (Glossa, Genius dicitur Deus) dare se non oportere, & pejeraverit; vel dari sibi oportere: vel intra certum tempus juraverit se solutur um, nec solvit: Imperator noster cum patre rescripsit, fustibus eum castigandum dimittere; & ita ei superdici, ωσπῆλως μὴ ὀμνυε, id est, petu-lanter {1} 1 lanter ne jurato. Ex ultimis verbis, perjurium puniri liquet. Aliam poenam videre est ff. Stellionat. le. sin. De perjurio, si sua pignora esse quis in instrumento jurare erit, crimen stellionatus fit: & ideo ad tempus exulat. Gravior poena irrogatur leg. 3. §.
units.tr: One who has sworn falsely about money denied does not repay the fifth until he confesses of his own accord; but if witnesses come forward and he persists in denying, he repays only the principal on the testimony of the witnesses, and does not add the fifth. For since the fifth goes with the offering for atonement, it is brought only upon his voluntary confession. But if these words were taken to mean that a perjurer and wrongdoer who aggravates his crime by obstinacy were held to less than one whose repentance is shown by his deed, then this master's opinion would rightly be rejected on the authority of the divine law, Ex. 22.9. ⁷ Yet Maimonides also seems to have misunderstood it from the words of the Mishnah that follow. The method of proceeding is shown in two cases, and each in two forms: where speakers are introduced, though it is not always expressed whose words are being put forward. This manner of speaking and writing often occurs in the writings and speeches of the Prophets: since it is certain that the words are God's and the prophet's, yet it is clear only from the sense and circumstances which speech is attributed to which. Let the song given by Moses in Deut. 32 be our example. Where God had just spoken, Moses holds forth, vv. 29–33. Again God speaks, vv. 34 and 35. In the Song of Songs how often do the speakers change, for instance in the dialogue of bride and bridegroom? The speakers are not to be introduced at a nod; but when it is clear that different people are speaking, I say that it is not always expressly stated who is speaking, because this would spoil the emphasis of speeches so closely joined, and that constant repetition, besides being superfluous, would be unpleasant to the ear. The Gemara authors affected this way of writing so awkwardly that it is the cause and source of the great obscurity found in the Gemara. Similarly in this Mishnah and the following one, the indication and mark of the speakers was sometimes omitted; therefore, where the wording was made more obscure by this, I have inserted them. The first case is twofold: when the man is convicted, or when he confesses his guilt of his own accord. And since from the convicted man only the lot or principal sum is demanded, whereas in the second case of the following Mishnah only double is demanded from the thief or depositary who has been convicted, it is clear from this comparison of cases, which they do not explain in full, that the Jews demanded a smaller fine, often only restitution of the principal, for a consumed deposit and the other enumerated kinds of injustice, except theft. Unless this is corrected by another penalty, it is unfair. In this Mishnah the restitution of the deposit and of the fifth is urged. So the Digest law (16.3.1) pronounces against the depositary, but in different ways: The praetor says: where a deposit is made not for the sake of a riot, fire, collapse, or shipwreck, [the depositary must restore] a single amount; but for those things which are included above, [he must pay] double; against the heir of one who has died, for what is said to have been done by his bad faith, a single amount; for what was his own, double; I shall grant judgment. Likewise concerning robbery, if the heir at last confesses the father's sin, etc., l. cit. Maimonides c. 7 sect. 6: [Hebrew: If he robbed and swore falsely, and died, the heir when he confesses the fault repays only the principal; and in this case, as in that case (where the father confesses the fault before death), the heir is absolved from offering the guilt offering.] The Mishnah teachers hold that the reason for robbery and deposit is the same. In a loan this must be considered: under [the Hebrew term] the loan is included together with the commodatum (a loan for use); so if either is withheld contrary to equity and justice, the masters demand the same fine in this case as in those described before. Yet the divine law usually demands double in such cases, Ex. 22.9: Concerning every matter of stolen goods, of ox, of ass, etc., let the matter of both come before the magistrates: whomever the magistrates condemn, he shall repay double to his neighbour. The Institutes (4.6.22) decree this about a loan: It is sued for a single amount, as from a stipulation, from the giving of a loan, etc. On a withheld commodatum see Title 6 of Digest book 13. The praetor says: Concerning what someone is said to have lent, I shall grant judgment, namely to the lender against the one who received it. See many things under the same title that bear on this, so that the commodatum may be restored. Next comes payment of wages, of which the Romans' care is taught by a single passage, §9 of law 20, Locati conducti: When a certain stenographer had let out his services, and then the one who had hired them died, the emperor Antoninus, together with the deified Severus, replied to the stenographer's petition in these words: since you allege that it was not your fault that you did not render the services hired to Antonius Aquilia, it is right that the agreement be fulfilled, if you have not received wages from another in the same year. A similar case occurs in §10. Finally, that the thing may be recovered from one who has found a lost object is shown by the action for theft which is then granted, and from it the penalty is also known. Digest, De furtis, l. 43 §4: One who has taken up something belonging to another, lying about, for the sake of gain, is bound by theft, whether he knows whose it is or does not know. For the fact that he does not know whose it is does not lessen the theft. But since in the Mishnah a case is proposed in which the defendant strives to cover his sin by perjury, let us add the penalty for perjury from Roman civil law. I am not unaware that it is debated whether a perjurer should be punished by human penalty, since he has God as sufficient avenger; nevertheless this opinion is confirmed by the laws, which impose a penalty to be inflicted by men on such a shameful person. Digest 12.2.13 §6: If anyone has sworn, by the genius of the prince (the gloss says genius means God) that in a money matter he ought not to give, and has perjured himself; or that something ought to be given to him; or has sworn within a certain time that he will pay, and does not pay: our emperor, together with his father, rescripted that he be let go with a beating, and that this be said to him: [Greek: do not swear so wantonly], that is, do not swear playfully. From the last words it is clear that perjury was punished. Another penalty may be seen in the Digest, De stellionatu, law: If someone swears in a document that his pledges are his own, it becomes the crime of stellionate; and so he is exiled for a time. A heavier penalty is imposed in law 3 §

units.la: 2. Infames quoque fieri perjuros, collataq; beneficia adimi, ab aliis annotatum. Praeterea Novel. quaedam Leonis & Constantini perjuro abscindi linguam jubet. Consule Cujac. 7. Obf. 14. Itaque dextre exponenda Imp. Alexandri verba Cod. l. 4. t. 1. non procul ab initio, Iusiurandi contempta religio satis Deum ultorem habet. Periculum autem corporis, vel majestatis crimen, secundum constituta divorum parentum meorum, etsi per principis venerationem quodam calore fuerit pejeratum, inferri non placet. Quia Deus perjuros singulari ratione ulciscitur, non quodvis perjurium, sed subito quodam animi impetu ex magna infirmitate praestitum, gravius puniri non postulant. vel etiam, uti ex antecedentibus colligitur, jusiurandum ab adversario, alicui ad causam decidendam in judicio delatum spectatur: quo iterum ad examen revocato, decisam causam retractari noluit Imperator: ut tandem controversiae finis imponeretur. Atque hoc expendendum, quamvis gravissima poena non exigatur, quae Periculo corporis & majestatis crimine describitur; nihilominus gravem poenam aliis legibus irrogari, non negatur. Hoc pacto istae leges conciliari queunt, ut diversae perjurii causae, species denique poenae expendantur.
units.tr: 2. It has also been noted by others that perjurers are made infamous and that benefices conferred on them are taken away. Moreover, certain Novels of Leo and Constantine order that the tongue of a perjurer be cut out. Consult Cujacius, Observations 7.14. Therefore the words of the emperor Alexander in Code 4.1, not far from the beginning, should be understood correctly: "Contempt for the religion of an oath has God as its avenger enough. But it is not our pleasure that danger to the body, or the crime of treason, be inflicted, according to the constitutions of my divine parents, even if the perjury was committed out of a certain heat of feeling from reverence for the prince." Because God avenges perjurers in a unique way, they do not require that every perjury, but only one committed from a sudden impulse of the mind and from great weakness, be punished more severely. Or, as may be gathered from what precedes, the oath is one that an opponent has tendered to another in a lawsuit to decide the case. When the matter has been brought back again for examination, the emperor did not wish the settled case to be reopened, so that an end might at last be put to the controversy. This must be weighed: although the most severe penalty, which is described as "danger to the body and the crime of treason," is not required, nevertheless it is not denied that a serious penalty is imposed by other laws. In this way those laws can be reconciled, once the different causes of perjury and finally the kinds of penalty have been weighed.

units.la: Vbi est depositum meum? Respondet, furto ablatum. (Proprietarius). Adjuro te. Respondet (alter) Amen. Testes contra ipsum testantur, eum id esse furatum. Tum1 rependit duplum. Si2 sua sponte fateatur; fortem cum quinta & reatu rependit. היכן פקדוני אשר לו נגנב משביעך אני ואמר אמן והעדים מעידין אותו שנגנבו משל' השלומי כפל הודה מעצמו משלם קרן וחומש ואשם׃
units.tr: Where is my deposit? He answers, it was stolen. (The owner.) I adjure you. He answers (the other), Amen. Witnesses testify against him that he stole it. Then he repays double. If he confesses of his own accord, he pays the principal with a fifth and the guilt offering. [היכן פקדוני אשר לו נגנב משביעך אני ואמר אמן והעדים מעידין אותו שנגנבו משל' השלומי כפל הודה מעצמו משלם קרן וחומש ואשם׃]
ANNOTATIONES.

units.la: Jam secundum exemplum, & quidem duplici modo proponit, quo depositum intervertenti, quibusdam antegressis, tandem multa irrogatur. Præcedenti Mișna sub finem, multa depositi dilapidati ac consumpti; hîc verò furto ablati exhibetur. quod furtum vel ultrò reus agnoscit ac fatetur; vel eò testibus adigitur. Hoc si fiat, ut alicubi clam depositum sepositte, aliave ratione integrum à proprietarii oculis occultasse convincatur, duplum (quæ est communior furti pœna, licet quadruplum & quintuplum alibi in quibusdam exigatur,) pendere cogitur. Quamvis Maimon. (si recte memini) duplum non exigat, si illud depositum quidem penes se habeat; nondum tamen manum ipsi admoverit: idque è prava expositione Ex.22.8. At si ultro fateatur & satisfacere velit, summam principalem, puta rem furtivam reppendit, cum quinta parte quam superaddit & proprietario unà tradit; oblatio vero pro reatu Deo offerenda ad sacerdotem adducitur. Quandoquidem in alienato depositio dupli pœna sancitur, quia depositarius furtum commisit, qui alioqui depositi valorem solummodo restituceret; & si furtum in depositio commissum ultro fateatur, ultra sortem sola quinta proprietario debetur: hinc liquet, furti pœnam, quamvis dupli quadrupli & quintupli sit, in fatente reo & ultro restituere cupiente non esse ulterius extendendam, quam ut ex lege Levit. 6. circa principium, exigitur. Hoc etiam Magistri è comm. 9. cap. 22. Ex. colligunt. Siquidem Deus ait, Quem condemnabunt magistratus, rependito duplum. Ergo, inquiunt, quum seipsum reus condemnat, duplum non reppendit. Cæterum quum videamus simpliciter pth, amen hic & in proxime præcedentibus pro toto juramento adhiberi, merito illa voce, quum à Servatore nostro etiam geminatur, legitimum juramentum defenditur. Hic passim de jusjurando sermonem esse voces נשבע, juravit & משבע, adjuravit, indicio sunt: quum verò reus jurare dicitur, vocem amen ore proferens introducitur. quasi dicat, jusiurandum suum ita effert, ut amen pronunciet. Itaque amen jusiurandi nota est: cui hic quod juramento stabilitur, non subjicitur, quia è præcedentibus patet. ט'ו הנחל את אביו ונשבע לו ומת הרי זה משלם קרן וחוש לבניו או לאחיו ואם אינו רוצה או שאין לו לוה ובעלי החוב באיכם ונפרעים׃
units.tr: Now he sets out the second example, and in two ways, by which a penalty is finally imposed on a depositary who has, after certain preliminary steps, misappropriated the deposit. In the preceding Mishnah, at the end, the penalty is for a deposit that has been squandered and used up; here it is for a deposit that has been taken by theft. This theft the defendant either admits of his own accord, or is compelled to admit by witnesses. If this happens, and it is proved that he hid the deposit secretly somewhere, or by some other means concealed it wholly from the owner's eyes, he is forced to pay double (which is the more usual penalty for theft, although elsewhere fourfold and fivefold are exacted in some cases). Maimonides (if I remember rightly) does not demand double if he still has the deposit in his possession but has not yet laid hands on it, and he bases this on a faulty reading of Exodus 22:8. But if he confesses freely and wishes to make restitution, he repays the principal sum, that is, the stolen thing itself, together with a fifth part, which he adds and hands over to the owner at the same time; but the offering to be brought to God for the guilt is taken to the priest. Since, in the case of a deposit that has been alienated, a penalty of double is sanctioned, because the depositary has committed theft (whereas otherwise he would restore only the value of the deposit), and since, if he freely confesses the theft committed in the deposit, only a fifth beyond the principal is owed to the owner, it is clear that the penalty for theft, although it is double, fourfold or fivefold, is not to be extended further when the defendant confesses and is willing to restore of his own accord, than what is exacted by the law in Leviticus 6, near the beginning. The Masters also gather this from Mishnah 9, chapter 22 of Exodus. For God says: Whom the magistrates shall condemn, let him repay double. Therefore, they say, when the defendant condemns himself, he does not repay double. Furthermore, since we see that the simple amen is used here and in the immediately preceding passages for the whole oath, the lawful oath is rightly defended by that word, which is also doubled by our Saviour. That the words niš'ba' (he swore) and mašbi'a (he adjured) are used here throughout of an oath is evident; but when the defendant is said to swear, he is introduced as uttering the word amen with his mouth, as if to say that he pronounces his oath in such a way that he says amen. So amen is the sign of an oath, and what is confirmed by the oath is not added here, because it is clear from what precedes. [Ṭo ha-nifal ... ṭo ha-nifal eto ve-niš'ba' lo, u-meth, harei zeh meshalem keren ve-ḥomesh li-venav o le-aḥav, ve-im eino rozeh o she-eino lo lavveh, u-ba'alei ha-ḥov ba'im ve-nifra'im׃]

units.la: Qui aliquid surripuit & pejeravit patri suo, qui postea mortuus est; ecce hic fortem cum quinta filiis ipsius, aut ejus fratribus rependit: quod si nolit, aut non habeat, mutuatur; & creditores accedunt ac debitum recipiunt.
units.tr: If someone has stolen something from his father and perjured himself against him, and afterwards he dies, behold, he repays the principal with a fifth to his sons, or to his brothers. If he is unwilling, or has nothing, he borrows, and the creditors come and receive the debt.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Totius legis fundamentum in Legislatoris edicto Levit. 6. 4. interpretes collocant: Restituet rapinam ipsam quam rapuit. Unde concludunt, quamvis in hæreditate paterna filius raptor suam portionem habeat, adeoque quod rapuerat ut portionem quandam sibi debitam post obitum patris jure hæreditatis retinere videatur; quo legislatoris edicto satisfiat, quod raptum erat, prius aliis hæredibus (quia patri non potest) restituendum, ut postea demum raptor cum illis hæreditatem cernat. ubi quod sibi in rapto hæreditatis jure debebatur, sibi vendicare & recipere poterit. Quam scrupulosi hic sunt Judæi! Quasi verò legislatoris menti non satisfieret, si raptum pro portione sibi debita raptor hæres retineret; modo quod ultra sortis restitutionem patri debuerat, hæredibus in commune traderet. Sanè hoc perinde est, sive quinque aureos (exempli gratia) quos antea rapuerat, pro sua portione ejusve parte retineat raptor; sive in commune conferat, posteaque in cernenda hæreditate eorundem valorem recipiat. Porrò quum dicitur reddendum esse ꞑꞑ ꞑ ꞑꞑꞑ, dupliciter enarratur. Maimonides Cod. ꞑꞑ c. 8. sect. tertia, ita accipit, ac si de raptoris filiis & fratribus ageretur. ideo inquit, ꞑꞑꞑ ꞑꞑ ꞑꞑꞑꞑ ꞑꞑ ꞑꞑꞑꞑ ꞑꞑ ꞑꞑꞑ ꞑꞑꞑꞑ ꞑꞑ ꞑꞑꞑ ꞑꞑ, Si fratres non habeat, quod hic solus raptor deprehendatur hæres, raptum è potestate sua auferens tradit filiis suis; quod si filios non habeat hic filius raptor, idipsum creditori ejus, aut pro mutuato, aut in eleemosynam expendunt. Melius tamen ab aliis illa verba ipsum patrem respicere judicantur. ipsius proximè facta fuit mentio; nec qui filiis suis, sæpè puerulis, aliquid tradit, è potestate sua amittit; quod tamen quidam Judæorum magistri exigunt, uti verba jam citata ostendunt.■ Iterum sequentia, Nolit, aut non habeat, &c. diversum sensum admittunt. quorum prior, Si nolit suam portionem in isto rapto reddere, aut non habeat fratres vel liberos; ne sua restituat mutuatur ab aliis, & quia fratres &c. non habet, creditoribus inde satisfacit. uti superioribus Maimonidæ verbis docetur. posterior sensus, isque genuinus, est, Si nolit portionem suam amittere, ab aliis mutuatur unde raptum restituat, aut si non habeat solvendi facultatem, alios sollicitat quibus suppeditantibus debitum exolvat: ipsi vero creditores ex isto rapto jam restituto portionem repetunt, quæ raptori in isto rapto ex paternis bonis competebat. Hæredibus & successoribus rapta restitui vult Misna: quod cum ff. Vi bon. raptorum l. 2. §. sin. convenit: ubi actio Vi bonorum raptorum, hæredibus ipsius, cui bona erepta fuere, competit. Hæc actio hæredi caterisque successoribus dabitur. Quod vero Misnæ autor fratrum faciat mentionem, id suum in lege Num. 27.9. fundamentum habet: Quod si filia non erit ei, tunc tradetis possessionem ejus fratribus patris ejus. Deficientibus liberis, succedebant fratres. At hoc casu filius quidem superest;
units.tr: The interpreters base the whole of the law on the Lawgiver's command in Lev. 6.4: He shall restore the very thing he stole. From this they conclude that, although a son who has stolen may have his own share in his father's inheritance, and so may seem to keep by right of inheritance some portion of what he took that is due to him after his father's death, the Lawgiver's command is satisfied if what was taken is first restored to the other heirs (since it cannot be restored to the father), so that the thief then takes up the inheritance together with them. In that case he may claim and receive for himself, by right of inheritance, what was owed to him out of the stolen property. How scrupulous the Jews are here! As if the Lawgiver's intention were not satisfied when the thief, as heir, kept the stolen property as his share, provided that he handed over to the heirs in common whatever he owed beyond the restitution of the principal to the father. Indeed it makes no difference whether the thief keeps five gold coins (for example) that he had stolen as his share or part of it, or brings them into the common stock and later receives their value when he takes up the inheritance. Further, when it is said that it must be restored [ꞑꞑ ꞑ ꞑꞑꞑ], it is explained in two ways. Maimonides, in the Code, Nedarim c. 8, sect. 3, takes it as if the matter concerned the thief's sons and brothers. Hence he says: If he has no brothers, then, since this thief alone is found to be the heir, he hands over what he took from his possession to his sons; but if this thief has no sons, they spend the same on his creditor, either as repayment of a loan or as alms. However, others judge more fairly that those words refer to the father himself, who was mentioned just before. Nor does a man who hands something over to his sons, often little children, lose it from his possession; yet certain Jewish teachers require this, as the words already cited show. ■ Again, the following words, if he is unwilling, or does not have, etc., admit a different sense. On the first reading: if he is unwilling to restore his share in this stolen property, or has no brothers or children, he borrows from others so as not to restore it himself, and because he does not have brothers etc., he satisfies the creditors from that source, as is taught in the words of Maimonides above. The second sense, which is the genuine one, is: If he is unwilling to lose his share, he borrows from others with which to restore what he took, or if he lacks the means of paying, he seeks others by whose help he may discharge the debt. The creditors themselves, however, claim from this restored property the share that belonged to the thief from his father's goods. The Mishnah wants the stolen property restored to heirs and successors, which agrees with the Digest, Vi bonorum raptorum, l. 2, §. sin., where the action for goods taken by force lies for the heirs of the one whose goods were seized: This action shall be given to the heir and the other successors. That the author of the Mishnah mentions brothers has its foundation in the law, Num. 27.9: But if he has no daughter, then you shall give his possession to the brothers of his father. Where there were no children, the brothers succeeded. But in this case a son is indeed left; [...]

units.la: {3} Iterum sequentia, Nolit, aut non habeat, &c. diversum sensum admittunt. superest; sed qui hic primo rei personam sustinet, non hæredis: quare & creditores ac unde mutuo accepit, tum hæredes secundum utramque expositionem potius censentur.
units.tr: Again, the following words, if he is unwilling, or does not have, etc., admit a different sense. [...] but he who here first bears the role of the debtor, not of the heir. Wherefore, according to either exposition, the creditors, and those from whom he borrowed, are rather to be counted as the heirs.

units.la: האומר לבנו קונם אי אתה נהנה ממני מה ירשנו בחייו ובמותו אם מת לא ירשנו ויחזיר לבניו או לאחיו ואם אין לו לה ובעלי החוב באים ונפרעים:
units.tr: If a man says to his son, "Qonam [קונם], you shall not benefit from me [אי אתה נהנה ממני]," then what we inherit from him, in his life and in his death: if he dies, we do not inherit it, and it returns to his sons or to his brothers; and if he has nothing for it, creditors come and are paid.

units.la: Si quis filio suo dixit, sanctè vovi¹, te ex meis non esse utilitatem percepturum; ubi obiit, ejus sit heres filius. Si de vita & ² morte sua hoc dixit; ubi obiit, ejus heres non sit filius: sed ³ illius filiis aut fratribus hereditatem tradit. Si nihil habeat,⁴ mutuatur: & creditores accedentes debitum ⁵ recipiunt.
units.tr: If someone said to his son, "I have solemnly vowed¹ that you shall gain no benefit from me," then when he dies, his son is his heir. If he said this about his life and his death,² then when he dies his son is not his heir, but he hands the inheritance to his sons or brothers.³ If he has nothing,⁴ he borrows, and the creditors who come forward receive the debt.⁵
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ קונם quare à lexicographis ita prætereatur, vix dici potest; nisi quod hanc vocem in Aruch non repererint. Satis frequenter tamen occurrit c.1. & seq. Cod. נדרים: unde ipsius notio elucescit, qua vovere & consecrare item devovere denotat. & plerumque קונם de voto ejusmodi usurpatur, quo alicujus rei usus interdicitur, vel in genere res aliqua quibusdam denegatur. Adeo ut juramenti etiam formula קונם videri queat, quæ illiusmodi interdicto sive voto negativo præmitti soleat, ad ejusdem confirmationem. Verbum tamen, nomenque inde deductum potius agnosco. Quandoque קונם cum ם ejusdem significationis est, quod è Nedar. 1. constat; licet passim per ם etiam scribatur. unde in Codice Nedarim f.86. קונמות, consecrata sive vota. & alibi קונמיס, interdictum: quia uti dictum fuit, in negativis votis plerumque adhibetur. Ita hoc loco קונם, vovens, id est, voveo, vel vovi, te ex meis &c. unde in quodam Codice additur פ pro ס, litera una transpositâ; ut אתה קונם fit vovens sum, id est, voveo. vel ut fit nomen : quasi dicas, votum conceptum est, te non &c. Quibus verbis parentum non religio, quemadmodum illi putant; sed impietas erga liberos sese prodit. Quid iniquius quam filiis ea denegare, quibus carere nequeunt? cujusmodi sunt alimenta, aliaque quibus in hac vita egemus. Parentum est liberos sustentare, eaque quoad fieri potest suppeditare, quibus instructi honestè vitam traducere queant. Similis illa est inhumanitas & improbitas filiorum, quam Clarissimus Coccæus è capite 11. Cod. Nedarim depromptam, convenire ostendit cum isto facto, quod Servator Iudæis Mat.15.5. improperavit: puta filios, qui sua bona consecrando, egenos parentes iis privarent, à magistris absolutos fuisse; quum tamen pietatem parentibus lege etiam naturæ debitam violarent. Cum hac filiorum impietate non inconcinne meo judicio conferam, quod apud Maimonidem invenio in Talmoud Thora c. 5. sect. 1. ubi amorem & reverentiam patri debitam, reverentiæ & amori præceptoribus exhibendo postponit. חייב ככבוד רבו ויראתו יותר מאביו Præceptorem suum magis honorare & revereri, quam patrem suum tenetur. & paulo post, ודא אבידת אביו ואבידת רבו של רבו קודמת, filius si videat patris sui interitum, & interitum præceptoris sui, cura de præceptore præcedet: vel pro interitum ponamus rem amissam. uti Iudæi vulgo accipiunt. Addit, ואם רבו שבויים בשביית פדה את רבו ואחר כך filius si pater & præceptor captivitate detineantur, prius præceptorem suum redimit; postea demum patrem suum liberat. An ergo mirum, si Scribæ & Pharisæi docuerint, filios bono animo bona sua, parentibus suis derelictis, consecrare posse; ubi isti doctores è consecratis utilitatem percipiebant? Si in illis & libertate (quæ ipsa vita charior) conservandis, magistros suos prætulerunt; ut in aliis bonis idem peccatum committerent, proclives fuisse mirum non est. Duplici vero modo filio suis bonis interdicebat parens: vel dum ipse viveret; vel in perpetuum, sive ut loquitur noster, de vita & morte, istud accipi volebat. Illo modo, post obitum patris cum reliquis hæreditatem cernebat; posteriori verò modo, hæreditate excidebat. ¹ Quum filius isto ⊃ʸp exhæreditatus fratribus suis vel parentis sui מיתר, restituere sive potius tradere dicitur, id Josephus Karo commentariis in Jad Chazaka sano sensu accipiendum docet. Nam ipse bona illa cæteris non tradit & largitur; alioqui habuisset & possedisset, eaque ratione contra voluntatem patris, qui emolumentum interdixerat, venisset: sed ostendit illis paterna bona, permittitq; ut accipiant & prout libitum fuerit iis utantur ac fruantur. מכ, filiis illius autem ad filios patris, non filii referendum satis ex Maimonide liquet: qui eo casu Cod. Nedarim c. 5. sect. 7. filium filii, sive patris nepotem, nonnisi avi expressa constitutione ad hæreditatem admittit. ⁴ At hoc pacto in gravem inopiam filius sæpe incidit, nec quo vitæ commoda sibi comparet, assequitur. quid hoc casu faciendum? Ab aliis mutuo accipiat, permittunt; unde vitam sustentet. ⁵ Creditoribus deinde permittitur, ut mutuum ab aliis hæredibus repetant, quantum portio quæ illi ex hæreditate obvenisset, suppeditat. Quod si objicias, hac via utilitatem magnam è paternis bonis percepturum esse filium; responsio duplex in promptu est. istum debita solvendi casum excipi ajunt, secundum sect. 2. c. 4. Cod. Nedarim. המור מכיר מיבא... Si quis voto prohibitus est utilitatem percipere à proximo suo, hic siclum ejus expendet, ejusque debitum solvet. siclum dimidium intelligit, quem singulis annis Israëlitæ ad oblationes totius cœtus conferebant. nam iste dimidius erat integer, si de communi siclo agas. Alia responsio in annotationibus Joseph K. de quibus antea dictum: ipsum filium debita non solvere; sed ipso licet invito, creditores ipsos accedere & debita sua exigere: atque eapropter non dici פורע ⊃ʸ solvit ipsis; sed ipsi פרעו, debitum exigunt & recipiunt. unde filius se habere ibidem dicitur, כמאחר פורע מלח מרמתו, instar alicujus qui contra propriam voluntatem solvit. Judæorum illam inhumanitatem filios omnino ab hæreditate excludentium, si quando lubueret; non approbari à jurisconsultis Romanorum vel initium leg. 7. t. 20. li. 48. Dig. demonstrat. Cum ratio naturalis quasi lex quædam tacita liberis parentum hæreditatem addiceret, velut ad debitam successionem eos vocando, propter quod & in jure civili suorum hæredum nomen eis inditum est; ac ne judicio quidem parentis, nisi meritis de causis summoveri ab ea successione possunt: æquissimum existimatum est, eo quoque casu, quo propter pœnam parentis aufert bona damnatio, rationem haberi liberorum, ne alieno admisso graviorem pœnam luerent, quos nulla contingeret culpa, interdum in summam egestatem devoluti,&c. Viden' quantopere lex liberis caveat, ne omnino à paternis bonis excludantur? Parentum quippe est filiis nondum natis prospicere, nedum adultis & quidem post mortem suam superstitibus: convenienter iis quæ Socrates proloquens introducitur à Xenoph. l. 2. memor. p. 586. edit. Baf. ὁ μὲν ἀνὴρ τὰ ... Vir quidem eam, quæ in procreatione ipsum adjuvat, nutrit; nascendisque liberis, omnia præparat, quæcunque ipsis ad vitam conducturæ existimat, eaque quam potest plurima. Quia id natura faciendum dictat, C. Tettium infantem à patre exheredatum Divus Augustus (ut loquitur Val. Max. l. 7. c. 7.) in bona paterna ire decreto suo jussit: patris patriæ animo usus. Quoniam Tettius in proprio jure procreato filio summa cum iniquitate paternum nomen abrogaverat.
units.tr: ¹ That the lexicographers have passed over קונם in this way can hardly be said, except that they did not find this word in the Aruch. It occurs quite often, however, in c. 1 and following of the Code Nedarim: from which its meaning becomes clear, namely that it signifies to vow, to consecrate, and also to devote. Usually קונם is used of a vow of this kind, by which the use of some thing is forbidden, or some thing is in general denied to certain persons. So that the formula קונם may also be regarded as an oath, which is commonly put before such a prohibition or negative vow, to confirm it. I recognise, however, that the verb and the noun derived from it are more correct. Sometimes קונם has the same meaning with ם, as appears from Nedarim 1; although it is also often written with ם. Hence in the Code Nedarim f. 86, קונמות means consecrated things or vows, and elsewhere קונמיס means a prohibition, because, as was said, it is mostly used in negative vows. So here קונם means "vowing", that is, I vow or I have vowed that you shall [receive no benefit] from my goods, etc. In some manuscript a פ is put in place of ס, with one letter transposed, so that אתה קונם becomes "I am vowing," that is, I vow, or as a noun: as if you said, "a vow has been made that you shall not..." By these words the impiety of the parents toward their children shows itself, not religious devotion, as they think. What is more unjust than to deny children those things without which they cannot live? Such things are food and other necessities of this life. It is the duty of parents to support their children and to supply, as far as possible, what enables them to live an honourable life. Similar to this is the inhumanity and wickedness of sons, which the most distinguished Coccejus, drawing on chapter 11 of the Code Nedarim, shows to agree with the act that the Saviour rebuked the Jews for in Matt. 15.5: namely that sons who consecrated their goods, and so deprived needy parents of them, were absolved by the teachers, although they violated a duty of piety to parents that is owed even by the law of nature. I think it not unfitting to compare with this filial impiety what I find in Maimonides, Talmud Torah c. 5, sect. 1, where he puts the love and reverence due to a father after the reverence and love to be shown to teachers: חייב ככבוד רבו ויראתו יותר מאביו He is bound to honour and revere his teacher more than his father. And a little later: ודא אבידת אביו ואבידת רבו של רבו קודמת, if a son sees his father's loss and the loss of his teacher, the care of the teacher comes first; or we may take loss to mean lost property, as the Jews commonly understand it. He adds: ואם רבו שבויים בשביית פדה את רבו ואחר כך if father and teacher are held captive, he first redeems his teacher; afterwards only then does he free his father. Is it then surprising if the Scribes and Pharisees taught that sons might with good conscience consecrate their goods and abandon their parents, when those teachers profited from what was consecrated? If they put their teachers before their own freedom, which is dearer than life itself, it is not surprising that they were inclined to commit the same sin with respect to other goods. Now a parent forbade his son the use of his goods in one of two ways: either while he himself was living, or for ever, which our author calls of life and death. In the former case the son took up the inheritance with the rest after his father's death; in the latter case he was cut off from the inheritance. ¹ When the son, disinherited by that ⊃ʸp, is said to restore or rather to hand over to his brothers or his father's מיתר, Joseph Karo, in his commentary on the Jad Chazaka, teaches that this must be taken in a sound sense. For he does not himself hand over and bestow those goods on the others; otherwise he would have had and possessed them, and so would have acted against the will of the father, who had forbidden the benefit. Rather he shows them the paternal goods and allows them to take them and to use and enjoy them as they please. That to his sons refers to the sons of the father, not to the son's sons, is sufficiently clear from Maimonides, who in that case, Code Nedarim c. 5, sect. 7, admits a son's son, that is, the father's grandson, to the inheritance only by an express decree of the grandfather. ⁴ But in this way the son often falls into grave want, and does not obtain the means of living. What is to be done in this case? They permit him to take a loan from others, by which he may sustain his life. ⁵ Then the creditors are allowed to claim the loan from the other heirs, to the extent that the share which would have fallen to him from the inheritance is sufficient. If you object that the son would in this way derive great benefit from his father's goods, there is a twofold answer ready to hand. They say that this case is excepted from the debt-paying clause, according to sect. 2 of c. 4 of the Code Nedarim: המור מכיר מיבא... If someone is forbidden by vow to derive benefit from his neighbour, let him pay out his shekel and discharge his debt. By the half-shekel they understand the one that the Israelites each year contributed to the offerings of the whole assembly; for that half was a whole shekel if you are speaking of the common shekel. The other answer is in the annotations of Joseph Karo, mentioned above: the son himself does not pay the debts, but, even against his will, the creditors come in and demand their debts; and therefore it is not said that he pays them, but that they have been paid, debt is demanded and received. Hence the son is said to be there like one who pays against his own will. That the Jews' inhumanity, which excludes sons altogether from the inheritance whenever it pleases them, is not approved by the Roman jurists, is shown by the beginning of l. 7, t. 20, bk. 48 of the Digest: Since natural reason, as a kind of unwritten law, assigns the inheritance to children, calling them to a due succession, for which reason in civil law they are called heirs of the household; and they cannot be removed from that succession even by a parent's judgement, except for serious causes: it has been thought most just that even in the case where the confiscation of goods is imposed as a penalty on the parent, account should be taken of the children, lest those who bore no fault should suffer a heavier punishment for another's offence, and sometimes fall into the greatest want, etc. Do you see how greatly the law takes care that children may not be wholly excluded from their father's goods? For it is the duty of parents to provide for children not yet born, much less for those already grown and surviving them after their death: in agreement with what Socrates, speaking in Xenophon, Memorabilia bk. 2, p. 586, Basel edition, says: ὁ μὲν ἀνὴρ τὰ ... [the man indeed nourishes her who helps him in procreation, and prepares everything for the children when they are born that he thinks will be useful for their life, and as much as he can.] Because nature dictates that this be done, the Divine Augustus (as Valerius Maximus says, bk. 7, c. 7) ordered by his decree that Gaius Tettius, an infant disinherited by his father, should enter into his paternal goods, using the feeling of a father of his country, since Tettius, in a son born to him by lawful marriage, had with the greatest injustice cancelled the paternal name.

units.tr: He who robs a stranger and swears falsely to him, and pays back the principal and a fifth [הגוזל ארץ הגר ונשבע לו ומהרי זה מסלם קרן וחומש]

units.tr: Having plundered a foreigner and sworn falsely, when he dies, behold, he repays the principal and the fifth to the priests,
§. II.
