units.la: bus, atque reatum altari, quia dicitur (Num. 5. 8.) Quod si non erit isti viro vindex ad restituendum ei reatum, reatus qui restituitur Jovae, sacerdotis esto, &c. Si cum affert pecuniam & reatum, moriatur; pecunia ejus filiis dabitur, & reatus pascetur donec vitium contrahat: tum vendetur, ejusque pretium in voluntaria sacrificia cedet.
units.tr: bus, and the guilt to the altar, because it is said (Num. 5. 8.): But if the man has no near kinsman to whom the guilt may be restored, the guilt that is restored to the LORD belongs to the priest, etc. If he brings the money and the guilt offering and dies, the money shall be given to his sons, and the guilt offering shall be pastured until it contracts a blemish; then it shall be sold, and its price shall go to voluntary sacrifices.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Quum peregrinus obiit, etsi liberos reliquit superstites, raptor ipsis raptum reddere non tenetur, secundum Rabbinorum placitum: cujus hoc est fundamentum, peregrinis nullos esse haeredes, si Iudaicam religionem non susceperint: nam si proselyti facti fuerint, pro haeredibus eorum, filios agnoscendos tradunt. Contingat Judaeum a peregrino decem siclos rapuisse, & perjurio negasse factum: Judaeorum magistri raptorem istos siclos filiis illius peregrini nondum proselytis non debere autumant. Ideoq; sacerdotibus summam cum superaddita quinta dandam pronuntiant: quod lege Dei defendere annituntur, quandoquidem Num. 5. 8. quod proprietario restitui non poterat, Jovae omnium domino afferendum ideoque sacerdoti tradendum praecipitur. Quid quaeso isto paragrapho habetur, quo putidus iste error statuminari queat? prima verba repugnant, Quod si non erit isti viro vindex ad restituendum ei reatum. si peregrinus patrem, fratres, liberos, cognatos & similes habeat, est ipsi vindex ad restituendum reatum. Reatus ut inquit Maimon. isto loco, est res rapta aut ejus pretium. atque eo nomine venit, quia rapina reus reddebatur: ideo Vf.7.dabitque illi in quem reus est. Et quod hic dicitur, restituet reatum quanti est, Levit. 6. 4.5. his verbis effertur, restituet rapinam ipsam... quanti est.Sed quo argumento è sacris literis elicient, peregrinis non esse vindices, sive propinquos qui ipsis sanguine & affinitate junăi sint, quosque Scriptura passim vindices nuncupat? Itaque cum ex initio Levit.6. c. & commate 7. hujus c. Dabitque illi in quem reus est, manifeste constet, Legislatoris mentem fuisse,ut cui res erepta esset restituerētur, aut saltem ipsius vindici sive propinquo; non est quod peregrinorum cognatis erepta bona denegemus, idque ex falsa hypothesi, peregrinis hæredes non esse, nisi Judaicam religionem susceperint. Quod de Israëlitis dicant Legem Num. 5. intelligi non posse; id negatur, quia fieri poterat ut pestis, vel bellum adeo consanguineos è medio tolleret, ut hæredes certi designari non possent. Itaque non est quod legem ad peregrinos restringant.' Profecto ex illa hypothesi deinde error & injustitia magna profluit. Si raptorem etiam, dum sacerdoti raptum affert, in via mori contingat, rem quam rapuerat filiis raptoris cedere pronuntiant. Nam, inquiunt, [Hebrew text], Iam raptor acquisiverat illam per mortem peregrini: verum restitutionem facere necesse erat, quò illi obtingeret expiatio sui perjurii. at nunc non restat amplius expiatio, quandoquidem mortuus est. Expende gravem errorem. Merito raptoris filios in peregrini bona erepta ire contendunt, quia simulac peregrinus obiisset, raptoris fierent. quod enim de afferendis bonis ad sacerdotem dicebatur, ad raptoris expiationem pertinebat, quæ ipsius morte evanuit. Raptori autem illa bona per mortem peregrini cedere statuunt, quia [Hebrew text], quicunque prius occupat illius peregrini bona,ea acquirit; atqui raptor prius occupavit, quandoquidem ista jam rapuerat. felices ergo raptores, qui peregrinis viventibus bona eripiunt: nam ipsis mortuis cum bona fiunt occupantium, ipsi tempore priores, ut qui jam rapuerint, jure potiores sunt, eorumque filii reliquis præferuntur. Eximia scilicet justitia eorum hominum, qui suis operibus salutem mereri contendunt. Profecto meritissimè Servator noster Matth. 5. 20. Dico vobis, nisi abundaverit vestra justitia plus quàm Scribarum & Pharisæorum, vos nequaquam ingressuros in regnum cœlorum. 4 Porrò ubi raptor ante oblatam pecudem obiit, pecus ita se habet sicuti aliæ victimæ quarum domini, antequam mactatæ sint, mortem opetierint. Quid fit? jam consecratæ sunt, aliis usibus adhiberi eas, fas non est: itaque hujusmodi pecus pascitur tam diu, donec ipsa, id est, vitium quoddam in ipsum incidat. Novimus autem qui Deus vitiatum pecus rejiciat Lev. 22. 20. Nullum in quo sit corporis vitium, affertote. Quare ad sacrificandum idoneum non est: ideoque vendere licet.
units.tr: When the foreigner dies, even if he leaves surviving children, the robber is not bound to return the plunder to them, according to the opinion of the rabbis. The foundation of this is that foreigners have no heirs, unless they have accepted the Jewish religion; for if they have become proselytes, they teach that their sons are to be acknowledged as heirs. Suppose a Jew has robbed a foreigner of ten shekels and denied the deed under oath. The masters of the Jews maintain that the robber is not to give those shekels to the sons of that foreigner, who are not yet proselytes. Therefore they pronounce that the sum, with the fifth added, is to be given to the priests; they strive to defend this by the law of God, since Num. 5. 8. commands that what could not be restored to the owner be brought to Jehovah, the lord of all, and therefore handed over to the priest. What, I ask, is contained in that paragraph by which this foul error can be supported? The first words contradict it: But if the man has no near kinsman to whom the guilt may be restored. If the foreigner has a father, brothers, children, kinsmen and the like, they are his near kinsman to whom the guilt may be restored. As Maimonides says in that place, the "guilt" is the stolen thing or its price, and it bears that name because the robber was made liable (reus) for the theft. Hence Vers. 7: and he shall give it to him against whom he is liable. And what is said here, he shall restore the guilt in full, is expressed in Lev. 6. 4, 5 by these words: he shall restore the stolen thing itself ... in full. But by what argument do they draw from the sacred letters that foreigners have no near kinsmen, that is, relatives joined to them by blood and marriage, whom Scripture everywhere calls near kinsmen? Therefore, since from the beginning of Lev. 6, and from verse 7 of this chapter, he shall give it to him against whom he is liable, it is manifest that the mind of the Lawgiver was that the stolen goods be restored to the one from whom they were taken, or at least to his near kinsman; there is no reason for us to deny the goods taken away to the relatives of foreigners, and that on the false hypothesis that foreigners have no heirs unless they have accepted the Jewish religion. That they say the law of Num. 5 cannot be understood of Israelites is denied, because it could happen that plague or war would so remove the blood relations that no definite heirs could be designated. Therefore there is no reason for them to restrict the law to foreigners. Indeed, from that hypothesis a great error and injustice follow. If the robber, while carrying the stolen goods to the priest, happens to die on the way, they pronounce that the thing he had stolen passes to the robber's sons. For, they say, the robber had already acquired it by the death of the foreigner; but restitution had to be made so that atonement for his perjury might come to him. But now there is no more atonement, since he is dead. Consider the grave error. They rightly contend that the robber's sons succeed to the goods taken from the foreigner, because as soon as the foreigner died they became the robber's. For what was said about bringing the goods to the priest pertained to the robber's atonement, which vanished at his death. But they lay down that those goods pass to the robber at the foreigner's death, because whoever first takes possession of the goods of that foreigner acquires them; but the robber took possession first, since he had already stolen them. Happy, then, are the robbers who snatch goods from foreigners while they are alive; for when they are dead, the goods become the property of those who seize them, and those who were first in time, as having already stolen them, are the stronger in right, and their sons are preferred to the rest. Such is, of course, the admirable justice of those men who contend that they merit salvation by their works. Surely our Saviour most rightly says, Matth. 5. 20: I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven. Moreover, where the robber dies before the animal is offered, the animal stands in the same position as other victims whose owners have died before they were slain. What follows? Since they are already consecrated, it is not lawful to use them for other purposes; so such an animal is pastured as long as it, that is, some blemish, falls upon it. We know, however, that God rejects a blemished animal, Lev. 22. 20: Bring nothing in which there is a bodily blemish. Therefore it is not fit for sacrifice, and so it may be sold.

units.la: ⁵ Pretio venumdati pecoris emitur voluntarium sacrificium. additque Maim. ubicunque dicitur voluntarium sacrificium, sensus est, holocaustum voluntarium. Melius tamen in Maaseh Korbanoth c. 14. f. 4. ubi etiam distinguit. Si quis dicat, ecce in me recipio holocaustum; aut, recipio in me eucharistica; aut, recipio in me fertum; aut, recipio in me pretium hujus pecudis convertendum in holocaustum vel eucharistica, tum est votum: sed si dicat, ecce hæc pecus, aut pretium hujus pecudis erit holocaustum vel eucharistica; aut hæc decima erit fertum, tum est voluntaria oblatio. Vbi videmus latius accipi quam ipse in superioribus docuerat. Ex hac distinctione & distinctius etiam intelligitur quid designetur Lev. 7. 16. Si votivum, aut voluntarium erit sacrificium &c. ita Lev. 22. 21. ac alibi. Distinctio in eo consistit, quod votivum sit minus definitum, quam voluntarium. Ideo cum votivum sacrificium descridescribatur in Maim. verbis, recipio in me pretium hujus pecudis, particulam hujus, id est, n, aliunde irrepsisse credo: nam ex initio c. 1. Cod. פיתּ omnino constat, in votivo sacrificio istam restrictionem non adhiberi. Nec mirum in hoc membro aberratum, cum in Codice longe antiquissimo in membrana exarato, quem à Nob. viro Gerardo à Renesse accepi, olim hic certam lectionem non fuisse animadvertam: utpote cujus contextus etiam פּוּא non habeat, cum tamen exemplar sit correctissimum, unde impressa exemplaria corrigi possunt. Cæterum ut eò redeam, unde digressus sum, scilicet ad pretium victimæ raptoris; ista sacrificia illo pretio empta præter necessaria cum publica, tum privata, offerebantur: quemadmodum enim singuli pro se præter necessitatem holocausta Deo grato animo adducere poterant; ita cœtui licebat holocausta voluntaria offerre, quibus Deus coleretur. nam id Deus liberum fecerat, ut præter necessitatem oblationes Deo pararent, quibus zelus & pietas ipsorum probaretur. Judæi hæc, de quibus agimus, vocant פּפ מִמִּמְמְ, æstivos fructus altaris: quia æstivorum fructuum instar se habebant. ficus, pruna, similes fructus, præter necessarios cibos opponi solent, atque unà cum iis eduntur & consumuntur; similiter dicta holocausta (quæ, ut alia sacrificia, cum cibis conferuntur Lev. c. 21. §. 6. ac alibi) apponebantur in altari & cum reliquis consumebantur. Quod politicam hujus Misnæ constitutionem spectat, legem parallelam non investigabo in Romanorum jure: quos tam ineptos nemo facile judicabit, ut tantam injustitiam stabiliverint, quam tamen Judæi, Scripturæ paragrapho male accepto, sancIverunt: quemadmodum exposui.
units.tr: 5 With the price of the animal sold, a voluntary sacrifice is bought. Maimonides adds: Wherever a voluntary sacrifice is mentioned, the sense is a voluntary burnt offering. Better, however, in Maaseh Korbanoth c. 14, f. 4, where he also distinguishes: If someone says, "Behold, I take upon myself a burnt offering," or "I take upon myself a thank offering," or "I take upon myself a tithe," or "I take upon myself the price of this animal, to be converted into a burnt offering or a thank offering," then it is a vow; but if he says, "Behold, this animal, or the price of this animal, shall be a burnt offering or a thank offering," or "this tithe shall be a tithe," then it is a voluntary offering. Here we see that the term is taken more broadly than he himself had taught in the earlier passage. From this distinction it is also more clearly understood what is meant by Lev. 7. 16: If the sacrifice is a votive or a voluntary offering, etc., and likewise Lev. 22. 21 and elsewhere. The distinction consists in this, that the votive offering is less definite than the voluntary. Therefore, since the votive sacrifice is described in Maimonides' words as I take upon myself the price of this animal, I believe the particle this, that is, the letter n, has crept in from elsewhere; for from the beginning of c. 1 of the Codex it is quite clear that this restriction is not applied to the votive sacrifice. Nor is it surprising that an error occurred in this member, since in the very ancient Codex written on parchment which I received from the noble man Gerard à Renesse, I noticed that there was no certain reading here, since its context does not even have the word [פּוּא]; yet it is a most accurate copy, from which printed copies can be corrected. But to return to where I digressed, namely the price of the robber's victim: those sacrifices bought with that price were offered, besides the necessary ones, both public and private; for just as individuals could bring burnt offerings to God gladly, beyond what was necessary, so the congregation was allowed to offer voluntary burnt offerings by which God would be honoured. For God made it free, so that beyond necessity they might prepare offerings to God by which their zeal and piety would be proved. The Jews call these, of which we speak, [פּפ מִמִּמְמְ] the summer fruits of the altar, because they stood in the place of summer fruits. Figs, plums and similar fruits are commonly set before necessary food, and are eaten and consumed together with it; similarly these said burnt offerings (which, like other sacrifices, are reckoned along with foods, Lev. c. 21, §. 6 and elsewhere) were set upon the altar and consumed with the rest. As for the political arrangement of this Mishnah, I will not look for a parallel law in Roman law; no one will easily judge the Romans so foolish as to have established such great injustice, which the Jews, having misused a paragraph of Scripture, nevertheless sanctioned, as I have set out.

units.la: להוציא מידם סנאמר איש אשר יחן לכהן לו יהיה נחן הכסף ליהוריב ואשם לירעיה יצא אשם ליהוריב וכסף לירעיה אם קיים האשם יקריבוהו בני ידעיה ואם לא יחזור ויביא אשם אחר שהסביא גזילו עד שלא הביא אשמו יצא הביא אשמו עד שלא הביא גזילו לא יצא נתן ארץ הקרן ולא נתן את החומש אין החומש מעכב׃
units.tr: For taking it out of their hands. As it is said: "If a man gives [it] to a priest, it shall be his" [איש אשר יתן לכהן לו יהיה]. If he gave the money to Jehoiarib and the guilt offering to Jedaiah, the guilt offering goes out to Jehoiarib and the money to Jedaiah. If the guilt offering is valid, the sons of Jedaiah shall offer it. But if not, he must bring another guilt offering. If he brought his guilt offering before he brought back what he had robbed, it is discharged; but if he brought back what he had robbed before he brought his guilt offering, it is not discharged. If he gave the principal but did not give the fifth, the fifth is not a hindrance.

units.la: ² repetere non possunt. quia dicitur (Num. 5.10.) Quod quis ulli sacerdoti dederit, illius esto. Si argentum dederit ³ Iojaribo; & reatum Iedaja satisfecit: quum reatum Iojaribo; & argentum Iedaja, si superfit reatus ⁴, cum offerent Iedaja posteri; sin minus, denuò offeret alium reatum. Etenim ⁵ qui affert rapinam suam, antequam reatum suum offerat, satisfacit: offert reatum suum, antequam afferat rapinam suam, non satisfacit. Si fortem quidem, at quintâ non dedit, quintâ ⁶ reatum non impedit.
units.tr: ² They cannot be repeated, because it is said (Num. 5.10): "Whatever anyone has given to any priest, it shall be his." If he gave the money to Jojarib and the guilt offering to Jedaiah, he has made satisfaction. If he gave the guilt offering to Jojarib and the money to Jedaiah, then, if the guilt offering is still in existence, the sons of Jedaiah shall offer it; but if not, he must again offer another guilt offering. For the one who brings his robbery before he offers his guilt offering makes satisfaction; the one who offers his guilt offering before he brings his robbery does not make satisfaction. If he gave the principal but did not give the fifth, the fifth does not hinder the guilt offering.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ In Ebraeo est homines custodiae. istos intelligit quorum tunc erat, excubias agere & observare quid in loco sacro agendum esset. Nam sacerdotes (de quibus agi docent praecedentia) in vigintiquatuor classes distincti, singulis septimanis vices permutabant, primaeque secunda, secundae tertia & ita deinceps succedebant: adeoque singulis septimanis singulae classes suo quaeque ordine & serie munera obibant. Qui ista septimana, qua raptor sortem cum quinta afferebat, in sacro munere versabantur, hi soli quod ab illo afferebatur accipiebant. Si autem accepissent, & raptor antequam victimam, quam unà debebat, obtulisset, moreretur, dubium oboriur, quid tunc juris esset: an sacerdotes acceptum retinerent; an verò raptoris filiis restituerent. quandoquidem in superioribus observata fuit Judaeorum sententia, qui raptoris filiis post obitum patris raptum cedere statuunt. ² Tamen ubi in sacerdotum manus pervenifset, quod is cui ereptum erat hæredes fecundum illorum mentem non haberet; filiis raptoris non fuisse restituendum affirmant: licet raptore in via mortuo antequam ad sacerdotes detulisset, raptoris filiis raptum assignent. Eoque referunt Num. 5. ⁊f. 10. Quod quis ulli sacerdoti dederit, illius esto: quasi hoc sibi Deus voluisset, sacerdoti semel datum repeti non posse; licet alioqui repetendi causa videretur, si aliis tradendum fuisset. Totus ille locus in hanc sententiam, quam subjicio, exponendus meo judicio. Commate nono & decimo idem diversis verbis prima fronte dici videtur, imo verba quædam redundare: nam quis dubitat, quin quod alteri datum est, illius sit. Verum quandoquidem in una classe multi erant sacerdotes, nec hi omnes simul sacris operari poterant, distincte munus suum obibant: & quia operarius dignus erat mercede sua, ejusdem esse emolumentum, cujus opus ac onus, æquitas suadebat. Itaque ait legislator com. 9. Si Israelitæ plures consecratum quid ad sacerdotem attulerint, ipsius erit quod sacerdotibus in sacro cedere solet. & com. 10. si unius tantum sit quod consecratum ad sacerdotem defertur, eadem erit ratio: idque plenius explicans subjungit, quod quis ad sacerdotem detulerit ut rem sacram faciat, istius sacerdotis erit, quicquid ex illo isti ordini debetur. Noluit enim Deus, alios sacerdotes illud isti sacerdoti eripere, eo prætextu quod sacerdotali ordini deberetur; quasi huic quidem traditum sit, sed omnibus istius classis in commune dividendum. Non ergo de quibusvis rebus consecratis agitur; sed ⁊f. 9. omnia sanctificata ad ea restringuntur quæ speciatim ad hunc vel illum sacerdotem afferuntur, quo rem divinam faciat; ut si qui ferta aliave sacerdoti ad offerendum adducant. Hanc loci varias interpretationibus distracti mentem esse existimo. ³ Sequitur casus duplex diversa expositione à Talmudistis in diversum sensum acceptus: in qua sententiarum differentia Salomonis Jarchi judicium praferendum autumo. 1 Chron. 24. 7. in sacerdotum classibus viginti quatuor, Jojaribi posteros primam; Jedajæ posteros secundam constituere liquet. Has ergo classes, utpote priores reliquis, in exemplum author producit, quò casum suum distincte proponere queat. Raptum unà cum reatu, sive piaculari victima, sacerdotibus afferendum, ita dispensari poterat, ut huic classi raptum; alteri reatus sive aries expiationum, traderetur: idque modo diverso, priori classi raptum, posteriori reatus; vel contra, priori reatus, posteriori raptum ejusve pretium. Priorem modum in hanc sententiam S. J. enarrat. Dum Jojaribi classis suo muneri incumbit, raptor Jojaribi posteris raptum reddat; piacularem hostiam sequentis septimanæ ministris è Jedajæ prosapia adducat: adeoque singulis, quum suo muneri sua quique septimana vacant, diversa tradat; & quidem servato ordine, quem è Num. 5. 8. deducunt. ubi raptum reatus nomine expressum (uti antea vidimus) præcedit, sequitur aries expiationum. Hic legi satisfacere & parere censetur: quia sacerdotibus licet diversarum classium, & quidem legitimo ordine offert, quæ offerenda constitutiones jubent. 4 Sin alio ordine rapinam & victimam ad sacerdotes adducat, licet sacerdotes nonnisi quum sua quique septimana sacris operantur conveniat; defunctus non judicatur. puta si primæ classi victimam adducat, sequenti pretium rapti vel ipsam rem quam rapuit. Etenim hic observandus erat ordo, ut reatus, id est, piacularis victima posterioribus sacerdotibus sive horum alicui traderetur: quia istorum erat ministerium posterius; illorum vero primæ classis, prius: & rapti restitutio præstanda antequam victima offerretur; victimaque demum post rapti restitutionem offerenda erat. Quare in isto retrogrado progressu, Jedajæ posteri, sive secunda sacerdotum classis, victimam à prima classe accipient, eamque secundum statuta offerent; modo res in integro sit: atque hac ratione qui
units.tr: ¹ In the Hebrew it is "men of the watch". He means those who were then on duty, keeping watch and observing what was to be done in the holy place. For the priests (of whom the preceding passages teach that we are speaking) were divided into twenty-four classes, which changed their turns every week, the first class being followed by the second, the second by the third, and so on; thus each class in its own order and sequence performed its duties each week. Those who were serving in the sacred office in the week in which the robber brought the principal with the fifth received alone what was brought by him. But if they had received it, and the robber died before he had offered the victim which he was bound to offer with it, a doubt arises as to what the law then was: whether the priests should keep what was received, or restore it to the sons of the robber. For in the earlier passages the opinion of the Jews was followed, who hold that what was taken by robbery passes to the sons of the robber after the father's death. ² Yet, when it had come into the hands of the priests, they affirm that it was not to be restored to the sons of the robber, since, in their view, the man from whom it had been taken would not have heirs; although, if the robber died on the way before he had brought it to the priests, they assign the stolen goods to the robber's sons. And they refer to Num. 5.10: "Whatever anyone gives to any priest shall be his," as if God had wished this: that what was once given to a priest could not be demanded back, although otherwise it would seem reasonable to demand it back, if it had been due to be given to others. In my judgment the whole of that passage must be explained in the sense which I here set out. In verses 9 and 10 the same thing seems to be said at first sight in different words; indeed some words seem superfluous, for who doubts that what has been given to another belongs to him? But since in one class there were many priests, and not all of them could perform sacred duties at the same time, each performed his own duty separately; and since the workman is worthy of his wages, reason suggested that the profit should belong to those whose work and burden it was. Thus the lawgiver says in verse 9: "If the children of Israel bring many consecrated things to a priest, what usually falls to the priests in the sacred service shall be his." And in verse 10: "If only one thing consecrated is brought to the priest, the same rule shall apply." Explaining this more fully, he adds that whatever a man brings to a priest so that he may perform the sacred rite shall belong to that priest, and whatever is owed to that order from it. For God did not wish other priests to snatch that from this priest, on the pretext that it was owed to the priestly order, as if it had indeed been given to him but was to be divided in common among all of that class. Therefore the passage does not deal with any kind of consecrated things, but verse 9, "all things sanctified," is restricted to those things which are brought specifically to this or that priest so that he may perform the divine service, such as gifts or other things brought to a priest for offering. I judge this to be the sense of the passage, which has been torn apart by various interpretations. ³ There follows a twofold case, taken in a different sense by the Talmudists through a different explanation; in the difference of these opinions I consider the judgment of Solomon Jarchi to be preferable. It is clear from 1 Chron. 24.7 that among the twenty-four classes of priests, the descendants of Jehoiarib constituted the first and the descendants of Jedaiah the second. The author therefore brings forward these classes, as the first above the rest, as an example, so that he may set out his case distinctly. The principal, together with the guilt, that is, the sin-offering, was to be brought to the priests, and it could be distributed so that the principal went to one class and the guilt, or the ram of atonement, to another, and this in different ways: the principal to the first class and the guilt to the second, or conversely, the guilt to the first and the principal or its price to the second. Solomon Jarchi explains the first way in this sense: while the class of Jehoiarib is occupied with its duty, the robber restores the principal to the descendants of Jehoiarib, and brings the sin-offering of the following week to the ministers from the family of Jedaiah. Thus he gives different things to each, since each class serves its own week, and indeed in the order which they derive from Num. 5.8, where the principal, expressed as the robbery-price (as we saw before), comes first, and the ram of atonement follows. Here he is judged to satisfy the law and to be compliant, because he offers to the priests of the different classes, and indeed in the lawful order which the regulations command to be offered. ⁴ But if he brings the robbery and the victim to the priests in another order, although the priests meet only when each class is performing sacred duties in its own week, he is not judged to have fulfilled his obligation. For example, if he brings the victim to the first class and the price of the robbery, or the thing itself which he stole, to the following class. For here the order had to be observed, so that the guilt, that is, the sin-offering, was to be given to the later priests, or to one of them, since the later ministry belonged to them; whereas the first class had the earlier ministry; and the restitution of the stolen goods had to be made before the victim was offered, and the victim had to be offered only after the restitution. Therefore, in this backward progression, the descendants of Jedaiah, that is, the second class of priests, will receive the victim from the first class and offer it according to the regulations, provided the thing is still intact; and in this way those who had received the robbery [...]

units.la: ¹ Chron. 24. 7. qui rem raptam receperant, postea accipient reatum sive victimam pro reatu, eamque suo ordine offerent & rapinam expiabunt. Quod si praevenerint Jojaribo prognati qui reatum praepostera serie acceperant, & victimam obtulerint, ista oblatione raptor defunctus non erit; sed aliam victimam raptor adducet, ne legitimus ordo violetur. eamque Jedajae posteri, accepta jam antea rapina ejusve pretio, offerent; quo omnia debite peragantur, nec rapinae restitutio victimam sequatur. 5 Ratio subjungitur qua praecedentia confirmant: & ratio quidem in ordine quo utrumque Num. 5. proponitur, reperitur. attamen ex his commatis 8. verbis eandem etiam exsculpunt, Quo ariete expiationem faciet pro eo: quatenus יבוא futurum esse observant, quasi dicas, incepta est expiatio per rapinae restitutionem; verum perficienda per arietem: ideoque quod raptum fuit prius restituendum; deinde aries offerendus. argumentum quamvis ipsis placeat, non satis solidum. Maimonides intricatam facit Misnam: quippe qui sapientum & D. Judae sententias simul proponi afferat; imo contrarias hypotheses expendi exstimet. Quasi primo quidem casu raptor rapinam ejusve pretium sacerdotibus, tempore quo a munere suo immunes erant, dare introduceretur; victimam vero iis, qui ea septimana muneri vacabant: sed hoc pacto, ut raptum ad posteriores transferendum esset, quia alii rapinam ejusve pretium alieno tempore recepissent. posteriori vero casu illud tempus in danda victima etiam attenderetur, quo posterior classis suo muneri incumberet; prior vero vacaret: sed quia prior victimam ante rapinam vel potius sine rapti restitutione accepisset, victima ad posteriorem classem reducenda esset. quae recepta jam rapina, postea demum victimam offerens, ordinem debitum observaret. quo casu & R. Judae sententiam de priori casu, quae Sapientum menti illic propositae repugnat, adumbrari censet. Haec fere est prolixi sermonis summa: quam ex ipsius annotationibus desumptam R. Salomonis expositioni merito postponere mihi videor. Quis enim Misnam adeo perplexe loquutam sine ulla necessitate credat?
units.tr: ¹ 1 Chron. 24.7 who had received the stolen thing will afterwards receive the guilt, or the victim in place of the guilt, and will offer it in its order and atone for the robbery. But if those descended from Jehoiarib, who had received the guilt in the reversed sequence, anticipate and offer the victim, the robber will not be discharged by that offering; the robber will bring another victim, so that the lawful order is not violated, and the descendants of Jedaiah, having already received the robbery or its price, will offer it, so that everything is duly performed and the restitution of the robbery does not follow the victim. ⁵ A reason is added by which the preceding statements are confirmed; and indeed the reason is found in the order in which both are set out in Num. 5. Yet from the words of verse 8 they also draw the same thing: "With the ram by which the atonement shall be made for him," inasmuch as they observe that the Hebrew [יבוא] means "shall come", as if you were to say: the atonement has begun through the restitution of the robbery, but is to be completed through the ram; therefore what was taken must first be restored, and then the ram offered. Although this argument pleases them, it is not solid enough. Maimonides makes the Mishnah intricate, since he holds that the opinions of the sages and of Rabbi Judah are proposed together, and indeed he thinks that contrary hypotheses are to be weighed. As if, in the first case, the robber were introduced to give the robbery or its price to the priests at a time when they were exempt from their office, but to give the victim to those who were then on duty that week; yet in such a way that the robbery was to be transferred to the later ones, because the others had received the robbery or its price at the wrong time. In the second case, the time for giving the victim would also be considered, when the later class was occupied with its duty and the earlier was free; but since the earlier class had received the victim before the robbery, or rather without restitution of the stolen goods, the victim was to be brought back to the later class, which, having now received the robbery, would afterwards offer the victim and so observe the due order. In this case he judges that Rabbi Judah's opinion about the first case, which is contrary to the mind of the sages proposed there, is hinted at. This is roughly the sum of the long discourse, which I think ought rightly to be preferred to Rabbi Solomon's exposition, taken from his own notes. For who would believe that the Mishnah speaks so obscurely without any necessity?

units.la: {a} Quum tandem subjicitur, quinta non moratur, hic est sensus; sors quidem ipsa sive res quae rapta fuerat, cum non restituitur ante oblatam victimam, moratur expiationem, ac quo minus reus absolvatur efficit; non itidem quinta superaddenda sorti: etenim si quis quintam istam differat, eamque demum ultimo loco solvat, non impedict quo minus a reatu suo absolvatur. Differunt hac in parte raptum & quinta, diversaque utriusque est ratio ac conditio: raptum nisi prius reddatur, subsequens victima non expiat; quinta licet in id tempus differatur quo victima oblata jam est, nihilominus antecedens oblatio reum a reatu mundat. His jam expensis quae in hac Misna ad ceremoniales constitutiones pertinent, ad politica statuta ulterius pergamus.
units.tr: {a} When it is finally added, "the fifth is not delayed," the meaning is this: the thing itself, that is, the property that was seized, if it is not restored before the guilt offering is brought, delays the expiation and prevents the offender from being absolved. The fifth part, however, need not be added to the principal in the same way. If someone postpones that fifth part and pays it only at the last, it does not stop him from being absolved of his guilt. In this respect the seized property and the fifth part differ, and their nature and condition are different: unless the stolen thing is first returned, a later offering does not make atonement; although the fifth may be deferred until the offering has already been made, the earlier offering still cleanses the guilty man from his guilt. Having now considered what in this Mishnah relates to the ceremonial regulations, let us proceed to the civil statutes.
CHAP. X. §. I.

units.la: Si aliquis ubi quid surripuit, indefilios suos cibat, vel id ipsis reliquit; hi rependere non tenentur. Si aliquid fuerit, in quo sit rerum evictio (id est, fundus,) rependere tenentur. Pecunias non permutant ex arca publicanorum, neque e loculo quaestorum aerariorum; nec inde eleemosynam accipiunt: sed ipse ex adibus suis desumit; aut e foro.
units.tr: If a man has stolen something and then feeds his sons, or leaves it to them, they are not bound to make restitution. If there is something in which there is eviction of the property (that is, a field), they are bound to make restitution. They do not exchange money from the chest of the publicans, nor from the purse of the treasurers of the sacred fund; nor do they receive alms from them. But he takes it from his own house, or from the market.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: 1 Reliquit coram ipsis (ut est in textu originali) synecdochice accè accipitur: nimirum ac si dictum fuisset, reliquit ipsis post mortem, ipsiq; tum comederunt. Synecdoche è verbis præcedentibus, quibus de alimento agitur, innotescit: ut ibi legitur, filios suos cibat; sic hoc loco de relicto cibo agitur, quo post mortem patris cibantur. 2 Hi restitutionem non debere judicantur; nisi parens fundum reliquerit. Verum, uti in Jad Chazaka & alibi docetur, כלאה, constitutio ex authoris istius mente, qui Misnam tradidit, non obtinet. Ad hunc modum Maim. c. 5. גמילה, sect. 6. בין לא הלכו בין לא הכו בין מן הקרקע בין מן הטלטלין טהנין Reppędere debent, sive ederint; sive non ederint (sed post patris obitum etiam habeant;) sive animum desponderint (proprietarii;) sive non desponderint animum; cum de fundo; tum de mobilibus quæ dereliquit. Idque hoc fundamento, quod posteriores doctores statuerint mobilia etiam creditori oppignerari; non solos fundos: quos ista tamen nota distinguere à mobilibus solent, uti è sequentibus patebit. Sed ubi pater raptor nulla bona filiis reliquit, filiisque quod raptum erat comederunt; siquidem antequam proprietarius desperavit de recuperatione, tenentur: sin postea, non tenentur. Ratio, quia tum sola actio in personam raptoris, si superesset, fuerit reliqua: etenim istam desperatione, qua proprietarius, rem amissam se recuperaturum, omnem spem abjicit, aliquo modo eam occupantis facere judicant. Quemadmodum in jure Romano non idem, sed simile quid legitur ff. 47. t. de furtis l. 44. §. 5. Quod si dominus id dereliquit, furtum non fit ejus, etiamsi ego furandi animum habuero. Nec enim furtum fit, nisi sit cui fiat. In propositio autem nulli fit: quippe cum placeat Sabini & Cassii sententia, existimantium statim nostram esse desinere rem, quam derelinquimus. 3 Deinde Misnæ author hoc sibi voluit, tum demum raptum restituendum à liberis, si hujusmodi quid hæreditatis jure à patre raptore accepissent, שיט כו אחריות, in quo esset rei evictio. quod nihil aliud est, quam si dixisset פרק, סתף, fundus, vel domus ac similia, quæ loco moveri non possunt: quæ immobilitas quum præcipuè in fundo spectatur, fundi nomine ista immobilia bona indigitare solent. In fundo autem חרמי, evictio esse agnoscitur: quia si quis inter Israëlitas ubi debendi reus esset, alteri agrum vendidisset; nec esset solvendo, is cui debebat, rei sibi debitæ evictionem in agro alteri vendito reperiebat. Ideoque ager dicebatur res חרמי כה טיט, in qua esset rei evictio, ut loquuntur jurisconsulti: quippe quæ creditori securitatem præstaret, quum rem sibi debitam in agro debitoris, licet ad alterum post contractum debitum venditione translato, quæreret & inveniret. Ni enim sibi satisfieret, agrum ejusve partem sibi vendicabat: pariterque in aliis immobilibus sua persequebatur. Consule Obadiam de Bartenora ad sectionem 5. ca. 1. Cod. Kiddoushin. 4 Constat è Cod. Maasar scheni, c. 2. siclum in minimos æreolos, & contra æreolos in siclum permutari solitos: nam qui secundas decimas ad urbem sanctam afferebant, ut onus esset levius, æreolos cum siclo permutabant; contra qui siclos eò detulerant, ut ex lege Deut. 14. v. 26. minima etiam emere commodè possent, siclos æreolis commutabant. Hinc autem noster, ne in ista frequenti permutatione, inprimis ad sacrbs usus destinata, numismata abusu contaminata recuperentur; nonnullis interdixit. ubi פרס pro commutare usurpatur, quia in hac actione פרוטות, æreoli tradebantur, vel recipiebantur. Primò publicanorum numi rejiciuntur. Verum inter publicanos distinguendum esse Gemara hoc loco observat, eosque hic spectari; פנים כסף, quibus exactio determinata non est; sed redemptis vectigalibus & similibus, quantum possunt extorquent, modo redemptionis suæ summam magistratui solvant: unde in eadem Gemara מוכס כהרי, publicani peregrini, utpote in Judæos magis austeri, mentio fit. Omnes enim publicani non erant Israëlitæ, nec omnes Ethnici; sed quidam, docente nos Gemara. unde verbis Servatoris Matth. 18. ῾Ϛ. 17. ὁ ἐθνικὸς ᾗ ὁ τελώνης, Ethnicus & publicanus distinguuntur: quod multi publicani non essent Ethnici. Et quemadmodum in Misna praesenti מוכסין, publicani, pro injustis publicanis ponuntur, quia utplurimum quantum possent exigebant, (quod ista universali formula, dum eos simpliciter publicanos vocant, testantur;) sic etiam Servatorem loco citato publicanum pro impio & injusto publicano accipere, tota docet oratio: & quidem jure, docet Misna. Ex istorum publicanorum arca numos commutari non ferebant constitutiones Judaicae, מבטס ... quia erant ipsius rapinae, id est, quod veluti per rapinam extorti essent. Ab aliis publicanis accipere permittebant, siquidem דינא דמלכותא דינא, jus regium est etiam jus, ut dicitur in Gemara: quasi dicas, quod rex vel magistratus sibi pendi exigit, id jure fieri subditi exististimare (ut est revera) debent. quo dicto, Servatoris apud Matth. 22. 21. sententia approbatur, Reddite quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari. Si itaque publicani nihil nisi constitutum exigerent, eorum numos ut justos admittebant Judaeorum magistri, & quin probos publicanos in republica habere possimus, minime negant. Quemadmodum Johannes ipsis publicanis, quid sibi agendum esset, quo viam vitae calcarent, percunctantibus respondebat, Luc. 3. 13. Nihil amplius quam quod constitutum est vobis exigite: ubi vox πράσσω, Talmudicae סדר, constitutum (de qua supra sub finem p. 271.) omnino respondet. Ita passim N. Test. dicta cum Talmudicis convenire identidem observamus. Par judicium de גזבר, quaestore aerario, ut si injusta exactione populum gravet, ejus numi respuantur; sin minus, admittantur. Sed in vocis interpretatione non conveniunt Ebraei: quidam quaestorem regium esse affirmant, cujus esset censum & tributum regis nomine a singulis recipere. Secundum aliam sententiam גזבר, quaestor est גזבר ... quaestor religiosus, qui eleemosynas colligit: e cujus aerario numos, ad effugiendam suspicionem, accipere non liceat: nam qui ex illo ærario accipientem observasset, nec quid prius ad permutandum dederat attendisset; è sacris bonis eum debita officia in decimis secundis comedendis & similibus peragere, facile crederet. verum prior expositio magis placet. Publicanus & quæstor ex suis ædibus sumere permittitur; sive potius, qui pecuniam permutare cupit, ab ipsis domo sua numos depromentibus accipere permittitur, par eleemosynæ ratio. Similiter si foris alicubi sint in loco publico (non tamen apud arcam suam publicam) eleemosynas &c. ab istis publicanis & quæstoribus accipere licet. Alia quæ affertur expositio durior est; hæc magis placet: statutique hæc videtur causa, quod interdictum in infinitum dilatari noluerint. Objici quidem potuisset, numos ex arca illa in ædes forte allatos, similiterque ex eadem in forum portatos fuisse: ideoque verendum ne isti numi quos recipere permittunt, iidem sint cum illis, quibus Magistri interdixerant. Sed ultra arcam illam publicanorum & quæstorum loculum nos inquirere noluerunt: quia de quavis pecunia dubitari posset, an non ab illis per emptionem variarum rerum profluxisset. Ita semper dubii hæsissent. Quod statutum politicum attinet supra ad prima Misnæ verba propositum, quo Misna correcta fuit; similiter statuunt jurisconsulti Romani: puta liberos plerunque convenire de rapto posse, ut à raptoris liberis quod ille rapuerat exigatur. Vide ff. l. 47. t. 8. le. 2. §. sin. An (actio rapti) in id quod locupletiores facti sint, dari debeat; videamus. Et ego puto ideo prætorem non esse pollicitum in hæredes in id quod ad eos pervenit, quia putavit sufficere conditionem.
units.tr: 1 "He left it before them" (as it stands in the original text) is taken figuratively, by synecdoche: as if it had been said that he left it to them after his death, and they then ate it. The synecdoche is made clear by the preceding words, which deal with food: there it is read he feeds his sons; so here too the subject is the food left behind, on which they feed after their father's death. 2 They are judged not to owe restitution unless the parent left the field. But, as is taught in the Jad Chazaka and elsewhere, the rule [כלאה] does not hold according to the mind of that author who handed down the Mishnah. In this manner, Maimonides, chapter 5 of the Laws of Theft, section 6: whether they walked or did not walk, whether they struck or did not strike, whether from the land or from movables, they must restore, whether they have eaten [of it]; or have not eaten (but even if they have it after the father's death); whether they have given up hope (as owners); or have not given up hope; as to the field; as well as to the movables which he left behind. And this rests on the ground that the later teachers ruled that movables too are pledged to a creditor, not only fields; which, nevertheless, they usually distinguish from movables by this mark, as will be clear from what follows. But where a father who was a thief left no goods to his sons, and the sons ate what had been stolen, they are bound, provided that before the owner gave up hope of recovery; but if afterwards, they are not bound. The reason is that then only the action against the person of the thief, if he survived, would remain: for by that despair, by which the owner abandons all hope of recovering his lost property, they judge that it has in some way become the property of the one who seizes it. Similarly in Roman law, not the same thing but something like it is read, Digest 47, title 'On Thefts,' law 44, section 5: If the owner has abandoned it, it is not theft of his, even if I have had the intention of stealing. For theft does not occur unless there is someone to whom it is done. In the present case it is done to no one, since the opinion of Sabinus and Cassius is accepted, who held that a thing immediately ceases to be ours when we abandon it. 3 Next, the author of the Mishnah meant this: that restitution of the seized property is due from the children only if they had received something of this kind by inheritance from the thief father, in which there was eviction of the property [שיט כו אחריות], which is nothing other than if he had said field [פרק, סתף], fundus, or a house and the like, which cannot be moved from place. Since this immovability is chiefly looked at in a field, they usually indicate such immovable goods by the name of field. Now in a field there is recognised eviction [חרמי], because if a man among the Israelites, who was a debtor, had sold a field to another, and he was not able to pay, the one to whom he owed found an eviction of his debt in the field sold to another. And so the field was called a thing [חרמי כה טיט] in which there is eviction of the property, as the jurists say, since it gave the creditor security, as he sought and found his debt in the debtor's field, even though it had been transferred to another by sale after the debt was contracted. For if he were not satisfied, he claimed the field or part of it for himself; and likewise in other immovable goods he pursued his claim. Consult Obadiah of Bertinoro on section 5, chapter 1 of the Tractate Kiddushin. 4 It is established from the Tractate Maaser Sheni, chapter 2, that a shekel was customarily exchanged for the smallest coins, and conversely small coins for a shekel: for those who brought the second tithes to the holy city, to lighten the burden, exchanged small coins for a shekel; and those who had brought shekels there, so that they might buy small things conveniently according to the law of Deuteronomy 14:26, exchanged the shekels for small coins. Hence our author, lest in this frequent exchange, chiefly destined for sacred uses, the coins should be recovered, contaminated by abuse, forbade some of them. Where exchange is expressed by [פרס], because in this transaction small coins [פרוטות], copper pieces, were handed over or received. First, the coins of the publicans are rejected. But the Gemara observes here that a distinction must be made among the publicans, and that these are the ones meant: [פנים כסף] those for whom no fixed exaction has been determined, but who, having farmed the taxes and similar dues, extort as much as they can, provided they pay the sum of their farm to the magistrate. Whence in the same Gemara [מוכס כהרי], foreign publicans, are mentioned, as being more severe against Jews. For not all publicans were Israelites, nor were all Gentiles; but some were, as the Gemara teaches us. Whence in the words of the Saviour, Matthew 18:17, ὁ ἐθνικὸς ᾗ ὁ τελώνης [ho ethnikos ē ho telōnēs], Gentile and publican are distinguished, since many publicans were not Gentiles. And just as in the present Mishnah the publicans [מוכסין] are put for unjust publicans, because for the most part they demanded as much as they could (which this general formula testifies, when they are simply called publicans); so also the whole discourse shows that the Saviour, in the passage cited, understands a publican to mean an impious and unjust publican: and rightly, the Mishnah teaches. The Jewish constitutions did not allow coins to be exchanged from the chest of those publicans, [מבטס ...] because they were the fruit of robbery, that is, because they had been extorted as if by plunder. They permitted acceptance from other publicans, since [דינא דמלכותא דינא], the law of the king is also law, as is said in the Gemara: as if you were to say that what the king or magistrate demands to be paid to himself, subjects ought to consider (as it truly is) to be lawfully done. By this saying the judgment of the Saviour in Matthew 22:21 is approved: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. If, therefore, the publicans demanded nothing except what was fixed, the Jewish masters admitted their coins as just, and they do not at all deny that we may have upright publicans in the commonwealth. Just as John, when the publicans asked what they ought to do in order to walk the path of life, answered them, Luke 3:13: Demand nothing more than what is fixed for you; where the Greek word πράσσω [prassō], corresponds entirely to the Talmudic [סדר], what is fixed (of which we spoke above near the end of p. 271). So we observe again and again that the sayings of the New Testament agree with the Talmudic ones. The same judgment holds concerning [גזבר], the treasurer: if he burdens the people with unjust exaction, his coins are rejected; otherwise they are admitted. But in the interpretation of the word the Hebrews do not agree: some affirm that the treasurer is a royal officer, whose task was to collect the census and tribute from each man in the king's name. According to another opinion, [גזבר], the treasurer, is [גזבר ...] the religious treasurer, who gathers alms: and it is not lawful to receive coins from his chest, to avoid suspicion; for anyone who observed a recipient from that treasury, and did not attend to what he had given earlier for exchange, would easily believe that he performed the due services with the sacred goods in eating the second tithes and similar things. Yet the former explanation pleases more. A publican and a treasurer are allowed to take from their own houses; or rather, one who wishes to exchange money is allowed to receive from them, when they bring out the coins from their own houses; the reason for alms is the same. Similarly, if they are somewhere outside in a public place (but not at their own public chest), it is lawful to receive alms &c. from these publicans and treasurers. The other explanation offered is harsher; this one pleases more: and the reason for the statute seems to be that they did not wish the prohibition to be extended indefinitely. It might indeed be objected that coins from that publicans' and treasurers' chest may have been brought into the houses, and likewise carried from the same into the market; so there is a fear that those coins which they permit to be received may be the same as those which the Masters had forbidden. But they did not wish us to inquire beyond that chest of the publicans and treasurers, because about any money one might doubt whether it had not flowed from them through the purchase of various goods. Thus they would always have remained in doubt. As for the political statute proposed above at the first words of the Mishnah, by which the Mishnah was corrected, the Roman jurists likewise lay down: namely, that children can generally be sued concerning the seizure, so that what the thief had seized may be demanded from the thief's children. See Digest 47, title 8, law 2, last section: Whether the action for seizure ought to be granted for what the wealthier have become; let us see. And I think that the praetor did not promise against the heirs for what came to them, because he thought the condition was sufficient.

units.la: §. 2. נטלו מוכסין את חמורו ונתנו לו חמור אחר גזלו ליסטים את כסותו ונתנו Si publicani sumant alicujus asinum, eique alium asinum restituant; latrones vestem cujusdam rapiant, eique
units.tr: §. 2. If tax collectors take a man's ass and give him another ass, or robbers take his garment and give him another garment: these are his own. [נטלו מוכסין את חמורו ונתנו לו חמור אחר גזלו ליסטים את כסותו ונתנו]

units.la: [Hebrew column, left, lines in printed order:] לו כסוח אחרת הרי אלו שלו ספני שחבעליםכהיאשין סהן הנהר או מן הנהר הסציל מן הגיים או מן חליסטים אם נחייאשו הבעליםהרי אלו שלו וכן נחיל של דבורי אם נחייאשו הבעליםהרי אלו שלו אשר רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא נאסנרת אשה או קטן לומר מכאן יצא נחיל זרה וסהלך בחיך שך׳ חבירו להציל ארת נחילו ואםחויק משלםמה שהויק אבל לא יקיץ ארת סוכו על סנרת ליחן ארת הדםים רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא אומר אף קוצץ ונוחן את הדםים׃
units.tr: ...another garment, these are his own. If someone rescues [property] from a river, from an army, or from robbers, and the owners have despaired of it, these are his own. Likewise a swarm of bees: if the owners have despaired of it, these are his own. Rabbi John son of Beroka says that a woman or a minor is believed when they say, "From here this swarm flew out and went into the field of my neighbour, so that he may recover his swarm," and if he damages [the field], he pays for the damage, but he must not cut down its branch on condition of giving the honey-combs. Rabbi Ishmael, son of Rabbi John son of Beroka, says: he may even cut it down and give the honey-combs. [הכסוח אחרת הרי אלו שלו ספני שחבעליםכהיאשין סהן הנהר או מן הנהר הסציל מן הגיים או מן חליסטים אם נחייאשו הבעליםהרי אלו שלו וכן נחיל של דבורי אם נחייאשו הבעליםהרי אלו שלו אשר רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא נאסנרת אשה או קטן לומר מכאן יצא נחיל זרה וסהלך בחיך שך׳ חבירו להציל ארת נחילו ואםחויק משלםמה שהויק אבל לא יקיץ ארת סוכו על סנרת ליחן ארת הדםים רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא אומר אף קוצץ ונוחן את הדםים׃]

units.la: eique vestem aliam restituant, ecce hae ipsius sunt: quia proprietarii de iis desperant. Si quis eripiat è flumine, ab exercitu, aut latronibus; quum proprietarii desperant, haec ipsius sunt. Similiter examen apum, si proprietarii desperent, occupantis est. Ita inquit D. Iohannes filius Beroka, creditur mulieri & pupillo dicenti, Hinc evolavit istud examen & in medium proximi agrum penetravit: quo alter suum examen repetat. Quod si lædat, rependit quantum læsit: sed non precidit ramum ejus hac conditione ut pretium restituat. D. Ismael filius D. Iohannis filii Beroka permittit etiam ut praecidat, & pretium restituat.
units.tr: ...another garment, these are his own, because the owners despair of them. If someone rescues [goods] from a river, from an army, or from robbers, when the owners despair, these are his own. Similarly a swarm of bees, if the owners despair, belongs to the one who takes it. So says Rabbi John son of Beroka: a woman or a minor is believed when saying, "From here this swarm flew out and entered the field of my neighbour," so that the other may recover his swarm. If it does damage, he pays for what he has damaged, but he may not cut down its branch on condition of paying the price. Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi John son of Beroka permits even cutting it down and paying the price.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Duo in bonis transferendis expendunt Judæi: despe- rationem, qua proprietarius animû de recuperatione desponder; ac præterea mutationem dominii, qua res alteri erepta, iterum ad tertium transfertur. Quæ duo, si tertius ille prioris peccati nullo modo sit conscius; ut bona hujusmodi retinere possit, saltem pretium ei restituendum sit, efficere tradunt: ita quidem ut ob solam illam dominii translationem, proprietarius pretium, quod tertius ille dederat, restituere teneatur; ob antecedentem autem proprietarii desperationem, ei qui ultimò accepit liceat, vel simpliciter retinere, vel saltem si valorem domino reddat: pro diversa Doctorum sententia, vide Maim. c. 5. ˈɔɔˈɔ & c. 6. ɔɔɲ; inprimis Chofchen Mifchpat ad Num. 369. Hinc sectionis praesentis verba lucem accipiunt: nam publicani iidem sunt cum praecedentibus, scilicet impii ac improbi, à quibus non magis quam latronibus se sua recuperaturos sperant proprietarii. Ideoque si publicani vel latrones tuum pecus vel aliud quid auferentes, aliud illius loco restituant, quod ab illis accipis retinere licet: quia ista permutatio est, ɲɔɔ ɲɔɔ, dominii translatio, & veluti venditio; quam praecessit dominorum desperatio, qui scilicet bovem vel vestem aliave sibi erepta tibique postea tradita se recepturos non credebant: utpote qui publicanorum istorum & latronum conditionem perspectam haberent. Vbi observandum est, (inquiunt Ebræi) de latronibus Israelitarum sermonem esse: quandoquidem enim Israelitæ nonnisi interveniente testium testimonio sententiam dicunt, Israelitæ omnem recipiendi spem abjiciunt; utpote quibus testium in hoc facto penuria satis constet. Quocirca in altero membro, ubi denuò latronum mentio fit, quò subjuncta conditio spectet, obscurum non est. Antea absolutè à latronibus permutata tibi ascribebantur; jam vero sub conditione si proprietarii desperent: cum tamen illic desperatio tanquam certa pro fundamento præstrueretur. Verum illic de aliis latronibus quam hoc loco agebatur: hic Gentilium latrones spectantur, à quibus bona restitutum iri, nonnulla spes est. Gentes (vel Idololatræ, vel Cuthæi, ut loquuntur, quorum complexu etiam Christianos comprehendunt) judicare etiam ɔɔɲɔ, per conjecturam solent: si deficiant testes, alia argumenta expendunt, quibus sagacitate quadam & conjectura verum eruere allaborant. Unde proprietarii majorem spem concipiunt: quia si desunt testes quibus latrones convincantur, aliæ rationes verum assequendi non deficiunt. Quapropter cum ɔɔʃ, desperatio, incerta sit, ac te lateat; illa bona tua censere, licet illo modo jam dicto acceperis, non debes, nisi prius de antecedenti desperatione constet. De qua desperatione etiam Num. 2. ad praecedentem Misnam dixi, eamque lege 44. §. 5. ff. de furtis, illustravi. Huc etiam non male revocabitur l.sin. ff. de evictionibus. Si alienam rem mihi tradideris, & eandem pro derelicto habuero, amitti auctoritatem id est actionem pro evictione placet. Vbi derelictio cum דיפ, desperatione, conferenda: nam illa, quemadmodum haec, evincendi actionem aufert.
units.tr: The Jews weigh two things in the transfer of goods: des- pair, by which the owner gives up hope of recovering it; and besides, the change of ownership, by which a thing taken from one person is again transferred to a third. They teach that if these two things occur, and that third person was in no way aware of the earlier wrong, then so that he may keep such goods, at least the price must be repaid to him. The effect is this: because of the transfer of ownership alone, the owner is bound to repay the price that the third party had given; but because of the owner's earlier despair, the one who received the goods last may either keep them outright or, at least, if he gives the value to the owner. For the differing opinions of the teachers, see Maimonides ch. 5 and ch. 6, and especially Chofchen Mishpat on Num. 369. Hence the words of the present section receive light. For the tax collectors are the same as in the preceding passages, namely the wicked and dishonest, from whom owners hope to recover their goods no more than from robbers. Therefore if tax collectors or robbers, carrying off your flock or something else, restore something else in its place, which you receive from them, you may keep it. This is because the exchange is a transfer of ownership, and as it were a sale; and it was preceded by the owners' despair, since they did not believe they would recover the ox or garment taken from them and later handed to you, knowing the character of those tax collectors and robbers. Here it must be observed (the Hebrews say) that the speech concerns robbers of Israelites. For since Israelites pronounce judgment only with the testimony of witnesses, Israelites give up all hope of recovery, since a lack of witnesses in such a case is well known. Hence in the second clause, where robbers are mentioned again, it is not unclear to what the added condition refers. Before, the goods exchanged by robbers were assigned to you absolutely; now, however, they are assigned under the condition if the owners despair, since there despair was laid down as a certain foundation. But there the robbers were other than those discussed here: here the robbers of the Gentiles are in view, from whom there is some hope that the goods will be restored. The Gentiles (whether idolaters, or Cuthaeans, as they call them, a name under which they also include Christians) are accustomed to judge by conjecture as well. If witnesses fail, they weigh other arguments and labour to draw out the truth by a certain shrewdness and surmise. Hence owners conceive greater hope, because if the witnesses by whom robbers are convicted are lacking, other ways of reaching the truth are not wanting. Therefore, since despair is uncertain and hidden from you, you ought not to regard those goods as yours merely because you received them in the manner just described, unless it is first established that there was earlier despair. I spoke of this despair at No. 2 on the preceding Mishnah, and illustrated it from law 44, §5, ff. de furtis. Here also the law sin. ff. de evictionibus may fittingly be recalled: If you have handed over to me another's thing, and I have held it as abandoned, it is agreed that the authority, that is, the action for eviction, is lost. Here abandonment is to be compared with despair, for that, like this, removes the action for eviction.

units.la: Plura isto titulo occurrunt, quae ad Judaeorum in hac materia constitutiones a lectoribus revocari queunt. Ex eodem fundamento Ebraeorum hoc de apum examine placitum profluit. Apes alvearis relictis alio saepe avolare solent; idque dum fit ignorantes proprietarii, ubi eas quaerere debeant ignorant; adeoque de recuperatione animum despondent: quae causa est, ut fiant occupantis. Quemadmodum instit. l, 2. t. 1. §. 14. legimus. Examen quod ex alveo tuo evolaverit, eousque intelligitur esse tuum, donec in conspectu tuo est, nec difficilis persecutio ejus est, alioquin occupantis fit. Alveus pro alvear—io hic adhibetur. Ratio illius placiti initio paragraphi ponitur, Apium quoque fera natura est: sicuti Maim. c. 6. §ect. 14. Apes non sunt in hominis potestate sicuti gallinae & anseres. Hoc exemplo utitur, siquidem gallinae & anseres ad fera animalia non pertinent: Inst. t. eod. §. 16. Gallinarum autem & anserum non est fera natura. Porro dum proprietarius rem suam, sive examen apum persequitur, mulieris vel pupilli indicio quo avolaverit subinde liquet. Unde quaeritur in Gem. mulier & pupillus an testari possunt? num in judicio eorum testimonium recipitur? Deinde respondetur, qua ratione quoque modo id fiat. Hoc loco quo in casu versamur? veluti, quum dominis apes persequentibus, mulier aut pupillus lus profert ex animi simplicitate, atque indicat, Hinc egressum est hoc examen. Hoc pacto coram tribunali quidem non testantur; nisi quod ultro & sponte sua occurrentes proprietarios & in rem suam inquirentes monent & instituunt, unde & quò apes evolaverint: quod non rejiciunt judices. 5 Eo vero casu suum examen proprietarius recipit; ea tamen lege ut ab apibus vel à se, dum examen persequitur & capit, illatum damnum praestet: idque secundum communem de illato damno doctrinam, in superioribus variè propositam. 6 Si tamen in ramo alterius tuum apum' examen consederit, non est quod dicas, vereor ליסל לחד לחד ... eas sigillatim auferre, ne avolent; ideoque totum ramum abscindam, ut omnes simul auferens in alveare meum colligam. Id prohibentur etiam Pomponii verbis in generali ista juris regula 206. Iure naturae aequum est, neminem cum alterius detrimento & injuria fieri locupletiorem. Tu apes amiseras, ideoque eas recuperans locupletior redderis; & quidem cum alterius detrimento, si integrum ramum ex alterius arbore amputes.
units.tr: Many more instances under this title can be referred by readers to the Jewish regulations on this matter. From the same principle the Hebrews' rule about the swarm of bees follows. Bees often fly off from the hive after they have left it, and while this happens the owners, not knowing where they should look for them, despair of recovering them; and this is the reason why they become the property of the one who takes them. As we read in Inst. 2.1.14: A swarm that has flown out of your hive is understood to remain yours as long as it is in your sight, and its pursuit is not difficult; otherwise it becomes the property of whoever takes it. Here alveus is used for the beehive. The reason for that rule is given at the beginning of the paragraph: The nature of bees, too, is wild, as in Maim. ch. 6, §14: Bees are not in man's power as hens and geese are. He uses this example, since hens and geese do not belong to wild animals: Inst. same title, §16: But the nature of hens and geese is not wild. Moreover, while the owner pursues his property, that is, the swarm of bees, it becomes clear from the information of a woman or a child where it has flown. Hence the Gemara asks: Can a woman and a child give testimony? that is, is their testimony received in judgment? Then it is answered in what way and in what manner this is done. What is the case in which we are involved here? For example, when the owners are pursuing the bees, a woman or a child, out of simplicity of mind, declares and points out, "This swarm came out from here." In this way, indeed, they do not give testimony before a tribunal; but since they, coming forward of their own accord and seeking the owners who are searching for their property, inform them and show them where and whither the bees have flown, judges do not reject this. 5 In that case the owner recovers his swarm, but on the condition that he makes good the damage done either by the bees or by himself while he pursues and captures the swarm; and this is according to the common doctrine on damage done, variously set out above. 6 If, however, your swarm of bees has settled on a branch of another's tree, it is not for you to say, "I am afraid one by one, one by one [ליסל לחד לחד] ... that they will fly away if I take them individually; therefore I will cut off the whole branch, so that by taking them all at once I may gather them into my hive." Pomponius' words in the general rule of law 206 also forbid this: By the law of nature it is fair that no one should become richer to the detriment and injury of another. You had lost the bees, and so by recovering them you become richer; and indeed you do so to another's detriment, if you cut off a whole branch from another's tree.

units.la: §. 3. הסכיר כליו וספריו ביד אחר ויצא לו שם גניבה בעיר ישבע לו לוקח כסה הוציא ויטול ואם לאו לא כל היסנו שאני אומר מכרן לאחר ולקחן זה היסנו ז
units.tr: §3. If a man has left his utensils and his books in another's hand, and a report of theft goes out in the city, the buyer shall swear to him, and he shall take back what he paid; but if not, nothing... [הסכיר כליו וספריו ביד אחר ויצא לו שם גניבה בעיר ישבע לו לוקח כסה הוציא ויטול ואם לאו לא כל היסנו שאני אומר מכרן לאחר ולקחן זה היסנו ז]

units.la: Qui vasa & libros suos in alterius manu agnoscit, si de eo rumor urbem pervadat, ei factum esse furtum; emptor juratus quantum dederit, id recipiet. si rumor non fit, id nullo modo fiet: dicam enim, ipse ista alteri vendidit, atque hic ista ab altero accepit, sive emit.
units.tr: He who recognises his vessels and books in another's hand: if a rumour of them spreads through the city, the theft is established for him; the buyer, having sworn, shall recover what he paid. If no rumour arises, this will in no way happen: for I say he himself sold those things to another, and this one received them from another, or bought them.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: Vt quis sua bona in alterius manu deprehensa recipiat, rumorem Misnae author requirit, quo fama isti viro aliquid furto ablatum fuisse ferat: alioqui cum bona sua vendidisse dicerent. Præterea aliam in isto viro conditionem magistri exigunt, ne hujusmodi res vendere solitus sit: etenim venditione rem alienatam exciperent.2 Alias rem furto ablatam à possessore recipiet, si tamen quanti emerit possessor, proprietarius ipsi restituerit. Nam rei evictionem in furto concedunt: quamvis in hac re magistrorum sententiæ varient, quas in materia frequentissima discrepantes breviter proponam; brevitatique studens prolixos discursus contraham: quorum summa capita in Chofchen Mischpat num. 356. & Maim. Cod. ב c. 5. sect. 3. invenire est. Si antequam proprietarius recuperandi spem amisit, rem furtivam quis emerit, eam domino recepta quam expenderat pecunia restituere tenetur (restitutio autem pretii præcipitur propter fori correctionem, id est, quo ad justitiam revocetur quod publicè in foro gestum, uti fere enarrat S. J. f. 114. Bab. Kam. alioqui venditio & emptio impedirentur:) nisi à noto fure emerit; tum enim gratis rem furtivam emptor restituit. Et hactenus quidem fermè conveniunt. verum si proprietarius animum recuperandi desponderit, sive ante, sive post venditionem, Maimonides loco annotato rem furtivam restituendam negat, & si publicè furem esse venditorem constiterit, pretium proprietario ab emptore dandum; sin furem esse vulgò ignoratur, nihil dandum pronuntiat. Medius tamen & juri convenientius D. Jacob loco citato: qui duas proponens sententias, priori loco secus statuit, hancque esse Maimonidæ mentem dicit; si de fure vulgò constat, scilicet esse furem famosum, emptori nihil à proprietario rem furtivam recipiente reddi; sin minus, id est, ubi venditorem furem esse vulgò non innotuit, solum pretium ab emptore reddendum esse proprietario. Posteriori loco alium citat, qui postquam proprietarius de re desperavit, ipsi ab emptore nullo casu rem restitui affirmat. quod etiam admodum durum est. Si Maimonides scripsit, quod R. Jacob eum scripsisse affirmat, ipsius sententia satis æqua videtur. Sed antiquissimus in membrana nitidissimè conscriptus codex (cujus aliquoties mentionem injicio) illam Maimonidæ attribuit sententiam quam etiam ex impressis codicibus expressi; non quam R. Jacob ei ascribit. Hoc quidem verum est, in manuscripto nonnulla deesse, quæ in utriusque impressionis exemplaribus reperiuntur; sed eorum defectus illi Maim. sententiæ nihil derogat. Etenim cum illo casu emptor quas emit merces retinere dicitur, & nonnisi pretium proprietario rependere si eas à famoso fure emisset; posterius illud membrum in manuscripto deficiens, quo merces absque compensatione retinere statuitur, si ab alio quodam emisset, subintelligi omnino constat. Porrò alia sententia, quam R. Jacob priori loco expressit, cum Rom. jure quodammodo convenit. Si emptor ab eo emerit quem furem ignoravit, obligatio ac emptio vim suam habet: similiter ff. 18. t. 1. l. 34. §. 3. Quod si venditor scivit (scilicet rem furtivam esse) emptor ignoravit: utrinque obligatio contrahitur. Et quemadmodum illic in R. J. verbis certo casu restitutio rei ipsius urgetur, ita tit. eod. l. 28. Rem alienam distrahere quem posse, nulla dubitatio est. nam emptio est & venditio: sed res emptori auferri potest. Etenim ut inquit Glossa, Nobis invitis non debet alius nostras res retinere. Ut in illis agnosco quandam similitudinem; ita nec dissimilitudinem nego. Similitudo major Cod. li. 4. initio t. 51. Si præsidi provinciæ probatum fuerit, Iulianum nullo jure munitum servos tuos scientibus vendidisse; restituere tibi emptores servos jubebit. Quod si ignoraverint, & eorum facti sint; pretium eorum Iulianum tibi solvere jubebit. Hic vides si emptor illegitimam venditionem cognoscat, rem sine pretio domino restituendam; sin ignoret, rei pretium domino rependendum. Idem in R. J. verbis Maimonidæ ascriptis: nisi quod illic pretium ab emptore, hic à venditore quia notus & solvendo est, exigatur; deinde hic in Cod. verba & eorum facti sunt, de usucapione accipiat glossa; illic vero absolute, etiam extra usucapionem, res emptori manere & pretium proprietario reddendum dicatur. Secus in Cod. faciendum praecipitur, uti t. eod. l. 6. ostenditur. Nemo res ad te pertinentes, non obligatas sibi, nec ex officio vendendi potestatem habens distrahendo, quicquam tibi nocere potuit. nempe quibusdam casibus exceptis. Itaque quod Judaeorum Doctores statuunt, si quis a fure quid emerit sincero & simplici animo, antequam proprietarius de recuperatione animum despondit, puta rem ab emptore, recepto pretio, esse restituendam domino cui erepta erat; idem in genere Romanae leges constituunt. Unicum tantum paragraphum eumque sin. t. 1. l. 4. Inst. producam. Ipsius rei persecutionem extrinsecus habet dominus, quam aut vindicando, aut condicendo potest auferre. Sed rei vindicatio quidem adversus possessorem est, sive fur ipse possidet, sive alius quilibet; condictio autem adversus furem ipsum, haeredemve ejus, licet non possideat, competit. De pretio tamen restituendo contrariae leges proferri solent; quas conciliare allaborant. ego pro utraque sententia singulas leges propositas contentus, ad alia pergam. Cod. l. 2. tit. 20. §. 3. Si vi vel metu fundum avus tuus distrahere coactus est, etiamsi maxime emptor eum alii vendidit; si tamen tu avo tuo haeres extitisti: ut tibi reddito a te pretio restituatur, postquam placuit in rem quoque dari actionem secundum formam perpetui edicti, adito praside provinciae poteris postulare. Contra Cod. lib. 6. t. 2. l. 2. Incivilem rem desideratis, ut agnitas res furtivas non prius reddatis, quam pretium fuerit solutum a dominis. Huic Severi & Antonini placito quae repugnant, ita conciliantur: in iis de pretio agi quod in utilitatem proprietarii conversum erat, ideoque ab ipso solvendum. Ex hisce Judaeorum injustitia palam fit, qui rem furtivam pignori datam nonnisi pecunia reddita, repeti posse contendunt. Ita in Gemara hujus Codicis f. 114. p. 1. Hebrew text. Si pignus valeat ducentis & pro eo centum acceperit (fur,) in eo fori correctionem faciunt, (id est, quod palam fecit, ad æquitatem uti censent revocant, ut proprietarius non recipiat pignus, nisi illis centum persolutis.) ita quum æquivalentem summam pro eo accepit, constitutio ac consuetudo fert ut in eo idem fiat. Hæc obscuriora sunt: ideoque Maimonidæ verbis c. 5. fect. 6. illustranda. Vbi quis rem furtivam pignori dedit, si eam oppigneravit sive supra pretium, sive infra pretium, proprietarii summam pigneratori reddere tenentur. Idem in Choschen Mischpat num. 356. lit. p. Melius Imperatores Cod. li. 8. t. 16. sub initium, quum de pignore agitur. Si tamen pecuniam creditoris in rem domini versam constabit, non inutilis erit exceptio, duntaxat quod numeratum est, exolvi desideranti. Ergo si in rem domini versa non sit, data pro pignore pecunia non exolvitur. Cæterum ut eò redeamus, unde digressi sumus: quum in Mishna emptor pretium, & proprietarius rem ipsam recepturus dicitur, author de eo tempore, quum proprietarius nondum desperavit, disserit. nam postquam dominus animum despondit, pretium ad summum domino restitui existimat.
units.tr: For someone to recover his goods when they are found in another's hands, the author of the Mishnah requires a public rumour, by which report would say that something was taken from that man by theft. Otherwise they would say that he had sold his own goods. Moreover, the teachers require another condition in that man, namely that he is not in the habit of selling such things, since they would count it as a sale of an alienated thing. Otherwise, a thing taken by theft is recovered by the owner from the possessor, provided that the owner pays back to the buyer what the possessor paid. For they also grant eviction in cases of theft, although the opinions of the teachers differ on this matter, which is very common, and which I will set out briefly, since they disagree, and I aim at brevity and shall shorten long discussions. Their main points may be found in Chofchen Mischpat, no. 356, and in Maimonides' Code [ב], ch. 5, sect. 3. If someone bought a stolen thing before the owner had lost hope of recovering it, he is bound to give back to the owner the money he had paid. (The restitution of the price, moreover, is enjoined for the correction of the forum, that is, so that what was done publicly in the forum is brought back to justice, as the Gemara of Bava Kamma, folio 114, mostly explains; otherwise buying and selling would be hindered.) The exception is if he bought from a known thief; for then the buyer gives back the stolen thing for nothing. And so far they mostly agree. But if the owner has given up the intention of recovering it, whether before or after the sale, Maimonides, in the passage noted, denies that the stolen thing is to be restored, and he pronounces that if it is publicly established that the seller was a thief, the price must be paid to the owner by the buyer; but if it is commonly unknown that he was a thief, he says nothing is to be paid. Yet the middle opinion, more in keeping with law, is that of R. Jacob in the place cited, who, proposing two opinions, decides the former point otherwise, and says this is Maimonides' meaning: if it is commonly established about the thief that he is a notorious thief, nothing is to be returned to the owner by the buyer when the owner receives the stolen thing; but if not, that is, where it is not commonly known that the seller is a thief, only the price is to be returned by the buyer to the owner. In the latter place he cites another authority, who affirms that, after the owner has despaired of the thing, it is in no case to be restored to him by the buyer. This too is very harsh. If Maimonides wrote what R. Jacob affirms he wrote, his opinion seems quite fair. But the very ancient codex, written most neatly on parchment (which I mention several times), attributes to Maimonides that opinion which I have also drawn from the printed codices, not the one R. Jacob ascribes to him. It is true that some things are missing in the manuscript which are found in the copies of both printed editions, but their absence does not detract from Maimonides' opinion. For since in that case the buyer is said to keep the goods he bought, and to return only the price to the owner if he had bought them from a notorious thief, it is entirely clear that the latter clause, missing in the manuscript, which lays down that he keeps the goods without compensation if he had bought them from some other person, is to be understood. Furthermore, the other opinion, which R. Jacob stated first, agrees in some measure with Roman law. If the buyer bought from one whom he did not know to be a thief, the obligation and the sale have their force: similarly, Digest 18, title 1, law 34, §3: But if the seller knew (namely that the thing was stolen) and the buyer did not know: an obligation is contracted on both sides. And just as there, in the words of R. J., restitution of the thing itself is pressed in a certain case, so in the same title, law 28: There is no doubt that a person can sell another's thing. For there is a purchase and a sale: but the thing can be taken from the buyer. For, as the Gloss says, Without our consent another ought not to keep our things. In these I recognise a certain likeness; nor do I deny a dissimilarity. The greater likeness is in the Code, book 4, at the beginning of title 51: If it has been proved to the governor of the province that Julianus, with no lawful right, sold your slaves knowing them to be yours, he will order the buyers to restore the slaves to you. But if they bought them in ignorance, and have become their owners, he will order Julianus to pay you the price of them. Here you see that if the buyer knew the sale was illegitimate, the thing is to be restored to the owner without price; but if he did not know, the price of the thing is to be repaid to the owner.
