The same holds in the words of Maimonides quoted, except that there the price is exacted from the buyer, here from the seller, because he is known and solvent; then, here in the Code, the gloss takes the words and have become their owners as referring to usucapion; there, however, it is said absolutely, even apart from usucapion, that the thing remains with the buyer and the price is to be returned to the owner. The Code, by contrast, orders the matter to be done otherwise, as is shown in the same title, law 6: No one could harm you by selling things that belong to you, which were not pledged to him, nor by disposing of them while holding the power of sale by virtue of his office, nor could he. namely with certain cases excepted. Therefore what the doctors of the Jews lay down, that if anyone bought something from a thief in sincere and simple good faith, before the owner gave up hope of recovery, the thing, when the price has been received by the buyer, is to be restored to the owner from whom it was snatched; the Roman laws establish the same thing in general. I shall produce only one paragraph, and that a short one, from Institutes, book 4, title 1: The owner has the pursuit of the thing from outside; he can take it away either by vindication or by condiction. But vindication lies against the possessor, whether the thief himself possesses it or any other person; condiction, however, lies against the thief himself, or his heir, even if he does not possess it. Yet contrary laws are usually brought forward about restoring the price, and people labour to reconcile them. I am content to have set out one law for each opinion, and will go on to other matters. Code, book 2, title 20, §3: If your grandfather was compelled by force or fear to sell the estate, even though the buyer sold it to another; yet if you became heir to your grandfather, you may, on repayment of the price by you, ask the governor of the province to have it restored to you, since it has been decided that an action in rem is also given, according to the form of the perpetual edict. Against this, Code, book 6, title 2, law 2: You want an unjust thing, that the stolen goods, once identified, should not be returned before the price has been paid by the owners. The rulings of Severus and Antoninus, which disagree with this, are reconciled thus: in those cases the price is to be claimed which was turned to the owner's advantage, and therefore must be paid by him. From these examples the injustice of the Jews is plainly seen, who contend that a stolen thing given in pledge can be reclaimed only when the money has been repaid. So in the Gemara of this Code, folio 114, side 1: If the pledge is worth two hundred and he received a hundred for it (the thief), they make a correction of the forum in this (that is, what he did openly they call back to equity, so that the owner does not receive the pledge unless those hundred have been paid). So when he has received a sum equivalent for it, the constitution and custom bring it about that the same is done in this case. These things are rather obscure, and so they must be clarified by the words of Maimonides, ch. 5, sect. 6: Where someone gave a stolen thing in pledge, if he pawned it either above or below its price, the owners are bound to repay the sum to the pledgee. The same is in Chofchen Mischpat, no. 356, letter p. The emperors speak better in Code, book 8, title 16, near the beginning, where pledge is treated: If, however, it is established that the creditor's money was turned to the owner's advantage, the exception will not be useless, provided that only what was counted out is paid to the one who demands it. Therefore if the money given for the pledge was not turned to the owner's advantage, it is not repaid. But to return to the point from which we digressed: since in the Mishnah the buyer and the owner about to recover the thing itself are spoken of, the author discusses the time when the owner has not yet despaired; for after the owner has given up hope, he thinks the price is to be restored to the owner only at most.

units.la: Verumenimverò si rumor, de quo in superiori membro, per urbem non feratur; quod exigitur non fiet: quia ipse qui de furto conqueritur, forte ista quæ furtiva dicit, alteri vendiderat, à quo inpræsentiarum possidens eadem emerit npb. Hæc vox accipere in genere significans, à Talmudistis sæpe ad emptionem restringitur: ut facile lectores observabunt.
units.tr: Moreover, if the rumour mentioned in the preceding clause is not spread through the city, what is demanded will not be done, because the one who complains of theft may have sold the things he calls stolen to another, from whom he now possesses them and emerit npb. This word, which signifies "to acquire" in general, is often restricted by the Talmudists to buying, as readers will easily notice.

units.la: Difficilior est phraseos istius explicatio, qua noster hoc loco utitur, quæque hic redditur, id nullo modo fiet. In textu originali [Hebrew] formula obscurior, ideoque à lexicographis omissa: saltem eam explicatam videre nondum contigit. loca tamen ubi occurrit in Rabbinorum scriptis, eam ignorari non sinunt; imo vel hæc sola Mishna satis ejus significationem, quam ei in versione assignavi, ostendit. Aliud sane ea designari nequit: originem tamen & usum plenius exhibebo. Omnibus quicunq; hæc studia tractamus notum, universali particulæ propositam negationem etiam in universum negare: ut לא לא significet quoque nemo, & nihil. Apud Rabbinos, præsertim antiquiores, כי in מכי pro בן, ex, vsurpari, compositamque vocem מכי esse idem quod מן ex eo, notius est, quam ut magnopere moneri debeat. Unde tota phrasis מכי לא לא sonat nihil ex eo, quasi dicas, istius nihil est. Vocabula autem quandoque non tam rem ipsam quæ proprie significatur, quam ejus debitum & obligationem notant. Quemadmodum hujus rei manifestum habemus exemplum Num. 35. 28. Deus vindicem non teneri pronuntiat, si interfecisset homicidam invitum, qui cum errore aliquem occidisset, è civitate receptus sui prodiisset: nam inquit legislator, in civitate receptus sui manebit, id est, manere debet sive debebat. Nam qui egreditur adeoque interficitur, in urbe non manet; sed hac formula ipsius officium & debitum ostenditur, manendi scilicet in ista civitate donec Sacerdos maximus moreretur. qua constitutione, gratia nostri summi sacerdotis J. Christi innuebatur; cujus morte libertas nobis parta. Alia exempla non subjiciam, licet plura non desint: satis liquet debitum quandoque rei, non rem ipsam designari. Hac ratione, מכי לא לא, nihil istius, non tantum designat, nihil istorum est, vel nihil istius erit, sive nullo modo istud fiet; sed etiam aversandi est formula: quasi dicas, Apage istam rem, vel, Id esse sive fieri nullo modo debet, sive, Iniquum est ut hoc vel illud ita fit aut fiat. In Rabboth sive antiquissimis collectaneis in Pentateuchum sol. edit. Salonic. 31. col. 4. Seculum divisionis linguarum dicebat, Id esse non debet, ut sibi eligat superiora, detque nobis inferiora; sed agedum, turrim nobis extruamus, ejusque summitati idolum imponamus, cujus manu ensem inferamus: ita videbitur ac si cum illo bellum gereret. Hic per כל היומו לא [?] nihil iftius, id fibi voluit author, Non decere, neque permittendum, Deum sibi coelefte dominium, omnemque religiosum cultum vendicare. Hujusmodi sermo in iftis Rabboth illius feculi hominibus attributur. Inde quædam depromens S. Jarchi ad initium c.11.Gen. eademque utens phrasi, inter alias dicti דכריס לחדיס [?], verba eadem, expofitiones & hanc producit, כלו בעב' לחת ולאמרו [?], Idem inive- runt confilium, dixeruntque, id non permittendum; ut fibi fuperiora deligat: afcendamus in expanfum & cum ipfo bellum geramus. Sed jam plus satis de hac Mifna; ut sequentem expendamus tempus poftulat.
units.tr: The explanation of the phrase our author uses here, rendered as id nullo modo fiet ("this will in no way happen"), is more difficult. In the original text the formula is more obscure, which is why the lexicographers have passed it over; at least I have not yet had the chance to see it explained. Still, the places where it occurs in the rabbinic writings do not allow it to be ignored, and this Mishnah alone shows well enough the sense I have given it in the translation. It certainly cannot mean anything else, but I will set out its origin and use more fully. Everyone who works on these studies knows that a universal negative particle also negates the whole proposition, so that לא לא [lo lo] means nemo and nihil. Among the rabbis, especially the older ones, כי in מכי [mikki] is used for בן, ex, and that the compound מכי is the same as מן, ex eo, is too familiar to need much pointing out. So the whole phrase מכי לא לא [mikki lo lo] sounds like nihil ex eo, as if you said, "nothing of that." Words, however, sometimes denote not so much the thing properly signified as its due and obligation. We have a clear example of this in Num. 35.28, where God declares that the avenger is not liable if he killed the manslayer unwillingly, who, having killed someone by mistake, came out of the city of refuge. For the lawgiver says, he shall remain in the city of his refuge, that is, he ought to remain, or was bound to remain. He who goes out and so is killed does not remain in the city; but by this formula his duty and obligation are shown, namely to remain in that city until the high priest died. By this ordinance the grace of our high priest Jesus Christ was signified, by whose death liberty was won for us. I will not add other examples, though many are not lacking: it is clear enough that the due of a thing is sometimes designated rather than the thing itself. In this way מכי לא לא [mikki lo lo], nothing of that, designates not only nothing of those is, or nothing of that will be, or that will in no way happen, but is also a formula of aversion: as if you said, Away with that thing, or, That ought in no way to be or to happen, or, It is unfair that this or that should be so or be done. In the Rabboth, that is the most ancient collections on the Pentateuch (ed. Salonica, p. 31, col. 4), we read: The generation of the division of tongues said, That ought not to be, that he should choose the higher things and give us the lower; come, let us build a tower and set on its summit an idol, into whose hand we will place a sword: so it will seem as if we were waging war with him. Here, by כל היומו לא [?] nothing of that, the author meant that it is not fitting, nor to be permitted, that God should claim for himself heavenly dominion and all religious worship. Such speech is attributed in those Rabboth to the men of that age. Hence S. Jarchi, drawing certain things from the beginning of chapter 11 of Genesis and using the same phrase, among other sayings with the same words, also gives this explanation: They took counsel together and said, That ought not to be permitted, that he should choose the higher things for himself; let us ascend into the expanse and wage war with him. But enough has been said about this Mishnah; the sequence now demands that we consider the following.

units.la: זח בא בחביתו של יין זוה בא בכרו של דבש נסרקרה חביה של דבש ושפך זה ארץ ייני והציל את הרבש להוכה אין לו אלא שכרו ואם אסר אציל את שלך ואתה נותן לי דמי שלי חיי ליתן לו שטף נהר חסורו וחסר חבירו שלו יפה מנה ושל חבירו טאחים הניח זח את שלו והציל ארץ של חבירו אין לו אלא שכרו ואם אסר לו אני אציל את שלך ואתה נותן דמי שלי חייב ליתן לו ו׳
units.tr: If one man comes with his jar of wine and another with his jar of honey, and the jar of honey breaks, and the first man pours out his wine and saves the other's honey, he has no claim beyond his wage. But if he says, "I will save yours, and you give me my due," then he must pay him. [זח בא בחביתו של יין זוה בא בכדו של דבש נשברה חביתו של דבש ושפך זה יינו והציל את הדבש לחבירו אין לו אלא שכרו ואם אמר אציל את שלך ואתה נותן לי דמי שלי חייב ליתן לו] ## §. 4.

units.la: Si ubi unus cum fuo vini vafe, alter cum fua mellis ampulla venit, mellis ampulla rumpatur 1, & ille effufo vino fuo, melin vas fuum colligat; nihil prater fuam mercedem habet: 2 at fi dixerit, Ego tuum colligam, tu vero mihi mei pretium folves; alter ei folvere tenetur. 3 Si cum flumen cujufdam afinum cum proximi afino inundaret, quorum qui illius erat valebat 4 minam, proximi vero, duas minas, ille fuo relicto eripuit proximi fui afinum; nihil prater fuam mercedem habet. quod fi dixerit, Ego tuum eripiam; & tu mei pretium folves, ipfi folvere tenetur.
units.tr: If, when one comes with his jar of wine and another with his jar of honey, the honey jar breaks, and the first, having poured out his wine, gathers up the honey jar, he has nothing but his wages.¹ But if he says, "I will gather yours, and you shall pay me my price," the other is bound to pay him.² If, when the flood of a river carries away one man's donkey along with his neighbour's donkey, the one whose donkey was worth a mina, and the neighbour's two minas, he leaves his own and rescues his neighbour's donkey, he has nothing but his wages. But if he says, "I will rescue yours, and you shall pay me my price," the other is bound to pay him.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: ¹ [?] cst quidem rumpitur; sed ex parte tantum: quod rimas agere dicimus, quum in fundo vel in lateribus fissura excitatur. Ita ampullæ vel lagenæ quadam sui parte fissæ latera separantur sæpe, & fissuras ac rimas admittunt: unde liquor contentus paulatim effluit. Contusione etiam particulæ quædam excutiuntur, ut per foramina mel, vinum, vel alia destillent ac perdantur. Hujusmodi quid hoc loco consideratur: nec ea spectatur fractura, qua mellis ampulla ita conteratur, ut liquor uno impetu in terram effusus dispergatur. Eo enim casu mel ab altero collectum, ipsius esse censetur; quemadmodum ait Maim. Cod. Abeda c. 12. sect. 5. [illegible, ~12 letters] Quod si mel effundatur in terram, ecce fit commune; & quicunque id ne perdatur servat, sibi servat. Itaque hoc tantum spectatur, quid juris sit, quum ampulla rimas agente mel effluere incipit, aliusque nihil pactus, lagena aliove vini vase evacuato, mel istud in vas suum recipit ne perdatur: atque hic solam laboris & commodati vasis mercedem assignatam habemus. ² At si pactus sit pretium vini, quod in alterius gratiam perditur; alter rependere tenetur. Pacisci autem cum hoc, tum sequenti membro censetur, si modo stipuletur pretium; licet alter non spondeat: siquidem cum longum colloquium non ferat res ipsa, suo silentio spondere judicatur. Etiam coram tribus viris stipulatus, ab altero pretium accipit, ac si coram id ipsi dixisset. ut in Chofchen Mifchpat & Jad Chazaka plenius exponitur. ³ Imo in altero exemplo, absente proprietario, quia ratio ipsa pretiosioris animalis, magis satagendum docet, & absens pretiosioris dominus, asini vilioris pretium potius solvere, quam cariorem amittere velle judicatur; absente inquam proprietario, alter illud ab ipso pactus ac stipulatus censetur: idcoque si absentis asinum tanto præstantiorem, uti hic expri-
units.tr: ¹ It is indeed said to be "broken," but only in part. This is what we call "making cracks" when a fissure arises in the bottom or the sides. Thus flasks and jars split in some part often have their sides separated and admit fissures and cracks, and the liquid they contain gradually leaks out. A blow can also knock loose certain fragments, so that honey, wine, or other liquids drip out through the holes and are lost. It is this kind of case that is considered here. We do not consider a breakage in which a honey jar is shattered so that the liquid, poured out on the ground in one rush, is scattered. In that case the honey collected by another is deemed to be his own, as Maimonides says (Cod. Abeda c. 12, sect. 5, [illegible]): "But if honey is poured out on the ground, behold, it becomes common; and whoever keeps it so that it is not lost, keeps it for himself." So the only question is this: what is the law when a jar with cracks begins to let its honey run out, and another person, having made no agreement, empties the jar or other wine vessel and puts that honey into his own vessel so that it is not lost? Here we have only the wages assigned for the labour and for the use of the vessel. ² But if he has agreed on a price for the wine that is lost for the other's benefit, the other is bound to repay it. An agreement of this kind, both here and in the following clause, is deemed to exist if he merely stipulates a price, even though the other does not promise. Since the matter itself does not allow a long conversation, the other is judged to have promised by his silence. Even one who has stipulated before three men and receives the price from the other is treated as if he had said it to him directly, as is more fully explained in Chofchen Mishpat and Jad Chazaka. ³ Indeed, in the other example, where the owner is absent, the reasoning of the more valuable animal itself teaches that one should take more care, and an absent owner is judged to prefer paying the price of the cheaper ass rather than losing the dearer one. So when the owner is absent, I say, the one who saved it is deemed to have agreed and stipulated with him. Therefore, if he saves the ass of the absent man, which is far more valuable, as is expressed here,

units.la: ¹ [?] cst: the Hebrew word at the start of the note and the Hebrew line in the middle of the paragraph are partly illegible; they are marked as such in the text. exprimitur, suo ac proprio celicto servet; sui pretium recuperat, quem proximi causâ æquitate id postulante neglexerat. Quantum ex Ascheris verbis, qui magnæ autoritatis Doctor in Talmud, adeoque & in hoc caput commentatus est, liquet. Exemplum posterius conjunctum volunt alii Talmudistæ, quod alioquin exceptiones & dubia exorirentur, quæ hac exemplorum diversitate auferuntur. * Cæterum quid sit mina sive מנה, paucis expendendum. Ex illa voce מנה, ducenta, facile mina æstimatur: quandoquidem in hac asinorum comparatione, vel ita numerus ducentarum accipiendus, quasi unus minâ, alter ducentis minis valeret, quæ esset insulsa pretiorum in hoc animali collatio; vel dualis numerus singulari ratione in voce מאתים attendendus est. Dualis ad singularem, dupli rationem habet: eamque satis aptam huic constitutioni, in præstantiæ unius asini præ altero differentia: ut hic illo, altero tanto carior sit. Sic cum unus ducentis valeat; alter centum valere statuitur: in ducentis autem exprimendis propria vox מאתים adhibetur; at pro centum in originali מאה. Unde מנה sive minam centum continere concludimus: & centum drachmæ sive denarii Romani hic admodum quadrant, quum asinus centum drachmis æstimatur. Mina itaque hac ratione centum drachmas continet, sive vigintiquinque siclos sacros: quod alia loca in hisce libris Nezikim affatim ostendunt. Nec in re non admodum obscura prolixus ero: sed pauca testimonia, quæ omnibus satisfacere queant, producam. Mina, מנה, inquit Glossator ad p. 2. f. 90. hujus Codicis ex edit. Ven. מנה, est viginti quinque siclorum, drachmarum autem sive denariorum centum. Atque hæc mina passim in Talmude adhibetur: & quia est alia quæ multo minus valet, distinctionis causa vocatur מנה צורית, Mina Tyria; altera vero, scilicet illius pars octava, מנה מדינה, Mina provincialis: quemadmodum siclus provincialis (uti observatum n. 2. sect. 6. c. 8.) Tyrii parte octava æstimatur. vide Sal. J. cum loco citato, tum etiam Exod. 25.39. [Hebrew line], Mina pendet libram qua ponderant argentum pondere Colonienſi: nimirum centum sunt denarii, ſicli vero vigintiquinque: ſiclus autem eſt quatuor denarior um. Nec dubitari potest minam eſse centum aureorum ſive denariorum (hos enim aureos vocant Ebræi) ſi 1 Reg. 10.17. conferatur cum 2 Chron. 9.16. Nam cum hic trecenti aurei ponantur; illic tres minas dicit author: ideoque mina centum Ebræorum aureos continet. Similiter Græcorum μνᾶ, licet diversissimæ sit quantitatis, (unde Hesychius, Λίτραι δύο, mina eſt duarum librarum; & postea, Λίτρας μιας δημοίρου, libra unius beſſis eſt,) ideoque jam pluris, jam minoris æstimetur; communior tamen, centum est drachmarum. Unde Plinius l.21.c.34. μνᾶ, quam noſtri minam vocant, pendet drachmas Atticas centum. Ibidem Plinius, Drachma Attica denarii argentei habet pondus. eadem ſex obolos pondere efficit. obolus decem chalcos. Hæc ideo adjeci, ut quomodo iſtis vocibus paſſim utar, lectori conſtaret. Drachmam enim, etiam Atticam, ſecundum Plinium pro Romano denario; & denarium pro numo ſex obolorum tempore ſecundæ ædis adhibeo; ita quidem, ut obolus decem chalcos proprie dictos contineat. chalcus autem proprie acceptus drachmæ Æginaſæ pars est circiter quinquagesima. Plinium vero idcirco sequor, quia à Judæis denarium pariter censeri video. Ita etiam mina Plinii cum Judæorum [Hebrew] convenit. Cæterum minam esse denariorum centum ex collatione quoque D. Halicarnassæi cum T. Livio constat: nam ubi Servii Tullii laudabile institutum narrant, quo populum in ſex classes divisit, quæ domi & militiæ munera & loca diversa obtinerent; in prima classe ille l.4. p.221. censum fuisse scribit πρὸς τὰ εκατον μνᾶν, non infra centum minas; hic vero li.1.c.43. primam classem ad minimum censum habuisse refert centum millium æris: id est, in bonis habuisse decem millia drachmarum sive denariorum: quia denarius decem æreos asses continebat. Iam si centum minæ sint decem millia denariorum; mina una centum denarios valet. Quò autem hic valor cum Judaica mina conveniat, denarios & drachmas Pliniano modo accipere & extendere oportet: sicuti etiam Judæos facere antea dictum fuit. Verumenimverò est & mina Judaica posterioris templi, quæ tempore secundæ ædis post captivitatem in usu erat: cujus Ezech. 45. 12. mentio fit. Hæc centum & viginti aureorum, sive drachmarum, sive denariorum erat: siquidem sexaginta siclis valere debebat, sicuti illic præcipitur. Sub templo posteriori pro obolis magnis sive tressibus quinque, denarius continebat sex: quo factum ut siclus sexta parte creseceret; similiter & mina: licet 100 tantum drachmas penderet. Sed cum Deus justitiam variis modis inculcaret, idque justum minæ pondus & valorem imperans; ne Judæi hac in parte errarent, siclis veteribus, ideoque cum hæc Ezechiel scriberet notissimis, novam minam (ad quam deinde numi examinarentur) definit. Ac si dixisset, posthac numi valor cresceret: etenim, exempli gratia, non eadem erit mina; sed siclis, cujusmodi hactenus usi estis, sexaginta valebit. sive numus viginti siclorum, & numus viginti quinque siclorum, cum numo quindecim siclorum veterum, eorumque communium, minam constituent. ideoque & siclorum & denariorum novorum valor secundum hujusmodi proportionem augebitur. Hæc est mens verborum, Ezechielis citato capite. Si hæc ita se habeant, quid sibi vult D. Kimchi in voce ? ubi testatur quosdam vocare libram viginti denarios. Atqui paulo ante scripserat, minam sive libram esse denariorum centum. Respondeo, numerum centenarium posteriori loco excidisse scribarum incuria: nam mina sive libra apud Ezechielem c. 45. centum & viginti denariis antiquis valet: tot enim hujusmodi denarii, in siclis veteribus sexaginta. Porrò hæc Misna non omnino cum jure Rom. convenire videtur, quum rem suam ante pactum in proximi commodum impendenti nihil nisi mercedem largitur. Attamen ff. l. 3. t. 5. l. 3. Ait prætor. Si quis negotia alterius, sive quis negotia quæ cujusque cum is moritur fuerint, gesserit: judicium eo nomine dabo. quæ conferenda cum his l. 2. verbis, Et sane sicut æquum est, ipsum actus sui rationem reddere, & eo nomine condemnari, quidquid vel non ut oportet gessit, vel ex his negotiis retinet: ita ex diverso justum est, si utiliter gessit, præstari ei quidquid eo nomine vel abest ei, vel abfuturum est. Nisi hinc hujusmodi infortunia, cum quis sua in alterius gratiam perdere cogitur &c. excludere velimus, argumento ff. l. 17. t. 1. l. 26. §. 6. Non omnia quæ impensurus non fuit, mandatori imputabit: veluti quod spoliatus sit à latronibus, aut naufragio res amiserit, vel languore suo, suorumve adprehensus, quaedam erogaverit. Hic tamen Paulum jurisconsultum ad ea quæ è Misna proposui respexisse, vix credo. Quod verò Misnæ author damnum in bonis alienis liberandis paffo postquam stipulatus est, à domino id præstandum asserat, id similitudine l. 56. §. sin. t. eod. confirmari videtur. Sumptus bona fide necessario factos, etsi negotio finem adhibere procurator non potuit, judicio mandati restitui necesse est. Similiter ergo damnum resarciendum, si suam rem amittere, ut alteri commodet, necesse sit. & quidem ab exitu restitutio non pendet secundum istam legem: verum Maimonides de eo agens qui alterius asinum cum sui pecoris interitu liberare nequit, quum id conatur; damnum restituendum negat. יד ולא הניח לו Si defecenderit ad eripiendum, nec tamen eripiat, nil nisi mercedem aufert.
units.tr: leaving his own behind, he recovers the price of his own animal, which he had neglected for his neighbour's sake, as equity demands. This is clear from the words of Ascheri, a teacher of great authority in the Talmud, who also commented on this chapter. Other Talmudists hold that the later example is to be joined to the earlier one, since otherwise exceptions and doubts would arise, and this variety of examples removes them. * As for what a mina [מנה] is, it should be considered briefly. From the word [מנה], meaning a hundred, the mina is easily estimated, since in this comparison of asses the number should be taken either as if one were worth a mina and the other two hundred minas, which would be a foolish comparison of values for this animal, or else the dual number must be considered in the special sense of the word [מאתים]. The dual has a double ratio to the singular, and this suits the present arrangement well, in the difference between the excellence of one ass and another, so that one is twice as dear as the other. Thus, since one is worth two hundred, the other is set at a hundred. For two hundred the proper word [מאתים] is used, but for a hundred the original has [מאה]. Whence we conclude that a mina [מנה] contains a hundred, and a hundred drachmas, or Roman denarii, fit very well here, since the ass is valued at a hundred drachmas. The mina in this sense therefore contains a hundred drachmas, or twenty-five sacred shekels, as other passages in these Nezikim books amply show. Nor will I be long on a matter that is not very obscure; I will produce a few testimonies that can satisfy everyone. "Mina" [מנה], says the Glossator on p. 2, f. 90 of this Codex (Venice edition), [מנה] "is twenty-five shekels, but of drachmas or denarii, a hundred." This mina is used everywhere in the Talmud, and because there is another mina worth much less, the one is called, for the sake of distinction, [מנה צורית], the Tyrian mina; the other, namely its eighth part, [מנה מדינה], the provincial mina, just as the provincial shekel (as observed n. 2, sect. 6, c. 8) is valued at an eighth part of the Tyrian. See Sal. J. with the passage cited, and also Exod. 25.39: "The mina weighs a pound, by which they weigh silver, by Cologne weight: that is, there are a hundred denarii, or twenty-five shekels; but the shekel is four denarii." Nor can it be doubted that the mina is a hundred gold pieces or denarii (for the Hebrews call these gold), if 1 Kings 10.17 is compared with 2 Chron. 9.16. For there three hundred gold pieces are mentioned here, and there the author speaks of three minas; so the mina contains a hundred gold pieces of the Hebrews. Similarly the Greek [μνᾶ], though of very different quantities (whence Hesychius: "[Λίτραι δύο]," a mina is two pounds; and later, "[Λίτρας μιας δημοίρου]," a pound is a half-unit), and so is valued now higher, now lower, is nevertheless commonly a hundred drachmas. Hence Pliny, book 21, c. 34: "[μνᾶ], which our people call the mina, weighs a hundred Attic drachmas." In the same place Pliny says: "The Attic drachma has the weight of a silver denarius; the same makes six obols by weight; the obol makes ten chalci." I have added this so that the reader will understand how I use these terms throughout. For I take the drachma, even the Attic, according to Pliny, for the Roman denarius, and the denarius for a coin of six obols at the time of the second temple; so that the obol contains ten chalci properly so called. A chalcus, properly taken, is about the fiftieth part of an Aeginetan drachma. I follow Pliny because I see that the Jews likewise reckon the denarius in this way. Thus also Pliny's mina agrees with the Jewish [mina]. Moreover, that the mina is a hundred denarii is clear from comparing Dionysius of Halicarnassus with Livy. For where they relate the praiseworthy institution of Servius Tullius, by which he divided the people into six classes, which held different duties and places in home and war, Dionysius writes that in the first class the census was "[πρὸς τὰ εκατον μνᾶν]," not less than a hundred minas (book 4, p. 221); and Livy (book 1, c. 43) reports that the first class had a census of at least "a hundred thousand of bronze," that is, it had ten thousand drachmas or denarii in goods, since the denarius contained ten bronze asses. Now if a hundred minas are ten thousand denarii, one mina is worth a hundred denarii. But for this value to agree with the Jewish mina, the denarii and drachmas must be taken and extended in Pliny's manner, as I said the Jews also do before. Yet there is also a Jewish mina of the later temple, which was in use in the time of the second temple after the captivity, and to which Ezek. 45.12 refers. This was a hundred and twenty gold pieces, whether drachmas or denarii, since it had to be worth sixty shekels, as is commanded there. Under the later temple, the denarius contained six obols, which were the large or three-fold obols, so that the shekel increased by a sixth; and similarly the mina, although it weighed only a hundred drachmas. But since God urged justice in various ways, and commanded a just weight and value for the mina, lest the Jews err in this matter, he defined a new mina (by which the coins would then be tested) in terms of the old shekels, which were well known when Ezekiel wrote this. It is as if he had said that henceforth the value of coins would increase: for example, the mina will not be the same, but will be worth sixty shekels of the kind you have used hitherto. Thus a coin of twenty shekels and a coin of twenty-five shekels, together with a coin of fifteen old shekels, and those common ones, will make up a mina; and so the value of new shekels and denarii will be increased in this proportion. This is the sense of the words of Ezekiel in the chapter cited. If this is so, what does Kimchi mean in the word [?], where he testifies that some "call the pound twenty denarii"? Yet a little before he had written that the mina or pound "is a hundred denarii." I reply that the number a hundred fell out in the later place through the carelessness of the copyists; for the mina or pound in Ezekiel chapter 45 is worth a hundred and twenty old denarii, since there are that many such denarii in sixty old shekels. Furthermore, this Mishnah does not seem entirely to agree with Roman law, since it grants nothing but a reward to one who spends his own goods, before any agreement, for the benefit of his neighbour. Yet Dig. l. 3, t. 5, l. 3: "The praetor says: If anyone has managed the affairs of another, or the affairs of a man who has died, I will grant an action on that account." This may be compared with these words of l. 2: "And indeed, just as it is right that he render an account of his own conduct and be condemned on that account for whatever he has managed improperly or retains from these affairs, so conversely it is just that, if he has managed them to advantage, he be repaid whatever he has lost or will lose on that account." Unless we wish to exclude from this such misfortunes, when someone is forced to lose his own goods for another's benefit, etc., by the argument of Dig. l. 17, t. 1, l. 26, §6: "The mandator will not charge to the mandatary what he was not going to spend, such as what he lost through robbers, or what was lost in shipwreck, or what he spent on account of his own or his family's illness." Yet I hardly believe that the jurist Paul had in mind the things I have proposed from the Mishnah. That the author of the Mishnah says the loss incurred in freeing another's goods, after he has stipulated, is to be made good by the owner, seems to be confirmed by the similar law of l. 56, §sin., same title: "Expenses necessarily incurred in good faith, even if the agent could not bring the business to an end, must be restored by the action of mandate." Similarly, then, the loss must be made good if one must lose his own goods in order to lend them to another. And indeed, under this law, restitution does not depend on the outcome; but Maimonides, discussing one who cannot free another's ass without the loss of his own flock when he tries, denies that the loss must be restored. [Hebrew phrase, illegible] "If he withdrew to rescue it, and did not rescue it, he takes nothing but the reward."

units.la: 1 Diversam in hac voce esse lectionem è Gemara constat: legunt quidam 'מסיקין' proprie oppressores, à מסף, opprimere; alii מניקיס, angustia afficientes, à פיץ, arctari. Sed eodem res recidit: siquidem graßatores designantur, qui agrorum possessores opprimunt, angustiaque afficiunt. Unde in Gemaræ initio R. Nachman dixisse fertur: מאן דתני מסיקין לא מטעבב דכתיב ירם הנלגל ומתרגמין יחסניהי ספס ומאן דתני מניקין לא מטעבב דכתיב במנור ובמנוך, Qui legit, מסיקין, oppressores, non aberrat; nam (Deut. 28.42.) scriptum extat, hereditario jure obtinebit locusta; quod Chaldaice exponimus, id hereditate obtinebit ספס oppressio: qui etiam legit, Angustia afficientes, non aberrat; quia scriptum est; (Deut. 28.53.) In oppressione & in מנוך angustia. Mens hæc est; idem pene significari, quia מסיקין sunt oppressores; quemadmodum liquet ex illo paragr. 42, c. 28. Deut. ubi locusta vel (ut alii) sideratio dicitur ספס, oppressio, quod homines & segetem opprimat: itaque 'מניקי', angustia afficientes non male nuncupari, ut מנוך est angustia eodem capite Deuteronomii. Verum ut alibi Talmudistæ sunt miseri grammatici; ita hoc loco ספס & מסיקין male ad eandem radicem revocantur: etsi significatione convenire inficias non eam. ספס permutatis ב & ם est ab Arabico شقي, miser fuit: sicuti in proverbio 18. centuriæ secundæ Anonymi cujusdam, مَنْ لاَ يُقَدِّمُ تَوْبَةً, Qui non anticipat pœnitentiam ante قَبْلَ المَوْتِ فَقَدْ شَقِيَ mortem mortem, miser est. Hinc in secunda conj. [?], miserum facere, affligere; ut Pf. 37. 8. secundum Arab. distinct. nonnemo in passivo legit [Arabic], afflictus sum. Hinc illud [Greek], affliction, oppressio. 2 Ad rem ipsam quod attinet, hic in mentem revocanda est Judaeorum hypothesis, cui Mishnae author incumbit, [Hebrew], fundus in potestate domini sui permanet. quae sententia conferri posset cum §. 25. l. 1. t. 16. li. 43. Dig. Quod vulgo dicitur, aestivorum hybernorumque saltuum nos possessiones animo retinere, id exempli causa didici. Proculum dicere: nam ex omnibus praediis, ex quibus non hac mente recedimus, ut omisisse possessionem vellemus, idem est. Quicquid fit, Judaei possessionem agri & fundi erepti penes proprietarium manere statuunt: nam etiamsi cum quis alterius fundum occupasset, & vendidisset alteri, hic tertio tradidisset, atque hoc saepius factum fuisset, semper fundum primi domini esse censent. Ergo quum communi quadam calamitate, quae raptoris culpa non accidit, tyrannus quis hujusmodi agrum occupat, fructusque percipit, modo ex vicini fundi calamitate communem esse constet; raptori dicere licet, capte tuum agrum. nam cum domini sive proprietarii ager maneat, ipsi ista miseria obvenisse judicatur; ideoque raptor absolvitur, [Hebrew], nec damnum ab ipso evinci potest. Sin vero secus se res habeat, ut raptor propria quadam culpa grassatores aliosque in se excitaverit, qui agrum devastent, aliove modo damnum dederit; ipse tenetur: quemadmodum alias damni autor id praestare obligatur. 3 Hinc ultimum membrum illustratur: cum enim inundatio plerumque sine possessoris culpa accidat; ita se res habet veluti si ingruens exercitus agrum vastaret. Quapropter cum ager in proprietarii dominio Ebraeorum judicio manere existimetur; quamvis cum latro occupasset, quodcunque eo modo contingit, ipsi domino contingit: neque id magis effugisset, quanquam raptor agrum non occupasset. ergo dicit raptor, Ecce tibi tuum. Quidquid vero raptoris culpa in isto agro proprietarius patitur, id saltem ab eo reparandum, leges etiam Rom. sanciunt. Hinc §. 31. le. 1. ff. de vi & vi armata, Qui vi dejectus est, quidquid damni senserit ab hoc quod dejectus est, recuperare debet. Pristina enim causa restitui debet, quam habiturus erat si non fuisset dejectus. Deinde par. 41. Non solum autem fructuum ratio in hoc interdicto habetur, verum caeterarum etiam utilitatum habenda est. Nam & Vivianus refert, in hoc interdicto omnia quaecunque habiturus vel adsecuturus erat is qui dejectus est, si vi dejectus non esset, restitui, aut eorum litem a judice aestimari debere: eumque tantum consecuturum, quanti sua interesset, se vi dejectum non esse.
units.tr: This reading is known to differ in this word in the Gemara. Some read 'מסיקין' [masikin], properly oppressors, from מסף, to oppress; others read מניקיס [maniqis], those who afflict with distress, from פיץ, to be straitened. But the matter comes to the same thing, since robbers are meant, who oppress the possessors of fields and afflict them with distress. Hence at the beginning of the Gemara R. Nachman is said to have remarked: "He who reads masikin, oppressors, does not err; for it is written (Deut. 28.42) that the locust will possess by hereditary right; what we render in Chaldee, it will possess by inheritance, is ספס [sps], oppression. He also who reads, those who afflict with distress, does not err, because it is written (Deut. 28.53): in oppression and in מנוך [manuk], distress." The meaning is this: the two terms signify almost the same thing, because masikin are oppressors, as is clear from that verse of Deut. 28.42, where the locust, or (as others say) blight, is called ספס [sps], oppression, because it oppresses both men and the crop. So מניקי [maniqi], those who afflict with distress, is not badly named, just as מנוך [manuk] is distress in the same chapter of Deuteronomy. But, as the Talmudists are elsewhere wretched grammarians, so here ספס [sps] and masikin are wrongly traced back to the same root, although I do not deny that they agree in meaning. ספס [sps], with ב and ם interchanged, comes from the Arabic shaqiya, he was wretched, as in the proverb of a certain anonymous author in the eighteenth century of the second hundred: man la yuqaddimu tawbatan qabla al-mawt faqad shaqiya, he who does not anticipate repentance before death is wretched. Hence in the second conjugation, to make wretched, to afflict; so that at Ps. 37.8, according to the Arabic, some read in the passive, [Arabic], I have been afflicted. Hence also that [Greek], affliction, oppression. 2 As far as the matter itself is concerned, here must be recalled the Jewish hypothesis to which the author of the Mishnah adheres, [Hebrew], the field remains in the power of its lord. This opinion may be compared with §. 25, l. 1, t. 16, lib. 43 of the Digest: What is commonly said, that we keep possession of summer and winter pastures in mind, I have learned by way of example; Proculus says so, for it is the same with all estates from which we do not withdraw with the intention of abandoning possession. Whatever the case, the Jews hold that the possession of a field or estate that has been seized remains with the owner; for even if someone had seized another's field and sold it to another, and this man had handed it on to a third, and this had been done repeatedly, they judge the field still to belong to the first owner. Therefore, when some tyrant seizes a field of this kind in a common calamity that did not happen through the robber's fault, and takes its produce, provided it is established that the calamity was common to the neighbouring estate as well, the robber may say, "The field was taken from you." For since the field remains the property of the owner, the misfortune is judged to have befallen him, and therefore the robber is acquitted: [Hebrew], nor can the loss be proved against him. But if the matter stands otherwise, so that the robber, through some fault of his own, has stirred up marauders against himself who lay waste the field, or has caused loss in some other way, he himself is liable, just as the author of any other damage is bound to make good. 3 Hence the last clause is illustrated: since a flood usually comes about without the possessor's fault, the case is as if an advancing army were laying waste the field. Therefore, since in the judgement of the Hebrews the field is held to remain under the ownership of the proprietor, whatever happens in that way, although the robber has seized it, happens to the owner himself; nor would he have escaped this even if the robber had not seized the field. So the robber says, "Behold, yours." But whatever the proprietor suffers in that field through the robber's fault, the robber at least must repair it; the Roman laws too so decree. Hence §. 31, l. 1, ff. de vi et vi armata: He who has been driven out by force must recover whatever loss he has suffered from being driven out. For the former state ought to be restored, which he would have had if he had not been driven out. Then par. 41: In this interdict account is taken not only of the fruits but also of the other advantages. For Vivianus also reports that in this interdict everything that he who was driven out would have had or obtained, had he not been driven out by force, ought to be restored, or its value assessed by the judge; and he will obtain only as much as his interest was in not having been driven out by force.

units.la: Qui proximo suo aliquid eripit; aut ab eo mutuatur, vel si quid apud hunc alter deponat in loco habitato, non restituet alteri in deserto: si ea conditione ut in desertum procedatur, restituet ipsi in deserto.
units.tr: He who snatches something from his neighbour, or borrows from him, or if another deposits something with this man in an inhabited place, shall not restore it to the other in the wilderness; but if the condition is that they go out into the wilderness, he shall restore it to him in the wilderness.
Annotations.

units.la: ¹ Locus habitatus Rabbinis יישוב nominatur: atque cum Ebraeorum יישוב in sacris literis usitato convenit. Ideo David Kimchi ad vocem יישוב annotat, היא כל ישוב, est nomen commune omnibus regionibus habitatis: ubi יישוב per יישוב explicat. Esse autem יישוב locum habitatum, & ipsi deserto opponi, edocet Esaiae comma 17. ca. 14. Disponens יישוב orbem habitabilem sicut desertum: quo loco maxima mutatio significatur, qua locus habitatus in vastitatem redigitur. Ergo in hac Misna יום idem cum בפה merito ipsi deserto opponitur. * Ad illa verba, quibus depositum in deserto restituere permittitur, si ea conditione depositum fuerit; excipit Gemarae author, id per se constare, neque addendum fuisse. Idcirco istud membrum explicans, quid istis verbis designetur ad hunc modum explicat, [Hebrew] Quum dicit ipsi, Sit hoc depositum penes te, quia in desertum prodeo; is vero respondet, Ego etiam in desertum prodire cupio: ubi inquam tum sic addit, Si velim restituere illud tibi illic (in deserto) an mihi restituere licet tibi? Quae verba a S. J. non satis intellecta videntur: ut qui ea de causa כעית in כעית immutaverit. Sensus verborum hic est: non quidem de expressa conditione agi, qua pacificatur se raptum, vel mutuum, vel depositum in deserto redditurum; sed quod si, exempli causa, quum depositarius novit proprietarium in desertum aliquod abire, quo & ipse profecturus sit, ita ipsum alloquatur, An si eo depositum ad te portare velim, id mihi licet? eum istis verbis ob alterius silentium, cum ipso pactum censeri, quod depositum in locum desertum deferre liceat. Vbi ex jure Rom. reddendum sit depositum, vel alia similia, docetur §. 1. t. Depositi vel contra, Depositum eo loco restitui debet, in quo sine dolo malo ejus est, apud quem depositum est: ubi vero depositum est, nihil interest. Eadem dicenda sunt communiter & in omnibus bonae fidei judiciis. Quemadmodum autem Misna ex pacto & veluti pacto, alibi quam ubi res deposita sit, ipsam reddi permittit; ita tit. eod. l. 5. §. 1. Si tamen cum sequestre convenit, ut certo loco rem depositam exhiberet, nec ibi exhibeat; teneri eum palam est. Quod si de pluribus locis convenit; in arbitrio ejus est, quo loci exhibeat.
units.tr: ¹ The rabbis call an inhabited place יישוב [yishuv], which agrees with the use of the Hebrew word יישוב in the sacred writings. Hence David Kimchi, on the word ישוב, notes: "it is a common name for all inhabited regions", where he explains ישוב by ישוב. That יישוב means an inhabited place, set against the desert itself, is taught by Isaiah 14:17: setting the inhabited world as a desert. That verse signifies the greatest change, by which an inhabited place is reduced to waste. So in this Mishnah the word יום, which is the same as בפה, is rightly set against the desert. * As to the words by which a deposit is allowed to be returned in the desert, if it was deposited on that condition, the author of the Gemara holds that this is self-evident and need not have been added. Therefore, explaining what these words mean, he explains this clause thus: [Hebrew] When one says to another, "Let this deposit be with you, because I am going out into the desert", and the other replies, "I too want to go out into the desert", then I say he goes on to add: "If I wish to restore it to you there (in the desert), may I restore it to you?" These words seem not to have been sufficiently understood by S. J., who for this reason changed כעית into כעית. The sense of the words here is this: it is not a question of an express condition by which the one who has seized something, or received a loan, or a deposit, agrees to return it in the desert. Rather, if, for example, the depositary knows that the owner is going off into some desert where he himself is also about to go, and he addresses him thus, "If I wish to carry the deposit to you there, may I?", then by the other's silence, the agreement is deemed to have been made, that it is lawful to carry the deposit to the desert place. Where, under Roman law, a deposit or similar thing must be returned, this is taught in §1, title "Of Deposit" or the reverse: A deposit must be restored in the place where the person with whom it was deposited has it without bad faith; but where it was deposited, it makes no difference. The same is to be said generally in all judgments of good faith. Just as the Mishnah, by agreement, or as if by agreement, allows the thing to be returned somewhere other than where it was deposited, so in the same title, law 5, §1: If, however, it was agreed with the depositary that he would produce the thing deposited at a certain place, and he does not produce it there, it is plain that he is liable. But if agreement was made about several places, it is at his discretion at which place he produces it.

units.la: האומר לחביריו גולחיך ‎הלויתני הפקדח אצלי ואיני ‎יודע אם החזרתי לך אם לא ‎החזרתיל לשלם אכל ‎אם אמר לו איני יודע אם ‎גולחיך אם הלויתני אם ‎הפקדת אצלי פטור מלטלם ;
units.tr: [Hebrew] האומר לחביריו גולחיך הלויתני הפקדח אצלי ואיני יודע אם החזרתי לך אם לא החזרתיל לשלם אכל אם אמר לו איני יודע אם גולחיך אם הלויתני אם הפקדת אצלי פטור מלטלם ;

units.la: Qui proximo suo fatetur, compilavi te, mutuasti mihi, apud me depositisti aliquid, sed nescio an tibi restituerim, annon restituerim; is rependere tenetur. at si ipse dicat, Ignoro an tibi quid eripuerim, an mihi mutuaveris, an apud me deposueris; a solutione absolvitur.
units.tr: Whoever says to his neighbour, "I have robbed you, you lent me money, you deposited something with me, but I do not know whether I have returned it to you or not", is bound to repay. But if he himself says, "I do not know whether I have taken anything from you, or whether you lent me something, or whether you deposited something with me", he is released from payment.
Annotations.

units.la: ¹ Quum dicitur, eum qui dubitat an debitum solverit, exigenti, modò debitum aliquando contractum agnoscat, obligari; id saltem si de conscientia sermo sit, omnes Judæi fatentur: ideoque in Gemara hoc dictum asseritur כפ לנפש ירי סמים, de eo qui conatur cœli, id est, Dei manus effugere. At si de foro civili agatur, id negat Doctor Nachman, cujus sententia in hujusmodi rebus obtinet. Nam alteri probandum censent, se non recepisse quod debitor se accepisse fatetur. ² Verum qui debitum à se contractum non agnoscit, secundum conscientiam & forum civile absolvitur. Ita tamen ut juramento se debitum ignorare confirmet: nam ut est in Gemara (quamvis ad aliud probandum) כרי ותמא כרי ערף, ubi quid asseveratur, & in dubium vocatur, affirmatio prævalet. Quapropter si unus sibi deberi afferat, alter dubitet; nisi intervenien te juramento se debitum istud ignorare afferat, exigens præferendus existimatur. Apud Romanos id quidem verum, si quis debitum fateretur id exigi posse. Vt Cod. l. 7. c.59. Confessos in jure pro judicatis haberi placet: quare sine causa desideras recedi à confessione tua, cum & solvere cogeris. Atque hinc prior Misnæ pars contra Nachmanem probari videtur. Verum
units.tr: ¹ When it is said that one who doubts whether he has paid a debt, when the creditor demands it, is bound provided he acknowledges that the debt was at some time contracted, all Jews agree, at least where the question concerns conscience. Hence in the Gemara this saying is asserted: [Hebrew] concerning one who tries to escape the hand of heaven, that is, of God. But if the matter is one of civil law, Doctor Nachman denies it, and his opinion prevails in such cases. For they hold that the other party must prove that he has not received what the debtor admits he has received. ² But one who does not acknowledge a debt contracted by himself is absolved both in conscience and in civil law, provided he confirms on oath that he does not know of the debt. For, as the Gemara says (although for another purpose), [Hebrew] where something is asserted and called in doubt, the affirmation prevails. Therefore, if one party claims that a debt is owed to him and the other doubts it, unless the other, by an oath, asserts that he does not know of that debt, the creditor is held to be preferred. Among the Romans this was indeed true, that if someone acknowledged a debt, it could be demanded. As in Cod. 7, title 59: "It is our pleasure that those who have confessed in court be held as adjudged; wherefore you seek in vain to withdraw from your confession, since you are also compelled to pay." And hence the first part of the Mishnah seems to be proved against Nachman. But

units.la: ¹ Quum dicitur, eum qui dubitat an debitum solverit, exigenti, &c.
units.tr: ¹ When it is said that one who doubts whether he has paid a debt, when the creditor demands it, etc.

units.la: Verum ibi de eo agitur qui non agnoscit se jam debere; sed an solverit dubitat. Quo applicari posset ff. de oblig. l. 47. Arrianus ait multum interesse, quaeras utrum aliquis obligetur, an aliquis liberetur. Vbi de obligando quaeritur, propensiores esse debere nos, si habeamus occasionem, ad negandum. Vbi de liberando ex diverso, ut facilior sis ad liberationem. In proposito autem casu res dubia est, ut propensiores ad absolvendum judices esse debeant. Hinc liquet quid de posteriori casu dicendum: cum ipsum debitum, an unquam fuerit, in dubium vocetur.
units.tr: But there the matter concerns one who does not acknowledge that he now owes, but doubts whether he has paid. This could be applied to Digest, "On Obligations", law 47: Arrianus says there is a great difference whether you ask whether someone is bound, or whether someone is released. Where the question is about binding, we ought to be more inclined, if we have the opportunity, to deny it. Where it is about releasing, on the contrary, you should be more ready to free him. But in the present case the matter is doubtful, so that judges ought to be more inclined to absolve. From this it is clear what must be said of the latter case, since the debt itself is called in doubt, whether it ever existed.

units.la: §. 8. Si furatus agnum e grege, restituat eum, & is postea moriatur, aut furto auferatur, eum compensare tenetur. Si ignoraverint proprietarii cum ejus furtum, tum restitutionem, & numerato grege inveniatur completus; a solutione ab-solvitur.
units.tr: §8. If he has stolen a lamb from the flock and restores it, and it afterwards dies or is taken by theft, he is bound to make compensation for it. If the owners were unaware both of the theft and of the restitution, and the flock, when counted, is found complete, he is released from payment.
Annotations.

units.la: Ratio quod agnum etiam restitutum fur compensare teneatur haec est, quia cum ipsum furatus sit, manet in ipsius dominio. puta, donec dominus eum sibi restitutum cognoscat, adeoque ejus curam suscipere queat. Fur igitur quodcunque interea evenerit, sibi imputare debet. Ipse enim in causa est, cur dominus illum negligat; & cum ad se agnum receperit, eum curare debet, donec alteri tradat. Hinc liquet, qui posterius membrum intelligendum sit. Saepe Mishna concisa est, & obscura, ipsamque rem indefinite enuntiat; uti hoc loco videre est. Quicquid infortunii agno accidat, fur absolvitur, quum dominus furto, cum fieret, ipsum latente, postea pecudes numerans numerum completũ deprehendit: verum cum hac cautione, si dominus pecudis eam restitutam post commissum furtum (licet tempus ignoret furti & restitutionis) ante computum cognoverit; sin semper ignoraverit, donec manifestum damnum patiatur, fur infortunii istius tenetur. Causam assignant, quia fur pecudem aberrantem utplurimum intercipit: quare nisi id cognoscat dominus, agnum suum hoc aberrandi & discurrendi vitio laborare, eum non servabit. ideoque quum fure eum abducente magis isti vitio assuevit, ut furi sequens damnum imputetur, æquum esse existimant. Non dissimili ratione Paulus, ut est §. sin. l. 22. ff. de furtis, Qui lancem rasit, totius fur est: & furti tenetur ad id quod domini interest. Vbi postrema verba expendantur cum glossa, & hoc generaliter in similibus. Quæ hic est partis ad totum ratio; ea in uno ejusdem rei furto ad duplicatum spectatur. Et si consideremus, quod Judæi de pecudis conditione mutata asserunt; non alienum ab hac materia l. 47. t. eod. Si dominium rei surreptæ quacunque ratione mutatum sit, domino furti actio competit.
units.tr: The reason why the thief must make compensation even for a lamb that has been returned is this: because, when he stole it, it remained in the ownership of its owner, that is, until the owner recognises that it has been restored to him and can therefore take charge of it. Whatever misfortune befalls the animal in the meantime, the thief must therefore blame himself. He is himself the cause of the owner's neglect, and once he has taken the lamb back into his own keeping he must look after it until he hands it over to someone else. From this it is clear what the latter clause means. The Mishnah is often terse and obscure and states the matter in indefinite terms, as is the case here. Whatever harm comes to the lamb, the thief is released from liability when the owner, who was unaware of the theft at the time it occurred, later counts his flock and finds the number complete. This holds with a proviso: if the owner learned of the restoration after the theft was committed (even if he does not know when the theft and the restoration took place) and before the count, the thief is liable for that misfortune; but if the owner remained ignorant of it until he suffered a definite loss, the thief is liable for that misfortune. They give the reason: a thief usually catches a straying animal, so unless the owner knows that his lamb has this habit of straying and running about, he will not keep it safe. Therefore, since the animal has grown more accustomed to this vice while in the thief's hands, they think it fair that the loss which follows should be charged to him. Paulus reasons in a not dissimilar way, in the paragraph at the end of law 22 of the Digest, de furtis: "Whoever shaves a dish is a thief of the whole, and is liable for theft to the extent of the owner's interest." Where the last words are weighed together with the gloss, and this generally in similar cases, the principle that the part stands for the whole applies, in a single theft of the same thing, to the doubled penalty. And if we consider what the Jews assert about a change in the condition of the animal, law 47 of the same title is not foreign to this matter: if the ownership of a stolen thing has been changed by any means, the action for theft belongs to the owner.

units.la: Non emunt à pastoribus, lanam, lac, vel hœdos; nec à fructuum custodibus, arbores, vel fructus: sed emunt à mulieribus laneas vestes in Iudæa, & lineas in Galilæa, & vitulos in Sarone. Quæcunque verò abscondi jubentur, vetita sunt. Cæterum ova & gallinaceos à quovis loco accipiunt.
units.tr: They do not buy wool, milk or kids from shepherds, nor trees or fruit from the keepers of orchards; but they buy woollen garments from women in Judea, linen in Galilee, and calves in Sharon. Whatever they are commanded to hide is forbidden. Otherwise they accept eggs and poultry from any place.
ANNOTATIONS.

units.la: {1} Causa interdicti, quo lanam, lac, vel hœdos à pastoribus, arbores vel fructus à fructuum custodibus accipere interdicitur, hæc est; quod pastores istos & custodes non esse proprietarios satis constet: ideoque si ista ab iis emantur, ab iis emi, quibus in ista nihil juris est. Quare si jus in ista habeant, sicuti hujusmodi casus dari observant Doctores Gemarici, ab iis emere licet. Exempli gratia lac emi à pastore interdicit Misna; at Gemara, [?Hebrew: לקחיו מזה חלב ונבניב במדבר ולא כייסוב], emunt ab iis lac & caseum in deserto, non tamen in loco habitato. ratio distinctionis, quia dominus deserta petere non solet, sed ista pastoribus in victum & mercedem relinquit; alibi vero cum pecus pascunt, lac caseosque ad domini ædes deferre debent. Ita fere Ebræi explicant. Hujusmodi circumstantiæ plures emptionem alias vetitam, faciunt licitam: sed ne omnes istos casus è Gemara, Maimonide, & R. Jacobo repetere necesse sit, regulam quandam generalem quæ plurimos casus complectitur, è Gemara subjicio. [?Hebrew line], Summa rei est, quicquid pastor vendit, & proprietarius ei animum advertit, ab illo emere licet; si non advertat animum, ab ipsis emere non licet. Vbi dominus rem perspectam habere potest, & in pastorem furem animadvertere, emptorem absolvunt. ut si pastor quatuor vel quinque pecudes è caula ædibus vicina vendat, dominus id facile animadvertit; itaque si hic taceat, nihilque agat, consentiente domino pastor vendere censetur: verum si unam vendat, eam emere non licet, quia pastor eam furari commodè potuit, & domino imponere, afferens (ut est in Glossa) [?Hebrew], lupum eam discerpsisse. Sic quicquid conscio domino venditur, ut lac in deserto, quod pastoribus permittit, emere licet. {2} Et quemadmodum ubi est furti suspicio, meritoque furtivam rem esse existimamus, emptio
units.tr: {1} The reason for the prohibition, that one may not take wool, milk or kids from shepherds, or fruit or trees from keepers of fruit, is this: it is clear enough that these shepherds and keepers are not owners. So if such things are bought from them, they are bought from people who have no right to them. Therefore, if the shepherds do have a right to them, as the Gemara doctors observe in such cases, it is lawful to buy from them. For example, the Mishnah forbids buying milk from a shepherd, but the Gemara says: they may buy milk and cheese from them in the desert, but not in an inhabited place [לקחיו מזה חלב ונבניב במדבר ולא כייסוב]. The reason for the distinction is that the owner does not usually go out into the desert, but leaves these things to the shepherds for their food and wages; elsewhere, when they pasture the flock, they must carry the milk and cheese to the owner's house. The Hebrews explain it roughly this way. Several circumstances of this kind make a purchase that is otherwise forbidden lawful. But so that it is not necessary to draw all these cases from the Gemara, Maimonides and R. Jacob, I set down from the Gemara one general rule that covers most cases: The sum of the matter is this: whatever the shepherd sells, if the owner takes notice of it, one may buy it from him; if the owner does not take notice, one may not buy it from them. Where the owner can have the matter in view and can catch the shepherd as a thief, they acquit the buyer. For example, if a shepherd sells four or five animals from a fold near the house, the owner easily notices it; so if he keeps silent and does nothing, the shepherd is deemed to sell with the owner's consent. But if he sells one, it is not lawful to buy it, because the shepherd could easily have stolen it and told the owner that a wolf had torn it apart (as the Gloss puts it) [?Hebrew]. So whatever is sold with the owner's knowledge, such as milk in the desert, which he allows the shepherds, may be bought. {2} And just as, where there is a suspicion of theft, and we rightly think the thing is stolen, the purchase is forbidden, so conversely, where we rightly think the seller is the owner of the thing, we buy it without fear.

units.la: {1} Causa interdicti ... [marks only; no printed foot note on this page] emptio prohibetur; ita vice versa, ubi merito vendentis rem esse exiſtimamus, eam intrepidè emimus. Atque hac de causa pannos & lintea iſtis quos annotat Miſnæ author locis à mulieribus emere licet: quia ﬠﬠ Hoc est ipsarum opus, quod ipsa cum faciunt, tum vendunt maritis conscii. Et in genere obtinet regula, Emere non licet à mulieribus, nisi res, quæ ipsarum habentur conscii maritis: sive quæ ita censentur esse uxorum, ut mariti hoc voluerint.
units.tr: Hence, for this reason, cloths and linen which the author of the Mishnah mentions may be bought from women in those places, because ﬠﬠ this is their own work, which they both make and sell with their husbands' knowledge. And the general rule holds: It is not lawful to buy from women unless the goods are regarded as theirs with their husbands' knowledge; or which are so regarded as the wives' property that the husbands have wished it so.

units.la: Ex eodem fundamento, quia Saronis paſtores ipsi pecoris sui proprietarii sunt, ab iis vitulos, quos magno numero iſtic paſcunt, emere licet. Maimon. c. 6. Cod. Gezela, ad mulieres refert, quas Sarone vitulos paſcere scribit. Hoc enim etiam virginum fuisse, docent sacræ literæ: sic Gen. 29. 9. legimus, Advenit Rachel cum pecudibus quæ erant patris sui, nàm paſcebat. Cæterum Sarone multa paſcua pecori accommoda fuisse vel id demonstrat, quod Davidi illic tot pecora fuerint, ut inter primarios præfectos unum habuerit, qui iſtis vacaret. 1 Chron. 27. פ. 29. His accedit epitheton decoris Ef. 35. 2. Decor arvi & Scharonis. Nonnemo tria loca hoc nomine venire putat; ego tantum duo invenio. Fuit Saron cis Jardenem, uti manifestè Jof. c. 12. פ. 7. collato cum 18. continetur. Vrbs fuit forte & regio, non procul à mari mediterraneo, nec procul à Lydda: de qua videre est Actor. 9. 35. Quum Petrus Lyddæ (Ebraicè לוד) Æneam quendam ab annis octo decumbentem verbis, Sanet te Iesus Christus, sanitati restituisset, Æneam viderunt Lyddæ & Saronis incolæ: unde Saroni Lyddam vicinam fuisse constat. utraque non procul à Joppe (Ebr. יפו) פ. 38. Quum Lydda (ergo & Saron, quæ apud Lyddam) esset prope Ioppen, &c. Joppe autem maritimâ erat civitas: Act. 10. 5. 6. Saron (sive Scharon) regionis etiam nomen est ultra Jardenem versus Orientem: in qua regione tamen oppidum vel oppida quædam fuisse non nego, utpote quæ late pateret. Hinc 1 Chron. 5. 16. Gadis posteri cum alibi, tum in Baschane, & in omnibus municipiis Scharonis habitasse leguntur. unde varia municipia in Sarone fuisse observavimus. Es. autem 65. 10. cum de restitutione agitur, de Sarone dicitur, erit caula gregis: ubi pascuam regionem designari videmus: eundemque locum cum præcedenti 1 Chr. 5. autumo. Et quia aliquando cum Carmelo Basanis (nam Carmelus diversorum locorum nomen) conjungitur, non sine causa regio Saron isti Carmelo vicina statuitur: sed præcipuè ipsius situs è primo 1 Chr. 5. Deut. 3. eruitur. Hic ÿ f. 12. & 13. Gaditis locum inter Rubenitas & Menasitas assignatum fuisse videmus: ita quidem ut cum tota pene Basanis regio Menassitis cederet; aliquam ejus partem incolerent Gaditæ, Deut. 3. 13. cum 1 Chron. 5. 11. cui Basani vicinam fuisse Saronem ibi ostendit ÿ f. 16. & confirmat ÿ f. 9. c. 33. Esaiæ. ubi etiam cum Libano conjungitur. quemadmodum Es. 35. 2. cum Sarone memoratur Libanus: cui ad orientem objacet Mons Hermon, qui ad Austrum protensus Basanem & Saronem ab Orientalioribus regionibus separat, variisque nominibus nuncupatur. Quod verò Saron in sacris literis præfixum ו (cum scribitur שרון) admittat, cujus in propriis nominibus notio non adeo apparet, quia satis restricta sunt; observandum id etiam in aliis locorum nominibus fieri, quamvis hominum nomina ו respuant. Nam locorum nomina cum sæpe notione sua communia sint, isto articulo ad certam regionem & locum restringuntur. ut שרון est locus irriguus qui facilè ad fructus emittendos resolvitur, quemadmodum etymologia probat. & per ו ad certum locum istis dotibus præditum applicatur, qui ob similitudinem quandam alium cognomine habuit. Porrò ubi Saron ab aliis inter mare Tiberiadis & Taborem montem collocetur, satis notum est: sed cum id unius autoritate, non ratione certoque argumento fieri animadvertam, à propositæ sententia non discedo. do.† Ad Misnam redeo, ubi cautio generalis in emptionibus adhibenda proponitur. Si venditor rem quam venundat clam haberi & occultari jubeat, cavendum ne hujusmodi emamus. Ratio est, quia rem furtivam esse merito suspicamur: etenim si is proprietarius esset, potius eam innotescere omnibus, operam daret; quò multis licitantibus, ei qui plus liceretur, venderet. Vbicunque igitur justa furti suspicio, vel quod venum exponitur raptum fuisse opinantur, emere prohibent. ³ Subjicitur de ovis & gallinis, e quovis loco comparari posse: cum tamen c. 7. sect. 7. quibusdam locis gallinaceum genus non aleretur. Itaque sensus est ac si dictum suisset, Vbicunque aluntur gallinæ, à quibusvis eas earumque ova emere licet, modo venum dent: nam cum hic tantum res furtiva vel rapta rejiciatur, autor promiscuè sine delectu ova & gallinaceos emi posse statuit, quum omnium sit alere ista animalia; non solum divitum, sed etiam pauperum, etiam fœminarum, & ministrorum. Qua tamen sententia illi constitutioni 7. c. 7. derogatum non voluit: siquidem tantum ab iis personis qui venderent, emi poterant, & quidem isto loco ubi venum darentur. Præterea licet Hierosolymis non alerentur, nec ullibi à sacerdotibus; nihil tamen impedit quin illic gallinæ alibi educatæ cum ovis venderentur; & quidem per sacerdotum institutores, si dono cum aliis rebus consecratis accepissent. Atque hoc ultimum Misnæ membrum cum præcedenti etiam cautione accipiendum esse juste Maimonides judicavit: ut qui adjecerit, si vero vendens dicat gallinam vel ova abscondenda esse, tum emptionem prohiberi. Huc omnia redeunt quodcunque tenetur habetur sive judicatur furto ablatum, id emere interdictum est. Cum hoc Judæorum placito conveniunt Imperatorum verba Cod. l. 6. t. de furtis, l. 12. sub finem, Nam extra pœnam, rei persecutionem esse, nulla juris quæstio est; cum etiam hi qui aliena mancipia comparaverint, si hanc
units.tr: On the same principle, since the shepherds of Saron are themselves the owners of their flocks, it is lawful to buy from them the calves which they pasture there in great numbers. Maimonides, ch. 6, Cod. Gezela, refers this to women, whom he writes pastured calves at Saron. For this was also the work of maidens, as holy letters teach: thus we read in Gen. 29. 9, Rachel came with the sheep which belonged to her father, for she was a shepherdess. Moreover, that Saron had many pastures suited to flocks is shown by the fact that David had so many herds there that he appointed one of the chief officers to look after them (1 Chron. 27. 29). To this is added the epithet of beauty in Isa. 35. 2, the beauty of the field and of Sharon. Some think three places come under this name; I find only two. Saron lay on this side of the Jordan, as is clearly shown in Josh. 12. 7, compared with v. 18. It was perhaps a town and a region, not far from the Mediterranean Sea and not far from Lydda, which may be seen in Acts 9. 35. When Peter at Lydda [לוד] restored to health with the words, Jesus Christ heals you, a certain Aeneas who had been bedridden for eight years, the inhabitants of Lydda and Saron saw Aeneas; whence it is clear that Lydda was near Saron. Both were not far from Joppa [יפו] (v. 38): since Lydda (therefore also Saron, which is near Lydda) was near Joppa, etc. Joppa was a seaport city (Acts 10. 5, 6). Saron (or Sharon) is also the name of a region beyond the Jordan toward the east; I do not deny that in that region there were some town or towns, since it extended widely. Hence in 1 Chron. 5. 16 it is read that the sons of Gad lived elsewhere, in Bashan, and in all the towns of Sharon; whence we have observed that there were various towns in Saron. In Isa. 65. 10, where restoration is spoken of, it is said of Saron that it will be a fold for the flock, where we see a pasture region is meant; and I judge it to be the same place as in the earlier passage, 1 Chron. 5. And because at times it is joined with Carmel and Bashan (for Carmel is the name of several places), the region of Saron is rightly placed near that Carmel; but its position is chiefly drawn from 1 Chron. 5 and Deut. 3. Here, in vv. 12 and 13, we see that Gad was assigned a place between the Reubenites and the Manassites, so that almost the whole region of Bashan went to the Manassites, and the Gadites inhabited some part of it (Deut. 3. 13 with 1 Chron. 5. 11), where v. 16 shows Saron was near Bashan, and v. 9 of ch. 33 of Isaiah confirms it, where it is also joined with Lebanon, just as in Isa. 35. 2 Lebanon is mentioned with Saron. Lying to the east of Lebanon is Mount Hermon, which stretches to the south, separates Bashan and Saron from the more eastern regions, and is called by various names. As for Saron in holy letters taking the prefixed ו (when it is written שרון), whose meaning does not appear so clearly in proper names, since they are sufficiently restricted, this should be observed as happening also in other place-names, although personal names reject the ו. For place-names, since they often share their general meaning, are restricted by this article to a certain region and place. Thus שרון is a well-watered place which readily yields its fruits, as its etymology proves; and through the ו it is applied to a certain place endowed with these qualities, which, because of a certain resemblance, had another place of the same name. Furthermore, that Saron is placed by others between the Sea of Tiberias and Mount Tabor is well known; but since I notice this is done on one man's authority, not on reason and a sure argument, I do not depart from the opinion I have proposed. I return to the Mishnah, where a general caution to be applied in purchases is laid down. If the seller orders the thing he is selling to be kept secret and hidden, we must beware of buying such things. The reason is that we rightly suspect the thing to be stolen; for if he were the owner, he would make every effort to make it known to all, so that he might sell it to whoever bid most, with many bidding. Wherever, therefore, there is a just suspicion of theft, or people think that what is put up for sale was seized, they forbid buying. ³ It is added concerning eggs and hens, that they may be obtained from any place, although in ch. 7, sect. 7, the poultry species was not reared in some places. So the sense is as if it had been said: wherever hens are kept, it is lawful to buy them and their eggs from anyone, provided they sell them. For since here only a stolen or seized thing is rejected, the author holds without distinction that eggs and poultry may be bought indiscriminately, since it is for everyone to rear these animals: not only the rich, but also the poor, women, and servants. Yet he did not wish this opinion to override that regulation of ch. 7; for they could be bought only from the persons who were selling them, and indeed in that place where they were put up for sale. Moreover, although they were not reared at Jerusalem, nor anywhere by priests, nothing prevents hens reared elsewhere from being sold with eggs; and indeed through the priests' agents, if they had received them as a gift along with other consecrated things. And Maimonides rightly judged that this last clause of the Mishnah is to be taken together with the preceding caution, as one who added: but if the seller says the hen or eggs must be hidden, then the purchase is forbidden. All of this comes down to this: whatever is held, or judged, to be taken by theft, it is forbidden to buy. The words of the emperors in Cod. l. 6, t. de furtis, l. 12, near the end, agree with this Jewish decision: For apart from the penalty, there is no question of law that the thing is to be pursued; since even those who have bought other people's slaves, if they did not know this cause, are liable to an action for theft.

units.la: † Hebrew words in the text, printed in Hebrew letters: כל דבר שהוא בחזקת גניבה (rendered as printed in the original). hanc causam non ignorent, furti actione teneantur. Quemadmodum qui à fure mancipia emit, furti tenetur; pariter qui alia quævis eo modo mercatur. Similia habes l.14. Eos qui à fervo furtim ablata scientes susceperint, non tantum de suscepta convenire, sed etiam pœnali furti actione potes. Si suscipere res furtivas non licet, multo magis peccat, qui emptione suas facere studet. Unde merito, casu quodam excepto, pretio hujusmodi emptor excidit: ut est li.8. le.27. Si fundum sciens alienum vel obligatum comparavit Athenocles, neque quicquam de evictione convenit, quod eo nomine dedit, contra juris poscit rationem.
units.tr: † Hebrew words in the text, printed in Hebrew letters: "every thing that is in the state of theft" [כל דבר שהוא בחזקת גניבה] (rendered as printed in the original). Let them not be ignorant of this case: they are liable to the action for theft. Just as one who buys slaves from a thief is liable for theft, so too is one who buys any other thing in that way. You have a similar rule in book 14: Those who knowingly receive things stolen from a slave are liable not only for what they received but can also be sued with the penal action for theft. If it is not lawful to receive stolen goods, much more does he sin who tries to make them his own by purchase. Hence, with one certain exception, the buyer rightly loses the price of such a thing, as in book 8, title 27: If Athenocles knowingly bought another's land, or land under encumbrance, and has made no agreement about eviction, he cannot demand back what he gave on that account, since this is contrary to the reason of law.

units.la: Flocculi quos1 fullo abstergit, hi ipsius sunt; quos2 carminator abradit (vel panni tonsor,) hi sunt patrisfamilias. Fullo tria3 fila sumit, atque ipsius sunt; si plura reperiantur, sunt patrisfamilias: si4 nigrum incumbat albo, totum illud capit, atque ipsius est. Si sartor ex filo tantum fecit residuum ut eo confuere queat; vel e panno quadratu trium digitorum segmen, ecce ista sunt patrisfamilias. Quicquid faber5 runcina dedolat, id ipsius est; securi vero, patrisfamilias; & si apud patremfamilias operetur,6 serrago etiam est patrisfamilias.
units.tr: The lint which the fuller wipes off belongs to him; what the carder (or the cloth-shearer) scrapes off belongs to the householder. The fuller takes three threads, and they are his; if more are found, they belong to the householder. If black lies on white, he takes the whole and it is his. If a tailor has made from the thread only what remains that can be sewn with it, or from a square of cloth a strip of three fingers' breadth, behold, these belong to the householder. Whatever the carpenter hews off with the adze is his; but what he cuts with the axe belongs to the householder; and if he works in the householder's house, the sawdust too belongs to the householder.
