units.la: Fullo, ut inquit Vlpianus, est qui curanda poliendaque vestimenta accepit, ff. de furtis, l. 12. in principio: id quo ordine fieret Plinius l. 35. c. 17. enarrat, ubi & fullonum curam majoribus fuisse præmittit. Neque pigebit hanc quoque partem attingere, cum lex Metella extet fullonibus dicta, quam C. Flaminius, L. Æmilius Censores dedere ad populum ferendam. Adeo omnia majoribus cura fuere. Ergo ordo hic est. primum abluitur vestis Sarda; dein sulfure suffitur; mox desquamatur Cimolia, quæ est coloris veri. Hujusmodi fullo Marco 9. 3. dicitur γναφεὺς, quum transfigurationem Christi narrat, Vestimenta ejus facta sunt coruscantia, candida valde ut nix, qualia non potest fullo in terra dealbare. Non quod fullo quivis vestes alterius coloris albas reddat, hoc enim quoad fieri potest, proprie infectorum est; sed hoc ideo dicitur, quia fullo vestibus cujuscunque sint coloris, si conspurcatæ sint, nativum & nitidum colorem restituere allaborat; si vero candidæ fuerint, suum ipsis candorem & albedinem restituit. Vnde Christi vestimenta tam candida imo candidiora facta fuisse testatur, quam peritissimus fullo ea reddere potuisset, licet etiam ab initio candida & alba fuissent. Adeo albæ apparebant Christi vestes: licet quo colore antea fuerint hinc concludi nequeat. A fullone differunt carminatores, qui dentatis suis instrumentis lanam pannosque veluti pectinant, & pannos etiam in villos attollunt, & quicquid inhæret vi extrahunt. Fullo & carminator è veste vel panno quasdam minutias auferunt: quas fullo retinet, carminator vero restituit ipsi פטר רחם, patrifamilias. quo nomine Iudæis venit proprietarius: ut sæpius paterfamilias fit rei ipsius dominus; quemadmodum paterfamilias plerunque quæcunque domi suæ inveniuntur possidet, eorumque proprietarius est. Et licet carminator majores flocculos reddere debeat; fulloni tamen trium filorum texturam abscindere sibiq; servare licet. Quo id melius percipiatur, quid sint תלת חוטין, tria fila, videamus. nulla explicatio planior quam illa R. Jomi Tob: cujus ideo verba subjicere non gravabor: דרך פתורגים פתורגים כפיך ... [Hebrew line] Moris est textoribus ut ad extremitatem panni tria vel quatuor fila texant, procul à reliqua textura: idque faciunt ut pannum conservent, ne ipsius textura in extremitate panni per fullonis ablutionem corrumpatur. ifiaque fila, cum inde evelluntur dum pannum mundat, accipit fullo: quia proprietarius ad ea non attendit. Id sibi vult author, sub finem telæ sive panni, per totam ejus latitudinem subtegmen aliquoties per longa staminis fila transmitti, idque non proximum reliquam texturam, sed interposito spatio ubi sola staminis fila sine subtegmine conspiciuntur. Hæc autem pars in eum finem adjicitur, quo fullo eam liberè attrectare, atque interea reliquam telam illæsam relinquere queat. ita subinde fit, quia fila ista pauca sunt, ut ob texturæ infirmitatem inter abluendum evellantur, adeoque illic nudum staminen relinquatur. Hoc casu, inquit Misnæ author, fullo ista fila retinebit. Imo etiamsi quatuor vel quinque fila ibi ad extremitatem intexta fuerint, ipsius erunt; si albo panno sive telæ nigrum filum unum vel plura intexantur: quia ista deformitatem inducunt. Pergit author, aliosque sub finem casus producit, quos determinat. exempli gratia: faber lignarius schidia frequentissime dedolat è lignis, quæ ab alio accepit, ut inde utensilia pararet. quid dicemus, schidia fabri sunt, an locatoris? Distinguitur hoc loco inter majores & minores assulas: has fabro, illas locatori assignant. Id hoc modo effertur, schidia תקר, runcina abrasa esse fabri, majores assulas כפס, securi abscissas, utpote majores, locatori cedere. Verum si כפטיר, mercenarii instar se habeat faber, ut apud dominum diurnos labores subeat, etiam ipsa ferrago, quæ ferra abraditur ipsi domino (quem patremfamilias vocat Misna) cedet. Serram autem S. J. aliique vocant מקדח: nam teste Maimonide כסומרין ferrago est מחיקת הנייס, est minutia lignorum, quum ligna serrant, quò inde afferes faciant. Ergo instrumentum quo ferrago fit, scilicet מקדח, quicquid lexicographi dicant, est etiam ferra. Ex hisce nominibus cum suo usu vario, differentia inter מנדר, כטיל & מקדח omnino liquet. adeoque ἐν παρόδῳ nonnulla Scripturæ loca illustrantur, ubi duarum priorum vocum fit mentio: quandoquidem è circumstantiis in hac Misna dubium esse nequit, quid istis vocibus significetur. Atq; ob hujusmodi vocabula dubia hoc attentè observari velim, non tantum V. Testamentum; sed & volumen Misnajoth antiqua lingua Ebræa conscriptum fuisse; imo & multas sententias veterum in Gemara recensitas: quandoquidem istæ constitutiones antiquissimæ sunt. uti vel ex illis Servatoris verbis liquet, quibus illas reprehendit ut jam tum receptas; imò earum autores antiquos, ἀρχαίως nuncupat Matth. 5. & constitutiones istas à majoribus istorum qui tum vivebant traditas agnoscit Mat. 15. 2. 3. Nam quæ hic traditio reprehenditur, eam legere est Cod. כדריס c. 11. sect. 4. & quod caput Matth. 5. concernit, omnia ista quæ Christus reprehendit ex antiquis non enarrabo: unum in exemplum proponam. commate 43. Audivisti dictum fuisse (scilicet ab antiquis, ut in præcedentibus aliquoties dixerat Servator, ideoque jam subintelligi vult,) Diliges proximum tuum, & odio habebis inimicum tuum. Antiquos Doctores posterius membrum contra Dei legem adjecisse; indicio nobis est codex Joma sive de die expiationis cap. 2. sol. 22. p. 2. sub finem, ubi hæc leguntur verba; מפני מה נטל מפני מחמל על כבודו שנאמר וכו כליטל אמרו מה יוציאנו וּ וִיבַּוּוּהוּ וְלֹא הָכִּיאוּ לוֹ מִכְּתַּח וַיהִי כִּמְחֻרִיס וּכְתִיב וַיִּטוֹל ... וְאָמַר ר׳ יוחנן מִפְּנֵי מָה כָּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁיִּנְּנוּ בִּיעֹק וְנֹאמַר כָּאֵת תַּלְמִיד. סמוך מלחמה, Quare punitus fuit Saul? quia honorem suum violantibus ignovit: nam legitur 1 Sam.10.27. At homines nequam dicebant, quid servaret nos iste? contemnentes eum, ut ne afferrent quidem ei munus: tamen plane conticuit. ideo sequitur c.11.1. Et ascendens Nachasch Hammonita castra habuit contra Jabeschun Gileadis, &c. Itaque Doctor Iohannes inquit nomine D. Simeonis filii Iotsedeci, Omnis sapientia studiosus qui non ulciscitur & servat inimicitiam (ita S. Jarchi recte in explicatione addit ססמ inimicitiam) instar serpentis, non est discipulus sapientis, sive sapientiae studiosus. Vides lector non immerito Servatorem nostrum istos Doctores carpsisse: ut qui vindictam & iram ac inimicitias permitterent, si quis verbis vel factis honori detraheret. Quod posteriores enarrant, si publice detraheret nec supplex veniam & remissionem peteret. Cum igitur huiusmodi placita ab antiquis tradita sint, cum lingua Ebraea adhuc in usu esset; nonne merito ex illis constitutionibus vocum significatio dubia hauritur? Itaque vel ob solam linguam illas legamus; nec putemus e solis sacris literis totam linguam sanctam addisci posse: quandoquidem in illis Misnajoth, & quamplurimis antiquorum dictis, quae sparsim in Gemara, alioqui misti idiomatis ac styli, occurrunt; multa vocabula, variae phrases reperiuntur, quae in sacris desiderantur, vel minus innotescere queunt. Porro ista quae in Misna operariorum esse, vel dominis reddenda dicuntur, recte Maimonides perpetui juris non censeri observavit; sed pro regionum varietate mutari, ut quod hoc loco sartori, vel fabro conceditur, alibi denegetur. Scopus ipsius Misnae spectandus, qui est servare justitiam: eoque ista omnia collimant. quorum haec summa est, ne operarii, quicunque sint, aliquid subtrahant, quod locatorum est, a quibus opera facienda conduxerunt. Quemadmodum justissime Vlpianus (ut est li. Dig. 19. t. 2. l. 39.) Non solet locatio Dominium mutare. Quod vero istas minutias attiattinet, quæ operariis permittuntur, eas retinendo furtum non faciunt; quia proprietarii eas pro derelictis habent: nam ff. de furtis 43. §. 5. statuitur, statim nostram esse desinere rem, quam derelinquimus. Huc facit §. 10. Si quis sponte rem jecit vel jactauit, non quasi pro derelicto habiturus, tuque hanc rem tuleris: an furti teneacalis, Celsus libro duodecimo Digestorum quaerit: & ait, si quidem putasti pro derelicto habitam, non teneris. Atqui fullo, faber, aliusve operarius ista minuta pro derelictis haberi censent: ergo dum secundum Misnam nostram ista retinerent, nulla dabatur furti actio. & quidem eo minus, quod ipse operis locator qui vestem poliendam, scamnum aliave paranda locaverat, istis locis de quibus Misna agit, omninò hujusmodi minuta pro derelictis haberet: atqui lex Romanorum factum excusat, etiamsi haec conditio non adesset; modo alius jure ac merito ita judicaret. Caeterum cum Iudaei alias justitiae tanti patroni non sint, uti vidimus, neque de sacris mysteriis fide amplectendis admodum laborent; hic vero schidiorum & serraginis ac assularum adeo satagant: merito Servatoris dicto finiam: Mat. 23. 24. τυφλοὶ ὁδηγοὶ διυλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα, τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες. Quid quaeso magis in S. Literis V.T. nobis expendendum proponitur, quam summa Dei patris clementia, & justa Dei judicis ira; atque pavenda & stupenda ejus majestas? Ergo illos homines potius satagere oportebat, qui clementiam Dei obtinere & iram effugere possent. quandoquidem major est Dei majestas, quam ut paucorum dierum jejunio, precibus quibusdam aliisque exercitiis, justissima & pavenda in peccatores ira averruncari queat. Peccata indesinenter commissa, atrociaque flagitia tot myriadum, longè graviora sunt, quam ut imperfectis operibus, quae & ipsa commaculata sunt, expiari possint apud eum, qui fontes sine justa satisfactione non absolvit, Nahu. 1. 3. Pariter plura illa & majora sunt, Deusque spiritus infinitus longè purioris & gravioris ac celsoris naturæ, quam ut sanguine brutorum propitiaretur; si solus sanguis spectetur, neq; ad Messiæ passionem referatur. Cujus vulnera nec antiquos Iudæos ignorasse, alibi docuimus. Enim Deus simpliciter (ut hoc, alio testimonio, iterum confirmemus) sine satisfactione se non remittere peccata tum etiam testatur, quum suam clementiam maximè exaggerat, Deut. 34. 6. 7. Verum quid dicas? Nunquam veritatem huius dogmatis in proprio etiam Talmude non praetermissam, poterunt ἐξαναδιζήν, ὲ spinosis suis quæstionibus Talmudicis eruere; antequam suam miseriam spiritualem agnoscant: ut hic incipiant τῷ καρδίαν ἀδχνισθῳ, in corde conscientiæ sensu morderi. Tum (Hos. 3. 5.) ויראו אל יהוה ואל טובו, paventes accedent ad Iovam & bonitatem ejus. ista
units.tr: A fuller, as Ulpian says, is one who receives clothes to be cleaned and polished (Dig. De furtis, l. 12, at the beginning). Pliny explains how this was done in book 35, chapter 17, where he also says that the care of fullers was a concern of our ancestors even earlier. Nor will I be ashamed to touch on this part too, since there is a law called the Metellan law concerning fullers, which the censors Gaius Flaminius and Lucius Aemilius drew up to be brought before the people. So completely did our ancestors attend to everything. The order is this: first the garment is washed in Sardian earth; then it is fumigated with sulphur; soon afterward it is scoured with Cimolian earth, which is of the true colour. A fuller of this kind is called γναφεύς [gnapheus] in Mark 9:3, where he describes the transfiguration of Christ: His garments became shining, exceedingly white as snow, such as no fuller on earth can whiten. This does not mean that any fuller makes garments of another colour white, for that, as far as it can be done, is properly the work of dyers. It is said because a fuller, whatever colour the garments are, if they are soiled, labours to restore their native and bright colour; but if they are white, he restores their own whiteness and brightness. Hence the evangelist testifies that Christ's garments were made so white, indeed whiter, than the most skilled fuller could have made them, although they had been white and bright from the beginning. So bright did Christ's garments appear, though from this one cannot conclude what colour they had been before. Carders differ from fullers. They comb wool and cloth with their toothed tools, as it were, raise the nap of the cloth, and draw out whatever clings to it. A fuller and a carder remove certain small bits from a garment or cloth. The fuller keeps them, but the carder gives them back to the owner, פטר רחם [peter rechem], the head of the family. By this name the Jews mean the owner, as the paterfamilias is often the lord of the thing itself, just as the paterfamilias generally possesses whatever is found in his house and is its owner. Although the carder must return the larger tufts, the fuller may nevertheless cut off the three-thread weaving and keep it for himself. To understand better what תלת חוטין [telat chutin], three threads, are, let us look at this. No explanation is plainer than that of Rabbi Jom Tob, whose words I will not hesitate to quote: It is the custom of weavers to weave three or four threads at the edge of the cloth, apart from the rest of the weaving. They do this so that the cloth may be kept, lest the weaving at its edge be spoiled by the fuller's washing. When these threads are pulled out while he cleans the cloth, the fuller takes them, because the owner does not attend to them. The author means this: near the end of the web or cloth, across its whole width, the weft is passed several times through the long threads of the warp, and not close to the rest of the weaving, but with a space left between where only the warp threads are seen without weft. This part is added for the purpose that the fuller may handle it freely and meanwhile leave the rest of the cloth unharmed. It happens thus, because these threads are few, so that through the weakness of the weaving they are pulled out during washing, and so bare warp is left there. In this case, says the author of the Mishnah, the fuller keeps these threads. Indeed, even if four or five threads woven in at the edge belong to him; if black threads are woven into a white cloth or web, one or more, these are his, because they cause a blemish. The author goes on and brings forward other cases near the end, which he decides. For example, a carpenter very often shaves chips from wood that he has received from another in order to make tools from it. What shall we say: are the chips the carpenter's or the employer's? Here a distinction is made between larger and smaller splinters: the smaller are assigned to the carpenter, the larger to the employer. This is set out thus: the chips shaved off with תקר [tiqer], the plane, belong to the carpenter; the larger splinters cut off with כפס [kaphas], the axe, as being larger, go to the employer. But if the carpenter is in the position of כפטיר [kaphtir], a hired labourer, so that he undertakes daily labour for the master, then even the sawdust scraped off by the saw belongs to the master himself, whom the Mishnah calls the paterfamilias. Now S. J. and others call the saw מקדח [miqdach]; for according to Maimonides, sawdust, which is כסומרין [ksomarin]... is the scraping of wood, a small piece of wood, which arises when they saw wood so that they may make planks from it. Therefore the instrument by which sawdust is made, namely מקדח, whatever the lexicographers say, is also a saw. From these words, with their varied use, the difference between מנדר, כטיל and מקדח is wholly clear. Thus, in passing, some passages of Scripture are illustrated where mention is made of the first two words, since from the circumstances in this Mishnah there can be no doubt what these words signify. Because of such doubtful words I would have this carefully observed, not only in the Old Testament but also in the Mishnayot, which were written in the ancient Hebrew language; indeed also in the many opinions of the ancients recorded in the Gemara, since those rules are very ancient, as is clear even from the words of the Saviour, by which he rebukes them as already received; and he calls their ancient authors ἀρχαίως [archaiōs], the ancients, in Matthew 5, and recognises that these rules were handed down by the forefathers of those who were then living (Matt. 15:2, 3). For the tradition that is rebuked here can be read in the Codex כדריס [kadris], chapter 11, section 4. As for Matthew 5, I will not recount from the ancients all the things Christ rebukes; I will set forth one example. In verse 43: You have heard that it was said (namely by the ancients, as the Saviour had several times said in what precedes, and so he wishes it now to be understood), You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy. That the ancient teachers added the latter part against the law of God is shown to us by the Codex Joma, or on the Day of Atonement, chapter 2, page 22, b, near the end, where these words are read: Why was Saul punished? Because he spared those who violated his honour; for it is read (1 Sam. 10:27). But wicked men said, "How shall this man save us?" despising him, so that they did not even bring him a gift; yet he kept silent. Therefore it follows (11:1): And Nahash the Ammonite went up and encamped against Jabesh Gilead, etc. So Doctor John says in the name of Rabbi Simeon son of Jotsedeq: Every student of wisdom who does not take vengeance and keeps enmity (so S. Jarchi rightly adds in explanation, enmity) like a serpent, is not a disciple of a sage, that is, a student of wisdom. You see, reader, that our Saviour did not without reason rebuke those teachers, who allowed vengeance, anger and enmity if anyone dishonoured them by word or deed. Later writers explain that this applied if one dishonoured them publicly and did not seek pardon and forgiveness as a suppliant. Since therefore such opinions were handed down by the ancients, while the Hebrew language was still in use, is it not rightly from these rules that the meaning of doubtful words is drawn? Therefore, if only for the sake of the language, let us read them, and let us not think that the whole holy language can be learned from the sacred letters alone. For in those Mishnayot and in very many sayings of the ancients, scattered through the Gemara and otherwise of mixed idiom and style, many words and various phrases are found which are lacking in the sacred books or can be less known. Moreover, Maimonides rightly observed that those things which are said to belong to workmen, or to be given back to the owners, are not regarded as a perpetual law, but are changed according to the variety of regions; so what is conceded here to the tailor or the smith is refused elsewhere. The aim of the Mishnah itself must be considered, which is to keep justice, and all these things aim at that. The sum of them is that workmen, whoever they are, should not take away anything that belongs to those by whom they were hired to do the work. As Ulpian most justly says (Dig. 19, t. 2, l. 39): Hiring does not usually transfer ownership. As for those small scraps which are allowed to workmen, they do not commit theft by keeping them, because the owners regard them as abandoned; for in Dig. De furtis 43, §5, it is laid down that a thing we abandon at once ceases to be ours. To this point is §10: If anyone of his own accord threw away or cast off a thing, not intending to hold it as abandoned, and you took this thing, Celsus asks in the twelfth book of the Digest whether you are liable to theft; and he says, if indeed you thought it had been regarded as abandoned, you are not liable. But a fuller, a carpenter, or another workman judges that these small things are regarded as abandoned; therefore, while they kept them according to our Mishnah, no action for theft was given. And all the more so, because the employer himself, who had hired out a garment to be polished, or a bench or other thing to be prepared, would regard such small things, in the places of which the Mishnah treats, as abandoned. But the Roman law excuses the deed even if this condition were absent, provided that another judge rightly and justly so decides. Moreover, since the Jews are not such great champions of justice in other respects, as we have seen, nor do they labour greatly over embracing the faith in the sacred mysteries, yet they are so busy about these chips and sawdust and splinters, I shall rightly end with the word of the Saviour: Matt. 23:24: Blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. What, I ask, should we weigh more in the Old Testament Scriptures than the supreme clemency of God the Father, and the just wrath of God the judge, and his fearful and astonishing majesty? Therefore those men ought rather to have been busy who could obtain God's mercy and escape his wrath. For the majesty of God is too great to be turned away from the most just and dreadful wrath against sinners by a fast of a few days, by certain prayers, or by other exercises. The sins committed without ceasing, and the atrocious crimes of so many myriads, are far too grave to be atoned for before him, who does not absolve the guilty without just satisfaction, by imperfect works which are themselves stained (Nah. 1:3). Likewise those sins are many and greater, and God is an infinite spirit of a far purer, weightier and loftier nature, so that he could not be propitiated by the blood of brute beasts, if the blood alone is considered and not referred to the passion of the Messiah. We have shown elsewhere that the ancient Jews were not ignorant of his wounds. For God, simply (to confirm this once more by another testimony), testifies that he does not remit sins without satisfaction, even when he most magnifies his mercy (Deut. 34:6, 7). But what will you say? The Talmudists will never be able to draw out of their thorny Talmudic questions the truth of this doctrine, which is not omitted even in their own Talmud, until they recognise their spiritual misery, so that they begin to be stung in the heart, in the sense of conscience. Then (Hos. 3:5): They shall come trembling to the Lord and to his goodness, this...
Christ has appeared [Χριστὸς ἐπιφάνη].
